# 00 — Hello, Dojo (C#)

Welcome to the C# track. This course teaches you C# by making you write it —
every line, yourself, in a real .NET solution that really compiles. Nothing
here fills in a method body for you. You edit a `.cs` file, you run one
command, and an automated gate tells you whether you were right; when you
weren't, it shows you the evidence and the sentence you need to reread.

The first thing to get straight is where things live, because C# splits a
lesson across two places and the split is not arbitrary. Your *code* lives in
a normal class library, `src/Lessons/`, one folder per lesson — because the
compiler needs it there, and because you should be reading real project
structure from day one, not a scratchpad. The *lesson* — this README, the
theory, the hints, the reference solutions — lives under `lessons/00_hello_dojo/`.
The gate that grades you lives in a third place, `tests/Gates/`, which is
exactly where tests live in every C# repository you will ever join.

So: **you edit files under `src/Lessons/`. You read files under `lessons/`.
You never edit `tests/Gates/`** — though you should absolutely read it, and
it is quoted verbatim at the bottom of this page.

## The loop

For this lesson the map is:

```
tracks/csharp/
├── src/Lessons/L00_HelloDojo/     <- YOU EDIT THESE
│   ├── Ex1.cs                        namespace CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo
│   ├── Ex2.cs
│   └── Ex3.cs
├── tests/Gates/L00_HelloDojoTests.cs  <- the gate (read it, never edit it)
└── lessons/00_hello_dojo/            <- this README, reading.md, hints
    ├── README.md
    ├── reading.md
    └── ex1/hints.md   ex2/hints.md   ex3/hints.md
```

The commands you will live in:

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo        # grade the whole lesson
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo ex2    # grade just one exercise
uv run dojo hint csharp 00_hello_dojo ex2    # stuck? reveal the next tier
uv run dojo read csharp 00_hello_dojo ex2    # the theory behind it
uv run dojo status csharp                    # the progress dashboard
uv run dojo next csharp                      # what should I do now?
```

`csharp` also answers to `cs`, so `uv run dojo test cs 00 ex2` is the same
command with less typing. If a run ever fails with a build error rather than a
test failure, `uv run dojo doctor` will tell you whether the solution itself
is broken.

Before you write a single line, run the gate and watch it fail:

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo
```

Three red tests, each one a `NotImplementedException` thrown by a stub. That
is the correct state of a fresh checkout. Note what it is *not*: a compiler
error. Every stub in this course is written so the solution always builds —
`throw new NotImplementedException()` is a perfectly valid method body, and
shipping stubs that compile means a half-finished exercise never breaks the
lesson next to it.

## Concept — a method is a signature plus a body

Here is the smallest complete C# method:

```csharp
public static int Double(int n)
{
    return n * 2;
}
```

Read it left to right, because every word is load-bearing. `public` means
other code can call it. `static` means it belongs to the type rather than to
an instance, so you call it as `Calculator.Double(21)` and never have to
create a `Calculator` first. `int` is the return type — and unlike TypeScript,
C# never infers it for you: you always write it. `Double` is the name, and C#
convention is PascalCase for methods. `(int n)` is the parameter list, with
the type first and the name second.

That "always write the return type" rule is worth pausing on. It means C#
signatures are self-documenting in a way inferred languages are not: you can
read a method's contract without reading its body. It also means the compiler
checks your body against the promise you made, on every path, every time.

Two more pieces you will need below. String interpolation puts a `$` in front
of the string literal and `{}` around expressions:

```csharp
string track = "react";
string line = $"{track} has {11 + 1} lessons";   // "react has 12 lessons"
```

…and the conditional operator picks between two values inline:

```csharp
string label = count == 1 ? "item" : "items";
```

Both should feel familiar if you have written JavaScript. The `$` prefix is
the part people forget: without it, `"{track}"` is just those seven
characters.

## Exercise 1 — your first method

Edit `src/Lessons/L00_HelloDojo/Ex1.cs`. Implement `Greeter.Greet` so that it
returns a greeting built from the `name` it is given:

- `Greet("Eli")` must return `"Hello, Eli! Welcome to the dojo."`
- `Greet("Ada")` must return `"Hello, Ada! Welcome to the dojo."`

Exact string, including the comma, the exclamation mark and the final full
stop. Replace the `throw` with a `return`; leave the signature alone.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two parameters, and a decision

Edit `src/Lessons/L00_HelloDojo/Ex2.cs`. Implement `TrackInfo.Describe(name, lessons)`
so it returns a one-line summary:

- `Describe("csharp", 14)` → `"csharp: 14 lessons"`
- `Describe("react", 1)` → `"react: 1 lesson"`
- `Describe("dotnet", 0)` → `"dotnet: 0 lessons"`

Read those three lines again. Two of them are the same shape and one is not:
English pluralises on "exactly one", not on "more than one", so zero is
plural. Your method has to make that decision at runtime — there is no single
interpolated string that produces all three.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — parse the number out of a slug

Edit `src/Lessons/L00_HelloDojo/Ex3.cs`. Implement `SlugParser.LessonNumber(slug)`,
which takes a lesson slug and returns its number as an `int`:

- `LessonNumber("07_generics")` → `7`
- `LessonNumber("00_hello_dojo")` → `0`
- `LessonNumber("13_async_await")` → `13`

The slug can contain more than one underscore, so take the *first* segment
rather than everything before the last one. Then turn that segment of text
into an `int` — the method's declared return type says `int`, and the compiler
will not let you hand back a `string`, which is the whole point of writing the
return type down.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo ex3
```

# Reading - csharp/00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course.
This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you
just solved. It is meant to be read **after** you attempt a problem, whether
the gate went green or red. Failing first and reading second is not a
consolation prize; it is the version of studying that actually sticks.

## Notes

**What actually happened when you ran the gate.** `dojo test csharp` shells
out to `dotnet test`, which does four things in order: restores NuGet
packages, compiles `src/Lessons` into `Lessons.dll`, compiles `tests/Gates`
into `Gates.dll` (which references the first), and then hands the test
assembly to the xUnit runner. Two of those four steps are a *compiler*, which
is why C# feedback feels different from JavaScript feedback: a typo in a
method name is caught before a single test runs, and the error names a file
and a line. This is the trade — a slower loop that catches a larger class of
mistakes without you having to think of a test for them.

**Static, and why almost everything in this lesson is.** A `static` member
belongs to the type; an instance member belongs to an object you have to
create first. `Greeter.Greet("Eli")` works without `new Greeter()` because
`Greet` is static. Static is the right default for a pure function of its
arguments — no state to hold, nothing to configure — and the wrong default for
almost everything else, which is why `03_classes_objects` will spend a whole
lesson on the alternative. If it helps: `Math.Max` is static, your
`OrderService` should not be.

**Namespaces are for organisation, not access control.** `namespace CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo;`
at the top of your files means their full names are
`CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo.Greeter` and so on, and the gate reaches them with a
`using CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo;` line. Namespaces do not restrict anything —
that is what `public`/`internal`/`private` are for. They exist so that two
libraries can both define a `Logger` without a fight, and in this course so
that one lesson's `TrackInfo` cannot collide with another's. Note the trailing
semicolon: that is the modern *file-scoped* namespace form, which saves you a
level of indentation over the older braced version you will see in older code.

**Nullable reference types are on.** `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in
`Lessons.csproj` means `string` promises not to be null and `string?` admits
it might be. The compiler then warns when you dereference something that could
be null. It is a warning, not an error, and it is not enforced at runtime —
which makes it much weaker than C#'s value/reference distinction but much
better than nothing. `01_types_variables` covers it properly.

## ex1 — your first method

The interesting part of this exercise is how little of it is C#. The body is
one `return` of one interpolated string; the same three lines in JavaScript,
Python or Ruby would look almost identical. What is different is everything
*around* the body: the return type you were given, the `static` you didn't
have to think about, the fact that a missing `$` on the string literal is a
compile error and not a silently wrong value.

The classic beginner mistake here is `"Hello, {name}!"` without the `$`.
Nothing fails to compile — that is a perfectly good string containing braces —
so the first time you find out is when the gate prints the expected and actual
side by side and you see your literal braces staring back. Getting caught by
that once is worth more than reading about it three times.

## ex2 — a decision the compiler cannot make for you

Pluralisation is a deliberately unglamorous problem, chosen because it splits
cleanly into "what the type system guarantees" and "what it doesn't". The
types guarantee you were handed a `string` and an `int` and must hand back a
`string`. They have nothing whatsoever to say about whether `0` is plural.
Type systems eliminate a *category* of mistakes — wrong shape, wrong
conversion, null where a value was assumed — and leave logic entirely to you
and your tests.

The classic mistake is `lessons > 1 ? "lessons" : "lesson"`, which is right for
14, right for 1, and wrong for 0. English pluralises on "is it exactly one",
so the condition to write is `lessons == 1`. Interviewers use almost exactly
this question — usually as "render '1 file' / '2 files'" — precisely because
the zero case separates people who tested their function from people who
eyeballed it.

For the record, real applications do not hand-roll this: .NET has
`System.Globalization` and localisation frameworks for it, because plural
rules in Polish and Arabic are not a ternary. Knowing that the naive version
is naive is enough for now.

## ex3 — text in, number out

`Split('_')` returns a `string[]`, and `[0]` takes the first element — which
is where the "first segment, not everything before the last one" rule comes
from. `"13_async_await".Split('_')` is `["13", "async", "await"]`, so index 0
is `"13"` no matter how many underscores follow.

Converting that to an `int` is where C# offers you a genuine choice, and it is
worth knowing all three now because they come up in interviews.
`int.Parse(text)` throws a `FormatException` if the text is not a number.
`int.TryParse(text, out int value)` returns a `bool` and never throws.
`Convert.ToInt32(text)` throws too, but maps `null` to `0` rather than
throwing. The rule of thumb professionals use: `Parse` when malformed input is
a *bug* and you want the loud failure, `TryParse` when malformed input is
*expected* and you have a plan for it. Here the slugs come from the course's
own directory names, so a bad one is a bug, and `Parse` is the honest choice.

Two smaller notes. `int.Parse("00")` is `0` — leading zeros are just digits,
and there is no octal surprise in C# the way there historically was in
JavaScript's `parseInt`. And the return type doing real work: had you tried to
`return slug.Split('_')[0];` the compiler would have stopped you with
"cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'int'". In a language that
inferred the return type, that same mistake would have compiled and failed
later, somewhere else.

## Further reading

- [A tour of C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/tour-of-csharp/) — Microsoft's official overview. Read the first three pages now; the rest becomes useful around lesson 05.
- [String interpolation in C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/tokens/interpolated) — the `$""` form, including alignment and format specifiers you will want later.
- [`int.Parse` vs `int.TryParse`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.int32.tryparse) — the API page, and the standard example of the "throw or return false" design question.
- [C# coding conventions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/coding-style/coding-conventions) — naming, braces, `var` usage. Skim it once; this course follows it, and so does every team you will join.
- [Nullable reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references) — what `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` bought you, and what it deliberately did not.

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L00_HelloDojoTests.cs`:

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L00_HelloDojoTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_GreetBuildsAGreetingFromAName()
    {
        Teach.Equal(
            "Hello, Eli! Welcome to the dojo.",
            Greeter.Greet("Eli"),
            "Greet(\"Eli\") must return exactly \"Hello, Eli! Welcome to the dojo.\" - "
                + "compare it character by character, punctuation included.");

        Teach.Equal(
            "Hello, Ada! Welcome to the dojo.",
            Greeter.Greet("Ada"),
            "The name has to come from the parameter, not be hard-coded - reread README ex1.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_DescribeAgreesWithItsOwnNumber()
    {
        Teach.Equal(
            "csharp: 14 lessons",
            TrackInfo.Describe("csharp", 14),
            "Describe(\"csharp\", 14) must return \"csharp: 14 lessons\".");

        Teach.Equal(
            "react: 1 lesson",
            TrackInfo.Describe("react", 1),
            "One lesson is a \"lesson\", not \"lessons\" - the plural is a decision your code "
                + "has to make, not a string you can interpolate once.");

        Teach.Equal(
            "dotnet: 0 lessons",
            TrackInfo.Describe("dotnet", 0),
            "Zero is plural in English: expect \"dotnet: 0 lessons\".");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_LessonNumberReturnsAnInt()
    {
        Teach.Equal(
            7,
            SlugParser.LessonNumber("07_generics"),
            "LessonNumber(\"07_generics\") must return the int 7 - note \"07\" has a leading zero.");

        Teach.Equal(
            0,
            SlugParser.LessonNumber("00_hello_dojo"),
            "The first lesson is number 0. Parsing \"00\" gives 0, not an exception.");

        Teach.Equal(
            13,
            SlugParser.LessonNumber("13_async_await"),
            "Split on '_' and parse the first part - the rest of the slug can contain "
                + "more underscores, so take the first segment, not everything before the last one.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: each `[Fact]` is one exercise. `Teach.Equal(expected, actual, why)`
is this course's assertion helper — it behaves like xUnit's `Assert.Equal` but
prints the sentence first and the expected/actual pair underneath, so a
failure tells you what to reread rather than just what didn't match. You can
read it in `tests/Gates/Teach.cs`; there is nothing clever in there.

every lesson in this track follows.

and C# that doesn't.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **00 — Hello, Dojo (C#)**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex1` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex2` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex3` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex1` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex2` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex3` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex1` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - csharp/00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course.
This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you
just solved. It is meant to be read **after** you attempt a problem, whether
the gate went green or red. Failing first and reading second is not a
consolation prize; it is the version of studying that actually sticks.

## Notes

**What actually happened when you ran the gate.** `dojo test csharp` shells
out to `dotnet test`, which does four things in order: restores NuGet
packages, compiles `src/Lessons` into `Lessons.dll`, compiles `tests/Gates`
into `Gates.dll` (which references the first), and then hands the test
assembly to the xUnit runner. Two of those four steps are a *compiler*, which
is why C# feedback feels different from JavaScript feedback: a typo in a
method name is caught before a single test runs, and the error names a file
and a line. This is the trade — a slower loop that catches a larger class of
mistakes without you having to think of a test for them.

**Static, and why almost everything in this lesson is.** A `static` member
belongs to the type; an instance member belongs to an object you have to
create first. `Greeter.Greet("Eli")` works without `new Greeter()` because
`Greet` is static. Static is the right default for a pure function of its
arguments — no state to hold, nothing to configure — and the wrong default for
almost everything else, which is why `03_classes_objects` will spend a whole
lesson on the alternative. If it helps: `Math.Max` is static, your
`OrderService` should not be.

**Namespaces are for organisation, not access control.** `namespace CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo;`
at the top of your files means their full names are
`CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo.Greeter` and so on, and the gate reaches them with a
`using CSharpDojo.L00_HelloDojo;` line. Namespaces do not restrict anything —
that is what `public`/`internal`/`private` are for. They exist so that two
libraries can both define a `Logger` without a fight, and in this course so
that one lesson's `TrackInfo` cannot collide with another's. Note the trailing
semicolon: that is the modern *file-scoped* namespace form, which saves you a
level of indentation over the older braced version you will see in older code.

**Nullable reference types are on.** `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in
`Lessons.csproj` means `string` promises not to be null and `string?` admits
it might be. The compiler then warns when you dereference something that could
be null. It is a warning, not an error, and it is not enforced at runtime —
which makes it much weaker than C#'s value/reference distinction but much
better than nothing. `01_types_variables` covers it properly.

## ex1 — your first method

The interesting part of this exercise is how little of it is C#. The body is
one `return` of one interpolated string; the same three lines in JavaScript,
Python or Ruby would look almost identical. What is different is everything
*around* the body: the return type you were given, the `static` you didn't
have to think about, the fact that a missing `$` on the string literal is a
compile error and not a silently wrong value.

The classic beginner mistake here is `"Hello, {name}!"` without the `$`.
Nothing fails to compile — that is a perfectly good string containing braces —
so the first time you find out is when the gate prints the expected and actual
side by side and you see your literal braces staring back. Getting caught by
that once is worth more than reading about it three times.

## ex2 — a decision the compiler cannot make for you

Pluralisation is a deliberately unglamorous problem, chosen because it splits
cleanly into "what the type system guarantees" and "what it doesn't". The
types guarantee you were handed a `string` and an `int` and must hand back a
`string`. They have nothing whatsoever to say about whether `0` is plural.
Type systems eliminate a *category* of mistakes — wrong shape, wrong
conversion, null where a value was assumed — and leave logic entirely to you
and your tests.

The classic mistake is `lessons > 1 ? "lessons" : "lesson"`, which is right for
14, right for 1, and wrong for 0. English pluralises on "is it exactly one",
so the condition to write is `lessons == 1`. Interviewers use almost exactly
this question — usually as "render '1 file' / '2 files'" — precisely because
the zero case separates people who tested their function from people who
eyeballed it.

For the record, real applications do not hand-roll this: .NET has
`System.Globalization` and localisation frameworks for it, because plural
rules in Polish and Arabic are not a ternary. Knowing that the naive version
is naive is enough for now.

## ex3 — text in, number out

`Split('_')` returns a `string[]`, and `[0]` takes the first element — which
is where the "first segment, not everything before the last one" rule comes
from. `"13_async_await".Split('_')` is `["13", "async", "await"]`, so index 0
is `"13"` no matter how many underscores follow.

Converting that to an `int` is where C# offers you a genuine choice, and it is
worth knowing all three now because they come up in interviews.
`int.Parse(text)` throws a `FormatException` if the text is not a number.
`int.TryParse(text, out int value)` returns a `bool` and never throws.
`Convert.ToInt32(text)` throws too, but maps `null` to `0` rather than
throwing. The rule of thumb professionals use: `Parse` when malformed input is
a *bug* and you want the loud failure, `TryParse` when malformed input is
*expected* and you have a plan for it. Here the slugs come from the course's
own directory names, so a bad one is a bug, and `Parse` is the honest choice.

Two smaller notes. `int.Parse("00")` is `0` — leading zeros are just digits,
and there is no octal surprise in C# the way there historically was in
JavaScript's `parseInt`. And the return type doing real work: had you tried to
`return slug.Split('_')[0];` the compiler would have stopped you with
"cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'int'". In a language that
inferred the return type, that same mistake would have compiled and failed
later, somewhere else.

## Further reading

- [A tour of C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/tour-of-csharp/) — Microsoft's official overview. Read the first three pages now; the rest becomes useful around lesson 05.
- [String interpolation in C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/tokens/interpolated) — the `$""` form, including alignment and format specifiers you will want later.
- [`int.Parse` vs `int.TryParse`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.int32.tryparse) — the API page, and the standard example of the "throw or return false" design question.
- [C# coding conventions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/coding-style/coding-conventions) — naming, braces, `var` usage. Skim it once; this course follows it, and so does every team you will join.
- [Nullable reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references) — what `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` bought you, and what it deliberately did not.

## Exercise 2 — two parameters, and a decision

Edit `src/Lessons/L00_HelloDojo/Ex2.cs`. Implement `TrackInfo.Describe(name, lessons)`
so it returns a one-line summary:

- `Describe("csharp", 14)` → `"csharp: 14 lessons"`
- `Describe("react", 1)` → `"react: 1 lesson"`
- `Describe("dotnet", 0)` → `"dotnet: 0 lessons"`

Read those three lines again. Two of them are the same shape and one is not:
English pluralises on "exactly one", not on "more than one", so zero is
plural. Your method has to make that decision at runtime — there is no single
interpolated string that produces all three.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo ex2
```


You need a value that is `"lesson"` in exactly one case and `"lessons"` in
every other case — including zero. Compute it into a local variable *before*
you build the result, then interpolate it like any other value.

The conditional operator (`condition ? a : b`) is the compact way; a plain
`if`/`else` is equally correct and equally readable.

and disagree on 0.

The shape is:

```csharp
string noun = /* the condition */ ? "lesson" : "lessons";
```

not `>`. Note that interpolating the `int` directly is fine: C# calls
`ToString()` on it for you, so you do not need a conversion here.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two of the three expected outputs are the same shape and one is not. Write
the three of them out and circle the single character that differs:

```
csharp: 14 lessons
react: 1 lesson
dotnet: 0 lessons
```

That character is the whole exercise. Everything else is the same interpolated
string you wrote for ex1.

## Hint 2

You need a value that is `"lesson"` in exactly one case and `"lessons"` in
every other case — including zero. Compute it into a local variable *before*
you build the result, then interpolate it like any other value.

The conditional operator (`condition ? a : b`) is the compact way; a plain
`if`/`else` is equally correct and equally readable.

Be careful with the condition. "More than one" and "exactly one" agree on 14
and disagree on 0.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
string noun = /* the condition */ ? "lesson" : "lessons";
return $"{name}: {lessons} {noun}";
```

The condition compares `lessons` to `1`, and it is an equality test — `==`,
not `>`. Note that interpolating the `int` directly is fine: C# calls
`ToString()` on it for you, so you do not need a conversion here.

## Exercise 3 — parse the number out of a slug

Edit `src/Lessons/L00_HelloDojo/Ex3.cs`. Implement `SlugParser.LessonNumber(slug)`,
which takes a lesson slug and returns its number as an `int`:

- `LessonNumber("07_generics")` → `7`
- `LessonNumber("00_hello_dojo")` → `0`
- `LessonNumber("13_async_await")` → `13`

The slug can contain more than one underscore, so take the *first* segment
rather than everything before the last one. Then turn that segment of text
into an `int` — the method's declared return type says `int`, and the compiler
will not let you hand back a `string`, which is the whole point of writing the
return type down.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 00_hello_dojo ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two steps, in this order: cut the slug into pieces, then turn the piece you
want into a number.

Note that `"13_async_await"` has two underscores. "Everything before the last
underscore" is the wrong rule and will bite you on that input; "the first
piece" is the right one.

## Hint 2

`string` has a `Split` method that takes a separator and hands back a
`string[]`. Arrays are indexed from zero, so the first piece is at `[0]`.

For the conversion, `int.Parse(text)` is the direct route. (There is also
`int.TryParse`, which returns a `bool` instead of throwing — the reading
explains when each one is right. For this exercise the input is always
well-formed, so the simple one is the honest choice.)

Predict the answer for `"00_hello_dojo"` before you run the gate.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
return int.Parse(slug.Split(/* what separator? */)[0]);
```

One decision left for you: the separator. It is a single character, so use a
`char` literal in single quotes (`'x'`) rather than a `string` in double
quotes — both overloads exist, but the `char` one is the one to reach for.

If the compiler complains that it "cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to
'int'", you have written the split but not the parse. That error is the
declared return type doing its job.

lessons.briefing:
# 01 — Types and variables

Every C# question you will ever be asked in an interview eventually walks back
to one sentence: **is this a value type or a reference type?** Not because
interviewers are pedants, but because the answer changes what an assignment
does, what passing to a method does, what equality means, and where the bytes
live. Get it wrong and you write a method that mutates its caller's data by
accident — or one that quietly doesn't, which is worse, because it fails in
production and not in the debugger.

The rest of this lesson is the machinery around that sentence. C# is a
statically typed language: every variable has a type at compile time, and the
compiler will not let you put a `string` in an `int`-shaped hole. That
strictness buys you conversions that are explicit about their cost, a
`decimal` type that money can trust, and — since C# 8 — a nullability layer
that tells you which references are allowed to be missing.

You already wrote one method in lesson 00. Now you find out what the values
flowing through it actually are.

## Concept — two families, one distinction

C# types come in two families and the difference is *where the value lives and
what a copy copies*.

A **value type** — `int`, `double`, `bool`, `decimal`, `char`, every `enum`,
every `struct` — holds its data directly. Assigning it, or passing it to a
method, copies all of that data:

```csharp
int a = 5;
int b = a;    // b is a second, independent 5
b = 99;       // a is still 5
```

A **reference type** — `string`, arrays, every `class`, every interface — holds
a *reference*: an arrow pointing at an object that lives somewhere else. Copying
the variable copies the arrow:

```csharp
int[] first  = { 1, 2, 3 };
int[] second = first;    // one array, two arrows
second[0] = 99;          // first[0] is now 99 as well
```

Nothing about that second snippet is a trick. It is the single most common
source of "why did my list change?" bugs in every language with references,
and C# makes it visible because you chose `class` or `struct` when you declared
the type.

**Conversions are explicit when they can lose.** A `long` fits every `int`, so
`long big = someInt;` needs no ceremony — that is an *implicit* conversion. The
other direction can lose data, so C# makes you write the cast and take
responsibility: `int small = (int)someLong;`. A cast from a floating-point type
truncates toward zero — `(int)3.9` is `3` and `(int)(-3.9)` is `-3` — which is
not the same as rounding and not the same as `Math.Floor`.

**`decimal` is for money.** `double` stores base-2 fractions, so 0.1 is not
exactly 0.1 and errors accumulate; `decimal` stores base-10 fractions in 128
bits and is exact for the numbers humans write on invoices. It is slower and
smaller in range, and nobody cares, because a cent that goes missing is a bug
report:

```csharp
double  d = 0.1 + 0.2;   // 0.30000000000000004
decimal m = 0.1m + 0.2m; // 0.3
```

**`var` infers, it does not weaken.** `var total = 0m;` declares a `decimal`,
full stop — the compiler works out the type from the right-hand side and the
variable is as statically typed as if you had written it out. Use it when the
right-hand side already names the type (`var order = new Order();`) and write
the type out when it doesn't (`var x = Parse(s);` tells the reader nothing).

**Nullable annotations.** With `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` — which this
project has — `string` means "I promise this is not null" and `string?` means
"this might be missing, and the compiler will nag you until you check". For
value types the `?` is older and stronger: `int?` is a genuinely different type
(`Nullable<int>`) with `.HasValue` and `.Value`, and it cannot hold an `int`
without wrapping it. The `??` operator supplies a fallback for either:

```csharp
string display = maybeName ?? "unknown";
```

## Exercise 1 — the same code, two answers

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Ex1.cs`. The file gives you two types that
differ by exactly one keyword — `struct ReadingValue` and `class ReadingRef` —
and two methods to implement.

In each method: copy the parameter into a local variable, set the **local's**
`Degrees` to `99`, and return the **original's** `Degrees`. Write literally the
same three lines in both bodies. The gate expects `12` from the struct version
and `99` from the class version, and the entire lesson is in that difference.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 01_types_variables ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — conversions that lose things

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Ex2.cs`. Three small methods:

`Truncate(double)` chops the fraction off toward zero: `3.9 -> 3`, `-3.9 -> -3`.

`RoundHalfAwayFromZero(double)` rounds to the nearest whole number, and sends
an exact `.5` away from zero: `2.5 -> 3`, `3.5 -> 4`. This is not what
`Math.Round` does by default — its default is *banker's rounding*, which sends
`2.5` to `2` because 2 is even. That default exists for good statistical
reasons and surprises approximately everyone the first time.

`SafeAdd(int, int)` returns a `long` that is correct even for
`int.MaxValue + 1`. Careful: `a + b` is computed in `int` and the overflow has
already happened before anything widens.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 01_types_variables ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — things that might not be there

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`Labels.Describe(string? name, int? age)`:

- `Describe("Ada", 36)` -> `"Ada (36)"`
- `Describe(null, 36)` -> `"anonymous (36)"`
- `Describe("   ", 36)` -> `"anonymous (36)"` — blank counts as missing
- `Describe("Ada", null)` -> `"Ada (age unknown)"`
- `Describe(null, null)` -> `"anonymous (age unknown)"`

Two independent decisions, not five cases. Note the two different `?`s in that
signature: `string?` is an annotation the compiler checks, and `int?` is a real
wrapper type with `.HasValue`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 01_types_variables ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — money

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`Money.LineTotal(decimal unitPrice, int quantity, decimal discountPercent)`:
multiply, take the discount off, and round to two decimal places with halves
going away from zero.

- `LineTotal(19.99m, 3, 0m)` -> `59.97m`
- `LineTotal(10m, 3, 10m)` -> `27.00m` (ten *percent*)
- `LineTotal(0.25m, 1, 50m)` -> `0.13m` (0.125 rounds away from zero)

Keep every intermediate value a `decimal`. The `m` suffix on a literal is what
makes it one; `100` is an `int` and `100.0` is a `double`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 01_types_variables ex4
```

## Challenge — a line of text in, a line of text out

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`ReceiptLine.Format(string line)`, which takes `"widget|19.99|3"` and returns
`"widget x3 = $59.97"`.

Honest difficulty note: nothing here is new, but it is the first time you have
to hold four ideas at once — splitting, parsing to two different types, decimal
arithmetic, and formatted output. The one genuinely new detail is culture:
`decimal.Parse` reads `"19.99"` differently on a machine whose locale writes
`19,99`, so pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` when parsing and when
formatting. That `using System.Globalization;` at the top of the file is there
for you.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 01_types_variables challenge
```

## Review

`review1` comes back later, scheduled by `dojo review`, not now. It asks for
`SensorRow.Summarize(string? label, double? celsius)` — the null fallbacks of
ex3 and the rounding of ex2 in one method — and you will meet it again in three
days, then a week, then three weeks.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/01_types_variables

## Notes

**The stack and the heap, at the level worth caring about.** The usual
one-liner is "value types live on the stack, reference types live on the heap",
and it is close enough to be useful and wrong often enough to be worth
correcting. What is actually true: a *local variable* of value type holds its
data inline, wherever that variable lives. If the variable is a local, that is
the stack frame. If it is a field of a class, it lives inside that class's
object — on the heap, embedded in it. An `int[]` of a million ints is one heap
object holding a million inline ints, not a million boxes. So the honest
version is: **value types are stored where they are declared; reference types
are stored as an arrow to somewhere else.** In an interview, say that, then say
"and the stack/heap answer is the usual shorthand" — it demonstrates you know
the difference between a model and a rule.

**Passing to a method is assignment.** Every parameter in C# is assigned from
the argument, so parameter passing follows exactly the same rule as `=`. A
struct argument is copied; a class argument copies the arrow, so the method can
mutate the object you handed it but cannot make your variable point somewhere
else. That last clause is the one people miss: reassigning a reference
parameter inside a method (`order = new Order();`) changes nothing for the
caller. Lesson 02's `ref` is the keyword that changes it.

**Boxing, in one paragraph, because it will come up again.** If you assign a
value type to a variable of type `object` (or of an interface type it
implements), the runtime allocates a heap box and copies the value into it.
That is *boxing*, and it is a real allocation with a real cost in hot loops. It
also copies, so mutating the value afterwards leaves the box unchanged. You
will meet this properly in `06_structs_records` and again in
`i1_interview_concepts`, where it is a [***] question.

**Nullable reference types are compile-time only.** `string?` and `string`
compile to exactly the same IL; the annotation drives a compiler analysis and
nothing else. Nothing stops a badly-behaved library, a reflection call, or a
deserialiser from putting a null in a non-nullable field at runtime — which is
why library authors still write argument checks. `int?`, by contrast, is a real
struct (`Nullable<int>`) with real runtime behaviour. Same punctuation, two
completely different mechanisms, and interviewers love asking you to tell them
apart.

## ex1

The two methods have identical bodies and different answers, which is as close
as a language gets to an experiment you can run. The struct version copies six
bytes and mutates the copy; the class version copies a pointer, so `copy` and
`original` are two names for one object.

What makes this worth doing by hand instead of reading: the code contains no
hint about which one you are getting. There is no `&`, no `*`, no `clone()`,
nothing at the call site at all. The behaviour is a property of the *type*, and
it was decided by whoever wrote `struct` or `class` — possibly years ago, in
another file. That is exactly why the question "is this a value type or a
reference type?" has to be reflexive, and why the .NET framework documents it
prominently for every type it ships.

The follow-up an interviewer will ask: "So is `string` a value type or a
reference type?" `string` is a *reference* type that is *immutable*, so it
behaves like a value in the ways you notice (you cannot mutate someone else's
string) but copies like a reference (assigning is cheap regardless of length).
That combination is deliberate and is why `==` on strings compares text rather
than arrows — the one operator overload that trips up people coming from Java.

## ex2

Three conversions, three different mechanisms, and it is worth naming them.

`(int)someDouble` is a *conversion operator* built into the language. It
truncates toward zero, which means it is `Math.Truncate`, not `Math.Floor`:
they agree for positive numbers and disagree for negative ones, and the day
that difference matters is the day you are computing a negative offset.

`Math.Round`'s default is **banker's rounding** (`MidpointRounding.ToEven`),
which sends 2.5 to 2 and 3.5 to 4. This is not a bug and not a .NET quirk — it
is IEEE 754's default, and it exists because always rounding halves up biases a
long series of sums upward. It is also, reliably, a surprise, so pass the mode
explicitly whenever a human is going to check your arithmetic with a
calculator.

`SafeAdd` is about *where the arithmetic happens*. C# picks the operator
overload from the operand types, so `int + int` is int addition, which wraps
silently on overflow; the widening to `long` happens afterwards, to a value
that is already wrong. Cast one operand and the compiler picks `long + long`
instead. C# also has a `checked` context that turns overflow into an
`OverflowException` — worth knowing it exists, and worth knowing it is off by
default for performance.

## ex3

The two `?`s in `Describe(string? name, int? age)` look like one feature and are
two. `string?` is an annotation: it changes the compiler's flow analysis and
nothing about the generated code. `int?` is `Nullable<int>`, an actual struct
with a `bool` and an `int` inside it, and `age.Value` on an empty one throws.

The blank-string case is there because `null` and `""` and `"   "` are three
different values that mean the same thing to a human, and a nullable annotation
only protects you from one of them. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the standard
answer, and it carries a `[NotNullWhen(false)]` attribute that tells the
compiler's null analysis "if this returned false, the argument is not null" —
which is why the `else` branch does not warn. Attribute-driven null analysis is
a small thing that makes the whole feature usable.

The related operators worth having at your fingertips: `??` (fallback if null),
`??=` (assign if currently null), and `?.` (call only if not null, result is
nullable). `name?.Trim() ?? "anonymous"` is idiomatic C# and reads exactly as
it behaves.

## ex4

`decimal` is a 128-bit type storing a 96-bit integer, a sign, and a base-10
exponent from 0 to 28. That representation is what makes `0.1m` exact where
`0.1` (double) is not. It also means `decimal` carries *scale*: `27m` and
`27.00m` are equal but not identical — `ToString()` prints them differently
because the trailing zeros are stored. That is a feature for money, where "$27.00"
is the correct rendering, and a small surprise the first time you see it in a
log.

The rounding call takes three arguments for a reason: value, digits, mode. Skip
the mode and you have silently chosen banker's rounding for someone's invoice.
Skip the rounding entirely and you get a total with four decimal places that
disagrees with the printed receipt by a fraction of a cent — the classic
accumulating-error bug, where each line is nearly right and the sum is visibly
wrong.

One more habit: do the rounding once, at the end, on the value you are about to
show or store. Rounding intermediate values is how you end up with a total that
does not equal the sum of its parts.

## challenge

Parsing and formatting are the two places a program touches the outside world,
and both are culture-sensitive. `decimal.Parse("19.99")` on a machine set to
German reads a *thousands* separator and can hand you 1999, and
`total.ToString("0.00")` there writes `19,99` — so the round trip that works on
your laptop breaks on a colleague's, or on a server set to a different locale.
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` says "use the machine-readable convention,
regardless of who is looking", and it is the right answer for anything that
crosses a wire, a file, or a test assertion. Its opposite number,
`CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, is right when the string is being *shown to a
human*.

The format string `"0.00"` is a custom numeric format: `0` means "a digit, and
a zero if there isn't one". The standard alternative is `"F2"` (fixed-point,
two decimals). Both are worth recognising; neither is worth memorising beyond
that.

## review1

This one folds three of the lesson's ideas into one method: the null fallback,
the nullable value type's `HasValue`, and the rounding mode. It also changes
the *shape* of the output when a value is missing rather than substituting a
different value, which is why an early `return` reads better than a conditional
expression — the two branches are not two values, they are two sentences.

If this came back to you cold and the rounding mode was the part you had to
look up, that is the expected outcome and exactly what the spaced-review ladder
is for. If the `double?` unwrapping was the part you had to look up, reread the
ex3 notes above: the annotation and the wrapper type look alike and behave
differently, and that confusion is durable.

## Further reading

- [Value types (C# reference)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) — the official statement of what a value type is, including the list of built-in ones.
- [Reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/reference-types) — the other half, and where `string`'s special status is spelled out.
- [Casting and type conversions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/casting-and-type-conversions) — implicit, explicit, and user-defined conversions in one page.
- [Nullable reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references) — what the annotations mean, and the honest list of what they do not guarantee.
- [`decimal` keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/floating-point-numeric-types) — precision, range, and the `m` suffix, next to `float` and `double` for comparison.
- [`MidpointRounding` enum](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.midpointrounding) — all the modes, with the banker's-rounding rationale.

12 and asserts that only the class version sees the 99. `Ex2` pins truncation
in both directions, the two midpoint cases, and one overflow. `Ex3` walks all
five null combinations. `Ex4` checks exact decimal results, including the
halfway case that separates the two rounding modes. `Challenge` runs three
lines through the formatter, and `Review1` is the spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

In production the value/reference distinction shows up as a rule of thumb you
will hear on every team: **make types that behave like values immutable**. A
`struct` you can mutate through a field, like this lesson's `ReadingValue`, is
a well-known footgun — put one in a `List<T>` and `list[0].Degrees = 5` won't
even compile, because the indexer hands you a copy. Real codebases declare
`readonly struct` for small value-like things (money, coordinates, dates) and
`class` for everything with identity and a lifecycle (an order, a customer, a
connection). Lesson 06 gives you the modern tools for both.

The other production habit is the one ex4 drills: pick the numeric type by what
the number *means*, not by what is convenient. Money is `decimal`, measurements
and physics are `double`, counts and IDs are `int` or `long`. Every codebase
that stores money in a `double` eventually files a bug titled "invoice is off
by one cent".

Next: **02_control_flow_methods**, where the method you have been filling in
grows parameters that can hand results back, defaults, and a `switch` that
returns a value.

# Reading - csharp/01_types_variables

## Notes

**The stack and the heap, at the level worth caring about.** The usual
one-liner is "value types live on the stack, reference types live on the heap",
and it is close enough to be useful and wrong often enough to be worth
correcting. What is actually true: a *local variable* of value type holds its
data inline, wherever that variable lives. If the variable is a local, that is
the stack frame. If it is a field of a class, it lives inside that class's
object — on the heap, embedded in it. An `int[]` of a million ints is one heap
object holding a million inline ints, not a million boxes. So the honest
version is: **value types are stored where they are declared; reference types
are stored as an arrow to somewhere else.** In an interview, say that, then say
"and the stack/heap answer is the usual shorthand" — it demonstrates you know
the difference between a model and a rule.

**Passing to a method is assignment.** Every parameter in C# is assigned from
the argument, so parameter passing follows exactly the same rule as `=`. A
struct argument is copied; a class argument copies the arrow, so the method can
mutate the object you handed it but cannot make your variable point somewhere
else. That last clause is the one people miss: reassigning a reference
parameter inside a method (`order = new Order();`) changes nothing for the
caller. Lesson 02's `ref` is the keyword that changes it.

**Boxing, in one paragraph, because it will come up again.** If you assign a
value type to a variable of type `object` (or of an interface type it
implements), the runtime allocates a heap box and copies the value into it.
That is *boxing*, and it is a real allocation with a real cost in hot loops. It
also copies, so mutating the value afterwards leaves the box unchanged. You
will meet this properly in `06_structs_records` and again in
`i1_interview_concepts`, where it is a [***] question.

**Nullable reference types are compile-time only.** `string?` and `string`
compile to exactly the same IL; the annotation drives a compiler analysis and
nothing else. Nothing stops a badly-behaved library, a reflection call, or a
deserialiser from putting a null in a non-nullable field at runtime — which is
why library authors still write argument checks. `int?`, by contrast, is a real
struct (`Nullable<int>`) with real runtime behaviour. Same punctuation, two
completely different mechanisms, and interviewers love asking you to tell them
apart.

## ex1

The two methods have identical bodies and different answers, which is as close
as a language gets to an experiment you can run. The struct version copies six
bytes and mutates the copy; the class version copies a pointer, so `copy` and
`original` are two names for one object.

What makes this worth doing by hand instead of reading: the code contains no
hint about which one you are getting. There is no `&`, no `*`, no `clone()`,
nothing at the call site at all. The behaviour is a property of the *type*, and
it was decided by whoever wrote `struct` or `class` — possibly years ago, in
another file. That is exactly why the question "is this a value type or a
reference type?" has to be reflexive, and why the .NET framework documents it
prominently for every type it ships.

The follow-up an interviewer will ask: "So is `string` a value type or a
reference type?" `string` is a *reference* type that is *immutable*, so it
behaves like a value in the ways you notice (you cannot mutate someone else's
string) but copies like a reference (assigning is cheap regardless of length).
That combination is deliberate and is why `==` on strings compares text rather
than arrows — the one operator overload that trips up people coming from Java.

## ex2

Three conversions, three different mechanisms, and it is worth naming them.

`(int)someDouble` is a *conversion operator* built into the language. It
truncates toward zero, which means it is `Math.Truncate`, not `Math.Floor`:
they agree for positive numbers and disagree for negative ones, and the day
that difference matters is the day you are computing a negative offset.

`Math.Round`'s default is **banker's rounding** (`MidpointRounding.ToEven`),
which sends 2.5 to 2 and 3.5 to 4. This is not a bug and not a .NET quirk — it
is IEEE 754's default, and it exists because always rounding halves up biases a
long series of sums upward. It is also, reliably, a surprise, so pass the mode
explicitly whenever a human is going to check your arithmetic with a
calculator.

`SafeAdd` is about *where the arithmetic happens*. C# picks the operator
overload from the operand types, so `int + int` is int addition, which wraps
silently on overflow; the widening to `long` happens afterwards, to a value
that is already wrong. Cast one operand and the compiler picks `long + long`
instead. C# also has a `checked` context that turns overflow into an
`OverflowException` — worth knowing it exists, and worth knowing it is off by
default for performance.

## ex3

The two `?`s in `Describe(string? name, int? age)` look like one feature and are
two. `string?` is an annotation: it changes the compiler's flow analysis and
nothing about the generated code. `int?` is `Nullable<int>`, an actual struct
with a `bool` and an `int` inside it, and `age.Value` on an empty one throws.

The blank-string case is there because `null` and `""` and `"   "` are three
different values that mean the same thing to a human, and a nullable annotation
only protects you from one of them. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the standard
answer, and it carries a `[NotNullWhen(false)]` attribute that tells the
compiler's null analysis "if this returned false, the argument is not null" —
which is why the `else` branch does not warn. Attribute-driven null analysis is
a small thing that makes the whole feature usable.

The related operators worth having at your fingertips: `??` (fallback if null),
`??=` (assign if currently null), and `?.` (call only if not null, result is
nullable). `name?.Trim() ?? "anonymous"` is idiomatic C# and reads exactly as
it behaves.

## ex4

`decimal` is a 128-bit type storing a 96-bit integer, a sign, and a base-10
exponent from 0 to 28. That representation is what makes `0.1m` exact where
`0.1` (double) is not. It also means `decimal` carries *scale*: `27m` and
`27.00m` are equal but not identical — `ToString()` prints them differently
because the trailing zeros are stored. That is a feature for money, where "$27.00"
is the correct rendering, and a small surprise the first time you see it in a
log.

The rounding call takes three arguments for a reason: value, digits, mode. Skip
the mode and you have silently chosen banker's rounding for someone's invoice.
Skip the rounding entirely and you get a total with four decimal places that
disagrees with the printed receipt by a fraction of a cent — the classic
accumulating-error bug, where each line is nearly right and the sum is visibly
wrong.

One more habit: do the rounding once, at the end, on the value you are about to
show or store. Rounding intermediate values is how you end up with a total that
does not equal the sum of its parts.

## challenge

Parsing and formatting are the two places a program touches the outside world,
and both are culture-sensitive. `decimal.Parse("19.99")` on a machine set to
German reads a *thousands* separator and can hand you 1999, and
`total.ToString("0.00")` there writes `19,99` — so the round trip that works on
your laptop breaks on a colleague's, or on a server set to a different locale.
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` says "use the machine-readable convention,
regardless of who is looking", and it is the right answer for anything that
crosses a wire, a file, or a test assertion. Its opposite number,
`CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, is right when the string is being *shown to a
human*.

The format string `"0.00"` is a custom numeric format: `0` means "a digit, and
a zero if there isn't one". The standard alternative is `"F2"` (fixed-point,
two decimals). Both are worth recognising; neither is worth memorising beyond
that.

## review1

This one folds three of the lesson's ideas into one method: the null fallback,
the nullable value type's `HasValue`, and the rounding mode. It also changes
the *shape* of the output when a value is missing rather than substituting a
different value, which is why an early `return` reads better than a conditional
expression — the two branches are not two values, they are two sentences.

If this came back to you cold and the rounding mode was the part you had to
look up, that is the expected outcome and exactly what the spaced-review ladder
is for. If the `double?` unwrapping was the part you had to look up, reread the
ex3 notes above: the annotation and the wrapper type look alike and behave
differently, and that confusion is durable.

## Further reading

- [Value types (C# reference)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) — the official statement of what a value type is, including the list of built-in ones.
- [Reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/reference-types) — the other half, and where `string`'s special status is spelled out.
- [Casting and type conversions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/casting-and-type-conversions) — implicit, explicit, and user-defined conversions in one page.
- [Nullable reference types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references) — what the annotations mean, and the honest list of what they do not guarantee.
- [`decimal` keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/floating-point-numeric-types) — precision, range, and the `m` suffix, next to `float` and `double` for comparison.
- [`MidpointRounding` enum](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.midpointrounding) — all the modes, with the banker's-rounding rationale.

## Challenge — a line of text in, a line of text out

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`ReceiptLine.Format(string line)`, which takes `"widget|19.99|3"` and returns
`"widget x3 = $59.97"`.

Honest difficulty note: nothing here is new, but it is the first time you have
to hold four ideas at once — splitting, parsing to two different types, decimal
arithmetic, and formatted output. The one genuinely new detail is culture:
`decimal.Parse` reads `"19.99"` differently on a machine whose locale writes
`19,99`, so pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` when parsing and when
formatting. That `using System.Globalization;` at the top of the file is there
for you.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 01_types_variables challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves: get three values out of the text, then build one string from them.
Do not try to do both in one expression.

The middle field is money and the last field is a count, so they do not become
the same type. Read the expected output and ask which of the three fields is
still a `string` when you print it.

## Hint 2

`line.Split('|')` gives you a `string[]` of length three. Index 0 is the name,
1 the unit price, 2 the quantity.

`decimal.Parse` and `int.Parse` both take an optional `IFormatProvider`. Pass
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` — the `using System.Globalization;` at the top
of the file is there for exactly this. On a machine whose locale writes
`19,99`, parsing `"19.99"` without it either throws or silently reads 1999.

Printing has the same problem in reverse: `total.ToString("0.00", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
string[] fields = line.Split('|');
decimal unitPrice = decimal.Parse(fields[1], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
int quantity = /* the same idea, one field along */;

decimal total = /* multiply, then round to 2 places away from zero */;
return $"{fields[0]} x{quantity} = ${/* two-decimal-place text */}";
```

Mind the `$` twice in that last line: one starts the interpolated string, and
the other is the literal dollar sign in the output. `"$"` inside an
interpolated string is just a character; only `$` *before* the quote is
special.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two halves: get three values out of the text, then build one string from them.
Do not try to do both in one expression.

The middle field is money and the last field is a count, so they do not become
the same type. Read the expected output and ask which of the three fields is
still a `string` when you print it.

## Hint 2

`line.Split('|')` gives you a `string[]` of length three. Index 0 is the name,
1 the unit price, 2 the quantity.

`decimal.Parse` and `int.Parse` both take an optional `IFormatProvider`. Pass
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` — the `using System.Globalization;` at the top
of the file is there for exactly this. On a machine whose locale writes
`19,99`, parsing `"19.99"` without it either throws or silently reads 1999.

Printing has the same problem in reverse: `total.ToString("0.00", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
string[] fields = line.Split('|');
decimal unitPrice = decimal.Parse(fields[1], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
int quantity = /* the same idea, one field along */;

decimal total = /* multiply, then round to 2 places away from zero */;
return $"{fields[0]} x{quantity} = ${/* two-decimal-place text */}";
```

Mind the `$` twice in that last line: one starts the interpolated string, and
the other is the literal dollar sign in the output. `"$"` inside an
interpolated string is just a character; only `$` *before* the quote is
special.

## Exercise 2 — conversions that lose things

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Ex2.cs`. Three small methods:

`Truncate(double)` chops the fraction off toward zero: `3.9 -> 3`, `-3.9 -> -3`.

`RoundHalfAwayFromZero(double)` rounds to the nearest whole number, and sends
an exact `.5` away from zero: `2.5 -> 3`, `3.5 -> 4`. This is not what
`Math.Round` does by default — its default is *banker's rounding*, which sends
`2.5` to `2` because 2 is even. That default exists for good statistical
reasons and surprises approximately everyone the first time.

`SafeAdd(int, int)` returns a `long` that is correct even for
`int.MaxValue + 1`. Careful: `a + b` is computed in `int` and the overflow has
already happened before anything widens.

```

```

## Exercise 3 — things that might not be there

Edit `src/Lessons/L01_TypesVariables/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`Labels.Describe(string? name, int? age)`:

- `Describe("Ada", 36)` -> `"Ada (36)"`
- `Describe(null, 36)` -> `"anonymous (36)"`
- `Describe("   ", 36)` -> `"anonymous (36)"` — blank counts as missing
- `Describe("Ada", null)` -> `"Ada (age unknown)"`
- `Describe(null, null)` -> `"anonymous (age unknown)"`

Two independent decisions, not five cases. Note the two different `?`s in that
signature: `string?` is an annotation the compiler checks, and `int?` is a real
wrapper type with `.HasValue`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two independent decisions here, not four cases. Compute the name
part, compute the age part, then glue them together with one interpolated
string at the end. If you are writing four `if` branches you are treating one
problem as two.

Watch the blank-string case: `"   "` is not null, and it is not `""` either.

## Hint 2

`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)` answers "missing or blank" in one call, and
the compiler is smart enough to know `name` is not null in the `else` branch.

`int? age` gives you `age.HasValue` and `age.Value`. You may also see
`age is null`, and `age?.ToString() ?? "age unknown"` — all three are fine.
Pick the one you can read back in six months.

## Hint 3

```csharp
string who = /* blank or null? */ ? "anonymous" : name;
string years = /* has a value? */ ? ... : "age unknown";
return $"{who} ({years})";
```

Note that `years` is a `string` in both branches — the conditional operator
needs both arms to be the same type, so the `int` has to become text before it
can sit next to `"age unknown"`. Interpolating it is one way; `ToString()` is
another.

## Hint 1

There are two independent decisions here, not four cases. Compute the name
part, compute the age part, then glue them together with one interpolated
string at the end. If you are writing four `if` branches you are treating one
problem as two.

Watch the blank-string case: `"   "` is not null, and it is not `""` either.

## Hint 2

`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)` answers "missing or blank" in one call, and
the compiler is smart enough to know `name` is not null in the `else` branch.

`int? age` gives you `age.HasValue` and `age.Value`. You may also see
`age is null`, and `age?.ToString() ?? "age unknown"` — all three are fine.
Pick the one you can read back in six months.

## Hint 3

```csharp
string who = /* blank or null? */ ? "anonymous" : name;
string years = /* has a value? */ ? ... : "age unknown";
return $"{who} ({years})";
```

Note that `years` is a `string` in both branches — the conditional operator
needs both arms to be the same type, so the `int` has to become text before it
can sit next to `"age unknown"`. Interpolating it is one way; `ToString()` is
another.

## Hint 1

Three steps in order: gross (price times quantity), then the discount taken
off, then the rounding. Do them in that order and each one is a single
expression.


The literal suffix matters: `100m` is a `decimal`, `100` is an `int`, and
