lessons.briefing:
# 02 — Control flow and methods

So far every method you have written took a value and returned a value, in one
straight line. Real code branches, repeats, hands back more than one answer,
and gets called by people who do not want to supply every argument every time.
This lesson is the grammar for all of that — and it is deliberately the last
lesson before objects, because once you have classes you will be tempted to
solve everything with them, and a good half of C# is still just methods that
compute things.

There is a second thread running through it. C# has spent the last decade
growing *expression* forms of things that used to be *statements*: a `switch`
that produces a value instead of jumping around, a method body that is one
`=>`, a conditional that sits inside an interpolated string. Expression-shaped
code is easier to read because it has one exit and no in-between states, and
modern C# style reaches for it first. You will write both forms here and feel
the difference.

## Concept — the pieces

**Loops.** `for` when you know the shape of the counting, `foreach` when you
have a collection and don't care about indices, `while` when the trip count is
genuinely unknown until it stops:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }          // initialiser; condition; step
foreach (string word in words) { }        // no index, no off-by-one
while (queue.Count > 0) { }               // until something changes
```

`foreach` is the default in idiomatic C#. Reach for `for` when the index is
part of the problem, not out of habit.

**Parameters that hand things back.** A method returns one value. When you need
two, C# gives you `out`:

```csharp
if (int.TryParse(text, out int number))
{
    // number is usable here
}
```

`out` means "I will assign this before I return" and the compiler *checks* it —
every return path must assign every `out` parameter. `ref` is the cousin that
passes an existing variable in and out (the caller must have assigned it
first), and it is rare in application code. The `Try...` pattern above — a
`bool` result plus an `out` value — is the standard .NET way to say "this might
not work, and that is not exceptional".

**`params`.** A final `params T[]` parameter lets callers pass loose arguments:
`Sum(1, 2, 3)` instead of `Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 })`. Inside the method it is an
ordinary array, and an empty call gives you a zero-length array, never null.

**Optional and named arguments.** A parameter with a default may be omitted;
a named argument (`shout: true`) lets you skip the ones in between:

```csharp
static string Log(string message, string level = "info", bool stamp = false) { }

Log("started");
Log("started", stamp: true);   // level stays "info"
```

The catch worth knowing: defaults are baked in **at the call site** by the
compiler, so changing a default in a library does nothing for callers who
haven't recompiled. That is why public APIs often prefer overloads.

**`switch` as an expression.** The old statement form still exists; the
expression form is what modern code uses, and it returns a value:

```csharp
string size = count switch
{
    0 => "empty",
    1 => "single",
    < 10 => "small",
    _ => "large",
};
```

`< 10` is a *relational pattern*, `_` is the discard that catches the rest, and
arms are tried in order — so put the specific ones first. The compiler warns
when it cannot prove every input is covered, which is a genuinely useful
safety net you will meet again in lesson 06.

**Expression-bodied members.** When a method is one expression, `=>` says so:

```csharp
public static int Square(int n) => n * n;
```

Same method, less ceremony. Use it when the body really is one expression, not
to compress three statements into an unreadable one.

## Exercise 1 — count down

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`Sequences.Countdown(int from)`:

- `Countdown(5)` -> `"5, 4, 3, 2, 1, liftoff"`
- `Countdown(1)` -> `"1, liftoff"`
- `Countdown(0)` -> `"liftoff"`
- `Countdown(-3)` -> `"liftoff"`

Separator is a comma and a space, with none trailing. That last pair of cases
is the design pressure: the version where you append `"5, "` as you go has to
special-case the end, and the version that collects pieces and joins them once
does not.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two answers and a variable number of arguments

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex2.cs`. Two methods.

`Stats.TryMinMax(int[] values, out int min, out int max)` returns `true` and
fills both out parameters for a non-empty array. For an empty array it sets
both to `0` and returns `false` — no exception; "empty" is an ordinary
outcome here, not a bug.

`Stats.Sum(params int[] numbers)` adds up whatever it is given. `Sum()` is `0`,
`Sum(1, 2, 3)` is `6`, and `Sum(someArray)` works too.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — defaults, and calling by name

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`Greeting.For(string name, string salutation = "Hello", bool shout = false)`:

- `For("Ada")` -> `"Hello, Ada."`
- `For("Ada", "Hi")` -> `"Hi, Ada."`
- `For("Ada", shout: true)` -> `"HELLO, ADA!"`
- `For("Ada", "Hi", true)` -> `"HI, ADA!"`

Shouting changes two things: the whole line goes upper-case *and* the full stop
becomes an exclamation mark. Leave the signature exactly as it is — the gate
calls the third case by argument name, which only works because the parameter
is called `shout`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a switch that returns

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`Grades.Letter(int score)`: 90 and up is `"A"`, 80 up `"B"`, 70 up `"C"`, 60 up
`"D"`, anything lower `"F"`. A score below 0 or above 100 is not a grade at
all — throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Two jobs, and they want to stay separate: a guard clause that rejects
impossible input, then a switch expression that maps the possible input. Notice
that `0` is a valid score and an `F`, while `-1` is neither.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex4
```

## Challenge — the loop that doesn't know when it will stop

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Challenge.cs`. The Collatz rule: from
any positive integer, halve it if it is even, otherwise triple it and add one.
Every number anyone has tried eventually reaches 1; nobody has proved they all
do.

`Collatz.Steps(int start)` counts the steps to reach 1 — `Steps(1)` is `0`,
`Steps(6)` is `8`. `Collatz.LongestUnder(int limit, out int steps)` returns
which starting number below `limit` takes the most steps, handing the count
back through `steps`; on a tie the smaller start wins.

Honest difficulty note: neither method is long, but three separate details bite
— an unbounded loop, an intermediate value that climbs far above where it
started, and a tie-break rule that is one character of difference.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods challenge
```

## Review

`review1` asks for `Words.TryLongest(string sentence, out string longest)` —
ex2's running-maximum loop and `Try...` shape, with strings. `dojo review` will
bring it back in a few days.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/02_control_flow_methods

## Notes

**Statements do, expressions are.** The through-line of this lesson is a shift
that C# has been making for years: replacing constructs that *perform steps*
with constructs that *produce values*. A `switch` statement jumps to a label
and relies on you to assign the right variable in each arm; a `switch`
expression *is* the value, so there is no arm that forgets to assign and no
variable that exists in a half-built state. Same for `?:` against `if`/`else`,
and for `=>` bodies against braces. The practical payoff is that expressions
compose — you can pass one to a method, return it, or drop it inside an
interpolated string — and that the compiler can check exhaustiveness, which it
cannot do for a statement that merely assigns.

**Argument passing, exactly.** By default C# passes arguments *by value*: the
parameter is a fresh variable initialised from the argument. For a class that
means the reference is copied, so the method can mutate the object but cannot
repoint the caller's variable. `ref` and `out` change this: the parameter
becomes an alias for the caller's variable itself, so an assignment inside the
method is visible outside. The difference between them is who must assign
first — `ref` requires the caller to, `out` requires the method to. There is
also `in`, which passes a read-only alias and exists mainly to avoid copying
large structs.

**Why `out` feels clumsy, and what replaced it.** Writing `out` at the call
site is noise, which is why C# 7 added inline declarations
(`TryParse(s, out int n)`) and why modern APIs increasingly return a tuple
instead: `static (int min, int max) MinMax(...)`. Tuples are usually the better
choice for two ordinary results; `out` earns its keep in the `Try...` pattern,
where the `bool` is the *primary* answer and the value is conditional on it.
Knowing both, and knowing when each reads better, is a reasonable interview
answer.

**Loop choice is a communication decision, not a performance one.** All three
loop forms compile to nearly identical IL for an array. `foreach` says "every
element, in order, no index arithmetic"; `for` says "the position matters";
`while` says "I do not know how many times". Choosing the one that matches your
intent is how a reader knows what to check for. The classic bug `foreach`
eliminates is the off-by-one, and the classic bug it introduces is trying to
modify the collection while enumerating it — which throws
`InvalidOperationException` at runtime, by design.

## ex1

The interesting part is not the loop, it is where the separator lives.
Appending `n + ", "` inside the loop builds the string *and* the punctuation
together, which means the last element is special and the empty case is
special. Collecting the pieces and calling `string.Join(", ", parts)` at the
end separates "what are the items" from "how are they rendered", and the two
awkward cases evaporate.

That is a small instance of a large idea: **build the data, then format it**.
The same reflex is why you will hear "don't build HTML with string
concatenation" and "don't build SQL by gluing text together". The formatting
step is where the edge cases live, so give it one place to live in.

Performance footnote, since someone always asks: repeated `+=` on a `string` in
a loop allocates a new string every iteration, because strings are immutable.
For a handful of items nobody cares. For thousands, use `StringBuilder`, which
keeps a mutable buffer and produces the string once. `string.Join` already does
the efficient thing internally.

## ex2

`out` parameters exist because a method returns exactly one value and sometimes
one is not enough. The compiler's definite-assignment analysis is doing real
work here: it will not let you `return false;` before assigning `min` and
`max`, which is why assigning both at the top of the method is the tidy
pattern rather than a trick.

The `Try...` convention is worth internalising because .NET is full of it and
because interviewers ask the design question behind it. `int.Parse` throws;
`int.TryParse` returns a `bool`. The rule: **if the caller can reasonably
expect this input to fail, do not make failure an exception.** Exceptions are
expensive (stack capture, unwinding) and, more importantly, they are a
different control-flow channel — using them for ordinary outcomes makes normal
code read like error handling.

`params` is a compiler trick, not a runtime feature: at the call site, the
compiler collects the loose arguments into a real array and passes that. Which
means every call allocates one, so hot paths sometimes offer overloads for one
and two arguments to avoid it — `string.Format` does exactly that. Notice also
that `params` must be the last parameter, for the obvious reason that the
compiler would otherwise not know where the array stops.

## ex3

Optional arguments are the feature people most often get subtly wrong, because
of *where* the default lives. The compiler embeds the default value into the
**caller's** compiled code. If a library ships `Log(string m, string level = "info")`
and version 2 changes the default to `"warn"`, existing callers that were not
recompiled keep passing `"info"` forever. That is why public library APIs
often prefer overloads (`Log(m)` calling `Log(m, "info")`), where the default
lives in one place that ships with the library.

Named arguments solve the other problem: a call like `Configure(true, false, true)`
tells the reader nothing. `Configure(retry: true, verbose: false, cache: true)`
tells them everything, and it costs nothing at runtime. The rule of thumb most
teams use: name your booleans at the call site. Which also means your parameter
names are part of your public API, and renaming one is a breaking change for
anyone who used it by name.

`ToUpperInvariant` over `ToUpper` is the other habit in this exercise.
Culture-sensitive upper-casing is right for text shown to a human and wrong for
anything you compare or store — the standard example is Turkish, where the
upper-case of `i` is `I` and `"file".ToUpper() == "FILE"` is false.

## ex4

Switch expressions with relational patterns replace the `if/else if` ladder
that every grading function used to be, and they are better for a specific
reason: the compiler checks them. Leave a gap and you get a warning that not
all inputs are handled; write an arm that can never be reached — put `>= 60`
above `>= 90` — and you get a warning for that too. An `if` ladder gets neither.

Keeping the range guard *out* of the switch is the design point. You could
write an arm for `< 0` that throws, and it would work, but then the switch is
doing two jobs: validating and classifying. Guard clauses at the top are the
convention because they let a reader skip to the interesting part knowing
exactly what is already ruled out.

`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` rather than a plain `ArgumentException` is a
small piece of etiquette worth copying: .NET has a specific exception for "the
value is the right type but outside the allowed range", and its constructor
takes the parameter name and the offending value so the message writes itself.
`nameof(score)` keeps that name correct through a rename. Lesson 12 covers the
whole family.

## challenge

The Collatz sequence is the standard teaching example for `while` because you
cannot express the trip count as a `for` header — there is no formula for how
many steps a number takes, and proving there always *is* a finite number is an
open problem in mathematics. That is the honest reason the loop form exists.

Two details worth keeping. First, the intermediate value climbs: starting at
27, the sequence reaches 9232 before descending. Nothing here overflows an
`int`, but the habit of widening the running value to `long` is the right one —
run the same search up to a million and the peaks reach into the billions.
Second, the tie-break. `if (count > best)` keeps the first winner and
`if (count >= best)` keeps the last, and no test you write by accident will
tell you which you meant. Deciding tie-breaks explicitly is the same discipline
as writing `ORDER BY` with a unique tiebreaker column in SQL.

A performance aside, because it is the natural follow-up question: this brute
force recomputes the whole chain for every start, and the standard improvement
is memoising the step counts in a dictionary, since most chains merge into ones
you have already walked. That is a fine thing to try after the gate is green —
`08_collections` gives you the dictionary.

## review1

Same `Try...` shape, same running-best loop, different element type — and the
tie-break question again, now as "which of two five-letter words wins". If the
`>` versus `>=` decision was the part you had to think about, that is the point
of the review appearing at all: the shape is easy to recall and the tie-break
is the part that decays.

The `StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries` detail is the other thing this
variant is quietly teaching. `"a  b".Split(' ')` produces three items, the
middle one empty, because splitting is literal about separators. Every language
has this and every developer gets bitten by it once.

## Further reading

- [Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) — `for`, `foreach`, `while`, `do`, and what `foreach` actually compiles into.
- [Method parameters: `ref`, `out`, `in`, `params`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters) — the whole family in one page, with the definite-assignment rules.
- [Named and optional arguments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/named-and-optional-arguments) — including the call-site-baking behaviour that makes defaults a versioning decision.
- [Pattern matching and `switch` expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/patterns) — relational patterns, `and`/`or`, and exhaustiveness.
- [The `Try...` pattern (`int.TryParse`)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.int32.tryparse) — the canonical example, with the design rationale in the remarks.

# 02 — Control flow and methods

So far every method you have written took a value and returned a value, in one
straight line. Real code branches, repeats, hands back more than one answer,
and gets called by people who do not want to supply every argument every time.
This lesson is the grammar for all of that — and it is deliberately the last
lesson before objects, because once you have classes you will be tempted to
solve everything with them, and a good half of C# is still just methods that
compute things.

There is a second thread running through it. C# has spent the last decade
growing *expression* forms of things that used to be *statements*: a `switch`
that produces a value instead of jumping around, a method body that is one
`=>`, a conditional that sits inside an interpolated string. Expression-shaped
code is easier to read because it has one exit and no in-between states, and
modern C# style reaches for it first. You will write both forms here and feel
the difference.

## Concept — the pieces

**Loops.** `for` when you know the shape of the counting, `foreach` when you
have a collection and don't care about indices, `while` when the trip count is
genuinely unknown until it stops:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }          // initialiser; condition; step
foreach (string word in words) { }        // no index, no off-by-one
while (queue.Count > 0) { }               // until something changes
```

`foreach` is the default in idiomatic C#. Reach for `for` when the index is
part of the problem, not out of habit.

**Parameters that hand things back.** A method returns one value. When you need
two, C# gives you `out`:

```csharp
if (int.TryParse(text, out int number))
{
    // number is usable here
}
```

`out` means "I will assign this before I return" and the compiler *checks* it —
every return path must assign every `out` parameter. `ref` is the cousin that
passes an existing variable in and out (the caller must have assigned it
first), and it is rare in application code. The `Try...` pattern above — a
`bool` result plus an `out` value — is the standard .NET way to say "this might
not work, and that is not exceptional".

**`params`.** A final `params T[]` parameter lets callers pass loose arguments:
`Sum(1, 2, 3)` instead of `Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 })`. Inside the method it is an
ordinary array, and an empty call gives you a zero-length array, never null.

**Optional and named arguments.** A parameter with a default may be omitted;
a named argument (`shout: true`) lets you skip the ones in between:

```csharp
static string Log(string message, string level = "info", bool stamp = false) { }

Log("started");
Log("started", stamp: true);   // level stays "info"
```

The catch worth knowing: defaults are baked in **at the call site** by the
compiler, so changing a default in a library does nothing for callers who
haven't recompiled. That is why public APIs often prefer overloads.

**`switch` as an expression.** The old statement form still exists; the
expression form is what modern code uses, and it returns a value:

```csharp
string size = count switch
{
    0 => "empty",
    1 => "single",
    < 10 => "small",
    _ => "large",
};
```

`< 10` is a *relational pattern*, `_` is the discard that catches the rest, and
arms are tried in order — so put the specific ones first. The compiler warns
when it cannot prove every input is covered, which is a genuinely useful
safety net you will meet again in lesson 06.

**Expression-bodied members.** When a method is one expression, `=>` says so:

```csharp
public static int Square(int n) => n * n;
```

Same method, less ceremony. Use it when the body really is one expression, not
to compress three statements into an unreadable one.

## Exercise 1 — count down

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`Sequences.Countdown(int from)`:

- `Countdown(5)` -> `"5, 4, 3, 2, 1, liftoff"`
- `Countdown(1)` -> `"1, liftoff"`
- `Countdown(0)` -> `"liftoff"`
- `Countdown(-3)` -> `"liftoff"`

Separator is a comma and a space, with none trailing. That last pair of cases
is the design pressure: the version where you append `"5, "` as you go has to
special-case the end, and the version that collects pieces and joins them once
does not.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two answers and a variable number of arguments

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex2.cs`. Two methods.

`Stats.TryMinMax(int[] values, out int min, out int max)` returns `true` and
fills both out parameters for a non-empty array. For an empty array it sets
both to `0` and returns `false` — no exception; "empty" is an ordinary
outcome here, not a bug.

`Stats.Sum(params int[] numbers)` adds up whatever it is given. `Sum()` is `0`,
`Sum(1, 2, 3)` is `6`, and `Sum(someArray)` works too.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — defaults, and calling by name

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`Greeting.For(string name, string salutation = "Hello", bool shout = false)`:

- `For("Ada")` -> `"Hello, Ada."`
- `For("Ada", "Hi")` -> `"Hi, Ada."`
- `For("Ada", shout: true)` -> `"HELLO, ADA!"`
- `For("Ada", "Hi", true)` -> `"HI, ADA!"`

Shouting changes two things: the whole line goes upper-case *and* the full stop
becomes an exclamation mark. Leave the signature exactly as it is — the gate
calls the third case by argument name, which only works because the parameter
is called `shout`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a switch that returns

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`Grades.Letter(int score)`: 90 and up is `"A"`, 80 up `"B"`, 70 up `"C"`, 60 up
`"D"`, anything lower `"F"`. A score below 0 or above 100 is not a grade at
all — throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Two jobs, and they want to stay separate: a guard clause that rejects
impossible input, then a switch expression that maps the possible input. Notice
that `0` is a valid score and an `F`, while `-1` is neither.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex4
```

## Challenge — the loop that doesn't know when it will stop

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Challenge.cs`. The Collatz rule: from
any positive integer, halve it if it is even, otherwise triple it and add one.
Every number anyone has tried eventually reaches 1; nobody has proved they all
do.

`Collatz.Steps(int start)` counts the steps to reach 1 — `Steps(1)` is `0`,
`Steps(6)` is `8`. `Collatz.LongestUnder(int limit, out int steps)` returns
which starting number below `limit` takes the most steps, handing the count
back through `steps`; on a tie the smaller start wins.

Honest difficulty note: neither method is long, but three separate details bite
— an unbounded loop, an intermediate value that climbs far above where it
started, and a tie-break rule that is one character of difference.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods challenge
```

## Review

`review1` asks for `Words.TryLongest(string sentence, out string longest)` —
ex2's running-maximum loop and `Try...` shape, with strings. `dojo review` will
bring it back in a few days.

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L02_ControlFlowMethodsTests.cs`:

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L02_ControlFlowMethods;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L02_ControlFlowMethodsTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_CountdownEndsInLiftoff()
    {
        Teach.Equal("5, 4, 3, 2, 1, liftoff", Sequences.Countdown(5),
            "Count DOWN to 1, then append \"liftoff\". Separator is a comma and a space, "
                + "with no trailing separator - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("1, liftoff", Sequences.Countdown(1),
            "Starting at 1 still counts 1 before liftoff.");

        Teach.Equal("liftoff", Sequences.Countdown(0),
            "A start below 1 means the loop body never runs, so there is nothing to separate "
                + "- and no leading comma. If you got \", liftoff\" you glued the separator on "
                + "by hand instead of letting string.Join do it - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("liftoff", Sequences.Countdown(-3),
            "A negative start is the same case: the loop condition is false immediately.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_TryMinMaxAndSumHandTheirResultsBack()
    {
        bool found = Stats.TryMinMax(new[] { 4, -2, 9, 9 }, out int min, out int max);

        Teach.True(found, "A non-empty array has a minimum and a maximum, so TryMinMax returns "
            + "true - reread README ex2.");
        Teach.Equal(-2, min, "The smallest of 4, -2, 9, 9 is -2. Starting your running minimum "
            + "at 0 instead of at values[0] is the classic way to miss it.");
        Teach.Equal(9, max, "The largest of 4, -2, 9, 9 is 9, and a repeat of the maximum "
            + "changes nothing.");

        bool empty = Stats.TryMinMax(Array.Empty<int>(), out int emptyMin, out int emptyMax);

        Teach.True(!empty, "An empty array has no minimum: return false rather than throwing "
            + "- that is the whole point of the Try- prefix - reread README ex2.");
        Teach.Equal(0, emptyMin, "Even on the false path, C# requires every out parameter to be "
            + "assigned before you return. Set both to 0.");
        Teach.Equal(0, emptyMax, "Same for max: assigned, even though the caller should ignore it.");

        Teach.Equal(6, Stats.Sum(1, 2, 3), "params lets the caller pass loose arguments; inside "
            + "the method they are an int[] you can loop over.");
        Teach.Equal(0, Stats.Sum(), "params also allows NO arguments, which arrives as an empty "
            + "array - not null. Summing nothing is 0.");
        Teach.Equal(10, Stats.Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }), "A caller may also pass a real array; "
            + "the same method handles both.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_ForUsesItsDefaultsUntilYouOverrideThem()
    {
        Teach.Equal("Hello, Ada.", Greeting.For("Ada"),
            "Two arguments were left out, so both defaults apply - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("Hi, Ada.", Greeting.For("Ada", "Hi"),
            "The second positional argument replaces the salutation only.");

        Teach.Equal("HELLO, ADA!", Greeting.For("Ada", shout: true),
            "A named argument skips over the one in between, so the salutation is still the "
                + "default \"Hello\" - upper-cased, and ending in \"!\" - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("HI, ADA!", Greeting.For("Ada", "Hi", true),
            "Shouting upper-cases the whole line, salutation included.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_LetterIsASwitchOverRanges()
    {
        Teach.Equal("A", Grades.Letter(90), "90 is the bottom of the A band - the boundary is "
            + "inclusive.");
        Teach.Equal("B", Grades.Letter(89), "89 is one below the A band. Off-by-one at the "
            + "boundary is what this pair of checks is for - reread README ex4.");
        Teach.Equal("C", Grades.Letter(70), "70 is the bottom of the C band.");
        Teach.Equal("D", Grades.Letter(60), "60 is the bottom of the D band.");
        Teach.Equal("F", Grades.Letter(0), "0 is a valid score and an F. Valid and failing are "
            + "different things.");

        Teach.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => Grades.Letter(101),
            "101 is not a score at all, so this is an argument problem, not an F. Throw "
                + "ArgumentOutOfRangeException - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => Grades.Letter(-1),
            "A negative score is the other end of the same guard clause.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Challenge_CollatzCountsStepsAndFindsTheLongest()
    {
        Teach.Equal(0, Collatz.Steps(1), "1 is already 1, so the loop never runs - reread "
            + "README challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(8, Collatz.Steps(6), "6 -> 3 -> 10 -> 5 -> 16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1 is eight "
            + "steps. Count the arrows, not the numbers.");
        Teach.Equal(111, Collatz.Steps(27), "27 is the famous one: 111 steps, and the sequence "
            + "climbs to 9232 before it comes back down. A loop with no fixed trip count is "
                + "exactly what while is for - reread README challenge.");

        int start = Collatz.LongestUnder(1000, out int steps);

        Teach.Equal(871, start, "Under 1000 the longest chain starts at 871 - reread README "
            + "challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(178, steps, "871 takes 178 steps, and that number has to come back through "
            + "the out parameter, not through the return.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Review1_TryLongestPicksTheFirstLongestWord()
    {
        bool found = Words.TryLongest("the quick brown fox", out string longest);

        Teach.True(found, "There are words here, so TryLongest returns true.");
        Teach.Equal("quick", longest, "\"quick\" and \"brown\" are both five letters, and the "
            + "FIRST one wins - which is what a strictly-greater-than comparison gives you, "
                + "and what >= would not.");

        Teach.True(Words.TryLongest("hi", out string only) && only == "hi",
            "One word is trivially the longest word.");

        bool empty = Words.TryLongest("   ", out string nothing);

        Teach.True(!empty, "Whitespace holds no words: return false.");
        Teach.Equal("", nothing, "The out parameter still has to be assigned - use \"\", not null.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: `Ex1` pins the separator behaviour and both empty cases.
`Ex2` calls `TryMinMax` twice — once with data, once empty — and checks the
`out` values on both paths, then calls `Sum` three different ways. `Ex3` calls
`For` four ways, including one named argument. `Ex4` checks each band's
boundary and both ends of the guard clause. `Challenge` checks three step
counts and the search, and `Review1` is the spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The `Try...` pattern in ex2 is worth more than its size suggests. Every .NET
API that might fail for an ordinary reason offers it — `int.TryParse`,
`Dictionary.TryGetValue`, `Queue.TryDequeue` — and the alternative is a thrown
exception, which costs a stack unwind and turns "the user typed nonsense" into
a control-flow event. The rule teams settle on: **exceptions are for the
unexpected**; a caller who can reasonably expect failure deserves a return
value. You will meet the other half of that rule in `12_exceptions`.

The other habit is the guard clause in ex4. Validating at the top and throwing
immediately keeps the interesting part of the method flat — no nesting, no
`else`, no reader wondering which of four conditions is still true down at line
40. It reads as "here is what must be true; now here is the work", and once you
notice it you will see it in every well-kept C# codebase you open.

Next: **03_classes_objects**, where state stops living in parameters and starts
living in objects that own it.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **02 — Control flow and methods**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex3` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `review1` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `challenge` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex1` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex2` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex3` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - csharp/02_control_flow_methods

## Notes

**Statements do, expressions are.** The through-line of this lesson is a shift
that C# has been making for years: replacing constructs that *perform steps*
with constructs that *produce values*. A `switch` statement jumps to a label
and relies on you to assign the right variable in each arm; a `switch`
expression *is* the value, so there is no arm that forgets to assign and no
variable that exists in a half-built state. Same for `?:` against `if`/`else`,
and for `=>` bodies against braces. The practical payoff is that expressions
compose — you can pass one to a method, return it, or drop it inside an
interpolated string — and that the compiler can check exhaustiveness, which it
cannot do for a statement that merely assigns.

**Argument passing, exactly.** By default C# passes arguments *by value*: the
parameter is a fresh variable initialised from the argument. For a class that
means the reference is copied, so the method can mutate the object but cannot
repoint the caller's variable. `ref` and `out` change this: the parameter
becomes an alias for the caller's variable itself, so an assignment inside the
method is visible outside. The difference between them is who must assign
first — `ref` requires the caller to, `out` requires the method to. There is
also `in`, which passes a read-only alias and exists mainly to avoid copying
large structs.

**Why `out` feels clumsy, and what replaced it.** Writing `out` at the call
site is noise, which is why C# 7 added inline declarations
(`TryParse(s, out int n)`) and why modern APIs increasingly return a tuple
instead: `static (int min, int max) MinMax(...)`. Tuples are usually the better
choice for two ordinary results; `out` earns its keep in the `Try...` pattern,
where the `bool` is the *primary* answer and the value is conditional on it.
Knowing both, and knowing when each reads better, is a reasonable interview
answer.

**Loop choice is a communication decision, not a performance one.** All three
loop forms compile to nearly identical IL for an array. `foreach` says "every
element, in order, no index arithmetic"; `for` says "the position matters";
`while` says "I do not know how many times". Choosing the one that matches your
intent is how a reader knows what to check for. The classic bug `foreach`
eliminates is the off-by-one, and the classic bug it introduces is trying to
modify the collection while enumerating it — which throws
`InvalidOperationException` at runtime, by design.

## ex1

The interesting part is not the loop, it is where the separator lives.
Appending `n + ", "` inside the loop builds the string *and* the punctuation
together, which means the last element is special and the empty case is
special. Collecting the pieces and calling `string.Join(", ", parts)` at the
end separates "what are the items" from "how are they rendered", and the two
awkward cases evaporate.

That is a small instance of a large idea: **build the data, then format it**.
The same reflex is why you will hear "don't build HTML with string
concatenation" and "don't build SQL by gluing text together". The formatting
step is where the edge cases live, so give it one place to live in.

Performance footnote, since someone always asks: repeated `+=` on a `string` in
a loop allocates a new string every iteration, because strings are immutable.
For a handful of items nobody cares. For thousands, use `StringBuilder`, which
keeps a mutable buffer and produces the string once. `string.Join` already does
the efficient thing internally.

## ex2

`out` parameters exist because a method returns exactly one value and sometimes
one is not enough. The compiler's definite-assignment analysis is doing real
work here: it will not let you `return false;` before assigning `min` and
`max`, which is why assigning both at the top of the method is the tidy
pattern rather than a trick.

The `Try...` convention is worth internalising because .NET is full of it and
because interviewers ask the design question behind it. `int.Parse` throws;
`int.TryParse` returns a `bool`. The rule: **if the caller can reasonably
expect this input to fail, do not make failure an exception.** Exceptions are
expensive (stack capture, unwinding) and, more importantly, they are a
different control-flow channel — using them for ordinary outcomes makes normal
code read like error handling.

`params` is a compiler trick, not a runtime feature: at the call site, the
compiler collects the loose arguments into a real array and passes that. Which
means every call allocates one, so hot paths sometimes offer overloads for one
and two arguments to avoid it — `string.Format` does exactly that. Notice also
that `params` must be the last parameter, for the obvious reason that the
compiler would otherwise not know where the array stops.

## ex3

Optional arguments are the feature people most often get subtly wrong, because
of *where* the default lives. The compiler embeds the default value into the
**caller's** compiled code. If a library ships `Log(string m, string level = "info")`
and version 2 changes the default to `"warn"`, existing callers that were not
recompiled keep passing `"info"` forever. That is why public library APIs
often prefer overloads (`Log(m)` calling `Log(m, "info")`), where the default
lives in one place that ships with the library.

Named arguments solve the other problem: a call like `Configure(true, false, true)`
tells the reader nothing. `Configure(retry: true, verbose: false, cache: true)`
tells them everything, and it costs nothing at runtime. The rule of thumb most
teams use: name your booleans at the call site. Which also means your parameter
names are part of your public API, and renaming one is a breaking change for
anyone who used it by name.

`ToUpperInvariant` over `ToUpper` is the other habit in this exercise.
Culture-sensitive upper-casing is right for text shown to a human and wrong for
anything you compare or store — the standard example is Turkish, where the
upper-case of `i` is `I` and `"file".ToUpper() == "FILE"` is false.

## ex4

Switch expressions with relational patterns replace the `if/else if` ladder
that every grading function used to be, and they are better for a specific
reason: the compiler checks them. Leave a gap and you get a warning that not
all inputs are handled; write an arm that can never be reached — put `>= 60`
above `>= 90` — and you get a warning for that too. An `if` ladder gets neither.

Keeping the range guard *out* of the switch is the design point. You could
write an arm for `< 0` that throws, and it would work, but then the switch is
doing two jobs: validating and classifying. Guard clauses at the top are the
convention because they let a reader skip to the interesting part knowing
exactly what is already ruled out.

`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` rather than a plain `ArgumentException` is a
small piece of etiquette worth copying: .NET has a specific exception for "the
value is the right type but outside the allowed range", and its constructor
takes the parameter name and the offending value so the message writes itself.
`nameof(score)` keeps that name correct through a rename. Lesson 12 covers the
whole family.

## challenge

The Collatz sequence is the standard teaching example for `while` because you
cannot express the trip count as a `for` header — there is no formula for how
many steps a number takes, and proving there always *is* a finite number is an
open problem in mathematics. That is the honest reason the loop form exists.

Two details worth keeping. First, the intermediate value climbs: starting at
27, the sequence reaches 9232 before descending. Nothing here overflows an
`int`, but the habit of widening the running value to `long` is the right one —
run the same search up to a million and the peaks reach into the billions.
Second, the tie-break. `if (count > best)` keeps the first winner and
`if (count >= best)` keeps the last, and no test you write by accident will
tell you which you meant. Deciding tie-breaks explicitly is the same discipline
as writing `ORDER BY` with a unique tiebreaker column in SQL.

A performance aside, because it is the natural follow-up question: this brute
force recomputes the whole chain for every start, and the standard improvement
is memoising the step counts in a dictionary, since most chains merge into ones
you have already walked. That is a fine thing to try after the gate is green —
`08_collections` gives you the dictionary.

## review1

Same `Try...` shape, same running-best loop, different element type — and the
tie-break question again, now as "which of two five-letter words wins". If the
`>` versus `>=` decision was the part you had to think about, that is the point
of the review appearing at all: the shape is easy to recall and the tie-break
is the part that decays.

The `StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries` detail is the other thing this
variant is quietly teaching. `"a  b".Split(' ')` produces three items, the
middle one empty, because splitting is literal about separators. Every language
has this and every developer gets bitten by it once.

## Further reading

- [Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) — `for`, `foreach`, `while`, `do`, and what `foreach` actually compiles into.
- [Method parameters: `ref`, `out`, `in`, `params`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters) — the whole family in one page, with the definite-assignment rules.
- [Named and optional arguments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/named-and-optional-arguments) — including the call-site-baking behaviour that makes defaults a versioning decision.
- [Pattern matching and `switch` expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/patterns) — relational patterns, `and`/`or`, and exhaustiveness.
- [The `Try...` pattern (`int.TryParse`)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.int32.tryparse) — the canonical example, with the design rationale in the remarks.

## Challenge — the loop that doesn't know when it will stop

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Challenge.cs`. The Collatz rule: from
any positive integer, halve it if it is even, otherwise triple it and add one.
Every number anyone has tried eventually reaches 1; nobody has proved they all
do.

`Collatz.Steps(int start)` counts the steps to reach 1 — `Steps(1)` is `0`,
`Steps(6)` is `8`. `Collatz.LongestUnder(int limit, out int steps)` returns
which starting number below `limit` takes the most steps, handing the count
back through `steps`; on a tie the smaller start wins.

Honest difficulty note: neither method is long, but three separate details bite
— an unbounded loop, an intermediate value that climbs far above where it
started, and a tie-break rule that is one character of difference.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods challenge
```

## Hint 1

int count = 0;
while (current != 1)
{

like the running maximum in ex2.

## Hint 3

The tie-break rule decides one character. Keeping the best with
`if (count > bestSteps)` keeps the *first* winner; `>=` would keep the last.
The prompt says the smaller starting number wins.

Remember `steps` is an `out` parameter, so it must be assigned on every path
that returns — assigning it once at the end, from the best you tracked, is
enough here. And do not print anything: the gate reads your return values, not
your console.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — count down

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`Sequences.Countdown(int from)`:

- `Countdown(5)` -> `"5, 4, 3, 2, 1, liftoff"`
- `Countdown(1)` -> `"1, liftoff"`
- `Countdown(0)` -> `"liftoff"`
- `Countdown(-3)` -> `"liftoff"`

Separator is a comma and a space, with none trailing. That last pair of cases
is the design pressure: the version where you append `"5, "` as you go has to
special-case the end, and the version that collects pieces and joins them once
does not.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two decisions: how to walk the numbers downward, and how to glue the pieces
together with commas. Solve them separately — collect the pieces first, join
them second.

The `Countdown(0)` case is the one that decides your design. If you build the
string by appending `"5, "` as you go, you have to remember to trim the last
separator, and the empty case has nothing to trim.

## Hint 2

A `for` loop can count down as easily as up: the initialiser, the condition and
the step are three independent expressions.

```csharp
for (int n = from; n >= 1; n--)
```

Collect into a `List<string>` with `.Add(...)`, then `string.Join(", ", parts)`
puts the separator *between* the pieces and nowhere else — which is exactly why
the empty case then costs you nothing.

## Hint 3

Add `"liftoff"` to the same list, after the loop, and join once at the end. An
`int` needs to become text before it can go into a `List<string>`:
`n.ToString()` or `$"{n}"`.

If you would rather use a `StringBuilder` or plain concatenation, that is fine
too — but then re-check `Countdown(0)` yourself before you run the gate.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two decisions: how to walk the numbers downward, and how to glue the pieces
together with commas. Solve them separately — collect the pieces first, join
them second.

The `Countdown(0)` case is the one that decides your design. If you build the
string by appending `"5, "` as you go, you have to remember to trim the last
separator, and the empty case has nothing to trim.

## Hint 2

A `for` loop can count down as easily as up: the initialiser, the condition and
the step are three independent expressions.

```csharp
for (int n = from; n >= 1; n--)
```

Collect into a `List<string>` with `.Add(...)`, then `string.Join(", ", parts)`
puts the separator *between* the pieces and nowhere else — which is exactly why
the empty case then costs you nothing.

## Hint 3

Add `"liftoff"` to the same list, after the loop, and join once at the end. An
`int` needs to become text before it can go into a `List<string>`:
`n.ToString()` or `$"{n}"`.

If you would rather use a `StringBuilder` or plain concatenation, that is fine
too — but then re-check `Countdown(0)` yourself before you run the gate.

## Exercise 2 — two answers and a variable number of arguments

Edit `src/Lessons/L02_ControlFlowMethods/Ex2.cs`. Two methods.

`Stats.TryMinMax(int[] values, out int min, out int max)` returns `true` and
fills both out parameters for a non-empty array. For an empty array it sets
both to `0` and returns `false` — no exception; "empty" is an ordinary
outcome here, not a bug.

`Stats.Sum(params int[] numbers)` adds up whatever it is given. `Sum()` is `0`,
`Sum(1, 2, 3)` is `6`, and `Sum(someArray)` works too.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 02_control_flow_methods ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`TryMinMax` returns a `bool` *and* produces two values. That is what `out` is
for, and the compiler enforces the contract: every path that returns must have
assigned both out parameters first. Try returning early without assigning them
and read the error — it is one of the clearest messages the C# compiler emits.

`Sum` has a `params` array. Inside the method it is an ordinary `int[]`; the
keyword only changes what callers may write.

## Hint 2

Assign both out parameters at the very top of the method, before any branch.
Then the empty-array early return costs you nothing and no path can be missed.

For the running minimum and maximum, seed them from `values[0]` rather than
from `0` — an array of all-positive numbers would otherwise report a minimum of
0, which is not in the array at all.

```csharp
min = 0;
max = 0;
if (values.Length == 0) { return false; }
min = values[0];
```

## Hint 3

The loop is one `foreach` with two `if`s inside it, comparing each value
against the current `min` and `max`. Both `if`s look at the same element, so
they belong in one pass, not two.

`Sum` is a `foreach` over `numbers` adding into a local total that starts at 0.
An empty `params` array arrives as a zero-length array, never null, so no guard
is needed — check that claim by reading what the gate expects from `Sum()`.

`TryMinMax` returns a `bool` *and* produces two values. That is what `out` is
for, and the compiler enforces the contract: every path that returns must have
assigned both out parameters first. Try returning early without assigning them

`Grades.Letter(int score)`: 90 and up is `"A"`, 80 up `"B"`, 70 up `"C"`, 60 up

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate jobs in one method, and they should stay separate: reject the
scores that are not scores, then map the ones that are onto a letter.

Do the rejecting first, at the top, and return nothing from that part — a guard
clause throws and gets out of the way.

## Hint 2

A `switch` *expression* produces a value, so it can be returned directly:

```csharp
return score switch
{
    >= 90 => "A",
    // ...
    _ => "F",
};
```

Those `>= 90` arms are *relational patterns*. Order matters: arms are tried top
to bottom, so a 95 matches the first arm that fits and never reaches the rest.
`_` is the discard pattern — the catch-all, and the compiler will tell you if
you leave it out and it cannot prove you covered everything.

## Hint 3

The guard is:

```csharp
if (score < 0 || score > 100)
{
    throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(score), score, "A score must be between 0 and 100.");
}
```

`nameof(score)` is a compile-time string of the parameter's name — rename the
parameter and it follows, which a string literal would not. Then write the four
bands in the order that lets each arm assume the ones above it already
failed, and let `_` handle everything below 60.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two separate jobs in one method, and they should stay separate: reject the
scores that are not scores, then map the ones that are onto a letter.

Do the rejecting first, at the top, and return nothing from that part — a guard
clause throws and gets out of the way.

## Hint 2

A `switch` *expression* produces a value, so it can be returned directly:

```csharp
return score switch
{
    >= 90 => "A",
    // ...
    _ => "F",
};
```

Those `>= 90` arms are *relational patterns*. Order matters: arms are tried top
to bottom, so a 95 matches the first arm that fits and never reaches the rest.
`_` is the discard pattern — the catch-all, and the compiler will tell you if
you leave it out and it cannot prove you covered everything.

## Hint 3

The guard is:

```csharp
if (score < 0 || score > 100)
{
    throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(score), score, "A score must be between 0 and 100.");
}
```

`nameof(score)` is a compile-time string of the parameter's name — rename the
parameter and it follows, which a string literal would not. Then write the four
bands in the order that lets each arm assume the ones above it already
failed, and let `_` handle everything below 60.

## Hint 1

This is ex2's running-maximum loop with strings instead of numbers, wearing
ex2's `Try...`/`out` shape. The thing you compare is not the word but its
length.

The tie-break rule is the same one the challenge asked about, so the comparison
operator is the same one.

## Hint 2

`sentence.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` gives you the
words and drops the empty strings that runs of spaces would otherwise produce.
Without that option, `"a  b"` splits into three pieces, one of them `""`.

Assign `longest` before any branch — `""` is a good starting value, because
every real word is longer than it, which quietly removes the need for a
separate "first word" case.

## Hint 3

```csharp
longest = "";
string[] words = /* split */;
if (words.Length == 0) { return false; }

foreach (string word in words)
{
    // keep it if it beats what you have
}
return true;
```

If you seeded `longest` with `""` you can drop the length check inside the
loop's first iteration entirely — but you still need the `words.Length == 0`
guard, because a sentence of pure whitespace has to return false rather than
report `""` as the winner.

# 03 — Classes and objects

Everything you have written so far has been a `static` method: a pure function
of its arguments, holding nothing between calls. That is a fine way to write a
calculator and a hopeless way to write a bank account, because an account *is*
a piece of state with rules attached — a balance that must never go negative, an
owner that must never change, a history of things that happened to it.

A class is how C# packages state together with the only code allowed to touch
it. That last clause is the whole idea, and it is worth being blunt about: the
point of a class is not that it groups related things, it is that it *forbids*
things. A `private` field can only be changed by methods you wrote, so if the
balance is ever wrong, the suspects are in one file. Losing that is what makes
a codebase of public fields miserable to change.

This lesson is the mechanics — fields, constructors, properties, static
members, access modifiers — but keep the idea in view, because lesson 04 and 05
are both about who gets to see what.

## Concept — an object is state plus its rules

The smallest useful class:

```csharp
public class Counter
{
    private int _count;                     // state: private, so it is ours

    public int Count => _count;             // a read-only view of it

    public void Increment() => _count++;    // the only way it ever changes
}
```

`new Counter()` makes an instance; each instance has its own `_count`. The
underscore prefix on private fields is a .NET convention, not a rule.

**Properties are methods that look like fields.** `public int Count => _count;`
compiles to a `get_Count()` method. That matters because you can change the
implementation later — validate, compute, log — without every caller having to
change. Which is why C# code exposes properties and not public fields, even
when the property does nothing but hand a field back.

The short forms, in increasing order of freedom:

```csharp
public string Name { get; }              // set only in the constructor
public string Name { get; init; }        // set in an object initialiser, then frozen
public int Balance { get; private set; } // anyone reads, only this class writes
public int Age { get => _age; set => _age = value; }  // your own logic; `value` is the incoming one
```

**Constructors put the object into a legal state.** They run once, they can
take arguments, and until one finishes there is no object:

```csharp
public class Account
{
    public Account(string owner)
    {
        Owner = owner;      // a get-only auto-property IS assignable here
    }

    public string Owner { get; }
}
```

If you write no constructor at all, C# gives you a parameterless one for free.
Write one and that gift disappears — which is how you make it impossible to
create an `Account` with no owner.

**Object initialisers and `init`.** For data-shaped types, an initialiser reads
better than a constructor with six arguments:

```csharp
var card = new LessonCard { Slug = "07_generics", Exercises = 4 };
```

`init` accessors allow exactly this and nothing after it: the property is
writable while the object is being built and read-only forever afterwards.
`required` (which `LessonCard.Slug` uses) makes the compiler insist the caller
supplies it, giving you a constructor's guarantee with an initialiser's syntax.

**Static means "belongs to the type".** A static field exists once, no matter
how many instances there are; a static method has no `this` and cannot touch
instance state. Shared counters, factory methods and `Math.Max` are static.
Nearly everything else should not be — static state is global state, with all
of global state's problems.

**Access modifiers** you need today: `public` (everyone), `private` (this type
only — the default for members), `internal` (this assembly). Start everything
`private` and open it only when something outside genuinely needs it.

## Exercise 1 — an object that protects an invariant

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Ex1.cs`. Finish the `Account` class:

The constructor takes an owner and leaves the balance at zero. `Deposit(amount)`
adds money, and throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for an amount of zero or
less. `Withdraw(amount)` takes money out and returns `true` — unless the balance
cannot cover it, in which case it changes **nothing** and returns `false`.

Notice the deliberate asymmetry: overdrawing is an ordinary thing customers do,
so it is a return value; depositing minus five pounds is a bug in the calling
code, so it is an exception. That distinction is lesson 12's whole subject, met
early.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — properties that compute

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Ex2.cs`. `LessonCard` already declares
three `init`-only properties. Implement the two computed members:

`TotalExercises` is the core count plus one when there is a challenge.

`Display` reads `"07_generics: 4 exercises + challenge"` — and
`"00_hello_dojo: 3 exercises"` when there is no challenge, and
`"23_transactions: 1 exercise + challenge"` for exactly one exercise. The
pluralisation rule is lesson 00's, again.

Neither member stores anything. They are read at the moment someone asks, from
data that cannot change after construction.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — one counter, many objects

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Ex3.cs`. `Robot.Built` is a static count of
how many have been made; `robot.Serial` is the number this particular robot got.
Implement the constructor so the first robot built is serial 1, and implement
`Reset()` so the counter goes back to zero — without disturbing the serials of
robots that already exist.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a property with a body

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Ex4.cs`. `Thermostat` keeps a private
`_celsius` field. Implement the `Celsius` property so reading hands the field
back and writing **clamps** into `Minimum..Maximum` (5 to 30) instead of
throwing — a physical dial cannot argue with you. Then implement `Fahrenheit`,
a get-only property computing `C × 9/5 + 32`, rounded to a whole degree.

Setting `Celsius = 100` and reading back `30` is the point: a property is a
method, and methods can have opinions.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects ex4
```

## Challenge — a class that owns a collection

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Challenge.cs`. `ShoppingCart` holds a
private `List<CartItem>`. Implement `Add` (which **merges** by product name
rather than appending a second line, and rejects a quantity of zero or less),
`Remove` (`true` if there was such a line), `ItemCount` (total units, not
lines), `Total`, and `Items`.

Honest difficulty note: `Items` is the interesting one and it is a trap.
Returning the private list as an `IReadOnlyList<CartItem>` compiles and looks
right — but the caller can cast it straight back to `List<CartItem>` and mutate
your internals, and the gate checks that they cannot. `List<T>.AsReadOnly()` is
the tool. `List<T>` itself is lesson 08's subject; `Add`, `Count`, indexing and
`RemoveAt` are all you need here.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is `Scoreboard` — a constructor, a static creation counter, a
`private set` property and one guard clause. `dojo review` schedules it.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/03_classes_objects

## Notes

**Why properties, when a public field is shorter?** Three reasons, in the order
they will bite you. First, binary compatibility: a property is a method call, so
changing `public int Count;` to `public int Count { get; set; }` later is a
*breaking change* for anything compiled against the old version, while changing
the body of a property is not. Second, interception: validation, lazy loading,
change notification and logging all need a method, and if there was never one
you cannot add it without touching every caller. Third, everything in .NET that
reflects over your objects — serialisers, data binding, ORMs like EF Core,
model binders in ASP.NET — looks for properties and ignores fields. The
convention is so strong that a public field in a code review reads as a
mistake, even when it would have worked.

**Auto-properties are a compiler trick.** `public int Count { get; private set; }`
generates a hidden backing field plus two tiny methods, which the JIT inlines
away, so the runtime cost is zero. That is why the idiomatic style is to start
with an auto-property and only write a full property body when you need one, as
ex4 did.

**Constructors, and the default you lose.** A class with no declared
constructor gets a public parameterless one. Declare any constructor and that
default disappears — deliberately, because "you must supply an owner" is
usually the rule you were trying to express. If you want both, declare both.
Constructor chaining with `: this(...)` lets one forward to another so the real
initialisation lives in one place.

**Static is global state wearing a namespace.** The `Robot.Built` counter in ex3
is shared by every robot in the process, which is exactly what the exercise
wanted and exactly what makes static state dangerous elsewhere: it is invisible
at the call site, it survives between tests (which is why the gate calls
`Reset()` first), and it is not thread-safe unless you make it so. The two
places static is unambiguously right: pure functions with no state at all
(`Math.Max`, your `Conversions` class from lesson 01), and constants.
Everything in between deserves a second look, and "I need one of these
globally" is usually dependency injection's job — the whole subject of the
.NET track's lesson 02.

**`readonly` versus `const`.** `const` is compile-time and baked into callers
(same versioning trap as optional arguments); `readonly` is assigned at
construction and fixed afterwards. `Thermostat.Minimum` is `const` because 5 is
5 forever. A `readonly` field is what you want for anything computed once per
object — `private readonly List<CartItem> _items = new();` in the challenge
means the *reference* cannot be repointed, though the list it points at is
still mutable. That distinction catches people: `readonly` protects the arrow,
not the object at the end of it.

## ex1

Two failures, two different mechanisms, and choosing between them is a genuine
design decision you will be asked to defend. The rule most teams use:
**exceptions are for situations the caller could not reasonably have
anticipated or handled**. An overdraft is anticipated — the caller is a cash
machine, and "insufficient funds" is a screen it already has. A negative
deposit is a programming error, and the loud failure is a service to whoever
wrote it.

The other half of ex1 is the ordering inside `Withdraw`. Checking before
mutating means the object is never observably in an illegal state. That matters
more than it looks: if a later version of this class raises an event, writes to
a log, or is read by another thread, "briefly negative" becomes "visibly
negative to someone". Getting into the habit of computing the new state, then
committing it, is what makes concurrent and transactional code possible later.

The interview follow-up here is usually "how would you make this thread-safe?"
The honest answer is that `Balance += amount` is three operations (read, add,
write) and two threads can interleave them; a `lock` around the mutation, or an
immutable design where every operation returns a new account, are the two
standard answers.

## ex2

`init` accessors solved a real problem. Before them you either wrote a
constructor with a long positional parameter list — where `new Card("07", 4, true)`
tells the reader nothing — or you used a settable property and gave up
immutability forever. `init` gives you the readable initialiser syntax *and*
the guarantee that nothing changes afterwards, and `required` restores the
constructor's other guarantee: that the caller cannot forget one.

Computed properties are the second idea. `TotalExercises` could have been a
field set by the constructor, and then it would be a second copy of the truth,
free to drift out of sync the moment anything changed. Deriving it means it
cannot be wrong. The trade is cost: a computed property runs its body on every
read, so a property that does real work (a database call, a sort of ten
thousand items) is a trap for callers who reasonably assume property access is
cheap. The convention: properties are for things that are cheap and
side-effect-free; anything else should be a method with a verb in its name.

## ex3

Instance state and static state in the same constructor is the clearest way to
see the difference. `Built++` reaches for one variable that the type owns;
`Serial = Built` writes into this object's own storage. Reset afterwards and
the shared number changes while every robot keeps what it was given, because
they were copies made at construction time, not live views.

Two production notes. First, this counter is a textbook race condition:
`Built++` reads, adds and writes, so two threads can both read 7 and both
become robot 8. `Interlocked.Increment(ref _built)` is the standard fix and the
standard interview answer. Second, static mutable state and tests are natural
enemies — your gate has to call `Reset()` first precisely because a previous
test could have left the counter anywhere. When a test needs to reset global
state, that is the design telling you something.

## ex4

The `value` keyword inside a setter is the incoming assignment, and the fact
that a property can *change* it on the way in is what makes properties more
than syntax sugar. Clamping was chosen over throwing to make the point that a
setter is a policy: this thermostat's policy is "I will do my best with what
you asked for". A different class might reject, log, or raise an event instead.

`Math.Clamp` exists so you do not write `Math.Max(low, Math.Min(high, value))`
and get the nesting backwards, which everybody does once.

`Fahrenheit` demonstrates the other half of the lesson: some state should never
be stored. If both `Celsius` and `Fahrenheit` had setters, someone would
eventually set one and not the other, and the object would hold two
contradictory truths. Derive the second from the first and that bug cannot be
written. The integer-division trap (`21 * 9 / 5` is 37, not 37.8) is the same
"where does the arithmetic happen" question as lesson 01 ex2, in new clothes.

## challenge

The `Items` trap is real and common. `IReadOnlyList<T>` documents an intention;
it does not enforce one, because the concrete `List<T>` you returned still
implements `IList<T>` and a determined caller can cast to it. Whether that
matters depends on the room — inside one team, the interface is a clear enough
signal; across a public API boundary, it is not. `AsReadOnly()` gives you the
enforcement for the price of one wrapper object.

The `Add` merge is the other lesson: **the class decides what its state means**.
Two lines for the same product is a representation the rest of the cart would
have to keep handling forever — `Total` would still work, `Remove` would only
remove one of them, and a UI would show the item twice. Normalising on the way
in, at the one place that can, is why `Add` is a method and not a public list.
The SQL analogy is exact: this is a unique constraint on the product name,
enforced by the only code that can insert.

A note on the `internal set` on `CartItem.Quantity`: it lets the cart update a
line it owns while keeping the setter out of the public API. `internal` means
"anything in this assembly", which is a blunter tool than you would like — it
is the pragmatic C# answer to a genuine gap in the language's access model.

## review1

Three of the lesson's ideas in one small class, and the one that decays fastest
is the ordering in the constructor plus the exact boundary of the guard. Zero
points is legal; minus one is not. If you guarded with `<= 0` and the gate told
you so, that is the review doing its job — boundary conditions are the most
forgettable part of any specification, which is why they are the most valuable
thing to write a test for.

Notice the `Reset()` at the top of the review gate, for the same reason as ex3.
When you see a test that has to reset something before it can run, you are
looking at shared mutable state, and you now know both why it is there and what
it costs.

## Further reading

- [Classes (C# programming guide)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/classes) — declaring, instantiating, and what reference semantics mean for objects.
- [Properties](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/properties) — auto-properties, `init`, expression-bodied accessors, and `value`.
- [Constructors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/constructors) — including chaining with `: this(...)` and the default you lose.
- [Static classes and static members](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/static-classes-and-static-class-members) — what static actually means and when it is appropriate.
- [Access modifiers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/access-modifiers) — the full table, including `protected internal` and `private protected`.
- [`required` members](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/required) — the compiler check behind `required string Slug`.

using CSharpDojo.L03_ClassesObjects;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L03_ClassesObjectsTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_AccountProtectsItsOwnBalance()
    {
        Account account = new Account("Ada");

                + "its parameter - reread README ex1.");

                + "constructor is where you say so out loud.");

        Teach.True(account.Withdraw(20m),
            "A withdrawal the balance can cover succeeds and returns true.");
        Teach.Equal(30m, account.Balance, "50 in, 20 out, 30 left.");

            "There is only 30 in the account, so this withdrawal must be refused - return false "
                + "rather than throwing - reread README ex1.");
        Teach.Equal(30m, account.Balance,
            "A refused withdrawal must change NOTHING. If the balance moved, you subtracted "
                + "before you checked - reread README ex1.");

            "A negative deposit is not an ordinary outcome, it is a caller bug: throw "
                + "ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Note the difference from the refused withdrawal, "
                + "which is an ordinary outcome - reread README ex1.");
    }

    {

            "Four core exercises plus one challenge is five - reread README ex2.");
        Teach.Equal("07_generics: 4 exercises + challenge", generics.Display,
            "Display reads its own properties; it stores nothing - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(3, hello.TotalExercises,
            "HasChallenge was never set in the object initialiser, so it is the default false, "

In plain English: `Ex1` builds an account, deposits, withdraws successfully,
withdraws too much and checks the balance did not move, then checks the
negative deposit throws. `Ex2` builds three cards with object initialisers and
reads the computed members. `Ex3` resets the counter, builds three robots, and
checks the shared count and the per-robot serials — then resets again to prove
instance state survives. `Ex4` reads the default, then writes out-of-range
values in both directions. `Challenge` walks a small shopping session including
the merge and the read-only check, and `Review1` is the spaced-repetition
variant.

## The teaching point

Every design decision in this lesson is the same decision in a different
costume: **who is allowed to change this, and when?** The constructor is "at
birth". `init` is "while it is being built". `private set` is "only by my own
methods". A get-only computed property is "never — it is derived". Reading a
class you have never seen before, those four answers tell you most of what the
author was worried about.

The invariant idea in ex1 is what senior code review looks for. A class whose
public surface makes an illegal state unreachable — no negative balance, no
account without an owner, no cart line with zero quantity — cannot be misused
by a colleague in a hurry. A class with public fields and a comment saying
"don't set this to null" will be, by Thursday.

Next: **04_inheritance_polymorphism**, where several classes agree to answer the
same question in different ways.
