# Reading - csharp/03_classes_objects

## Notes

**Why properties, when a public field is shorter?** Three reasons, in the order
they will bite you. First, binary compatibility: a property is a method call, so
changing `public int Count;` to `public int Count { get; set; }` later is a
*breaking change* for anything compiled against the old version, while changing
the body of a property is not. Second, interception: validation, lazy loading,
change notification and logging all need a method, and if there was never one
you cannot add it without touching every caller. Third, everything in .NET that
reflects over your objects — serialisers, data binding, ORMs like EF Core,
model binders in ASP.NET — looks for properties and ignores fields. The
convention is so strong that a public field in a code review reads as a
mistake, even when it would have worked.

**Auto-properties are a compiler trick.** `public int Count { get; private set; }`
generates a hidden backing field plus two tiny methods, which the JIT inlines
away, so the runtime cost is zero. That is why the idiomatic style is to start
with an auto-property and only write a full property body when you need one, as
ex4 did.

**Constructors, and the default you lose.** A class with no declared
constructor gets a public parameterless one. Declare any constructor and that
default disappears — deliberately, because "you must supply an owner" is
usually the rule you were trying to express. If you want both, declare both.
Constructor chaining with `: this(...)` lets one forward to another so the real
initialisation lives in one place.

**Static is global state wearing a namespace.** The `Robot.Built` counter in ex3
is shared by every robot in the process, which is exactly what the exercise
wanted and exactly what makes static state dangerous elsewhere: it is invisible
at the call site, it survives between tests (which is why the gate calls
`Reset()` first), and it is not thread-safe unless you make it so. The two
places static is unambiguously right: pure functions with no state at all
(`Math.Max`, your `Conversions` class from lesson 01), and constants.
Everything in between deserves a second look, and "I need one of these
globally" is usually dependency injection's job — the whole subject of the
.NET track's lesson 02.

**`readonly` versus `const`.** `const` is compile-time and baked into callers
(same versioning trap as optional arguments); `readonly` is assigned at
construction and fixed afterwards. `Thermostat.Minimum` is `const` because 5 is
5 forever. A `readonly` field is what you want for anything computed once per
object — `private readonly List<CartItem> _items = new();` in the challenge
means the *reference* cannot be repointed, though the list it points at is
still mutable. That distinction catches people: `readonly` protects the arrow,
not the object at the end of it.

## ex1

Two failures, two different mechanisms, and choosing between them is a genuine
design decision you will be asked to defend. The rule most teams use:
**exceptions are for situations the caller could not reasonably have
anticipated or handled**. An overdraft is anticipated — the caller is a cash
machine, and "insufficient funds" is a screen it already has. A negative
deposit is a programming error, and the loud failure is a service to whoever
wrote it.

The other half of ex1 is the ordering inside `Withdraw`. Checking before
mutating means the object is never observably in an illegal state. That matters
more than it looks: if a later version of this class raises an event, writes to
a log, or is read by another thread, "briefly negative" becomes "visibly
negative to someone". Getting into the habit of computing the new state, then
committing it, is what makes concurrent and transactional code possible later.

The interview follow-up here is usually "how would you make this thread-safe?"
The honest answer is that `Balance += amount` is three operations (read, add,
write) and two threads can interleave them; a `lock` around the mutation, or an
immutable design where every operation returns a new account, are the two
standard answers.

## ex2

`init` accessors solved a real problem. Before them you either wrote a
constructor with a long positional parameter list — where `new Card("07", 4, true)`
tells the reader nothing — or you used a settable property and gave up
immutability forever. `init` gives you the readable initialiser syntax *and*
the guarantee that nothing changes afterwards, and `required` restores the
constructor's other guarantee: that the caller cannot forget one.

Computed properties are the second idea. `TotalExercises` could have been a
field set by the constructor, and then it would be a second copy of the truth,
free to drift out of sync the moment anything changed. Deriving it means it
cannot be wrong. The trade is cost: a computed property runs its body on every
read, so a property that does real work (a database call, a sort of ten
thousand items) is a trap for callers who reasonably assume property access is
cheap. The convention: properties are for things that are cheap and
side-effect-free; anything else should be a method with a verb in its name.

## ex3

Instance state and static state in the same constructor is the clearest way to
see the difference. `Built++` reaches for one variable that the type owns;
`Serial = Built` writes into this object's own storage. Reset afterwards and
the shared number changes while every robot keeps what it was given, because
they were copies made at construction time, not live views.

Two production notes. First, this counter is a textbook race condition:
`Built++` reads, adds and writes, so two threads can both read 7 and both
become robot 8. `Interlocked.Increment(ref _built)` is the standard fix and the
standard interview answer. Second, static mutable state and tests are natural
enemies — your gate has to call `Reset()` first precisely because a previous
test could have left the counter anywhere. When a test needs to reset global
state, that is the design telling you something.

## ex4

The `value` keyword inside a setter is the incoming assignment, and the fact
that a property can *change* it on the way in is what makes properties more
than syntax sugar. Clamping was chosen over throwing to make the point that a
setter is a policy: this thermostat's policy is "I will do my best with what
you asked for". A different class might reject, log, or raise an event instead.

`Math.Clamp` exists so you do not write `Math.Max(low, Math.Min(high, value))`
and get the nesting backwards, which everybody does once.

`Fahrenheit` demonstrates the other half of the lesson: some state should never
be stored. If both `Celsius` and `Fahrenheit` had setters, someone would
eventually set one and not the other, and the object would hold two
contradictory truths. Derive the second from the first and that bug cannot be
written. The integer-division trap (`21 * 9 / 5` is 37, not 37.8) is the same
"where does the arithmetic happen" question as lesson 01 ex2, in new clothes.

## challenge

The `Items` trap is real and common. `IReadOnlyList<T>` documents an intention;
it does not enforce one, because the concrete `List<T>` you returned still
implements `IList<T>` and a determined caller can cast to it. Whether that
matters depends on the room — inside one team, the interface is a clear enough
signal; across a public API boundary, it is not. `AsReadOnly()` gives you the
enforcement for the price of one wrapper object.

The `Add` merge is the other lesson: **the class decides what its state means**.
Two lines for the same product is a representation the rest of the cart would
have to keep handling forever — `Total` would still work, `Remove` would only
remove one of them, and a UI would show the item twice. Normalising on the way
in, at the one place that can, is why `Add` is a method and not a public list.
The SQL analogy is exact: this is a unique constraint on the product name,
enforced by the only code that can insert.

A note on the `internal set` on `CartItem.Quantity`: it lets the cart update a
line it owns while keeping the setter out of the public API. `internal` means
"anything in this assembly", which is a blunter tool than you would like — it
is the pragmatic C# answer to a genuine gap in the language's access model.

## review1

## Challenge — a class that owns a collection

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Challenge.cs`. `ShoppingCart` holds a
private `List<CartItem>`. Implement `Add` (which **merges** by product name
rather than appending a second line, and rejects a quantity of zero or less),
`Remove` (`true` if there was such a line), `ItemCount` (total units, not
lines), `Total`, and `Items`.

Honest difficulty note: `Items` is the interesting one and it is a trap.
Returning the private list as an `IReadOnlyList<CartItem>` compiles and looks
right — but the caller can cast it straight back to `List<CartItem>` and mutate
your internals, and the gate checks that they cannot. `List<T>.AsReadOnly()` is
the tool. `List<T>` itself is lesson 08's subject; `Add`, `Count`, indexing and
`RemoveAt` are all you need here.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The cart owns a `List<CartItem>` and nobody else is allowed to touch it. Every
member you write is either a question about that list (`Items`, `ItemCount`,
`Total`) or a controlled change to it (`Add`, `Remove`).

`ItemCount` and `Total` are both a loop that accumulates. `Add` is a search
followed by either an update or an append.

## Hint 2

A `List<T>` is a growable array: `.Add(item)`, `.Count`, `_items[i]`,
`.RemoveAt(i)`. Lesson 08 covers the family properly; that much is enough here.

For the merge in `Add`, walk the existing items looking for one with the same
`Name`. If you find it, add to its `Quantity` and return immediately — the
early return is what stops you also appending a duplicate.

`Remove` needs the index to remove at, so a `for` loop reads better than a
`foreach` here. Removing from a list while a `foreach` is walking it throws.

## Hint 3

The subtle one is `Items`. Returning `_items` directly compiles and passes a
naive test — but `IReadOnlyList<CartItem>` is an *interface* the private
`List<CartItem>` happens to implement, so a caller can write
`((List<CartItem>)cart.Items).Clear()` and gut your cart. The gate checks for
exactly that.

`List<T>.AsReadOnly()` returns a `ReadOnlyCollection<T>` that wraps the list
without copying it: reads pass through, writes do not exist. Note it is a
*wrapper*, not a snapshot — later `Add` calls are visible through it, which is
what you want here and worth knowing when it isn't.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The cart owns a `List<CartItem>` and nobody else is allowed to touch it. Every
member you write is either a question about that list (`Items`, `ItemCount`,
`Total`) or a controlled change to it (`Add`, `Remove`).

`ItemCount` and `Total` are both a loop that accumulates. `Add` is a search
followed by either an update or an append.

## Hint 2

A `List<T>` is a growable array: `.Add(item)`, `.Count`, `_items[i]`,
`.RemoveAt(i)`. Lesson 08 covers the family properly; that much is enough here.

For the merge in `Add`, walk the existing items looking for one with the same
`Name`. If you find it, add to its `Quantity` and return immediately — the
early return is what stops you also appending a duplicate.

`Remove` needs the index to remove at, so a `for` loop reads better than a
`foreach` here. Removing from a list while a `foreach` is walking it throws.

## Hint 3

The subtle one is `Items`. Returning `_items` directly compiles and passes a
naive test — but `IReadOnlyList<CartItem>` is an *interface* the private
`List<CartItem>` happens to implement, so a caller can write
`((List<CartItem>)cart.Items).Clear()` and gut your cart. The gate checks for
exactly that.

`List<T>.AsReadOnly()` returns a `ReadOnlyCollection<T>` that wraps the list
without copying it: reads pass through, writes do not exist. Note it is a
*wrapper*, not a snapshot — later `Add` calls are visible through it, which is
what you want here and worth knowing when it isn't.

## Exercise 1 — an object that protects an invariant

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Ex1.cs`. Finish the `Account` class:

The constructor takes an owner and leaves the balance at zero. `Deposit(amount)`
adds money, and throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for an amount of zero or
less. `Withdraw(amount)` takes money out and returns `true` — unless the balance
cannot cover it, in which case it changes **nothing** and returns `false`.

Notice the deliberate asymmetry: overdrawing is an ordinary thing customers do,
so it is a return value; depositing minus five pounds is a bug in the calling
code, so it is an exception. That distinction is lesson 12's whole subject, met
early.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three bodies to fill in, and the interesting one is `Withdraw`, because it has
to decide *before* it acts. Write it in that order: check, then change.

Notice the two different failure styles the prompt asks for. Not enough money
is an ordinary thing that happens to real accounts, so it is a return value.
A negative deposit is a bug in the calling code, so it is an exception.

## Hint 2

The constructor's job is to leave the object in a state where every other
method can assume things. Assign `Owner` from the parameter — a get-only
auto-property is assignable *inside the constructor*, which is exactly why that
form exists.

`Balance` has a `private set`, so `Balance += amount;` works inside the class
and `account.Balance = 100m;` does not compile outside it. That asymmetry is
the whole point of the exercise.

For the guards, copy the shape from lesson 02 ex4:

```csharp
if (amount <= 0m)
{
    throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(amount), amount, "...");
}
```

## Hint 3

`Withdraw` is:

```csharp
// guard against a non-positive amount, as Deposit does
if (amount > Balance)
{
    return false;      // and nothing else has happened yet
}
// take the money and report success
```

The ordering is the lesson. If you subtract first and check afterwards, there
is a moment where the balance is negative — and in real systems something else
reads it in exactly that moment. Decide what the invariant is ("balance is
never negative") and never let the object exist outside it.

```csharp
public string Display
```

## Exercise 3 — one counter, many objects

Edit `src/Lessons/L03_ClassesObjects/Ex3.cs`. `Robot.Built` is a static count of
how many have been made; `robot.Serial` is the number this particular robot got.
Implement the constructor so the first robot built is serial 1, and implement
`Reset()` so the counter goes back to zero — without disturbing the serials of
robots that already exist.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 03_classes_objects ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are exactly two pieces of state here and they live in different places.
`Built` belongs to the *type* — one of it, no matter how many robots exist.
`Serial` belongs to each *object* — one per robot, fixed for life.

The constructor is where the two meet: it changes the shared one and reads the
result into the private one.

## Hint 2

Order matters. The first robot must get serial 1, not 0, so increment the
shared counter *before* you read it into `Serial`.

`Serial` is declared `{ get; }` with no setter, which means only the
constructor may assign it — that is the compiler enforcing "fixed for life".

`Reset` is `static`, so it has no `this` and cannot touch any robot's `Serial`.
That is not a limitation to work around; it is the correct behaviour, and the
gate checks it.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public Robot()
{
    Built++;
    // now Serial gets the number you just produced
}
```

`Built` has a `private set`, so the increment compiles inside the class and
`Robot.Built = 0;` from a test would not. `Reset` is one assignment.

Worth pausing on before you move to ex4: this shared counter is not
thread-safe. Two threads calling `new Robot()` at the same moment can both read the
same value. `Interlocked.Increment` is the fix, and lesson 13 is where that
conversation belongs.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There are exactly two pieces of state here and they live in different places.
`Built` belongs to the *type* — one of it, no matter how many robots exist.
`Serial` belongs to each *object* — one per robot, fixed for life.

The constructor is where the two meet: it changes the shared one and reads the
result into the private one.

## Hint 2

Order matters. The first robot must get serial 1, not 0, so increment the
shared counter *before* you read it into `Serial`.

`Serial` is declared `{ get; }` with no setter, which means only the
constructor may assign it — that is the compiler enforcing "fixed for life".

`Reset` is `static`, so it has no `this` and cannot touch any robot's `Serial`.
That is not a limitation to work around; it is the correct behaviour, and the
gate checks it.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public Robot()
{
    Built++;
    // now Serial gets the number you just produced
}
```

`Built` has a `private set`, so the increment compiles inside the class and
`Robot.Built = 0;` from a test would not. `Reset` is one assignment.

Worth pausing on before you move to ex4: this shared counter is not
thread-safe. Two threads calling `new Robot()` at the same moment can both read the
same value. `Interlocked.Increment` is the fix, and lesson 13 is where that
conversation belongs.

# 04 — Inheritance and polymorphism

Lesson 03 gave you objects that own their state. This one gives you objects
that can *stand in for each other*. A method that takes a `Shape` will happily
be handed a `Circle`, call `Area()` on it, and get the circle's answer — without
the method containing the word "circle" anywhere. That substitution is
polymorphism, and it is the mechanism behind almost every extensible design in
.NET: the logging framework that accepts your custom logger, the test runner
that finds your test class, the middleware pipeline in ASP.NET Core.

Inheritance is one way to get there and it is the one with the worst
reputation, deservedly. Deep hierarchies — `Animal -> Mammal -> Dog -> Poodle` —
are the standard textbook example and a standard production mistake, because
every subclass inherits every decision the base made, forever. The rule most
teams settle on is "inherit for *is-a* plus shared implementation, compose for
everything else", and lesson 05 gives you the composition half.

So learn this properly, then be sparing with it. Two levels deep is usually
plenty.

## Concept — one word to the base, one word to the derived

```csharp
public abstract class Shape          // cannot be instantiated
{
    public abstract double Area();   // no body: subclasses must supply one
    public virtual string Unit() => "cm2";  // has a body: subclasses may replace it
}

public class Square : Shape
{
    public Square(double side) { Side = side; }
    public double Side { get; }
    public override double Area() => Side * Side;
}
```

Four keywords carry the whole feature:

- **`abstract`** on a class means "you cannot make one of these"; on a member it
  means "there is no sensible default, so every concrete subclass must supply
  one". The compiler enforces both.
- **`virtual`** means "here is a default, and a subclass may replace it".
- **`override`** is how the subclass replaces it, and it is required — C# will
  not let you silently override by accident, which is a deliberate difference
  from Java.
- **`sealed`** on a class means "no further derivation"; on a member, "this
  override is the last one".

**`base`** does two jobs. `: base(args)` in a constructor hands work to the base
class's constructor, which runs *first*, so the state the base owns is
initialised before your body runs. And `base.Method()` calls the implementation
you just overrode, which is how a subclass adds to behaviour rather than
replacing it:

```csharp
public override decimal Pay() => base.Pay() + Bonus;
```

**Virtual dispatch, in one sentence.** When you call a virtual member, the
runtime looks at what the object *is*, not at what the variable was declared
as. That is why this prints the circle's area:

```csharp
Shape s = new Circle(2);
s.Area();          // Circle.Area, every time
```

**And its evil twin, `new`.** You can declare a method that merely *hides* one
of the same name in the base class:

```csharp
public class Sneaky : Duck
{
    public new string Speak() => "shh";   // NOT an override
}
```

Now the answer depends on the type of the *variable*, not the object: a
`Duck`-typed variable gets `Duck.Speak`, a `Sneaky`-typed variable gets
`Sneaky.Speak`. One object, two answers. This is almost never what you want —
it exists so that a base class adding a method cannot break a derived class
that already had one — and it is asked about in interviews constantly, because
knowing the difference proves you understand what `virtual` actually does.

## Exercise 1 — an abstract base and two formulas

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex1.cs`. `Shape` is abstract and
declares `Area()` with no body. Implement `Rectangle.Area()` and
`Circle.Area()` — width × height, and pi r² using `Math.PI`.

Look at what is already written while you are there: both subclasses call
`: base("rectangle")` / `: base("circle")`, so the `Name` property lives in one
place and each subclass supplies its own word.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — adding to inherited behaviour

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex2.cs`. `Employee.MonthlyPay()`
is one twelfth of the annual salary, rounded to the cent, halves away from
zero. `Manager.MonthlyPay()` is that, plus the manager's flat monthly bonus —
and it must **call** the base version rather than repeating the division.

The gate then assigns the manager to an `Employee`-typed variable and calls
`MonthlyPay()` again. Predict what you will get before you run it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — `override` versus `new`

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex3.cs`. `Duck.Speak()` is
`virtual` and says `"quack"`. Two subclasses are waiting, each missing a
modifier:

`LoudDuck` must **override**, returning `"QUACK"`, so every caller hears it.

`SneakyDuck` must **hide** with `new`, returning `"shh"`, so only a caller
holding a `SneakyDuck`-typed reference hears it — a `Duck`-typed variable still
gets `"quack"`.

Add the right keyword to each and fill in the bodies. The compiler is already
warning you about both methods; read those warnings, one of them names the
keyword it thinks you meant.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — one loop, every kind

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`EmailNotification.Render()` -> `"email to ada@example.com: Welcome"` and
`SmsNotification.Render()` -> `"sms to 07700900123: Your code is 1234"`, then
`Notifier.RenderAll(...)`, which renders every notification in order and joins
them with `" | "`. An empty sequence renders as `""`.

`RenderAll` must contain no type checks at all — no `is`, no `switch` on type,
no casting. If you find yourself asking "what kind is this?", the abstract
method already answered.

One more thing: `SmsNotification` is meant to be the end of its line. Add the
modifier that makes deriving from it a compile error.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex4
```

## Challenge — the template method

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Challenge.cs`. `Report.Render()`
defines the fixed skeleton — a header line, a body, a footer, joined by `"\n"`:

```
== Sales ==
3 sales totalling 60
-- 3 rows --
```

`Render` itself is not virtual: subclasses fill in the parts and never
rearrange the whole. Implement `Render`, then `SalesReport.Body()` (count and
total, with "sale"/"sales" pluralised) and `SalesReport.Footer()`, then
`EmptyReport.Body()` -> `"(no data)"`.

Honest difficulty note: the code is short; the design is the difficulty.
Notice that `EmptyReport` deliberately does not override `Footer()` and gets
`"-- end --"` from the base — the difference between `abstract` (you must) and
`virtual` (you may) in one working example. This shape has a name, the
*template method pattern*, and you have already used it: this is how every
ASP.NET Core `ControllerBase` and every xUnit fixture works.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is `Vehicle` / `Car` / `Motorbike`: one abstract property everyone
must answer, one virtual method most can ignore, and a `Describe()` written in
the base class that calls both. `dojo review` will bring it back.

# Reading - csharp/04_inheritance_polymorphism

## Notes

**How virtual dispatch actually works.** Every object on the .NET heap carries a
pointer to its type's *method table*. A non-virtual call is compiled to "call
this exact address"; a virtual call is compiled to "look in the object's method
table at slot 4 and call whatever is there". A subclass that overrides a method
puts its own implementation in that slot, so the same call site reaches
different code depending on what it is holding. That one indirection is the
entire mechanism, and it is why `override` costs a pointer hop and `sealed`
sometimes lets the JIT skip it (it can prove there is only one candidate and
inline the call).

**Construction order is base-first.** When you write `new Manager(...)`, the
base constructor body runs before the derived constructor body. Field
initialisers, though, run in the *other* order: a derived class's field
initialisers run before the base constructor. The practical consequence is the
one bug everyone hits once: **never call a virtual method from a constructor.**
The base constructor runs while the derived object is only half-built, and a
virtual call from there lands in the derived override, which then reads fields
that have not been assigned yet. C# will not stop you; a static analyser will
warn you.

**Single inheritance, many interfaces.** A C# class has exactly one base class.
That is a deliberate restriction — multiple inheritance of *implementation*
creates the diamond problem, where two bases both define `Save()` and nobody
can say which one wins. Interfaces (lesson 05) have no implementation to
conflict, so you may have as many as you like. This is the structural reason
that "favour composition over inheritance" is not just style advice: you get
one inheritance slot, so spend it carefully.

**`sealed`, honestly.** It communicates intent ("this is not an extension
point") and occasionally helps the JIT devirtualise a call. It also stops
people mocking your class in tests, which is the usual reason a team regrets
sealing something. The .NET guideline is to seal by default *in libraries you
version publicly*, because unsealing later is easy and sealing later is a
breaking change. In application code, most teams do not bother.

**Where inheritance goes wrong.** The classic failure is inheriting for code
reuse rather than for substitutability. If `Square : Rectangle` and rectangles
have independent `Width` and `Height` setters, then a method that sets width
and expects height to stay put is now broken by every square — the
Liskov substitution principle, in its original example. When the base's
contract does not honestly hold for the derived type, you wanted composition:
hold a rectangle in a field, expose the two members that make sense, and be
free of the rest.

## ex1

`abstract` is the compiler enforcing a design decision. `Shape` has no area
because "a shape" has no formula, and making `Area()` abstract means the
question is answered exactly once per concrete type, never forgotten, never
defaulted to something meaningless like zero. Delete one override and the build
fails with a message naming the member you did not implement — a genuinely
useful failure, at compile time, in the file that is wrong.

The base constructor doing the `Name` assignment is worth noticing separately.
Shared *state* in the base plus abstract *behaviour* in the subclasses is the
shape most healthy hierarchies take. When the base has no state at all and only
abstract members, you have discovered an interface — which is lesson 05.

For the record: comparing `double`s with `==` is normally a mistake, because
0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. The gate gets away with `12.0` because 3 × 4 is exact in
binary, and rounds the circle's area to four places precisely because pi r² is
not. When you write your own tests over floating point, compare with a
tolerance.

## ex2

`base.MonthlyPay()` is the difference between *extending* behaviour and
*replacing* it, and choosing extension keeps the salary formula in one place.
Copy the division into the override instead and you have created the bug that
appears six months later, when payroll changes to thirteen payments a year and
managers keep getting twelve.

Omit the `base.` and you get infinite recursion, because `MonthlyPay()` inside
`Manager.MonthlyPay` resolves to the method you are inside. The
`StackOverflowException` that results cannot be caught in .NET — the process
dies immediately — which makes it one of the more memorable mistakes available
to you.

The final assertion is the payoff: `Employee asEmployee = manager;` then
`asEmployee.MonthlyPay()` gives 5500. Upcasting changes what the *compiler*
lets you call; it changes nothing about what the object *is*. Every framework
that hands you back a base type — `object`, `Exception`, `IEnumerable<T>` —
relies on this.

## ex3

This is the single most-asked C# inheritance question in interviews, and the
answer worth memorising is one sentence: **`override` is resolved by the
runtime type of the object; `new` is resolved by the compile-time type of the
variable.**

The reason `new` exists at all is versioning. Suppose you write
`class MyList : SomeLibraryList` with a `Sort()` method. Version 2 of the
library adds its own virtual `Sort()`. Without `new`, your method would suddenly
become an override of something you have never seen, and might be called by
library code expecting different semantics. C# makes you say which you meant,
and warns when you say nothing.

In application code, hiding is almost always a bug. The tell is exactly what
the gate demonstrates: the same object gives two different answers depending on
how the caller happened to be holding it, which means behaviour depends on a
detail no one thinks about. If you ever *need* hiding, that is usually a sign
the two methods should have different names.

## ex4

`RenderAll` is the argument for polymorphism in six lines. The alternative —
`if (n is EmailNotification e) ... else if (n is SmsNotification s) ...` —
works, and then someone adds a push notification and the compiler says nothing,
because the `if` chain is still valid code. It just silently does not handle
the new case. Virtual dispatch makes "handle every kind" the compiler's problem
rather than yours.

`IEnumerable<Notification>` as the parameter type is the other habit worth
copying: take the least specific type you can actually use. A method that only
foreaches has no business demanding a `List<T>`, and demanding one means
callers with an array or a LINQ query have to materialise a copy for you.
Lesson 08 covers the interface hierarchy this sits in.

`typeof(SmsNotification).IsSealed` is the gate reaching for reflection, because
a modifier is not observable any other way at runtime. Reflection is how test
frameworks, serialisers and dependency-injection containers work, and seeing it
used once here is enough for now — `07_generics` and the .NET track use it
again.

## challenge

The template method pattern inverts who is in charge. Normally your code calls
the library's; here the base class calls *yours*, at the moments it chooses.
That inversion is the whole point of a framework, and once you recognise it you
will see it everywhere: `ControllerBase` calls your action, xUnit constructs
your test class and calls your `[Fact]`, `BackgroundService` calls your
`ExecuteAsync`.

Making `Render` non-virtual is a real design decision. It says: the *shape* of
a report — header, body, footer, in that order — is not up for negotiation, and
only the content varies. If a subclass could override `Render`, it could omit
the footer, and then "every report has a footer" stops being true and every
consumer needs a null check.

The `abstract` versus `virtual` contrast between `Body()` and `Footer()` is the
other half. `Body()` is abstract because there is no such thing as a default
report body; `Footer()` is virtual because `"-- end --"` is a perfectly good
answer for most reports. Choosing between them per member, rather than making
everything virtual "just in case", is what keeps a base class honest.

## review1

The abstract *property* is the wrinkle here. Properties can be abstract or
virtual exactly like methods — `public abstract int Wheels { get; }` says every
vehicle must be able to answer, and `public override int Wheels => 4;` answers
with an expression body. There is no field anywhere, which is the point: an
abstract property is a question, not storage.

`Describe()` in the base class is the ex4 idea in miniature. It was written
once, it never changed, and it printed "brap" for the motorbike — because the
call to `Sound()` inside it is virtual and the object decided. Code you wrote
before a subclass existed calls into that subclass correctly. That is the
sentence to keep from this whole lesson.

## Further reading

- [Inheritance in C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/object-oriented/inheritance) — the base/derived relationship, with construction order spelled out.
- [Polymorphism](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/object-oriented/polymorphism) — including the `new` versus `override` section, which is worth reading twice.
- [Abstract and sealed classes and class members](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/abstract-and-sealed-classes-and-class-members) — when each modifier is appropriate.
- [`base` keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/base) — calling base constructors and base implementations.
- [Knowing when to use `override` and `new`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/knowing-when-to-use-override-and-new-keywords) — Microsoft's own worked comparison, with output.

# 04 — Inheritance and polymorphism

Lesson 03 gave you objects that own their state. This one gives you objects
that can *stand in for each other*. A method that takes a `Shape` will happily
be handed a `Circle`, call `Area()` on it, and get the circle's answer — without
the method containing the word "circle" anywhere. That substitution is
polymorphism, and it is the mechanism behind almost every extensible design in
.NET: the logging framework that accepts your custom logger, the test runner
that finds your test class, the middleware pipeline in ASP.NET Core.

Inheritance is one way to get there and it is the one with the worst
reputation, deservedly. Deep hierarchies — `Animal -> Mammal -> Dog -> Poodle` —
are the standard textbook example and a standard production mistake, because
every subclass inherits every decision the base made, forever. The rule most
teams settle on is "inherit for *is-a* plus shared implementation, compose for
everything else", and lesson 05 gives you the composition half.

So learn this properly, then be sparing with it. Two levels deep is usually
plenty.

## Concept — one word to the base, one word to the derived

```csharp
public abstract class Shape          // cannot be instantiated
{
    public abstract double Area();   // no body: subclasses must supply one
    public virtual string Unit() => "cm2";  // has a body: subclasses may replace it
}

public class Square : Shape
{
    public Square(double side) { Side = side; }
    public double Side { get; }
    public override double Area() => Side * Side;
}
```

Four keywords carry the whole feature:

- **`abstract`** on a class means "you cannot make one of these"; on a member it
  means "there is no sensible default, so every concrete subclass must supply
  one". The compiler enforces both.
- **`virtual`** means "here is a default, and a subclass may replace it".
- **`override`** is how the subclass replaces it, and it is required — C# will
  not let you silently override by accident, which is a deliberate difference
  from Java.
- **`sealed`** on a class means "no further derivation"; on a member, "this
  override is the last one".

**`base`** does two jobs. `: base(args)` in a constructor hands work to the base
class's constructor, which runs *first*, so the state the base owns is
initialised before your body runs. And `base.Method()` calls the implementation
you just overrode, which is how a subclass adds to behaviour rather than
replacing it:

```csharp
public override decimal Pay() => base.Pay() + Bonus;
```

**Virtual dispatch, in one sentence.** When you call a virtual member, the
runtime looks at what the object *is*, not at what the variable was declared
as. That is why this prints the circle's area:

```csharp
Shape s = new Circle(2);
s.Area();          // Circle.Area, every time
```

**And its evil twin, `new`.** You can declare a method that merely *hides* one
of the same name in the base class:

```csharp
public class Sneaky : Duck
{
    public new string Speak() => "shh";   // NOT an override
}
```

Now the answer depends on the type of the *variable*, not the object: a
`Duck`-typed variable gets `Duck.Speak`, a `Sneaky`-typed variable gets
`Sneaky.Speak`. One object, two answers. This is almost never what you want —
it exists so that a base class adding a method cannot break a derived class
that already had one — and it is asked about in interviews constantly, because
knowing the difference proves you understand what `virtual` actually does.

## Exercise 1 — an abstract base and two formulas

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex1.cs`. `Shape` is abstract and
declares `Area()` with no body. Implement `Rectangle.Area()` and
`Circle.Area()` — width × height, and pi r² using `Math.PI`.

Look at what is already written while you are there: both subclasses call
`: base("rectangle")` / `: base("circle")`, so the `Name` property lives in one
place and each subclass supplies its own word.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — adding to inherited behaviour

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex2.cs`. `Employee.MonthlyPay()`
is one twelfth of the annual salary, rounded to the cent, halves away from
zero. `Manager.MonthlyPay()` is that, plus the manager's flat monthly bonus —
and it must **call** the base version rather than repeating the division.

The gate then assigns the manager to an `Employee`-typed variable and calls
`MonthlyPay()` again. Predict what you will get before you run it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — `override` versus `new`

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex3.cs`. `Duck.Speak()` is
`virtual` and says `"quack"`. Two subclasses are waiting, each missing a
modifier:

`LoudDuck` must **override**, returning `"QUACK"`, so every caller hears it.

`SneakyDuck` must **hide** with `new`, returning `"shh"`, so only a caller
holding a `SneakyDuck`-typed reference hears it — a `Duck`-typed variable still
gets `"quack"`.

Add the right keyword to each and fill in the bodies. The compiler is already
warning you about both methods; read those warnings, one of them names the
keyword it thinks you meant.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — one loop, every kind

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`EmailNotification.Render()` -> `"email to ada@example.com: Welcome"` and
`SmsNotification.Render()` -> `"sms to 07700900123: Your code is 1234"`, then
`Notifier.RenderAll(...)`, which renders every notification in order and joins
them with `" | "`. An empty sequence renders as `""`.

`RenderAll` must contain no type checks at all — no `is`, no `switch` on type,
no casting. If you find yourself asking "what kind is this?", the abstract
method already answered.

One more thing: `SmsNotification` is meant to be the end of its line. Add the
modifier that makes deriving from it a compile error.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex4
```

## Challenge — the template method

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Challenge.cs`. `Report.Render()`
defines the fixed skeleton — a header line, a body, a footer, joined by `"\n"`:

```
== Sales ==
3 sales totalling 60
-- 3 rows --
```

`Render` itself is not virtual: subclasses fill in the parts and never
rearrange the whole. Implement `Render`, then `SalesReport.Body()` (count and
total, with "sale"/"sales" pluralised) and `SalesReport.Footer()`, then
`EmptyReport.Body()` -> `"(no data)"`.

Honest difficulty note: the code is short; the design is the difficulty.
Notice that `EmptyReport` deliberately does not override `Footer()` and gets
`"-- end --"` from the base — the difference between `abstract` (you must) and
`virtual` (you may) in one working example. This shape has a name, the
*template method pattern*, and you have already used it: this is how every
ASP.NET Core `ControllerBase` and every xUnit fixture works.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is `Vehicle` / `Car` / `Motorbike`: one abstract property everyone
must answer, one virtual method most can ignore, and a `Describe()` written in
the base class that calls both. `dojo review` will bring it back.

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L04_InheritancePolymorphismTests.cs`:

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L04_InheritancePolymorphism;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L04_InheritancePolymorphismTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_EachShapeKnowsItsOwnArea()
    {
        Shape rectangle = new Rectangle(3, 4);
        Shape circle = new Circle(2);

        Teach.Equal(12.0, rectangle.Area(),
            "A 3 x 4 rectangle has area 12 - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal(12.5664, Math.Round(circle.Area(), 4),
            "A circle of radius 2 has area pi x 2 x 2 = 12.5664. Use Math.PI rather than a "
                + "typed-out 3.14 - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("rectangle", rectangle.Name,
            "Name comes from the base constructor, which each subclass calls with its own "
                + "word. The base class holds the state every shape shares.");

        Teach.Equal(24.0, new Rectangle(6, 4).Area(),
            "The formula reads the instance's own Width and Height, so a different rectangle "
                + "gives a different answer.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_ManagerReusesTheBaseCalculation()
    {
        Employee employee = new Employee("Ada", 60000m);
        Manager manager = new Manager("Grace", 60000m, 500m);

        Teach.Equal(5000m, employee.MonthlyPay(),
            "60000 a year is 5000 a month - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(5500m, manager.MonthlyPay(),
            "A manager earns the ordinary monthly pay plus the bonus. Call base.MonthlyPay() "
                + "rather than repeating the division - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal("Grace", manager.Name,
            "Name is stored once, by the base constructor. If you added another Name field to "
                + "Manager you now have two, and they will disagree one day.");

        Employee asEmployee = manager;
        Teach.Equal(5500m, asEmployee.MonthlyPay(),
            "This is the whole point of virtual: the variable's type is Employee, but the "
                + "OBJECT is a Manager, and the object decides - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(4166.67m, new Employee("Bo", 50000m).MonthlyPay(),
            "50000 / 12 is 4166.666..., which rounds to 4166.67. Round to the cent, away from "
                + "zero.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_OverrideAndNewAreResolvedByDifferentThings()
    {
        Duck loud = new LoudDuck();
        Teach.Equal("QUACK", loud.Speak(),
            "LoudDuck OVERRIDES Speak, so a Duck-typed variable holding a LoudDuck still gets "
                + "the loud version: the runtime type decides - reread README ex3.");

        Duck sneaky = new SneakyDuck();
        Teach.Equal("quack", sneaky.Speak(),
            "SneakyDuck HIDES Speak with `new`, so a Duck-typed variable gets Duck's version. "
                + "The compiler decided this at compile time from the variable's type - "
                + "reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("shh", ((SneakyDuck)sneaky).Speak(),
            "Cast the same object to SneakyDuck and the hidden method appears. One object, "
                + "two answers, depending only on how you were holding it. That is why `new` "
                + "is almost never what you want.");

        Teach.Equal("QUACK", ((LoudDuck)loud).Speak(),
            "An overridden method gives the same answer through either type - which is the "
                + "difference in one line.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_OneLoopRendersEveryKind()
    {
        List<Notification> outbox = new List<Notification>
        {
            new EmailNotification("ada@example.com", "Welcome"),
            new SmsNotification("07700900123", "Your code is 1234"),
            new EmailNotification("bo@example.com", "Receipt"),
        };

        Teach.Equal(
            "email to ada@example.com: Welcome | sms to 07700900123: Your code is 1234 | "
                + "email to bo@example.com: Receipt",
            Notifier.RenderAll(outbox),
            "RenderAll should call Render() on each item and join with \" | \". If you wrote "
                + "an `if (n is EmailNotification)` you have re-implemented what virtual "
                + "dispatch does for free - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal("", Notifier.RenderAll(new List<Notification>()),
            "Nothing to render is an empty string, not a crash - string.Join handles it.");

        Teach.True(typeof(SmsNotification).IsSealed,
            "SmsNotification is meant to be the last word: mark the class sealed so nobody can "
                + "derive from it - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.True(!typeof(EmailNotification).IsSealed,
            "EmailNotification is NOT sealed - only the SMS one is. Sealing everything is as "
                + "thoughtless as sealing nothing.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Challenge_TheSkeletonIsFixedAndThePartsVary()
    {
        Report sales = new SalesReport(10m, 20m, 30m);

        Teach.Equal("== Sales ==\n3 sales totalling 60\n-- 3 rows --", sales.Render(),
            "Render builds header, body and footer in that order, joined by newlines. The "
                + "header is \"== \" + Title + \" ==\" - reread README challenge.");

        Report empty = new EmptyReport();

        Teach.Equal("== Empty ==\n(no data)\n-- end --", empty.Render(),
            "EmptyReport does not override Footer, so it inherits the virtual default. That "
                + "is the difference between abstract (you must) and virtual (you may) - "
                + "reread README challenge.");

        Teach.Equal("== Sales ==\n1 sale totalling 99\n-- 1 rows --", new SalesReport(99m).Render(),
            "One sale is a \"sale\". The footer's \"rows\" is deliberately not pluralised - "
                + "match the specification, not your instincts.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Review1_WheelsAreRequiredAndSoundIsOptional()
    {
        Vehicle car = new Car("hatchback");
        Vehicle bike = new Motorbike("scrambler");

        Teach.Equal("hatchback: 4 wheels, vroom", car.Describe(),
            "Car supplies Wheels and keeps the inherited Sound - reread README review.");

        Teach.Equal("scrambler: 2 wheels, brap", bike.Describe(),
            "Describe lives in the base class and never changed, yet it printed \"brap\": it "
                + "calls the virtual member, and the object chose the implementation.");

        Teach.Equal("vroom", car.Sound(),
            "Not overriding a virtual member is a legitimate choice - the base version stands.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: `Ex1` holds both shapes in `Shape`-typed variables and checks
each formula. `Ex2` checks the base calculation, the derived one, and then the
same manager through an `Employee` variable. `Ex3` calls `Speak` through both
the base type and the derived type for each duck — four calls, and the two
duck kinds differ in exactly one of them. `Ex4` renders a mixed list, checks
the empty case, and reflects over both classes to check which one is sealed.
`Challenge` renders two reports, and `Review1` is the spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The `new`-versus-`override` distinction in ex3 looks like trivia and is not.
It exists because inheritance creates a contract between two pieces of code
that may be versioned separately: if a base class in someone else's library
adds a `Save()` method, and your derived class already had one, your code must
keep compiling and keep meaning what it meant. `new` is the escape hatch for
exactly that, and the compiler's warning when you omit it is asking "which of
these two things did you mean?"

The deeper habit is the one ex4 drills: **let the object decide**. Every `if`
that asks "what kind of thing is this?" is a place where adding a new kind
means editing existing code — and missing one of the places. Replace it with a
virtual call and the new kind arrives complete, with nothing to update. When
you see `switch` on a type name in a code review, that is the question to ask,
and the answer is usually a base method or an interface.

Next: **05_interfaces**, which is the same substitutability without the
inheritance — and the tool you will actually reach for most days.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **04 — Inheritance and polymorphism**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex3` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `review1` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `challenge` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex1` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex2` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex3` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - csharp/04_inheritance_polymorphism

## Notes

**How virtual dispatch actually works.** Every object on the .NET heap carries a
pointer to its type's *method table*. A non-virtual call is compiled to "call
this exact address"; a virtual call is compiled to "look in the object's method
table at slot 4 and call whatever is there". A subclass that overrides a method
puts its own implementation in that slot, so the same call site reaches
different code depending on what it is holding. That one indirection is the
entire mechanism, and it is why `override` costs a pointer hop and `sealed`
sometimes lets the JIT skip it (it can prove there is only one candidate and
inline the call).

**Construction order is base-first.** When you write `new Manager(...)`, the
base constructor body runs before the derived constructor body. Field
initialisers, though, run in the *other* order: a derived class's field
initialisers run before the base constructor. The practical consequence is the
one bug everyone hits once: **never call a virtual method from a constructor.**
The base constructor runs while the derived object is only half-built, and a
virtual call from there lands in the derived override, which then reads fields
that have not been assigned yet. C# will not stop you; a static analyser will
warn you.

**Single inheritance, many interfaces.** A C# class has exactly one base class.
That is a deliberate restriction — multiple inheritance of *implementation*
creates the diamond problem, where two bases both define `Save()` and nobody
can say which one wins. Interfaces (lesson 05) have no implementation to
conflict, so you may have as many as you like. This is the structural reason
that "favour composition over inheritance" is not just style advice: you get
one inheritance slot, so spend it carefully.

**`sealed`, honestly.** It communicates intent ("this is not an extension
point") and occasionally helps the JIT devirtualise a call. It also stops
people mocking your class in tests, which is the usual reason a team regrets
sealing something. The .NET guideline is to seal by default *in libraries you
version publicly*, because unsealing later is easy and sealing later is a
breaking change. In application code, most teams do not bother.

**Where inheritance goes wrong.** The classic failure is inheriting for code
reuse rather than for substitutability. If `Square : Rectangle` and rectangles
have independent `Width` and `Height` setters, then a method that sets width
and expects height to stay put is now broken by every square — the
Liskov substitution principle, in its original example. When the base's
contract does not honestly hold for the derived type, you wanted composition:
hold a rectangle in a field, expose the two members that make sense, and be
free of the rest.

## ex1

`abstract` is the compiler enforcing a design decision. `Shape` has no area
because "a shape" has no formula, and making `Area()` abstract means the
question is answered exactly once per concrete type, never forgotten, never
defaulted to something meaningless like zero. Delete one override and the build
fails with a message naming the member you did not implement — a genuinely
useful failure, at compile time, in the file that is wrong.

The base constructor doing the `Name` assignment is worth noticing separately.
Shared *state* in the base plus abstract *behaviour* in the subclasses is the
shape most healthy hierarchies take. When the base has no state at all and only
abstract members, you have discovered an interface — which is lesson 05.

For the record: comparing `double`s with `==` is normally a mistake, because
0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. The gate gets away with `12.0` because 3 × 4 is exact in
binary, and rounds the circle's area to four places precisely because pi r² is
not. When you write your own tests over floating point, compare with a
tolerance.

## ex2

`base.MonthlyPay()` is the difference between *extending* behaviour and
*replacing* it, and choosing extension keeps the salary formula in one place.
Copy the division into the override instead and you have created the bug that
appears six months later, when payroll changes to thirteen payments a year and
managers keep getting twelve.

Omit the `base.` and you get infinite recursion, because `MonthlyPay()` inside
`Manager.MonthlyPay` resolves to the method you are inside. The
`StackOverflowException` that results cannot be caught in .NET — the process
dies immediately — which makes it one of the more memorable mistakes available
to you.

The final assertion is the payoff: `Employee asEmployee = manager;` then
`asEmployee.MonthlyPay()` gives 5500. Upcasting changes what the *compiler*
lets you call; it changes nothing about what the object *is*. Every framework
that hands you back a base type — `object`, `Exception`, `IEnumerable<T>` —
relies on this.

## ex3

This is the single most-asked C# inheritance question in interviews, and the
answer worth memorising is one sentence: **`override` is resolved by the
runtime type of the object; `new` is resolved by the compile-time type of the
variable.**

The reason `new` exists at all is versioning. Suppose you write
`class MyList : SomeLibraryList` with a `Sort()` method. Version 2 of the
library adds its own virtual `Sort()`. Without `new`, your method would suddenly
become an override of something you have never seen, and might be called by
library code expecting different semantics. C# makes you say which you meant,
and warns when you say nothing.

In application code, hiding is almost always a bug. The tell is exactly what
the gate demonstrates: the same object gives two different answers depending on
how the caller happened to be holding it, which means behaviour depends on a
detail no one thinks about. If you ever *need* hiding, that is usually a sign
the two methods should have different names.

## ex4

`RenderAll` is the argument for polymorphism in six lines. The alternative —
`if (n is EmailNotification e) ... else if (n is SmsNotification s) ...` —
works, and then someone adds a push notification and the compiler says nothing,
because the `if` chain is still valid code. It just silently does not handle
the new case. Virtual dispatch makes "handle every kind" the compiler's problem
rather than yours.

`IEnumerable<Notification>` as the parameter type is the other habit worth
copying: take the least specific type you can actually use. A method that only
foreaches has no business demanding a `List<T>`, and demanding one means
callers with an array or a LINQ query have to materialise a copy for you.
Lesson 08 covers the interface hierarchy this sits in.

`typeof(SmsNotification).IsSealed` is the gate reaching for reflection, because
a modifier is not observable any other way at runtime. Reflection is how test
frameworks, serialisers and dependency-injection containers work, and seeing it
used once here is enough for now — `07_generics` and the .NET track use it
again.

## challenge

The template method pattern inverts who is in charge. Normally your code calls
the library's; here the base class calls *yours*, at the moments it chooses.
That inversion is the whole point of a framework, and once you recognise it you
will see it everywhere: `ControllerBase` calls your action, xUnit constructs
your test class and calls your `[Fact]`, `BackgroundService` calls your
`ExecuteAsync`.

Making `Render` non-virtual is a real design decision. It says: the *shape* of
a report — header, body, footer, in that order — is not up for negotiation, and
only the content varies. If a subclass could override `Render`, it could omit
the footer, and then "every report has a footer" stops being true and every
consumer needs a null check.

The `abstract` versus `virtual` contrast between `Body()` and `Footer()` is the
other half. `Body()` is abstract because there is no such thing as a default
report body; `Footer()` is virtual because `"-- end --"` is a perfectly good
answer for most reports. Choosing between them per member, rather than making
everything virtual "just in case", is what keeps a base class honest.

## review1

The abstract *property* is the wrinkle here. Properties can be abstract or
virtual exactly like methods — `public abstract int Wheels { get; }` says every
vehicle must be able to answer, and `public override int Wheels => 4;` answers
with an expression body. There is no field anywhere, which is the point: an
abstract property is a question, not storage.

`Describe()` in the base class is the ex4 idea in miniature. It was written
once, it never changed, and it printed "brap" for the motorbike — because the
call to `Sound()` inside it is virtual and the object decided. Code you wrote
before a subclass existed calls into that subclass correctly. That is the
sentence to keep from this whole lesson.

## Further reading

- [Inheritance in C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/object-oriented/inheritance) — the base/derived relationship, with construction order spelled out.
- [Polymorphism](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/object-oriented/polymorphism) — including the `new` versus `override` section, which is worth reading twice.
- [Abstract and sealed classes and class members](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/abstract-and-sealed-classes-and-class-members) — when each modifier is appropriate.
- [`base` keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/base) — calling base constructors and base implementations.
- [Knowing when to use `override` and `new`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/knowing-when-to-use-override-and-new-keywords) — Microsoft's own worked comparison, with output.

## Challenge — the template method

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Challenge.cs`. `Report.Render()`
defines the fixed skeleton — a header line, a body, a footer, joined by `"\n"`:

```
== Sales ==
3 sales totalling 60
-- 3 rows --
```

`Render` itself is not virtual: subclasses fill in the parts and never
rearrange the whole. Implement `Render`, then `SalesReport.Body()` (count and
total, with "sale"/"sales" pluralised) and `SalesReport.Footer()`, then
`EmptyReport.Body()` -> `"(no data)"`.

Honest difficulty note: the code is short; the design is the difficulty.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both bodies are one line of arithmetic. The exercise is not the maths — it is
noticing that `Shape` deliberately has no formula, and that the `override`
keyword on each subclass is a promise to supply one.

If you are unsure what `abstract` bought you, try deleting one of the two
`Area` overrides and reading the compiler error.

## Hint 2

A rectangle's area is width times height; both are already properties on the
class.

A circle's is pi r². Use `Math.PI` rather than typing 3.14159 — the constant is
a `double` with full precision, and the gate rounds to four decimal places
expecting exactly that.

There is no `Math.Square`; `Radius * Radius` is idiomatic, and `Math.Pow(r, 2)`
is slower and less readable for a square.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public override double Area()
{
    return Width * Height;
}
```

The circle is the same shape of method with a different expression. Neither
subclass needs a field, a constructor change, or a call to `base` — everything
they need is already stored.

One thing to notice before you move on: the gate declares its variables as
`Shape`, not as `Rectangle`. Your code is being called through the base type,
and it works anyway. That is the payoff the next three exercises build on.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both bodies are one line of arithmetic. The exercise is not the maths — it is
noticing that `Shape` deliberately has no formula, and that the `override`
keyword on each subclass is a promise to supply one.

If you are unsure what `abstract` bought you, try deleting one of the two
`Area` overrides and reading the compiler error.

## Hint 2

A rectangle's area is width times height; both are already properties on the
class.

A circle's is pi r². Use `Math.PI` rather than typing 3.14159 — the constant is
a `double` with full precision, and the gate rounds to four decimal places
expecting exactly that.

There is no `Math.Square`; `Radius * Radius` is idiomatic, and `Math.Pow(r, 2)`
is slower and less readable for a square.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public override double Area()
{
    return Width * Height;
}
```

The circle is the same shape of method with a different expression. Neither
subclass needs a field, a constructor change, or a call to `base` — everything
they need is already stored.

One thing to notice before you move on: the gate declares its variables as
`Shape`, not as `Rectangle`. Your code is being called through the base type,
and it works anyway. That is the payoff the next three exercises build on.

## Exercise 2 — adding to inherited behaviour

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex2.cs`. `Employee.MonthlyPay()`
is one twelfth of the annual salary, rounded to the cent, halves away from
zero. `Manager.MonthlyPay()` is that, plus the manager's flat monthly bonus —
and it must **call** the base version rather than repeating the division.

The gate then assigns the manager to an `Employee`-typed variable and calls
`MonthlyPay()` again. Predict what you will get before you run it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 04_inheritance_polymorphism ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two bodies. The base one divides; the derived one adds a bonus to whatever the
base one produced.

That second sentence is the exercise. There is a way to say "whatever the base
one produced" without retyping the division, and using it means a change to the
pay formula happens in one place.

## Hint 2

`base.MonthlyPay()` calls the base class's version of the method you are
currently overriding — the one you would otherwise have replaced entirely.

The division needs rounding to the cent, exactly like lesson 01 ex4:
`Math.Round(value, 2, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero)`. Keep it in `decimal`
throughout; this is money.

Note the constructor is already written and already says `: base(name, annualSalary)`.
Read it: that is how the base class gets the chance to initialise the state it
owns before your constructor body runs.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public override decimal MonthlyPay()
{
    return base.MonthlyPay() + MonthlyBonus;
}
```

Without `base.`, writing `MonthlyPay()` inside `Manager.MonthlyPay` would call
*itself*, and the stack overflow would tell you so within a second. That is a
mistake worth making once deliberately, in a scratch project, so you recognise
the exception when it happens for real.

The last check in the gate assigns the manager to an `Employee` variable and
calls the method again. Predict the answer before you run it.

## Exercise 3 — `override` versus `new`

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex3.cs`. `Duck.Speak()` is

## Exercise 4 — one loop, every kind

Edit `src/Lessons/L04_InheritancePolymorphism/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`EmailNotification.Render()` -> `"email to ada@example.com: Welcome"` and
`SmsNotification.Render()` -> `"sms to 07700900123: Your code is 1234"`, then
`Notifier.RenderAll(...)`, which renders every notification in order and joins
them with `" | "`. An empty sequence renders as `""`.

`RenderAll` must contain no type checks at all — no `is`, no `switch` on type,
no casting. If you find yourself asking "what kind is this?", the abstract
method already answered.

modifier that makes deriving from it a compile error.

## Hint 1

Three small bodies and one keyword.

The two `Render` overrides are interpolated strings built from the properties
each class already has — note that `Recipient` lives on the base and is
available to both.

`RenderAll` is a loop that does not care what kind of notification it is
holding. If you catch yourself testing the type, stop: that is the code
`abstract` exists to delete.

## Hint 2

The two formats, exactly:

```
email to ada@example.com: Welcome
sms to 07700900123: Your code is 1234
```

For `RenderAll`, collect each `notification.Render()` into a `List<string>` and
finish with `string.Join(" | ", lines)` — the same collect-then-join shape as
lesson 02 ex1, which also gives you the empty case for free.

The keyword the gate checks for goes on the `SmsNotification` *class*
declaration, not on any member.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public static string RenderAll(IEnumerable<Notification> notifications)
{
    List<string> lines = new List<string>();
    foreach (Notification notification in notifications)
    {
        // one line each
    }
    return /* joined */;
}
```

`IEnumerable<Notification>` is the loosest thing you can ask for — anything you
can `foreach` over. Taking the loosest parameter type your code actually needs
is a habit worth starting now; lesson 08 explains what else it buys you.

The class modifier is the one that means "no further derivation". If you cannot
remember it, the gate's failure message names the property it checks
(`IsSealed`), which is a strong hint.

## Hint 1

Three small bodies and one keyword.

The two `Render` overrides are interpolated strings built from the properties
each class already has — note that `Recipient` lives on the base and is
available to both.

`RenderAll` is a loop that does not care what kind of notification it is
holding. If you catch yourself testing the type, stop: that is the code
`abstract` exists to delete.

## Hint 2

The two formats, exactly:

```
email to ada@example.com: Welcome
sms to 07700900123: Your code is 1234
```

For `RenderAll`, collect each `notification.Render()` into a `List<string>` and
finish with `string.Join(" | ", lines)` — the same collect-then-join shape as
lesson 02 ex1, which also gives you the empty case for free.

The keyword the gate checks for goes on the `SmsNotification` *class*
declaration, not on any member.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public static string RenderAll(IEnumerable<Notification> notifications)
{
    List<string> lines = new List<string>();
    foreach (Notification notification in notifications)
    {
        // one line each
    }
    return /* joined */;
}
```

`IEnumerable<Notification>` is the loosest thing you can ask for — anything you
can `foreach` over. Taking the loosest parameter type your code actually needs
is a habit worth starting now; lesson 08 explains what else it buys you.

The class modifier is the one that means "no further derivation". If you cannot
remember it, the gate's failure message names the property it checks
(`IsSealed`), which is a strong hint.

Three tiny members, and the question behind each one is "must every subclass

`Sound()` already has a base implementation, so `Car` can simply not mention

Nothing here needs a field, a constructor or a `base.` call — every override is
a single expression.

`"vroom"` explicitly. It would pass. It is also the kind of code that makes a
future reader wonder what is different about a car, so the gate's message about
"not overriding is a legitimate choice" is the answer being pointed at.
