lessons.briefing:
# 05 — Interfaces

An interface is a list of things a type promises to be able to do, with no
statement about what it *is*. That sounds like a small difference from lesson
04's abstract class and it changes everything about how you design: a class has
one base and can implement as many interfaces as it likes, so interfaces are
how a type joins many worlds at once. `string` is comparable, enumerable,
cloneable and equatable, and it did not have to pick one parent to get there.

The practical consequence is the sentence you will hear in every code review:
**depend on interfaces, not on concrete types**. A `Checkout` that says
`DateTime.Now` can never be tested at midnight on the 31st. A `Checkout` that
takes an `IClock` can be handed any moment in history by a three-line fake, and
in production it gets the real one. Same code, and the difference is entirely
in what it asked for.

This lesson is also where C# gets slightly weird — explicit implementations
that are invisible on the class, default methods that only exist through the
interface — and both of those oddities are interview favourites precisely
because they reveal whether you know how the dispatch works.

## Concept — a contract, and four ways to satisfy it

Declaring one is short:

```csharp
public interface IPriced
{
    decimal Price { get; }        // members are public and abstract by default
}
```

No `public` on the members, no bodies (usually), no state — an interface cannot
have fields. A class opts in by listing it after a colon, and the compiler
checks that every member is there:

```csharp
public class Book : IPriced
{
    public decimal Price { get; }     // implicit implementation: also on the class
}
```

**Implicit implementation** is the normal way: the member is public on the
class *and* satisfies the interface. **Explicit implementation** nails a member
to one interface and hides it from the class's own surface:

```csharp
string IEnglish.Greet() => "hello";   // no access modifier; not callable on the class
```

You need it when two interfaces demand the same signature and you want two
different answers, and you sometimes want it to keep a noisy interface out of
your public API — `IDisposable.Dispose` implemented explicitly, say, when your
type prefers to expose `Close()`.

**Default interface members** (C# 8 and later) let an interface ship a body:

```csharp
public interface IAuditEvent
{
    string Actor { get; }
    string Describe() => $"{Actor} did something";   // implementers may skip it
}
```

They exist so a library can add a member to a published interface without
breaking every implementer. The catch, and it is a real one: a default member is
only callable through the interface type, not through the implementing class.
`new LoginEvent("ada").Describe()` does not compile; casting to `IAuditEvent`
first does.

**Composition over inheritance.** Instead of inheriting behaviour, hold an
object that has it and hand it in from outside:

```csharp
public class Checkout
{
    private readonly IClock _clock;
    public Checkout(IClock clock) => _clock = clock;   // constructor injection
}
```

That is dependency injection, before any framework gets involved: the class
names what it needs as an interface and someone else decides which
implementation to supply. The .NET track's lesson 02 is the container that
automates the "someone else".

## Exercise 1 — one contract, two unrelated types

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Ex1.cs`. `IPriced` demands a `Label` and a
`Price`. `Book` and `Subscription` share no base class and no fields.

Implement `Book.Label` (the title in double quotes: `"Dune"`),
`Subscription.Label` (`news x3`), `Subscription.Price` (the whole subscription:
monthly × months), and `Basket.Total`, which adds up an
`IEnumerable<IPriced>` — mentioning neither concrete type.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two contracts, one name

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Ex2.cs`. `IEnglish.Greet()` and
`IFrench.Greet()` have identical signatures, and `Bilingual` implements both.
As shipped it has one public `Greet` that satisfies both at once — which is why
it can only ever give one answer.

Replace it with two **explicit** implementations, so that
`((IEnglish)person).Greet()` is `"hello"` and `((IFrench)person).Greet()` is
`"bonjour"`. Remember: an explicit implementation takes no access modifier.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a default that most implementers keep

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Ex3.cs`. Implement `IAuditEvent.Describe()` —
the body inside the *interface* — so it returns `"ada performed login"`, built
from the two properties every implementer promises. `LoginEvent` then needs no
`Describe` at all. `AdminEvent` supplies its own:
`"[ADMIN] root performed delete-user"`.

Watch how the gate declares its variables. `IAuditEvent login = new LoginEvent("ada");`
is not stylistic — a default interface member is unreachable through the class
type, and that is the detail worth taking away.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — collaborators handed in from outside

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Ex4.cs`. `Checkout` needs the current date and
a discount rule, and is given both as interfaces. Implement the constructor
(store them in the two `readonly` fields) and `Receipt(amount)`, which returns
`"2026-08-20: 90"` — the clock's date formatted `yyyy-MM-dd`, then the amount
after the policy has had it.

`Checkout` must never write `DateTime.Now` and never construct a policy. The
gate supplies a `FixedClock` pinned to 20 August 2026 and a `TenOff` policy that
subtracts 10 — read those three-line classes in the gate; they are what
testability looks like.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces ex4
```

## Challenge — implement an interface the framework already knows

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Challenge.cs`. `SemVer` holds a major, minor
and patch number. Implement `CompareTo(SemVer? other)` — major first, then
minor, then patch, with `null` sorting before everything — and `ToString()` ->
`"1.2.3"`.

Then read the gate's last block: it calls `versions.Sort()` and you wrote no
sorting code. `List<T>.Sort` found your `CompareTo` through `IComparable<T>`.
That is the deal interfaces offer — implement the contract the framework
already understands, and the framework's machinery starts working on your type.

Honest difficulty note: the trap is comparing the parts as text (`"10"` sorts
before `"9"`) or subtracting to get the sign (fine until the numbers are large
enough to overflow). Both are common enough that the gate checks for them.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is a shipping-rate strategy: one interface, two implementations
(`FlatRate`, `ByWeight`), and an `Order` that takes whichever it is given.
`dojo review` schedules it.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/05_interfaces

## Notes

**Interface versus abstract class, the answer to give.** An abstract class can
hold state, constructors, and non-public members, and a type may have only one.
An interface holds no state, and a type may implement any number. So: use an
abstract class when the implementers genuinely share *implementation and data*
and form one family; use an interface when you want to describe a *capability*
that unrelated types can have. The .NET framework itself is the worked example
— `Stream` is an abstract class (real shared buffering machinery, and every
stream is a stream), while `IDisposable` is an interface (a file, a database
connection and a subscription have nothing else in common). If you find
yourself wanting both, that is fine and normal: `List<T>` derives from nothing
interesting and implements six interfaces.

**Structural promise, nominal check.** C# interfaces are *nominal*: a type
implements `IPriced` only if it says so. Having a matching `Price` property is
not enough, which is the opposite of TypeScript's structural typing. That
matters when you meet a type you cannot edit — you cannot retrofit an interface
onto someone else's class, and the standard workaround is the *adapter*: a
small class of yours that implements the interface and forwards to theirs.

**How the runtime dispatches an interface call.** Each type carries an
interface map alongside its method table, so calling `item.Price` on an
`IPriced` variable is a lookup plus a call — slightly more expensive than a
virtual call, and irrelevant outside very hot loops. What is *not* irrelevant:
calling an interface member on a struct **boxes** it unless the call is
constrained by a generic type parameter. That is one of the reasons lesson 07's
generic constraints exist, and a real interview question.

**Interfaces name the seam.** The design value of `IClock` is not
polymorphism — you will probably only ever have two implementations, the real
one and the fake. It is that the interface marks the boundary between "my
logic" and "the messy outside world" (time, the network, the file system,
randomness). Code on your side of that line is deterministic and testable; code
on the other side is not. Every hard-to-test class you meet in the wild has that
line running straight through the middle of a method.

## ex1

The point of this exercise is what `Basket.Total` *cannot* see. It holds
`IPriced`, so `Title` and `Months` do not exist as far as it is concerned. That
narrowing is the whole trade: you give up access to everything a type offers in
return for accepting anything that offers this much.

That trade is also why interfaces should be small. An interface with fifteen
members is a promise almost nothing can make honestly, and the classes that do
implement it end up throwing `NotSupportedException` from half of them —
the standard example being `System.Array` implementing `IList<T>` and throwing
on `Add`. "Interface segregation", the I in SOLID, is exactly this observation:
prefer several small contracts to one large one.

`Subscription.Price` computing rather than storing is lesson 03's point coming
back. The interface says "you can be asked for a price"; it says nothing about
where the number lives, and the subscription's answer is arithmetic over data it
already has.

## ex2

Explicit implementation is the answer to a real collision: two interfaces, one
signature, two meanings. It is rare in application code and common in framework
code, where the second reason for it matters more — hiding a member from your
type's public surface.

The mechanical detail worth knowing: an explicitly implemented member has no
access modifier because it genuinely is not part of the class's interface. It
lives in the type's interface map, reachable only by casting. That also means
calling it on a **struct** boxes the struct, which is why the guidance for value
types is to implement interface members implicitly wherever you can.

The classic use in the wild is `IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` — the old
non-generic one — implemented explicitly so that only `IEnumerable<T>`'s typed
version shows up on your class. You will write exactly that in lesson 08.

## ex3

Default interface members arrived in C# 8 for a specific reason: API
versioning. Before them, adding a member to a published interface broke every
implementer on the planet at compile time, which is why .NET's interfaces were
frozen for a decade and why "extension methods on the interface" became the
standard workaround. Now a library can add a member *with* a default and
existing implementers keep compiling.

The oddity you met — a default member being invisible on the implementing class
— follows from how it is implemented. The body lives in the interface, so the
call has to be dispatched through the interface; the class never got a copy.
This makes default members good for "here is the obvious implementation in
terms of the other members" and bad as a general code-sharing mechanism. When
you want shared implementation available everywhere, an abstract base class or
a plain helper is still the better tool.

Worth knowing for interviews: this is *not* multiple inheritance of state.
Interfaces still cannot have fields. If two interfaces supply conflicting
defaults, the implementing class must resolve it explicitly, which is the
diamond problem being handed back to you rather than guessed at.

## ex4

The design in ex4 has three names depending on who you ask: *dependency
injection* (the collaborators arrive from outside), *inversion of control* (the
class no longer decides which implementation it gets), and the *strategy
pattern* (the discount policy is an interchangeable algorithm). They describe
the same shape from different angles.

What makes it worth the extra constructor parameter is the gate's `FixedClock`.
Time, randomness, the network, the clock on the wall and the file system are
all *ambient dependencies* — things a method reaches out and grabs rather than
being handed. Every one of them makes a test either flaky or impossible, and
every one of them has a standard interface-shaped fix. In real .NET you would
use `TimeProvider` (built in since .NET 8) rather than rolling your own
`IClock`, but the mechanism is exactly what you just wrote.

Note the fields are `readonly`. A collaborator assigned once in the constructor
and never repointed is easier to reason about, and the compiler will hold you to
it — the same lesson-03 note applies, that `readonly` protects the arrow rather
than the object it points at.

## challenge

`IComparable<T>` is the deal interfaces offer in its clearest form: implement
one method to the framework's specification, and `List<T>.Sort`,
`Array.Sort`, `OrderBy`, `SortedSet<T>`, `Max` and `Min` all start working on
your type. You wrote no sorting algorithm. You described an order.

The contract has rules, and violating them corrupts sorts in ways that are hard
to debug: the comparison must be *consistent* (if a < b and b < c then a < c),
*antisymmetric* (if a < b then b > a), and stable for equal items in the sense
that `x.CompareTo(x)` is 0. `List<T>.Sort` uses an introsort that will happily
produce nonsense — or throw `InvalidOperationException: IComparer.Compare()
method returns inconsistent results` — if you break them.

Two traps the gate checks. Comparing `ToString()` values is text ordering, and
`"1.2.10"` sorts before `"1.2.9"`. Returning `Major - other.Major` works until
someone compares `int.MinValue`, at which point the subtraction overflows and
the sign flips. `int.CompareTo(int)` has neither problem and reads better.

The related interface is `IEquatable<T>`, and the two together raise the
question lesson 06 answers: what does it mean for two of your objects to be
"equal"?

## review1

The strategy pattern again, in the smallest possible form: `Order` adds goods
to whatever number the rate hands back, and cannot tell a flat rate from a
weight-based one. Adding a third rate — free shipping over £50, say — means
writing one new class and changing nothing that already works. That is the
"open for extension, closed for modification" line, and this is what it looks
like when it is not a slogan.

The rounding-up trick, `(n + 999) / 1000`, is worth keeping. Integer division
truncates, so rounding up needs either that idiom or a float round trip via
`Math.Ceiling`, and the integer version has no precision question at all. Where
the minimum charge lives is the design question: inside the rate, because
`Order` should not know that one policy has a floor.

## Further reading

- [Interfaces (C# programming guide)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/interfaces) — declaring, implementing, and what an interface may contain.
- [Explicit interface implementation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/interfaces/explicit-interface-implementation) — the collision case and the hiding case, with examples.
- [Default interface methods tutorial](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/whats-new/tutorials/default-interface-methods-versions) — the versioning problem they were designed to solve.
- [`IComparable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.icomparable-1) — the contract, including the null rule and the consistency requirements.
- [Dependency injection in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection) — where constructor injection goes once a container is involved.
- [`TimeProvider`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timeprovider) — the framework's own `IClock`, and what to use in real code.

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L05_Interfaces;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L05_InterfacesTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_OneContractCoversTwoUnrelatedTypes()
    {
        Book book = new Book("Dune", 12.50m);
        Subscription news = new Subscription("news", 4m, 3);

        Teach.Equal("\"Dune\"", book.Label,
            "A book's label is its title wrapped in double quotes - escape them as \\\" inside "
                + "a C# string - reread README ex1.");
        Teach.Equal("news x3", news.Label,
            "A subscription's label is the service, an x, and the number of months.");
        Teach.Equal(12m, news.Price,
            "Price is the WHOLE subscription: 4 a month for 3 months is 12. The interface asked "
                + "for a price, and each type decides what that means - reread README ex1.");

        List<IPriced> basket = new List<IPriced> { book, news };

        Teach.Equal(24.50m, Basket.Total(basket),
            "12.50 plus 12 is 24.50. Total never mentions Book or Subscription: it only knows "
                + "IPriced - reread README ex1.");
        Teach.Equal(0m, Basket.Total(new List<IPriced>()),
            "An empty basket costs nothing.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_ExplicitImplementationsGiveTwoAnswers()
    {
        Bilingual person = new Bilingual();

        Teach.Equal("hello", ((IEnglish)person).Greet(),
            "Through IEnglish, Greet says \"hello\". One class, two contracts, two "
                + "implementations - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal("bonjour", ((IFrench)person).Greet(),
            "Through IFrench, the same object says \"bonjour\". If both calls give the same "
                + "answer you still have one method implementing both interfaces implicitly - "
                + "reread README ex2.");

        Teach.True(person is IEnglish && person is IFrench,
            "Bilingual must still declare BOTH interfaces. Explicit implementation changes how "
                + "the members are reached, not what the class promises.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_DefaultMethodsAreInheritedUnlessReplaced()
    {
        IAuditEvent login = new LoginEvent("ada");

        Teach.Equal("ada performed login", login.Describe(),
            "LoginEvent writes no Describe at all - it takes the default implementation from "
                + "the interface, which reads the two properties - reread README ex3.");

        IAuditEvent admin = new AdminEvent("root", "delete-user");

        Teach.Equal("[ADMIN] root performed delete-user", admin.Describe(),
            "AdminEvent supplies its own Describe, which wins over the interface's default - "
                + "reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("login", login.Action,
            "Action is an ordinary property on the implementer; only Describe has a default.");
    }

    private sealed class FixedClock : IClock
    {
        public DateTime Now => new DateTime(2026, 8, 20);
    }

    private sealed class TenOff : IDiscountPolicy
    {
        public decimal Apply(decimal amount) => amount - 10m;
    }

    private sealed class NoDiscount : IDiscountPolicy
    {
        public decimal Apply(decimal amount) => amount;
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_CheckoutUsesWhateverItWasGiven()
    {
        Checkout discounted = new Checkout(new FixedClock(), new TenOff());

        Teach.Equal("2026-08-20: 90", discounted.Receipt(100m),
            "The date comes from the injected clock (never DateTime.Now) and the amount from "
                + "the injected policy, which here takes 10 off - reread README ex4.");

        Checkout plain = new Checkout(new FixedClock(), new NoDiscount());

        Teach.Equal("2026-08-20: 100", plain.Receipt(100m),
            "Same Checkout code, a different policy object, a different answer - and Checkout "
                + "needed no changes at all. That is what depending on an interface buys you.");

        Teach.Equal("2026-08-20: 40", discounted.Receipt(50m),
            "The collaborators are stored once in the constructor and reused on every call.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Challenge_SemVerTeachesTheFrameworkHowToSortIt()
    {
        SemVer one = new SemVer(1, 2, 3);
        SemVer same = new SemVer(1, 2, 3);

        Teach.Equal(0, one.CompareTo(same),
            "Equal versions compare to 0 - and note that CompareTo says \"same order\", not "
                + "\"same object\" - reread README challenge.");

        Teach.True(new SemVer(1, 9, 9).CompareTo(new SemVer(2, 0, 0)) < 0,
            "1.9.9 sorts before 2.0.0: major wins outright, whatever the other parts say - "
                + "reread README challenge.");

        Teach.True(new SemVer(1, 2, 10).CompareTo(new SemVer(1, 2, 9)) > 0,
            "Compare the parts as NUMBERS: 10 is after 9, though \"10\" sorts before \"9\" as "
                + "text. Comparing the ToString values is the classic wrong answer here.");

        Teach.True(one.CompareTo(null) > 0,
            "By convention every object sorts after null, so CompareTo(null) is positive.");

        List<SemVer> versions = new List<SemVer>
        {
            new SemVer(2, 0, 0), new SemVer(1, 2, 3), new SemVer(1, 0, 0), new SemVer(1, 2, 0),
        };
        versions.Sort();

        Teach.Equal("1.0.0, 1.2.0, 1.2.3, 2.0.0", string.Join(", ", versions),
            "List<T>.Sort found your CompareTo through IComparable<T> - you wrote no sorting "
                + "code at all. string.Join calls ToString on each item, which is the other "
                + "half of this exercise - reread README challenge.");
    }

    public void Review1_TheOrderDoesNotKnowWhichRateItHas()
    {
        Teach.Equal(5m, new FlatRate(5m).For(20000),
            "A flat rate ignores the weight entirely.");

        Teach.Equal(2m, new ByWeight().For(0),
            "Nothing weighs less than the minimum charge of 2.");
        Teach.Equal(2m, new ByWeight().For(1000),
            "Exactly one kilogram is one kilogram, not two - watch the boundary.");
        Teach.Equal(4m, new ByWeight().For(1001),
            "One gram over rounds UP to the next whole kilogram: 4. Integer division alone "
                + "rounds down, so this needs a deliberate rounding up.");

        Order flat = new Order(new FlatRate(5m));
        Order weighed = new Order(new ByWeight());

        Teach.Equal(35m, flat.TotalFor(30m, 1500),
            "Goods plus shipping, with the flat policy.");
        Teach.Equal(34m, weighed.TotalFor(30m, 1500),
            "The same order, the same Order class, a different injected policy - reread README "
                + "review.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: `Ex1` prices a book and a subscription and totals them through
the interface. `Ex2` calls `Greet` through each interface on one object. `Ex3`
checks the inherited default and the replaced version. `Ex4` builds two
`Checkout`s with different fake policies and compares the receipts. `Challenge`
checks the comparison contract in four ways and then lets `List<T>.Sort` use
it. `Review1` is the spaced-repetition variant. The little `FixedClock`,
`TenOff` and `NoDiscount` classes inside the gate are test doubles — the whole
reason ex4's design is worth the extra constructor parameter.

## The teaching point

Interfaces are how .NET is extensible without knowing about you. `IEnumerable<T>`
is why your class can be `foreach`ed; `IComparable<T>` is why it can be sorted;
`IDisposable` is why `using` knows to clean it up; `ILogger` is why your custom
logger drops into ASP.NET Core. Every one of those is the same deal: implement
the contract, inherit the ecosystem.

The design habit — ex4's — is the one that changes how your code feels to work
with. A class that constructs its own collaborators has hard-coded a decision
that belongs to whoever assembles the application. A class that asks for them by
interface can be tested with fakes, reconfigured per environment, and reused in
a context you never imagined. The cost is one constructor parameter and the
discipline of not reaching for `new` in the middle of your logic.

Next: **06_structs_records**, where you meet the types that behave like values —
and the equality rules that come with them.

# Reading - csharp/05_interfaces

## Notes

**Interface versus abstract class, the answer to give.** An abstract class can
hold state, constructors, and non-public members, and a type may have only one.
An interface holds no state, and a type may implement any number. So: use an
abstract class when the implementers genuinely share *implementation and data*
and form one family; use an interface when you want to describe a *capability*
that unrelated types can have. The .NET framework itself is the worked example
— `Stream` is an abstract class (real shared buffering machinery, and every
stream is a stream), while `IDisposable` is an interface (a file, a database
connection and a subscription have nothing else in common). If you find
yourself wanting both, that is fine and normal: `List<T>` derives from nothing
interesting and implements six interfaces.

**Structural promise, nominal check.** C# interfaces are *nominal*: a type
implements `IPriced` only if it says so. Having a matching `Price` property is
not enough, which is the opposite of TypeScript's structural typing. That
matters when you meet a type you cannot edit — you cannot retrofit an interface
onto someone else's class, and the standard workaround is the *adapter*: a
small class of yours that implements the interface and forwards to theirs.

**How the runtime dispatches an interface call.** Each type carries an
interface map alongside its method table, so calling `item.Price` on an
`IPriced` variable is a lookup plus a call — slightly more expensive than a
virtual call, and irrelevant outside very hot loops. What is *not* irrelevant:
calling an interface member on a struct **boxes** it unless the call is
constrained by a generic type parameter. That is one of the reasons lesson 07's
generic constraints exist, and a real interview question.

**Interfaces name the seam.** The design value of `IClock` is not
polymorphism — you will probably only ever have two implementations, the real
one and the fake. It is that the interface marks the boundary between "my
logic" and "the messy outside world" (time, the network, the file system,
randomness). Code on your side of that line is deterministic and testable; code
on the other side is not. Every hard-to-test class you meet in the wild has that
line running straight through the middle of a method.

## ex1

The point of this exercise is what `Basket.Total` *cannot* see. It holds
`IPriced`, so `Title` and `Months` do not exist as far as it is concerned. That
narrowing is the whole trade: you give up access to everything a type offers in
return for accepting anything that offers this much.

That trade is also why interfaces should be small. An interface with fifteen
members is a promise almost nothing can make honestly, and the classes that do
implement it end up throwing `NotSupportedException` from half of them —
the standard example being `System.Array` implementing `IList<T>` and throwing
on `Add`. "Interface segregation", the I in SOLID, is exactly this observation:
prefer several small contracts to one large one.

`Subscription.Price` computing rather than storing is lesson 03's point coming
back. The interface says "you can be asked for a price"; it says nothing about
where the number lives, and the subscription's answer is arithmetic over data it
already has.

## ex2

Explicit implementation is the answer to a real collision: two interfaces, one
signature, two meanings. It is rare in application code and common in framework
code, where the second reason for it matters more — hiding a member from your
type's public surface.

The mechanical detail worth knowing: an explicitly implemented member has no
access modifier because it genuinely is not part of the class's interface. It
lives in the type's interface map, reachable only by casting. That also means
calling it on a **struct** boxes the struct, which is why the guidance for value
types is to implement interface members implicitly wherever you can.

The classic use in the wild is `IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` — the old
non-generic one — implemented explicitly so that only `IEnumerable<T>`'s typed
version shows up on your class. You will write exactly that in lesson 08.

## ex3

Default interface members arrived in C# 8 for a specific reason: API
versioning. Before them, adding a member to a published interface broke every
implementer on the planet at compile time, which is why .NET's interfaces were
frozen for a decade and why "extension methods on the interface" became the
standard workaround. Now a library can add a member *with* a default and
existing implementers keep compiling.

The oddity you met — a default member being invisible on the implementing class
— follows from how it is implemented. The body lives in the interface, so the
call has to be dispatched through the interface; the class never got a copy.
This makes default members good for "here is the obvious implementation in
terms of the other members" and bad as a general code-sharing mechanism. When
you want shared implementation available everywhere, an abstract base class or
a plain helper is still the better tool.

Worth knowing for interviews: this is *not* multiple inheritance of state.
Interfaces still cannot have fields. If two interfaces supply conflicting
defaults, the implementing class must resolve it explicitly, which is the
diamond problem being handed back to you rather than guessed at.

## ex4

The design in ex4 has three names depending on who you ask: *dependency
injection* (the collaborators arrive from outside), *inversion of control* (the
class no longer decides which implementation it gets), and the *strategy
pattern* (the discount policy is an interchangeable algorithm). They describe
the same shape from different angles.

What makes it worth the extra constructor parameter is the gate's `FixedClock`.
Time, randomness, the network, the clock on the wall and the file system are
all *ambient dependencies* — things a method reaches out and grabs rather than
being handed. Every one of them makes a test either flaky or impossible, and
every one of them has a standard interface-shaped fix. In real .NET you would
use `TimeProvider` (built in since .NET 8) rather than rolling your own
`IClock`, but the mechanism is exactly what you just wrote.

Note the fields are `readonly`. A collaborator assigned once in the constructor
and never repointed is easier to reason about, and the compiler will hold you to
it — the same lesson-03 note applies, that `readonly` protects the arrow rather
than the object it points at.

## challenge

`IComparable<T>` is the deal interfaces offer in its clearest form: implement
one method to the framework's specification, and `List<T>.Sort`,
`Array.Sort`, `OrderBy`, `SortedSet<T>`, `Max` and `Min` all start working on
your type. You wrote no sorting algorithm. You described an order.

The contract has rules, and violating them corrupts sorts in ways that are hard
to debug: the comparison must be *consistent* (if a < b and b < c then a < c),
*antisymmetric* (if a < b then b > a), and stable for equal items in the sense
that `x.CompareTo(x)` is 0. `List<T>.Sort` uses an introsort that will happily
produce nonsense — or throw `InvalidOperationException: IComparer.Compare()
method returns inconsistent results` — if you break them.

Two traps the gate checks. Comparing `ToString()` values is text ordering, and
`"1.2.10"` sorts before `"1.2.9"`. Returning `Major - other.Major` works until
someone compares `int.MinValue`, at which point the subtraction overflows and
the sign flips. `int.CompareTo(int)` has neither problem and reads better.

The related interface is `IEquatable<T>`, and the two together raise the
question lesson 06 answers: what does it mean for two of your objects to be
"equal"?

## review1

The strategy pattern again, in the smallest possible form: `Order` adds goods
to whatever number the rate hands back, and cannot tell a flat rate from a
weight-based one. Adding a third rate — free shipping over £50, say — means
writing one new class and changing nothing that already works. That is the
"open for extension, closed for modification" line, and this is what it looks
like when it is not a slogan.

The rounding-up trick, `(n + 999) / 1000`, is worth keeping. Integer division
truncates, so rounding up needs either that idiom or a float round trip via
`Math.Ceiling`, and the integer version has no precision question at all. Where
the minimum charge lives is the design question: inside the rate, because
`Order` should not know that one policy has a floor.

## Further reading

- [Interfaces (C# programming guide)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/interfaces) — declaring, implementing, and what an interface may contain.
- [Explicit interface implementation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/interfaces/explicit-interface-implementation) — the collision case and the hiding case, with examples.
- [Default interface methods tutorial](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/whats-new/tutorials/default-interface-methods-versions) — the versioning problem they were designed to solve.
- [`IComparable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.icomparable-1) — the contract, including the null rule and the consistency requirements.
- [Dependency injection in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection) — where constructor injection goes once a container is involved.
- [`TimeProvider`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timeprovider) — the framework's own `IClock`, and what to use in real code.

## Challenge — implement an interface the framework already knows

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Challenge.cs`. `SemVer` holds a major, minor
and patch number. Implement `CompareTo(SemVer? other)` — major first, then
minor, then patch, with `null` sorting before everything — and `ToString()` ->
`"1.2.3"`.

Then read the gate's last block: it calls `versions.Sort()` and you wrote no
sorting code. `List<T>.Sort` found your `CompareTo` through `IComparable<T>`.
That is the deal interfaces offer — implement the contract the framework
already understands, and the framework's machinery starts working on your type.

Honest difficulty note: the trap is comparing the parts as text (`"10"` sorts
before `"9"`) or subtracting to get the sign (fine until the numbers are large
enough to overflow). Both are common enough that the gate checks for them.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two members. `ToString()` is one interpolated string. `CompareTo` is the
interesting one, and it has three parts to compare in priority order.

Think of it as a tie-break chain: compare the majors, and only if they are
equal look at the minors, and only if those are equal look at the patches. That
is the same "ORDER BY a, b, c" idea you know from SQL.

## Hint 2

`int` already implements `IComparable<int>`, so `Major.CompareTo(other.Major)`
gives you the negative/zero/positive answer for one part without writing any
subtraction. Comparing with `-` works for small ints and overflows for large
ones, which is why `CompareTo` is the habit.

The shape:

```csharp
int major = Major.CompareTo(other.Major);
if (major != 0)
{
    return major;
}
// ... and so on down the parts
```

Handle the `null` argument first, before you touch `other` at all.

## Hint 3

The contract you are implementing has rules, and the gate checks two of them:
`x.CompareTo(x)` must be 0, and `null` sorts before everything, so
`x.CompareTo(null)` is positive. It must also be *consistent* — if `a` is
before `b` and `b` before `c`, then `a` must be before `c`. A comparison built
from a chain of part comparisons gets that for free; one built from a clever
formula usually does not.

Left to you: whether to return the raw result of the final `CompareTo` or
normalise everything to -1/0/1. Both satisfy the contract — the framework only
looks at the sign.

```csharp
int major = Major.CompareTo(other.Major);

}
```

`x.CompareTo(x)` must be 0, and `null` sorts before everything, so

formula usually does not.

normalise everything to -1/0/1. Both satisfy the contract — the framework only

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Ex2.cs`. `IEnglish.Greet()` and
`IFrench.Greet()` have identical signatures, and `Bilingual` implements both.

`"bonjour"`. Remember: an explicit implementation takes no access modifier.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The class as shipped compiles: one public `Greet()` satisfies both interfaces at
once, because C# matches interface members by signature. That is exactly the
problem — one method, one answer, two contracts that want different ones.

You need to delete that method and write two, each one nailed to a specific
interface.

## Hint 2

An *explicit* implementation names the interface in the member declaration and
takes no access modifier at all:

```csharp
string IEnglish.Greet() => "hello";
```

No `public`. There cannot be one, because the member is not part of the class's
own surface — it exists only through that interface. Write the French one the
same way.

## Hint 3

After both are written, try adding `person.Greet()` (with `person` typed as
`Bilingual`) somewhere and read the compiler error. That inaccessibility is the
feature: the only way to reach either greeting is to say which contract you are
asking under, by casting to `IEnglish` or `IFrench` — which is what the gate
does.

The decision left to you: whether either greeting should *also* be available
directly on the class. It can be, by implementing one implicitly and the other
explicitly. Try it and see which reads better.

## Hint 1

The class as shipped compiles: one public `Greet()` satisfies both interfaces at
once, because C# matches interface members by signature. That is exactly the
problem — one method, one answer, two contracts that want different ones.

You need to delete that method and write two, each one nailed to a specific
interface.

## Hint 2

An *explicit* implementation names the interface in the member declaration and
takes no access modifier at all:

```csharp
string IEnglish.Greet() => "hello";
```

No `public`. There cannot be one, because the member is not part of the class's
own surface — it exists only through that interface. Write the French one the
same way.

## Hint 3

After both are written, try adding `person.Greet()` (with `person` typed as
`Bilingual`) somewhere and read the compiler error. That inaccessibility is the
feature: the only way to reach either greeting is to say which contract you are
asking under, by casting to `IEnglish` or `IFrench` — which is what the gate
does.

The decision left to you: whether either greeting should *also* be available
directly on the class. It can be, by implementing one implicitly and the other
explicitly. Try it and see which reads better.

## Exercise 4 — collaborators handed in from outside

Edit `src/Lessons/L05_Interfaces/Ex4.cs`. `Checkout` needs the current date and
a discount rule, and is given both as interfaces. Implement the constructor
(store them in the two `readonly` fields) and `Receipt(amount)`, which returns
`"2026-08-20: 90"` — the clock's date formatted `yyyy-MM-dd`, then the amount
after the policy has had it.

`Checkout` must never write `DateTime.Now` and never construct a policy. The
gate supplies a `FixedClock` pinned to 20 August 2026 and a `TenOff` policy that
subtracts 10 — read those three-line classes in the gate; they are what
testability looks like.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 05_interfaces ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two bodies, both short. The constructor stores what it is handed; `Receipt`
asks its two collaborators for their answers and formats the result.

The rule to hold on to: `Checkout` must never say `DateTime.Now` and never say
`new SomethingDiscountPolicy()`. Everything variable arrives through the
constructor.

## Hint 2

The fields are already declared and already `readonly` — assign both in the
constructor and the compiler will stop anyone (including you) from repointing
them later.

The receipt is one interpolated string with a format specifier on the date:

```csharp
return $"{_clock.Now:yyyy-MM-dd}: {/* the discounted amount */}";
```

That colon inside the braces separates the value from its format string; it is
not the literal colon in the output, which comes after the closing brace.

## Hint 3

The amount comes from `_policy.Apply(amount)`, not from any arithmetic of your
own. If `Checkout` knew that a discount is "ten percent", the whole exercise
would be pointless — the interface exists so that the policy can be a flat
amount, a percentage, a loyalty table or nothing at all, without `Checkout`
changing.

Read the gate's little `FixedClock` and `TenOff` classes before you run it.
They are three lines each, they live in the test file, and they are the reason
this design is testable: a clock you can pin to a date, a policy that takes
exactly 10 off. Try to test a class that calls `DateTime.Now` directly and you
will understand why this pattern is everywhere.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two bodies, both short. The constructor stores what it is handed; `Receipt`
asks its two collaborators for their answers and formats the result.

The rule to hold on to: `Checkout` must never say `DateTime.Now` and never say
`new SomethingDiscountPolicy()`. Everything variable arrives through the
constructor.

## Hint 2

The fields are already declared and already `readonly` — assign both in the
constructor and the compiler will stop anyone (including you) from repointing
them later.

The receipt is one interpolated string with a format specifier on the date:

```csharp
return $"{_clock.Now:yyyy-MM-dd}: {/* the discounted amount */}";
```

That colon inside the braces separates the value from its format string; it is
not the literal colon in the output, which comes after the closing brace.

## Hint 3

The amount comes from `_policy.Apply(amount)`, not from any arithmetic of your
own. If `Checkout` knew that a discount is "ten percent", the whole exercise
would be pointless — the interface exists so that the policy can be a flat
amount, a percentage, a loyalty table or nothing at all, without `Checkout`
changing.

Read the gate's little `FixedClock` and `TenOff` classes before you run it.
They are three lines each, they live in the test file, and they are the reason
this design is testable: a clock you can pin to a date, a policy that takes
exactly 10 off. Try to test a class that calls `DateTime.Now` directly and you
will understand why this pattern is everywhere.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three bodies: two implementations of the same one-method interface, and a
consumer that asks the interface for an answer without knowing which one it has.

`FlatRate` is the trivial one — deliberately, because it proves the consumer
really is indifferent.

## Hint 2

`ByWeight` charges 2 per kilogram *or part of a kilogram*, with a minimum of 2.
So 0 g and 1000 g both cost 2, and 1001 g costs 4.

Integer division rounds down, which is the opposite of what you need. The
standard trick for rounding an integer division up is to add one less than the
divisor first:

```csharp
int kilos = (weightGrams + 999) / 1000;
```

Then clamp the minimum so a zero-gram order still pays.

## Hint 3

`Order.TotalFor` is `goods + _rate.For(weightGrams)` and nothing else. No `if`,
no type test, no knowledge of which rate arrived.

The decision left to you is where the minimum charge belongs — inside
`ByWeight.For`, or as a `Math.Max` in `Order`. Put it in the rate: the order
should not know that one particular policy has a floor, or you will be editing
`Order` every time a policy gains a rule.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three bodies: two implementations of the same one-method interface, and a
consumer that asks the interface for an answer without knowing which one it has.

`FlatRate` is the trivial one — deliberately, because it proves the consumer
really is indifferent.

## Hint 2

`ByWeight` charges 2 per kilogram *or part of a kilogram*, with a minimum of 2.
So 0 g and 1000 g both cost 2, and 1001 g costs 4.

Integer division rounds down, which is the opposite of what you need. The
standard trick for rounding an integer division up is to add one less than the
divisor first:

```csharp
int kilos = (weightGrams + 999) / 1000;
```

Then clamp the minimum so a zero-gram order still pays.

## Hint 3

`Order.TotalFor` is `goods + _rate.For(weightGrams)` and nothing else. No `if`,
no type test, no knowledge of which rate arrived.

The decision left to you is where the minimum charge belongs — inside
`ByWeight.For`, or as a `Math.Max` in `Order`. Put it in the rate: the order
should not know that one particular policy has a floor, or you will be editing
`Order` every time a policy gains a rule.

# 06 — Structs and records

Lesson 01 told you that `struct` copies and `class` points. This lesson is
about what you do with that: which of your own types should behave like values,
and what "equal" means for each kind. It is also where C# has changed most in
the last five years — `record`, `init`, `with`, `record struct` and positional
patterns all arrived since 2020, and together they make writing immutable
data types about as short as writing a JSON object.

The question underneath is one interviewers ask constantly and most candidates
answer vaguely: **when two objects hold the same data, are they the same
thing?** For a coordinate, a money amount, a date — obviously yes; nobody cares
*which* `(3, 7)` they have. For a customer, an order, a database connection —
obviously no; two customers with the same name are two people. C# gives you
types that default to each answer, and the skill is picking the right one.

## Concept — three kinds of type, two kinds of equality

**A `struct` is a value type.** It copies on assignment, lives inline where it
is declared, and gets **memberwise equality** for free — two structs are equal
when every field is. Make it `readonly` and the compiler enforces that nothing
can mutate it after construction:

```csharp
public readonly struct Money
{
    public Money(decimal amount, string currency) { Amount = amount; Currency = currency; }
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public string Currency { get; }
}
```

Guidance from Microsoft, worth memorising: make a struct when the thing is
logically a single value, is under about 16 bytes, is immutable, and will not
be boxed often. Otherwise write a class. A *mutable* struct is a well-known
footgun — because every copy is independent, changes you make often land on a
copy you did not know you had.

**A `record` is a class with value semantics bolted on.** One line gets you
properties, a constructor, value equality, `GetHashCode`, a readable
`ToString`, a `Deconstruct`, and `with`:

```csharp
public record Reading(string Sensor, int Degrees);

var a = new Reading("kiln", 20);
var b = new Reading("kiln", 20);
a == b            // true - compared by value
a.ToString()      // "Reading { Sensor = kiln, Degrees = 20 }"
```

It is still a reference type: assigning copies the arrow, and `record struct`
is the value-type version.

**`with` copies and changes in one expression:**

```csharp
var shipped = order with { Status = "shipped" };   // order itself is untouched
```

The copy is **shallow**. If a member is a `List<T>`, the copy points at the
same list — which is also why record equality on such a member is reference
equality, and both facts bite in the same exercise below.

**A plain `class` compares by reference.** Two `ReadingClass` objects holding
identical data are not equal, because `object.Equals` asks "are you the same
object?". To change that you override `Equals` **and** `GetHashCode`, and they
must agree: equal objects must produce equal hash codes, or hashed collections
break in ways that look like the dictionary is lying to you.

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is CacheKey k && k.Id == Id;
public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Id);
```

**Deconstruction and positional patterns.** Records (and any type with a
`Deconstruct` method) can be taken apart:

```csharp
var (x, y) = point;
string where = point switch { (0, 0) => "origin", (_, 0) => "on the x axis", _ => "somewhere" };
```

## Exercise 1 — a value type of your own

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Ex1.cs`. `Money` is a `readonly struct`.
Implement `Add(Money other)`, which returns a **new** `Money` holding the sum
and throws `InvalidOperationException` when the currencies differ, and
`ToString()`, which returns `"GBP 5.00"` — currency, space, two decimal places,
formatted with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`.

You cannot assign to `Amount` inside `Add`; the struct is `readonly`. That is
the shape immutable value types take: every operation is a function returning a
new value, exactly like `DateTime.AddDays` or `string.Replace`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the same data, three answers

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Ex2.cs`. `Reading` is a record;
`ReadingClass` holds the same two values as a plain class. Implement four tiny
methods: `SameReading` (ask the records), `SameLegacyData` (compare the class's
two properties by hand), `ClassEqualsSays` (ask the class's own `Equals` and
report what it says — do not fix it), and `Describe` (the record's own
`ToString`).

Predict all four results before running the gate. The one that surprises people
is `ClassEqualsSays`, and it is the reason ex4 exists.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — copy-and-change

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Ex3.cs`. Implement `Reprice` (a copy at a
new unit price), `AddOneUnit` (a copy with one more unit **and** the status set
to `"amended"`), and `DiffersOnlyInStatus`, which is true when two orders match
on everything except status.

That last one has a one-line answer that uses `with` and `==` together and does
not name a single property except `Status`. Finding it is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — earning value equality by hand

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Ex4.cs`. `CacheKey` is meant to be a
dictionary key: two keys with the same region and id are the same key. Override
`Equals(object?)` and `GetHashCode()` so that a `Dictionary<CacheKey, string>`
can find an entry using a *different but equal* key object.

`Equals` will be handed nulls and objects of other types — deal with both. And
the two methods must agree: the gate builds a dictionary with one key and looks
it up with the twin, which only works if the hash codes match.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records ex4
```

## Challenge — patterns over a record struct

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Challenge.cs`. `Point` is a
`readonly record struct`. Implement `Classify(Point)` returning `"origin"`,
`"on the x axis"`, `"on the y axis"`, or `"quadrant 1"` through
`"quadrant 4"` (anticlockwise from the top right); and `Mirror(Point)`, which
swaps the coordinates.

Honest difficulty note: the switch itself is easy and the **order of the arms**
is the whole problem — three of your patterns match `(0, 0)`, and only the
first one written wins. Use positional patterns (`(0, 0)`, `(_, 0)`,
`( > 0, > 0)`), which work because a record struct generates `Deconstruct`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records challenge
```

## Review

`review1` asks how deep record equality goes when a member is a `List<string>`,
and what `with` does about it. Both answers are "not as deep as you assumed".
`dojo review` will bring it back.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/06_structs_records

## Notes

**Why mutable structs are a footgun.** Because a struct copies on every
assignment, argument pass and collection read, a mutation can land somewhere
you did not expect. The classic demonstration: put a mutable struct in a
`List<T>` and write `list[0].Value = 5`. C# refuses to compile it, because the
indexer returns a *copy* and the assignment would be silently thrown away —
one of the few places the language protects you from a design mistake rather
than the mistake itself. Arrays are the exception (`array[0].Value = 5` works,
because array indexing gives a real reference), which means the same line
behaves differently for an array and a list. `readonly struct` sidesteps the
whole category by making mutation impossible.

**Records are classes, not magic.** `record Reading(string Sensor, int Degrees)`
compiles to a sealed-ish class with two get-only properties, a constructor, an
`Equals(Reading)` implementing `IEquatable<Reading>`, an `Equals(object)`
override, a `GetHashCode` combining the members, a `ToString` override, a
`Deconstruct`, a protected copy constructor and a `<Clone>$` method that `with`
calls. You can see all of it with a decompiler, and everything you can do by
hand you can still do — declare extra members, override `ToString`, write your
own constructor. The type is ordinary; only the boilerplate is generated.

**Record equality is member-by-member, using each member's own equality.**
Which is why two records holding equal-but-distinct `List<T>`s are not equal:
`List<T>` never overrode `Equals`. This surprises people who read "value
equality" as "deep equality". It is not deep; it is one level, delegating.

**`with` is a shallow copy, for the same reason.** It clones the record's
fields and replaces the ones you named. A field holding a reference is copied
as a reference, so both records share the object. If you need a deep copy you
write it, and the fact that nobody can write a general deep copy for you is
exactly why the language does not pretend to.

**Boxing, properly this time.** Assigning a struct to `object`, or to an
interface variable, allocates a heap box and copies the value in. `object o = someMoney;`
boxes. `IComparable c = someInt;` boxes. Calling an interface method on a
struct through a generic constrained to that interface does *not* box, which is
one of the main reasons generic constraints exist (lesson 07). Boxing matters
in hot loops and in allocation-sensitive code, and it is a [***] interview
question because it demonstrates you know that value types have somewhere else
to be.

## ex1

The signature of `Add` is the lesson: it takes a `Money` and returns a `Money`,
and there is nowhere for a mutation to happen. Compare `DateTime.AddDays`,
`string.ToUpper`, `decimal.Round` — the whole immutable-value vocabulary in
.NET looks like this, and once you notice the pattern you stop expecting
`list.Sort()`-style in-place methods from value types.

Choosing `InvalidOperationException` over `ArgumentException` is a real
distinction worth having an opinion about. `ArgumentException` says "the value
you passed is wrong"; `InvalidOperationException` says "the object is not in a
state where this makes sense". Adding EUR to GBP is arguably either, and the
framework itself is inconsistent about such calls — but the second reads better
here, because neither amount is wrong on its own.

The free memberwise `Equals` you did not write is worth pausing on: it is
implemented in `ValueType.Equals`, and for a struct containing a reference
member (the `string`) it falls back to *reflection over the fields*, which is
correct but slow. Structs used in hot paths or as dictionary keys should
override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` explicitly — or be `record struct`s, which
generate fast ones.

## ex2

Three ways of asking "the same?", three answers, and the reason is inheritance.
`ReadingClass` inherits `object.Equals`, which is `ReferenceEquals`. `Reading`
is a record, so the compiler generated an `Equals` that compares members.
Nothing about the *data* differs; only the type's opinion about identity.

The follow-up interviewers ask: "what does `==` do for a record?" Records
overload `==` to call the generated value equality, which makes them one of the
few reference types where `==` and `Equals` agree. For a plain class, `==` is
reference comparison unless someone overloaded it, and for `string` it was
overloaded to compare text — which is why `"ab" + "c" == "abc"` is true.
Knowing which of those three worlds you are in is the actual skill.

The generated `ToString` format is stable and documented:
`TypeName { Prop = value, Prop = value }`. It exists because the first thing
anyone does with a data object is print it in a log or a debugger, and
`Namespace.Reading` — what a plain class prints — helps nobody.

## ex3

`with` is the immutable-update idiom, and it matters more than it looks.
Immutable data means no method you call can change your object behind your
back, which removes an entire category of bug in concurrent and event-driven
code. The reason immutability used to be painful in C# was the boilerplate:
copying nine properties to change one. `with` deletes that boilerplate, and
that is the whole reason records exist.

`DiffersOnlyInStatus` is worth keeping in your toolkit as a pattern: *normalise
the difference away, then compare*. The by-hand alternative — comparing sku,
quantity and price — is longer, and worse, it silently stops being right when
someone adds a fourth property to `Order`. The `with`-and-compare version keeps
working, because `==` covers whatever the record holds today.

The trap in `AddOneUnit` is reading `with` as a sequence of assignments. It is
not: all the values in the braces are computed against the *original*, and one
new object is constructed from the result. If you write
`order with { Quantity = Quantity + 1 }` inside a member of the record, the
same rule applies.

## ex4

The `Equals`/`GetHashCode` contract is the most consequential unwritten rule in
.NET, and the failure mode is memorable: a dictionary that cannot find a key
you are certain you added. The mechanism is worth being able to draw. A
`Dictionary` computes `key.GetHashCode()`, reduces it to a bucket index, and
only compares (with `Equals`) the entries already in that bucket. Two equal
keys with different hash codes land in different buckets, so the comparison
that would have matched never happens.

The rules, precisely: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects
*may* share one (a collision, handled by the comparison step); and a hash code
must not change while the object is in use as a key. That last one is why keys
should be immutable — mutate a property that feeds the hash and the entry is
stranded in the old bucket forever.

`HashCode.Combine` is the modern answer to "how do I mix several members?" It
implements a proper avalanche mix, so small differences in inputs produce very
different outputs. The old folklore (`hash = hash * 31 + field.GetHashCode()`)
is fine too; XOR-ing fields is not, because `Combine(a, b)` and `Combine(b, a)`
then collide, and so does any pair of equal fields.

`obj is CacheKey other && ...` is worth reading as three checks in one: not
null, right type, and a typed variable to compare with. Before pattern
matching, this took four lines and everybody wrote at least one of them wrong.

## challenge

Positional patterns come from `Deconstruct`, which the record struct generated.
Any type can join in by writing a `Deconstruct` method with `out` parameters —
including your own classes, which is a pleasant way to make a type feel
first-class in modern C#.

Arm order in a switch expression is not a detail: arms are tested top to
bottom, so more specific patterns must come first. The compiler helps in one
direction — it warns about an arm that can never be reached because an earlier
one subsumes it — but it cannot tell you that you *meant* the origin to be
tested before the axes. Exhaustiveness is the other half: the compiler will
warn when it cannot prove every input is handled, which for two unbounded ints
means you always need a catch-all.

Where this pays off is modelling. Once you are comfortable with records plus
positional patterns, "a discriminated union and a match" becomes idiomatic C#:
a hierarchy of records and one switch expression covering them. It is not as
tight as F# or TypeScript, and it is a great deal better than a chain of `if`s
casting to concrete types.

## review1

Two ideas that trip people up for the same underlying reason: a record holds
*references*, and both its equality and its `with` stop at the reference. Two
baskets with equal-looking lists are not equal, because `List<T>` compares by
reference. A renamed basket shares its list with the original, because copying a
reference copies the arrow. One sentence — "a record's value semantics are one
level deep" — covers both, and it is a good sentence to have ready in an
interview.

The practical guidance that follows: when a record must be genuinely immutable,
make its collection members immutable too. `IReadOnlyList<string>` documents the
intent, and `ImmutableArray<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` (in
`System.Collections.Immutable`) enforce it. A record with a `List<T>` inside is
an immutable wrapper around a mutable thing, which is often exactly the bug
report you will spend an afternoon on.

## Further reading

- [Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record) — what the compiler generates, including the exact `ToString` format and `with` semantics.
- [Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) — `readonly struct`, `record struct`, and the parameterless-constructor rules.
- [Choosing between class and struct](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/choosing-between-class-and-struct) — the official size/immutability/boxing guidance.
- [`Object.GetHashCode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) — the contract, spelled out, with the consequences of breaking it.
- [`HashCode.Combine`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.hashcode.combine) — the modern way to mix members.
- [Patterns](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/patterns) — positional, property, relational and logical patterns in one reference.
- [Deconstructing tuples and other types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/functional/deconstruct) — how to add `Deconstruct` to your own types.

```csharp
        Money three = new Money(3m, "GBP");

        Teach.Equal(new Money(8m, "GBP"), five.Add(three),
            "Add returns a NEW Money. A readonly struct cannot mutate itself, which is exactly "
                + "the property that makes it safe to pass around - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal(5m, five.Amount,
            "The original is untouched: Add produced a new value rather than changing this one.");

        Teach.Equal("GBP 5.00", five.ToString(),
            "The currency, a space, and two decimal places. Format with \"0.00\" and "
                + "CultureInfo.InvariantCulture so the output does not change with the "
                + "machine's locale - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => five.Add(new Money(3m, "EUR")),
            "Pounds plus euros is not a number - throw InvalidOperationException rather than "
                + "silently producing nonsense - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.True(new Money(5m, "GBP").Equals(new Money(5m, "GBP")),
            "Structs get memberwise equality for free: two Moneys with the same amount and "
                + "currency are equal without you writing a line.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_RecordsBringEqualityAndToStringWithThem()
    {
        Reading a = new Reading("kiln", 20);
        Reading b = new Reading("kiln", 20);

        Teach.True(!ReferenceEquals(a, b), "These really are two separate objects.");

        Teach.True(Equality.SameReading(a, b),
            "A record compares by VALUE, so two separate records holding the same data are "
                + "equal - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.True(!Equality.SameReading(a, new Reading("kiln", 21)),
            "Different data, not equal. Value equality means every member has to match.");

        ReadingClass c = new ReadingClass("kiln", 20);
        ReadingClass d = new ReadingClass("kiln", 20);

        Teach.True(Equality.SameLegacyData(c, d),
            "Compared property by property, these two obviously hold the same data.");

        Teach.True(!Equality.ClassEqualsSays(c, d),
            "...but the CLASS says they are not equal, because a plain class inherits "
                + "reference equality from object: same data, different objects - reread "
                + "README ex2. Return what Equals says; do not fix it up.");

        Teach.Equal("Reading { Sensor = kiln, Degrees = 20 }", Equality.Describe(a),
            "A record's generated ToString prints the type name and every property. Hand back "
                + "reading.ToString() rather than building the string yourself.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_WithCopiesAndChangesInOneStep()
    {
        Order original = new Order("SKU-1", 2, 10m);

        Order repriced = Orders.Reprice(original, 12m);
        Teach.Equal(new Order("SKU-1", 2, 12m), repriced,
            "Reprice changes the price and copies everything else, Status included - reread "
                + "README ex3.");
        Teach.Equal(10m, original.UnitPrice,
            "`with` never modifies the record you started from. If the original moved, you "
                + "mutated instead of copying - reread README ex3.");

        Order amended = Orders.AddOneUnit(original);
        Teach.Equal(new Order("SKU-1", 3, 10m, "amended"), amended,
            "One `with` expression can set several properties at once - a comma-separated "
                + "list inside the braces.");

        Teach.True(Orders.DiffersOnlyInStatus(
                new Order("SKU-1", 2, 10m, "new"),
                new Order("SKU-1", 2, 10m, "shipped")),
            "Copy one order with the other's status and compare: if they are equal now, the "
                + "status was the only difference - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.True(!Orders.DiffersOnlyInStatus(
                new Order("SKU-1", 2, 10m, "new"),
                new Order("SKU-1", 9, 10m, "new")),
            "Different quantities differ in more than the status.");

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_EqualKeysMustHashTheSame()
    {
        CacheKey key = new CacheKey("eu", 7);
        CacheKey twin = new CacheKey("eu", 7);
        CacheKey other = new CacheKey("us", 7);

        Teach.True(key.Equals(twin),
            "Same region, same id: the same key - reread README ex4.");
        Teach.True(!key.Equals(other),
            "A different region is a different key.");
        Teach.True(!key.Equals("eu"),
            "Equals takes an object, so it can be handed anything at all. Something that is "
                + "not a CacheKey is never equal to one - a type test is the first thing "
                + "Equals does.");
        Teach.True(!key.Equals(null),
            "And null is never equal to a real object. `obj is CacheKey other` handles that "
                + "case for free, which is why it is the idiomatic opening line.");

        Teach.Equal(key.GetHashCode(), twin.GetHashCode(),
            "Two objects that are Equal MUST return the same hash code. Break that and hashed "
                + "collections stop working - reread README ex4.");

        Dictionary<CacheKey, string> cache = new Dictionary<CacheKey, string>
        {
            [key] = "cached value",
        };

        Teach.True(cache.ContainsKey(twin),
            "This is the payoff: a Dictionary finds an entry using a DIFFERENT but equal key "
                + "object, because it hashes to the same bucket and then compares equal. "
                + "Without GetHashCode this lookup fails even though Equals is correct.");

        HashSet<CacheKey> seen = new HashSet<CacheKey> { key, twin, other };
        Teach.Equal(2, seen.Count,
            "A HashSet keeps one of each: key and twin are the same key, so only two remain.");
    }

        Teach.Equal("on the y axis", Geometry.Classify(new Point(0, -2)),

        Teach.Equal("quadrant 2", Geometry.Classify(new Point(-2, 5)), "Left and up.");
        Teach.Equal("quadrant 3", Geometry.Classify(new Point(-2, -5)), "Left and down.");
        Teach.Equal("quadrant 4", Geometry.Classify(new Point(2, -5)), "Right and down.");

                + "`var (x, y) = point;` takes it apart in one line - reread README challenge.");

    [Fact]
    public void Review1_RecordEqualityStopsAtTheReference()
    {
        List<string> firstList = new List<string> { "milk", "bread" };
        List<string> secondList = new List<string> { "milk", "bread" };

        Basket a = new Basket("ada", firstList);
        Basket b = new Basket("ada", secondList);

        Teach.True(!Baskets.RecordSays(a, b),
            "The two lists hold the same strings but ARE different objects, and List<T> uses "
                + "reference equality. A record compares its members with THEIR equality, so "
                + "these baskets are not equal - reread README review.");

        Teach.True(Baskets.RecordSays(a, new Basket("ada", firstList)),
            "Point both records at the SAME list and they are equal again.");

        Teach.True(Baskets.SameContents(a, b),
            "The question a human meant needs a real comparison of the contents.");
        Teach.True(!Baskets.SameContents(a, new Basket("bo", firstList)),
            "A different owner is a different basket, however the items line up.");

        Basket original = new Basket("ada", new List<string> { "milk" });
        Basket renamed = Baskets.Rename(original, "bo");

        Teach.Equal("bo", renamed.Owner, "Rename is a with-expression on the owner.");

        renamed.Items.Add("bread");
        Teach.Equal(2, original.Items.Count,
            "`with` makes a SHALLOW copy: the new record points at the very same list, so "
                + "adding through one is visible through the other. Copying a record does not "
                + "copy what its members point at - reread README review.");
    }
```

In plain English: `Ex1` adds money, checks the original did not move, formats
it, and mixes currencies to see the exception. `Ex2` builds two records and two
class instances with identical data and asks all four questions. `Ex3` checks
each `with` result against a freshly constructed expected record — which works
only because records compare by value. `Ex4` tests `Equals` against a twin, a
different key, a string, and null, then checks the hash codes match and puts
the keys in a `Dictionary` and a `HashSet`. `Challenge` walks all seven
classifications, and `Review1` is the spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The everyday version of this lesson is: **use records for data, classes for
behaviour, structs for small values.** A DTO coming off an HTTP request, an
event in a queue, a query result, a configuration snapshot — all records; they
are data, they should be immutable, and comparing them by value is what you
meant. A service, a repository, a controller — classes; they have identity and
dependencies and no sensible notion of equality.

The `Equals`/`GetHashCode` contract in ex4 is not academic. Break it and you get
one of the nastiest bug classes in .NET: a `Dictionary` that "loses" an entry
you know you added, or a `HashSet` with two items you can see are identical.
The reason is exactly what the gate demonstrates — the lookup hashes to a
bucket first and only compares within it — and the reason `record` exists is
that nobody should have to write those two methods by hand for the hundredth
time.
