# Reading - csharp/06_structs_records

## Notes

**Why mutable structs are a footgun.** Because a struct copies on every
assignment, argument pass and collection read, a mutation can land somewhere
you did not expect. The classic demonstration: put a mutable struct in a
`List<T>` and write `list[0].Value = 5`. C# refuses to compile it, because the
indexer returns a *copy* and the assignment would be silently thrown away —
one of the few places the language protects you from a design mistake rather
than the mistake itself. Arrays are the exception (`array[0].Value = 5` works,
because array indexing gives a real reference), which means the same line
behaves differently for an array and a list. `readonly struct` sidesteps the
whole category by making mutation impossible.

**Records are classes, not magic.** `record Reading(string Sensor, int Degrees)`
compiles to a sealed-ish class with two get-only properties, a constructor, an
`Equals(Reading)` implementing `IEquatable<Reading>`, an `Equals(object)`
override, a `GetHashCode` combining the members, a `ToString` override, a
`Deconstruct`, a protected copy constructor and a `<Clone>$` method that `with`
calls. You can see all of it with a decompiler, and everything you can do by
hand you can still do — declare extra members, override `ToString`, write your
own constructor. The type is ordinary; only the boilerplate is generated.

**Record equality is member-by-member, using each member's own equality.**
Which is why two records holding equal-but-distinct `List<T>`s are not equal:
`List<T>` never overrode `Equals`. This surprises people who read "value
equality" as "deep equality". It is not deep; it is one level, delegating.

**`with` is a shallow copy, for the same reason.** It clones the record's
fields and replaces the ones you named. A field holding a reference is copied
as a reference, so both records share the object. If you need a deep copy you
write it, and the fact that nobody can write a general deep copy for you is
exactly why the language does not pretend to.

**Boxing, properly this time.** Assigning a struct to `object`, or to an
interface variable, allocates a heap box and copies the value in. `object o = someMoney;`
boxes. `IComparable c = someInt;` boxes. Calling an interface method on a
struct through a generic constrained to that interface does *not* box, which is
one of the main reasons generic constraints exist (lesson 07). Boxing matters
in hot loops and in allocation-sensitive code, and it is a [***] interview
question because it demonstrates you know that value types have somewhere else
to be.

## ex1

The signature of `Add` is the lesson: it takes a `Money` and returns a `Money`,
and there is nowhere for a mutation to happen. Compare `DateTime.AddDays`,
`string.ToUpper`, `decimal.Round` — the whole immutable-value vocabulary in
.NET looks like this, and once you notice the pattern you stop expecting
`list.Sort()`-style in-place methods from value types.

Choosing `InvalidOperationException` over `ArgumentException` is a real
distinction worth having an opinion about. `ArgumentException` says "the value
you passed is wrong"; `InvalidOperationException` says "the object is not in a
state where this makes sense". Adding EUR to GBP is arguably either, and the
framework itself is inconsistent about such calls — but the second reads better
here, because neither amount is wrong on its own.

The free memberwise `Equals` you did not write is worth pausing on: it is
implemented in `ValueType.Equals`, and for a struct containing a reference
member (the `string`) it falls back to *reflection over the fields*, which is
correct but slow. Structs used in hot paths or as dictionary keys should
override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` explicitly — or be `record struct`s, which
generate fast ones.

## ex2

Three ways of asking "the same?", three answers, and the reason is inheritance.
`ReadingClass` inherits `object.Equals`, which is `ReferenceEquals`. `Reading`
is a record, so the compiler generated an `Equals` that compares members.
Nothing about the *data* differs; only the type's opinion about identity.

The follow-up interviewers ask: "what does `==` do for a record?" Records
overload `==` to call the generated value equality, which makes them one of the
few reference types where `==` and `Equals` agree. For a plain class, `==` is
reference comparison unless someone overloaded it, and for `string` it was
overloaded to compare text — which is why `"ab" + "c" == "abc"` is true.
Knowing which of those three worlds you are in is the actual skill.

The generated `ToString` format is stable and documented:
`TypeName { Prop = value, Prop = value }`. It exists because the first thing
anyone does with a data object is print it in a log or a debugger, and
`Namespace.Reading` — what a plain class prints — helps nobody.

## ex3

`with` is the immutable-update idiom, and it matters more than it looks.
Immutable data means no method you call can change your object behind your
back, which removes an entire category of bug in concurrent and event-driven
code. The reason immutability used to be painful in C# was the boilerplate:
copying nine properties to change one. `with` deletes that boilerplate, and
that is the whole reason records exist.

`DiffersOnlyInStatus` is worth keeping in your toolkit as a pattern: *normalise
the difference away, then compare*. The by-hand alternative — comparing sku,
quantity and price — is longer, and worse, it silently stops being right when
someone adds a fourth property to `Order`. The `with`-and-compare version keeps
working, because `==` covers whatever the record holds today.

The trap in `AddOneUnit` is reading `with` as a sequence of assignments. It is
not: all the values in the braces are computed against the *original*, and one
new object is constructed from the result. If you write
`order with { Quantity = Quantity + 1 }` inside a member of the record, the
same rule applies.

## ex4

The `Equals`/`GetHashCode` contract is the most consequential unwritten rule in
.NET, and the failure mode is memorable: a dictionary that cannot find a key
you are certain you added. The mechanism is worth being able to draw. A
`Dictionary` computes `key.GetHashCode()`, reduces it to a bucket index, and
only compares (with `Equals`) the entries already in that bucket. Two equal
keys with different hash codes land in different buckets, so the comparison
that would have matched never happens.

The rules, precisely: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects
*may* share one (a collision, handled by the comparison step); and a hash code
must not change while the object is in use as a key. That last one is why keys
should be immutable — mutate a property that feeds the hash and the entry is
stranded in the old bucket forever.

`HashCode.Combine` is the modern answer to "how do I mix several members?" It
implements a proper avalanche mix, so small differences in inputs produce very
different outputs. The old folklore (`hash = hash * 31 + field.GetHashCode()`)
is fine too; XOR-ing fields is not, because `Combine(a, b)` and `Combine(b, a)`
then collide, and so does any pair of equal fields.

`obj is CacheKey other && ...` is worth reading as three checks in one: not
null, right type, and a typed variable to compare with. Before pattern
matching, this took four lines and everybody wrote at least one of them wrong.

## challenge

Positional patterns come from `Deconstruct`, which the record struct generated.
Any type can join in by writing a `Deconstruct` method with `out` parameters —
including your own classes, which is a pleasant way to make a type feel
first-class in modern C#.

Arm order in a switch expression is not a detail: arms are tested top to
bottom, so more specific patterns must come first. The compiler helps in one
direction — it warns about an arm that can never be reached because an earlier
one subsumes it — but it cannot tell you that you *meant* the origin to be
tested before the axes. Exhaustiveness is the other half: the compiler will
warn when it cannot prove every input is handled, which for two unbounded ints
means you always need a catch-all.

Where this pays off is modelling. Once you are comfortable with records plus
positional patterns, "a discriminated union and a match" becomes idiomatic C#:
a hierarchy of records and one switch expression covering them. It is not as
tight as F# or TypeScript, and it is a great deal better than a chain of `if`s
casting to concrete types.

## review1

Two ideas that trip people up for the same underlying reason: a record holds
*references*, and both its equality and its `with` stop at the reference. Two
baskets with equal-looking lists are not equal, because `List<T>` compares by
reference. A renamed basket shares its list with the original, because copying a
reference copies the arrow. One sentence — "a record's value semantics are one
level deep" — covers both, and it is a good sentence to have ready in an
interview.

The practical guidance that follows: when a record must be genuinely immutable,
make its collection members immutable too. `IReadOnlyList<string>` documents the
intent, and `ImmutableArray<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` (in
`System.Collections.Immutable`) enforce it. A record with a `List<T>` inside is
an immutable wrapper around a mutable thing, which is often exactly the bug
report you will spend an afternoon on.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — patterns over a record struct

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Challenge.cs`. `Point` is a
`readonly record struct`. Implement `Classify(Point)` returning `"origin"`,
`"on the x axis"`, `"on the y axis"`, or `"quadrant 1"` through
`"quadrant 4"` (anticlockwise from the top right); and `Mirror(Point)`, which
swaps the coordinates.

Honest difficulty note: the switch itself is easy and the **order of the arms**
is the whole problem — three of your patterns match `(0, 0)`, and only the
first one written wins. Use positional patterns (`(0, 0)`, `(_, 0)`,
`( > 0, > 0)`), which work because a record struct generates `Deconstruct`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Classify` is one `switch` expression with seven arms, and the whole exercise is
their **order**. Three of your arms would happily match `(0, 0)`; only one of
them should get the chance.

`Mirror` is two lines: take the point apart, put a new one together the other
way round.

## Hint 2

Because `Point` is a record struct, it has a generated `Deconstruct`, which
unlocks *positional patterns* — you can match on the parts directly:

```csharp
point switch
{
    (0, 0) => "origin",
    (_, 0) => "on the x axis",
    // ...
}
```

`_` inside a positional pattern means "anything here". Relational patterns work
in the same position: `( > 0, > 0)` is the top-right quadrant.

Deconstruction also works in a declaration: `var (x, y) = point;`.

## Hint 3

Quadrants count anticlockwise from the top right: 1 is (+, +), 2 is (-, +), 3 is
(-, -), 4 is (+, -).

Once the origin and the two axis cases are out of the way, neither coordinate
can be zero, so three relational arms plus a `_` catch-all cover the rest — and
the compiler needs that `_` to prove the switch is exhaustive.

Decision left to you: whether to write the fourth quadrant explicitly as
`( > 0, < 0)` and add a `_` arm that throws. Being explicit and letting the
catch-all be unreachable-but-required is defensible; so is letting `_` be the
fourth quadrant. One of them survives someone adding a third dimension better
than the other.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Classify` is one `switch` expression with seven arms, and the whole exercise is
their **order**. Three of your arms would happily match `(0, 0)`; only one of
them should get the chance.

`Mirror` is two lines: take the point apart, put a new one together the other
way round.

## Hint 2

Because `Point` is a record struct, it has a generated `Deconstruct`, which
unlocks *positional patterns* — you can match on the parts directly:

```csharp
point switch
{
    (0, 0) => "origin",
    (_, 0) => "on the x axis",
    // ...
}
```

`_` inside a positional pattern means "anything here". Relational patterns work
in the same position: `( > 0, > 0)` is the top-right quadrant.

Deconstruction also works in a declaration: `var (x, y) = point;`.

## Hint 3

Quadrants count anticlockwise from the top right: 1 is (+, +), 2 is (-, +), 3 is
(-, -), 4 is (+, -).

Once the origin and the two axis cases are out of the way, neither coordinate
can be zero, so three relational arms plus a `_` catch-all cover the rest — and
the compiler needs that `_` to prove the switch is exhaustive.

Decision left to you: whether to write the fourth quadrant explicitly as
`( > 0, < 0)` and add a `_` arm that throws. Being explicit and letting the
catch-all be unreachable-but-required is defensible; so is letting `_` be the
fourth quadrant. One of them survives someone adding a third dimension better
than the other.

## Exercise 1 — a value type of your own

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Ex1.cs`. `Money` is a `readonly struct`.
Implement `Add(Money other)`, which returns a **new** `Money` holding the sum
and throws `InvalidOperationException` when the currencies differ, and
`ToString()`, which returns `"GBP 5.00"` — currency, space, two decimal places,
formatted with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`.

You cannot assign to `Amount` inside `Add`; the struct is `readonly`. That is
the shape immutable value types take: every operation is a function returning a
new value, exactly like `DateTime.AddDays` or `string.Replace`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 06_structs_records ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two bodies. `Add` has a guard and a return; `ToString` is one interpolated
string.

The thing to notice while you write `Add`: you cannot assign to `Amount`. The
struct is `readonly`, so the only way to "change" money is to produce a
different `Money`. That constraint is the feature.

## Hint 2

The guard compares `other.Currency` with this instance's `Currency` and throws
`InvalidOperationException` when they differ — not `ArgumentException`; the
problem is the *state* the operation was attempted in, not one bad argument.
(Both are defensible; the gate wants the first.)

Then return `new Money(...)` with the summed amount and the shared currency.

For `ToString`, two decimal places and no surprises from the machine's locale:

```csharp
Amount.ToString("0.00", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)
```

The `using System.Globalization;` at the top of the file is already there.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public Money Add(Money other)
{
    if (/* currencies differ */)
    {
        throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot add {other.Currency} to {Currency}.");
    }

    return new Money(/* the sum */, Currency);
}
```

One thing left to look at rather than write: the gate's last check asserts that
two separately constructed `Money` values are `Equals`. You did not implement
that — structs compare memberwise out of the box. Lesson 06's ex4 shows what a
class has to do to earn the same behaviour.

Two bodies. `Add` has a guard and a return; `ToString` is one interpolated

```csharp

    if (/* currencies differ */)

}
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

All three bodies are one line, and all three use the same operator.

`with` produces a copy of a record with some properties replaced:
`order with { Status = "shipped" }`. Everything you do not name is carried over
unchanged, and the record you started from is untouched.

## Hint 2

`AddOneUnit` needs two changes in one copy. The braces take a comma-separated
list:

```csharp
return order with { Quantity = order.Quantity + 1, Status = "amended" };
```

Note that the right-hand side reads `order.Quantity` — the *old* value. A
`with` expression is not a sequence of assignments; every value is computed
from the original.

## Hint 3

`DiffersOnlyInStatus` is the clever one, and the prompt tells you the trick:
make one comparable to the other. Copy `a` with `b`'s status, then compare with
`==`. If they are equal now, status was the only thing that differed.

```csharp
return a with { Status = b.Status } == b;
```

That works because records compare by value, so one `==` covers every remaining
property — including ones added to the record later, which the by-hand version
would silently ignore. Whether you find that clever or too clever is a
legitimate style call; know that it is available.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

All three bodies are one line, and all three use the same operator.

`with` produces a copy of a record with some properties replaced:
`order with { Status = "shipped" }`. Everything you do not name is carried over
unchanged, and the record you started from is untouched.

## Hint 2

`AddOneUnit` needs two changes in one copy. The braces take a comma-separated
list:

```csharp
return order with { Quantity = order.Quantity + 1, Status = "amended" };
```

Note that the right-hand side reads `order.Quantity` — the *old* value. A
`with` expression is not a sequence of assignments; every value is computed
from the original.

## Hint 3

`DiffersOnlyInStatus` is the clever one, and the prompt tells you the trick:
make one comparable to the other. Copy `a` with `b`'s status, then compare with
`==`. If they are equal now, status was the only thing that differed.

```csharp
return a with { Status = b.Status } == b;
```

That works because records compare by value, so one `==` covers every remaining
property — including ones added to the record later, which the by-hand version
would silently ignore. Whether you find that clever or too clever is a
legitimate style call; know that it is available.

## Exercise 4 — earning value equality by hand

Edit `src/Lessons/L06_StructsRecords/Ex4.cs`. `CacheKey` is meant to be a
dictionary key: two keys with the same region and id are the same key. Override
`Equals(object?)` and `GetHashCode()` so that a `Dictionary<CacheKey, string>`
can find an entry using a *different but equal* key object.

`Equals` will be handed nulls and objects of other types — deal with both. And
the two methods must agree: the gate builds a dictionary with one key and looks
it up with the twin, which only works if the hash codes match.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two methods that must agree with each other. `Equals` decides which keys are
the same; `GetHashCode` decides which bucket a key lands in. If they disagree,
a `Dictionary` puts a key in one bucket and then looks for it in another.

`Equals` takes an `object?`, so it can be handed a string, a null, or anything
else. Deal with that first.

## Hint 2

The idiomatic opening is a type-testing pattern, which rules out null and wrong
types in one go:

```csharp
return obj is CacheKey other && /* compare the two properties */;
```

`other` is only in scope when the pattern matched, and the `&&` short-circuits,
so nothing dereferences a null.

For the hash, `HashCode.Combine(Region, Id)` does the right thing — it mixes
the members' own hash codes properly. Adding or XOR-ing them by hand is a
classic source of clustering, where too many keys land in one bucket and your
dictionary degrades to a linear scan.

## Hint 3

The contract, in the order it matters:

1. Equal objects **must** return equal hash codes. (Unequal ones may collide;
   that is allowed and normal.)
2. `GetHashCode` must be stable for as long as the object is a key. Hashing a
   property that can change is how entries get lost inside a live dictionary —
   which is one reason both properties here are get-only.

Left to you: whether to also implement `IEquatable<CacheKey>` for a strongly
typed `Equals` that avoids the cast. The framework will use it when it is
there, and it is what a record generates for you behind the scenes.

`Equals` takes an `object?`, so it can be handed a string, a null, or anything
else. Deal with that first.

## Hint 2

The idiomatic opening is a type-testing pattern, which rules out null and wrong
types in one go:

```csharp
return obj is CacheKey other && /* compare the two properties */;
```

`other` is only in scope when the pattern matched, and the `&&` short-circuits,
so nothing dereferences a null.

For the hash, `HashCode.Combine(Region, Id)` does the right thing — it mixes
the members' own hash codes properly. Adding or XOR-ing them by hand is a
classic source of clustering, where too many keys land in one bucket and your
dictionary degrades to a linear scan.

## Hint 3

The contract, in the order it matters:

1. Equal objects **must** return equal hash codes. (Unequal ones may collide;
   that is allowed and normal.)
2. `GetHashCode` must be stable for as long as the object is a key. Hashing a
   property that can change is how entries get lost inside a live dictionary —
   which is one reason both properties here are get-only.

Left to you: whether to also implement `IEquatable<CacheKey>` for a strongly
typed `Equals` that avoids the cast. The framework will use it when it is
there, and it is what a record generates for you behind the scenes.

lessons.briefing:
# 07 — Generics

Before generics, a collection that could hold anything held `object`, and every
read came back as `object`. You cast on the way out, you found out at *runtime*
when you cast wrong, and every value type you put in got boxed onto the heap.
`ArrayList` still exists in .NET so you can see what that was like. C# 2.0
added generics in 2005 and the entire library was rewritten around them, which
is why `List<T>` is the one you have been using without thinking about it.

A generic type or method has a *type parameter* — a placeholder the caller
fills in. `List<T>` is not a list of objects pretending to be typed; the
runtime creates a genuinely distinct `List<int>` with `int`-shaped storage, no
casts and no boxing. That last detail is where .NET generics differ from
Java's, and it is worth knowing why: Java erases type arguments at compile
time, .NET keeps them at runtime. Hence `typeof(List<int>)` is a real thing you
can ask questions about, and it is how the reflection in this lesson's ex4
works.

## Concept — a parameter that happens to be a type

A generic method declares its parameter in angle brackets:

```csharp
public static T FirstOr<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, T fallback) { ... }

int n  = FirstOr(new[] { 1, 2 }, -1);        // T inferred as int
string s = FirstOr(new List<string>(), "?"); // T inferred as string
```

You rarely write `FirstOr<int>(...)` because the compiler infers `T` from the
arguments. A generic *type* declares its parameters on the type itself:

```csharp
public class Box<T>
{
    public Box(T value) => Value = value;
    public T Value { get; }
}
```

**Constraints say what you may assume about T.** Inside an unconstrained
generic method, `T` might be anything, so you can barely do a thing with it:
no `+`, no `<`, no `new T()`, not even a guaranteed `null`. Constraints buy
those back one at a time:

```csharp
where T : IComparable<T>   // T has CompareTo, so you may order Ts
where T : class            // T is a reference type; null is available
where T : struct           // T is a non-nullable value type
where T : new()            // T has a public parameterless constructor
where T : notnull          // T is never null - what Dictionary<TKey,...> wants
where T : Shape            // T derives from Shape, so Shape's members are available
```

Several can be combined (`where T : class, IDisposable, new()`), and each type
parameter gets its own clause.

**Variance says which conversions are allowed.** An `IProducer<string>` and an
`IProducer<object>` are, by default, unrelated types — even though every string
is an object. Annotating the parameter changes that:

```csharp
public interface IProducer<out T> { T Produce(); }     // covariant: T only comes OUT
public interface IConsumer<in T> { void Consume(T x); } // contravariant: T only goes IN

IProducer<object> p = someStringProducer;   // legal with `out`
IConsumer<string> c = someObjectConsumer;   // legal with `in`
```

You have already used both without noticing: `IEnumerable<out T>` is why a
`List<string>` can be passed to a method taking `IEnumerable<object>`, and
`Action<in T>`/`IComparer<in T>` are contravariant for the same reason in
reverse. The compiler enforces the safety condition — a covariant `T` may only
appear in output positions — which is precisely the check that C# arrays skip,
and why `object[] a = new string[1]; a[0] = 42;` compiles and then throws.

**Generic maths, briefly.** Since .NET 7, interfaces can require *static*
members, which finally makes "sum any numeric type" expressible:
`where T : INumber<T>` gives you `T.Zero`, the operators, and
`T.CreateChecked`. That is the challenge.

## Exercise 1 — one method, any element type

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex1.cs`. Implement `FirstOr<T>` (the first item,
or the fallback when the sequence is empty), `Swap<T>(ref T, ref T)`, and
`CountOf<T>`.

None of the three may name a concrete type, and none needs a constraint —
because none of them asks anything of `T` beyond existing. Notice on the way
past that `FirstOr` cannot return `null` for "nothing found": `T` might be an
`int`, which is exactly why the fallback is a parameter.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — constraints, and what each one buys

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex2.cs`. `Max<T>` is constrained
`where T : IComparable<T>` and returns the largest item, throwing
`InvalidOperationException` for an empty sequence. `Fill<T>` is constrained
`where T : new()` and returns a list of `count` freshly constructed `T`s.

The seeding question in `Max` is the interesting one: you cannot start from `0`
and you cannot start from `default(T)` — the gate passes a set of negative
numbers precisely to catch that. Take the first item you actually see.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a generic type of your own

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex3.cs`. `Result<T>` holds either a value or a
reason there isn't one. The private constructor is written; implement the two
static factories `Ok` and `Fail`, and the `Value` and `Error` properties.

`Value` on a failed result must throw `InvalidOperationException`, not hand
back `default(T)`. A silent zero that means "no answer" travels a long way
before anything notices.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — variance

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex4.cs`. The two method bodies are
`return producer;` and `return consumer;` — and they do not compile until you
annotate each interface's type parameter. `IProducer<T>` only ever hands a `T`
out, so it wants `out`. `IConsumer<T>` only ever takes a `T` in, so it wants
`in`.

Write the returns first, read the errors, then fix the interfaces. The gate
also reflects over both interfaces to check the annotations landed.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex4
```

## Challenge — one algorithm for every numeric type

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Challenge.cs`. Implement `Total<T>` and
`Average<T>`, both constrained `where T : INumber<T>`, so they work over
`int[]`, `double[]` and `decimal[]` alike. `Average` throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence.

Honest difficulty note: the loop is trivial and the two unfamiliar pieces are
`T.Zero` (the additive identity, whatever `T` is) and `T.CreateChecked(count)`
(turning the `int` count into a `T` so the division type-checks). Static
abstract interface members are recent and genuinely strange the first time; the
hints walk you through them.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is two more constrained generic methods — `FirstAbove` and
`CountBetween` — where the words "strictly" and "inclusive" decide the
comparison. `dojo review` will bring it back.

# Reading - csharp/07_generics

## Notes

**Reified generics, and why they matter.** .NET keeps type arguments at
runtime. The JIT compiles a separate machine-code specialisation for each value
type argument — `List<int>` really does store ints inline, with no boxing — and
shares one specialisation among all reference types, since every reference is
the same size. Java, by contrast, *erases* type arguments: `List<String>` and
`List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime, everything is boxed, and you
cannot ask an object what its element type is. The practical consequences in C#
are that `typeof(List<int>) != typeof(List<string>)`, that reflection can
inspect type arguments (which is how ex4's gate works, and how JSON
serialisers and DI containers work), and that generic collections of value
types are genuinely fast.

**Constraints are a contract in both directions.** They tell the compiler what
the body may do with `T`, and they tell callers what types are allowed. Adding
one is a breaking change for callers; removing one is a breaking change for the
body. So the discipline is: add the fewest constraints that let you write the
method. `where T : notnull` in particular is what `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`
requires of its key, and it is a nullable-annotation constraint rather than a
runtime one.

**Where generic code cannot go.** You cannot constrain to "has a `+` operator"
(before .NET 7), cannot constrain to a specific constructor signature other
than the parameterless one, and cannot write `where T : Enum`... except that
you now can, since C# 7.3. The general shape of the gaps: the CLR's constraint
system is deliberately simple, and generic maths finally filled the biggest
hole by letting interfaces declare `static abstract` members.

**`default(T)` is a trap worth naming.** For a reference type it is `null`, for
a numeric it is `0`, for a `bool` it is `false`, for a struct it is the
all-zero value. So `default(T)` as "no result" is ambiguous exactly when `0` or
`false` is a legitimate result. That is why `FirstOrDefault` has a
`FirstOrDefault(source, defaultValue)` overload now, why the `Try...` pattern
returns a `bool`, and why ex3's `Result<T>` exists.

**Variance in one line each.** Covariance (`out`) preserves the direction of
the type relationship: `IEnumerable<string>` is an `IEnumerable<object>`.
Contravariance (`in`) reverses it: an `Action<object>` is an `Action<string>`.
Invariance is neither, and is the default — `List<string>` is *not* a
`List<object>`, and it must not be, because you could then add an `int` to it.

## ex1

The three methods have no constraints because they need none: they store,
return and count `T`s without asking anything of them. That is the cleanest
case for generics, and it is worth noticing how much you *cannot* do in such a
method — no comparison, no arithmetic, no `null` check that means anything.

`ref` is the other half of ex1. A `ref` parameter is an alias for the caller's
variable, so `Swap` assigns to the caller's storage directly. It is one of
three modifiers in the family: `ref` (read and write), `out` (write only, must
assign), `in` (read only, avoids copying a large struct). C# also requires
`ref` at the *call* site, which is unusual among languages and deliberate:
seeing `Swap(ref a, ref b)` tells a reader that `a` and `b` may change, without
looking up the signature.

The LINQ note in the hints is not a throwaway. `FirstOrDefault` and `Count()`
are exactly these methods, already written, tested and optimised — `Count()`
even checks whether the sequence is secretly an `ICollection<T>` and asks for
its `Count` rather than walking it. Writing them by hand once means the LINQ
version is a shortcut rather than a mystery.

## ex2

Each constraint unlocks precisely one capability, and the exercise is designed
so you feel the lack. Without `IComparable<T>`, `item.CompareTo(best)` does not
compile — because `T` could be a `Random`, and `Random` has no ordering. The
constraint is you telling the compiler which types are allowed, so the compiler
can let you write the body.

The seeding problem in `Max` is a genuine generic-programming difficulty. In
non-generic code you would start `best` at `int.MinValue`; there is no such
value for an arbitrary `T`. The two honest options are a `seenAny` flag or
splitting the first element out with an enumerator (`if (!e.MoveNext()) throw;`),
and LINQ's own `Max` uses the second. Returning `default(T)` for an empty
sequence would be the third, and it is exactly what `Max` deliberately does not
do — because `0` is a plausible maximum and "there wasn't one" is not the same
statement.

`new()` is the weakest constraint in practice, because it only promises a
*parameterless* constructor, and most real types need arguments. That is why
factory *functions* (`Func<T>`, lesson 09) and dependency-injection containers
exist: they express "here is how to make one" without the type having to
support a no-argument construction.

## ex3

`Result<T>` is a small, real design worth carrying with you: it makes "this
might have failed" part of the return *type*, so a caller cannot accidentally
ignore it the way they can ignore an exception they never thought about. Rust
and F# and Go all lean on this pattern; C# is starting to, and every ASP.NET
Core codebase eventually grows one.

The static factory methods (`Ok`, `Fail`) are the other pattern here.
Constructors have a fixed name, so when a type has two meaningfully different
ways to come into existence, factories give each one a name and let you hide the
constructor. `TimeSpan.FromMinutes`, `Task.FromResult` and
`ImmutableArray.Create` are the framework doing the same thing.

The choice to have `Value` throw is the important one, and the reasoning
generalises: **fail where the mistake is, not three method calls later**. A
`Result` that hands back `default(T)` when it failed produces a `0` that means
"no answer" and a `null` that means "no answer", and both of those look exactly
like real data until they cause a wrong number in a report.

## ex4

Variance is where generics stop being obvious, and the way to remember it is by
direction of data flow. If a type only ever *produces* `T`, it is safe to treat
it as producing something more general — hence `out`, hence
`IEnumerable<out T>`. If it only ever *consumes* `T`, it is safe to treat it as
consuming something more specific — hence `in`, hence `Action<in T>` and
`IComparer<in T>`. If it does both, neither is safe, and the type must be
invariant: `List<T>` and `IList<T>` are invariant for exactly this reason.

The compiler enforces the condition at declaration time, which is why you get
an error if you add a `void Accept(T item)` to a covariant interface. That
check is what makes variance sound, and it is what C# arrays lack: `string[]`
is treated as `object[]`, which was a Java-era decision, and the price is a
runtime `ArrayTypeMismatchException` on the store instead of a compile error.
Being able to explain that trade is a solid interview answer.

Note that variance applies only to interfaces and delegates, and only to
reference type arguments. `IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`,
because boxing an `int` changes its representation and the conversion cannot be
a no-op reference reinterpretation.

## challenge

Static abstract interface members are the newest thing in this course.
`INumber<T>` declares `static abstract T Zero { get; }`, so the *type* `T` — not
an instance — must supply it, and `T.Zero` inside your generic method resolves
at compile time to whichever type was substituted. That closes a hole that made
"sum any number" genuinely impossible to express for twenty years; the old
workarounds involved `dynamic`, expression trees, or a switch over `typeof(T)`.

`T.CreateChecked(count)` is the generic conversion. The family is
`CreateChecked` (throws if the value does not fit), `CreateSaturating` (clamps
to the type's range) and `CreateTruncating` (wraps). Being asked to pick one is
the same "what should happen when this cannot be represented?" question that
lesson 01's `SafeAdd` asked, generalised.

Counting and summing in one pass is not premature optimisation. An
`IEnumerable<T>` might be a database query, a file being read, or a generator —
walking it twice can be slow, or wrong, or impossible. That habit is the whole
subject of lesson 10 ex3.

## review1

Both methods are `CompareTo` in a loop, and the review is really checking two
things: that you reach for `CompareTo` rather than `<` when `T` is generic, and
that you translate specification words into the right comparison. "Strictly
greater" is `> 0`; "inclusive" is `>= 0` and `<= 0`. Getting a boundary wrong is
the most common bug in this kind of code, which is why every gate in this
course tests the boundary rather than the middle.

`FirstAbove` returning early is worth a thought too: it stops as soon as it has
an answer, which for a lazy or expensive sequence is the difference between
reading one item and reading a million. LINQ's `First` does the same, and
knowing which operators are lazy and which are greedy is lesson 10.

## Further reading

- [Generics in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/) — the overview, including what the runtime does with type arguments.
- [Constraints on type parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters) — every constraint, with what each one permits.
- [Covariance and contravariance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/concepts/covariance-contravariance/) — with the list of variant interfaces and delegates in the BCL.
- [Generic math](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/math) — `INumber<T>`, static abstract members, and the `Create*` conversions.
- [`default` operator](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/default) — what `default(T)` produces for each kind of type.

# 07 — Generics

Before generics, a collection that could hold anything held `object`, and every
read came back as `object`. You cast on the way out, you found out at *runtime*
when you cast wrong, and every value type you put in got boxed onto the heap.
`ArrayList` still exists in .NET so you can see what that was like. C# 2.0
added generics in 2005 and the entire library was rewritten around them, which
is why `List<T>` is the one you have been using without thinking about it.

A generic type or method has a *type parameter* — a placeholder the caller
fills in. `List<T>` is not a list of objects pretending to be typed; the
runtime creates a genuinely distinct `List<int>` with `int`-shaped storage, no
casts and no boxing. That last detail is where .NET generics differ from
Java's, and it is worth knowing why: Java erases type arguments at compile
time, .NET keeps them at runtime. Hence `typeof(List<int>)` is a real thing you
can ask questions about, and it is how the reflection in this lesson's ex4
works.

## Concept — a parameter that happens to be a type

A generic method declares its parameter in angle brackets:

```csharp
public static T FirstOr<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, T fallback) { ... }

int n  = FirstOr(new[] { 1, 2 }, -1);        // T inferred as int
string s = FirstOr(new List<string>(), "?"); // T inferred as string
```

You rarely write `FirstOr<int>(...)` because the compiler infers `T` from the
arguments. A generic *type* declares its parameters on the type itself:

```csharp
public class Box<T>
{
    public Box(T value) => Value = value;
    public T Value { get; }
}
```

**Constraints say what you may assume about T.** Inside an unconstrained
generic method, `T` might be anything, so you can barely do a thing with it:
no `+`, no `<`, no `new T()`, not even a guaranteed `null`. Constraints buy
those back one at a time:

```csharp
where T : IComparable<T>   // T has CompareTo, so you may order Ts
where T : class            // T is a reference type; null is available
where T : struct           // T is a non-nullable value type
where T : new()            // T has a public parameterless constructor
where T : notnull          // T is never null - what Dictionary<TKey,...> wants
where T : Shape            // T derives from Shape, so Shape's members are available
```

Several can be combined (`where T : class, IDisposable, new()`), and each type
parameter gets its own clause.

**Variance says which conversions are allowed.** An `IProducer<string>` and an
`IProducer<object>` are, by default, unrelated types — even though every string
is an object. Annotating the parameter changes that:

```csharp
public interface IProducer<out T> { T Produce(); }     // covariant: T only comes OUT
public interface IConsumer<in T> { void Consume(T x); } // contravariant: T only goes IN

IProducer<object> p = someStringProducer;   // legal with `out`
IConsumer<string> c = someObjectConsumer;   // legal with `in`
```

You have already used both without noticing: `IEnumerable<out T>` is why a
`List<string>` can be passed to a method taking `IEnumerable<object>`, and
`Action<in T>`/`IComparer<in T>` are contravariant for the same reason in
reverse. The compiler enforces the safety condition — a covariant `T` may only
appear in output positions — which is precisely the check that C# arrays skip,
and why `object[] a = new string[1]; a[0] = 42;` compiles and then throws.

**Generic maths, briefly.** Since .NET 7, interfaces can require *static*
members, which finally makes "sum any numeric type" expressible:
`where T : INumber<T>` gives you `T.Zero`, the operators, and
`T.CreateChecked`. That is the challenge.

## Exercise 1 — one method, any element type

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex1.cs`. Implement `FirstOr<T>` (the first item,
or the fallback when the sequence is empty), `Swap<T>(ref T, ref T)`, and
`CountOf<T>`.

None of the three may name a concrete type, and none needs a constraint —
because none of them asks anything of `T` beyond existing. Notice on the way
past that `FirstOr` cannot return `null` for "nothing found": `T` might be an
`int`, which is exactly why the fallback is a parameter.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — constraints, and what each one buys

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex2.cs`. `Max<T>` is constrained
`where T : IComparable<T>` and returns the largest item, throwing
`InvalidOperationException` for an empty sequence. `Fill<T>` is constrained
`where T : new()` and returns a list of `count` freshly constructed `T`s.

The seeding question in `Max` is the interesting one: you cannot start from `0`
and you cannot start from `default(T)` — the gate passes a set of negative
numbers precisely to catch that. Take the first item you actually see.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a generic type of your own

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex3.cs`. `Result<T>` holds either a value or a
reason there isn't one. The private constructor is written; implement the two
static factories `Ok` and `Fail`, and the `Value` and `Error` properties.

`Value` on a failed result must throw `InvalidOperationException`, not hand
back `default(T)`. A silent zero that means "no answer" travels a long way
before anything notices.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — variance

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex4.cs`. The two method bodies are
`return producer;` and `return consumer;` — and they do not compile until you
annotate each interface's type parameter. `IProducer<T>` only ever hands a `T`
out, so it wants `out`. `IConsumer<T>` only ever takes a `T` in, so it wants
`in`.

Write the returns first, read the errors, then fix the interfaces. The gate
also reflects over both interfaces to check the annotations landed.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex4
```

## Challenge — one algorithm for every numeric type

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Challenge.cs`. Implement `Total<T>` and
`Average<T>`, both constrained `where T : INumber<T>`, so they work over
`int[]`, `double[]` and `decimal[]` alike. `Average` throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence.

Honest difficulty note: the loop is trivial and the two unfamiliar pieces are
`T.Zero` (the additive identity, whatever `T` is) and `T.CreateChecked(count)`
(turning the `int` count into a `T` so the division type-checks). Static
abstract interface members are recent and genuinely strange the first time; the
hints walk you through them.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is two more constrained generic methods — `FirstAbove` and
`CountBetween` — where the words "strictly" and "inclusive" decide the
comparison. `dojo review` will bring it back.

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L07_GenericsTests.cs`:

```csharp
using System.Reflection;

using CSharpDojo.L07_Generics;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L07_GenericsTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_OneMethodServesEveryElementType()
    {
        Teach.Equal(10, Utils.FirstOr(new[] { 10, 20 }, -1),
            "The first item of a non-empty sequence - reread README ex1.");
        Teach.Equal(-1, Utils.FirstOr(Array.Empty<int>(), -1),
            "Nothing to take, so the fallback comes back. Note you cannot write `return null` "
                + "here: T might be an int - reread README ex1.");
        Teach.Equal("none", Utils.FirstOr(new List<string>(), "none"),
            "The same method, a different T, no cast anywhere.");

        string first = "left";
        string second = "right";
        Utils.Swap(ref first, ref second);

        Teach.Equal("right", first,
            "Swap must exchange the CALLER's variables, which is what ref means - reread "
                + "README ex1.");
        Teach.Equal("left", second, "And the other way for the second one.");

        Teach.Equal(3, Utils.CountOf(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }), "Three items.");
        Teach.Equal(0, Utils.CountOf(Array.Empty<string>()), "No items.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_ConstraintsUnlockWhatYouCanDoWithT()
    {
        Teach.Equal(9, Constrained.Max(new[] { 3, 9, 2 }),
            "IComparable<T> is what makes item.CompareTo(best) legal - without the constraint "
                + "the compiler will not let you compare two Ts at all - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal("pear", Constrained.Max(new[] { "apple", "pear", "fig" }),
            "string implements IComparable<string>, so the same method sorts words - and "
                + "\"pear\" is last alphabetically here.");

        Teach.Equal(-2, Constrained.Max(new[] { -9, -2, -5 }),
            "Seeding your running maximum with 0 or default(T) instead of the first item is "
                + "the classic bug: every value here is negative.");

        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => Constrained.Max(Array.Empty<int>()),
            "There is no largest item in an empty sequence, and default(T) would be a lie - "
                + "throw InvalidOperationException, which is what LINQ's own Max does.");

        List<Widget> made = Constrained.Fill<Widget>(3);
        Teach.Equal(3, made.Count, "Fill produces exactly count items - reread README ex2.");
        Teach.True(made[0] is not null && !ReferenceEquals(made[0], made[1]),
            "Each item must be a SEPARATE new T(). Adding the same instance three times is a "
                + "different thing entirely.");
    }

    public sealed class Widget
    {
        public int Value { get; set; }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_ResultCarriesEitherAValueOrAReason()
    {
        Result<int> ok = Result<int>.Ok(42);

        Teach.True(ok.IsOk, "Ok produces a successful result - reread README ex3.");
        Teach.Equal(42, ok.Value, "...carrying the value it was given.");
        Teach.Equal("", ok.Error, "A successful result has nothing to explain, so Error is \"\".");

        Result<int> failed = Result<int>.Fail("not found");

        Teach.True(!failed.IsOk, "Fail produces a failed result.");
        Teach.Equal("not found", failed.Error, "...carrying the reason.");
        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => _ = failed.Value,
            "Asking a failed Result for its value must throw rather than hand back a silent "
                + "default(T) - a zero that means \"no answer\" is how bad data spreads - "
                + "reread README ex3.");

        Result<string> text = Result<string>.Ok("hello");
        Teach.Equal("hello", text.Value,
            "The same generic type at a different T, with no casting and no boxing.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_VarianceDecidesWhichConversionsAreLegal()
    {
        Type producerParameter = typeof(IProducer<>).GetGenericArguments()[0];
        Teach.True(producerParameter.GenericParameterAttributes.HasFlag(GenericParameterAttributes.Covariant),
            "IProducer only ever hands a T out, so its parameter should be COVARIANT: declare "
                + "it `out T` - reread README ex4.");

        Type consumerParameter = typeof(IConsumer<>).GetGenericArguments()[0];
        Teach.True(consumerParameter.GenericParameterAttributes.HasFlag(GenericParameterAttributes.Contravariant),
            "IConsumer only ever takes a T in, so its parameter should be CONTRAVARIANT: "
                + "declare it `in T` - reread README ex4.");

        object produced = Variance.Widen(new GreetingProducer()).Produce();
        Teach.Equal("hello", produced,
            "Widen just returns its argument: with `out T`, an IProducer<string> already IS an "
                + "IProducer<object> and no conversion code is needed - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal("consumed abc", Variance.Narrow(new AnythingConsumer()).Consume("abc"),
            "And with `in T`, a consumer of objects already IS a consumer of strings.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Challenge_OneSumForEveryNumericType()
    {
        Teach.Equal(6, Statistics.Total(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }),
            "T.Zero is the generic way to say \"the additive identity of whatever T is\" - "
                + "reread README challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(4.0, Statistics.Total(new[] { 1.5, 2.5 }),
            "The same method over doubles.");
        Teach.Equal(3.3m, Statistics.Total(new[] { 1.1m, 2.2m }),
            "...and over decimals, where 1.1 + 2.2 is exactly 3.3.");
        Teach.Equal(0, Statistics.Total(Array.Empty<int>()),
            "The sum of nothing is zero, and T.Zero already said so.");

        Teach.Equal(4, Statistics.Average(new[] { 2, 4, 6 }),
            "12 over 3. Turning the int count into a T is the interesting line: "
                + "T.CreateChecked(count) - reread README challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(2.5, Statistics.Average(new[] { 2.0, 3.0 }),
            "Over doubles the same code gives a fractional answer.");
        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => Statistics.Average(Array.Empty<double>()),
            "Dividing by zero items is undefined - throw rather than returning NaN.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Review1_ConstrainedGenericsOverTwoDifferentTs()
    {
        Teach.Equal(7, Thresholds.FirstAbove(new[] { 2, 5, 7, 9 }, 5, -1),
            "Strictly greater: 5 itself does not qualify - reread README review.");
        Teach.Equal(-1, Thresholds.FirstAbove(new[] { 1, 2 }, 99, -1),
            "Nothing qualifies, so the fallback comes back.");
        Teach.Equal("cat", Thresholds.FirstAbove(new[] { "ant", "cat", "dog" }, "b", "none"),
            "The same method over strings, comparing alphabetically.");

        Teach.Equal(3, Thresholds.CountBetween(new[] { 1, 5, 7, 9, 12 }, 5, 9),
            "Inclusive at both ends: 5, 7 and 9 all count - reread README review.");
        Teach.Equal(0, Thresholds.CountBetween(Array.Empty<int>(), 0, 10),
            "Nothing in an empty sequence falls anywhere.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: `Ex1` calls each method at two different `T`s, including the
empty cases, and checks `Swap` really moved the caller's variables. `Ex2`
checks `Max` over ints, strings and all-negative ints, the empty throw, and
that `Fill` produced distinct instances. `Ex3` walks a successful and a failed
`Result`, including the throw. `Ex4` reflects over both interfaces for the
variance annotations and then exercises the conversions. `Challenge` sums three
different numeric types, and `Review1` is the spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The rule of thumb for when to make something generic: **when the algorithm is
genuinely the same and only the type differs.** `FirstOr` is a real candidate —
the logic has nothing to do with what is in the sequence. A method that takes a
`T` and then immediately switches on `typeof(T)` is not: that is a normal
method wearing a costume, and it will be harder to read than the two methods it
replaced.

The constraint half of the rule is where the design lives. Every constraint you
add makes the method more capable and less applicable, so add the fewest that
let you write the body. When you find yourself wanting five constraints, that
is usually the signal to pass an interface — or, once lesson 09 gives you
delegates, a function — instead of demanding the type have the members baked in.

Next: **08_collections**, where the generic types you have been handed —
`List<T>`, `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` and their relatives — finally get taught
properly.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **07 — Generics**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex3` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `review1` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `challenge` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex1` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex2` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex3` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - csharp/07_generics

## Notes

**Reified generics, and why they matter.** .NET keeps type arguments at
runtime. The JIT compiles a separate machine-code specialisation for each value
type argument — `List<int>` really does store ints inline, with no boxing — and
shares one specialisation among all reference types, since every reference is
the same size. Java, by contrast, *erases* type arguments: `List<String>` and
`List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime, everything is boxed, and you
cannot ask an object what its element type is. The practical consequences in C#
are that `typeof(List<int>) != typeof(List<string>)`, that reflection can
inspect type arguments (which is how ex4's gate works, and how JSON
serialisers and DI containers work), and that generic collections of value
types are genuinely fast.

**Constraints are a contract in both directions.** They tell the compiler what
the body may do with `T`, and they tell callers what types are allowed. Adding
one is a breaking change for callers; removing one is a breaking change for the
body. So the discipline is: add the fewest constraints that let you write the
method. `where T : notnull` in particular is what `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`
requires of its key, and it is a nullable-annotation constraint rather than a
runtime one.

**Where generic code cannot go.** You cannot constrain to "has a `+` operator"
(before .NET 7), cannot constrain to a specific constructor signature other
than the parameterless one, and cannot write `where T : Enum`... except that
you now can, since C# 7.3. The general shape of the gaps: the CLR's constraint
system is deliberately simple, and generic maths finally filled the biggest
hole by letting interfaces declare `static abstract` members.

**`default(T)` is a trap worth naming.** For a reference type it is `null`, for
a numeric it is `0`, for a `bool` it is `false`, for a struct it is the
all-zero value. So `default(T)` as "no result" is ambiguous exactly when `0` or
`false` is a legitimate result. That is why `FirstOrDefault` has a
`FirstOrDefault(source, defaultValue)` overload now, why the `Try...` pattern
returns a `bool`, and why ex3's `Result<T>` exists.

**Variance in one line each.** Covariance (`out`) preserves the direction of
the type relationship: `IEnumerable<string>` is an `IEnumerable<object>`.
Contravariance (`in`) reverses it: an `Action<object>` is an `Action<string>`.
Invariance is neither, and is the default — `List<string>` is *not* a
`List<object>`, and it must not be, because you could then add an `int` to it.

## ex1

The three methods have no constraints because they need none: they store,
return and count `T`s without asking anything of them. That is the cleanest
case for generics, and it is worth noticing how much you *cannot* do in such a
method — no comparison, no arithmetic, no `null` check that means anything.

`ref` is the other half of ex1. A `ref` parameter is an alias for the caller's
variable, so `Swap` assigns to the caller's storage directly. It is one of
three modifiers in the family: `ref` (read and write), `out` (write only, must
assign), `in` (read only, avoids copying a large struct). C# also requires
`ref` at the *call* site, which is unusual among languages and deliberate:
seeing `Swap(ref a, ref b)` tells a reader that `a` and `b` may change, without
looking up the signature.

The LINQ note in the hints is not a throwaway. `FirstOrDefault` and `Count()`
are exactly these methods, already written, tested and optimised — `Count()`
even checks whether the sequence is secretly an `ICollection<T>` and asks for
its `Count` rather than walking it. Writing them by hand once means the LINQ
version is a shortcut rather than a mystery.

## ex2

Each constraint unlocks precisely one capability, and the exercise is designed
so you feel the lack. Without `IComparable<T>`, `item.CompareTo(best)` does not
compile — because `T` could be a `Random`, and `Random` has no ordering. The
constraint is you telling the compiler which types are allowed, so the compiler
can let you write the body.

The seeding problem in `Max` is a genuine generic-programming difficulty. In
non-generic code you would start `best` at `int.MinValue`; there is no such
value for an arbitrary `T`. The two honest options are a `seenAny` flag or
splitting the first element out with an enumerator (`if (!e.MoveNext()) throw;`),
and LINQ's own `Max` uses the second. Returning `default(T)` for an empty
sequence would be the third, and it is exactly what `Max` deliberately does not
do — because `0` is a plausible maximum and "there wasn't one" is not the same
statement.

`new()` is the weakest constraint in practice, because it only promises a
*parameterless* constructor, and most real types need arguments. That is why
factory *functions* (`Func<T>`, lesson 09) and dependency-injection containers
exist: they express "here is how to make one" without the type having to
support a no-argument construction.

## ex3

`Result<T>` is a small, real design worth carrying with you: it makes "this
might have failed" part of the return *type*, so a caller cannot accidentally
ignore it the way they can ignore an exception they never thought about. Rust
and F# and Go all lean on this pattern; C# is starting to, and every ASP.NET
Core codebase eventually grows one.

The static factory methods (`Ok`, `Fail`) are the other pattern here.
Constructors have a fixed name, so when a type has two meaningfully different
ways to come into existence, factories give each one a name and let you hide the
constructor. `TimeSpan.FromMinutes`, `Task.FromResult` and
`ImmutableArray.Create` are the framework doing the same thing.

The choice to have `Value` throw is the important one, and the reasoning
generalises: **fail where the mistake is, not three method calls later**. A
`Result` that hands back `default(T)` when it failed produces a `0` that means
"no answer" and a `null` that means "no answer", and both of those look exactly
like real data until they cause a wrong number in a report.

## ex4

Variance is where generics stop being obvious, and the way to remember it is by
direction of data flow. If a type only ever *produces* `T`, it is safe to treat
it as producing something more general — hence `out`, hence
`IEnumerable<out T>`. If it only ever *consumes* `T`, it is safe to treat it as
consuming something more specific — hence `in`, hence `Action<in T>` and
`IComparer<in T>`. If it does both, neither is safe, and the type must be
invariant: `List<T>` and `IList<T>` are invariant for exactly this reason.

The compiler enforces the condition at declaration time, which is why you get
an error if you add a `void Accept(T item)` to a covariant interface. That
check is what makes variance sound, and it is what C# arrays lack: `string[]`
is treated as `object[]`, which was a Java-era decision, and the price is a
runtime `ArrayTypeMismatchException` on the store instead of a compile error.
Being able to explain that trade is a solid interview answer.

Note that variance applies only to interfaces and delegates, and only to
reference type arguments. `IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`,
because boxing an `int` changes its representation and the conversion cannot be
a no-op reference reinterpretation.

## challenge

Static abstract interface members are the newest thing in this course.
`INumber<T>` declares `static abstract T Zero { get; }`, so the *type* `T` — not
an instance — must supply it, and `T.Zero` inside your generic method resolves
at compile time to whichever type was substituted. That closes a hole that made
"sum any number" genuinely impossible to express for twenty years; the old
workarounds involved `dynamic`, expression trees, or a switch over `typeof(T)`.

`T.CreateChecked(count)` is the generic conversion. The family is
`CreateChecked` (throws if the value does not fit), `CreateSaturating` (clamps
to the type's range) and `CreateTruncating` (wraps). Being asked to pick one is
the same "what should happen when this cannot be represented?" question that
lesson 01's `SafeAdd` asked, generalised.

Counting and summing in one pass is not premature optimisation. An
`IEnumerable<T>` might be a database query, a file being read, or a generator —
walking it twice can be slow, or wrong, or impossible. That habit is the whole
subject of lesson 10 ex3.

## review1

Both methods are `CompareTo` in a loop, and the review is really checking two
things: that you reach for `CompareTo` rather than `<` when `T` is generic, and
that you translate specification words into the right comparison. "Strictly
greater" is `> 0`; "inclusive" is `>= 0` and `<= 0`. Getting a boundary wrong is
the most common bug in this kind of code, which is why every gate in this
course tests the boundary rather than the middle.

`FirstAbove` returning early is worth a thought too: it stops as soon as it has
an answer, which for a lazy or expensive sequence is the difference between
reading one item and reading a million. LINQ's `First` does the same, and
knowing which operators are lazy and which are greedy is lesson 10.

## Further reading

- [Generics in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/) — the overview, including what the runtime does with type arguments.
- [Constraints on type parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters) — every constraint, with what each one permits.
- [Covariance and contravariance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/concepts/covariance-contravariance/) — with the list of variant interfaces and delegates in the BCL.
- [Generic math](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/math) — `INumber<T>`, static abstract members, and the `Create*` conversions.
- [`default` operator](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/default) — what `default(T)` produces for each kind of type.

## Challenge — one algorithm for every numeric type

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Challenge.cs`. Implement `Total<T>` and
`Average<T>`, both constrained `where T : INumber<T>`, so they work over
`int[]`, `double[]` and `decimal[]` alike. `Average` throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence.

Honest difficulty note: the loop is trivial and the two unfamiliar pieces are
`T.Zero` (the additive identity, whatever `T` is) and `T.CreateChecked(count)`
(turning the `int` count into a `T` so the division type-checks). Static
abstract interface members are recent and genuinely strange the first time; the
hints walk you through them.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are the accumulate-in-a-loop shape you have written four times
now. The new thing is the constraint: `where T : INumber<T>` says T is a
number, which is what lets you use `+` and `/` on two Ts at all.

The problem it solves: what do you initialise the running total to, when you do
not know whether T is `int`, `double` or `decimal`?

## Hint 2

`T.Zero` — a *static abstract member* on the interface, new since .NET 7. The
interface can demand statics, so `T.Zero`, `T.One` and `T.CreateChecked(...)`
are all available through the constraint.

```csharp
T total = T.Zero;
foreach (T value in values)
{
    total += value;
}
```

`Average` needs to divide by the count. `count` is an `int` and the total is a
`T`, and C# will not mix them — `T.CreateChecked(count)` converts, throwing if
the value would not fit.

## Hint 3

Count and total in the *same* loop rather than calling `Total` and then
counting separately: an `IEnumerable<T>` may be a lazy sequence that is
expensive (or impossible) to walk twice. That habit is exactly what lesson 10's
deferred-execution exercise is about, and it starts here.

The empty check comes after the loop, when you know the count, and throws
`InvalidOperationException` — the same choice `Max` made in ex2.

Left to you: whether to use `T.CreateChecked` or `T.CreateSaturating`. The
first throws on overflow and the second clamps; for a count either is fine, and
knowing they are different is the point.

## Exercise 1 — one method, any element type

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex1.cs`. Implement `FirstOr<T>` (the first item,
or the fallback when the sequence is empty), `Swap<T>(ref T, ref T)`, and
`CountOf<T>`.

None of the three may name a concrete type, and none needs a constraint —
because none of them asks anything of `T` beyond existing. Notice on the way
past that `FirstOr` cannot return `null` for "nothing found": `T` might be an
`int`, which is exactly why the fallback is a parameter.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three short bodies, and none of them may mention a concrete type. If you catch
yourself writing `int`, `string` or `object` anywhere, back out — the method
signature already gave you a name for the type: `T`.

`FirstOr` has a subtlety worth spotting before you start: you cannot write
`return null` for "no first item", because `T` might be an `int`.

## Hint 2

The simplest way to take the first item of an `IEnumerable<T>` is to `foreach`
and `return` inside the loop — the first iteration is the first item, and if
the loop body never runs there was nothing there.

```csharp
foreach (T item in items)
{
    return item;
}
return fallback;
```

`Swap` needs a third variable to hold one value while you overwrite it. `ref`
means both parameters are aliases for the caller's variables, so assigning to
them is what the caller sees.

`CountOf` is a counter and a `foreach`.

## Hint 3

Everything here works for *any* `T` because none of it asks anything of `T` —
no comparison, no construction, no member access. That is why no constraint is
needed, and it is the honest test of whether a method should be generic at all.

One decision left: `FirstOr` could use LINQ's `FirstOrDefault`, and `CountOf`
could use `Count()`. Both exist and both are what you would write in real code
(lesson 10). Writing the loops once, by hand, is what makes the LINQ versions
stop being magic.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three short bodies, and none of them may mention a concrete type. If you catch
yourself writing `int`, `string` or `object` anywhere, back out — the method
signature already gave you a name for the type: `T`.

`FirstOr` has a subtlety worth spotting before you start: you cannot write
`return null` for "no first item", because `T` might be an `int`.

## Hint 2

The simplest way to take the first item of an `IEnumerable<T>` is to `foreach`
and `return` inside the loop — the first iteration is the first item, and if
the loop body never runs there was nothing there.

```csharp
foreach (T item in items)
{
    return item;
}
return fallback;
```

`Swap` needs a third variable to hold one value while you overwrite it. `ref`
means both parameters are aliases for the caller's variables, so assigning to
them is what the caller sees.

`CountOf` is a counter and a `foreach`.

## Hint 3

Everything here works for *any* `T` because none of it asks anything of `T` —
no comparison, no construction, no member access. That is why no constraint is
needed, and it is the honest test of whether a method should be generic at all.

One decision left: `FirstOr` could use LINQ's `FirstOrDefault`, and `CountOf`
could use `Count()`. Both exist and both are what you would write in real code
(lesson 10). Writing the loops once, by hand, is what makes the LINQ versions
stop being magic.

## Exercise 2 — constraints, and what each one buys

Edit `src/Lessons/L07_Generics/Ex2.cs`. `Max<T>` is constrained
`where T : IComparable<T>` and returns the largest item, throwing
`InvalidOperationException` for an empty sequence. `Fill<T>` is constrained
`where T : new()` and returns a list of `count` freshly constructed `T`s.

The seeding question in `Max` is the interesting one: you cannot start from `0`
and you cannot start from `default(T)` — the gate passes a set of negative
numbers precisely to catch that. Take the first item you actually see.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 07_generics ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two constraints in these signatures are not decoration: each one unlocks
exactly one thing you would otherwise be unable to write.

`where T : IComparable<T>` is what makes `a.CompareTo(b)` legal.
`where T : new()` is what makes `new T()` legal. Delete either constraint and
read the compiler error — it is a good way to feel what constraints are for.

## Hint 2

`Max` is the running-maximum loop from lesson 02, with `CompareTo` in place of
`>`. `item.CompareTo(best) > 0` means "item sorts after best".

The seeding question is the one that bites: you cannot start `best` at 0, and
`default(T)` is null for a class and 0 for an int — both wrong. Track a
`bool seenAny` and take the first item you see, or split the sequence's first
element out before the loop.

`Fill` is a `for` loop adding `new T()` to a list.

## Hint 3

```csharp
bool seenAny = false;
T best = default!;
foreach (T item in items)
{
    if (!seenAny || item.CompareTo(best) > 0)
    {
        best = item;
        seenAny = true;
    }
}
```

The `!` in `default!` tells the compiler "I know this looks null-unfriendly, I
have it covered" — the null-forgiving operator. Without it, a nullable-reference
warning appears, and the warning is not wrong: the value is only safe because
`seenAny` guards every read of it.

Then throw `InvalidOperationException` when nothing was seen. Left to you: what
message to put in it. Say what was empty and what was being asked.

## Hint 1

The two constraints in these signatures are not decoration: each one unlocks
exactly one thing you would otherwise be unable to write.

`where T : IComparable<T>` is what makes `a.CompareTo(b)` legal.
`where T : new()` is what makes `new T()` legal. Delete either constraint and
read the compiler error — it is a good way to feel what constraints are for.

## Hint 2

`Max` is the running-maximum loop from lesson 02, with `CompareTo` in place of
`>`. `item.CompareTo(best) > 0` means "item sorts after best".

The seeding question is the one that bites: you cannot start `best` at 0, and
`default(T)` is null for a class and 0 for an int — both wrong. Track a
`bool seenAny` and take the first item you see, or split the sequence's first
element out before the loop.

`Fill` is a `for` loop adding `new T()` to a list.

## Hint 3

```csharp
bool seenAny = false;
T best = default!;
foreach (T item in items)
{
    if (!seenAny || item.CompareTo(best) > 0)
    {
        best = item;
        seenAny = true;
    }
}
```

The `!` in `default!` tells the compiler "I know this looks null-unfriendly, I
have it covered" — the null-forgiving operator. Without it, a nullable-reference
warning appears, and the warning is not wrong: the value is only safe because
`seenAny` guards every read of it.

Then throw `InvalidOperationException` when nothing was seen. Left to you: what
message to put in it. Say what was empty and what was being asked.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two method bodies are `return producer;` and `return consumer;`. That is
not a joke — the exercise is making those two lines *compile*, which they do
not until each interface's type parameter carries a variance annotation.

Try writing them first and read the two compiler errors. They are unusually
clear about what is missing.

## Hint 2

`out T` means "T only ever comes out of this interface" and permits
`IProducer<string>` to be used as `IProducer<object>`. That is safe because
every string that comes out is an object.

`in T` means "T only ever goes into this interface" and permits
`IConsumer<object>` to be used as `IConsumer<string>`. That is safe because a
consumer that accepts anything certainly accepts strings.

The annotation goes on the interface declaration:
`public interface IProducer<out T>`.

## Hint 3

The reason the compiler insists on the annotation rather than working it out
itself is safety in the *other* direction. If `IProducer<out T>` had a method
taking a `T`, you could hand an `IProducer<object>` where an
`IProducer<string>` was expected and then feed it an `int` — so C# checks that
`T` appears only in return positions before it lets you write `out`.

That is the same reason arrays are a known hole in the type system: C# allows
`object[] a = new string[1];` and then throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException` at
runtime when you store the wrong thing. Generic variance was designed to not
repeat that mistake, which is worth saying out loud in an interview.

Left to you: whether to write the bodies as expression-bodied members. Both
forms are one line.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The two method bodies are `return producer;` and `return consumer;`. That is
not a joke — the exercise is making those two lines *compile*, which they do
not until each interface's type parameter carries a variance annotation.

Try writing them first and read the two compiler errors. They are unusually
clear about what is missing.

## Hint 2

`out T` means "T only ever comes out of this interface" and permits
`IProducer<string>` to be used as `IProducer<object>`. That is safe because
every string that comes out is an object.

`in T` means "T only ever goes into this interface" and permits
`IConsumer<object>` to be used as `IConsumer<string>`. That is safe because a
consumer that accepts anything certainly accepts strings.

The annotation goes on the interface declaration:
`public interface IProducer<out T>`.

## Hint 3

The reason the compiler insists on the annotation rather than working it out
itself is safety in the *other* direction. If `IProducer<out T>` had a method
taking a `T`, you could hand an `IProducer<object>` where an
`IProducer<string>` was expected and then feed it an `int` — so C# checks that
`T` appears only in return positions before it lets you write `out`.

That is the same reason arrays are a known hole in the type system: C# allows
`object[] a = new string[1];` and then throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException` at
runtime when you store the wrong thing. Generic variance was designed to not
repeat that mistake, which is worth saying out loud in an interview.

Left to you: whether to write the bodies as expression-bodied members. Both
forms are one line.

## Hint 1

Two loops, both constrained by `IComparable<T>`, both deciding something with
`CompareTo`.

The words in the prompt are load-bearing: "strictly greater" for the first,
"inclusive" for the second. Each one picks a different comparison operator

## Hint 2

`x.CompareTo(y)` is negative when x sorts first, zero when they tie, positive
when x sorts last. So:

- strictly greater than the threshold: `item.CompareTo(threshold) > 0`
- at or above the low bound: `item.CompareTo(low) >= 0`

`FirstAbove` returns as soon as it finds one — no need to look at the rest —
and returns the fallback if the loop finishes.

`CountBetween` needs both bounds true at once, which is one `if` with `&&`, not
two nested ones.

The decision left to you: whether to also guard against `low` being greater
than `high`. The gate never does that, so either behaviour passes — but think
about what your method would return, and whether silently returning 0 for an
impossible range is a kindness or a way to hide someone's bug.

lessons.briefing:
# 08 — Collections

You have been using `List<T>` since lesson 02 on the strength of "it is a
growable array", which is true and is about a fifth of what you need. This
lesson is the rest: which collection to reach for, what each one is fast at,
and what `IEnumerable<T>` — the type that keeps showing up in these signatures
— actually promises.

The choice matters more than beginners expect. Deduplicating a million strings
with `List.Contains` takes minutes; with a `HashSet` it takes a fraction of a
second, and the code is shorter. That is not micro-optimisation, it is picking
the data structure that matches the question you keep asking. "Is this in
there?" is a `HashSet`. "What is the value for this key?" is a `Dictionary`.
"Who is next?" is a `Queue`. "What was the most recent?" is a `Stack`.

The other half of the lesson is `yield`, which lets you write a sequence that
does not exist yet — computed one item at a time, as somebody reads it. That is
the machinery underneath every LINQ query you are about to write in lesson 10,
and meeting it here means LINQ will look like a library rather than magic.

## Concept — the family, and what each is for

