```csharp
names.Add("cy");                 // append: fast
names[0];                        // by position: fast
names.Contains("bo");            // by value: walks the whole list

Dictionary<string, int> ages = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["ada"] = 36 };
ages["bo"] = 41;                 // add or overwrite
ages.TryGetValue("cy", out int a);   // safe lookup: false, and a is 0
// ages["cy"] would THROW KeyNotFoundException

HashSet<string> seen = new HashSet<string>();
seen.Add("ada");                 // returns true the first time, false after

Queue<string> line = new Queue<string>();
line.Enqueue("ada"); line.Dequeue();     // first in, first out

Stack<string> undo = new Stack<string>();
undo.Push("typed"); undo.Pop();          // last in, first out
```

`Dictionary` and `HashSet` are both hash tables, which is why lesson 06's
`GetHashCode` contract mattered: they hash the key to pick a bucket and only
compare within it.

```

  ICollection<T>     ...and it has Count, Add, Remove, Contains

IReadOnlyList<T>     positions, no mutation
IDictionary<K,V>     keyed access
```

promise.** A method that only loops should take `IEnumerable<T>`, so callers
can pass an array, a list, or a lazy query without materialising anything.

compiled into a state machine:

```csharp

{
    foreach (int n in numbers)
    {
        if (n % 2 == 0)
        {
            yield return n;      // hand one out, pause here
        }
    }
}
```

that body — it hands back an object that will run it when enumerated. And each
`foreach` over the result runs the whole thing again from the start. Lesson 10
ex3 is where that second one bites.

## Exercise 1 — a dictionary and the key that isn't there

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex1.cs`. `Words.Count(text)` returns how many
times each word appears, lower-cased, ignoring runs of spaces.
`Words.CountOf(counts, word)` returns a word's count, or `0` when it is absent.

missing key throws `KeyNotFoundException`. `TryGetValue` is the way round it,
and its `out` parameter comes back as `0` when the key was absent — which is
conveniently the count you wanted to start from.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a set

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex2.cs`. `DistinctInOrder` returns each item
once, in the order first seen (case-sensitively — `"Cat"` and `"cat"` are two
items). `SharedCount` returns how many distinct items appear in both sequences.

`HashSet<T>.Add` returns `false` when the item was already there, which turns
"check, then add" into one line. A `HashSet` has no order, so keeping the
order is the `List`'s job.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a queue and a stack

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex3.cs`. `Serve(queue, count)` takes up to
`count` items off the front, in service order, and serves nothing rather than
throwing when the queue runs dry. `IsBalanced(text)` checks that every
`( [ {` is closed by the right partner in the right order, ignoring all other
characters.

smallest problem where a counter is *not enough*: `"(]"` has one opener and one
closer and is still wrong. A stack remembers not just how many are open but
which.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — sequences that are computed as they are read

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex4.cs`. Implement `Evens` and `WhileBelow`
as **iterators** — methods that use `yield return`, never building a list.

The gate can tell the difference. It hands you a source of 1,000 numbers that
counts how many were read, checks that calling your method read **zero** of
them, then takes three results and checks that far fewer than 1,000 were
touched. `WhileBelow` must stop at the first item that fails the test — `yield
break` — and never look at what follows.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections ex4
```

## Challenge — a collection of your own

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Challenge.cs`. `RingBuffer<T>` keeps the most
recent `Capacity` items: adding to a full buffer drops the oldest. Implement
`Count`, `Add`, and `GetEnumerator()` so `foreach` and `string.Join` work on
it.

Honest difficulty note: the storage is a `List<T>` and the logic is three
lines; the new idea is that implementing `IEnumerable<T>` is what lets *other
people's code* — `foreach`, `string.Join`, every LINQ operator — work with your
type. The non-generic `IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` at the bottom
is written for you, and it is lesson 05's explicit implementation in the wild.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections challenge
```

# Reading - csharp/08_collections

## Notes

**What each collection actually costs.** `List<T>` is an array that doubles
when it fills: indexing and appending are O(1) (appending *amortised* — the
occasional resize copies everything), inserting or removing in the middle is
O(n) because everything after it shifts, and `Contains` is O(n).
`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` and `HashSet<T>` are hash tables: lookup, insert and
remove are O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case, when every key hashes to
the same bucket. `Queue<T>` and `Stack<T>` are arrays with clever indices —
O(1) at their respective ends. Knowing this table is the difference between
code that scales and code that works on your laptop's test data.

**The hidden cost of the wrong one.** The classic accident is a `List.Contains`
inside a loop over another list: 10,000 × 10,000 comparisons for something a
`HashSet` does in 10,000. The second classic is `list.Insert(0, item)` in a
loop, which shifts the entire array every time — that is what `Queue<T>` and
`LinkedList<T>` exist for.

**`IEnumerable<T>` is a promise, not data.** It says only "you can ask me for
an enumerator". The thing behind it might be a list already in memory, a file
being read line by line, a database query that has not run yet, or an infinite
generator. That is why enumerating one twice is a smell — it might do the
expensive thing twice — and why `ToList()` exists: to say "I want this
materialised now, once".

**Iterators are state machines.** The compiler rewrites a method containing
`yield` into a class with a `MoveNext` and a `Current`, with your locals
promoted to fields and a state number tracking which `yield` you paused at.
That is why the body does not run when you call it (you got the state machine
back, not a result) and why every enumeration starts over (each `foreach` asks
for a fresh one). You can see the generated class in any decompiler, and it is
worth doing once.

**The `Try...` pattern, everywhere.** `TryGetValue`, `TryDequeue`, `TryPop`,
`TryPeek`, `TryAdd`. Every one exists because the alternative — an exception on
an ordinary outcome — is both slow and wrong-shaped. Lesson 02 introduced the
idea; the collections are where you will use it every day.

## ex1

`TryGetValue(key, out int soFar)` writing 0 into the out parameter when the key
is missing is not an accident you are exploiting — it is `default(TValue)`,
documented, and the reason counting dictionaries read so cleanly. The
alternatives are `ContainsKey` followed by an index (two lookups where one
would do) and `GetValueOrDefault` (one lookup, added in .NET Core 2.0, and the
shortest correct answer for `CountOf`).

The indexer's asymmetry is worth memorising because it catches everyone once:
**reading** a missing key throws, **writing** a missing key adds it. So
`counts[key] = counts[key] + 1` throws on the first occurrence, while
`counts[key] = soFar + 1` is fine. `Add` is stricter still — it throws if the
key is already present, which is the right choice when a duplicate means a bug.

`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` passed to the dictionary constructor is how
you would really do case-insensitive keys, and it is worth knowing why the
comparer belongs to the *dictionary* rather than to each lookup: the hash code
has to be computed the same way for storing and for finding, so both sides must
agree on what "equal" means. It is lesson 06's contract again, parameterised.

## ex2

`HashSet<T>.Add` returning a `bool` is the API design worth stealing: a method
that both performs an action and reports what it found saves the caller a
second lookup and, more importantly, removes the race between checking and
acting. `Dictionary.TryAdd` does the same.

The set operations — `UnionWith`, `IntersectWith`, `ExceptWith`,
`SymmetricExceptWith`, `IsSubsetOf`, `Overlaps` — mutate in place and are the
fast paths. LINQ has non-mutating equivalents (`Union`, `Intersect`, `Except`)
that return new sequences, which is usually what you want when the input is not
yours to modify. The SQL parallel is exact: these are `UNION`, `INTERSECT` and
`EXCEPT`, and the SQL course's lesson 11 is the same ideas over rows.

Order is the thing a `HashSet` does not give you. It has *an* order when you
enumerate it — the bucket order — but it is unspecified, can change when the
set grows, and must never be relied on. When you need both uniqueness and
order, you need both structures, which is exactly what the exercise made you
write.

## ex3

The queue and the stack are the two ends of the same idea, and the reason both
exist is that "next" means different things. A print queue, a message queue, a
breadth-first search: first in, first out. An undo history, a call stack, a
depth-first search, and bracket matching: last in, first out.

`IsBalanced` is the canonical stack interview question because a counter looks
like it should work and does not. `"([)]"` has matching counts of each kind and
is still wrong, because the *nesting* is wrong, and nesting is precisely what a
stack records. When you see a problem where "the most recent unfinished thing"
matters — parsing, tree traversal, expression evaluation — reach for a stack
before you reach for recursion, because recursion is the same stack with less
control.

`TryDequeue` over `Dequeue` matters here for the reason lesson 02 gave: an
empty queue is an ordinary state, not an exceptional one. Serving fewer people
than asked for is a normal Tuesday.

## ex4

This is the most important exercise in the lesson, because everything in lesson
10 rests on it. Three facts:

1. **The body does not run when you call the method.** You get a state machine
   back. Any argument validation you wanted to do eagerly therefore does not
   happen until enumeration — which is why the framework's own iterator methods
   are usually split into a public method that validates and a private iterator
   it returns.
2. **Enumeration is pull-based.** The consumer asks for one item; your code
   runs until the next `yield return`; then it pauses again. `Take(3)` simply
   stops asking, so your loop never runs a fourth time. That is how an infinite
   sequence can be useful.
3. **Each enumeration starts from scratch.** A second `foreach` calls
   `GetEnumerator` again and reruns your whole method.

The gate's counting source measures all three. If you build a `List` and return
it, everything is computed up front — the values are identical and the
behaviour is completely different, which is exactly the sort of bug that only
shows up when the input gets large or expensive.

`yield break` versus `continue` is the other check. `TakeWhile` semantics
("stop at the first failure") and `Where` semantics ("skip the failures") look
similar on the sample data and diverge on `{ 1, 2, 3, 9, 4 }`. Knowing which
one you meant is what makes the LINQ operator names worth learning precisely.

## challenge

Implementing `IEnumerable<T>` is how your type joins the ecosystem: `foreach`,
`string.Join`, every LINQ operator, collection initialisers and pattern
matching over sequences all key off it. That is lesson 05's point — implement
the contract the framework already understands — applied to the most useful
contract in the library.

The two-interface arrangement (`IEnumerable<T>` deriving from the old
non-generic `IEnumerable`) is a piece of history: the generic one arrived in
2005 and had to remain compatible with 2002-era code. Explicit implementation
is how everybody hides the old one, and now you have written that idiom
yourself.

Worth knowing: `foreach` does not actually require the interface. The compiler
looks for a public `GetEnumerator()` method with the right shape — a rare bit
of duck typing in a nominal language — which is what allows `foreach` over
`Span<T>` without any interface at all. Implement the interface anyway; LINQ
and everything else do require it.

The `RemoveAt(0)` in `Add` is O(n) and a real ring buffer would keep a fixed
array with head and tail indices, overwriting in place. Writing that version is
a good hour's work and a genuinely common interview task.

## review1

`Dictionary<char, List<string>>` is the shape you build by hand about twice
before you discover LINQ's `GroupBy` (lesson 11), and doing it by hand first is
what makes `GroupBy` legible when you meet it. The awkward moment — no list yet
for a new key — is the same TryGetValue-shaped hole as ex1, and the same
`Dictionary.TryAdd` / `CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault` tricks apply
if you go looking.

Adding the empty list to the dictionary *before* filling it works because the
dictionary stores a reference. If `List<T>` were a struct, that code would
silently drop every word — which is precisely the mutable-struct trap from
lesson 06, and a good reminder that "value or reference?" is a question with
practical consequences every day.

Returning an empty list rather than null from `For` is the *null object
pattern*: give callers something harmless to work with instead of something
they must check. `Enumerable.Empty<T>()` and `Array.Empty<T>()` exist for this
and allocate nothing, because they hand back a cached singleton — safe only
because both are immutable, which is why an empty `List<T>` singleton would be
a bug waiting to happen.

## Further reading

- [Collections and data structures](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/) — the overview, with the complexity table for each type.
- [`Dictionary<TKey,TValue>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2) — including the indexer's add-or-overwrite behaviour and the comparer constructor.
- [`HashSet<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.hashset-1) — set operations and what `Add`'s return value means.
- [Iterators](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/iterators) — `yield return`, `yield break`, and what the compiler generates.
- [`IEnumerable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.ienumerable-1) — the contract every sequence in .NET implements.
- [When to use generic collections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/when-to-use-generic-collections) — the "which one should I pick" page, worth a skim before every design.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a collection of your own

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Challenge.cs`. `RingBuffer<T>` keeps the most
recent `Capacity` items: adding to a full buffer drops the oldest. Implement
`Count`, `Add`, and `GetEnumerator()` so `foreach` and `string.Join` work on
it.

Honest difficulty note: the storage is a `List<T>` and the logic is three
lines; the new idea is that implementing `IEnumerable<T>` is what lets *other
people's code* — `foreach`, `string.Join`, every LINQ operator — work with your
type. The non-generic `IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` at the bottom
is written for you, and it is lesson 05's explicit implementation in the wild.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three members to write, and one of them is what makes `foreach` work on your
own type.

Keep the storage boring: a `List<T>` field is already declared. The buffer's
behaviour is entirely in `Add` — append, and if that made it too long, drop the
oldest.

## Hint 2

`Count` is the list's count. `Add` is two lines: add, then trim if over
capacity (`_items.RemoveAt(0)` drops the oldest).

`GetEnumerator` can be an iterator, exactly like ex4:

```csharp
public IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator()
{
    foreach (T item in _items)
    {
        yield return item;
    }
}
```

The compiler turns that into a state machine implementing `IEnumerator<T>` for
you — which is a lot of code you are not writing.

## Hint 3

Two things worth understanding rather than copying.

First, `foreach` does not actually require `IEnumerable<T>`: the compiler looks
for a public `GetEnumerator()` method by name (duck typing, uniquely in this
one place). Implementing the interface is still right, because that is what
LINQ and `string.Join` demand.

Second, the explicit `IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` at the bottom is
written for you, and it is lesson 05's explicit implementation earning its
keep: the old non-generic interface is required, and hiding it behind an
explicit implementation keeps it off your type's public surface.

Left to you: the real ring buffer keeps a fixed array and two indices, so
nothing is ever shifted. `RemoveAt(0)` is O(n). Worth doing once the gate is
green if you want the version that would survive a code review.

## Exercise 2 — a set

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex2.cs`. `DistinctInOrder` returns each item
once, in the order first seen (case-sensitively — `"Cat"` and `"cat"` are two
items). `SharedCount` returns how many distinct items appear in both sequences.

`HashSet<T>.Add` returns `false` when the item was already there, which turns
"check, then add" into one line. A `HashSet` has no order, so keeping the
order is the `List`'s job.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `HashSet<T>` answers one question extremely fast: have I seen this before? It
does not remember order, which is why `DistinctInOrder` needs both a set and a
list — the set decides, the list remembers.

`SharedCount` is set arithmetic: build one set, then keep only what is also in
the other sequence.

## Hint 2

`HashSet<T>.Add` returns a `bool`: true if the item was new, false if it was
already there. That single return value collapses the whole "check then add"
dance into one line:

```csharp
if (seen.Add(item))
{
    result.Add(item);
}
```

For the second method, `new HashSet<string>(left)` builds a set from a sequence
(dropping duplicates on the way), and `IntersectWith(right)` removes everything
not in the other side, in place.

## Hint 3

The reason a `HashSet` is the right tool rather than
`if (!result.Contains(item))` on the list: `List<T>.Contains` walks the whole
list every time, so deduplicating n items costs n² comparisons.
`HashSet<T>.Contains` hashes and looks in one bucket — constant time on average.
For 10 items nobody notices; for 100,000 it is the difference between instant
and a coffee break.

That performance claim rests on `GetHashCode` being well distributed, which is
lesson 06 ex4 coming back around: give a `HashSet` a key type whose hash code
is a constant and it degrades to exactly the list you were avoiding.

Left to you: whether `SharedCount` should build its set from the left or the
right sequence. Think about which one you would rather be the smaller.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `HashSet<T>` answers one question extremely fast: have I seen this before? It
does not remember order, which is why `DistinctInOrder` needs both a set and a
list — the set decides, the list remembers.

`SharedCount` is set arithmetic: build one set, then keep only what is also in
the other sequence.

## Hint 2

`HashSet<T>.Add` returns a `bool`: true if the item was new, false if it was
already there. That single return value collapses the whole "check then add"
dance into one line:

```csharp
if (seen.Add(item))
{
    result.Add(item);
}
```

For the second method, `new HashSet<string>(left)` builds a set from a sequence
(dropping duplicates on the way), and `IntersectWith(right)` removes everything
not in the other side, in place.

## Hint 3

The reason a `HashSet` is the right tool rather than
`if (!result.Contains(item))` on the list: `List<T>.Contains` walks the whole
list every time, so deduplicating n items costs n² comparisons.
`HashSet<T>.Contains` hashes and looks in one bucket — constant time on average.
For 10 items nobody notices; for 100,000 it is the difference between instant
and a coffee break.

That performance claim rests on `GetHashCode` being well distributed, which is
lesson 06 ex4 coming back around: give a `HashSet` a key type whose hash code
is a constant and it degrades to exactly the list you were avoiding.

Left to you: whether `SharedCount` should build its set from the left or the
right sequence. Think about which one you would rather be the smaller.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a queue and a stack

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex3.cs`. `Serve(queue, count)` takes up to
`count` items off the front, in service order, and serves nothing rather than
throwing when the queue runs dry. `IsBalanced(text)` checks that every
`( [ {` is closed by the right partner in the right order, ignoring all other
characters.

`IsBalanced` is a classic interview question and the reason is that it is the
smallest problem where a counter is *not enough*: `"(]"` has one opener and one
closer and is still wrong. A stack remembers not just how many are open but
which.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two collections that differ by one word: a `Queue` gives back what went in
first, a `Stack` gives back what went in last. Each exercise here is the
smallest problem that genuinely needs one of them.

`IsBalanced` needs a stack because the answer to "what should close next?" is
always "whatever opened most recently".

## Hint 2

`Queue<T>` has `Enqueue`, `Dequeue`, `Peek`, `Count` and — the one you want —
`TryDequeue(out T item)`, which returns false rather than throwing on an empty
queue. Loop up to `count` times and stop early when it comes back false.

`Stack<T>` has `Push`, `Pop`, `Peek`, `Count`, and `TryPop(out T item)`.

For the brackets: push every opener; on a closer, pop and check the popped
character is the matching opener. At the end, the stack must be empty.

## Hint 3

The three ways `IsBalanced` can be false are worth listing before you write it,
because each one is a different line of code:

1. a closer arrives when the stack is empty — `"())"`;
2. a closer arrives that does not match the top — `"(]"`;
3. the text ends with something still open — `"(()"`.

Mapping a closer to its opener is a small `switch` expression, and
`c is '(' or '[' or '{'` is the tidy way to ask "is this an opener" (a *logical
or* pattern, from lesson 02's family).

Left to you: whether to push the *expected closer* instead of the opener. That
version compares the popped character directly against `c` and needs no mapping
on the way out. Both are correct; one is a nice thing to notice.

## Exercise 4 — sequences that are computed as they are read

Edit `src/Lessons/L08_Collections/Ex4.cs`. Implement `Evens` and `WhileBelow`
as **iterators** — methods that use `yield return`, never building a list.

The gate can tell the difference. It hands you a source of 1,000 numbers that
counts how many were read, checks that calling your method read **zero** of
them, then takes three results and checks that far fewer than 1,000 were
touched. `WhileBelow` must stop at the first item that fails the test — `yield
break` — and never look at what follows.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 08_collections ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods return `IEnumerable<int>`, and both must be *iterators* — methods
containing `yield`. The gate proves it: it checks that calling your method
reads **nothing** from the source, and that taking three results does not walk
a thousand items.

If you build a `List<int>` and return it, both of those checks fail, even
though the values would be right.

## Hint 2

`yield return x;` hands one item to whoever is enumerating and *pauses the
method there*. The next `MoveNext` resumes on the following line, with every
local variable exactly as you left it.

```csharp
foreach (int number in numbers)
{
    if (/* even */)
    {
        yield return number;
    }
}
```

`yield break;` ends the sequence immediately — the equivalent of `return` in an
ordinary method.

## Hint 3

`WhileBelow` is the one where the difference shows. "Stopping at the first item
that is not below the limit" means `yield break` on that item — not `continue`,
which would skip it and carry on, and not a filter, which would keep looking.
The gate's `{ 1, 2, 3, 9, 4 }` case separates the two: a filter would return the
4, and stopping does not.

Left to you: whether to write these with LINQ instead (`numbers.Where(...)` and
`numbers.TakeWhile(...)` are exactly these two methods). Lesson 10 does that,
and the whole reason it will make sense is that you wrote the iterator version
first and know there is no list hiding inside it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A dictionary whose values are lists has one awkward moment, and it is the same
one as ex1: the first time a key appears, there is no list to add to yet.

`For` has the mirror problem on the way out — a caller asking about a letter
that was never seen.

## Hint 2

The standard shape:

```csharp
if (!groups.TryGetValue(key, out List<string>? group))
{
    group = new List<string>();
    groups[key] = group;
}
group.Add(word);
```

Note the list is added to the dictionary *before* it is filled. That works
because the dictionary holds a reference to the list, not a copy of it — lesson
01's value-versus-reference distinction doing real work.

`word[0]` is the first character of a string.

## Hint 3

`For` must return an empty list rather than null, so the caller can `foreach`
the result without a null check. That is a small kindness with a name — the
*null object pattern* — and it removes a whole class of `NullReferenceException`
from calling code.

Left to you: whether the empty list you return should be a fresh one each time
or a shared static. A fresh one is safe; a shared one is cheaper and becomes a
bug the moment a caller adds to what they were given. Think about which
guarantee you would rather make.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A dictionary whose values are lists has one awkward moment, and it is the same
one as ex1: the first time a key appears, there is no list to add to yet.

`For` has the mirror problem on the way out — a caller asking about a letter
that was never seen.

## Hint 2

The standard shape:

```csharp
if (!groups.TryGetValue(key, out List<string>? group))
{
    group = new List<string>();
    groups[key] = group;
}
group.Add(word);
```

Note the list is added to the dictionary *before* it is filled. That works
because the dictionary holds a reference to the list, not a copy of it — lesson
01's value-versus-reference distinction doing real work.

`word[0]` is the first character of a string.

## Hint 3

`For` must return an empty list rather than null, so the caller can `foreach`
the result without a null check. That is a small kindness with a name — the
*null object pattern* — and it removes a whole class of `NullReferenceException`
from calling code.

Left to you: whether the empty list you return should be a fresh one each time
or a shared static. A fresh one is safe; a shared one is cheaper and becomes a
bug the moment a caller adds to what they were given. Think about which
guarantee you would rather make.

lessons.briefing:
# 09 — Delegates, events and lambdas

Every method you have written so far was called by name. This lesson makes
methods into *values*: things you can store in a variable, pass as an argument,
return from a method, and keep in a list. Once behaviour can travel, a method
can take "what to do" as a parameter — which is how `List.Sort` sorts by
whatever you like, how a button knows what your click means, and how every
single LINQ operator in lesson 10 works.

The name for a variable that holds a method is a **delegate**. C# has had them
since version 1, back when you had to declare a named type for every shape;
today you use the two built-in families, `Func<...>` and `Action<...>`, and
write the methods inline as lambdas. The old declaration form still exists and
you will meet it in older code and in `EventHandler`.

There is one genuinely tricky thing here and it is worth arriving braced for
it: what a lambda *captures*. Not the value — the variable. Getting that
backwards produces one of the most famous surprises in C#, and ex2 walks you
straight into it on purpose.

## Concept — behaviour in a variable

```csharp
Func<int, int> twice = n => n * 2;        // takes an int, returns an int
Func<string, bool> isEmpty = s => s.Length == 0;
Action<string> log = message => Console.WriteLine(message);   // returns nothing
Func<int> now = () => 42;                 // no parameters

twice(21);      // 42 - call it exactly like a method
```

`Func<A, B, R>` reads "takes an A and a B, returns an R" — the **last** type
parameter is always the return type. `Action<...>` is the same with no return.
A method that takes one of these is *higher-order*: it decides when to call,
the caller decides what happens.

```csharp
public static int CountWhere<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, bool> predicate)
{
    int count = 0;
    foreach (T item in items) { if (predicate(item)) { count++; } }
    return count;
}
```

**Lambdas are closures.** A lambda can use variables from the method that
created it, and those variables *live on* after that method returns — the
compiler hoists them into a hidden object:

```csharp
public static Func<int> MakeCounter()
{
    int count = 0;
    return () => ++count;      // count outlives MakeCounter
}
```

Two calls to `MakeCounter` produce two independent counters. And the capture is
**by variable, not by value** — if the variable changes later, the lambda sees
the change. That is the ex2 trap.

**Events are a delegate with etiquette.** An `event` is a delegate field that
only the declaring class may raise, while anyone may subscribe with `+=` and
unsubscribe with `-=`:

```csharp
public event EventHandler<PriceChangedEventArgs>? PriceChanged;

PriceChanged?.Invoke(this, args);   // ?. because an event with no subscribers is null
```

The .NET convention is `(object? sender, TEventArgs e)`, with the raiser
passing `this` as the sender. Delegates are also **multicast**: `+=` adds
another subscriber, and invoking calls them all, in subscription order.

## Exercise 1 — behaviour as an argument

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex1.cs`. Implement `Apply` (every
item through a `Func<T, T>`, collected in order), `CountWhere` (how many items
a `Func<T, bool>` says yes to), and `Repeat` (call an `Action<int>` once for
each number from 1 to `times`, inclusive).

None of the three knows or cares what the delegate does. That indifference is
the entire feature.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — what a lambda captures

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex2.cs`. Implement `MakeCounter`
(a `Func<int>` handing back 1, then 2, then 3…), then two methods that build
three `() => i` lambdas — one from a `for` loop, one from a `foreach`.

Write both the obvious way. **Do not** copy the loop variable into a local
inside `FromForLoop`; the gate wants the naive version, because the naive
version is the famous one. Predict what each list of functions returns before
you run the gate — one of your two predictions is probably wrong, and that is
the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — an event

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`StockTicker.Update(newPrice)`: record the price, and raise `PriceChanged` with
the old and new values — but only when the price actually moved, and without
throwing when nobody has subscribed.

Three details to get right: capture the old price before you overwrite it,
update the state before you raise (a handler that reads `ticker.Price` should
see the new one), and use `?.Invoke`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — functions that build functions

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex4.cs`. `Compose(params steps)`
returns a single `Func<string, string>` that runs every step left to right,
feeding each result into the next — and with no steps returns the input
unchanged. `Combine(first, second)` returns one `Action` that runs both in
order, tolerating either (or both) being null.

Both methods return a lambda. Nothing happens when you call them; everything
happens when someone calls what they gave back.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas ex4
```

## Challenge — the middleware pipeline

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Challenge.cs`. A middleware here
is a `Func<Func<string,string>, Func<string,string>>`: hand it the next
handler and it gives you back a new handler that wraps it. `Build` wraps a core
handler in each middleware so that the **first one listed is the outermost**.

Honest difficulty note: the type is harder to read than the code is to write —
three lines, once the direction is clear. Get it right and you have built, in
miniature, the exact mechanism behind ASP.NET Core's request pipeline: order of
registration is order of nesting, and a middleware that never calls `next`
short-circuits everything inside it. The gate checks both.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is `MakeAdder` (a running total in a closure) and `Not` (a predicate
wrapped in its opposite). `dojo review` will bring it back.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/09_delegates_events_lambdas

## Notes

**A delegate is an object, not a function pointer.** It holds two things: a
target (the object the method belongs to, or null for a static method) and a
method. That is why a delegate can keep an object alive — the delegate
references the target — and it is the mechanism behind the most common memory
leak in .NET, described under ex3 below. It is also why delegates can be
*multicast*: the object holds an invocation list, and `+` appends to it.

**`Func` and `Action` are just declared delegate types.** The framework
declares `Func<TResult>` through `Func<T1,...,T16,TResult>` and `Action`
through `Action<T1,...,T16>`, so you almost never declare your own. When you do
see a custom `public delegate int Comparison<in T>(T x, T y);`, the reason is
usually a name that documents intent better than `Func<T,T,int>` does — and
occasionally `ref`/`out` parameters, which `Func` cannot express.

**Lambdas capture variables, not values.** The compiler rewrites a capturing
lambda into a hidden class with a field per captured variable, and rewrites the
*enclosing method* to use that field too. So there is genuinely only one
variable, shared between the method and every lambda that captured it. That
explains both the useful case (a counter that persists) and the surprising one
(three lambdas all seeing the loop's final value).

**Lambdas versus local functions.** A local function (`int Twice(int n) => n * 2;`
declared inside a method) is often better when you do not need a delegate: it
can be recursive, it can use `ref` and `out`, and it allocates nothing unless it
is captured. If you are writing a helper for the current method only, prefer a
local function; if the helper needs to be *passed* somewhere, you need a
delegate.

**Allocation, briefly.** A non-capturing lambda is cached by the compiler and
allocates once for the whole program. A capturing lambda allocates a closure
object each time the enclosing scope runs. That matters in hot loops and
nowhere else, and the fix — passing state through an overload that takes it as
an argument, like `List.Sort(Comparison<T>)` versus a captured comparer — is
worth recognising when you see it in framework source.

## ex1

The three methods are `Select`, `Count(predicate)` and a `for` loop by another
name, which is exactly what lesson 10 is going to point out. Writing them by
hand is the same trick as writing the iterators by hand in lesson 08: LINQ
stops being magic when you have already built two of its operators.

The design idea worth taking away is *inversion*: `CountWhere` owns the loop
and the counting, and hands the interesting decision back to the caller. When
you see a method with a `bool includeInactive` parameter, or three near-copies
differing by one `if`, that is the shape a `Func<T, bool>` collapses.

`Action<int>` versus `Func<int, T>` marks the divide between something done for
its *effect* and something done for its *result*. It is a useful signal in a
signature: an `Action` tells the reader "this changes the world" and a `Func`
tells them "this computes an answer".

## ex2

The `for` loop giving `3, 3, 3` is one of the most-asked C# interview questions,
and the answer is one sentence: **the lambda captured the variable, and the
loop has only one of them.** By the time you invoke the lambdas, that variable
holds the value that ended the loop.

The `foreach` version giving `0, 1, 2` is the same sentence with a different
fact attached: since C# 5, `foreach` declares a fresh iteration variable each
time round. Before C# 5 it did not, and the change was a rare *breaking* change
to the language — accepted because the old behaviour was, in the design team's
own words, wrong more often than right.

If you want the per-iteration behaviour in a `for` loop, copy into a local
inside the loop body:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
{
    int captured = i;         // a new variable per iteration
    functions.Add(() => captured);
}
```

Which is precisely what you were told *not* to do in the exercise, because
seeing the trap once is worth more than avoiding it. The same bug appears with
`Task.Run(() => Process(i))` inside a loop, with event handlers wired in a
loop, and with timers — and the symptom is always "they all processed the last
item".

## ex3

Events are delegates with two restrictions: outside the declaring class you may
only `+=` and `-=`, and you may not invoke. That is what stops a consumer of
your class from raising `PriceChanged` on your behalf or wiping the subscriber
list with `=`.

`?.Invoke(...)` is the required idiom, and it does two things. It skips the
call when nobody has subscribed (an event with no subscribers is genuinely
`null`), and it reads the delegate into a temporary first, so a subscriber
unsubscribing on another thread between the check and the call cannot cause a
`NullReferenceException`.

The "only raise on an actual change" rule matters more than it looks. Handlers
often trigger more work — a redraw, a save, another event — and an event that
fires when nothing happened turns into a feedback loop or a performance
problem. The same discipline appears in `INotifyPropertyChanged`
implementations everywhere.

The leak worth knowing about: subscribing with `+=` gives the *publisher* a
reference to the *subscriber*. If a long-lived ticker holds a handler belonging
to a short-lived window, that window can never be collected — the classic .NET
memory leak. The fix is symmetric unsubscription (`-=`) or a weak event pattern,
and it is a good interview answer because it shows you understand a delegate
holds its target.

## ex4

Returning a function is where higher-order code starts feeling powerful. Both
methods here are *combinators*: they take behaviour and produce new behaviour
without doing anything themselves. `Compose` is function composition;
`Combine` is what `+` already does for delegates, written out by hand.

The `params` empty case falling out for free is worth noticing — the loop that
never runs returns the input unchanged, so "compose nothing" is the identity
function without a special case. Whenever an operation has a natural "do
nothing" value (0 for addition, "" for concatenation, identity for composition),
your code gets shorter by leaning on it instead of branching around it.

`Combine(null, null)` returning a working no-op `Action` rather than `null` is
the null-object pattern again. The rule of thumb it comes from: **make the
absent case something the caller can use**, so they do not need a null check
that they will eventually forget.

## challenge

This is ASP.NET Core's pipeline, and building it once makes the whole framework
legible. `app.UseAuthentication()`, `app.UseRouting()`, `app.UseEndpoints()` are
each registering a `Func<RequestDelegate, RequestDelegate>` — a function taking
"the rest of the pipeline" and returning a new "rest of the pipeline". Order of
registration is order of nesting. A middleware that does not call `next` never
reaches your endpoint, which is exactly how a 401 happens.

The reverse loop is the part that catches people. To make the first-listed
middleware outermost, you must wrap it *last*, so you build from the core
outward — iterating the array backwards. Getting this wrong produces code that
still runs every middleware but nests them inside out, and the tell is that the
"on the way out" work happens in the wrong order. The gate's two orderings are
designed so that a sequence-not-a-nest implementation gives the same answer to
both, which is the fastest way to spot it.

The general pattern has a name — the decorator — and it is the composition
answer to "I want to add behaviour to something I do not own". Logging,
caching, retries, timing and authorisation are all decorators in real
codebases, and none of them requires touching the thing being decorated.

## review1

`MakeAdder` is the counter with an argument, and the gate's second adder is
the check that matters: if your state was `static`, both adders would share it
and the second would start at 5. Each call to `MakeAdder` creates a new
closure; that is the whole difference between captured state and global state,
and it is why closures are a reasonable alternative to small classes.

`Not` is a combinator like ex4's, and the assertion that the original predicate
still works is not a formality. Delegates are immutable in the way that
matters: `+`, `-` and any wrapping produce *new* delegates. Nothing you do to a
`Func` can change what the caller's copy points at, which is what makes passing
them around safe.

The extension-method note in the hints is a small preview of how LINQ is
actually shaped: `items.Where(...)` is a static method with `this` on its first
parameter, and lesson 10 is where that syntax finally pays off.

## Further reading

- [Delegates](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/delegates/) — what a delegate is, multicast invocation, and the older declaration syntax.
- [Lambda expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions) — including the capture rules and expression versus statement bodies.
- [`Func<T,TResult>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.func-2) and [`Action<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.action-1) — the two families you will use every day.
- [Events](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/events-overview) — the pattern, the naming conventions, and raising safely.
- [Local functions versus lambda expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/local-functions#local-functions-vs-lambda-expressions) — when each one is the better tool.
- [ASP.NET Core middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/) — the challenge's pattern, at production scale.

your code gets shorter by leaning on it instead of branching around it.

`Combine(null, null)` returning a working no-op `Action` rather than `null` is
the null-object pattern again. The rule of thumb it comes from: **make the
absent case something the caller can use**, so they do not need a null check
that they will eventually forget.

## challenge

This is ASP.NET Core's pipeline, and building it once makes the whole framework
legible. `app.UseAuthentication()`, `app.UseRouting()`, `app.UseEndpoints()` are
each registering a `Func<RequestDelegate, RequestDelegate>` — a function taking
"the rest of the pipeline" and returning a new "rest of the pipeline". Order of
registration is order of nesting. A middleware that does not call `next` never
reaches your endpoint, which is exactly how a 401 happens.

The reverse loop is the part that catches people. To make the first-listed
middleware outermost, you must wrap it *last*, so you build from the core
outward — iterating the array backwards. Getting this wrong produces code that
still runs every middleware but nests them inside out, and the tell is that the
"on the way out" work happens in the wrong order. The gate's two orderings are
designed so that a sequence-not-a-nest implementation gives the same answer to
both, which is the fastest way to spot it.

The general pattern has a name — the decorator — and it is the composition
answer to "I want to add behaviour to something I do not own". Logging,
caching, retries, timing and authorisation are all decorators in real
codebases, and none of them requires touching the thing being decorated.

## review1

`MakeAdder` is the counter with an argument, and the gate's second adder is
the check that matters: if your state was `static`, both adders would share it
and the second would start at 5. Each call to `MakeAdder` creates a new
closure; that is the whole difference between captured state and global state,
and it is why closures are a reasonable alternative to small classes.

`Not` is a combinator like ex4's, and the assertion that the original predicate
still works is not a formality. Delegates are immutable in the way that
matters: `+`, `-` and any wrapping produce *new* delegates. Nothing you do to a
`Func` can change what the caller's copy points at, which is what makes passing
them around safe.

The extension-method note in the hints is a small preview of how LINQ is
actually shaped: `items.Where(...)` is a static method with `this` on its first
parameter, and lesson 10 is where that syntax finally pays off.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the middleware pipeline

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Challenge.cs`. A middleware here
is a `Func<Func<string,string>, Func<string,string>>`: hand it the next
handler and it gives you back a new handler that wraps it. `Build` wraps a core
handler in each middleware so that the **first one listed is the outermost**.

Honest difficulty note: the type is harder to read than the code is to write —
three lines, once the direction is clear. Get it right and you have built, in
miniature, the exact mechanism behind ASP.NET Core's request pipeline: order of
registration is order of nesting, and a middleware that never calls `next`
short-circuits everything inside it. The gate checks both.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the type slowly, because it is the hardest part:

```
Func<Func<string,string>, Func<string,string>>
```

A middleware is a function that **takes the next handler and returns a new
handler**. Given `next`, it hands back something that can do a bit of work,
call `next`, and do a bit more work on the way out.

`Build` starts from the core handler and wraps it, one middleware at a time.

## Hint 2

The wrapping direction is the whole exercise. The first middleware listed must
end up **outermost** — so it must be applied **last**:

```csharp
Func<string, string> handler = core;
for (int i = middleware.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
{
    handler = middleware[i](handler);
}
return handler;
```

Walk it with two middlewares on paper before you trust it. `middleware[1]` wraps
`core`; then `middleware[0]` wraps that.

## Hint 3

Check your result against the gate's two orderings. `brackets` then `exclaim`
gives `"[hi!]"`; `exclaim` then `brackets` gives `"[hi]!"`. If both come out
the same you built a *sequence*, not a nest — the "on the way out" half of each
middleware never happened.

This is exactly ASP.NET Core's request pipeline. `app.Use(...)` registers a
middleware in this shape, order of registration is order of wrapping, and a
middleware that does not call `next` short-circuits the request — which is how
authentication returns 401 without your controller ever running.

Left to you: whether to reject a null middleware in the array, and whether
`Build` should copy the array before closing over it. Both matter more the
moment the caller can mutate what they passed.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the type slowly, because it is the hardest part:

```
Func<Func<string,string>, Func<string,string>>
```

A middleware is a function that **takes the next handler and returns a new
handler**. Given `next`, it hands back something that can do a bit of work,
call `next`, and do a bit more work on the way out.

`Build` starts from the core handler and wraps it, one middleware at a time.

## Hint 2

The wrapping direction is the whole exercise. The first middleware listed must
end up **outermost** — so it must be applied **last**:

```csharp
Func<string, string> handler = core;
for (int i = middleware.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
{
    handler = middleware[i](handler);
}
return handler;
```

Walk it with two middlewares on paper before you trust it. `middleware[1]` wraps
`core`; then `middleware[0]` wraps that.

## Hint 3

Check your result against the gate's two orderings. `brackets` then `exclaim`
gives `"[hi!]"`; `exclaim` then `brackets` gives `"[hi]!"`. If both come out
the same you built a *sequence*, not a nest — the "on the way out" half of each
middleware never happened.

This is exactly ASP.NET Core's request pipeline. `app.Use(...)` registers a
middleware in this shape, order of registration is order of wrapping, and a
middleware that does not call `next` short-circuits the request — which is how
authentication returns 401 without your controller ever running.

Left to you: whether to reject a null middleware in the array, and whether
`Build` should copy the array before closing over it. Both matter more the
moment the caller can mutate what they passed.

## Exercise 1 — behaviour as an argument

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex1.cs`. Implement `Apply` (every
item through a `Func<T, T>`, collected in order), `CountWhere` (how many items
a `Func<T, bool>` says yes to), and `Repeat` (call an `Action<int>` once for
each number from 1 to `times`, inclusive).

None of the three knows or cares what the delegate does. That indifference is
the entire feature.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

All three methods are loops you have written before. The only new thing is that
part of the work arrives as a parameter, and you call it like a method.

A `Func<T, T>` is "give me a T, get a T back". A `Func<T, bool>` is a question
about a T. An `Action<int>` takes an int and returns nothing — you call it for
what it *does*, not for what it gives you.

## Hint 2

Calling one looks exactly like calling a method:

```csharp
T changed = transform(item);
if (predicate(item)) { ... }
action(i);
```

`Apply` collects the results into a `List<T>` and returns it. `CountWhere`
counts the items the predicate says yes to. `Repeat` loops from 1 to `times`
**inclusive** — read the gate if you are unsure which end is which.

## Hint 3

Nothing here inspects the delegate, checks it for null, or cares what it does.
That indifference is the point: `Apply` works for doubling ints and trimming
strings without knowing about either.

Left to you: whether to guard against a null `transform`. Production library
code would (`ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(transform)` is the one-liner);
the gate never passes null. Deciding when a guard is worth its line is a real
judgement call, not a rule.

## Hint 1

All three methods are loops you have written before. The only new thing is that
part of the work arrives as a parameter, and you call it like a method.

A `Func<T, T>` is "give me a T, get a T back". A `Func<T, bool>` is a question
about a T. An `Action<int>` takes an int and returns nothing — you call it for
what it *does*, not for what it gives you.

## Hint 2

Calling one looks exactly like calling a method:

```csharp
T changed = transform(item);
if (predicate(item)) { ... }
action(i);
```

`Apply` collects the results into a `List<T>` and returns it. `CountWhere`
counts the items the predicate says yes to. `Repeat` loops from 1 to `times`
**inclusive** — read the gate if you are unsure which end is which.

## Hint 3

Nothing here inspects the delegate, checks it for null, or cares what it does.
That indifference is the point: `Apply` works for doubling ints and trimming
strings without knowing about either.

Left to you: whether to guard against a null `transform`. Production library
code would (`ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(transform)` is the one-liner);
the gate never passes null. Deciding when a guard is worth its line is a real
judgement call, not a rule.

## Hint 1

Three tiny methods, and two of them are deliberately the *same code* in two
loop shapes. Write them the obvious way. Do not try to be clever, and
specifically do not copy the loop variable into a local inside `FromForLoop` —

## Hint 2

`MakeCounter` declares a local, returns a lambda that touches it, and the local
outlives the method:

```csharp
int count = 0;
return () => ++count;
```

`++count` increments and hands back the new value, which is why the first call
is 1 and not 0.

The two loop methods each build a `List<Func<int>>` and add `() => i` three
times — one with `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)`, one with
`foreach (int i in new[] { 0, 1, 2 })`.

## Hint 3

Before you run the gate, predict both lists out loud. Most people get one of
them wrong, and the reason is worth having in your own words:

A lambda captures the **variable**, not the value it had at the time. A `for`
loop declares its variable once for the whole loop; a `foreach` declares a
fresh one each iteration (it has done since C# 5, and the change was made
precisely because everybody got this wrong).

So one of your two methods hands back three functions sharing one variable, and
the other hands back three functions with one variable each. The gate's message
tells you which is which if your prediction was off — but predict first.

## Exercise 3 — an event

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`StockTicker.Update(newPrice)`: record the price, and raise `PriceChanged` with
the old and new values — but only when the price actually moved, and without
throwing when nobody has subscribed.

Three details to get right: capture the old price before you overwrite it,
update the state before you raise (a handler that reads `ticker.Price` should
see the new one), and use `?.Invoke`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One method, three decisions in it: is this actually a change, what do the
subscribers need to know, and what happens when nobody is listening.

Take them in that order and the body writes itself. Note the order matters in
one more way — you need the *old* price for the event arguments, so capture it
before you overwrite it.

## Hint 2

The null-safe raise is the idiom to learn:

```csharp
PriceChanged?.Invoke(this, new PriceChangedEventArgs(oldPrice, newPrice));
```

An event with no subscribers is `null`, so a bare `PriceChanged(...)` would
throw. `?.Invoke` is the standard form, and by convention the first argument is
`this` — the object raising the event.

The "only when it changed" guard is an early `return` at the top.

## Hint 3

The shape:

```csharp
if (/* nothing changed */) { return; }

decimal oldPrice = Price;
Price = newPrice;
// tell whoever is listening
```

Raising *after* the state is updated is deliberate: a subscriber that reads
`ticker.Price` inside its handler should see the new value, not a half-applied
change.

Left to you: the thread-safe version of the raise copies the event to a local
first (`var handler = PriceChanged; handler?.Invoke(...)`), so that a
subscriber unsubscribing on another thread between the null check and the call
cannot cause a `NullReferenceException`. `?.Invoke` already does that copy for
you — which is one reason it is the recommended form.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One method, three decisions in it: is this actually a change, what do the
subscribers need to know, and what happens when nobody is listening.

Take them in that order and the body writes itself. Note the order matters in
one more way — you need the *old* price for the event arguments, so capture it
before you overwrite it.

## Hint 2

The null-safe raise is the idiom to learn:

```csharp
PriceChanged?.Invoke(this, new PriceChangedEventArgs(oldPrice, newPrice));
```

An event with no subscribers is `null`, so a bare `PriceChanged(...)` would
throw. `?.Invoke` is the standard form, and by convention the first argument is
`this` — the object raising the event.

The "only when it changed" guard is an early `return` at the top.

## Hint 3

The shape:

```csharp
if (/* nothing changed */) { return; }

decimal oldPrice = Price;
Price = newPrice;
// tell whoever is listening
```

Raising *after* the state is updated is deliberate: a subscriber that reads
`ticker.Price` inside its handler should see the new value, not a half-applied
change.

Left to you: the thread-safe version of the raise copies the event to a local
first (`var handler = PriceChanged; handler?.Invoke(...)`), so that a
subscriber unsubscribing on another thread between the null check and the call
cannot cause a `NullReferenceException`. `?.Invoke` already does that copy for
you — which is one reason it is the recommended form.

## Exercise 4 — functions that build functions

Edit `src/Lessons/L09_DelegatesEventsLambdas/Ex4.cs`. `Compose(params steps)`
returns a single `Func<string, string>` that runs every step left to right,
feeding each result into the next — and with no steps returns the input
unchanged. `Combine(first, second)` returns one `Action` that runs both in
order, tolerating either (or both) being null.

Both methods return a lambda. Nothing happens when you call them; everything
happens when someone calls what they gave back.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 09_delegates_events_lambdas ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods **return a function**. Neither of them does the work now — they
build something that will do the work later, when someone calls it.

So the body of each is mostly a lambda, and everything inside that lambda runs
per invocation, not once at build time.

## Hint 2

`Compose` returns a lambda that loops the steps, feeding each result into the
next:

```csharp
return input =>
{
    string current = input;
    foreach (Func<string, string> step in steps)
    {
        // current becomes the result of this step
    }
    return current;
};
```

With no steps, the loop never runs and `current` is still the input — the empty
case falls out for free, exactly as `string.Join` did in lesson 02.

`Combine` returns a lambda that calls each half with `?.Invoke()`, so a null
half is skipped.

## Hint 3

Note what `Combine` must NOT do: return `null` when both arguments are null.
The gate calls the result immediately, so it has to be a real (if empty)
`Action`. Returning something harmless rather than null is the same null-object
idea as lesson 08's review.

Left to you: C# can also combine delegates with `+` (`first + second`), which
is *multicast* — the same mechanism events use, and it handles nulls
correctly all by itself. Try that version too and decide which one you would
rather read in six months.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods **return a function**. Neither of them does the work now — they
build something that will do the work later, when someone calls it.

So the body of each is mostly a lambda, and everything inside that lambda runs
per invocation, not once at build time.

## Hint 2

`Compose` returns a lambda that loops the steps, feeding each result into the
next:

```csharp
return input =>
{
    string current = input;
    foreach (Func<string, string> step in steps)
    {
        // current becomes the result of this step
    }
    return current;
};
```

With no steps, the loop never runs and `current` is still the input — the empty
case falls out for free, exactly as `string.Join` did in lesson 02.

`Combine` returns a lambda that calls each half with `?.Invoke()`, so a null
half is skipped.

## Hint 3

Note what `Combine` must NOT do: return `null` when both arguments are null.
The gate calls the result immediately, so it has to be a real (if empty)
`Action`. Returning something harmless rather than null is the same null-object
idea as lesson 08's review.

Left to you: C# can also combine delegates with `+` (`first + second`), which
is *multicast* — the same mechanism events use, and it handles nulls
correctly all by itself. Try that version too and decide which one you would
rather read in six months.

## Hint 1

Two methods, both returning functions, both from ex2 and ex4's playbook.

`MakeAdder` keeps a running total in a captured local — the counter from ex2,
with an argument. `Not` wraps a predicate you were handed and flips its answer.

## Hint 2

The adder's lambda needs a body with two statements, so it takes braces:

```csharp
int total = 0;
return amount =>
{
    total += amount;
    return total;
};
```

`Not` is a single expression: `value => !predicate(value)`.

## Hint 3

The gate checks that a second adder starts from zero. If yours does not, the
state is in the wrong place — a `static` field is shared by everything, while a
local captured by the lambda belongs to that one call of `MakeAdder`. Each call
creates a fresh closure, which is the whole difference.

It also checks that the predicate you were given still works afterwards. `Not`
returns a NEW function; it cannot and must not modify the original, because a
`Func<T, bool>` is a value, not an object with settings.

Left to you: whether `Not` should be an extension method
(`predicate.Not()`), which is how LINQ-style fluent APIs are built. The
signature would barely change and the call site would read very differently.

`Func<T, bool>` is a value, not an object with settings.

Left to you: whether `Not` should be an extension method
(`predicate.Not()`), which is how LINQ-style fluent APIs are built. The
signature would barely change and the call site would read very differently.

# 10 — LINQ, part 1

You already know this lesson. You learned it in SQL.

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM orders o
WHERE o.amount >= 100
ORDER BY o.amount DESC, o.customer;
```

```csharp
orders.Where(o => o.Amount >= 100)
      .OrderByDescending(o => o.Amount)
      .ThenBy(o => o.Customer)
      .Select(o => o.Customer);
```

Same query, same three ideas — restrict, sort, project — over a `List<Order>`
instead of a table. LINQ was designed by people who wanted SQL's expressiveness
inside a general-purpose language, and the resemblance is not a coincidence; it
goes all the way down to the vocabulary. `Where` is `WHERE`. `Select` is
`SELECT`. `OrderBy`/`ThenBy` are `ORDER BY` with its comma. `Skip`/`Take` are
`OFFSET`/`LIMIT`. `Any` is `EXISTS`. `Distinct` is `DISTINCT`. Lesson 11 adds
`GroupBy`, `Join` and the aggregates.

There is one difference that matters enormously, and it is the subject of ex3.
In SQL you hand the planner a description of the answer and it decides how to
get it. In LINQ-to-objects the operators run in the order you wrote them, and —
crucially — **not until somebody asks**. A LINQ query is a plan you are holding,
and every time you enumerate it, it runs again.

Everything you need to read this lesson's code you already built by hand:
lesson 08's iterators are how the laziness works, and lesson 09's lambdas are
what you pass to every operator.

## Concept — the operators, and when they run

LINQ operators are extension methods on `IEnumerable<T>`, which is why they
chain. They come in two families.

**Deferred operators return a new sequence and read nothing yet:**

```csharp
IEnumerable<Order> big = orders.Where(o => o.Amount >= 100);   // nothing has happened
foreach (Order o in big) { }                                    // NOW the filtering runs
```

`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `Skip`, `Take`, `Distinct`, `SelectMany`,
`GroupBy` — all deferred. (`OrderBy` is a special case: it defers, but when it
does run it must read *everything* before it can yield the first item.)

**Greedy operators read the sequence immediately and return an answer:**

```csharp
orders.Count();          orders.ToList();      orders.First();
orders.Any(o => ...);    orders.All(o => ...); orders.Single(o => ...);
```

The consequences of that split are worth stating plainly, because they are what
interviewers ask about:

1. A query built and never enumerated never runs at all.
2. A query enumerated twice runs **twice**. Over a `List` that is wasted CPU;
   over a database or a network stream it is two round trips.
3. `.ToList()` is how you say "run it now, once, and give me the data".

**The end-of-query operators and their failure modes.** `First` throws when
there is nothing; `FirstOrDefault` gives `null` (or `default(T)`). `Single`
throws unless there is **exactly one** — use it when "more than one" would mean
your data is broken, which is exactly what a unique id promises. `All` over an
empty sequence is `true`, vacuously, which surprises everyone once.

**Ordering.** `OrderBy(...).ThenBy(...)` is one sort with two keys. Writing
`OrderBy(...).OrderBy(...)` throws the first ordering away and sorts again —
the LINQ equivalent of writing two separate `ORDER BY` clauses and expecting
them to combine.

## Exercise 1 — restrict, sort, project

Edit `src/Lessons/L10_Linq1/Ex1.cs`. The shared `Order` record lives in
`Model.cs` and you never edit it; the gate builds five sample orders and hands
them to you.

## Exercise 3 — the query is not the answer

Edit `src/Lessons/L10_Linq1/Ex3.cs`. Three methods that look almost identical
and behave completely differently.

# Reading - csharp/10_linq_1

## Notes

**What a LINQ operator actually is.** `Where` is a static extension method on
`IEnumerable<T>` that returns an iterator — roughly the `Evens` method you wrote
by hand in lesson 08, generalised over a predicate you supply. That is the whole
trick: lesson 08 gave you laziness, lesson 09 gave you behaviour-as-a-value, and
LINQ is those two ideas plus about forty well-chosen method names. There is no
compiler magic in `orders.Where(...)`; you could write every operator yourself
in an afternoon, and people did, before 2007.

**Method syntax versus query syntax.** Everything in this lesson can also be
written as `from o in orders where o.Amount >= 100 select o.Customer`, which
the compiler rewrites into exactly the method calls you have been writing. Query
syntax reads better for joins and multi-level groupings (lesson 11 shows both);
method syntax is what most C# codebases use for everything else, mostly because
not every operator has a keyword.

**LINQ to Objects versus LINQ to a database.** The methods you are calling take
`Func<T, bool>` — a compiled lambda, a piece of executable code. The versions
on `IQueryable<T>` take `Expression<Func<T, bool>>` — a *data structure
describing* the lambda, which EF Core walks and turns into SQL. Identical
source code, two completely different execution stories: one runs your delegate
per item in memory, the other sends a `WHERE` clause to Postgres. Knowing which
one you are holding is the single most valuable LINQ skill in a .NET job, and
the tell is the static type: `IEnumerable<T>` means "in this process",
`IQueryable<T>` means "there is a translator downstream".

**Deferred execution, precisely.** `orders.Where(p)` constructs an object that
holds a reference to `orders` and to `p`. Nothing else. The filtering happens
inside `MoveNext`, one item at a time, when someone enumerates it. Consequences:
the query sees the source *as it is at enumeration time*; enumerating twice does
the work twice; and an exception in your predicate surfaces at the `foreach`,
not at the line that looks like it built the query.

**Which operators are greedy.** `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `Count`,
`Sum`, `Min`, `Max`, `Average`, `First`, `Single`, `Last`, `Any`, `All`,
`Contains`, `Aggregate`. Everything else you have met defers. `OrderBy` is the
subtle one: it is deferred, but it cannot yield its first item until it has read
every item, so it buffers the whole sequence — which is why sorting an infinite
sequence hangs and filtering one does not.

## ex1

The chain order is the lesson: `Where` before `OrderBy` before `Select`. It
matters for both cost and correctness. Filtering first means sorting fewer
items. Projecting last means the ordering can still see fields the projection
throws away — try to sort by `Amount` after `Select(o => o.Customer)` and the
`Amount` is simply gone.

That is a genuine difference from SQL, where `ORDER BY` may reference columns
the `SELECT` list omits, because the database orders the *rows* before
projecting. In LINQ the pipeline is literal, so the order you write is the
order things happen.

`ThenBy` versus a second `OrderBy` is the most common LINQ ordering bug.
`OrderBy(a).OrderBy(b)` is not a two-key sort — it is a sort by `a`, thrown
away, then a sort by `b`. It compiles, it runs, and it silently gives the wrong
answer whenever there are ties. `.NET`'s sort is stable, which makes the wrong
version look right often enough to survive review.

## ex2

These operators are where a query stops being a query. Each one walks the
sequence until it can answer and then stops: `Any` returns on the first match,
`First` returns the first item, `All` returns on the first counterexample.
`Count` has to walk everything — unless the sequence is secretly an
`ICollection<T>`, in which case it asks for `.Count` and returns instantly, a
small optimisation worth knowing when someone claims `Count()` is O(n).

The `First`/`Single` distinction is a design statement about your data. `First`
says "there may be several; give me one". `Single` says "there is exactly one,
and if there is not, something upstream is broken". Using `Single` on a unique
key is self-documenting and gives you a loud failure at the right moment; using
`First` there hides a duplicate-key bug forever.

The `...OrDefault` variants are where lesson 07's `default(T)` trap returns.
`FirstOrDefault` on a sequence of `int` gives `0` when there was no match, which
is indistinguishable from a real `0`. That is why .NET 6 added an overload
taking an explicit default value, and why a nullable reference type is a
friendlier signature.

`All` over an empty sequence being `true` follows from the logic — "every
element satisfies p" is only false if you can produce an element that does not —
and it is a real source of bugs in validation code: `items.All(IsValid)` happily
approves an empty basket.

## ex3

This exercise is the reason lesson 10 exists in this course.

A LINQ query is a *plan*. The `CountingOrders` source in the gate makes that
observable: building the query touches nothing, and each enumeration walks the
source again. In memory that is a wasted loop. Against EF Core it is a second
`SELECT`. Against a network stream or a one-shot iterator it is either an
exception or, worse, silently different data.

The two production symptoms to recognise:

```csharp
if (query.Any()) { foreach (var x in query) { } }   // two executions
var count = query.Count(); var total = query.Sum(...); // two executions
```

Both are fixed the same way — materialise once at the point where you stop
composing and start consuming: `var results = query.ToList();`.

The mirror-image mistake is materialising too early: calling `.ToList()` in the
middle of a chain forces everything into memory and throws away the database's
chance to do the filtering. The rule of thumb: compose lazily, materialise once,
at the boundary.

The snapshot-versus-live pair is the other half. `Snapshot` is data and cannot
change; `Query` is a question re-asked every time. Neither is right in general,
and choosing without noticing is how a method ends up returning results that
depend on when the caller looked at them.

## ex4

`Skip` and `Take` are `OFFSET` and `LIMIT`, with the same well-known problem:
offset paging gets slower the deeper you go (the source still walks the skipped
items) and is unstable if the ordering has ties. The SQL course's lesson on
keyset pagination is the same critique with the same fix — order by something
unique and remember where you stopped, rather than counting from the start.

Ordering before taking is not a style preference. `Take` is deferred, so
`Take(3).OrderByDescending(...)` builds a pipeline that takes the first three
items *in source order* and then sorts those three. It produces a plausible
list of three orders that are simply not the biggest three. Errors like this
never throw; you find them when a report looks odd.

`OrderBy` buffering the whole sequence is worth remembering here too: `Take(3)`
after an `OrderBy` still sorts everything first. .NET's implementation is
smarter than a naive full sort for small takes, but the mental model — "sorting
reads everything" — is the one to keep.

## challenge

The pipeline is routine by now; the interesting line is the last one. LINQ hands
you an empty sequence for "no matches", `string.Join` hands you `""`, and
whether the *user* should see an empty line or the word "none" is a product
decision that no library can make.

That is a small instance of a large habit: the library's default for the empty
case is almost never the right answer for the user's. Empty baskets, months with
no sales, searches with no hits — every one of them needs a deliberate decision,
and every one of them is a bug report when nobody made it.

## review1

`Distinct` uses the element's `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, which is lesson 06's
contract turning up in a place you would not have predicted. Over a sequence of
`string` it does what you expect. Over a sequence of `Order` **records** it also
does what you expect, because records generate value equality. Over a sequence
of a plain class holding identical data it does nothing at all, because every
instance is distinct by reference — and that is the interview question hiding in
this exercise.

`DistinctBy` (since .NET 6) is the operator you actually want most of the time:
`orders.DistinctBy(o => o.Customer)` keeps the first order per customer without
any equality plumbing. Worth knowing it exists before you write a `GroupBy` to
fake it.

The laziness check on `LazyNames` is the ex3 point again in a smaller frame. If
you have started reaching for `.ToList()` reflexively to make the types line up,
this is the review catching that habit early: return type
`IEnumerable<string>` means "I am handing you a query", and the caller decides
when it runs.

## Further reading

- [LINQ overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/) — the concepts, with query syntax and method syntax side by side.
- [Standard query operators overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/) — the full catalogue, grouped by what they do.
- [Deferred execution and lazy evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/linq/deferred-execution-lazy-evaluation) — with the classification of which operators defer.
- [Classification of standard query operators by manner of execution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/query-expression-syntax-for-standard-query-operators) — the deferred/immediate table worth bookmarking.
- [`IQueryable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.iqueryable-1) — the other LINQ, and why expression trees exist.

```csharp
using System.Collections;

using CSharpDojo.L10_Linq1;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L10_Linq1Tests
{
    private static List<Order> Sample() => new List<Order>
    {
        new Order(1, "ada", "books", 120m, 2025),
        new Order(2, "bo", "toys", 45m, 2025),
        new Order(3, "ada", "toys", 300m, 2026),
        new Order(4, "cy", "books", 120m, 2026),
        new Order(5, "bo", "books", 90m, 2026),
    };

    /// <summary>A source that reports how many times somebody walked it.</summary>
    private sealed class CountingOrders : IEnumerable<Order>
    {
        public CountingOrders(List<Order> items) => Items = items;

        public List<Order> Items { get; }

        public int Enumerations { get; private set; }

        public IEnumerator<Order> GetEnumerator()
        {
            Enumerations++;
            return Items.GetEnumerator();
        }

        IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => GetEnumerator();
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_FilterProjectAndOrder()
    {

            "Three orders are 100 or more: 300 (ada), 120 (ada) and 120 (cy). Largest first, "
                + "and the two 120s are broken by customer name - which is what ThenBy is for. "
                + "A second OrderBy would throw the first ordering away - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("ada, ada, cy, bo, bo", string.Join(", ", Queries.NamesOfOrdersOver(Sample(), 45m)),
            "A minimum of 45 keeps the 45 itself: \"at least\" is >=, not >. Five orders, "
                + "largest first - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("ada: 300, ada: 120, bo: 90, bo: 45, cy: 120",
            string.Join(", ", Queries.SortedLabels(Sample())),
            "Customer A-Z first, then largest amount first WITHIN each customer - so ada's 300 "
                + "leads and cy comes last despite the 120 - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal(0, Queries.NamesOfOrdersOver(Sample(), 1000m).Count,
            "Nothing qualifies, so the result is empty - not null, and not an exception.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_AskingQuestionsOfASequence()
    {
        Order? firstToy = Questions.FirstIn(Sample(), "toys");
        Teach.Equal(2, firstToy!.Id,
            "FIRST in sequence order, not smallest or largest: order 2 appears before order 3 "
                + "- reread README ex2.");

        Teach.True(Questions.FirstIn(Sample(), "shoes") is null,
            "No shoes here. FirstOrDefault returns null for a reference type rather than "
                + "throwing - First would have thrown - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.True(Questions.AnyOver(Sample(), 250m), "The 300 is over 250.");
        Teach.True(!Questions.AnyOver(Sample(), 300m), "Nothing is over 300 - the 300 itself "
            + "is not over 300. Any takes a strict comparison here because the prompt said "
            + "\"above\".");

        Teach.True(Questions.AllUnder(Sample(), 500m), "Every order is under 500.");
        Teach.True(!Questions.AllUnder(Sample(), 100m), "The 120s and the 300 are not.");
        Teach.True(Questions.AllUnder(new List<Order>(), 1m),
            "All over an EMPTY sequence is true - vacuously, because there is no "
                + "counterexample. Every language does this and it surprises people every "
                + "time - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(3, Questions.CountIn(Sample(), "books"), "Orders 1, 4 and 5 are books.");
        Teach.Equal(0, Questions.CountIn(Sample(), "shoes"), "None at all.");

        Teach.Equal("cy", Questions.WithId(Sample(), 4).Customer,
            "Single finds the one match - reread README ex2.");
        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => Questions.WithId(Sample(), 99),
            "There is no order 99. Single THROWS when there is not exactly one match, and "
                + "that loudness is the point: an id that matches nothing is a bug, not a "
                + "null - reread README ex2.");
    }
```
