    public void Ex3_AQueryIsAPlanUntilSomebodyRunsIt()
    {

        IEnumerable<Order> query = Deferred.Query(source, 100m);

        Teach.Equal(0, source.Enumerations,
            "Building the query must not read the source at all. If this is not 0 you called "
                + "ToList - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal(3, query.Count(), "Three orders are 100 or more.");
        Teach.Equal(1, source.Enumerations, "Counting them walked the source once.");

        Teach.Equal(3, query.Count(), "The same query, asked again, gives the same answer...");
        Teach.Equal(2, source.Enumerations,
            "...but it walked the source AGAIN. That is the multiple-enumeration bug: over a "
                + "database or a network stream, this is two round trips. reread README ex3.");

        CountingOrders snapshotSource = new CountingOrders(Sample());
        IReadOnlyList<Order> snapshot = Deferred.Snapshot(snapshotSource, 100m);

        Teach.Equal(1, snapshotSource.Enumerations,
            "Snapshot reads the source exactly once, immediately - ToList is what does that - "
                + "reread README ex3.");
        Teach.Equal(3, snapshot.Count, "Three matching orders.");

        snapshotSource.Items.Add(new Order(6, "zed", "books", 500m, 2026));
        Teach.Equal(3, snapshot.Count,
            "A snapshot is data. Adding to the source afterwards cannot change it.");
        Teach.Equal(1, snapshotSource.Enumerations,
            "And reading the snapshot again does not touch the source at all.");

        CountingOrders liveSource = new CountingOrders(Sample());
        IEnumerable<Order> live = Deferred.Query(liveSource, 100m);
        liveSource.Items.Add(new Order(6, "zed", "books", 500m, 2026));

        Teach.Equal(4, live.Count(),
            "The live query ran AFTER the source changed, so it saw the new order. Same two "
                + "lines of code, opposite behaviour - reread README ex3.");

        CountingOrders onePass = new CountingOrders(Sample());
        (int count, decimal total) = Deferred.CountAndTotal(onePass);

        Teach.Equal(5, count, "Five orders.");
        Teach.Equal(675m, total, "120 + 45 + 300 + 120 + 90.");
        Teach.Equal(1, onePass.Enumerations,
            "Both numbers had to come from ONE pass. Calling .Count() and then .Sum() walks "
                + "the source twice - reread README ex3.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_SkipAndTakeArePagingAndTopN()
    {
        Teach.Equal("1, 2", string.Join(", ", Paging.PageOfIds(Sample(), 1, 2)),
            "Page 1 of size 2 is the first two ids - pages are numbered from 1, so page 1 "
                + "skips nothing - reread README ex4.");
        Teach.Equal("3, 4", string.Join(", ", Paging.PageOfIds(Sample(), 2, 2)),
            "Page 2 skips (2-1) x 2 = 2 rows.");
        Teach.Equal("5", string.Join(", ", Paging.PageOfIds(Sample(), 3, 2)),
            "The last page can be short.");
        Teach.Equal("", string.Join(", ", Paging.PageOfIds(Sample(), 9, 2)),
            "A page past the end is empty rather than an error - Skip past the end simply "
                + "yields nothing.");

        Teach.Equal("3, 1, 4", string.Join(", ", Paging.TopIds(Sample(), 3)),
            "300 first, then the two 120s with ada before cy. Order BEFORE you take - taking "
                + "first would give you three arbitrary rows - reread README ex4.");
        Teach.Equal("3", string.Join(", ", Paging.TopIds(Sample(), 1)), "Just the biggest.");
        Teach.Equal(5, Paging.TopIds(Sample(), 50).Count,
            "Asking for more than there are gives everything, without complaint.");
    }

    public void Challenge_OnePipelineFromRowsToReport()
    {
        Teach.Equal("ada: 300 | cy: 120 | bo: 90", Reports.TopOfYear(Sample(), 2026, 3),
            "Filter to the year, order by amount descending with the customer as tie-break, "
                + "take 3, format each, join with \" | \" - reread README challenge.");

        Teach.Equal("ada: 120 | bo: 45", Reports.TopOfYear(Sample(), 2025, 3),
            "2025 has only two orders, so the report is shorter - no padding, no blanks.");

        Teach.Equal("ada: 300", Reports.TopOfYear(Sample(), 2026, 1),
            "count really does limit the report.");

        Teach.Equal("(none)", Reports.TopOfYear(Sample(), 1999, 3),
            "A year with no orders reports \"(none)\" - string.Join over an empty sequence "
                + "gives \"\", so this case needs a decision from you - reread README challenge.");
    }

    public void Review1_DistinctFilteredProjectionsAndLaziness()
    {
        Teach.Equal("books, toys", string.Join(", ", Catalogue.CategoriesOver(Sample(), 100m)),
            "Orders of 100+ are in books (twice) and toys - Distinct collapses the repeat, and "
                + "the result is alphabetical - reread README review.");

        Teach.Equal("books, toys", string.Join(", ", Catalogue.CategoriesOver(Sample(), 45m)),
            "Every order qualifies now, and there are still only two categories.");

        Teach.Equal(0, Catalogue.CategoriesOver(Sample(), 9999m).Count, "Nothing qualifies.");

        CountingOrders source = new CountingOrders(Sample());
        IEnumerable<string> names = Catalogue.LazyNames(source);

        Teach.Equal(0, source.Enumerations,
            "Select is deferred too: building the projection reads nothing - reread README "
                + "review.");
        Teach.Equal("ada, bo, ada, cy, bo", string.Join(", ", names),

In plain English: `Ex1` checks the ordering, the tie-break, the `>=` boundary
and the empty result. `Ex2` walks every operator's found and not-found case,
including `All` over an empty sequence and `Single` throwing. `Ex3` is the
interesting one — the `CountingOrders` class in the gate records every walk of
the source, and the assertions read as a story about when your code ran.
`Ex4` pages three times plus past the end, then takes the top 1, 3 and 50.
`Challenge` reports two years and an empty one, and `Review1` is the
spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The SQL habits transfer, and so do the SQL mistakes. Ordering with no unique
tie-break makes paging unstable in both languages — a row can appear on page 1
and again on page 2 — which is why `PageOfIds` orders by the id. Filtering
after you have already materialised everything is `WHERE` applied by hand after
a full table scan. And LINQ's `Select` is `SELECT`: projecting to just the
columns you need is as good an idea here as it is there.

The habit that is *not* from SQL is watching for double enumeration. The
symptom in production is a method that takes `IEnumerable<T>`, calls `.Any()`
to check it is not empty, and then `foreach`es it — two walks, and if the
argument was a database query or a stream, two of something expensive. The fix
is one word: materialise once with `.ToList()` at the boundary where you stop
composing and start consuming. This is the same instinct as the SQL course's
"don't N+1", and it comes from the same place: knowing when the work actually
happens.

Next: **11_linq_2**, where `GroupBy`, `Join` and the aggregates finish the
translation.

# Reading - csharp/10_linq_1

## Notes

**What a LINQ operator actually is.** `Where` is a static extension method on
`IEnumerable<T>` that returns an iterator — roughly the `Evens` method you wrote
by hand in lesson 08, generalised over a predicate you supply. That is the whole
trick: lesson 08 gave you laziness, lesson 09 gave you behaviour-as-a-value, and
LINQ is those two ideas plus about forty well-chosen method names. There is no
compiler magic in `orders.Where(...)`; you could write every operator yourself
in an afternoon, and people did, before 2007.

**Method syntax versus query syntax.** Everything in this lesson can also be
written as `from o in orders where o.Amount >= 100 select o.Customer`, which
the compiler rewrites into exactly the method calls you have been writing. Query
syntax reads better for joins and multi-level groupings (lesson 11 shows both);
method syntax is what most C# codebases use for everything else, mostly because
not every operator has a keyword.

**LINQ to Objects versus LINQ to a database.** The methods you are calling take
`Func<T, bool>` — a compiled lambda, a piece of executable code. The versions
on `IQueryable<T>` take `Expression<Func<T, bool>>` — a *data structure
describing* the lambda, which EF Core walks and turns into SQL. Identical
source code, two completely different execution stories: one runs your delegate
per item in memory, the other sends a `WHERE` clause to Postgres. Knowing which
one you are holding is the single most valuable LINQ skill in a .NET job, and
the tell is the static type: `IEnumerable<T>` means "in this process",
`IQueryable<T>` means "there is a translator downstream".

**Deferred execution, precisely.** `orders.Where(p)` constructs an object that
holds a reference to `orders` and to `p`. Nothing else. The filtering happens
inside `MoveNext`, one item at a time, when someone enumerates it. Consequences:
the query sees the source *as it is at enumeration time*; enumerating twice does
the work twice; and an exception in your predicate surfaces at the `foreach`,
not at the line that looks like it built the query.

**Which operators are greedy.** `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `Count`,
`Sum`, `Min`, `Max`, `Average`, `First`, `Single`, `Last`, `Any`, `All`,
`Contains`, `Aggregate`. Everything else you have met defers. `OrderBy` is the
subtle one: it is deferred, but it cannot yield its first item until it has read
every item, so it buffers the whole sequence — which is why sorting an infinite
sequence hangs and filtering one does not.

## ex1

The chain order is the lesson: `Where` before `OrderBy` before `Select`. It
matters for both cost and correctness. Filtering first means sorting fewer
items. Projecting last means the ordering can still see fields the projection
throws away — try to sort by `Amount` after `Select(o => o.Customer)` and the
`Amount` is simply gone.

That is a genuine difference from SQL, where `ORDER BY` may reference columns
the `SELECT` list omits, because the database orders the *rows* before
projecting. In LINQ the pipeline is literal, so the order you write is the
order things happen.

`ThenBy` versus a second `OrderBy` is the most common LINQ ordering bug.
`OrderBy(a).OrderBy(b)` is not a two-key sort — it is a sort by `a`, thrown
away, then a sort by `b`. It compiles, it runs, and it silently gives the wrong
answer whenever there are ties. `.NET`'s sort is stable, which makes the wrong
version look right often enough to survive review.

## ex2

These operators are where a query stops being a query. Each one walks the
sequence until it can answer and then stops: `Any` returns on the first match,
`First` returns the first item, `All` returns on the first counterexample.
`Count` has to walk everything — unless the sequence is secretly an
`ICollection<T>`, in which case it asks for `.Count` and returns instantly, a
small optimisation worth knowing when someone claims `Count()` is O(n).

The `First`/`Single` distinction is a design statement about your data. `First`
says "there may be several; give me one". `Single` says "there is exactly one,
and if there is not, something upstream is broken". Using `Single` on a unique
key is self-documenting and gives you a loud failure at the right moment; using
`First` there hides a duplicate-key bug forever.

The `...OrDefault` variants are where lesson 07's `default(T)` trap returns.
`FirstOrDefault` on a sequence of `int` gives `0` when there was no match, which
is indistinguishable from a real `0`. That is why .NET 6 added an overload
taking an explicit default value, and why a nullable reference type is a
friendlier signature.

`All` over an empty sequence being `true` follows from the logic — "every
element satisfies p" is only false if you can produce an element that does not —
and it is a real source of bugs in validation code: `items.All(IsValid)` happily
approves an empty basket.

## ex3

This exercise is the reason lesson 10 exists in this course.

A LINQ query is a *plan*. The `CountingOrders` source in the gate makes that
observable: building the query touches nothing, and each enumeration walks the
source again. In memory that is a wasted loop. Against EF Core it is a second
`SELECT`. Against a network stream or a one-shot iterator it is either an
exception or, worse, silently different data.

The two production symptoms to recognise:

```csharp
if (query.Any()) { foreach (var x in query) { } }   // two executions
var count = query.Count(); var total = query.Sum(...); // two executions
```

Both are fixed the same way — materialise once at the point where you stop
composing and start consuming: `var results = query.ToList();`.

The mirror-image mistake is materialising too early: calling `.ToList()` in the
middle of a chain forces everything into memory and throws away the database's
chance to do the filtering. The rule of thumb: compose lazily, materialise once,
at the boundary.

The snapshot-versus-live pair is the other half. `Snapshot` is data and cannot
change; `Query` is a question re-asked every time. Neither is right in general,
and choosing without noticing is how a method ends up returning results that
depend on when the caller looked at them.

## ex4

`Skip` and `Take` are `OFFSET` and `LIMIT`, with the same well-known problem:
offset paging gets slower the deeper you go (the source still walks the skipped
items) and is unstable if the ordering has ties. The SQL course's lesson on
keyset pagination is the same critique with the same fix — order by something
unique and remember where you stopped, rather than counting from the start.

Ordering before taking is not a style preference. `Take` is deferred, so
`Take(3).OrderByDescending(...)` builds a pipeline that takes the first three
items *in source order* and then sorts those three. It produces a plausible
list of three orders that are simply not the biggest three. Errors like this
never throw; you find them when a report looks odd.

`OrderBy` buffering the whole sequence is worth remembering here too: `Take(3)`
after an `OrderBy` still sorts everything first. .NET's implementation is
smarter than a naive full sort for small takes, but the mental model — "sorting
reads everything" — is the one to keep.

## challenge

The pipeline is routine by now; the interesting line is the last one. LINQ hands
you an empty sequence for "no matches", `string.Join` hands you `""`, and
whether the *user* should see an empty line or the word "none" is a product
decision that no library can make.

That is a small instance of a large habit: the library's default for the empty
case is almost never the right answer for the user's. Empty baskets, months with
no sales, searches with no hits — every one of them needs a deliberate decision,
and every one of them is a bug report when nobody made it.

## review1

`Distinct` uses the element's `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, which is lesson 06's
contract turning up in a place you would not have predicted. Over a sequence of
`string` it does what you expect. Over a sequence of `Order` **records** it also
does what you expect, because records generate value equality. Over a sequence
of a plain class holding identical data it does nothing at all, because every
instance is distinct by reference — and that is the interview question hiding in
this exercise.

`DistinctBy` (since .NET 6) is the operator you actually want most of the time:
`orders.DistinctBy(o => o.Customer)` keeps the first order per customer without
any equality plumbing. Worth knowing it exists before you write a `GroupBy` to
fake it.

The laziness check on `LazyNames` is the ex3 point again in a smaller frame. If
you have started reaching for `.ToList()` reflexively to make the types line up,
this is the review catching that habit early: return type
`IEnumerable<string>` means "I am handing you a query", and the caller decides
when it runs.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a whole report in one pipeline

Edit `src/Lessons/L10_Linq1/Challenge.cs`. `TopOfYear(orders, year, count)`
returns the biggest `count` orders of one year as
`"ada: 300 | cy: 120 | bo: 90"`, biggest first with the customer name as
tie-break — and `"(none)"` for a year with no orders.

Honest difficulty note: the chain is five steps you have already written; the
only genuinely new thing is that `string.Join` over an empty sequence gives
`""`, so the "no rows" case is a decision the library will not make for you.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 10_linq_1 challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One chain, five steps, and then one decision at the end.

The chain is everything you did in ex1 and ex4 in a row: filter to the year,
order by amount (biggest first, customer as tie-break), take `count`, project
each row to text.

The decision is what to return when the chain produced nothing.

## Hint 2

Materialise the projected lines into a `List<string>` before you join them, so
you can ask whether it is empty:

```csharp
List<string> lines = orders
    .Where(order => order.Year == year)
    // ... order, take, select ...
    .ToList();

return lines.Count == 0 ? "(none)" : string.Join(" | ", lines);
```

Each line is `$"{order.Customer}: {order.Amount}"`, and the separator is a
space, a pipe, a space.

## Hint 3

`string.Join` over an empty sequence gives `""`, not `"(none)"` — which is why
the empty case needs you rather than the library. That is the same
"the empty case is a design decision" point as lesson 02's countdown, one level
up.

Left to you: whether to check `lines.Count == 0` or use `Any()` on the query
before materialising. The first reads better here; the second is what you would
want if the source were a database and you did not want to fetch rows twice.
Note that asking a *query* `Any()` and then enumerating it is exactly the
double-enumeration ex3 warned about.

## Hint 1

One chain, five steps, and then one decision at the end.

The chain is everything you did in ex1 and ex4 in a row: filter to the year,
order by amount (biggest first, customer as tie-break), take `count`, project
each row to text.

The decision is what to return when the chain produced nothing.

## Hint 2

Materialise the projected lines into a `List<string>` before you join them, so
you can ask whether it is empty:

```csharp
List<string> lines = orders
    .Where(order => order.Year == year)
    // ... order, take, select ...
    .ToList();

return lines.Count == 0 ? "(none)" : string.Join(" | ", lines);
```

Each line is `$"{order.Customer}: {order.Amount}"`, and the separator is a
space, a pipe, a space.

## Hint 3

`string.Join` over an empty sequence gives `""`, not `"(none)"` — which is why
the empty case needs you rather than the library. That is the same
"the empty case is a design decision" point as lesson 02's countdown, one level
up.

Left to you: whether to check `lines.Count == 0` or use `Any()` on the query
before materialising. The first reads better here; the second is what you would
want if the source were a database and you did not want to fetch rows twice.
Note that asking a *query* `Any()` and then enumerating it is exactly the
double-enumeration ex3 warned about.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are one chain each, and both chains are the same four steps in a
different order: keep some rows, sort them, turn each row into something
smaller, produce a list.

Write the clauses in the order LINQ wants them, which is not the order SQL
writes them: the source comes first, then `Where`, then the ordering, then
`Select`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
return orders
    .Where(order => /* the condition */)
    .OrderByDescending(order => order.Amount)
    .ThenBy(order => order.Customer)
    .Select(order => order.Customer)
    .ToList();
```

`ThenBy` is the tie-break. Writing a second `OrderBy` instead throws the first
ordering away completely — it re-sorts from scratch — which is the single most
common LINQ ordering bug.

`SortedLabels` sorts by customer first and then by amount *descending* within
each customer, and projects to `$"{order.Customer}: {order.Amount}"`.

## Hint 3

"At least `minimum`" is `>=`. The gate passes a minimum equal to one of the
amounts precisely to check which comparison you used.

`ToList()` at the end is what turns the query into the `List<string>` the
signature promised. Without it you have an `IEnumerable<string>` and the
compiler will tell you so — and *why* that final step exists at all is exactly
what ex3 is about.

Left to you: `OrderByDescending(...).ThenBy(...)` can also be written as
`OrderBy(o => (-o.Amount, o.Customer))` with a tuple. Try it if you like;
decide which one you would rather read next year.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Five one-liners. Each one is a LINQ operator that ends the query and returns an
answer rather than another sequence — these are the *greedy* operators, and
each has a matching idea in SQL: `Any` is `EXISTS`, `Count` is `count(*)`,

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the query is not the answer

Edit `src/Lessons/L10_Linq1/Ex3.cs`. Three methods that look almost identical
and behave completely differently.

`Query` returns the query itself — built, unrun, touching nothing. `Snapshot`
returns the results, read from the source exactly once, immune to later
changes. `CountAndTotal` returns a count and a sum from **one** pass over the
sequence.

The gate hands all three a source that counts how many times it is walked. It
checks that building the query walks it zero times, that enumerating the same
query twice walks it twice, that the snapshot does not see an order added
afterwards while the live query does, and that `CountAndTotal` walks it once.
This is the multiple-enumeration bug, made visible.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 10_linq_1 ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two of these three methods are one line, and the difference between them is a
single call. The third is deliberately not LINQ at all.

`Query` must hand back the query itself — unrun. `Snapshot` must run it once,
now, and keep the results. `CountAndTotal` must produce two numbers from **one**
walk of the sequence.

## Hint 2

`orders.Where(...)` returns an `IEnumerable<Order>` and reads nothing until
somebody enumerates it. That is `Query`, complete.

Adding `.ToList()` is what runs it: one pass over the source, results copied
into a list you own. That is `Snapshot`.

`CountAndTotal` is the interesting one. `orders.Count()` walks the sequence and
`orders.Sum(o => o.Amount)` walks it again — the gate counts enumerations and
will see the second walk. Write a `foreach` and accumulate both.

## Hint 3

The gate tells the whole story if you read its assertions in order: the query
that reads nothing, the same query counted twice reading the source twice, the
snapshot that is immune to a later `Add`, and the live query that is not.

That last pair is the point. Two lines of code that differ only by `.ToList()`
have completely different semantics: one is a *plan* re-run on demand against
whatever the source holds at that moment, the other is *data*.

Left to you: `CountAndTotal` could also be done by materialising once
(`var list = orders.ToList();`) and then using LINQ twice on the list. That is
one enumeration of the source and perfectly defensible — the gate accepts it.
Deciding between "one pass, no allocation" and "one pass, then convenience" is
the real judgement call.

## Hint 1

Two of these three methods are one line, and the difference between them is a
single call. The third is deliberately not LINQ at all.

`Query` must hand back the query itself — unrun. `Snapshot` must run it once,
now, and keep the results. `CountAndTotal` must produce two numbers from **one**
walk of the sequence.

## Hint 2

`orders.Where(...)` returns an `IEnumerable<Order>` and reads nothing until
somebody enumerates it. That is `Query`, complete.

Adding `.ToList()` is what runs it: one pass over the source, results copied
into a list you own. That is `Snapshot`.

`CountAndTotal` is the interesting one. `orders.Count()` walks the sequence and
`orders.Sum(o => o.Amount)` walks it again — the gate counts enumerations and
will see the second walk. Write a `foreach` and accumulate both.

## Hint 3

The gate tells the whole story if you read its assertions in order: the query
that reads nothing, the same query counted twice reading the source twice, the
snapshot that is immune to a later `Add`, and the live query that is not.

That last pair is the point. Two lines of code that differ only by `.ToList()`
have completely different semantics: one is a *plan* re-run on demand against
whatever the source holds at that moment, the other is *data*.

Left to you: `CountAndTotal` could also be done by materialising once
(`var list = orders.ToList();`) and then using LINQ twice on the list. That is
one enumeration of the source and perfectly defensible — the gate accepts it.
Deciding between "one pass, no allocation" and "one pass, then convenience" is
the real judgement call.

## Exercise 4 — paging and top-N

Edit `src/Lessons/L10_Linq1/Ex4.cs`. `PageOfIds(orders, pageNumber, pageSize)`
returns one page of ids ordered by id, with pages numbered from 1 and a page
past the end coming back empty. `TopIds(orders, count)` returns the ids of the
biggest `count` orders, largest first, ties broken by customer A–Z.

Order before you take. `Take(3).OrderByDescending(...)` sorts three arbitrary
rows and looks plausible while being wrong — the same trap as putting `LIMIT`
in front of the wrong `ORDER BY` in SQL.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods end with "take some of them", and both need an explicit ordering
first — otherwise "the first two" and "the top three" mean whatever order the
source happened to arrive in.

Page numbers start at 1, which means page 1 skips nothing.

## Hint 2

```csharp
orders
    .OrderBy(order => order.Id)
    .Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
    .Take(pageSize)
```

`Skip` past the end yields nothing rather than throwing, and `Take` more than
there are gives you everything — so neither edge case needs a guard.

`TopIds` orders by amount descending with the customer name as tie-break, takes
`count`, and projects the ids.

## Hint 3

Order **before** you take. `Take(3).OrderByDescending(...)` sorts three
arbitrary rows; `OrderByDescending(...).Take(3)` gives the three biggest. The
same mistake in SQL is putting `LIMIT` before you decide the `ORDER BY`, and it
produces plausible-looking wrong answers rather than errors.

The other habit worth carrying over from the SQL course: **paging without a
unique tie-break is unstable**. If two rows sort equally, nothing says which
page each lands on, so a row can appear on page 1 and again on page 2. Ordering
by the id here makes the paging deterministic; ordering only by amount would
not.

Left to you: what a caller passing `pageNumber = 0` should get. The gate never
asks. Silently returning page 1, returning empty, and throwing are all
defensible — pick one deliberately rather than by accident.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two methods, and they differ in exactly the way ex3 was about: one ends with
`ToList()` and one deliberately does not.

`CategoriesOver` filters, projects to the category name, removes duplicates,
sorts, and materialises. `LazyNames` projects and stops.

## Hint 2

`Distinct()` is the LINQ operator for "each value once" — it is `SELECT
DISTINCT`, and like SQL's it works on the *projected* values, so project first
and then distinct.

```csharp
orders
    .Where(...)
    .Select(order => order.Category)
    .Distinct()
    .OrderBy(category => category)
    .ToList();
```

`LazyNames` is a single `Select` with no `ToList` — the return type is
`IEnumerable<string>` for exactly that reason.

## Hint 3

Order matters between `Distinct` and `OrderBy` in principle, though not for the
answer here: distinct-then-sort sorts fewer items. In SQL the planner would
make that decision for you; in LINQ-to-objects the order you write is the order

# 11 — LINQ, part 2

Lesson 10 covered the operators that keep a sequence a sequence. This one
covers the operators that change its *shape*: many rows into groups, two
sequences into one, one row into many. If lesson 10 was `SELECT ... WHERE ...
ORDER BY`, this is `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, `HAVING` and the aggregates — and the
translation is close enough that you can read most of it straight across from
the SQL course.

The one place the analogy is worth pushing on is what a *group* is. In SQL, a
`GROUP BY` collapses rows and you may only see aggregates afterwards. In LINQ,
`GroupBy` hands you a sequence of groups and **each group is still a sequence
you can look inside**. That is strictly more powerful — you can take the three
biggest sales per category without a window function — and it is the reason
LINQ's grouping feels different for the first hour.

The other reason this lesson matters: this is what you will actually write at
work. EF Core queries are these operators, translated to SQL by an expression
tree walker. Getting the grouping and joining right in memory, where you can see
every step, is how you learn to predict what EF will send to the database.

## Concept — four operators that reshape

**`GroupBy`** turns rows into groups. Each group has a `Key` and *is* an
`IEnumerable<T>` of its members:

```csharp
sales.GroupBy(s => s.Category)                       // IEnumerable<IGrouping<string, Sale>>
     .Select(g => $"{g.Key}: {g.Sum(s => s.Amount)}")
```

Grouping an empty sequence gives no groups — not one empty group — which is the
same as SQL.

**`Join`** matches two sequences on a key and gives you one row per matched
pair. It is an **inner** join: anything unmatched on either side disappears.

```csharp
sales.Join(customers,
    sale => sale.CustomerId,      // key on the left
    customer => customer.Id,      // key on the right
    (sale, customer) => new { customer.Name, sale.Amount });
```

**`GroupJoin`** is the left join: one row per *outer* item, paired with a
(possibly empty) group of matches. That empty group is how a customer with no
sales still appears.

**`SelectMany`** flattens. Where `Select` gives one output per input,
`SelectMany` takes a lambda returning a sequence and concatenates the lot:

```csharp
shipments.SelectMany(s => s.Items);                              // just the items
shipments.SelectMany(s => s.Items, (s, item) => $"{s.Code}:{item}");  // paired with their parent
```

**`Aggregate`** is the general fold — `Sum`, `Min`, `Max` and `Count` are named
special cases:

```csharp
words.Aggregate((best, w) => w.Length > best.Length ? w : best);
```

The seedless version starts from the first element and **throws on an empty
sequence**; the overload taking a seed does not.

**Query syntax** is the other way to write all of this, and for grouping and
joining it often reads better:

```csharp
from customer in customers
group customer by customer.City into city
orderby city.Count() descending, city.Key
select $"{city.Key}: {city.Count()}"
```

The compiler rewrites that into exactly the method calls above — `group ... into`
becomes `GroupBy`, the comma in `orderby` becomes `ThenBy`, `join ... on ... equals`
becomes `Join`. Neither form is faster; use whichever is clearer, and be able to
read both, because every codebase has some of each.

## Exercise 1 — GROUP BY

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex1.cs`. `TotalByCategory` returns
`"category: total"` per category, biggest total first with the category name as
tie-break. `CountByCategory` returns a `Dictionary<string, int>` of how many
sales each category had.

The shared model is in `Model.cs` and you never edit it. Watch the difference
between `group.Count()` (this group) and `sales.Count()` (everything) — the same
mistake as an aggregate outside its `GROUP BY`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex2.cs`. `SaleLabels` returns
`"customer - category"` for every sale, matched to its customer, in sale-id
order. `SaleCounts` returns `"name: count"` for **every** customer, A–Z —
including zed, who has no sales and must report `0`.

One of those is `Join` and the other is `GroupJoin`, and picking the wrong one
silently drops a row. That is the LINQ version of the inner/outer join decision
from the SQL course's lesson 09.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — one row in, many out

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex3.cs`. `AllItems` flattens every shipment's items
into one sequence. `LabelledItems` does the same but tags each item with its
shipment code: `"A:hat"`.

Note what shipment B — the one with no items — does to the output: nothing at
all. It does not appear as a blank. A row whose child collection is empty
contributes no rows, which is exactly why an inner join drops unmatched rows.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — folding, and the other syntax

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex4.cs`. `Longest` returns the longest word using
`Aggregate` — earlier word wins a tie, and an empty sequence is allowed to
throw. `CitiesByCustomerCount` returns `"city: count"`, most customers first
with the city name as tie-break.

Write the second one in **query syntax**. The gate cannot tell which syntax you
used, and that is not the point: you are here to be able to read both, and this
is the query where the keyword form earns its keep.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex4
```

## Challenge — a revenue report from two tables

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Challenge.cs`. `TopCustomers(customers, sales, count)`
returns the biggest-spending customers as `"bo: 390 | ada: 165 | cy: 120"` —
biggest first, ties by name, customers with no sales excluded, `"(none)"` when
there is nothing at all.

Honest difficulty note: four operators in one chain, and the design decision is
in the first line. Start from `sales` and join to `customers` and the
no-sales customer is excluded automatically; start from `customers` with a
`GroupJoin` and you have to exclude them by hand. Read the requirement, then
pick the join — which is exactly the conversation you will have about a real
report.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is `HAVING`: filtering the groups rather than the rows, plus a `Max`
per group. `dojo review` will bring it back.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/11_linq_2

## Notes

**`GroupBy` is greedy in a way that matters.** It is a deferred operator — it
returns without doing anything — but the moment you enumerate it, it must read
the *entire* source before it can hand you the first group, because a later row
could belong to a group it has already yielded. So `GroupBy` buffers everything
in memory, which is fine for a list and worth knowing for a large stream. The
same is true of `OrderBy`, `Join` (it builds a lookup of the inner sequence),
and `Distinct` in its own way.

**`IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` is an `IEnumerable<TElement>` with a `Key`.** That
is the whole type. Everything you can do to a sequence — `Count`, `Sum`,
`OrderBy`, `Take` — you can do inside a group, which is what makes "top 3 per
category" a two-line LINQ query and a window function in SQL.

**Join builds a lookup.** `Join` and `GroupJoin` read the *inner* sequence into
a hash lookup first, then stream the outer sequence past it. So the cost is
roughly one pass over each, not the n × m a nested loop would give — the same
hash-join strategy a database planner picks. It also means the inner sequence is
fully materialised, which is another reason to pass the smaller side as the
inner one.

**Query syntax is a rewrite, not a runtime.** `from x in xs where ... select ...`
is turned into method calls by the compiler before anything else happens. There
is no performance difference and no operator available only in one form —
though the reverse is true: many operators (`Count`, `Take`, `Distinct`) have no
keyword and need a method call anyway, which is why most codebases lean on
method syntax and switch to query syntax for joins and multi-level groups.

**Anonymous types are the glue.** `new { customer.Name, sale.Amount }` creates
an unnamed class with two read-only properties, value equality and a sensible
`ToString` — records, essentially, before records existed. They exist for
precisely this: carrying a few values through the middle of a query without
declaring a type for them. They cannot leave the method (you have no name to
declare a return type with), which is a deliberate limit, not an oversight.

## ex1

The mental shift is that a group is a sequence. In SQL, after `GROUP BY
category` you cannot see individual sales any more — only aggregates. In LINQ
you can: `group.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).Take(3)` gives you the biggest
three sales *within* each category, which in SQL needs `ROW_NUMBER() OVER
(PARTITION BY ...)`. That extra power is the single biggest difference between
the two grouping models, and it is worth remembering when a report gets
awkward.

`ToDictionary(keySelector, valueSelector)` is the standard way to finish a
grouping when the caller wants lookups rather than a list. Two things to know:
it throws on duplicate keys (which is a feature — it catches a grouping mistake
immediately), and `ToLookup` is its sibling for when duplicates are expected,
returning a multi-value dictionary that never throws and returns an empty
sequence for a missing key.

The empty-source behaviour — no groups rather than one empty group — is the
same as SQL's, and it is the reason a "no data" report needs the explicit
decision that lesson 10's challenge made.

## ex2

`Join` is an inner join and `GroupJoin` is a left join, and if you take one
sentence from this lesson, take that one. The failure mode is asymmetric and
nasty: an inner join where you wanted a left join does not error, it just
silently returns fewer rows. Zed vanishes from the report, and nobody notices
until someone asks why the customer count is 3 when the CRM says 4.

The LINQ shape differs from SQL's in a way that is worth stating. SQL's `LEFT
JOIN` produces one row per match *with nulls* when there are none.
`GroupJoin` produces one row per outer item with a **group** of matches, which
is usually more useful — you can `Count()` it, `Sum()` it, or check whether it
is empty, all without a null in sight. When you genuinely want SQL's shape, the
idiom is `GroupJoin(...).SelectMany(g => g.Inner.DefaultIfEmpty(), ...)`, and
that is exactly what EF Core generates for a left join.

`DefaultIfEmpty` is worth meeting on its own: it turns an empty sequence into a
one-element sequence holding `default(T)`. That is the whole mechanism behind
LINQ's outer joins, and it is a neat trick to have in your pocket.

## ex3

`SelectMany` is the flattening operator and also, quietly, the join operator.
`from shipment in shipments from item in shipment.Items select ...` compiles to
`SelectMany` — a nested `from` **is** a join, and if the inner collection were
a whole other sequence rather than a child property, that is a cross join with
a filter.

Which explains the empty-shipment behaviour: shipment B contributes nothing
because flattening an empty collection contributes nothing, and that is the
same reason an inner join drops unmatched rows. Two facts, one mechanism.

The two-lambda overload exists because flattening loses the parent. Once the
items are in one flat sequence, "which shipment was this from?" is
unanswerable, so the pairing must happen *during* the flattening. Every time you
find yourself flattening and then trying to look the parent back up, that
overload is what you wanted.

`SelectMany` is also the reason LINQ is a monad, if you have met the word — it
is `bind`. You do not need the theory; you do need to recognise that "map, then
flatten" is one operation with a name.

## ex4

`Aggregate` is the fold, and its two overloads encode a real decision. The
seedless version starts from the first element and throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence — correct, because "the longest
of nothing" has no answer. The seeded version (`Aggregate(seed, func)`) never
throws and returns the seed. Choosing between them is choosing whether empty is
an error or a legitimate base case, which is the same question `Max` answers by
throwing and `Sum` answers by returning 0.

Most `Aggregate` calls in the wild should have been something else — `Sum`,
`Max`, `string.Join`, or a `foreach`. It earns its place when the fold is
genuinely custom and the sequence is being consumed once. When you catch
yourself writing `Aggregate` to build a string, use `string.Join`: it is
clearer and it does not allocate a new string per element.

The query-syntax half is worth practising even though most code you write will
be method syntax. `group x by key into g` is the piece that has no obvious
method-syntax counterpart at a glance (it is `GroupBy` plus a continuation), and
`join x in xs on a equals b into g` is how a left join looks in keywords.
Reading a colleague's query-syntax `join ... into ... from ... in ...
DefaultIfEmpty()` without flinching is a genuine skill.

## challenge

Real reports are exactly this: two tables, a join, a grouping, an aggregate, a
ranking, and a formatting decision at the end. The interesting part is that the
*specification* decides the join type, and the specification here says "the
customers who spent the most" — which cannot include somebody who spent
nothing.

If the specification had said "every customer, with their spend", the same
report would need `GroupJoin` and would show `zed: 0`. Neither is more correct;
they answer different questions. The mistake to avoid is picking a join because
it is the one you remembered.

Grouping by name rather than by id is the other thing a reviewer would flag.
Two customers called "ada" would silently merge into one row, and the test data
cannot show you that. In production, group by the key that is actually unique
and carry the display name along for the projection.

## review1

`Where` after `GroupBy` is `HAVING`, and the reason SQL needs two keywords is
the reason this matters: a condition about a *group* cannot be expressed as a
condition about a *row*. "Its category has at least three sales" is not a fact
about any individual sale. Try to write it as a pre-grouping filter and you will
find there is nothing to write.

The order does matter for cost as well as meaning. Filtering rows before
grouping (a real `WHERE`) means fewer rows to group; filtering groups after
means you grouped everything first. When both are possible — "categories with
three or more sales over 100" — you want both: `Where` the rows, `GroupBy`, then
`Where` the groups. That is precisely how the SQL version reads too.

`group.Max(...)` versus `sales.Max(...)` is the same scope question as ex1's
`Count`. Inside a `Select` over groups, `group` is your world; reaching back out
to the whole sequence gives a number that is the same for every row, which is
occasionally what you want and usually a bug.

## Further reading

- [`GroupBy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.groupby) — every overload, including the element-selector and result-selector forms.
- [`Join` and `GroupJoin`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/join-operations) — inner joins, group joins, and the left-outer-join idiom.
- [`SelectMany`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/projection-operations#selectmany) — flattening, with the two-lambda overload explained.
- [`Aggregate`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.aggregate) — the seeded and seedless versions and what each does with an empty sequence.
- [Query syntax versus method syntax](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/get-started/query-expression-basics) — the rewrite rules, keyword by keyword.
- [Grouping data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/grouping-data) — worked examples including nested groupings.

# 11 — LINQ, part 2

Lesson 10 covered the operators that keep a sequence a sequence. This one
covers the operators that change its *shape*: many rows into groups, two
sequences into one, one row into many. If lesson 10 was `SELECT ... WHERE ...
ORDER BY`, this is `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, `HAVING` and the aggregates — and the
translation is close enough that you can read most of it straight across from
the SQL course.

The one place the analogy is worth pushing on is what a *group* is. In SQL, a
`GROUP BY` collapses rows and you may only see aggregates afterwards. In LINQ,
`GroupBy` hands you a sequence of groups and **each group is still a sequence
you can look inside**. That is strictly more powerful — you can take the three
biggest sales per category without a window function — and it is the reason
LINQ's grouping feels different for the first hour.

The other reason this lesson matters: this is what you will actually write at
work. EF Core queries are these operators, translated to SQL by an expression
tree walker. Getting the grouping and joining right in memory, where you can see
every step, is how you learn to predict what EF will send to the database.

## Concept — four operators that reshape

**`GroupBy`** turns rows into groups. Each group has a `Key` and *is* an
`IEnumerable<T>` of its members:

```csharp
sales.GroupBy(s => s.Category)                       // IEnumerable<IGrouping<string, Sale>>
     .Select(g => $"{g.Key}: {g.Sum(s => s.Amount)}")
```

Grouping an empty sequence gives no groups — not one empty group — which is the
same as SQL.

**`Join`** matches two sequences on a key and gives you one row per matched
pair. It is an **inner** join: anything unmatched on either side disappears.

```csharp
sales.Join(customers,
    sale => sale.CustomerId,      // key on the left
    customer => customer.Id,      // key on the right
    (sale, customer) => new { customer.Name, sale.Amount });
```

**`GroupJoin`** is the left join: one row per *outer* item, paired with a
(possibly empty) group of matches. That empty group is how a customer with no
sales still appears.

**`SelectMany`** flattens. Where `Select` gives one output per input,
`SelectMany` takes a lambda returning a sequence and concatenates the lot:

```csharp
shipments.SelectMany(s => s.Items);                              // just the items
shipments.SelectMany(s => s.Items, (s, item) => $"{s.Code}:{item}");  // paired with their parent
```

**`Aggregate`** is the general fold — `Sum`, `Min`, `Max` and `Count` are named
special cases:

```csharp
words.Aggregate((best, w) => w.Length > best.Length ? w : best);
```

The seedless version starts from the first element and **throws on an empty
sequence**; the overload taking a seed does not.

**Query syntax** is the other way to write all of this, and for grouping and
joining it often reads better:

```csharp
from customer in customers
group customer by customer.City into city
orderby city.Count() descending, city.Key
select $"{city.Key}: {city.Count()}"
```

The compiler rewrites that into exactly the method calls above — `group ... into`
becomes `GroupBy`, the comma in `orderby` becomes `ThenBy`, `join ... on ... equals`
becomes `Join`. Neither form is faster; use whichever is clearer, and be able to
read both, because every codebase has some of each.

## Exercise 1 — GROUP BY

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex1.cs`. `TotalByCategory` returns
`"category: total"` per category, biggest total first with the category name as
tie-break. `CountByCategory` returns a `Dictionary<string, int>` of how many
sales each category had.

The shared model is in `Model.cs` and you never edit it. Watch the difference
between `group.Count()` (this group) and `sales.Count()` (everything) — the same
mistake as an aggregate outside its `GROUP BY`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex2.cs`. `SaleLabels` returns
`"customer - category"` for every sale, matched to its customer, in sale-id
order. `SaleCounts` returns `"name: count"` for **every** customer, A–Z —
including zed, who has no sales and must report `0`.

One of those is `Join` and the other is `GroupJoin`, and picking the wrong one
silently drops a row. That is the LINQ version of the inner/outer join decision
from the SQL course's lesson 09.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — one row in, many out

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex3.cs`. `AllItems` flattens every shipment's items
into one sequence. `LabelledItems` does the same but tags each item with its
shipment code: `"A:hat"`.

Note what shipment B — the one with no items — does to the output: nothing at
all. It does not appear as a blank. A row whose child collection is empty
contributes no rows, which is exactly why an inner join drops unmatched rows.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — folding, and the other syntax

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex4.cs`. `Longest` returns the longest word using
`Aggregate` — earlier word wins a tie, and an empty sequence is allowed to
throw. `CitiesByCustomerCount` returns `"city: count"`, most customers first
with the city name as tie-break.

Write the second one in **query syntax**. The gate cannot tell which syntax you
used, and that is not the point: you are here to be able to read both, and this
is the query where the keyword form earns its keep.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex4
```

## Challenge — a revenue report from two tables

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Challenge.cs`. `TopCustomers(customers, sales, count)`
returns the biggest-spending customers as `"bo: 390 | ada: 165 | cy: 120"` —
biggest first, ties by name, customers with no sales excluded, `"(none)"` when
there is nothing at all.

Honest difficulty note: four operators in one chain, and the design decision is
in the first line. Start from `sales` and join to `customers` and the
no-sales customer is excluded automatically; start from `customers` with a
`GroupJoin` and you have to exclude them by hand. Read the requirement, then
pick the join — which is exactly the conversation you will have about a real
report.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is `HAVING`: filtering the groups rather than the rows, plus a `Max`
per group. `dojo review` will bring it back.

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L11_Linq2Tests.cs`:

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L11_Linq2;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L11_Linq2Tests
{
    private static List<Customer> Customers() => new List<Customer>
    {
        new Customer(1, "ada", "london"),
        new Customer(2, "bo", "bristol"),
        new Customer(3, "cy", "london"),
        new Customer(4, "zed", "leeds"),
    };

    private static List<Sale> Sales() => new List<Sale>
    {
        new Sale(1, 1, "books", 120m),
        new Sale(2, 1, "toys", 45m),
        new Sale(3, 2, "books", 300m),
        new Sale(4, 3, "toys", 120m),
        new Sale(5, 2, "books", 90m),
    };

    private static List<Shipment> Shipments() => new List<Shipment>
    {
        new Shipment("A", new List<string> { "hat", "scarf" }),
        new Shipment("B", new List<string>()),
        new Shipment("C", new List<string> { "boots" }),
    };

    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_GroupByCollapsesRowsIntoGroups()
    {
        Teach.Equal("books: 510, toys: 165", string.Join(", ", Grouped.TotalByCategory(Sales())),
            "books is 120 + 300 + 90 = 510 and toys is 45 + 120 = 165, biggest first. GroupBy "
                + "gives you a sequence of groups; Sum turns each group back into one number - "
                + "reread README ex1.");

        Dictionary<string, int> counts = Grouped.CountByCategory(Sales());

        Teach.Equal(2, counts.Count, "Two distinct categories, so two entries.");
        Teach.Equal(3, counts["books"], "Three book sales - group.Count(), not sales.Count().");
        Teach.Equal(2, counts["toys"], "Two toy sales.");

        Teach.Equal(0, Grouped.CountByCategory(new List<Sale>()).Count,
            "No sales, no groups - and no exception. GroupBy over an empty sequence yields "
                + "nothing rather than one empty group.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_JoinKeepsMatchesAndGroupJoinKeepsEverybody()
    {
        Teach.Equal("ada - books, ada - toys, bo - books, cy - toys, bo - books",
            string.Join(", ", Joins.SaleLabels(Customers(), Sales())),
            "One line per SALE, matched to its customer on CustomerId = Id, in sale-id order. "
                + "Join is an INNER JOIN: zed has no sales so zed never appears - reread "
                + "README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal("ada: 2, bo: 2, cy: 1, zed: 0",
            string.Join(", ", Joins.SaleCounts(Customers(), Sales())),
            "Every customer appears, including zed with 0. That is a LEFT JOIN, and in LINQ it "
                + "is GroupJoin - which hands you each customer together with THEIR sales as a "
                + "(possibly empty) group. A plain Join would silently drop zed - reread "
                + "README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(4, Joins.SaleCounts(Customers(), new List<Sale>()).Count,
            "With no sales at all, all four customers still appear - each with 0.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_SelectManyFlattensRowsThatHoldCollections()
    {
        Teach.Equal("hat, scarf, boots", string.Join(", ", Flatten.AllItems(Shipments())),
            "Three shipments, one flat list of items. Shipment B is empty and contributes "
                + "nothing - it does not appear as a blank - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("A:hat, A:scarf, C:boots",
            string.Join(", ", Flatten.LabelledItems(Shipments())),
            "The item alone loses which shipment it came from. SelectMany's second lambda "
                + "gets both the outer row and the inner item, which is exactly the pairing a "
                + "join produces - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal(0, Flatten.AllItems(new List<Shipment>()).Count, "Nothing to flatten.");

        Teach.Equal(0, Flatten.AllItems(new List<Shipment> { new Shipment("Z", new List<string>()) }).Count,
            "A shipment with an empty item list yields no rows - the same reason an INNER "
                + "JOIN drops a row with no matches.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_AggregateFoldsAndQuerySyntaxGroups()
    {
        Teach.Equal("three", Folding.Longest(new[] { "a", "three", "xx" }),
            "Aggregate carries a running best through the sequence - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal("aaa", Folding.Longest(new[] { "aaa", "bbb" }),
            "A tie keeps the EARLIER word, which is what a strictly-greater comparison gives "
                + "you - the same tie-break decision as lesson 02.");

        Teach.Equal("only", Folding.Longest(new[] { "only" }),
            "With one item, Aggregate never calls your lambda at all - the seed is the first "
                + "element.");

        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => Folding.Longest(Array.Empty<string>()),
            "The seedless Aggregate has nothing to start from, so it throws. Do not paper over "
                + "that with a \"\" - an empty sequence has no longest word - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal("london: 2, bristol: 1, leeds: 1",
            string.Join(", ", Folding.CitiesByCustomerCount(Customers())),
            "Two Londoners lead; bristol and leeds tie on 1 and are broken alphabetically - "
                + "reread README ex4.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Challenge_ARevenueReportFromTwoTables()
    {
        Teach.Equal("bo: 390 | ada: 165 | cy: 120",
            Revenue.TopCustomers(Customers(), Sales(), 3),
            "bo spent 300 + 90, ada 120 + 45, cy 120. Join the sales to their customers, group "
                + "by customer, sum, rank, take - reread README challenge.");

        Teach.Equal("bo: 390", Revenue.TopCustomers(Customers(), Sales(), 1),
            "Only the top spender.");

        Teach.Equal("(none)", Revenue.TopCustomers(Customers(), new List<Sale>(), 3),
            "No sales means no rows to report - zed and everyone else are absent, because a "
                + "customer with no sales does not appear - reread README challenge.");

        Teach.True(!Revenue.TopCustomers(Customers(), Sales(), 10).Contains("zed"),
            "Even asking for ten, zed has no sales and so does not appear. If zed showed up "
                + "with 0 you used GroupJoin where the prompt wanted an inner join.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Review1_FilteringGroupsIsHavingNotWhere()
    {
        Teach.Equal("books", string.Join(", ", Analysis.CategoriesWithAtLeast(Sales(), 3)),
            "Only books has three or more sales. The Where comes AFTER the GroupBy, so it "
                + "filters groups rather than rows - that is HAVING - reread README review.");

        Teach.Equal("books, toys", string.Join(", ", Analysis.CategoriesWithAtLeast(Sales(), 2)),
            "Both categories clear a threshold of 2.");

        Teach.Equal(0, Analysis.CategoriesWithAtLeast(Sales(), 4).Count,
            "Nothing has four sales.");

        Teach.Equal("books: 300, toys: 120", string.Join(", ", Analysis.MaxByCategory(Sales())),
            "The biggest sale within each group, categories A-Z. Max over the group, not over "
                + "everything - reread README review.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: `Ex1` checks both aggregates and the empty-sequence case.
`Ex2` compares the inner join's output with the group join's, and checks zed
appears in exactly one of them. `Ex3` flattens with and without labels and
checks that an empty child collection contributes nothing. `Ex4` folds four
sequences including the empty one that throws, then checks the grouped city
counts. `Challenge` runs the report three ways, and `Review1` is the
spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The SQL translation table is worth writing down once, because it is the whole
lesson:

```
WHERE          -> .Where(...)          before the grouping
GROUP BY       -> .GroupBy(...)
HAVING         -> .Where(...)          after the grouping
count(*)       -> group.Count()
sum(x)         -> group.Sum(s => s.X)
INNER JOIN     -> .Join(...)
LEFT JOIN      -> .GroupJoin(...)      (or GroupJoin + SelectMany + DefaultIfEmpty)
ORDER BY a, b  -> .OrderBy(a).ThenBy(b)
LIMIT / OFFSET -> .Take(n) / .Skip(n)
```

And the one that has no SQL equivalent: a LINQ group is still a sequence. You
can sort inside it, take the top three from each, or project it into a nested
shape — none of which plain `GROUP BY` can do.

The habit to carry into a .NET job is to keep asking *where the work happens*.
The exact same chain over a `List<Sale>` runs in memory as delegates; over an
EF Core `DbSet<Sale>` it becomes a `SELECT ... GROUP BY` and runs in Postgres.
Written badly — materialising with `.ToList()` too early, or calling a method
EF cannot translate — it quietly turns into "fetch the whole table, then group
in C#". That is the same N+1 conversation the SQL course had, and it starts
with knowing which of the two worlds your query is in.

Next: **12_exceptions**, where things go wrong on purpose.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **11 — LINQ, part 2**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex3` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `review1` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `challenge` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex1` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex2` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex3` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - csharp/11_linq_2

## Notes

**`GroupBy` is greedy in a way that matters.** It is a deferred operator — it
returns without doing anything — but the moment you enumerate it, it must read
the *entire* source before it can hand you the first group, because a later row
could belong to a group it has already yielded. So `GroupBy` buffers everything
in memory, which is fine for a list and worth knowing for a large stream. The
same is true of `OrderBy`, `Join` (it builds a lookup of the inner sequence),
and `Distinct` in its own way.

**`IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` is an `IEnumerable<TElement>` with a `Key`.** That
is the whole type. Everything you can do to a sequence — `Count`, `Sum`,
`OrderBy`, `Take` — you can do inside a group, which is what makes "top 3 per
category" a two-line LINQ query and a window function in SQL.

**Join builds a lookup.** `Join` and `GroupJoin` read the *inner* sequence into
a hash lookup first, then stream the outer sequence past it. So the cost is
roughly one pass over each, not the n × m a nested loop would give — the same
hash-join strategy a database planner picks. It also means the inner sequence is
fully materialised, which is another reason to pass the smaller side as the
inner one.

**Query syntax is a rewrite, not a runtime.** `from x in xs where ... select ...`
is turned into method calls by the compiler before anything else happens. There
is no performance difference and no operator available only in one form —
though the reverse is true: many operators (`Count`, `Take`, `Distinct`) have no
keyword and need a method call anyway, which is why most codebases lean on
method syntax and switch to query syntax for joins and multi-level groups.

**Anonymous types are the glue.** `new { customer.Name, sale.Amount }` creates
an unnamed class with two read-only properties, value equality and a sensible
`ToString` — records, essentially, before records existed. They exist for
precisely this: carrying a few values through the middle of a query without
declaring a type for them. They cannot leave the method (you have no name to
declare a return type with), which is a deliberate limit, not an oversight.

## ex1

The mental shift is that a group is a sequence. In SQL, after `GROUP BY
category` you cannot see individual sales any more — only aggregates. In LINQ
you can: `group.OrderByDescending(s => s.Amount).Take(3)` gives you the biggest
three sales *within* each category, which in SQL needs `ROW_NUMBER() OVER
(PARTITION BY ...)`. That extra power is the single biggest difference between
the two grouping models, and it is worth remembering when a report gets
awkward.

`ToDictionary(keySelector, valueSelector)` is the standard way to finish a
grouping when the caller wants lookups rather than a list. Two things to know:
it throws on duplicate keys (which is a feature — it catches a grouping mistake
immediately), and `ToLookup` is its sibling for when duplicates are expected,
returning a multi-value dictionary that never throws and returns an empty
sequence for a missing key.

The empty-source behaviour — no groups rather than one empty group — is the
same as SQL's, and it is the reason a "no data" report needs the explicit
decision that lesson 10's challenge made.

## ex2

`Join` is an inner join and `GroupJoin` is a left join, and if you take one
sentence from this lesson, take that one. The failure mode is asymmetric and
nasty: an inner join where you wanted a left join does not error, it just
silently returns fewer rows. Zed vanishes from the report, and nobody notices
until someone asks why the customer count is 3 when the CRM says 4.

The LINQ shape differs from SQL's in a way that is worth stating. SQL's `LEFT
JOIN` produces one row per match *with nulls* when there are none.
`GroupJoin` produces one row per outer item with a **group** of matches, which
is usually more useful — you can `Count()` it, `Sum()` it, or check whether it
is empty, all without a null in sight. When you genuinely want SQL's shape, the
idiom is `GroupJoin(...).SelectMany(g => g.Inner.DefaultIfEmpty(), ...)`, and
that is exactly what EF Core generates for a left join.

`DefaultIfEmpty` is worth meeting on its own: it turns an empty sequence into a
one-element sequence holding `default(T)`. That is the whole mechanism behind
LINQ's outer joins, and it is a neat trick to have in your pocket.

## ex3

`SelectMany` is the flattening operator and also, quietly, the join operator.
`from shipment in shipments from item in shipment.Items select ...` compiles to
`SelectMany` — a nested `from` **is** a join, and if the inner collection were
a whole other sequence rather than a child property, that is a cross join with
a filter.

Which explains the empty-shipment behaviour: shipment B contributes nothing
because flattening an empty collection contributes nothing, and that is the
same reason an inner join drops unmatched rows. Two facts, one mechanism.

The two-lambda overload exists because flattening loses the parent. Once the
items are in one flat sequence, "which shipment was this from?" is
unanswerable, so the pairing must happen *during* the flattening. Every time you
find yourself flattening and then trying to look the parent back up, that
overload is what you wanted.

`SelectMany` is also the reason LINQ is a monad, if you have met the word — it
is `bind`. You do not need the theory; you do need to recognise that "map, then
flatten" is one operation with a name.

## ex4

`Aggregate` is the fold, and its two overloads encode a real decision. The
seedless version starts from the first element and throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence — correct, because "the longest
of nothing" has no answer. The seeded version (`Aggregate(seed, func)`) never
throws and returns the seed. Choosing between them is choosing whether empty is
an error or a legitimate base case, which is the same question `Max` answers by
throwing and `Sum` answers by returning 0.

Most `Aggregate` calls in the wild should have been something else — `Sum`,
`Max`, `string.Join`, or a `foreach`. It earns its place when the fold is
genuinely custom and the sequence is being consumed once. When you catch
yourself writing `Aggregate` to build a string, use `string.Join`: it is
clearer and it does not allocate a new string per element.

The query-syntax half is worth practising even though most code you write will
be method syntax. `group x by key into g` is the piece that has no obvious
method-syntax counterpart at a glance (it is `GroupBy` plus a continuation), and
`join x in xs on a equals b into g` is how a left join looks in keywords.
Reading a colleague's query-syntax `join ... into ... from ... in ...
DefaultIfEmpty()` without flinching is a genuine skill.

## challenge

Real reports are exactly this: two tables, a join, a grouping, an aggregate, a
ranking, and a formatting decision at the end. The interesting part is that the
*specification* decides the join type, and the specification here says "the
customers who spent the most" — which cannot include somebody who spent
nothing.

If the specification had said "every customer, with their spend", the same
report would need `GroupJoin` and would show `zed: 0`. Neither is more correct;
they answer different questions. The mistake to avoid is picking a join because
it is the one you remembered.

Grouping by name rather than by id is the other thing a reviewer would flag.
Two customers called "ada" would silently merge into one row, and the test data
cannot show you that. In production, group by the key that is actually unique
and carry the display name along for the projection.

## review1

`Where` after `GroupBy` is `HAVING`, and the reason SQL needs two keywords is
the reason this matters: a condition about a *group* cannot be expressed as a
condition about a *row*. "Its category has at least three sales" is not a fact
about any individual sale. Try to write it as a pre-grouping filter and you will
find there is nothing to write.

The order does matter for cost as well as meaning. Filtering rows before
grouping (a real `WHERE`) means fewer rows to group; filtering groups after
means you grouped everything first. When both are possible — "categories with
three or more sales over 100" — you want both: `Where` the rows, `GroupBy`, then
`Where` the groups. That is precisely how the SQL version reads too.

`group.Max(...)` versus `sales.Max(...)` is the same scope question as ex1's
`Count`. Inside a `Select` over groups, `group` is your world; reaching back out
to the whole sequence gives a number that is the same for every row, which is
occasionally what you want and usually a bug.

## Further reading

- [`GroupBy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.groupby) — every overload, including the element-selector and result-selector forms.
- [`Join` and `GroupJoin`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/join-operations) — inner joins, group joins, and the left-outer-join idiom.
- [`SelectMany`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/projection-operations#selectmany) — flattening, with the two-lambda overload explained.
- [`Aggregate`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.aggregate) — the seeded and seedless versions and what each does with an empty sequence.
- [Query syntax versus method syntax](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/get-started/query-expression-basics) — the rewrite rules, keyword by keyword.
- [Grouping data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/grouping-data) — worked examples including nested groupings.

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Challenge.cs`. `TopCustomers(customers, sales, count)`

## Hint 1

Four of this lesson's operators in one chain, in this order: join the sales to

automatically — an inner join drops the customer with nothing to join to, which

real data; ids are. The gate's data cannot tell the difference, and a code
reviewer would.

## Exercise 1 — GROUP BY

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex1.cs`. `TotalByCategory` returns
`"category: total"` per category, biggest total first with the category name as
tie-break. `CountByCategory` returns a `Dictionary<string, int>` of how many
sales each category had.

The shared model is in `Model.cs` and you never edit it. Watch the difference
between `group.Count()` (this group) and `sales.Count()` (everything) — the same
mistake as an aggregate outside its `GROUP BY`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`GroupBy` turns a sequence of rows into a sequence of *groups*. Each group is
itself a little sequence, with a `Key` — so after grouping you can run any of
lesson 10's operators on each group.

Both methods here are "group, then turn each group into one thing". The
difference is only what that one thing is and how the results come out.

## Hint 2

```csharp
sales.GroupBy(sale => sale.Category)     // IEnumerable<IGrouping<string, Sale>>
     .Select(group => new { Category = group.Key, Total = group.Sum(s => s.Amount) })
```

That anonymous type gives you two named values to order by before you format
them — order first, format last, exactly as in lesson 10.

`ToDictionary(keySelector, valueSelector)` turns the groups into the dictionary
the second method promises: `group => group.Key` and `group => group.Count()`.

## Hint 3

`group.Sum(...)` and `group.Count()` are the aggregates operating *inside* one
group. `sales.Count()` would count every sale in the whole sequence — the same
mistake as putting `count(*)` outside a `GROUP BY` in SQL.

Note that grouping an empty sequence produces no groups at all, not one empty
group. That is why the empty case needs no special handling here, and it is the
same behaviour SQL has.

Left to you: `GroupBy` has an overload taking both a key selector and an element
selector, so you can group and project in one call. Worth finding in the docs;
it makes the first method a little shorter.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`GroupBy` turns a sequence of rows into a sequence of *groups*. Each group is
itself a little sequence, with a `Key` — so after grouping you can run any of
lesson 10's operators on each group.

Both methods here are "group, then turn each group into one thing". The
difference is only what that one thing is and how the results come out.

## Hint 2

```csharp
sales.GroupBy(sale => sale.Category)     // IEnumerable<IGrouping<string, Sale>>
     .Select(group => new { Category = group.Key, Total = group.Sum(s => s.Amount) })
```

That anonymous type gives you two named values to order by before you format
them — order first, format last, exactly as in lesson 10.

`ToDictionary(keySelector, valueSelector)` turns the groups into the dictionary
the second method promises: `group => group.Key` and `group => group.Count()`.

## Hint 3

`group.Sum(...)` and `group.Count()` are the aggregates operating *inside* one
group. `sales.Count()` would count every sale in the whole sequence — the same
mistake as putting `count(*)` outside a `GROUP BY` in SQL.

Note that grouping an empty sequence produces no groups at all, not one empty
group. That is why the empty case needs no special handling here, and it is the
same behaviour SQL has.

Left to you: `GroupBy` has an overload taking both a key selector and an element
selector, so you can group and project in one call. Worth finding in the docs;
it makes the first method a little shorter.

## Exercise 2 — INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN

Edit `src/Lessons/L11_Linq2/Ex2.cs`. `SaleLabels` returns
`"customer - category"` for every sale, matched to its customer, in sale-id
order. `SaleCounts` returns `"name: count"` for **every** customer, A–Z —
including zed, who has no sales and must report `0`.

One of those is `Join` and the other is `GroupJoin`, and picking the wrong one
silently drops a row. That is the LINQ version of the inner/outer join decision
from the SQL course's lesson 09.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 11_linq_2 ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two joins, and the whole exercise is which one drops rows.

`SaleLabels` wants one line per sale, so start from `sales` and match each one
to its customer. `SaleCounts` wants one line per customer *including the ones
with nothing*, so start from `customers` — and a plain `Join` will not do it.

## Hint 2

`Join` takes four arguments: the other sequence, the key on the left, the key on
the right, and what to make from each matched pair.

```csharp
sales.Join(
    customers,
    sale => sale.CustomerId,
    customer => customer.Id,
    (sale, customer) => /* the pair */)
```

`GroupJoin` has the same shape, but the last lambda receives the outer row and
**a group** of matching inner rows — empty when there are none. That empty group
is your LEFT JOIN.

## Hint 3

Ordering by sale id in the first method needs the id to survive the projection,
so project to an anonymous type holding both the id and the label, order, and
then select the label. Projecting straight to the label throws away what you
need to sort by — lesson 10's "order before you narrow" again.

The `zed: 0` line is the whole point of the second method. In SQL you would
write `LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY`; here `GroupJoin` hands you the same thing
without the join-then-regroup dance.

Left to you: LINQ's other way to write a left join is
`GroupJoin(...).SelectMany(g => g.Sales.DefaultIfEmpty(), ...)`, which gives you
one row per match with nulls for the missing side — literally what SQL returns.
Try it once so the shape is familiar when you meet it in EF Core.

## Hint 1

Two joins, and the whole exercise is which one drops rows.

`SaleLabels` wants one line per sale, so start from `sales` and match each one
to its customer. `SaleCounts` wants one line per customer *including the ones
with nothing*, so start from `customers` — and a plain `Join` will not do it.

## Hint 2

`Join` takes four arguments: the other sequence, the key on the left, the key on
the right, and what to make from each matched pair.

```csharp
sales.Join(
    customers,
    sale => sale.CustomerId,
    customer => customer.Id,
    (sale, customer) => /* the pair */)
```

`GroupJoin` has the same shape, but the last lambda receives the outer row and
**a group** of matching inner rows — empty when there are none. That empty group
is your LEFT JOIN.

## Hint 3

Ordering by sale id in the first method needs the id to survive the projection,
so project to an anonymous type holding both the id and the label, order, and
then select the label. Projecting straight to the label throws away what you
need to sort by — lesson 10's "order before you narrow" again.

The `zed: 0` line is the whole point of the second method. In SQL you would
write `LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY`; here `GroupJoin` hands you the same thing
without the join-then-regroup dance.

Left to you: LINQ's other way to write a left join is
`GroupJoin(...).SelectMany(g => g.Sales.DefaultIfEmpty(), ...)`, which gives you
one row per match with nulls for the missing side — literally what SQL returns.
Try it once so the shape is familiar when you meet it in EF Core.
