exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two different jobs. `Longest` folds a whole sequence down to one value with
`Aggregate`. `CitiesByCustomerCount` is ex1's grouping again, written in the
*other* LINQ syntax.

`Aggregate` is the general case of `Sum`, `Count`, `Min` and `Max` — the one
you reach for when the fold you want does not already have a name.

## Hint 2

The seedless `Aggregate` takes the first element as the starting value and then
calls your lambda for each remaining one:

```csharp
words.Aggregate((best, word) => /* whichever should survive */)
```

Query syntax for the second one:

```csharp
from customer in customers
group customer by customer.City into city
orderby /* ... */
select $"{city.Key}: {city.Count()}"
```

`into` names the grouped result so the rest of the query can work with it, and
the whole `from ... select` expression is an `IEnumerable<string>` you can
`.ToList()` — put the query in parentheses to call it.

## Hint 3

The empty case is the interesting one. Seedless `Aggregate` throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence because there is nothing to
start from — and the gate wants that, not a `""`. If you want a different
answer, the three-argument overload takes an explicit seed and never throws;
choosing between them is a real decision about whether "no items" is an error.

`orderby a descending, b` in query syntax is `OrderByDescending(a).ThenBy(b)` —
the comma is the `ThenBy`, exactly as in SQL.

Left to you: whether to call `city.Count()` twice (once in `orderby`, once in
`select`) or project to an intermediate. Twice is clearer and walks each group
twice; over a database, the translator would collapse them anyway.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two different jobs. `Longest` folds a whole sequence down to one value with
`Aggregate`. `CitiesByCustomerCount` is ex1's grouping again, written in the
*other* LINQ syntax.

`Aggregate` is the general case of `Sum`, `Count`, `Min` and `Max` — the one
you reach for when the fold you want does not already have a name.

## Hint 2

The seedless `Aggregate` takes the first element as the starting value and then
calls your lambda for each remaining one:

```csharp
words.Aggregate((best, word) => /* whichever should survive */)
```

Query syntax for the second one:

```csharp
from customer in customers
group customer by customer.City into city
orderby /* ... */
select $"{city.Key}: {city.Count()}"
```

`into` names the grouped result so the rest of the query can work with it, and
the whole `from ... select` expression is an `IEnumerable<string>` you can
`.ToList()` — put the query in parentheses to call it.

## Hint 3

The empty case is the interesting one. Seedless `Aggregate` throws
`InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence because there is nothing to
start from — and the gate wants that, not a `""`. If you want a different
answer, the three-argument overload takes an explicit seed and never throws;
choosing between them is a real decision about whether "no items" is an error.

`orderby a descending, b` in query syntax is `OrderByDescending(a).ThenBy(b)` —
the comma is the `ThenBy`, exactly as in SQL.

Left to you: whether to call `city.Count()` twice (once in `orderby`, once in
`select`) or project to an intermediate. Twice is clearer and walks each group
twice; over a database, the translator would collapse them anyway.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods start with the same `GroupBy`. The first then *filters the
groups*; the second aggregates each one.

Filtering after a `GroupBy` is `HAVING`. Filtering before it is `WHERE`. They
are different questions and they give different answers, so be clear which one
the prompt is asking for.

## Hint 2

```csharp
sales.GroupBy(sale => sale.Category)
     .Where(group => group.Count() >= minCount)     // HAVING
     .Select(group => group.Key)
     .OrderBy(category => category)
```

`group.Key` is the category name; `group.Max(sale => sale.Amount)` is the
biggest sale inside one group.

## Hint 3

Try writing the first method with the `Where` *before* the `GroupBy` and work
out what it would mean: "keep the sales that ... " — there is no per-sale
condition that expresses "its category has at least three sales", because that
fact belongs to the group, not the row. That impossibility is exactly why SQL
has both `WHERE` and `HAVING`.

Left to you: whether to order before or after the `Select`. Ordering by
`group.Key` and then selecting it is identical here; when the projection is
expensive, ordering first means projecting fewer items.

## Hint 1

Both methods start with the same `GroupBy`. The first then *filters the
groups*; the second aggregates each one.

Filtering after a `GroupBy` is `HAVING`. Filtering before it is `WHERE`. They
are different questions and they give different answers, so be clear which one
the prompt is asking for.

## Hint 2

```csharp
sales.GroupBy(sale => sale.Category)
     .Where(group => group.Count() >= minCount)     // HAVING
     .Select(group => group.Key)
     .OrderBy(category => category)
```

`group.Key` is the category name; `group.Max(sale => sale.Amount)` is the
biggest sale inside one group.

## Hint 3

Try writing the first method with the `Where` *before* the `GroupBy` and work
out what it would mean: "keep the sales that ... " — there is no per-sale
condition that expresses "its category has at least three sales", because that
fact belongs to the group, not the row. That impossibility is exactly why SQL
has both `WHERE` and `HAVING`.

Left to you: whether to order before or after the `Select`. Ordering by
`group.Key` and then selecting it is identical here; when the projection is
expensive, ordering first means projecting fewer items.

# 12 — Exceptions

Every method you have written so far assumed things went well. This lesson is
about the other path — and, more importantly, about the judgement call that
comes first: **is this failure exceptional at all?**

You have already met both answers. `int.TryParse` returns `false` because text
from a user is expected to be wrong sometimes. `int.Parse` throws because a
malformed number in code you control is a bug. `Withdraw` in lesson 03 returned
`false` for an overdraft and threw for a negative amount — the same distinction,
in one class. The rule teams settle on: **an exception is for a situation the
caller could not reasonably have anticipated or handled.** Everything else is a
return value.

Get that wrong in the cheap direction and you get code where the happy path is
buried in error handling. Get it wrong in the expensive direction — swallowing
exceptions with `catch (Exception) { }` — and you get a system that fails
silently, which is the worst kind of failure there is.

## Concept — throw, catch, filter, clean up

```csharp
try
{
    return a / b;
}
catch (DivideByZeroException)
{
    return fallback;
}
finally
{
    // runs on the way out, whichever way you leave
}
```

**Catch the specific type.** `catch (Exception)` catches configuration errors,
your own bugs, and out-of-memory alike, and reports them all as the same thing.
The narrower the catch, the more the code says.

**`finally` always runs** — normal exit, `return`, or exception. It is where
"whatever happens, undo this" goes.

**Exception filters** split one type by its data, and are evaluated *before*
the stack unwinds:

```csharp
catch (TransientException e) when (e.StatusCode >= 500) { ... }
catch (TransientException) { ... }
```

**Rethrowing:** `throw;` continues the current exception with its stack trace
intact. `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to this line and destroys the
evidence. The difference is one word and it costs debugging hours.

**Your own exception types** are worth it when a caller might want to catch
*that* specifically. Derive from `Exception`, offer the standard constructors,
and — this is the part people skip — pass the original exception as the
**inner** one when you wrap:

```csharp
catch (FormatException original)
{
    throw new ConfigurationException($"bad port: {text}", original);
}
```

**`IDisposable` and `using`.** Anything holding something the garbage collector
cannot clean up — a file, a socket, a database connection — implements
`IDisposable`, and `using` guarantees `Dispose()` runs even if the block throws:

```csharp
using Resource resource = new Resource();   // disposed at the end of the enclosing block
```

That guarantee is why cleanup written at the bottom of a `try` block is a bug
waiting for its first exception.

## Exercise 1 — the three blocks

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Ex1.cs`. `SafeDivide(a, b, fallback)` returns
`a / b`, catching `DivideByZeroException` and returning the fallback.

`Trace(shouldThrow)` writes a diary: `"try"` at the top of the `try`, a thrown
`InvalidOperationException` when asked, `"after"` on the path where nothing was
thrown, `"catch"` in the catch, `"finally"` in a `finally`. Return the log.

Predict both diaries before you run the gate. The question worth asking
yourself: does `"finally"` appear on the path where nothing went wrong?

```
uv run dojo test csharp 12_exceptions ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — your own exception, with the cause attached

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Ex2.cs`. `ConfigurationException` has two
constructors, and one of them quietly drops its `inner` argument on the way to
`base` — fix it. Then implement `Configuration.LoadPort(text)`: parse the
number, and turn any parse failure into a `ConfigurationException` whose message
is `"bad port: abc"` (or `"bad port: null"`) and whose `InnerException` is
whatever `int.Parse` actually threw.

`int.Parse` throws `FormatException` for `"abc"` and `ArgumentNullException` for
`null`, and the gate checks that *both* arrive with the right inner exception.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 12_exceptions ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — catching the right thing

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Ex3.cs`. `Classifier.Attempt(work)` reports
`"ok"` when nothing was thrown, `"retry"` for a `TransientException` with a
status of 500 or more, `"give up"` for any other `TransientException` — and
lets everything else through untouched.

That last clause is written by *not* writing a catch. A catch-all here would
report your own `NullReferenceException` as "give up", and the bug would live
in production for months.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 12_exceptions ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — cleanup that happens anyway

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Ex4.cs`. Implement `Resource.Dispose()` — it
logs `"dispose"`, but only the first time, because disposing twice must be
harmless. Then implement `Session.Run(shouldThrow)`: open a `Resource` in a
`using`, `Use()` it, throw when asked, catch that exception *outside* the using,
and return the log.

The two logs come out in a different order, and that difference is the lesson:
on the failure path the resource is released while the stack unwinds, before
the catch block runs.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 12_exceptions ex4
```

## Challenge — retry the retryable

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Challenge.cs`. `Resilient.Run(work, maxAttempts)`
calls `work` until it succeeds or until it has failed `maxAttempts` times with a
`TransientException`, returning `(attempts, value, "ok")` or
`(maxAttempts, 0, "exhausted")`. Anything that is not transient must escape
immediately, without another attempt.

Honest difficulty note: the loop is easy and the exit conditions are fiddly.
The gate counts calls, so "one attempt too many" and "gave up one early" both
show up as an exact number. The neat solution uses an exception filter to say
"transient, *and* there are attempts left".

```
uv run dojo test csharp 12_exceptions challenge
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/12_exceptions

## Notes

**What an exception costs.** Throwing is not just a jump: the runtime captures a
stack trace, walks the stack looking for a handler, and runs any `finally`
blocks on the way. That is measured in microseconds, not nanoseconds — fine for
something that happens when a request fails, terrible for something that happens
per row of a million-row import. This is the concrete reason behind "don't use
exceptions for control flow", and the reason `TryParse`, `TryGetValue` and
`TryDequeue` all exist.

**The exception hierarchy, in the bit you need.** Everything derives from
`Exception`. `SystemException` and its descendants (`ArgumentException`,
`InvalidOperationException`, `NullReferenceException`, `FormatException`) come
from the framework. `ApplicationException` was meant to be the base for yours and
is now explicitly *not* recommended — derive from `Exception` directly. A few
are special: `OutOfMemoryException` and `StackOverflowException` cannot be
meaningfully handled (the latter cannot be caught at all), and
`OperationCanceledException` is the polite one you will meet in lesson 13.

**Which exception to throw.** `ArgumentNullException` for a null argument,
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for one outside a valid range,
`ArgumentException` for anything else wrong with an argument,
`InvalidOperationException` when the *object* is not in a state where the call
makes sense, `NotSupportedException` for an operation this implementation will
never support. Using the right one lets callers write a specific catch — and
tells the reader what kind of mistake was made.

**`throw;` versus `throw ex;`.** `throw;` rethrows the current exception,
preserving the original stack trace. `throw ex;` throws the same object with the
stack trace reset to *this* line, so the log now says the failure happened in
your catch block. There is almost never a reason for the second. If you need to
add context, wrap: `throw new MyException("...", ex);`.

**Where exceptions should be caught.** Usually not where they are thrown.
Low-level code should let failures out; some boundary — a request handler, a
message consumer, a `Main` — should catch, log, and turn it into a response.
That is exactly what ASP.NET Core's exception middleware does, and it is why the
.NET track spends a lesson on it. A `try/catch` in every method is a sign
nobody decided where the boundary is.

## ex1

The diary in `Trace` makes the control flow visible. Two things worth noticing.
`"after"` never runs on the throwing path — a `throw` abandons the rest of the
block immediately, which is why "clean up at the bottom of the try" is a bug.
And `"finally"` runs on *both* paths, which is the guarantee that makes cleanup
possible at all.

`finally` also runs when the `try` block `return`s — the return value is
computed first, then the `finally` runs, then the method actually returns. That
occasionally surprises people writing `finally` blocks that modify the variable
being returned; the returned value was already captured.

`SafeDivide` is the exercise being deliberately artificial. In real code
`if (b == 0)` is faster, clearer, and does not pay for a stack trace. The
version worth writing is whichever makes the *reason* obvious: a check when the
condition is expected, a catch when the failure is genuinely surprising.

One detail worth having: integer division by zero throws, but floating-point
division by zero does **not** — `1.0 / 0.0` is `double.PositiveInfinity`, and
`0.0 / 0.0` is `NaN`. Same operator, two completely different failure models,
because IEEE 754 says so.

## ex2

Custom exceptions earn their place when a caller might want to catch *that*
specifically. If nobody will ever write `catch (ConfigurationException)`, a
plain `InvalidOperationException` with a good message is fine, and one more type
in the codebase is a cost with no benefit.

The inner exception is the part that gets dropped and the part that matters. Your
`ConfigurationException`'s stack trace starts at the line where you threw it —
which is the catch block, not the failure. The inner exception remembers where
the parse actually blew up, and every logger and every debugger prints the chain.
Dropping it produces the log entry everyone has seen: a friendly message with no
information in it.

The other half is the message. `"bad port: abc"` names the offending value;
`"Configuration error"` does not, and someone will have to reproduce the failure
locally to find out which setting was wrong. The rule of thumb: put in the
message whatever you would want to grep for.

`int.Parse(null)` throwing `ArgumentNullException` rather than `FormatException`
is a small trap the gate checks deliberately. Two failure types from one call is
normal in .NET, and a catch that handles only the one you thought of leaves the
other escaping raw.

## ex3

Exception filters are a C# 6 feature that people underuse. Beyond the obvious —
splitting one type by its data — the mechanism matters: a `when` clause runs
**before** the stack unwinds, in a first pass over the handlers. If it returns
false, the exception carries on from its original throw point with everything
intact, and a debugger breaking on unhandled exceptions still stops at the real
site.

Catch-and-rethrow does not have that property. `catch (X) { if (...) throw; }`
has already unwound the stack by the time it decides, so any `finally` blocks
between the throw and the catch have already run. For a logging filter this is a
genuine trick people use: `catch (Exception ex) when (Log(ex))`, where `Log`
returns false — it logs at the throw site and never catches anything.

The "do not catch what you cannot handle" rule is the real lesson here though.
The catch-all version of `Attempt` would classify a `NullReferenceException` in
your own code as `"give up"` and return normally, and the bug would never
surface. The narrower each catch is, the smaller the set of failures your code
can hide.

## ex4

The two orderings in this exercise are the whole reason `using` exists. On the
failure path, `Dispose` runs as the stack unwinds, before any outer catch — so
the file is closed before the code that decides what to tell the user runs. Get
that wrong (cleanup after the catch, or at the bottom of the `try`) and you leak
a handle exactly when things are going badly, which is when leaks hurt most.

`using` is `try/finally` with less typing: the compiler rewrites
`using X x = ...;` into a `try` whose `finally` calls `x.Dispose()`. The
declaration form (no braces) disposes at the end of the enclosing block; the
statement form (`using (...) { }`) disposes at the end of its own block, which
is what you want when the resource's life should be shorter than the method's.

Idempotent `Dispose` is part of the documented contract:
"If an object's Dispose method is called more than once, the object must ignore
all calls after the first." That is not pedantry — nested `using`s, a `Dispose`
called explicitly before the block ends, or a container disposing something you
also disposed all produce a second call.

The full disposal pattern (`protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)` plus
a finaliser) exists only for types owning *unmanaged* resources directly — a raw
handle, a pointer. If your class merely holds other `IDisposable`s, the simple
version you wrote is correct and the finaliser is actively harmful, because it
delays collection by a generation. `IAsyncDisposable` is the async sibling, and
lesson 13's world is where it belongs.

## challenge

Retry is where "which failures are worth retrying" stops being philosophy. A
timeout, a 503, a deadlocked transaction: retry. A 400, a null reference, a
parse failure: retrying just produces the same failure more slowly. The policy
belongs in one place, and everything it does not recognise must pass straight
through.

The filter `catch (TransientException) when (attempt < maxAttempts)` is the
elegant part. Without it you need an `if` inside the catch and a way to
distinguish "loop again" from "give up", and it is easy to end up with an
off-by-one — which is why the gate counts calls rather than trusting the
returned number.

Real retry adds two things this challenge deliberately omits. **Backoff**:
waiting longer between attempts, usually exponentially, so a struggling service
is not hammered by every client at once. **Jitter**: randomising that wait, so
ten thousand clients do not all retry at the same instant — the thundering-herd
problem. Polly is the .NET library that implements all of it, and by now you can
read its source.

The testability note in the hints is worth repeating: a real delay would make
this gate slow and flaky. Put the clock behind an interface (lesson 05 ex4) and
the policy stays instantly testable — which is why every serious retry library
takes an abstraction for time.

## Further reading

- [Exceptions and exception handling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/exceptions/) — the language mechanics, including filters and rethrow.
- [Best practices for exceptions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions) — when to throw, which type to pick, and what not to catch.
- [Creating and throwing exceptions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/exceptions/creating-and-throwing-exceptions) — the standard constructors your own type should offer.
- [Implement a Dispose method](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose) — the simple case and the full pattern, with guidance on which you need.
- [`using` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/using) — the declaration form, the statement form, and what each compiles to.

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L12_Exceptions;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L12_ExceptionsTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ex1_FinallyRunsOnBothPaths()
    {
        Teach.Equal(5, Basics.SafeDivide(10, 2, -1), "10 / 2 is 5 - the ordinary path.");
        Teach.Equal(-1, Basics.SafeDivide(10, 0, -1),
            "Integer division by zero throws DivideByZeroException; catching it and returning "
                + "the fallback is the whole method - reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("try, after, finally", string.Join(", ", Basics.Trace(shouldThrow: false)),
            "With nothing thrown, the catch block never runs and finally still does - reread "
                + "README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("try, catch, finally", string.Join(", ", Basics.Trace(shouldThrow: true)),
            "The throw skips the rest of the try block - \"after\" never happens - then the "
                + "catch runs, and finally runs last either way - reread README ex1.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex2_YourExceptionKeepsTheOriginalCause()
    {

        ConfigurationException bad = Teach.Throws<ConfigurationException>(
            () => Configuration.LoadPort("abc"),
            "Unparseable configuration should surface as YOUR exception type, not as a raw "
                + "FormatException from somewhere deep inside - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal("bad port: abc", bad.Message,
            "The message names the offending value, so a log line is enough to diagnose it.");
        Teach.True(bad.InnerException is FormatException,
            "The original FormatException must be kept as the InnerException. Dropping it "
                + "throws away the stack trace that says where it actually happened - pass it "
                + "to the base constructor - reread README ex2.");

        ConfigurationException missing = Teach.Throws<ConfigurationException>(
            () => Configuration.LoadPort(null),
            "Null is also unparseable configuration.");

        Teach.Equal("bad port: null", missing.Message,
            "With no text at all the message says \"null\" rather than being blank.");
        Teach.True(missing.InnerException is ArgumentNullException,
            "int.Parse(null) throws ArgumentNullException, not FormatException - and whatever "
                + "it threw is what the InnerException must be. If this failed, you caught one "
                + "specific type and missed the other.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex3_FiltersDecideWhichCatchWins()
    {
        Teach.Equal("ok", Classifier.Attempt(() => { }),
            "Nothing thrown, nothing to classify - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("retry", Classifier.Attempt(() => throw new TransientException("busy", 503)),
            "503 is 500 or above, so this one is worth retrying. A `when` filter on the catch "
                + "clause is how you split one exception type by its data - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("give up", Classifier.Attempt(() => throw new TransientException("bad request", 400)),
            "400 is the caller's fault and will not fix itself. Same type, different answer, "
                + "decided by the filter - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(
            () => Classifier.Attempt(() => throw new InvalidOperationException("bug")),
            "Anything that is not a TransientException must travel on untouched. A catch-all "
                + "here would swallow real bugs and report them as \"give up\" - reread "
                + "README ex3.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ex4_DisposeHappensWhateverElseDoes()
    {
        Teach.Equal("open, use, finished, dispose", string.Join(", ", Session.Run(shouldThrow: false)),
            "A `using` declaration disposes at the end of its enclosing block - so \"finished\" "
                + "comes first and the cleanup last - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal("open, use, dispose, caught", string.Join(", ", Session.Run(shouldThrow: true)),
            "When the throw happens, the resource is disposed as the stack unwinds - BEFORE "
                + "the catch outside it runs. That ordering is the whole reason using exists - "
                + "reread README ex4.");

        List<string> log = new List<string>();
        Resource resource = new Resource(log);
        resource.Dispose();
        resource.Dispose();

        Teach.Equal("open, dispose", string.Join(", ", log),
            "Dispose must be safe to call twice: the second call does nothing at all. Guard on "
                + "a bool field - reread README ex4.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Challenge_RetryOnlyWhatIsWorthRetrying()
    {
        (int attempts, int value, string outcome) = Resilient.Run(() => 42, 3);

        Teach.Equal(1, attempts, "It worked first time - reread README challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(42, value, "...and the value comes back with it.");
        Teach.Equal("ok", outcome, "Success is reported as \"ok\".");

        int calls = 0;
        (int lateAttempts, int lateValue, string lateOutcome) = Resilient.Run(
            () =>
            {
                calls++;
                if (calls < 3)
                {
                    throw new TransientException("busy", 503);
                }

                return 7;
            },
            5);

        Teach.Equal(3, lateAttempts, "Two failures then a success is three attempts.");
        Teach.Equal(7, lateValue, "The value from the attempt that worked.");
        Teach.Equal("ok", lateOutcome, "Recovering counts as success.");

        int hopeless = 0;
        (int outAttempts, int outValue, string outOutcome) = Resilient.Run(
            () =>
            {
                hopeless++;
                throw new TransientException("still busy", 503);
            },
            3);

        Teach.Equal(3, hopeless, "maxAttempts means exactly that many calls - not one more, "
            + "not one fewer - reread README challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(3, outAttempts, "The attempt count comes back so a caller can log it.");
        Teach.Equal(0, outValue, "There is no value to report.");
        Teach.Equal("exhausted", outOutcome, "Giving up is reported, not thrown.");

        int fatalCalls = 0;
        Teach.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(
            () => Resilient.Run(
                () =>
                {
                    fatalCalls++;
                    throw new InvalidOperationException("bug");
                },
                5),
            "A non-transient failure is a bug, and retrying a bug five times just makes five "
                + "identical stack traces. Let it out - reread README challenge.");
        Teach.Equal(1, fatalCalls,
            "...and let it out IMMEDIATELY: the work must have been called exactly once.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: `Ex1` divides both ways and reads both diaries. `Ex2` parses a
good port and two bad ones, checking the message and the inner exception type
each time. `Ex3` runs four kinds of work and checks the fourth escapes. `Ex4`
compares the two orderings and calls `Dispose` twice. `Challenge` runs work that
succeeds immediately, work that recovers on the third try, work that never
recovers, and work that fails fatally — counting the calls each time.

## The teaching point

The two rules that survive contact with production:

**Catch what you can do something about.** A `catch` that logs and rethrows is
fine. A `catch` that returns a default value is fine *if* the default is
genuinely correct. A `catch (Exception) { }` is almost never fine, and the
version with a comment saying "should never happen" is the one that eventually
hides a real outage.

**Preserve the evidence.** `throw;` not `throw ex;`. Inner exceptions when you
wrap. Enough context in the message to identify the input. The person reading
that log at 3am has only what you decided to keep — and it is often you.

The third thing, which the challenge hints at: exceptions are for *exceptional*
control flow, and they are not free. Throwing captures a stack trace, and doing
it in a loop over ten thousand items is measurably slow. When failure is
routine — parsing user input, looking up a key that might be absent, checking
whether a file exists — the `Try...` pattern exists so you do not pay for it.

across time.

# Reading - csharp/12_exceptions

## Notes

**What an exception costs.** Throwing is not just a jump: the runtime captures a
stack trace, walks the stack looking for a handler, and runs any `finally`
blocks on the way. That is measured in microseconds, not nanoseconds — fine for
something that happens when a request fails, terrible for something that happens
per row of a million-row import. This is the concrete reason behind "don't use
exceptions for control flow", and the reason `TryParse`, `TryGetValue` and
`TryDequeue` all exist.

**The exception hierarchy, in the bit you need.** Everything derives from
`Exception`. `SystemException` and its descendants (`ArgumentException`,
`InvalidOperationException`, `NullReferenceException`, `FormatException`) come
from the framework. `ApplicationException` was meant to be the base for yours and
is now explicitly *not* recommended — derive from `Exception` directly. A few
are special: `OutOfMemoryException` and `StackOverflowException` cannot be
meaningfully handled (the latter cannot be caught at all), and
`OperationCanceledException` is the polite one you will meet in lesson 13.

**Which exception to throw.** `ArgumentNullException` for a null argument,
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for one outside a valid range,
`ArgumentException` for anything else wrong with an argument,
`InvalidOperationException` when the *object* is not in a state where the call
makes sense, `NotSupportedException` for an operation this implementation will
never support. Using the right one lets callers write a specific catch — and
tells the reader what kind of mistake was made.

**`throw;` versus `throw ex;`.** `throw;` rethrows the current exception,
preserving the original stack trace. `throw ex;` throws the same object with the
stack trace reset to *this* line, so the log now says the failure happened in
your catch block. There is almost never a reason for the second. If you need to
add context, wrap: `throw new MyException("...", ex);`.

**Where exceptions should be caught.** Usually not where they are thrown.
Low-level code should let failures out; some boundary — a request handler, a
message consumer, a `Main` — should catch, log, and turn it into a response.
That is exactly what ASP.NET Core's exception middleware does, and it is why the
.NET track spends a lesson on it. A `try/catch` in every method is a sign
nobody decided where the boundary is.

## ex1

The diary in `Trace` makes the control flow visible. Two things worth noticing.
`"after"` never runs on the throwing path — a `throw` abandons the rest of the
block immediately, which is why "clean up at the bottom of the try" is a bug.
And `"finally"` runs on *both* paths, which is the guarantee that makes cleanup
possible at all.

`finally` also runs when the `try` block `return`s — the return value is
computed first, then the `finally` runs, then the method actually returns. That
occasionally surprises people writing `finally` blocks that modify the variable
being returned; the returned value was already captured.

`SafeDivide` is the exercise being deliberately artificial. In real code
`if (b == 0)` is faster, clearer, and does not pay for a stack trace. The
version worth writing is whichever makes the *reason* obvious: a check when the
condition is expected, a catch when the failure is genuinely surprising.

One detail worth having: integer division by zero throws, but floating-point
division by zero does **not** — `1.0 / 0.0` is `double.PositiveInfinity`, and
`0.0 / 0.0` is `NaN`. Same operator, two completely different failure models,
because IEEE 754 says so.

## ex2

Custom exceptions earn their place when a caller might want to catch *that*
specifically. If nobody will ever write `catch (ConfigurationException)`, a
plain `InvalidOperationException` with a good message is fine, and one more type
in the codebase is a cost with no benefit.

The inner exception is the part that gets dropped and the part that matters. Your
`ConfigurationException`'s stack trace starts at the line where you threw it —
which is the catch block, not the failure. The inner exception remembers where
the parse actually blew up, and every logger and every debugger prints the chain.
Dropping it produces the log entry everyone has seen: a friendly message with no
information in it.

The other half is the message. `"bad port: abc"` names the offending value;
`"Configuration error"` does not, and someone will have to reproduce the failure
locally to find out which setting was wrong. The rule of thumb: put in the
message whatever you would want to grep for.

`int.Parse(null)` throwing `ArgumentNullException` rather than `FormatException`
is a small trap the gate checks deliberately. Two failure types from one call is
normal in .NET, and a catch that handles only the one you thought of leaves the
other escaping raw.

## ex3

Exception filters are a C# 6 feature that people underuse. Beyond the obvious —
splitting one type by its data — the mechanism matters: a `when` clause runs
**before** the stack unwinds, in a first pass over the handlers. If it returns
false, the exception carries on from its original throw point with everything
intact, and a debugger breaking on unhandled exceptions still stops at the real
site.

Catch-and-rethrow does not have that property. `catch (X) { if (...) throw; }`
has already unwound the stack by the time it decides, so any `finally` blocks
between the throw and the catch have already run. For a logging filter this is a
genuine trick people use: `catch (Exception ex) when (Log(ex))`, where `Log`
returns false — it logs at the throw site and never catches anything.

The "do not catch what you cannot handle" rule is the real lesson here though.
The catch-all version of `Attempt` would classify a `NullReferenceException` in
your own code as `"give up"` and return normally, and the bug would never
surface. The narrower each catch is, the smaller the set of failures your code
can hide.

## ex4

The two orderings in this exercise are the whole reason `using` exists. On the
failure path, `Dispose` runs as the stack unwinds, before any outer catch — so
the file is closed before the code that decides what to tell the user runs. Get
that wrong (cleanup after the catch, or at the bottom of the `try`) and you leak
a handle exactly when things are going badly, which is when leaks hurt most.

`using` is `try/finally` with less typing: the compiler rewrites
`using X x = ...;` into a `try` whose `finally` calls `x.Dispose()`. The
declaration form (no braces) disposes at the end of the enclosing block; the
statement form (`using (...) { }`) disposes at the end of its own block, which
is what you want when the resource's life should be shorter than the method's.

Idempotent `Dispose` is part of the documented contract:
"If an object's Dispose method is called more than once, the object must ignore
all calls after the first." That is not pedantry — nested `using`s, a `Dispose`
called explicitly before the block ends, or a container disposing something you
also disposed all produce a second call.

The full disposal pattern (`protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)` plus
a finaliser) exists only for types owning *unmanaged* resources directly — a raw
handle, a pointer. If your class merely holds other `IDisposable`s, the simple
version you wrote is correct and the finaliser is actively harmful, because it
delays collection by a generation. `IAsyncDisposable` is the async sibling, and
lesson 13's world is where it belongs.

## challenge

Retry is where "which failures are worth retrying" stops being philosophy. A
timeout, a 503, a deadlocked transaction: retry. A 400, a null reference, a
parse failure: retrying just produces the same failure more slowly. The policy
belongs in one place, and everything it does not recognise must pass straight
through.

The filter `catch (TransientException) when (attempt < maxAttempts)` is the
elegant part. Without it you need an `if` inside the catch and a way to
distinguish "loop again" from "give up", and it is easy to end up with an
off-by-one — which is why the gate counts calls rather than trusting the
returned number.

Real retry adds two things this challenge deliberately omits. **Backoff**:
waiting longer between attempts, usually exponentially, so a struggling service
is not hammered by every client at once. **Jitter**: randomising that wait, so
ten thousand clients do not all retry at the same instant — the thundering-herd
problem. Polly is the .NET library that implements all of it, and by now you can
read its source.

The testability note in the hints is worth repeating: a real delay would make
this gate slow and flaky. Put the clock behind an interface (lesson 05 ex4) and
the policy stays instantly testable — which is why every serious retry library
takes an abstraction for time.

## Further reading

- [Exceptions and exception handling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/exceptions/) — the language mechanics, including filters and rethrow.
- [Best practices for exceptions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/best-practices-for-exceptions) — when to throw, which type to pick, and what not to catch.
- [Creating and throwing exceptions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/exceptions/creating-and-throwing-exceptions) — the standard constructors your own type should offer.
- [Implement a Dispose method](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose) — the simple case and the full pattern, with guidance on which you need.
- [`using` statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/using) — the declaration form, the statement form, and what each compiles to.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — retry the retryable

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Challenge.cs`. `Resilient.Run(work, maxAttempts)`
calls `work` until it succeeds or until it has failed `maxAttempts` times with a
`TransientException`, returning `(attempts, value, "ok")` or
`(maxAttempts, 0, "exhausted")`. Anything that is not transient must escape
immediately, without another attempt.

Honest difficulty note: the loop is easy and the exit conditions are fiddly.
The gate counts calls, so "one attempt too many" and "gave up one early" both
show up as an exact number. The neat solution uses an exception filter to say
"transient, *and* there are attempts left".

```
uv run dojo test csharp 12_exceptions challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A loop with a `try` inside it — not a `try` with a loop inside it. Each
iteration is one attempt.

Three ways out: the work returns (success), the work keeps throwing transiently
until the attempts run out (exhausted), or the work throws something else
(which is not yours to handle).

## Hint 2

```csharp
for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++)
{
    try
    {
        return (attempt, work(), "ok");
    }
    catch (TransientException) when (attempt < maxAttempts)
    {
        // there are attempts left: fall out of the catch and loop again
    }
    catch (TransientException)
    {
        return (attempt, 0, "exhausted");
    }
}
```

The filter is doing the work: "transient AND there is another attempt" means
carry on; "transient and this was the last one" means report exhaustion.

Note there is no catch for anything else, which is what lets a real bug out.

## Hint 3

The gate counts how many times `work` was called, so an off-by-one shows up
immediately: `maxAttempts` of 3 means exactly three calls, and a fatal
exception means exactly one.

The empty-looking catch block deserves a comment rather than an apology — a
`catch` that deliberately does nothing is fine when the *filter* has already
said what it means, and unreadable when it has not.

Left to you: real retry policies wait between attempts, usually with
exponential backoff and jitter, and that is what Polly does for you in
production. Adding a delay here would make the gate slow and flaky, which is
its own lesson about testable design — the *policy* is what you unit-test, and
the clock belongs behind an interface, exactly as in lesson 05 ex4.

## Exercise 2 — your own exception, with the cause attached

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Ex2.cs`. `ConfigurationException` has two
constructors, and one of them quietly drops its `inner` argument on the way to
`base` — fix it. Then implement `Configuration.LoadPort(text)`: parse the
number, and turn any parse failure into a `ConfigurationException` whose message
is `"bad port: abc"` (or `"bad port: null"`) and whose `InnerException` is
whatever `int.Parse` actually threw.

`null`, and the gate checks that *both* arrive with the right inner exception.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things to fix. One of the `ConfigurationException` constructors quietly
loses its `inner` argument — look at what it passes to `base`. And `LoadPort`
has to catch what `int.Parse` throws and rethrow it wrapped.

`int.Parse` throws two different things here: `FormatException` for `"abc"`,
`ArgumentNullException` for `null`. The gate checks both.

## Hint 2

The base `Exception` class has a constructor taking a message **and** an inner
exception. Passing the inner one through is a one-word change:

```csharp
public ConfigurationException(string message, Exception inner)
    : base(message, inner)
{
}
```

In `LoadPort`, catch, build the message, and throw yours with the original
attached:

```csharp
catch (Exception original) when (original is FormatException or ArgumentNullException)
{
    throw new ConfigurationException($"bad port: {text ?? "null"}", original);
}
```

`text ?? "null"` is what produces `"bad port: null"` rather than `"bad port: "`.

## Hint 3

Two catch blocks (one per exception type) work just as well as the single
filtered one above, and are arguably clearer. What you must *not* do is
`catch (Exception)` with no filter: that would also swallow an
`OutOfMemoryException` and report it as a bad port number.

Why keep the inner exception at all? Because your `ConfigurationException`'s
stack trace starts where *you* threw it. The inner one remembers where the
failure actually happened, and every logger prints the chain. Throwing away the
cause is the single most common way a team ends up staring at
"Configuration error" with no idea which line produced it.

Left to you: whether the caught variable should be named `original`, `ex`, or
`inner`. Small thing; the code reads differently for each.

## Hint 1

Two things to fix. One of the `ConfigurationException` constructors quietly
loses its `inner` argument — look at what it passes to `base`. And `LoadPort`
has to catch what `int.Parse` throws and rethrow it wrapped.

`int.Parse` throws two different things here: `FormatException` for `"abc"`,
`ArgumentNullException` for `null`. The gate checks both.

## Hint 2

The base `Exception` class has a constructor taking a message **and** an inner
exception. Passing the inner one through is a one-word change:

```csharp
public ConfigurationException(string message, Exception inner)
    : base(message, inner)
{
}
```

In `LoadPort`, catch, build the message, and throw yours with the original
attached:

```csharp
catch (Exception original) when (original is FormatException or ArgumentNullException)
{
    throw new ConfigurationException($"bad port: {text ?? "null"}", original);
}
```

`text ?? "null"` is what produces `"bad port: null"` rather than `"bad port: "`.

## Hint 3

Two catch blocks (one per exception type) work just as well as the single
filtered one above, and are arguably clearer. What you must *not* do is
`catch (Exception)` with no filter: that would also swallow an
`OutOfMemoryException` and report it as a bad port number.

Why keep the inner exception at all? Because your `ConfigurationException`'s
stack trace starts where *you* threw it. The inner one remembers where the
failure actually happened, and every logger prints the chain. Throwing away the
cause is the single most common way a team ends up staring at
"Configuration error" with no idea which line produced it.

Left to you: whether the caught variable should be named `original`, `ex`, or
`inner`. Small thing; the code reads differently for each.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four outcomes, and only three of them are things you write. The fourth —
"anything else" — is what you achieve by *not* writing a catch for it.

The two `TransientException` cases differ by a property on the exception, not
by its type. C# has a way to say that on the catch clause itself.

## Hint 2

An exception *filter*:

```csharp
catch (TransientException failure) when (failure.StatusCode >= 500)
{
    return "retry";
}
catch (TransientException)
{
    return "give up";
}
```

Order matters: the filtered clause must come first, or the unfiltered one
catches everything of that type and the filter never gets a look in.

The `try` block calls `work()` and then returns `"ok"`.

## Hint 3

You could write one catch and an `if` inside it. There is a real difference,
and it is worth knowing for interviews: a `when` filter is evaluated **before**
the stack unwinds, so if no clause matches, the exception continues from its
original throw point with the stack intact. Catching and rethrowing has already
unwound and, if you write `throw ex;` instead of `throw;`, has already reset the
stack trace.

Left to you: whether `"give up"` should be the filtered case instead
(`when (failure.StatusCode < 500)`), leaving the unfiltered clause for the
retryable one. Both work. Which reads better when a third status band appears?

## Exercise 4 — cleanup that happens anyway

Edit `src/Lessons/L12_Exceptions/Ex4.cs`. Implement `Resource.Dispose()` — it
logs `"dispose"`, but only the first time, because disposing twice must be
harmless. Then implement `Session.Run(shouldThrow)`: open a `Resource` in a

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two small bodies. `Dispose` writes one line to the log and must be safe to call
again. `Run` opens the resource in a `using`, uses it, maybe throws, and
catches that throw *outside* the using.

Before you write `Run`, predict the two logs. The order is the exercise.

## Hint 2

The `_disposed` field is already declared — guard on it:

```csharp
public void Dispose()
{
    if (_disposed) { return; }
    _disposed = true;
    _log.Add("dispose");
}
```

`Run` uses a *using declaration* — no braces, scoped to the enclosing block:

```csharp
try
{
    using Resource resource = new Resource(log);
    resource.Use();
    // maybe throw; otherwise log "finished"
}
catch (InvalidOperationException)
{
    log.Add("caught");
}
```

## Hint 3

The two orders are different and both are correct:

- no throw: `open, use, finished, dispose` — the using disposes at the end of
  the block, after your last statement;
- throw: `open, use, dispose, caught` — the stack unwinds out of the `try`
  block, which disposes on the way, and only then does the catch run.

That second ordering is the entire reason `using` exists. Cleanup written at
the bottom of a `try` block never happens on the failure path, which is exactly
when you most needed the file closed.

Left to you: the full `IDisposable` pattern for a class with unmanaged
resources adds a `protected virtual void Dispose(bool)` and a finaliser. It is
overkill here and worth reading about once — the reading notes say when you
actually need it.

lessons.briefing:
# 13 — async and await

A web server handling a thousand requests spends almost all of its time waiting
— for a database, for an HTTP call, for a disk. If each of those waits occupies
a thread, a thousand concurrent requests need a thousand threads, each with a
megabyte of stack, most of them asleep. `async`/`await` exists to make waiting
free: the method gives its thread back while it waits, and picks up where it
left off when the answer arrives.

The mental model that gets people through: **`await` does not run anything in
parallel.** It says "this result is not here yet; suspend me, and resume this
method when it is". Whether the work happens on another thread, on the network,
or on a disk controller is not `await`'s business. Concurrency is what
`Task.WhenAll` adds, and starting work in the background is what `Task.Run`
does — three different ideas that get merged into one under the name "async" in
conversation, and separating them is most of what an interviewer is checking.

Everything in this lesson's gates is deterministic: no `Task.Delay`, no
sleeping, no "usually finishes in time". The tasks are controlled by
`TaskCompletionSource`, so the gate decides exactly when each one completes.
That is also how you should write async tests of your own.

## Concept — tasks, awaiting, and the three ways to get it wrong

A `Task<T>` is a promise of a `T` that may not have arrived yet. An `async`
method returns one:

```csharp
public static async Task<int> LoadAsync(HttpClient client)
{
    string body = await client.GetStringAsync("https://example.com");  // suspends here
    return body.Length;                                                 // resumes here
}
```

`await` unwraps the result, and rethrows the original exception if the task
failed.

**Waiting for several things.** Awaiting in sequence takes as long as the sum;
`Task.WhenAll` takes as long as the slowest:

```csharp
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(first, second);   // results are in INPUT order
```

That input-order guarantee matters: however the tasks finish, the array lines up
with the tasks you passed.

**Cancellation is cooperative.** A `CancellationToken` is a signal, not a
weapon. Nothing can abort running code from outside; code that wants to be
cancellable must check:

```csharp
token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();       // between steps you control
await work.WaitAsync(token);                // stop waiting for something you don't
```

Both throw `OperationCanceledException`, which by convention is *not* an error
to log — it is the answer to "did the caller change their mind?".

**The three classic mistakes**, all of which this lesson makes you see:

1. **`.Result` / `.Wait()`** — blocks the thread instead of yielding it, and
   wraps any failure in an `AggregateException`. In an app with a
   synchronization context (WinForms, WPF, old ASP.NET), it deadlocks outright:
   the continuation needs the thread that is sitting there blocking on it.
2. **`async void`** — a method returning `void` has no task, so nobody can await
   it and nobody can catch its exceptions; they go straight to the
   synchronization context and usually take the process down. The only
   legitimate use is an event handler.
3. **Not passing the token down** — a cancellation chain works only if every
   link forwards it.

## Exercise 1 — awaiting two things

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex1.cs`. `SumAsync(first, second)` returns the
two results added together. `InOrderAsync(first, second)` returns
`"one+two"` — the results in **parameter** order, however the tasks actually
finish.

The gate hands you tasks it controls and completes them in the wrong order on
purpose, checking along the way that your returned task is not finished before
both inputs are.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — fanning out

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex2.cs`. `SumAllAsync` totals a sequence of
tasks. `JoinAsync` joins their results with `", "` — again in the order the
tasks were given, not the order they completed.

The gate finishes three tasks in exactly reverse order and expects the original
order back. That property of `Task.WhenAll` is worth knowing precisely: the
results array is positional.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — cancellation

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex3.cs`. `WaitOrCancelAsync(work, token)`
returns the work's result, unless the token fires first — in which case an
`OperationCanceledException` comes out. `SumUntilCancelledAsync(tasks, token)`
adds up the results, checking the token before each one so an already-cancelled
request does no work at all.

Read the gate's assertion after the cancellation: the underlying task is *still
pending*. Cancelling a wait does not stop the work. That is the single most
important thing to understand about cancellation in .NET.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — fix this code

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex4.cs`. `RunAsync(work)` returns the work's
result, and when the work has failed the caller must see the **original**
exception — not an `AggregateException` with it buried inside. That difference
is exactly what `.Result` gets wrong and `await` gets right, and the gate can
tell them apart.

`AlwaysFailsAsync()` throws an `InvalidOperationException` with the message
`"boom"` — but the failure must arrive **in the returned task**, not be thrown
at the caller before they have a task to await.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await ex4
```

## Challenge — fan out, wait, and describe what happened

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Challenge.cs`. `SummariseAsync(work, token)`
waits for every task and reports `"ok: <total>"` when all succeeded, or
`"failed: <exception type name>"` naming the first faulted task in list order —
and lets an `OperationCanceledException` straight out when the token fires.

Honest difficulty note: the catch-block ordering is the difficulty. A bare
`catch` written first swallows the cancellation and reports it as a failure,
and the gate checks for exactly that. Finding *which* task failed also needs a
look at the tasks themselves, because awaiting `WhenAll` only rethrows one of
the exceptions. Finish it with a `switch` expression over the exception type if
you like — a fitting last line for the language part of this course.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await challenge
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/13_async_await

## Notes

**What the compiler actually does.** An `async` method is rewritten into a state
machine, exactly like the iterators in lesson 08. Each `await` becomes: check
whether the awaited thing is already complete; if it is, carry straight on; if
it is not, register a continuation and **return** to the caller. The method's
locals become fields on the state machine object so they survive the gap. The
task you hand back is that state machine's promise. Two things follow: the code
before the first `await` runs *synchronously* on the calling thread, and there
is no thread sitting anywhere waiting for the result.

**Async is not a thread.** The most useful sentence about async I/O: while a
network read is in flight there is **no thread involved at all** — the operating
system holds the request and signals a completion port when data arrives. That
is why a server can have ten thousand pending requests and twenty threads. It is
also why `async` does nothing for CPU-bound work: burning CPU genuinely needs a
thread, and `Task.Run` is the tool for pushing that off the current one.

**The synchronization context, and where deadlocks come from.** In WinForms,
WPF and old ASP.NET, `await` captures a context and resumes the continuation on
it — the UI thread, or the request's thread. Now block that same thread with
`.Result` and the continuation can never run: the thread is waiting for a task
whose continuation needs the thread. Classic deadlock, and the reason
`ConfigureAwait(false)` exists — it says "resume anywhere, I do not need the
context". Modern ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so the deadlock
does not occur there, but library code still uses `ConfigureAwait(false)`
because it cannot know who will call it. In application code you generally do
not need it.

**`async void` is a trap with one legitimate use.** A `void`-returning async
method hands the caller nothing to await, so nobody can wait for it and nobody
can catch its exceptions — they are raised on the synchronization context and
usually terminate the process. The single legitimate case is an event handler,
because the event's delegate signature demands `void`. Everywhere else: return
`Task`.

**`ValueTask`, briefly.** A `Task` is a heap allocation, which matters when a
method is called millions of times and usually completes synchronously (a cache
hit, a buffered read). `ValueTask<T>` avoids the allocation in that case, at the
cost of stricter rules — you may await it only once, and never block on it. Use
`Task` by default; recognise `ValueTask` when you see it in high-performance
APIs.

## ex1

The gate's shape — assert "not completed", complete one input, assert "still not
completed", complete the other — is worth stealing for your own async tests.
`TaskCompletionSource` gives you a task whose completion *you* trigger, which
removes timing from the test entirely. Tests that call `Task.Delay(100)` and
hope are the reason people believe async tests are flaky.

The sequential-versus-concurrent point is the one to keep. `await first; await second;`
gives the same answer as `Task.WhenAll` here, because both tasks were already
running before your method was called. Change that to a method that *starts*
each call — `await LoadAsync(a); await LoadAsync(b);` — and the two versions
differ by the duration of the first call, every time. The rule of thumb: start
everything you can, then await; do not start-and-await in a loop unless the
calls genuinely depend on each other.

Reading `.Result` on an already-completed task, as `InOrderAsync` may do after
`WhenAll`, is safe and non-blocking. It is still a habit worth avoiding, because
the same expression a hundred lines later, on a task that has not completed, is
a blocked thread — and reviewers cannot tell the two apart at a glance.

## ex2

`Task.WhenAll`'s positional result array is a small guarantee with large
consequences: you can fan out over a list of ids and zip the results back
against it, with no correlation logic at all. Completion order tells you nothing
and you never need it.

Two behaviours worth knowing. If several tasks fault, awaiting `WhenAll` rethrows
only the **first** exception — the rest are still there on the task's
`AggregateException`, reachable through `task.Exception.InnerExceptions`, which
is what the challenge digs into. And `WhenAll` waits for *every* task even after
one has failed, which is usually right (no orphaned work continuing in the
background) and occasionally not.

The lazy-sequence trap deserves repeating because it combines two lessons.
`items.Select(i => FetchAsync(i))` is a lazy query whose *enumeration* starts the
tasks. Pass it to `WhenAll` and it is enumerated once, fine. Enumerate it twice —
`if (queries.Any())` and then `await Task.WhenAll(queries)` — and you have
started every request twice. `.ToList()` before you hand it over.

## ex3

Cancellation in .NET is cooperative and that is a design decision, not a
limitation. The alternative — killing a thread mid-operation — leaves locks
held, files half-written and invariants broken, which is why `Thread.Abort` was
deprecated and then removed. So a `CancellationToken` is a flag with a callback
list, and code that wants to be interruptible has to look at it.

The two idioms cover the two situations. When you control the loop, check
between steps with `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`. When you are waiting for
somebody else's task, `WaitAsync(token)` stops the *wait* — and, as the gate
proves, the work carries on regardless. That distinction is the interview
question: "how do you cancel a task?" The answer is that you do not cancel a
task, you signal an intent, and the task decides.

`OperationCanceledException` gets special treatment across the framework: a task
that ends with one is `TaskStatus.Canceled` rather than `Faulted`, and ASP.NET
Core does not log it as an error, because a client hanging up is not a bug. That
is also why catching it and returning a "failed" result is wrong — it turns a
non-event into an alert.

`TaskCanceledException` derives from `OperationCanceledException`, so catch the
base and stop worrying about which one you got.

## ex4

Two mistakes in one exercise, and both are [***] interview questions.

**`.Result` versus `await`.** Blocking on a task wraps whatever went wrong in an
`AggregateException`, because a task can hold several exceptions. `await`
unwraps and rethrows the first one with its stack trace preserved (via
`ExceptionDispatchInfo`), so your `catch (InvalidOperationException)` actually
catches. The gate distinguishes them by asserting the exception *type*, which is
the cleanest possible demonstration.

The other half of `.Result` is worse: it blocks a thread. On a server that is a
thread not serving a request; under a synchronization context it is the deadlock
described above. `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` at least avoids the wrapping, which
is why you see it in `Main` methods of older code, but it still blocks.

**Where an async method's exception lives.** Because the method body runs inside
a state machine, a `throw` anywhere in it is captured and placed on the returned
task. So `var t = FailsAsync();` does not throw — `await t` does. A
*non*-async method declared to return `Task` that throws directly does throw at
the call site, which is a genuine difference in behaviour and the reason the
guidance for argument validation is to do it in a small non-async wrapper that
returns the async part:

```csharp
public static Task<int> LoadAsync(string path)
{
    ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty(path);   // eagerly, at the call site
    return LoadCoreAsync(path);                    // the async part
}
```

## challenge

The catch-ordering trap is real and appears in production code constantly. A
`catch (Exception)` around an awaited operation catches `OperationCanceledException`
too, so a cancelled request gets logged as an error, alerts fire, and somebody
investigates a user who closed a browser tab. Catch cancellation explicitly and
rethrow, or filter it out — `catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)`
is the compact form, and lesson 12's filters are what make it possible.

Digging the causes out of the tasks rather than out of the thrown exception is
the other production habit. Awaiting `WhenAll` gives you one exception; the
tasks themselves know about all of them. When a batch of ten uploads fails, "one
of them timed out" is much less useful than "three timed out, one was
unauthorised, and here are the ids".

Ending with a `switch` expression over the exception type is a nice closing
image for the language half of this course, because it uses lesson 02's switch
expressions, lesson 04's type hierarchy, lesson 06's patterns and lesson 12's
exceptions in one line — which is roughly what idiomatic modern C# looks like.

## Further reading

- [Asynchronous programming with async and await](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/) — the task-based model from the top.
- [Async in depth](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/async-in-depth) — what actually happens during an I/O wait, and why no thread is involved.
- [Task asynchronous programming model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/task-asynchronous-programming-model) — the state machine, step by step.
- [Async guidance: avoid `async void`, avoid blocking](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices) — ASP.NET Core's list of the same mistakes at production scale.
- [`CancellationToken`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/cancellation-in-managed-threads) — the cooperative cancellation model in full.
- [`ConfigureAwait` FAQ](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/) — Stephen Toub's definitive answer on contexts and deadlocks.

# 13 — async and await

A web server handling a thousand requests spends almost all of its time waiting
— for a database, for an HTTP call, for a disk. If each of those waits occupies
a thread, a thousand concurrent requests need a thousand threads, each with a
megabyte of stack, most of them asleep. `async`/`await` exists to make waiting
free: the method gives its thread back while it waits, and picks up where it
left off when the answer arrives.

The mental model that gets people through: **`await` does not run anything in
parallel.** It says "this result is not here yet; suspend me, and resume this
method when it is". Whether the work happens on another thread, on the network,
or on a disk controller is not `await`'s business. Concurrency is what
`Task.WhenAll` adds, and starting work in the background is what `Task.Run`
does — three different ideas that get merged into one under the name "async" in
conversation, and separating them is most of what an interviewer is checking.

Everything in this lesson's gates is deterministic: no `Task.Delay`, no
sleeping, no "usually finishes in time". The tasks are controlled by
`TaskCompletionSource`, so the gate decides exactly when each one completes.
That is also how you should write async tests of your own.

## Concept — tasks, awaiting, and the three ways to get it wrong

A `Task<T>` is a promise of a `T` that may not have arrived yet. An `async`
method returns one:

```csharp
public static async Task<int> LoadAsync(HttpClient client)
{
    string body = await client.GetStringAsync("https://example.com");  // suspends here
    return body.Length;                                                 // resumes here
}
```

`await` unwraps the result, and rethrows the original exception if the task
failed.

**Waiting for several things.** Awaiting in sequence takes as long as the sum;
`Task.WhenAll` takes as long as the slowest:

```csharp
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(first, second);   // results are in INPUT order
```

That input-order guarantee matters: however the tasks finish, the array lines up
with the tasks you passed.

**Cancellation is cooperative.** A `CancellationToken` is a signal, not a
weapon. Nothing can abort running code from outside; code that wants to be
cancellable must check:

```csharp
token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();       // between steps you control
await work.WaitAsync(token);                // stop waiting for something you don't
```

Both throw `OperationCanceledException`, which by convention is *not* an error
to log — it is the answer to "did the caller change their mind?".

**The three classic mistakes**, all of which this lesson makes you see:

1. **`.Result` / `.Wait()`** — blocks the thread instead of yielding it, and
   wraps any failure in an `AggregateException`. In an app with a
   synchronization context (WinForms, WPF, old ASP.NET), it deadlocks outright:
   the continuation needs the thread that is sitting there blocking on it.
2. **`async void`** — a method returning `void` has no task, so nobody can await
   it and nobody can catch its exceptions; they go straight to the
   synchronization context and usually take the process down. The only
   legitimate use is an event handler.
3. **Not passing the token down** — a cancellation chain works only if every
   link forwards it.

## Exercise 1 — awaiting two things

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex1.cs`. `SumAsync(first, second)` returns the
two results added together. `InOrderAsync(first, second)` returns
`"one+two"` — the results in **parameter** order, however the tasks actually
finish.

The gate hands you tasks it controls and completes them in the wrong order on
purpose, checking along the way that your returned task is not finished before
both inputs are.

tasks were given, not the order they completed.

The gate finishes three tasks in exactly reverse order and expects the original

```

## Exercise 3 — cancellation

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex3.cs`. `WaitOrCancelAsync(work, token)`
returns the work's result, unless the token fires first — in which case an
`OperationCanceledException` comes out. `SumUntilCancelledAsync(tasks, token)`
adds up the results, checking the token before each one so an already-cancelled
request does no work at all.

Read the gate's assertion after the cancellation: the underlying task is *still
pending*. Cancelling a wait does not stop the work. That is the single most
important thing to understand about cancellation in .NET.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — fix this code

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex4.cs`. `RunAsync(work)` returns the work's
result, and when the work has failed the caller must see the **original**
exception — not an `AggregateException` with it buried inside. That difference
is exactly what `.Result` gets wrong and `await` gets right, and the gate can
tell them apart.

`AlwaysFailsAsync()` throws an `InvalidOperationException` with the message
`"boom"` — but the failure must arrive **in the returned task**, not be thrown
at the caller before they have a task to await.

```
