
## Challenge — fan out, wait, and describe what happened

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Challenge.cs`. `SummariseAsync(work, token)`
waits for every task and reports `"ok: <total>"` when all succeeded, or
`"failed: <exception type name>"` naming the first faulted task in list order —
and lets an `OperationCanceledException` straight out when the token fires.

Honest difficulty note: the catch-block ordering is the difficulty. A bare
`catch` written first swallows the cancellation and reports it as a failure,
and the gate checks for exactly that. Finding *which* task failed also needs a
look at the tasks themselves, because awaiting `WhenAll` only rethrows one of
the exceptions. Finish it with a `switch` expression over the exception type if
you like — a fitting last line for the language part of this course.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await challenge
```

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L13_AsyncAwaitTests.cs`:

```csharp
using CSharpDojo.L13_AsyncAwait;

namespace CSharpDojo.Gates;

public class L13_AsyncAwaitTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex1_AwaitBothBeforeYouAnswer()
    {
        TaskCompletionSource<int> first = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        TaskCompletionSource<int> second = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();

        Task<int> sum = Awaiting.SumAsync(first.Task, second.Task);

        Teach.True(!sum.IsCompleted,
            "Neither input has produced a value yet, so the result cannot be finished. If this "
                + "failed, you returned something without awaiting - reread README ex1.");

        second.SetResult(3);
        Teach.True(!sum.IsCompleted,
            "One of the two is in. Still not enough - reread README ex1.");

        first.SetResult(2);
        Teach.Equal(5, await sum, "2 + 3, whichever order they arrived in.");

        TaskCompletionSource<string> left = new TaskCompletionSource<string>();
        TaskCompletionSource<string> right = new TaskCompletionSource<string>();
        Task<string> joined = Awaiting.InOrderAsync(left.Task, right.Task);

        right.SetResult("two");
        left.SetResult("one");

        Teach.Equal("one+two", await joined,
            "The SECOND task finished first, and the answer still reads \"one+two\": the "
                + "output order comes from the parameters, not from who won - reread README ex1.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex2_WhenAllKeepsTheInputOrder()
    {
        TaskCompletionSource<int> a = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        TaskCompletionSource<int> b = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        TaskCompletionSource<int> c = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();

        Task<int> total = Fanout.SumAllAsync(new[] { a.Task, b.Task, c.Task });

        c.SetResult(3);
        a.SetResult(1);
        Teach.True(!total.IsCompleted, "Two of three: WhenAll waits for every one of them - "
            + "reread README ex2.");

        b.SetResult(2);
        Teach.Equal(6, await total, "1 + 2 + 3.");

        TaskCompletionSource<string> x = new TaskCompletionSource<string>();
        TaskCompletionSource<string> y = new TaskCompletionSource<string>();
        TaskCompletionSource<string> z = new TaskCompletionSource<string>();

        Task<string> joined = Fanout.JoinAsync(new[] { x.Task, y.Task, z.Task });

        z.SetResult("zebra");
        y.SetResult("yak");
        x.SetResult("xerus");

        Teach.Equal("xerus, yak, zebra", await joined,
            "They finished in exactly the reverse order, and the answer is still in input "
                + "order: Task.WhenAll's result array lines up with the tasks you gave it - "
                + "reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(0, await Fanout.SumAllAsync(Array.Empty<Task<int>>()),
            "WhenAll over nothing completes immediately, and the sum of nothing is 0.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex3_CancellationStopsTheWaitingNotTheWork()
    {
        Teach.Equal(7, await Cancellable.WaitOrCancelAsync(Task.FromResult(7), CancellationToken.None),
            "With nothing cancelled, this is just an await - reread README ex3.");

        TaskCompletionSource<int> never = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        CancellationTokenSource source = new CancellationTokenSource();
        Task<int> pending = Cancellable.WaitOrCancelAsync(never.Task, source.Token);

        Teach.True(!pending.IsCompleted, "Nothing has happened yet - the work is still running "
            + "and nobody has cancelled.");

        source.Cancel();

        await Teach.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => pending,
            "Once the token is cancelled, the wait must end with an OperationCanceledException "
                + "- Task.WaitAsync(token) does exactly this - reread README ex3. Note the "
                + "work itself is still running: cancelling a wait cannot un-start a task.");

        Teach.True(!never.Task.IsCompleted,
            "...and there is the proof: the underlying task is still pending.");

        Teach.Equal(6, await Cancellable.SumUntilCancelledAsync(
                new[] { Task.FromResult(1), Task.FromResult(2), Task.FromResult(3) },
                CancellationToken.None),
            "No cancellation, so every task contributes - reread README ex3.");

        CancellationTokenSource cancelled = new CancellationTokenSource();
        cancelled.Cancel();

        await Teach.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => Cancellable.SumUntilCancelledAsync(new[] { Task.FromResult(1) }, cancelled.Token),
            "An ALREADY cancelled token means do no work at all: check it at the top of the "
                + "loop with token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() - reread README ex3.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex4_AwaitUnwrapsWhatResultWrapsUp()
    {
        Teach.Equal(41, await Faults.RunAsync(Task.FromResult(41)), "The ordinary path.");

        TaskCompletionSource<int> broken = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        broken.SetException(new InvalidOperationException("inner boom"));

        InvalidOperationException caught = await Teach.ThrowsAsync<InvalidOperationException>(
            () => Faults.RunAsync(broken.Task),
            "await rethrows the ORIGINAL exception. Blocking on .Result or .Wait() instead "
                + "throws an AggregateException with the real one buried inside - which is why "
                + "this gate can tell the two apart - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal("inner boom", caught.Message, "...and it is the same exception object, "
            + "message and all.");

        Task<int> failing = Faults.AlwaysFailsAsync();

        Teach.True(failing.IsFaulted || !failing.IsCompleted,
            "Calling AlwaysFailsAsync must RETURN a task carrying the failure, not throw in "
                + "the caller's face. If the exception escaped at the call site this line "
                + "never even ran - which means the method is not `async` - reread README ex4.");

        InvalidOperationException later = await Teach.ThrowsAsync<InvalidOperationException>(
            () => failing,
            "The failure surfaces when the task is awaited.");

        Teach.Equal("boom", later.Message, "With the message the prompt asked for.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Challenge_SummariseReportsSuccessFailureAndCancellation()
    {
        TaskCompletionSource<int> a = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        TaskCompletionSource<int> b = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        Task<string> ok = Pipeline.SummariseAsync(
            new[] { a.Task, b.Task }, CancellationToken.None);

        a.SetResult(4);
        b.SetResult(5);
        Teach.Equal("ok: 9", await ok, "Everything succeeded, so report the total - reread "
            + "README challenge.");

        TaskCompletionSource<int> good = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        TaskCompletionSource<int> bad = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        Task<string> failed = Pipeline.SummariseAsync(
            new[] { good.Task, bad.Task }, CancellationToken.None);

        good.SetResult(1);
        bad.SetException(new TimeoutException("too slow"));

        Teach.Equal("failed: TimeoutException", await failed,
            "One task faulted, so report its exception type. Task.WhenAll waits for ALL of "
                + "them even after one fails, and its awaited exception is the first one - "
                + "reread README challenge.");

        TaskCompletionSource<int> pendingWork = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        CancellationTokenSource source = new CancellationTokenSource();
        Task<string> cancelled = Pipeline.SummariseAsync(new[] { pendingWork.Task }, source.Token);

        Teach.True(!cancelled.IsCompleted, "Nothing has finished and nothing is cancelled yet.");

        source.Cancel();

        await Teach.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => cancelled,
            "Cancellation is not a failure to report - it travels out as an "
                + "OperationCanceledException. A bare `catch` that swallows it and returns "
                + "\"failed: ...\" is the bug this check exists to catch - reread README "
                + "challenge.");
    }
}
```

In plain English: every gate here drives `TaskCompletionSource` objects, so
nothing depends on timing. `Ex1` completes two tasks in reverse order, checking
in between that your result is still pending. `Ex2` does the same with three.
`Ex3` cancels a wait and then proves the work is still running, and calls the
second method with an already-cancelled token. `Ex4` awaits a faulted task and
insists on the original exception type and message. `Challenge` runs the three
outcomes: all-succeed, one-faults, and cancelled-while-waiting.

## The teaching point

Two rules cover most async code you will write:

**Async all the way down.** If a method awaits, it returns a `Task`, and its
caller awaits it too — up to a boundary the framework owns (a controller
action, a `BackgroundService`, `Main`). The moment somebody blocks with
`.Result` in the middle, you have given away the benefit and possibly bought a
deadlock.

**Pass the token.** Every async API takes a `CancellationToken` as its last
parameter for a reason: cancellation only works if every layer forwards it. A
method that accepts one and quietly ignores it is worse than one that never
took it, because the caller believes it works.

And the honest limitation, which is the answer to the most common follow-up
question: async is about **not blocking a thread while waiting**, not about
going faster. It makes a server handle more concurrent requests with fewer
threads. It does nothing at all for CPU-bound work — that is what
`Task.Run` and `Parallel.For` are for, and reaching for `async` there is a
common and revealing mistake.

That is the end of the language part of the course. Next: **i1_interview_concepts**,
where everything you have built gets turned into answers you can say out loud.

# Reading - csharp/13_async_await

## Notes

**What the compiler actually does.** An `async` method is rewritten into a state
machine, exactly like the iterators in lesson 08. Each `await` becomes: check
whether the awaited thing is already complete; if it is, carry straight on; if
it is not, register a continuation and **return** to the caller. The method's
locals become fields on the state machine object so they survive the gap. The
task you hand back is that state machine's promise. Two things follow: the code
before the first `await` runs *synchronously* on the calling thread, and there
is no thread sitting anywhere waiting for the result.

**Async is not a thread.** The most useful sentence about async I/O: while a
network read is in flight there is **no thread involved at all** — the operating
system holds the request and signals a completion port when data arrives. That
is why a server can have ten thousand pending requests and twenty threads. It is
also why `async` does nothing for CPU-bound work: burning CPU genuinely needs a
thread, and `Task.Run` is the tool for pushing that off the current one.

**The synchronization context, and where deadlocks come from.** In WinForms,
WPF and old ASP.NET, `await` captures a context and resumes the continuation on
it — the UI thread, or the request's thread. Now block that same thread with
`.Result` and the continuation can never run: the thread is waiting for a task
whose continuation needs the thread. Classic deadlock, and the reason
`ConfigureAwait(false)` exists — it says "resume anywhere, I do not need the
context". Modern ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so the deadlock
does not occur there, but library code still uses `ConfigureAwait(false)`
because it cannot know who will call it. In application code you generally do
not need it.

**`async void` is a trap with one legitimate use.** A `void`-returning async
method hands the caller nothing to await, so nobody can wait for it and nobody
can catch its exceptions — they are raised on the synchronization context and
usually terminate the process. The single legitimate case is an event handler,
because the event's delegate signature demands `void`. Everywhere else: return
`Task`.

**`ValueTask`, briefly.** A `Task` is a heap allocation, which matters when a
method is called millions of times and usually completes synchronously (a cache
hit, a buffered read). `ValueTask<T>` avoids the allocation in that case, at the
cost of stricter rules — you may await it only once, and never block on it. Use
`Task` by default; recognise `ValueTask` when you see it in high-performance
APIs.

## ex1

The gate's shape — assert "not completed", complete one input, assert "still not
completed", complete the other — is worth stealing for your own async tests.
`TaskCompletionSource` gives you a task whose completion *you* trigger, which
removes timing from the test entirely. Tests that call `Task.Delay(100)` and
hope are the reason people believe async tests are flaky.

The sequential-versus-concurrent point is the one to keep. `await first; await second;`
gives the same answer as `Task.WhenAll` here, because both tasks were already
running before your method was called. Change that to a method that *starts*
each call — `await LoadAsync(a); await LoadAsync(b);` — and the two versions
differ by the duration of the first call, every time. The rule of thumb: start
everything you can, then await; do not start-and-await in a loop unless the
calls genuinely depend on each other.

Reading `.Result` on an already-completed task, as `InOrderAsync` may do after
`WhenAll`, is safe and non-blocking. It is still a habit worth avoiding, because
the same expression a hundred lines later, on a task that has not completed, is
a blocked thread — and reviewers cannot tell the two apart at a glance.

## ex2

`Task.WhenAll`'s positional result array is a small guarantee with large
consequences: you can fan out over a list of ids and zip the results back
against it, with no correlation logic at all. Completion order tells you nothing
and you never need it.

Two behaviours worth knowing. If several tasks fault, awaiting `WhenAll` rethrows
only the **first** exception — the rest are still there on the task's
`AggregateException`, reachable through `task.Exception.InnerExceptions`, which
is what the challenge digs into. And `WhenAll` waits for *every* task even after
one has failed, which is usually right (no orphaned work continuing in the
background) and occasionally not.

The lazy-sequence trap deserves repeating because it combines two lessons.
`items.Select(i => FetchAsync(i))` is a lazy query whose *enumeration* starts the
tasks. Pass it to `WhenAll` and it is enumerated once, fine. Enumerate it twice —
`if (queries.Any())` and then `await Task.WhenAll(queries)` — and you have
started every request twice. `.ToList()` before you hand it over.

## ex3

Cancellation in .NET is cooperative and that is a design decision, not a
limitation. The alternative — killing a thread mid-operation — leaves locks
held, files half-written and invariants broken, which is why `Thread.Abort` was
deprecated and then removed. So a `CancellationToken` is a flag with a callback
list, and code that wants to be interruptible has to look at it.

The two idioms cover the two situations. When you control the loop, check
between steps with `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`. When you are waiting for
somebody else's task, `WaitAsync(token)` stops the *wait* — and, as the gate
proves, the work carries on regardless. That distinction is the interview
question: "how do you cancel a task?" The answer is that you do not cancel a
task, you signal an intent, and the task decides.

`OperationCanceledException` gets special treatment across the framework: a task
that ends with one is `TaskStatus.Canceled` rather than `Faulted`, and ASP.NET
Core does not log it as an error, because a client hanging up is not a bug. That
is also why catching it and returning a "failed" result is wrong — it turns a
non-event into an alert.

`TaskCanceledException` derives from `OperationCanceledException`, so catch the
base and stop worrying about which one you got.

## ex4

Two mistakes in one exercise, and both are [***] interview questions.

**`.Result` versus `await`.** Blocking on a task wraps whatever went wrong in an
`AggregateException`, because a task can hold several exceptions. `await`
unwraps and rethrows the first one with its stack trace preserved (via
`ExceptionDispatchInfo`), so your `catch (InvalidOperationException)` actually
catches. The gate distinguishes them by asserting the exception *type*, which is
the cleanest possible demonstration.

The other half of `.Result` is worse: it blocks a thread. On a server that is a
thread not serving a request; under a synchronization context it is the deadlock
described above. `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` at least avoids the wrapping, which
is why you see it in `Main` methods of older code, but it still blocks.

**Where an async method's exception lives.** Because the method body runs inside
a state machine, a `throw` anywhere in it is captured and placed on the returned
task. So `var t = FailsAsync();` does not throw — `await t` does. A
*non*-async method declared to return `Task` that throws directly does throw at
the call site, which is a genuine difference in behaviour and the reason the
guidance for argument validation is to do it in a small non-async wrapper that
returns the async part:

```csharp
public static Task<int> LoadAsync(string path)
{
    ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty(path);   // eagerly, at the call site
    return LoadCoreAsync(path);                    // the async part
}
```

## challenge

The catch-ordering trap is real and appears in production code constantly. A
`catch (Exception)` around an awaited operation catches `OperationCanceledException`
too, so a cancelled request gets logged as an error, alerts fire, and somebody
investigates a user who closed a browser tab. Catch cancellation explicitly and
rethrow, or filter it out — `catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)`
is the compact form, and lesson 12's filters are what make it possible.

Digging the causes out of the tasks rather than out of the thrown exception is
the other production habit. Awaiting `WhenAll` gives you one exception; the
tasks themselves know about all of them. When a batch of ten uploads fails, "one
of them timed out" is much less useful than "three timed out, one was
unauthorised, and here are the ids".

Ending with a `switch` expression over the exception type is a nice closing
image for the language half of this course, because it uses lesson 02's switch
expressions, lesson 04's type hierarchy, lesson 06's patterns and lesson 12's
exceptions in one line — which is roughly what idiomatic modern C# looks like.

## Further reading

- [Asynchronous programming with async and await](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/) — the task-based model from the top.
- [Async in depth](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/async-in-depth) — what actually happens during an I/O wait, and why no thread is involved.
- [Task asynchronous programming model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/task-asynchronous-programming-model) — the state machine, step by step.
- [Async guidance: avoid `async void`, avoid blocking](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices) — ASP.NET Core's list of the same mistakes at production scale.
- [`CancellationToken`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/cancellation-in-managed-threads) — the cooperative cancellation model in full.
- [`ConfigureAwait` FAQ](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/) — Stephen Toub's definitive answer on contexts and deadlocks.

## Challenge — fan out, wait, and describe what happened

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Challenge.cs`. `SummariseAsync(work, token)`
waits for every task and reports `"ok: <total>"` when all succeeded, or

and the gate checks for exactly that. Finding *which* task failed also needs a
look at the tasks themselves, because awaiting `WhenAll` only rethrows one of
the exceptions. Finish it with a `switch` expression over the exception type if
you like — a fitting last line for the language part of this course.

## Exercise 1 — awaiting two things

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex1.cs`. `SumAsync(first, second)` returns the
two results added together. `InOrderAsync(first, second)` returns
`"one+two"` — the results in **parameter** order, however the tasks actually
finish.

The gate hands you tasks it controls and completes them in the wrong order on
purpose, checking along the way that your returned task is not finished before
both inputs are.

```
uv run dojo test csharp 13_async_await ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both tasks are already running when you receive them. You are not starting
work; you are deciding how to wait for it.

Awaiting them one after the other works and is not wrong here — but say out
loud what it means before you write it, because it is the difference between
"two seconds" and "one second" when the tasks are real network calls.

## Hint 2

`Task.WhenAll(first, second)` returns a task that completes when both do, and
for `Task<int>` inputs it hands back an `int[]` of the results in the order you
passed them:

```csharp
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(first, second);
return results[0] + results[1];
```

`InOrderAsync` is the same wait, then a string built from the two results in
parameter order.

## Hint 3

The gate checks that your returned task is **not** finished until both inputs
are, which is what `await` gives you and what returning early would not.

For `InOrderAsync`, after `await Task.WhenAll(...)` both tasks are complete, so
`first.Result` is safe — reading `.Result` on an *already completed* task never
blocks and never wraps. (It is reading `.Result` on a task that has not
finished that blocks the thread, which is ex4's subject.) Awaiting each one
again after the `WhenAll` is equally fine and reads better to some people.

Left to you: `await first; await second;` — two sequential awaits — passes this
gate too. Work out why it still gives the right answer here, and when it would
not be acceptable.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both tasks are already running when you receive them. You are not starting
work; you are deciding how to wait for it.

Awaiting them one after the other works and is not wrong here — but say out
loud what it means before you write it, because it is the difference between
"two seconds" and "one second" when the tasks are real network calls.

## Hint 2

`Task.WhenAll(first, second)` returns a task that completes when both do, and
for `Task<int>` inputs it hands back an `int[]` of the results in the order you
passed them:

```csharp
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(first, second);
return results[0] + results[1];
```

`InOrderAsync` is the same wait, then a string built from the two results in
parameter order.

## Hint 3

The gate checks that your returned task is **not** finished until both inputs
are, which is what `await` gives you and what returning early would not.

For `InOrderAsync`, after `await Task.WhenAll(...)` both tasks are complete, so
`first.Result` is safe — reading `.Result` on an *already completed* task never
blocks and never wraps. (It is reading `.Result` on a task that has not
finished that blocks the thread, which is ex4's subject.) Awaiting each one
again after the `WhenAll` is equally fine and reads better to some people.

Left to you: `await first; await second;` — two sequential awaits — passes this
gate too. Work out why it still gives the right answer here, and when it would
not be acceptable.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are one `await Task.WhenAll(...)` and one line of LINQ.

The interesting fact to notice is what order the results come back in when the
tasks finish in a completely different order from the one you passed them in.
Predict it before the gate tells you.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
return results.Sum();
```

`Task.WhenAll` accepts an `IEnumerable<Task<T>>` and returns a `Task<T[]>`.
The array is in the **input** order, always — completion order does not affect
it at all.

`JoinAsync` is the same call plus `string.Join(", ", results)`.

## Hint 3

`Task.WhenAll` over an empty sequence completes immediately with an empty
array, so `Sum()` gives 0 and no special case is needed.

One thing worth knowing that the gate does not check: `WhenAll` enumerates the
sequence you hand it once, immediately. If that sequence is a lazy LINQ query
that *creates* the tasks (`items.Select(i => FetchAsync(i))`), enumerating it
is what starts them — and enumerating it twice would start them twice. This is
lesson 10 ex3's multiple-enumeration trap with real consequences, and the fix
is the same: `.ToList()` before you pass it.

Left to you: `Task.WhenAny` is the sibling that completes when the *first* one
does. Read its signature and work out why it returns `Task<Task<T>>` rather
than `Task<T>`.

## Hint 1

## Exercise 4 — fix this code

Edit `src/Lessons/L13_AsyncAwait/Ex4.cs`. `RunAsync(work)` returns the work's
result, and when the work has failed the caller must see the **original**
exception — not an `AggregateException` with it buried inside. That difference
is exactly what `.Result` gets wrong and `await` gets right, and the gate can
tell them apart.

`AlwaysFailsAsync()` throws an `InvalidOperationException` with the message
`"boom"` — but the failure must arrive **in the returned task**, not be thrown
at the caller before they have a task to await.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are one line, and both are about *where the exception ends up*.

`RunAsync` must hand back the work's result — and when the work failed, the
caller has to see the original exception rather than something wrapped round
it. There is exactly one keyword that does that.

`AlwaysFailsAsync` must fail through the task it returns, not at the call site.

## Hint 2

`return await work;` is the whole of `RunAsync`. The tempting alternatives are
both wrong:

- `return work.Result;` blocks the calling thread AND wraps any failure in an
  `AggregateException`;
- `return work.GetAwaiter().GetResult();` also blocks, though it does not wrap.

For `AlwaysFailsAsync`, an `async` method that throws does not throw at the
call site — the compiler-generated state machine catches it and puts it on the
returned task. So an `async` method with a `throw` in it is exactly what you
want:

```csharp
await Task.Yield();
throw new InvalidOperationException("boom");
```

## Hint 3

The `await Task.Yield()` is there to make the method genuinely asynchronous and
to silence the "this async method has no await" warning. Without any `await`,
the method still behaves correctly — it is `async`, so the exception is still
captured — but the compiler warns, and warnings you ignore are warnings you
stop reading.

The contrast worth carrying out of this exercise: a **non**-async method
declared as `Task<int>` that throws directly (`public static Task<int> Fails() =>
throw new ...;`) throws *at the call site*, before the caller has a task to
await. Callers written as `var t = Fails(); ... await t;` never get to their
`try`. That asymmetry is why the guidance is to make argument validation happen
in a small non-async wrapper, deliberately, when you want it eager.

Left to you: work out what `async void` would do with this exception. (Nothing
catchable: it goes straight to the synchronization context and usually kills the
process. That is the interview answer.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are one line, and both are about *where the exception ends up*.

`RunAsync` must hand back the work's result — and when the work failed, the
caller has to see the original exception rather than something wrapped round
it. There is exactly one keyword that does that.

`AlwaysFailsAsync` must fail through the task it returns, not at the call site.

## Hint 2

`return await work;` is the whole of `RunAsync`. The tempting alternatives are
both wrong:

- `return work.Result;` blocks the calling thread AND wraps any failure in an
  `AggregateException`;
- `return work.GetAwaiter().GetResult();` also blocks, though it does not wrap.

For `AlwaysFailsAsync`, an `async` method that throws does not throw at the
call site — the compiler-generated state machine catches it and puts it on the
returned task. So an `async` method with a `throw` in it is exactly what you
want:

```csharp
await Task.Yield();
throw new InvalidOperationException("boom");
```

## Hint 3

The `await Task.Yield()` is there to make the method genuinely asynchronous and
to silence the "this async method has no await" warning. Without any `await`,
the method still behaves correctly — it is `async`, so the exception is still
captured — but the compiler warns, and warnings you ignore are warnings you
stop reading.

The contrast worth carrying out of this exercise: a **non**-async method
declared as `Task<int>` that throws directly (`public static Task<int> Fails() =>
throw new ...;`) throws *at the call site*, before the caller has a task to
await. Callers written as `var t = Fails(); ... await t;` never get to their
`try`. That asymmetry is why the guidance is to make argument validation happen
in a small non-async wrapper, deliberately, when you want it eager.

Left to you: work out what `async void` would do with this exception. (Nothing
catchable: it goes straight to the synchronization context and usually kills the
process. That is the interview answer.)

# d01 - Types and conversion drills

Eight problems on the arithmetic that C# does *before* you notice it did
anything: integer division, widening, overflow, rounding mode and parsing.
They drill lesson 01 - if the first three feel like guessing rather than
recall, reread `01_types_variables` and come back.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - the clock

Format a count of seconds as `H:MM:SS` and count whole minutes, using only
integer division and remainder. Hours are not padded and not wrapped at 24;
minutes and seconds always show two digits. A negative input throws
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - percentages, twice

`Percent(part, whole)` returns a `double` rounded to one decimal place with
halves going away from zero. `IntegerPercent(part, whole)` returns the
truncated whole-number percentage computed entirely in `int`. Both throw
`DivideByZeroException` when `whole` is 0.

The gate checks 1 in 3, 2 in 3, and 1 in 16 - the last one is exactly 6.25, so
it can tell your rounding mode from the default.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - the absent reading

Three small methods over `int?`: `SumOrNull` (null only when both inputs are
null, otherwise a null counts as 0), `AverageOfPresent` (mean of the readings
that exist, as a `double`, 0.0 when none do) and `Describe` (the number, or
`"none"`).

Zero is a value, not an absence. The gate checks that you know the difference.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - overflow, three ways

`AddChecked(a, b)` raises `OverflowException` instead of wrapping.
`AddSaturating(a, b)` clamps to `int.MaxValue` / `int.MinValue` and never
throws. The gate calls the second one with `int.MaxValue` twice, which catches
a clamp written one operation too late.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - double versus decimal

`DoubleTenthsReach(times)` adds `0.1` to a running total that many times and
reports whether it landed exactly on `times / 10.0`. `DecimalTenthsReach` runs
the same experiment in `decimal`. Then `RoundMoney` (2 dp, away from zero) and
`BankersRound` (2 dp, to even) on the same inputs.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - reading a money field

`TryReadAmount(raw, out amount)`: reject null, empty and whitespace-only text;
trim; allow one leading `$`; parse the number with the invariant culture
allowing a sign and `,` group separators. Failure returns `false` with `amount`
at 0 - and never throws.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - the ledger

`Balance(lines)` folds `"op,amount"` lines into a balance rounded to 2 dp,
halves away from zero. `credit` adds and `debit` subtracts, matched ignoring
case and surrounding whitespace. Blank lines are skipped but still count toward
the 1-based line number. Any other problem - wrong field count, unknown
operation, unparsable amount - throws `FormatException` whose message contains
`"line N"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - what a cast really does

`TruncateToInt`, `WrapToByte` (300 becomes 44, -1 becomes 255), `ToChar`, and
then the one that matters: `TrySafeToInt(value, out result)`, which returns
`false` for NaN, either infinity, and anything outside the `int` range -
without ever running the cast on a value it cannot represent.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d01_types_conversion

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same problem wearing a different hat: **C#
decides what kind of arithmetic to do from the operand types, and it decides
before it knows what you meant.** `1 / 3` is `0` because both operands are
`int`. `int.MaxValue + 1` is negative because `+` on two ints is unchecked by
default. `0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1` misses `0.3` because a `double` literal is the
nearest binary fraction, not the number you typed. `Math.Round(2.345m, 2)`
gives 2.34 because the default midpoint rule is to-even.

None of these are bugs in the language - each is a documented, defensible
choice - but every one of them is silent. The skill being drilled is spotting
the moment the decision gets made and taking it deliberately: widen before you
divide, widen before you add, pick a `MidpointRounding`, pick a `CultureInfo`,
and use `Try...` when the input came from a human.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that `/` and `%` on ints are exact tools rather
than approximations of real division. The classic mistake is `totalSeconds /
60 % 60` written as `totalSeconds % 60 / 60`, which is always 0 - the
precedence is left to right, so the remainder has to be taken from the larger
unit before the division. The model answer peels hours first, then takes the
sub-hour remainder and divides by 60. The second classic mistake is assuming
`-119 / 60` is `-2`: C# truncates toward zero, so it is `-1`, and that
difference has bitten every developer who has ever paged backwards through a
list.

## ex2

Really testing: whether you can see the exact instant an expression stops being
integer arithmetic. `part / whole` is evaluated in `int` no matter what the
method returns, so `1 / 3` is `0` and the widening to `double` happens on the
wrong side of the damage. Multiplying by `100.0` first drags the whole
expression into `double`. The mirror-image trap is in `IntegerPercent`, where
the fix is the opposite: keep everything in `int` but multiply *before* you
divide. The 1-in-16 case exists because 6.25 is exactly a midpoint, and the
default `Math.Round` overload rounds it to 6.2 - a silent one-cent-per-invoice
class of bug.

## ex3

Really testing: the difference between "the value is zero" and "there is no
value". `int?` makes that distinction representable, and the classic mistake is
throwing it away - `if (sum == 0) return null`, or `value ?? 0` used where the
absence itself is the answer. The model answer asks the *inputs* whether they
have values and never asks the result. `AverageOfPresent` hides the second
trap: `sum` and `count` are both `int`, so `sum / count` truncates and the mean
of 1 and 2 comes back as 1 - one cast fixes it, and it must be on the division,
not on the return value.

## ex4

Really testing: knowledge that C# integer arithmetic is unchecked by default,
and that this is a choice you can reverse per expression. The classic mistake
in the clamping method is `long sum = (long)(a + b)`: the addition still
happens in `int`, wraps, and then you faithfully widen the wrong number. The
gate calls it with `int.MaxValue` twice precisely to catch that. The model
answer widens one operand - `(long)a + b` - so the addition itself is done in
`long`, then compares against the `int` bounds before narrowing. Saturating
arithmetic is the right shape for counters and gauges; `checked` is the right
shape for anything where a wrong answer is worse than a stopped process.

## ex5

Really testing: that `double` and `decimal` are not "less precise" and "more
precise" versions of each other but different number systems. `double` is
binary and cannot represent a tenth at all; `decimal` is base 10 and
represents it exactly, at roughly a tenth of the speed and with a much smaller
exponent range. The classic mistake is comparing floating-point values with
`==` - which is exactly what this exercise makes you do, so you can watch it
fail. The rounding half is a different lesson: `Math.Round(x, n)` defaults to
banker's rounding, which is statistically sound and almost never what a
financial specification means. Say the mode out loud in the argument list.

## ex6

Really testing: that parsing is a *policy* decision, not a utility call. Which
culture reads the text? Which shapes count as a number? What happens on
failure? The classic mistake is `decimal.Parse(raw)` with no culture, which
reads `"1,234.50"` differently in Berlin than in Boston and throws on any
malformed keystroke. The model answer states the policy in the call itself:
invariant culture, `NumberStyles.Number`, `TryParse` so failure is a return
value rather than an exception. The guard order matters too - reject
null-or-whitespace first, so the later steps can assume there is something to
work with.

## ex7

Really testing: whether you can hold six small rules in your head at once and
still write a clean loop. The classic mistake is rounding inside the loop:
every line gets its own rounding error and the total drifts, which is exactly
the bug that makes an accountant distrust a system. The second classic mistake
is incrementing the line counter after the blank-line `continue`, so the number
in the error message does not match the file the user is looking at. The model
answer counts first, skips second, validates third, and rounds exactly once on
the way out. The error messages name the line because an error that does not
tell you where it happened costs someone an hour.

## ex8

Really testing: that an explicit cast is an instruction, not a request. `(int)`
on a `double` truncates toward zero; `(byte)` on an `int` keeps the low eight
bits; `(char)` on an `int` reinterprets it as a UTF-16 code unit. None of them
check anything at run time. The classic mistake in `TrySafeToInt` is doing the
range comparison before the NaN check: every comparison involving NaN is
`false`, so `value < int.MinValue || value > int.MaxValue` is `false` for NaN
and the value sails through to a cast whose result the specification leaves
unspecified. The model answer asks "is this a real number?" before it asks "is
it in range?", and only then performs the conversion.

## Further reading

- [Integral numeric types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types) - ranges, division, and what `/` does to ints.
- [Floating-point numeric types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/floating-point-numeric-types) - why `double` and `decimal` are different tools.
- [`checked` and `unchecked`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/checked-and-unchecked) - the statement, the expression, and the project-wide switch.
- [`MidpointRounding`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.midpointrounding) - all five modes, with the to-even default spelled out.
- [Parsing numeric strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/parsing-numeric) - `NumberStyles`, cultures, and the Try-pattern.
- [Casting and type conversions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/casting-and-type-conversions) - implicit widening versus explicit narrowing.

## Exercise 1 - the clock

Format a count of seconds as `H:MM:SS` and count whole minutes, using only
integer division and remainder. Hours are not padded and not wrapped at 24;
minutes and seconds always show two digits. A negative input throws
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D01_TypesConversion/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d01_types_conversion ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two operators do all the work here: `/` between two ints throws the fraction
away, and `%` gives you what `/` threw away. Neither one rounds, and both
truncate *toward zero* rather than downward.

The padding is a format specifier, not string surgery: `D2` on an int means
"at least two digits, zero-filled".

## Hint 2

Peel the units off largest first, and take each remainder from the right
quantity:

```csharp
int hours = totalSeconds / 3600;
int minutes = totalSeconds % 3600 / 60;   // seconds left over, then minutes
int seconds = totalSeconds % 60;
```

`totalSeconds / 60 % 60` gets you the same minutes by a different route - pick
one and be able to explain it.

Interpolation holds format specifiers directly: `$"{minutes:D2}"`. The hours
part has no specifier because it is not padded and not wrapped at 24.

## Hint 1

Two operators do all the work here: `/` between two ints throws the fraction
away, and `%` gives you what `/` threw away. Neither one rounds, and both
truncate *toward zero* rather than downward.

The padding is a format specifier, not string surgery: `D2` on an int means
"at least two digits, zero-filled".

## Hint 2

Peel the units off largest first, and take each remainder from the right
quantity:

```csharp
int hours = totalSeconds / 3600;
int minutes = totalSeconds % 3600 / 60;   // seconds left over, then minutes
int seconds = totalSeconds % 60;
```

`totalSeconds / 60 % 60` gets you the same minutes by a different route - pick
one and be able to explain it.

Interpolation holds format specifiers directly: `$"{minutes:D2}"`. The hours
part has no specifier because it is not padded and not wrapped at 24.

## Exercise 2 - percentages, twice

`Percent(part, whole)` returns a `double` rounded to one decimal place with
halves going away from zero. `IntegerPercent(part, whole)` returns the
truncated whole-number percentage computed entirely in `int`. Both throw
`DivideByZeroException` when `whole` is 0.

The gate checks 1 in 3, 2 in 3, and 1 in 16 - the last one is exactly 6.25, so
it can tell your rounding mode from the default.


## Hint 1

C# picks the arithmetic from the operand types, not from the type you are
assigning to. `int / int` is integer division even when the result is going
straight into a `double`, so `1 / 3` is `0` and `(double)(1 / 3)` is `0.0`.

The fix is to make one operand a `double` *before* the divide happens.

## Hint 2

Multiplying by `100.0` (note the `.0`) widens the whole expression:

```csharp
return Math.Round(part * 100.0 / whole, 1, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero);
```

`Math.Round`'s two-argument overload uses to-even rounding, which would answer
6.2 for 6.25. The specification says away from zero, so the third argument is
not optional.

For the integer version the order is the whole exercise: `part * 100 / whole`
keeps the precision that `part / whole * 100` has already lost.

## Exercise 3 - the absent reading

Three small methods over `int?`: `SumOrNull` (null only when both inputs are
null, otherwise a null counts as 0), `AverageOfPresent` (mean of the readings
that exist, as a `double`, 0.0 when none do) and `Describe` (the number, or
`"none"`).

Zero is a value, not an absence. The gate checks that you know the difference.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`int?` is `Nullable<int>`: a struct holding a value plus a flag. `HasValue`
asks the flag, `Value` reads the value (and throws when there is none), and
`??` supplies a fallback.

The trap in all three methods is the same one: `0` is a perfectly good value,
so anything that treats "is it zero?" as "is it missing?" is wrong.

## Hint 2

`SumOrNull` has to test the *inputs*, not the sum:

```csharp
if (a is null && b is null) return null;
return (a ?? 0) + (b ?? 0);
```

`AverageOfPresent` wants a plain `foreach` with a running total and a running
count, skipping anything where `HasValue` is false. Then the division: `sum`
and `count` are both `int`, so cast one of them - `sum / (double)count` - or
the mean of 1 and 2 comes back as 1.

`Describe` is one conditional. `Nullable<T>.ToString()` on an empty nullable
gives `""`, which is not the word the gate wants.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`int?` is `Nullable<int>`: a struct holding a value plus a flag. `HasValue`
asks the flag, `Value` reads the value (and throws when there is none), and
`??` supplies a fallback.

The trap in all three methods is the same one: `0` is a perfectly good value,
so anything that treats "is it zero?" as "is it missing?" is wrong.

## Hint 2

`SumOrNull` has to test the *inputs*, not the sum:

```csharp
if (a is null && b is null) return null;
return (a ?? 0) + (b ?? 0);
```

`AverageOfPresent` wants a plain `foreach` with a running total and a running
count, skipping anything where `HasValue` is false. Then the division: `sum`
and `count` are both `int`, so cast one of them - `sum / (double)count` - or
the mean of 1 and 2 comes back as 1.

`Describe` is one conditional. `Nullable<T>.ToString()` on an empty nullable
gives `""`, which is not the word the gate wants.

## Exercise 4 - overflow, three ways

`AddChecked(a, b)` raises `OverflowException` instead of wrapping.
`AddSaturating(a, b)` clamps to `int.MaxValue` / `int.MinValue` and never
throws. The gate calls the second one with `int.MaxValue` twice, which catches
a clamp written one operation too late.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

By default C# arithmetic is *unchecked*: an int addition that does not fit
wraps around silently, and `int.MaxValue + 1` is `int.MinValue`. The `checked`
keyword turns that same addition into an `OverflowException`.

Clamping needs the opposite trick - a type roomy enough to notice the problem
before it happens.

## Hint 2

`checked` works as a statement block or as an expression:

```csharp
checked { return a + b; }        // or: return checked(a + b);
```

For the clamping version, widen first and compare afterwards:

```csharp
long sum = (long)a + b;
```

The cast has to be on one operand of the addition. `(long)(a + b)` adds two
ints first, so the overflow has already happened and you are widening the
wrong answer - which is exactly the case the gate checks with two `int.MaxValue`
operands.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

By default C# arithmetic is *unchecked*: an int addition that does not fit
wraps around silently, and `int.MaxValue + 1` is `int.MinValue`. The `checked`
keyword turns that same addition into an `OverflowException`.

Clamping needs the opposite trick - a type roomy enough to notice the problem
before it happens.

## Hint 2

`checked` works as a statement block or as an expression:

```csharp
checked { return a + b; }        // or: return checked(a + b);
```

For the clamping version, widen first and compare afterwards:

```csharp
long sum = (long)a + b;
```

The cast has to be on one operand of the addition. `(long)(a + b)` adds two
ints first, so the overflow has already happened and you are widening the
wrong answer - which is exactly the case the gate checks with two `int.MaxValue`
operands.

`TryReadAmount(raw, out amount)`: reject null, empty and whitespace-only text;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`decimal.Parse` throws on bad input; `decimal.TryParse` returns a bool and
writes through an `out`. Text that came from a user is expected to be wrong
sometimes, so the Try-version is the right tool - an exception per bad
keystroke is both slow and noisy.

The four-argument overload is the one that lets you say which culture and which
shapes of number you will accept.

## Hint 2

```csharp
decimal.TryParse(text, NumberStyles.Number, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out amount);
```

`NumberStyles.Number` is the combination you want: leading and trailing
whitespace, a sign, a decimal point and group separators. `CultureInfo`
lives in `System.Globalization`.

Order matters before that call: reject null-or-whitespace, then `Trim`, then
strip at most one leading `"$"`. And note that a failed `TryParse` already sets
its `out` to 0 - but assigning `amount = 0m` on the first line makes that
guaranteed rather than inherited.

Left to you: whether to use `StartsWith("$", StringComparison.Ordinal)` or a
character comparison. Both are fine; the ordinal overload is the one that says
"this is a symbol, not language".

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`decimal.Parse` throws on bad input; `decimal.TryParse` returns a bool and
writes through an `out`. Text that came from a user is expected to be wrong
sometimes, so the Try-version is the right tool - an exception per bad
keystroke is both slow and noisy.

The four-argument overload is the one that lets you say which culture and which
shapes of number you will accept.

## Hint 2

```csharp
decimal.TryParse(text, NumberStyles.Number, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out amount);
```

`NumberStyles.Number` is the combination you want: leading and trailing
whitespace, a sign, a decimal point and group separators. `CultureInfo`
lives in `System.Globalization`.

Order matters before that call: reject null-or-whitespace, then `Trim`, then
strip at most one leading `"$"`. And note that a failed `TryParse` already sets
its `out` to 0 - but assigning `amount = 0m` on the first line makes that
guaranteed rather than inherited.

Left to you: whether to use `StartsWith("$", StringComparison.Ordinal)` or a
character comparison. Both are fine; the ordinal overload is the one that says
"this is a symbol, not language".

## Exercise 7 - the ledger

`Balance(lines)` folds `"op,amount"` lines into a balance rounded to 2 dp,
halves away from zero. `credit` adds and `debit` subtracts, matched ignoring
case and surrounding whitespace. Blank lines are skipped but still count toward
the 1-based line number. Any other problem - wrong field count, unknown
operation, unparsable amount - throws `FormatException` whose message contains
`"line N"`.


them: count the line, skip if blank, split into exactly two fields, read the
operation, read the amount, apply it. Every failure in that list becomes a

not a word in the user's language), and use the same

# d02 - Strings and formatting drills

Eight problems on the type you touch more than any other: padding and
truncating, format specifiers, splitting and joining, `StringBuilder`,
comparison rules, and three small text algorithms. They drill lesson 01's
string and culture material - if the format specifiers feel unfamiliar, reread
`01_types_variables` first.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/`. Nothing here depends
on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - fit a fixed column

`Fit(text, width)` returns a string of exactly `width` characters: padded on
the right when short, and truncated to `width - 3` plus `"..."` when long. A
width below 4 throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. `Center(text, width)`
centres inside the field, giving any odd space to the right, and returns text
that is already wide enough unchanged.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - three format specifiers

`Money(1234.5m)` is `"1,234.50"`. `Percent(0.1234)` is `"12.3%"` - one decimal,
always. `Hex(255)` is `"0x00FF"` - upper case, four digits minimum. All three
use the invariant culture, and none of them uses `Replace`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - the delimited line, both ways

`Join(fields)` trims each field, drops the null and blank ones, and joins with
`", "`. `Split(line)` does the inverse and returns a `List<string>`; a null or
blank line gives an empty list.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - build it with a builder

`Repeat(word, times, separator)` puts the separator between copies only, and
answers `""` for a count of zero or less. `Reverse(text)` reverses the
characters. Both use a `StringBuilder`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - which "equal" did you mean

`SameName(a, b)` trims and compares ordinally ignoring case, treating two nulls
as equal and one null as not. `SortKey(name)` returns the trimmed,
invariant-upper-cased grouping key. `StartsWithIgnoringCase(text, prefix)` does
what it says, ordinally.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - a tiny template engine

`Render(template, values)` replaces every `{key}` with its value. An unknown
key is left exactly as written, braces and all; a `{` with no matching `}` is
ordinary text; everything else is copied through. Braces do not nest.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - greedy word wrap

`Lines(text, width)` breaks text into lines no longer than `width`, filling
each line while the next word still fits. Runs of whitespace collapse, a word
longer than the width gets its own line rather than being broken, and text with
no words gives an empty list.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - the URL slug

`From(title)` keeps letters and digits (lower-cased, invariant), turns every
run of anything else into a single `-`, and leaves no hyphen at either end.
`"  C# 12 -- What's New?  "` becomes `"c-12-what-s-new"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex8
```

# Reading - csharp/d02_strings_formatting

## Notes

The thread running through all eight problems is that **a `string` in .NET is
an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units, and almost every question you can
ask about one has more than one defensible answer** - so the API makes you
choose. Which culture formats this number? Which comparison decides these two
names are equal? Does a run of separators collapse or not?

The everyday consequence of immutability is that concatenation in a loop is
quadratic and `StringBuilder` is not a micro-optimisation. The everyday
consequence of "more than one answer" is that any string method with a
`StringComparison` or `IFormatProvider` overload has a wrong default waiting
for you when your code meets a machine in another locale. Reach for the
explicit overload by reflex; the drills here are mostly about building that
reflex.

## ex1

Really testing: that the field width is a promise about the *result*, not about
the input. The classic mistake is `text.Substring(0, width) + "..."`, which
produces a string of `width + 3` characters and silently breaks the column
alignment the whole point of the method was to maintain. The model answer
subtracts the ellipsis from the budget before truncating. `Center` hides a
smaller version of the same discipline: the odd space has to go somewhere, the
specification says right, and `padding / 2` on the left with `padding - left`
on the right encodes that without a conditional.

## ex2

Really testing: that formatting is a lookup, not a construction. Everything
asked for here is one standard or custom specifier plus
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. The classic mistake is building the output by
hand - `Math.Round` then `ToString()` then inserting commas - which is longer,
slower and wrong on the first machine whose locale uses `.` as a group
separator. The percentage case teaches the other half: the built-in `"P1"`
specifier exists but inserts a culture-specific space before the sign, so the
model answer multiplies by 100 and uses `"0.0"`. Knowing *why* you did not use
the obvious specifier is the senior version of this answer.

## ex3

Really testing: that real delimited data has ragged whitespace and empty
fields, and that both directions need the same filter. The classic mistake is
filtering on one side only, so a round trip through `Join` and `Split` is not
the identity. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the single call that covers null,
empty and spaces, and it carries a `[NotNullWhen(false)]` annotation so the
compiler stops warning about the `Trim()` inside the `if` - a small example of
nullable annotations doing real work.

## ex4

Really testing: whether you reach for `StringBuilder` without being told, and
whether you can get "separator between items" right. The classic mistake is
appending the separator after each item and then trimming the last one off -
which works, allocates an extra string, and reads like an apology. Appending
the separator *before* every item except the first has no cleanup step. The
negative-count case exists to show that a `for` loop already handles it: a
guard clause there would be code that can never run, and code that can never
run still has to be read.

## ex5

Really testing: that "equal" is a question with several correct answers and
that C# makes you pick one. `==` is ordinal and case-sensitive; culture-aware
comparison sorts differently in different places; `OrdinalIgnoreCase` is the
right default for identifiers. The classic mistake is
`a.ToLower() == b.ToLower()`, which allocates two strings per comparison and is
locale-dependent into the bargain. The null handling is not defensive
programming: names arrive null from databases constantly, and `a.Trim()` on a
null is the `NullReferenceException` in your log at 3am.

## ex6

Really testing: single-pass scanning with an index, and the judgement call
about unknown tokens. The classic mistake is a `Replace` per dictionary entry,
which is O(keys x length), rewrites the string once per key, and cannot tell an
unknown token from ordinary text. The model answer walks the template once,
and at each `{` asks only two questions: is there a `}`, and is the key known.
Leaving an unknown token visible is the deliberate part of the design - a
renderer that drops what it does not recognise turns `{nmae}` into a blank
space that ships to a customer.

## ex7

Really testing: a greedy algorithm with an explicit invariant - "the buffer
always holds a line that fits". Splitting on whitespace first removes an entire
category of edge case, which is a habit worth generalising: normalise the input
so the loop only has one job. The classic mistake is forgetting the `+ 1` for
the space you are about to add, producing lines one character too wide; the
second is forgetting to flush the buffer after the loop, silently losing the
last line. Note that the over-long word needs no special case: the buffer is
empty, so the word starts the line, and the next word does not fit.

## ex8

Really testing: collapsing runs, which is the same shape as de-duplicating
adjacent items, and is best solved with a "separator owed" flag rather than by
post-processing. The classic mistake is `Regex.Replace(title, "[^a-z0-9]+",
"-")` followed by `Trim('-')` - which is not wrong, and is a perfectly good
answer if you can say why the `+` matters and why the trim is still needed. The
mistake proper is the version without the `+`, which produces `"hello--world"`
from a comma and a space. The lower-casing is invariant for the same reason as
ex5: a slug is machine data, and it must not change when the process starts on
a machine in Ankara.

## Further reading

- [`string` and string literals](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/strings/) - immutability, interpolation, raw literals.
- [Standard numeric format strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/standard-numeric-format-strings) - `N`, `X`, `P` and the rest, with examples.
- [Custom numeric format strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/custom-numeric-format-strings) - what `0.0` and `#.##` actually mean.
- [Comparing strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/comparing) - which `StringComparison` to use, with a decision table.
- [`StringBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.stringbuilder) - the API and when it stops being worth it.
- [Globalization and localization best practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/globalization-and-localization) - why invariant is the default for machine data.

names are equal? Does a run of separators collapse or not?

The everyday consequence of immutability is that concatenation in a loop is
quadratic and `StringBuilder` is not a micro-optimisation. The everyday
consequence of "more than one answer" is that any string method with a
`StringComparison` or `IFormatProvider` overload has a wrong default waiting
for you when your code meets a machine in another locale. Reach for the
explicit overload by reflex; the drills here are mostly about building that
reflex.

## ex1

Really testing: that the field width is a promise about the *result*, not about
the input. The classic mistake is `text.Substring(0, width) + "..."`, which
produces a string of `width + 3` characters and silently breaks the column
alignment the whole point of the method was to maintain. The model answer
subtracts the ellipsis from the budget before truncating. `Center` hides a
smaller version of the same discipline: the odd space has to go somewhere, the
specification says right, and `padding / 2` on the left with `padding - left`
on the right encodes that without a conditional.

## ex2

Really testing: that formatting is a lookup, not a construction. Everything
asked for here is one standard or custom specifier plus
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. The classic mistake is building the output by
hand - `Math.Round` then `ToString()` then inserting commas - which is longer,
slower and wrong on the first machine whose locale uses `.` as a group
separator. The percentage case teaches the other half: the built-in `"P1"`
specifier exists but inserts a culture-specific space before the sign, so the
model answer multiplies by 100 and uses `"0.0"`. Knowing *why* you did not use
the obvious specifier is the senior version of this answer.

## ex3

Really testing: that real delimited data has ragged whitespace and empty
fields, and that both directions need the same filter. The classic mistake is
filtering on one side only, so a round trip through `Join` and `Split` is not
the identity. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the single call that covers null,
empty and spaces, and it carries a `[NotNullWhen(false)]` annotation so the
compiler stops warning about the `Trim()` inside the `if` - a small example of
nullable annotations doing real work.

## ex4

Really testing: whether you reach for `StringBuilder` without being told, and
whether you can get "separator between items" right. The classic mistake is
appending the separator after each item and then trimming the last one off -
which works, allocates an extra string, and reads like an apology. Appending
the separator *before* every item except the first has no cleanup step. The
negative-count case exists to show that a `for` loop already handles it: a
guard clause there would be code that can never run, and code that can never
run still has to be read.

## ex5

Really testing: that "equal" is a question with several correct answers and
that C# makes you pick one. `==` is ordinal and case-sensitive; culture-aware
comparison sorts differently in different places; `OrdinalIgnoreCase` is the
right default for identifiers. The classic mistake is
`a.ToLower() == b.ToLower()`, which allocates two strings per comparison and is
locale-dependent into the bargain. The null handling is not defensive
programming: names arrive null from databases constantly, and `a.Trim()` on a
null is the `NullReferenceException` in your log at 3am.

## ex6

Really testing: single-pass scanning with an index, and the judgement call
about unknown tokens. The classic mistake is a `Replace` per dictionary entry,
which is O(keys x length), rewrites the string once per key, and cannot tell an
unknown token from ordinary text. The model answer walks the template once,
and at each `{` asks only two questions: is there a `}`, and is the key known.
Leaving an unknown token visible is the deliberate part of the design - a
renderer that drops what it does not recognise turns `{nmae}` into a blank
space that ships to a customer.

## ex7

Really testing: a greedy algorithm with an explicit invariant - "the buffer
always holds a line that fits". Splitting on whitespace first removes an entire
category of edge case, which is a habit worth generalising: normalise the input
so the loop only has one job. The classic mistake is forgetting the `+ 1` for
the space you are about to add, producing lines one character too wide; the
second is forgetting to flush the buffer after the loop, silently losing the
last line. Note that the over-long word needs no special case: the buffer is
empty, so the word starts the line, and the next word does not fit.

## ex8

Really testing: collapsing runs, which is the same shape as de-duplicating
adjacent items, and is best solved with a "separator owed" flag rather than by
post-processing. The classic mistake is `Regex.Replace(title, "[^a-z0-9]+",
"-")` followed by `Trim('-')` - which is not wrong, and is a perfectly good
answer if you can say why the `+` matters and why the trim is still needed. The
mistake proper is the version without the `+`, which produces `"hello--world"`
from a comma and a space. The lower-casing is invariant for the same reason as
ex5: a slug is machine data, and it must not change when the process starts on
a machine in Ankara.

## Further reading

- [`string` and string literals](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/strings/) - immutability, interpolation, raw literals.
- [Standard numeric format strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/standard-numeric-format-strings) - `N`, `X`, `P` and the rest, with examples.
- [Custom numeric format strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/custom-numeric-format-strings) - what `0.0` and `#.##` actually mean.
- [Comparing strings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/comparing) - which `StringComparison` to use, with a decision table.
- [`StringBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.stringbuilder) - the API and when it stops being worth it.
- [Globalization and localization best practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/globalization-and-localization) - why invariant is the default for machine data.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - fit a fixed column

`Fit(text, width)` returns a string of exactly `width` characters: padded on
the right when short, and truncated to `width - 3` plus `"..."` when long. A
width below 4 throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. `Center(text, width)`
centres inside the field, giving any odd space to the right, and returns text
that is already wide enough unchanged.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three built-ins do almost all of this: `PadRight(width)`, `Substring(start,
length)` and the `new string(char, count)` constructor. Nothing here needs a
loop.

Decide the three cases before you type: shorter than the field, exactly the
field, longer than the field.

## Hint 2

For `Fit`, note that the ellipsis is part of the width, not extra:

```csharp
return text.Substring(0, width - 3) + "...";
```

so the result is always exactly `width` characters. `PadRight` already returns
the string unchanged when it is long enough, which folds two of your three
cases into one line.

For `Center`, compute the total padding once and give the remainder to the
right: `int left = padding / 2;` then `padding - left` on the other side.
Integer division is doing the "odd space goes right" rule for you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three built-ins do almost all of this: `PadRight(width)`, `Substring(start,
length)` and the `new string(char, count)` constructor. Nothing here needs a
loop.

Decide the three cases before you type: shorter than the field, exactly the
field, longer than the field.

## Hint 2

For `Fit`, note that the ellipsis is part of the width, not extra:

```csharp
return text.Substring(0, width - 3) + "...";
```

so the result is always exactly `width` characters. `PadRight` already returns
the string unchanged when it is long enough, which folds two of your three
cases into one line.

For `Center`, compute the total padding once and give the remainder to the
right: `int left = padding / 2;` then `padding - left` on the other side.
Integer division is doing the "odd space goes right" rule for you.

## Exercise 2 - three format specifiers

`Money(1234.5m)` is `"1,234.50"`. `Percent(0.1234)` is `"12.3%"` - one decimal,
always. `Hex(255)` is `"0x00FF"` - upper case, four digits minimum. All three
use the invariant culture, and none of them uses `Replace`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every one of these is a *format specifier* plus a culture, not string surgery.
`ToString(format, provider)` is the overload you want, and
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` (in `System.Globalization`) is the provider that
makes the output the same on every machine.

Look up the standard specifiers before reaching for `Replace`: `N` for numbers
with group separators, `X` for hex, and `0.0` as a custom pattern.

## Hint 2

- `"N2"` - group separators plus exactly two decimals.
- `"0.0"` - exactly one decimal, and a leading zero when the value is below 1.
- `"X4"` - upper-case hex, zero-padded to at least four digits. (`"x4"` gives
  lower case, which is why the case of the letter matters.)

The percentage needs the multiply-by-100 done by you: the built-in `"P1"`
specifier also appends a `%` but inserts a culture-specific space before it,
which is not the shape the gate asks for. Being able to say *why* you did not
use `P1` is worth as much as the answer.

## Hint 1

Every one of these is a *format specifier* plus a culture, not string surgery.
`ToString(format, provider)` is the overload you want, and
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` (in `System.Globalization`) is the provider that
makes the output the same on every machine.

Look up the standard specifiers before reaching for `Replace`: `N` for numbers
with group separators, `X` for hex, and `0.0` as a custom pattern.

## Hint 2

- `"N2"` - group separators plus exactly two decimals.
- `"0.0"` - exactly one decimal, and a leading zero when the value is below 1.
- `"X4"` - upper-case hex, zero-padded to at least four digits. (`"x4"` gives
  lower case, which is why the case of the letter matters.)

The percentage needs the multiply-by-100 done by you: the built-in `"P1"`
specifier also appends a `%` but inserts a culture-specific space before it,
which is not the shape the gate asks for. Being able to say *why* you did not
use `P1` is worth as much as the answer.

## Exercise 4 - build it with a builder

`Repeat(word, times, separator)` puts the separator between copies only, and
answers `""` for a count of zero or less. `Reverse(text)` reverses the
characters. Both use a `StringBuilder`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex4
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `string` in .NET is immutable, so `result += word` in a loop allocates a
whole new string every time round - N appends cost O(N^2) copying.
`StringBuilder` keeps one growable buffer and copies once, at `ToString()`.

The separator rule is the usual off-by-one: it belongs *between* items, so
there is one fewer separator than there are copies.

## Hint 2

The cleanest way to get "between" right is to append the separator *before*
every item except the first:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < times; i++)
{
    if (i > 0) builder.Append(separator);
    builder.Append(word);
}
```

A negative `times` needs no guard - the loop condition is already false.

For `Reverse`, walk the indexer backwards from `text.Length - 1` down to 0.
`new string(chars)` over a reversed `char[]` and `string.Concat(text.Reverse())`
both work too; be ready to say which allocates less.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `string` in .NET is immutable, so `result += word` in a loop allocates a
whole new string every time round - N appends cost O(N^2) copying.
`StringBuilder` keeps one growable buffer and copies once, at `ToString()`.

The separator rule is the usual off-by-one: it belongs *between* items, so
there is one fewer separator than there are copies.

## Hint 2

The cleanest way to get "between" right is to append the separator *before*
every item except the first:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < times; i++)
{
    if (i > 0) builder.Append(separator);
    builder.Append(word);
}
```

A negative `times` needs no guard - the loop condition is already false.

For `Reverse`, walk the indexer backwards from `text.Length - 1` down to 0.
`new string(chars)` over a reversed `char[]` and `string.Concat(text.Reverse())`
both work too; be ready to say which allocates less.

## Hint 1

`==` on strings is an ordinal, case-sensitive comparison. Everything else -
ignoring case, using the current culture, using the invariant culture - is a
`StringComparison` you pass explicitly to `string.Equals`, `StartsWith`,
`IndexOf` or `Compare`.

## Hint 2

```csharp

```

Handle the nulls before that line, and handle both of them: two nulls are
equal, one null is not. Writing it as a single expression is possible but the
explicit guard reads better and cannot dereference a null.

`ToUpperInvariant()` rather than `ToUpper()` for the sort key, and upper rather

## Exercise 6 - a tiny template engine

`Render(template, values)` replaces every `{key}` with its value. An unknown
key is left exactly as written, braces and all; a `{` with no matching `}` is
ordinary text; everything else is copied through. Braces do not nest.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Scan the template once with an index and a `StringBuilder`. At each position
you are in one of two situations: the character is not a `{`, so copy it; or it
is, so look for the matching `}` and decide what to emit.

`string.IndexOf('}', startIndex)` finds the close brace and returns -1 when
there is none - which is the "ordinary text" case.

## Hint 2

The three outcomes at a `{`:

1. no `}` after it - append the rest of the template and stop;
2. a `}` and the key is known - append the value;

## Hint 1

Scan the template once with an index and a `StringBuilder`. At each position
you are in one of two situations: the character is not a `{`, so copy it; or it
is, so look for the matching `}` and decide what to emit.

`string.IndexOf('}', startIndex)` finds the close brace and returns -1 when
there is none - which is the "ordinary text" case.

## Hint 2

The three outcomes at a `{`:

1. no `}` after it - append the rest of the template and stop;
2. a `}` and the key is known - append the value;
3. a `}` and the key is unknown - append the token *including both braces*.

dropping an unknown token turns a typo into a missing word nobody notices.

guessing.

## Exercise 7 - greedy word wrap

`Lines(text, width)` breaks text into lines no longer than `width`, filling
each line while the next word still fits. Runs of whitespace collapse, a word
longer than the width gets its own line rather than being broken, and text with
no words gives an empty list.

Edit `src/Lessons/D02_StringsFormatting/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split into words first - that disposes of the whitespace-collapsing rule
entirely - then run one loop that keeps a "current line" buffer.

For each word there are exactly two questions: is the buffer empty (start the
line with this word, however long it is), and does the word still fit
(`current.Length + 1 + word.Length <= width`)?

## Hint 2

`text.Split((char[]?)null, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` splits on
any whitespace and throws away the empty entries, so `"  a   b "` gives
`["a", "b"]`.

The `+ 1` in the fit test is the space you are about to add. Forgetting it
produces lines one character too long, which is the classic off-by-one here.

Do not forget the last line: when the loop ends there is still text in the
buffer, and it only gets added if you say so. The empty-input case falls out of
that - the buffer is empty, so nothing is added.

Left to you: whether an over-long word gets its own line by luck (the buffer is
empty, so it starts the line) or by an explicit branch. Both work; know which
one you wrote.
