exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Split into words first - that disposes of the whitespace-collapsing rule
entirely - then run one loop that keeps a "current line" buffer.

For each word there are exactly two questions: is the buffer empty (start the
line with this word, however long it is), and does the word still fit
(`current.Length + 1 + word.Length <= width`)?

## Hint 2

`text.Split((char[]?)null, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` splits on
any whitespace and throws away the empty entries, so `"  a   b "` gives
`["a", "b"]`.

The `+ 1` in the fit test is the space you are about to add. Forgetting it
produces lines one character too long, which is the classic off-by-one here.

Do not forget the last line: when the loop ends there is still text in the
buffer, and it only gets added if you say so. The empty-input case falls out of
that - the buffer is empty, so nothing is added.

Left to you: whether an over-long word gets its own line by luck (the buffer is
empty, so it starts the line) or by an explicit branch. Both work; know which
one you wrote.

## Exercise 8 - the URL slug

`From(title)` keeps letters and digits (lower-cased, invariant), turns every
run of anything else into a single `-`, and leaves no hyphen at either end.
`"  C# 12 -- What's New?  "` becomes `"c-12-what-s-new"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d02_strings_formatting ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The hard part is not "replace bad characters with hyphens" - it is "a *run* of
bad characters becomes one hyphen, and runs at the ends become nothing". A
naive `Replace` per character gives `"hello--world-"`.

One pass with a flag solves it: instead of emitting a hyphen when you see a
separator, *remember that one is owed* and emit it only when the next keepable
character arrives.

## Hint 2

```csharp
bool pendingSeparator = false;
foreach (char c in title)
{
    if (!IsKeepable(c)) { pendingSeparator = slug.Length > 0; continue; }
    if (pendingSeparator) { slug.Append('-'); pendingSeparator = false; }
    slug.Append(char.ToLowerInvariant(c));
}
```

`slug.Length > 0` in the separator branch is what suppresses a leading hyphen,
and the fact that a pending separator is never flushed after the last keepable
character is what suppresses the trailing one. Both edge rules, one flag.

`char.ToLowerInvariant` rather than `ToLower` for the same reason as ex5: a
slug is part of a URL, not part of a language.

Left to you: whether "keepable" is `char.IsLetterOrDigit` or an explicit
ASCII range test. They differ - `char.IsLetterOrDigit('e')` with an accent is
true, and an accented letter in a URL is a different conversation. Pick one and
know what you picked.

lessons.briefing:
# d03 - Control flow drills

Eight problems on loops, conditions and patterns: counting, stopping early,
nesting, and three switch-expression forms. They drill lesson 02 - if the
relational and or-patterns in ex2 look unfamiliar, reread
`02_control_flow_methods` before starting.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D03_ControlFlow/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - count and accumulate

`SumOfMultiples(limit, a, b)` adds up every number from 1 up to but not
including `limit` that divides by `a` or by `b`, counting a number divisible by
both only once. `CountDigits(value)` returns how many decimal digits the number
has, ignoring the sign - and `int.MinValue` is in the gate for a reason.

Edit `src/Lessons/D03_ControlFlow/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d03_control_flow ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - switch expressions

`SeasonOf(month)` maps 12/1/2 to `"winter"`, 3-5 to `"spring"`, 6-8 to
`"summer"`, 9-11 to `"autumn"`, and anything else to an
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. `Ticket(age)` maps 0-4 to `"free"`, 5-17 to
`"child"`, 18-64 to `"adult"`, 65 and over to `"senior"`, and a negative age to
an exception.

Edit `src/Lessons/D03_ControlFlow/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d03_control_flow ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - stop as soon as you know

`FirstIndexOf(values, target)` and `LastIndexOf(values, target)` return the
index or -1. Both must work on an empty array.

Edit `src/Lessons/D03_ControlFlow/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d03_control_flow ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - run-length encoding

`Encode(text)` turns each run of identical characters into the character
followed by the run length, always - `"aaabbc"` becomes `"a3b2c1"`, and
`"aabaa"` becomes `"a2b1a2"`. `LongestRunLength(text)` returns the length of
the longest run, or 0 for empty text.

Edit `src/Lessons/D03_ControlFlow/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d03_control_flow ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - one switch, every pattern kind

`Describe(value)` classifies an `object?` in a single switch expression: null,
the constant 0, a negative int, any other int, an empty string, any other
string, an `int[]`, and everything else. The exact strings are in the file's
doc comment; the ordering is the exercise.

# Reading - csharp/d03_control_flow

## Notes

Control flow is the part of a language you stop noticing, which is exactly why
it is worth drilling. The pattern uniting these eight problems is **stating the
invariant before writing the loop**: what is true at the top of each iteration,
what the loop variable means, and what the answer is when the loop body never
runs at all.

Nearly every bug in this set is an edge that the middle of the range hides. An
empty array, a single element, a value of zero, the largest negative int, a run
of one character, the last line of the buffer. A loop that is right for
`{4, 7, 4, 9}` and wrong for `{}` is not almost right - it is a crash waiting
for a quiet Tuesday, and the habit that prevents it is naming the empty case
out loud before you type the `for`.

The other half of the set is patterns. C#'s switch expression has quietly grown
into a small language of its own - constants, types, ranges, properties,
combinators - and arms are tested strictly in order, so ordering *is* the
logic.

## ex1

Really testing: an accumulator loop with a compound condition, and one
notorious overflow. The classic mistake in `SumOfMultiples` is two separate
`if` statements, which counts 15 twice for divisors 3 and 5; one condition with
`||` cannot make that mistake. The classic mistake in `CountDigits` is
`while (n > 0)` with the counter starting at 0, which answers 0 for the input
0. The model answer starts the count at 1 and loops while there are ten or more
left. The sting is `Math.Abs(int.MinValue)`: the negative range of a
two's-complement int is one wider than the positive range, so there is no
positive `int` for it and `Math.Abs` throws. Widening to `long` first is the
fix, and knowing why is a good interview answer.

## ex2

Really testing: switch expressions with or-patterns and relational patterns,
and the fact that arms are ordered. The classic mistake in `Ticket` is putting
the negative-age guard anywhere but first, where `< 5` swallows it and a
-3-year-old travels free. The model answer leans on ordering so each arm names
only its upper bound - `< 5`, `< 18`, `< 65` - which halves the number of
boundary numbers in the code and therefore halves the places an off-by-one can
hide. The other lesson is the discard arm: a non-exhaustive switch expression
throws `SwitchExpressionException` at run time, which tells the caller nothing,
so the `_` arm is where you throw something useful.

## ex3

Really testing: early return, and the two ends of an array. The classic mistake
is the backwards loop written as `for (int i = values.Length; i > 0; i--)`,
which either indexes past the end or never looks at element 0 - and both
versions pass a four-element test and fail an empty one. The model answer
returns from inside the loop rather than tracking a `found` flag; the flag
version needs an extra variable and an extra branch to say the same thing. The
`-1` sentinel is worth a thought too: it is the BCL's convention
(`IndexOf`, `LastIndexOf`), which is why it is the right choice here even
though a nullable `int?` would be more honest in new code.

## ex4

Really testing: the "consume a run" loop shape, where the inner loop advances
the *outer* loop's index. The classic mistake is putting the array access
before the bounds check in the inner condition - `text[index] == current &&
index < text.Length` - which throws on the last run because `&&` evaluates left
to right. The second classic mistake belongs to the one-loop version: it
accumulates a run and emits it when the character changes, and then forgets
that the final run never triggers a change, so the last group vanishes.
`LongestRunLength` is the same idea with the emit step removed, and its empty
case (0, not 1) is the reminder that a counter initialised before the loop is a
claim about zero iterations.

## ex5

Really testing: pattern precedence and the fact that patterns do not convert.
The classic mistake is putting `int n` above `0` or above the negative arm, at
which point the more specific arms are unreachable - and the compiler will tell
you so, which is a good habit to lean on. The `null` arm has to be first
because a type pattern never matches null: `null is object` is false, which
surprises people. The `3.5` case is the deep one: a boxed `double` does not
match `int` even though 3.5 is "obviously" a number, because pattern matching
tests the runtime type and applies no numeric conversion. Same rule as
`(object)1 is long` being false.

## ex6

Really testing: nested loops where the inner bound depends on the outer
variable. The classic mistake in `CountPairs` is starting the inner loop at 0
or at `i`, which counts each pair twice or pairs an element with itself
respectively; `j = i + 1` is the standard fix and is worth having in your
fingers, because half the "count the pairs" interview questions are this loop.
The classic mistake in `Triangle` is a trailing newline, which every "why does
my output have a blank last line" bug report is made of. Appending the
separator before every row except the first has no cleanup step, exactly as in
d02 ex4.

## ex7

Really testing: whether you can turn a written specification into a loop
without rewriting the specification. The classic mistake is doubling from the
left - "every second digit" counted from the start gives the wrong parity for
odd-length inputs, which is why the model answer walks backwards. The second
classic mistake is counting characters rather than digits when deciding what to
double, so a hyphen shifts the parity and a number that a human typed with
separators fails. Keeping a separate `seen` counter, incremented only for
digits, makes the separators genuinely invisible. The length rule is worth
noticing as a design point: `"0"` passes the arithmetic and is still not a
card number, so validity is the *conjunction* of two independent checks.

## ex8

Really testing: writing a scanner - the same shape as every tokeniser,
`TryParse` and JSON reader in existence. One index that only moves forward, one
"while the character here is what I want" loop per grammar element, and one
final check that the whole input was consumed. The classic mistake is omitting
that final check, which turns "is this a number?" into "does this *start* with
a number?" and quietly accepts `"1.2.3"`, `"1a"` and `"12,34"`. The second
classic mistake is `char.IsDigit`, which is true for digits in every writing
system Unicode knows about - including many that no `decimal.Parse` in your
program will accept. `char.IsAsciiDigit` says what this grammar actually means.

## Further reading

- [Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) - `for`, `foreach`, `while`, `do`.
- [Selection statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/selection-statements) - `if` and the switch statement.
- [Pattern matching](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/patterns) - every pattern kind, in precedence order.
- [The switch expression](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/switch-expression) - exhaustiveness and `SwitchExpressionException`.
- [`char` methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.char) - `IsAsciiDigit`, `IsDigit`, `IsLetterOrDigit` and how they differ.
- [Jump statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/jump-statements) - `break`, `continue`, `return`, `goto`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are one switch *expression* - `input switch { ... }` - not a
switch statement. Two pattern forms carry the whole exercise:

- `12 or 1 or 2` - an or-pattern over constants;
- `>= 3 and <= 5`, or just `< 5` - relational patterns.

Arms are tried in order, so ordering them from most specific to least removes
most of the boundary arithmetic.

## Hint 2

For `Ticket`, put the guard first and then let the ordering do the work:

```csharp
age switch
{
    < 0 => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(age), "..."),
    < 5 => "free",
    < 18 => "child",
    ...
}
```

Each arm only has to name its upper bound, because everything below it was
already matched. Writing `>= 5 and < 18` is correct and says the same thing
twice.

A switch expression must be exhaustive: leave out the `_` arm and the compiler
warns, and at run time a value that matches nothing throws
`SwitchExpressionException`. Throwing your own exception from the `_` arm is
how you turn that into a message the caller can act on.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are one switch *expression* - `input switch { ... }` - not a
switch statement. Two pattern forms carry the whole exercise:

- `12 or 1 or 2` - an or-pattern over constants;
- `>= 3 and <= 5`, or just `< 5` - relational patterns.

Arms are tried in order, so ordering them from most specific to least removes
most of the boundary arithmetic.

## Hint 2

For `Ticket`, put the guard first and then let the ordering do the work:

```csharp
age switch
{
    < 0 => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(age), "..."),
    < 5 => "free",
    < 18 => "child",
    ...
}
```

Each arm only has to name its upper bound, because everything below it was
already matched. Writing `>= 5 and < 18` is correct and says the same thing
twice.

A switch expression must be exhaustive: leave out the `_` arm and the compiler
warns, and at run time a value that matches nothing throws
`SwitchExpressionException`. Throwing your own exception from the `_` arm is
how you turn that into a message the caller can act on.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are the same loop pointed in opposite directions, and both return
from inside the loop the moment they find a match. The `return` *is* the early
exit - no `break` and no found-flag needed.

The value to return when nothing matches is decided once, after the loop.

## Hint 2

Forwards is the familiar shape. Backwards is where the off-by-one lives:

```csharp
for (int i = values.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
```

`values.Length` is not a valid index, and `i > 0` would never look at element 0.
Both mistakes pass the four-element test in the gate and fail the empty one -
which is why the empty case is there.

Left to you: whether `LastIndexOf` walks backwards and returns early, or walks
forwards remembering the most recent hit. Both are correct; one reads the
target array fewer times on average, and being able to say which is the point.

## Exercise 4 - run-length encoding

`Encode(text)` turns each run of identical characters into the character
followed by the run length, always - `"aaabbc"` becomes `"a3b2c1"`, and
`"aabaa"` becomes `"a2b1a2"`. `LongestRunLength(text)` returns the length of
the longest run, or 0 for empty text.

## Hint 1

Run-length encoding is the classic "inner loop consumes the run" problem. An
outer `while` sits at the start of a run; an inner `while` advances past every
character equal to the one it started on. When the inner loop stops, you know
both the character and the length.

The alternative shape - one loop with a "previous character" variable - works
too, but then you have to remember to emit the final run after the loop, which
is where that version usually breaks.

## Hint 2

```csharp
while (index < text.Length)
{
    char current = text[index];
    int length = 0;
    while (index < text.Length && text[index] == current) { index++; length++; }
    encoded.Append(current).Append(length);
}
```

The order of the `&&` operands is load-bearing: the bounds check must come
first, because `&&` short-circuits and `text[index]` on an exhausted string
throws.

`LongestRunLength` does not need the inner loop at all - one pass comparing
each character with the one before it, resetting the counter when they differ,
is enough. Watch the empty case: the answer is 0, and any code that starts the
counter at 1 before the loop gets it wrong.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One switch expression, eight arms, tried top to bottom. The whole exercise is
ordering them so the specific cases get their turn before the general ones.

Four pattern kinds appear: the constant pattern (`null`, `0`), the type pattern
(`int`, `string`), the property pattern (`string { Length: 0 }`) and a
relational pattern combined with a type (`int and < 0`).

## Hint 2

The order that works:

```
null                    // first: no type pattern ever matches null
0                       // constant beats type
int and < 0             // still more specific than plain int
int n                   // captures the value for the message
string { Length: 0 }    // property pattern
string s
int[] a
_
```

`int and < 0` combines a type pattern with a relational one without declaring a
variable you never use.

The `3.5` case is worth pausing on: patterns do **not** perform numeric
conversions, so a boxed `double` never matches `int` even when the value is a
whole number. That is the same rule that makes `(object)1 is long` false, and
it surprises people who expect pattern matching to behave like `==`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One switch expression, eight arms, tried top to bottom. The whole exercise is
ordering them so the specific cases get their turn before the general ones.

Four pattern kinds appear: the constant pattern (`null`, `0`), the type pattern
(`int`, `string`), the property pattern (`string { Length: 0 }`) and a
relational pattern combined with a type (`int and < 0`).

## Hint 2

The order that works:

```
null                    // first: no type pattern ever matches null
0                       // constant beats type
int and < 0             // still more specific than plain int
int n                   // captures the value for the message
string { Length: 0 }    // property pattern
string s
int[] a
_
```

`int and < 0` combines a type pattern with a relational one without declaring a
variable you never use.

The `3.5` case is worth pausing on: patterns do **not** perform numeric
conversions, so a boxed `double` never matches `int` even when the value is a
whole number. That is the same rule that makes `(object)1 is long` false, and
it surprises people who expect pattern matching to behave like `==`.

## Exercise 7 - the Luhn check

`IsValidLuhn(input)` validates a card-style number. Ignore spaces and hyphens;
any other non-digit is invalid, and so is having fewer than two digits. Walking
from the rightmost digit leftwards, double every second digit and subtract 9
from any result above 9; the number is valid when the total divides by 10.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Walk the string from the END to the start. That removes the hardest part of
Luhn - "every second digit from the right" is a nuisance to work out from the
left when the length is unknown and separators are scattered through it.

Keep two counters: the running total, and how many *digits* you have seen
(which is not the same as how many characters you have visited).

## Hint 2

```csharp
for (int i = input.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
{
    char c = input[i];
    if (c == ' ' || c == '-') continue;
    if (!char.IsAsciiDigit(c)) return false;
    int digit = c - '0';
    if (seen % 2 == 1) { digit *= 2; if (digit > 9) digit -= 9; }
    total += digit;
    seen++;
}
```

`seen % 2 == 1` is the "every second digit" test, and it works because `seen`
counts digits rather than characters - so separators cannot shift the parity.

`c - '0'` converts a digit character to its value: `char` arithmetic promotes
to `int`, and the digits are contiguous in the character set.

Left to you: `digit -= 9` versus summing the two decimal digits of the doubled
value. They are the same for every input in range - be able to explain why.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - a number scanner, by hand

`IsNumber(text)` decides whether the whole text matches
`sign? digit* ('.' digit+)?` with at least one digit somewhere - without
calling any `Parse` or `TryParse`. `".5"` and `"007"` are numbers; `"5."`,
`"1.2.3"`, `"1a"` and `" 1"` are not.

Edit `src/Lessons/D03_ControlFlow/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d03_control_flow ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the grammar out before you write any code:

```
number := sign? digit* ( '.' digit+ )?
```

and then read it as instructions: consume an optional sign, consume digits,
optionally consume a point and *at least one* digit. Two facts have to be true
at the end - you reached the end of the string, and you saw at least one digit
somewhere.

## Hint 2

Keep one `index` and move it forward; never move it backwards. Each step is
"while the character here is what I want, advance".

```csharp
if (index < text.Length && (text[index] == '+' || text[index] == '-')) index++;
while (index < text.Length && char.IsAsciiDigit(text[index])) { index++; wholeDigits++; }
```

The final `return` is the part people forget:

```csharp
return index == text.Length && wholeDigits + fractionDigits > 0;
```

`index == text.Length` is what rejects `"1.2.3"`, `"1a"` and `" 1"` - the
scanner stops happily at the leftover character, and only the end-of-input
check notices. Without it your scanner recognises *prefixes*, which is a
different and much less useful function.

`char.IsAsciiDigit` is deliberate: `char.IsDigit` is true for digits in every
writing system, including ones no `Parse` in your program will accept.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the grammar out before you write any code:

```
number := sign? digit* ( '.' digit+ )?
```

and then read it as instructions: consume an optional sign, consume digits,
optionally consume a point and *at least one* digit. Two facts have to be true
at the end - you reached the end of the string, and you saw at least one digit
somewhere.

## Hint 2

Keep one `index` and move it forward; never move it backwards. Each step is
"while the character here is what I want, advance".

```csharp
if (index < text.Length && (text[index] == '+' || text[index] == '-')) index++;
while (index < text.Length && char.IsAsciiDigit(text[index])) { index++; wholeDigits++; }
```

The final `return` is the part people forget:

```csharp
return index == text.Length && wholeDigits + fractionDigits > 0;
```

`index == text.Length` is what rejects `"1.2.3"`, `"1a"` and `" 1"` - the
scanner stops happily at the leftover character, and only the end-of-input
check notices. Without it your scanner recognises *prefixes*, which is a
different and much less useful function.

`char.IsAsciiDigit` is deliberate: `char.IsDigit` is true for digits in every
writing system, including ones no `Parse` in your program will accept.

# d04 - Methods and parameters drills

Eight problems on the signature rather than the body: optional and named
arguments, `params`, `out`, `ref`, overload resolution, recursion, and two
larger methods that use most of them at once. They drill lesson 02 - if `out`
and `params` are not automatic yet, reread `02_control_flow_methods`.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - optional arguments

`Line(message, level = "INFO", source = null)` returns `"[LEVEL] message"`, or
`"[LEVEL] (source) message"` when a source is given. `Bullet(text, marker =
"-", indent = 0)` returns the indent spaces, the marker, a space, then the
text. The gate calls both with named arguments, in and out of order.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - params arrays

`Combine(params string?[] parts)` joins with `"/"`, ignoring null and blank
parts and stripping slashes from both ends of each part so no double slash can
appear. `First(params string?[] candidates)` returns the first non-blank
candidate, trimmed, or `""`. Both must survive being called with no arguments
at all.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - two out parameters

`TryRange(text, out low, out high)` reads `"3-9"`. Whitespace around either
number is ignored; both must be non-negative whole numbers and `low` must not
exceed `high`. Every failure returns `false` with both outs at 0.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - ref versus by value

`Scale(ref x, ref y, factor)` multiplies both of the caller's variables.
`SwapIfOutOfOrder(ref a, ref b)` swaps them when `a > b` and reports whether it
did. `BumpByValue(count)` returns `count + 1` and leaves the caller's variable
alone - the gate checks that it really is unchanged.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - overload resolution

Five overloads of `Describe`, each returning its own name: `int`, `long`,
`double`, `object`, and `params int[]`. The bodies are one line each; the
exercise is being able to predict, before you run it, which one
`Describe((short)3)`, `Describe(1.5f)`, `Describe(1)` and `Describe(1, 2)`
select.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - methods calling methods

`Gcd(a, b)` ignoring signs, with `Gcd(0, 0)` being 0. `Lcm(a, b)` built from
`Gcd`, always non-negative, 0 when either input is 0. `PowerOf(base, exponent)`
by recursion, with a negative exponent throwing
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - split the bill

`Split(total, ways)` returns one `decimal` per person, every share a whole
number of cents, adding up to the total exactly. Leftover cents go one each to
the earliest shares, so 10.00 between 3 is `3.34, 3.33, 3.33`. The total is
rounded to cents first, halves away from zero. A `ways` of 0 or less, or a
negative total, throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a command-line parser

`Parse(params string[] args)` returns the `--` options as a dictionary:
`--key=value` splits at the first `=`, `--key value` consumes the following
token unless it is itself an option, and a bare `--flag` stores `"true"`. Keys
are lower-cased without the dashes; a repeated key keeps the last value;
everything else is ignored. `ValueOr(options, key, fallback = "")` reads one
back.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex8
```

# Reading - csharp/d04_methods_params

## Notes

A method signature is a contract, and C# gives you an unusual number of ways to
write one: optional parameters, named arguments, `params`, `out`, `ref`, `in`,
and overloads. The pattern uniting these eight problems is that **each of those
features moves a decision to a different place**, and knowing which place is
the skill.

An optional parameter moves the default into the callee, where every caller
inherits it - and freezes it into every calling assembly at compile time, which
is why changing a default is a subtly breaking change. `params` moves the array
construction to the compiler. `out` moves "did it work?" out of the return
value so the return value can be a plain bool. `ref` moves the variable itself
across the boundary. Overloads move the choice to the compiler, using rules
that are precise, documented, and almost never what people guess.

The second thread is the Try-pattern, which appears twice: a bool return plus
`out` results, and the discipline that a false return leaves the outputs at a
known value rather than half-written.

## ex1

Really testing: that optional parameters and named arguments are two halves of
one feature. Without named arguments, a caller who wants to set the third
parameter must also pass the second, which is why long optional lists are
unusable in languages that lack them. The classic mistake is treating the
default as data - `string level = DateTime.Now.ToString()` will not compile,
because defaults must be compile-time constants. The subtler trap, worth
knowing before it bites you: the default is baked into the *caller's* compiled
code, so changing `"INFO"` to `"TRACE"` in a shipped library changes nothing
for callers until they recompile.

## ex2

Really testing: that `params` is a caller-side convenience and nothing more.
Inside the method it is an array, it is never null when the method is called
normally, and `foreach` over an empty one is a no-op - which is why neither
method here needs a guard. The classic mistake is a null check that can only
fire when someone explicitly passes `null` as the array. The `Trim().Trim('/')`
detail is the interesting part of `Combine`: the two overloads do different
jobs, and applying them in the wrong order leaves a slash behind on `" /a/ "`.

## ex3

Really testing: the Try-pattern's contract. The bool is the only trustworthy
output when the call fails, and the way to guarantee that is to assign the
outs on the first line rather than on each failure path. The classic mistake is
returning `false` after writing `low` but before writing `high`, leaving the
caller with a plausible half-parsed range - and the compiler will not stop you,
because `out` only requires *definite assignment*, not consistency. The
`"-3-9"` case is a small gift: splitting on `-` produces three fields, so the
length check rejects negative bounds before any parsing is attempted.

## ex4

Really testing: the difference between passing a value and passing a variable.
`ref` gives the method an alias for the caller's storage; a plain parameter
gives it a copy. The classic misconception is that this is about value types
versus reference types - it is not. Passing a `List<T>` by value still lets the
method call `.Add` (the object is shared) but not reassign the caller's
variable; passing it by `ref` allows both. The `BumpByValue` method mutates its
parameter deliberately so you can watch the caller's variable stay at 5. And
`ref`/`out` must be written at the call site, which is C# choosing readability
over convenience: your variable cannot be reassigned by a method invisibly.

## ex5

Really testing: whether you can predict overload resolution rather than
discover it. The rules in play, in order: applicable candidates first; a method
applicable in normal form beats one applicable only in expanded (`params`)
form; then the most specific parameter type wins, where "more specific" means
"converts implicitly to the other". So `short` picks `int` over `long`,
`double` and `object`; `float` picks `double` because widening beats boxing;
`bool` picks `object` because nothing else applies. The classic mistake is
assuming a `params` overload is a catch-all - it is the *last* resort, which is
why adding one to an existing API is usually safe.

## ex6

Really testing: composing small methods, and two arithmetic traps. Euclid's
loop handles `Gcd(0, n)` and `Gcd(0, 0)` with no special case, which is worth
noticing - a well-chosen loop condition often deletes the edge cases rather
than handling them. In `Lcm` the trap is `a * b / gcd`: the multiplication
overflows for inputs whose correct answer fits comfortably, so divide first.
In `PowerOf` the trap is guarding after the recursive call rather than before,
which turns a bad argument into a `StackOverflowException` - the one .NET
failure you cannot catch, because there is no stack left to run a handler on.

## ex7

Really testing: the standard fix for "the parts do not add up to the whole".
Work in the smallest indivisible unit - cents - as integers, and distribute the
remainder explicitly. The classic mistake is `Math.Round(total / ways, 2)` per
share, which loses or gains a cent and produces the support ticket that starts
"our invoices are off by one penny". Note that the remainder is always smaller
than the number of shares, so "one extra cent to the first `extra` shares"
always terminates and always uses up exactly the remainder. The guards are the
other half: a `ways` of 0 must be an `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` naming the
parameter, not a `DivideByZeroException` naming nothing.

## ex8

Really testing: a scanner with lookahead, which is the same shape as d03 ex8
plus one extra move - consuming a token. The classic mistake is `foreach`,
which cannot skip ahead, so `--level 3` leaves `3` to be re-examined as a
positional argument. The second classic mistake is `Split('=')` instead of
`IndexOf('=')`, which mangles any value containing an `=`. The lower-cased key
with a case-preserved value is a deliberate asymmetry: the key is a protocol
token and the value is user data, and the rule "normalise your protocol, never
your payload" generalises well past command lines.

## Further reading

- [Named and optional arguments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/named-and-optional-arguments) - the rules, and the versioning caveat.
- [`params` modifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/params) - including the newer `params` collections.
- [Method parameters: `ref`, `out`, `in`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters) - all the passing modes in one page.
- [Overload resolution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#1264-overload-resolution) - the specification section the ex5 answers come from.
- [The Try-pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/exceptions-and-performance) - when to return a bool instead of throwing.
- [`Math.Round`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.math.round) - the overloads ex7 depends on.

## Exercise 1 - optional arguments

`Line(message, level = "INFO", source = null)` returns `"[LEVEL] message"`, or
`"[LEVEL] (source) message"` when a source is given. `Bullet(text, marker =
"-", indent = 0)` returns the indent spaces, the marker, a space, then the
text. The gate calls both with named arguments, in and out of order.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An optional parameter is one with a default in the signature - and the default
must be a compile-time constant, which is why `string? source = null` works and
`= new object()` would not.

Both methods are a single interpolated string. The only decision in `Line` is
what to do when `source` is null.

## Hint 2

```csharp
return source is null ? $"[{level}] {message}" : $"[{level}] ({source}) {message}";
```

`new string(' ', indent)` builds the indent without a loop, and it gives `""`
for an indent of 0 rather than needing a special case.

The gate calls these methods with named arguments - `Log.Line("started",
source: "db")` - which is a caller-side feature you do not have to write
anything for. It works because the parameter is named `source`, which is why
renaming a public parameter is a breaking change even though nothing about the
type has changed.

## Exercise 2 - params arrays

`Combine(params string?[] parts)` joins with `"/"`, ignoring null and blank
parts and stripping slashes from both ends of each part so no double slash can
appear. `First(params string?[] candidates)` returns the first non-blank
candidate, trimmed, or `""`. Both must survive being called with no arguments
at all.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`params` is a caller-side convenience: inside the method the parameter is an
ordinary array, and it is **never null** when the method is called normally -
callers who pass nothing get an empty array. So `foreach` over it needs no
guard.

Both methods are one loop with one filter. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the
filter again.

## Hint 2

`Trim('/')` removes the character from both ends, and it is separate from
`Trim()`, which removes whitespace - you want both, in that order:

```csharp
string trimmed = part.Trim().Trim('/');
```

A part that was only slashes is now empty, so test the length again before
keeping it.

Collect the survivors into a `List<string>` and finish with
`string.Join("/", kept)`. Building the string as you go means handling "is this

## Hint 1

`params` is a caller-side convenience: inside the method the parameter is an
ordinary array, and it is **never null** when the method is called normally -
callers who pass nothing get an empty array. So `foreach` over it needs no
guard.

Both methods are one loop with one filter. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the
filter again.

## Hint 2

`Trim('/')` removes the character from both ends, and it is separate from
`Trim()`, which removes whitespace - you want both, in that order:

```csharp
string trimmed = part.Trim().Trim('/');
```

A part that was only slashes is now empty, so test the length again before
keeping it.

Collect the survivors into a `List<string>` and finish with
`string.Join("/", kept)`. Building the string as you go means handling "is this
the first one?" for the separator; the join has already solved that.

`FirstOrDefault`. The loop is what the exercise is about, but be ready to write
the one-liner too.

## Exercise 3 - two out parameters

`TryRange(text, out low, out high)` reads `"3-9"`. Whitespace around either
number is ignored; both must be non-negative whole numbers and `low` must not
exceed `high`. Every failure returns `false` with both outs at 0.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The Try-pattern has a contract worth stating: the bool is the *only* thing the
caller may trust when it is false. So assign both `out` parameters to 0 on the
very first line, and only write real values once every check has passed.

The checks, in order: is there text at all; does it split into exactly two
fields; do both fields parse; is `low <= high`.

## Hint 2

An `out` parameter must be definitely assigned on every path out of the method,
including the `return false` paths - which is exactly why assigning them both
up front is the tidy way rather than a defensive habit.

```csharp
low = 0; high = 0;
string[] parts = text.Split('-');
if (parts.Length != 2) return false;
```

`int.TryParse(parts[0].Trim(), NumberStyles.None, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
out int start)` accepts digits only - no sign, no whitespace, no separators -
which is what "non-negative whole number" means here.

Note what the split already does for you: `"-3-9"` splits into three fields, so
the length check rejects negative bounds before any parsing happens.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The Try-pattern has a contract worth stating: the bool is the *only* thing the
caller may trust when it is false. So assign both `out` parameters to 0 on the
very first line, and only write real values once every check has passed.

The checks, in order: is there text at all; does it split into exactly two
fields; do both fields parse; is `low <= high`.

## Hint 2

An `out` parameter must be definitely assigned on every path out of the method,
including the `return false` paths - which is exactly why assigning them both
up front is the tidy way rather than a defensive habit.

```csharp
low = 0; high = 0;
string[] parts = text.Split('-');
if (parts.Length != 2) return false;
```

`int.TryParse(parts[0].Trim(), NumberStyles.None, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture,
out int start)` accepts digits only - no sign, no whitespace, no separators -
which is what "non-negative whole number" means here.

Note what the split already does for you: `"-3-9"` splits into three fields, so
the length check rejects negative bounds before any parsing happens.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every method body here is a single string literal. There is nothing to work out
in the implementation at all - the exercise is reading the gate afterwards and
being able to predict every answer.

So: write the five one-liners, run the gate, and then for each assertion say
out loud *why* the compiler chose that overload before you accept the green.

## Hint 2

The rules the gate is exercising, in the order the compiler applies them:

1. Collect the applicable candidates - the ones whose parameters the arguments
   convert to implicitly.
2. Prefer a method applicable in **normal** form over one applicable only in
   **expanded** (params) form. That is why `Describe(1)` is not "params".
3. Among the rest, pick the one whose parameter type is most specific: a
   conversion exists from `int` to `long` and to `double`, so `int` is better
   than both, and any of them beats `object`.

`(short)3` is applicable to `int`, `long`, `double` and `object`, and `int`
wins by rule 3. `1.5f` is applicable to `double` and `object`, and widening
beats boxing. `true` converts to nothing but `object`.

If you can also say why `Describe(null)` would not compile against this set,
you have understood it properly.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Every method body here is a single string literal. There is nothing to work out
in the implementation at all - the exercise is reading the gate afterwards and
being able to predict every answer.

So: write the five one-liners, run the gate, and then for each assertion say
out loud *why* the compiler chose that overload before you accept the green.

## Hint 2

The rules the gate is exercising, in the order the compiler applies them:

1. Collect the applicable candidates - the ones whose parameters the arguments
   convert to implicitly.
2. Prefer a method applicable in **normal** form over one applicable only in
   **expanded** (params) form. That is why `Describe(1)` is not "params".
3. Among the rest, pick the one whose parameter type is most specific: a
   conversion exists from `int` to `long` and to `double`, so `int` is better
   than both, and any of them beats `object`.

`(short)3` is applicable to `int`, `long`, `double` and `object`, and `int`
wins by rule 3. `1.5f` is applicable to `double` and `object`, and widening
beats boxing. `true` converts to nothing but `object`.

If you can also say why `Describe(null)` would not compile against this set,
you have understood it properly.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Euclid's algorithm: replace `(a, b)` with `(b, a % b)` until `b` is 0; the
answer is what is left in `a`. Written that way, `Gcd(0, 5)` and `Gcd(0, 0)`
both come out right with no special case - work through them on paper to see
why.

`Lcm` is `a / Gcd(a, b) * b`. The order matters, and so does the type.

`PowerOf` is the standard recursion: the base case is exponent 0.

## Hint 2

```csharp
long x = Math.Abs((long)a), y = Math.Abs((long)b);
while (y != 0) { (x, y) = (y, x % y); }
```

The widening to `long` is for the same reason as d03 ex1: `Math.Abs` on
`int.MinValue` throws.

For `Lcm`, divide before multiplying. `a * b / Gcd(a, b)` overflows for values
that the correct answer would fit in comfortably - dividing first keeps every
intermediate no bigger than the result.

For `PowerOf`, the guard has to come before the recursive call, or a negative
exponent counts downwards forever and you get a `StackOverflowException` -
which, unlike almost every other .NET exception, cannot be caught and kills the
process.

Left to you: recursion or a loop for `PowerOf`, and whether to be clever with
exponentiation by squaring. State the complexity of whichever you pick.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Euclid's algorithm: replace `(a, b)` with `(b, a % b)` until `b` is 0; the
answer is what is left in `a`. Written that way, `Gcd(0, 5)` and `Gcd(0, 0)`
both come out right with no special case - work through them on paper to see
why.

`Lcm` is `a / Gcd(a, b) * b`. The order matters, and so does the type.

`PowerOf` is the standard recursion: the base case is exponent 0.

## Hint 2

```csharp
long x = Math.Abs((long)a), y = Math.Abs((long)b);
while (y != 0) { (x, y) = (y, x % y); }
```

The widening to `long` is for the same reason as d03 ex1: `Math.Abs` on
`int.MinValue` throws.

For `Lcm`, divide before multiplying. `a * b / Gcd(a, b)` overflows for values
that the correct answer would fit in comfortably - dividing first keeps every
intermediate no bigger than the result.

For `PowerOf`, the guard has to come before the recursive call, or a negative
exponent counts downwards forever and you get a `StackOverflowException` -
which, unlike almost every other .NET exception, cannot be caught and kills the
process.

Left to you: recursion or a loop for `PowerOf`, and whether to be clever with
exponentiation by squaring. State the complexity of whichever you pick.

## Exercise 8 - a command-line parser

`Parse(params string[] args)` returns the `--` options as a dictionary:
`--key=value` splits at the first `=`, `--key value` consumes the following
token unless it is itself an option, and a bare `--flag` stores `"true"`. Keys
are lower-cased without the dashes; a repeated key keeps the last value;
everything else is ignored. `ValueOr(options, key, fallback = "")` reads one
back.

Edit `src/Lessons/D04_MethodsParams/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d04_methods_params ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Use an indexed `for` loop, not a `foreach` - because the `"--key value"` form
has to *consume the next token*, and only an index lets you skip it.

At each token there are exactly three shapes: not an option (skip), an option
containing `=` (split it), an option without one (look ahead).

## Hint 2

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < args.Length; i++)
{
    string token = args[i];
    if (!token.StartsWith("--", StringComparison.Ordinal)) continue;
    ...
    if (i + 1 < args.Length && !args[i + 1].StartsWith("--", StringComparison.Ordinal))
    {
        options[key] = args[i + 1];
        i++;                       // consumed, so do not read it again
    }
    else options[key] = "true";
}
```

The `i++` inside the loop body is what stops `"3"` in `--level 3` being treated
as a positional argument on the next pass. Incrementing the loop variable from
inside the body is normally a smell; in a hand-written scanner it is the
standard technique, and worth being able to defend.

`IndexOf('=')` rather than `Split('=')`: a value may legitimately contain an
`=` (think `--filter=a=b`), and splitting at the first one is the rule every
real parser uses.

Left to you: whether an unknown `--flag` at the very end should be `"true"` or
an error. The specification here says `"true"`; know that real tools differ.

lessons.briefing:
# d05 - Classes and construction drills

Eight problems on getting an object born correctly: validating constructors,
constructor chaining, static factories, owning a collection, defensive copying,
`Deconstruct`, an invariant several methods share, and a fluent builder. They
drill lesson 03 - reread `03_classes_objects` if encapsulation is still fuzzy.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/`. Nothing here
depends on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - a constructor that refuses bad state

`Ticket(code, seats)` stores the code trimmed and upper-cased. A blank code is
an `ArgumentException`; fewer than one seat is an
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. `Describe()` returns `"CODE x2"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - one constructor calling another

`Box(width, height, depth)` validates that every dimension is at least 1.
`Box(side)` builds a cube by *delegating* to it with `: this(...)` - the gate
checks `new Box(0)` throws, which only works if you really chained. `Volume`
and `IsCube` are computed properties.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - static factories

`Temperature` has a private constructor and two factories: `FromCelsius` and
`FromFahrenheit`. Both reject anything below absolute zero (-273.15 C, which is
itself allowed). `Fahrenheit` is a computed property.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - a class that owns a collection

`Playlist` keeps a private `List<string>`, exposes it as `IReadOnlyList<string>
Tracks`, and offers `Add`, `Remove` (false when the track is not there) and
`MoveUp` (false when the track is missing or already first). The constructor
copies the tracks it is given.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - readonly does not mean immutable

`Poll(question, options)` copies the options array in, and `Options()` hands a
copy back out. The gate mutates the caller's array *and* the returned array and
checks the poll is unchanged both times. A blank question or fewer than two
options is an `ArgumentException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - Deconstruct

`Coordinate(latitude, longitude)` validates inclusive bounds of -90..90 and
-180..180. Two `Deconstruct` overloads: two components, and the same two plus
`"N"` or `"S"`. The gate uses tuple assignment, so the method names and shapes
have to be exactly right.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - one invariant, four methods

`SeatMap(rows, seatsPerRow)` with 1-based `IsReserved`, `Reserve` and `Release`
- each returning false when there is nothing to do - plus `Capacity` and
`AvailableCount`. The count must stay exactly right after every call,
*including* the calls that change nothing. Out-of-range rows or seats throw
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a fluent builder

`UrlBuilder` with `Host`, `Path`, `Query` - each returning the same builder -
and `Build()`. `Build` produces `"https://host/seg/seg?k=v&k=v"`, keeps query
parameters in insertion order, replaces a repeated key in place, and throws
`InvalidOperationException` when no host was set. Blank arguments throw
`ArgumentException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d05_classes_construction

## Notes

The skill drilled here is **making invalid states unrepresentable**, and every
problem is one tactic for it. A constructor that throws means no caller ever
holds a half-built object. Chaining means the validation exists once. A private
constructor with named factories means the caller cannot express an ambiguous
request. A private collection with a read-only view means nobody edits your
state behind your back. A copy on the way in and on the way out means nobody
edits it by accident either.

The pattern that unites them: **decide where each rule lives, and put it there
exactly once.** Duplicated validation drifts apart; validation spread across
callers is validation you cannot audit; validation that runs after the fields
are assigned leaves a corpse in memory for a debugger to find.

The last two exercises are about the object's life *after* construction - an
invariant that four methods have to maintain between them, and a builder that
accumulates state until someone asks for the result. Both are places where
"which method is allowed to break this rule?" has to have the answer "none".

## ex1

Really testing: guard-then-assign, and picking the right exception type. The
classic mistake is validating after assigning, which throws but leaves the
object partially initialised - harmless for a local, dangerous when the
constructor also registered the object somewhere. The type distinction is worth
memorising: `ArgumentException` for structurally wrong input, and its derived
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a value outside its range - and note the
constructor argument order flips between them, which is a genuine trap. The
normalisation is a design point rather than a rule: doing `Trim().ToUpperInvariant()`
once, in the constructor, means every later reader gets the canonical form.

## ex2

Really testing: `: this(...)`. The classic mistake is copying the three
assignments into the cube constructor, which compiles, works for good input,
and silently skips the validation - which is why the gate asserts `new Box(0)`
throws. Constructor chaining runs the target constructor *first*, then the
delegating constructor's own body, so the fields are already valid by the time
your extra code runs. The computed properties are the second half: `Volume` is
derived from state that cannot change, so storing it would create a second
source of truth for no benefit.

## ex3

Really testing: the named-constructor pattern. Constructors can only be
distinguished by their parameter *types*, so two ways of building a
`Temperature` from one `double` is impossible with constructors alone - and
`new Temperature(20)` would be ambiguous to a reader even if it compiled. Static
factories have names, can return a cached instance or a subclass, and can fail
by returning null or a `TryCreate` bool. The classic mistake here is repeating
the absolute-zero check in both factories; having `FromFahrenheit` convert and
then call `FromCelsius` keeps the rule in one place, and the gate's -500 F case
passes for free.

## ex4

Really testing: encapsulating a collection. Two leaks are possible - storing
the caller's collection rather than copying it, and handing the internal list
straight out - and this exercise closes the first. `IReadOnlyList<T>` is the
usual return type, and it is worth knowing exactly what it promises: the
*interface* has no mutators, but the object behind it is still your `List<T>`,
so a determined caller can cast back. `AsReadOnly()` returns a genuine wrapper
that cannot be cast back, at the cost of an allocation. The `index <= 0` test
in `MoveUp` folding "missing" and "already first" into one branch is a nice
trick and a comment-worthy one.

## ex5

Really testing: that `readonly` constrains the field, not the object. This is
the same distinction as lesson 01's value-versus-reference semantics, arriving
as a security problem: a `readonly string[]` can be rewritten element by element
by anyone who has a reference to it. Both directions matter, and the classic
mistake is closing only one - copying on the way in and then returning the
field, or vice versa. For `string` elements a shallow copy suffices because
strings are immutable; if the elements were mutable, you would have the same
question one level down. The alternative design - return `IReadOnlyList<T>` and
skip the copies - is cheaper and equally defensible, and knowing when to choose
each is the actual skill.

## ex6

Really testing: that `Deconstruct` is a convention, not an interface. Any void
method called `Deconstruct` whose parameters are all `out` enables tuple
assignment on the type, overload-resolved by the number of variables the caller
writes. The classic mistake is returning a tuple instead - `(double, double)
Deconstruct()` compiles but does nothing for `var (a, b) = x`. The second
detail worth noticing is that the bounds are inclusive: `new Coordinate(90,
180)` must succeed, and off-by-one at a boundary is the single most common
validation bug there is.

## ex7

Really testing: keeping a derived value in step with the data it summarises.
State the invariant first - `AvailableCount` equals the number of free seats -
and then every method has one obligation. The classic mistake is decrementing
the counter before checking whether the seat was already taken, so a
double-booking silently corrupts the count; the gate's repeated `Reserve` and
repeated `Release` exist to catch exactly that. The second classic mistake is
the index arithmetic: `(row - 1) * SeatsPerRow + (seat - 1)` multiplies by the
row *length*, and using `Rows` instead is the bug the `Reserve(2,3)` /
`IsReserved(1,3)` pair is designed to find. Putting the bounds checks in one
private helper is the other half of the lesson: validation written three times
eventually disagrees with itself.

## ex8

Really testing: the builder pattern, and the difference between an argument
error and a state error. `return this;` is the whole mechanism, and it means
the chain mutates one object rather than producing copies - which is why the
gate checks `ReferenceEquals`. The query-parameter rule (insertion order,
replace in place) is a deliberate nudge away from `Dictionary<,>`, whose
enumeration order is unspecified. The exception distinction is the interview
point: `ArgumentException` says "you passed me something wrong",
`InvalidOperationException` says "everything you passed was fine, but the
object is not in a state where this makes sense". Confusing the two is common
and tells a reviewer a lot.

## Further reading

- [Constructors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/constructors) - chaining, field initialisers, and the order they run in.
- [Using constructors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/using-constructors) - including private constructors and factories.
- [`readonly`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/readonly) - exactly what it does and does not freeze.
- [Deconstructing tuples and other types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/functional/deconstruct) - the `Deconstruct` convention.
- [Choosing exception types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/using-standard-exception-types) - `ArgumentException` versus `InvalidOperationException`.
- [`IReadOnlyList<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.ireadonlylist-1) - what the read-only interfaces promise.

## Exercise 1 - a constructor that refuses bad state

`Ticket(code, seats)` stores the code trimmed and upper-cased. A blank code is
an `ArgumentException`; fewer than one seat is an
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. `Describe()` returns `"CODE x2"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D05_ClassesConstruction/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d05_classes_construction ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A constructor's job is to make it impossible to hold an invalid object. So the
guards come first, the assignments come last, and anything that fails throws
before a single field is set.

Two exception types, and the distinction matters: `ArgumentException` for input
that is the wrong *shape*, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a value outside
its allowed *range*.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(code))
    throw new ArgumentException("A ticket needs a code.", nameof(code));
if (seats < 1)
    throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(seats), "A ticket covers at least one seat.");
```

Note the argument order differs between the two types -
`ArgumentException(message, paramName)` but
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException(paramName, message)`. Getting it backwards
compiles and produces a nonsense message, so it is worth checking once.

Normalise after validating: `code.Trim().ToUpperInvariant()`. Doing it in the
constructor means every reader of `Code` gets the canonical form and nobody
downstream has to remember.

`Code` and `Seats` are get-only auto-properties, which a constructor may assign
and nothing else can.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A constructor's job is to make it impossible to hold an invalid object. So the
guards come first, the assignments come last, and anything that fails throws
before a single field is set.

Two exception types, and the distinction matters: `ArgumentException` for input
that is the wrong *shape*, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a value outside
its allowed *range*.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(code))
    throw new ArgumentException("A ticket needs a code.", nameof(code));
if (seats < 1)
    throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(seats), "A ticket covers at least one seat.");
```

Note the argument order differs between the two types -
`ArgumentException(message, paramName)` but
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException(paramName, message)`. Getting it backwards
compiles and produces a nonsense message, so it is worth checking once.

Normalise after validating: `code.Trim().ToUpperInvariant()`. Doing it in the
constructor means every reader of `Code` gets the canonical form and nobody
downstream has to remember.

`Code` and `Seats` are get-only auto-properties, which a constructor may assign
and nothing else can.

## Exercise 3 - static factories

`Temperature` has a private constructor and two factories: `FromCelsius` and
`FromFahrenheit`. Both reject anything below absolute zero (-273.15 C, which is
itself allowed). `Fahrenheit` is a computed property.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A private constructor plus public static factory methods is the "named
constructor" pattern. Its point is right here in the signatures:
`new Temperature(20)` cannot say which scale 20 is in, but
`Temperature.FromCelsius(20)` can only mean one thing.

The constructor is written for you. You write the two factories and the
computed property.

## Hint 2

`FromFahrenheit` should convert and then call `FromCelsius`, not repeat the
range check:

```csharp
return FromCelsius((fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9);
```

That way the absolute-zero rule exists in exactly one place, and the gate's
`FromFahrenheit(-500)` case passes without you writing anything for it.

Watch the arithmetic types: `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9` is all `double` because
`fahrenheit` is, so there is no integer division here. If you had written this
with `int` temperatures, `5 / 9` would be 0 and every answer would be 32 -
which is d01 ex2's trap in a new costume.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A private constructor plus public static factory methods is the "named
constructor" pattern. Its point is right here in the signatures:
`new Temperature(20)` cannot say which scale 20 is in, but
`Temperature.FromCelsius(20)` can only mean one thing.

The constructor is written for you. You write the two factories and the
computed property.

## Hint 2

`FromFahrenheit` should convert and then call `FromCelsius`, not repeat the
range check:

```csharp
return FromCelsius((fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9);
```

That way the absolute-zero rule exists in exactly one place, and the gate's
`FromFahrenheit(-500)` case passes without you writing anything for it.

Watch the arithmetic types: `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9` is all `double` because
`fahrenheit` is, so there is no integer division here. If you had written this
with `int` temperatures, `5 / 9` would be 0 and every answer would be 32 -
which is d01 ex2's trap in a new costume.

`Playlist` keeps a private `List<string>`, exposes it as `IReadOnlyList<string>
Tracks`, and offers `Add`, `Remove` (false when the track is not there) and
`MoveUp` (false when the track is missing or already first). The constructor

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The field is `private readonly List<string>`; the property is
`IReadOnlyList<string>`. That pairing is the standard way to own a collection:
the class can add and remove, and callers can only look.

`List<T>` already has `Add`, `Remove` (which returns the bool you want) and
`IndexOf`. Most of this exercise is delegation.

## Hint 2

`_tracks.AddRange(tracks)` copies the incoming sequence rather than storing a
reference to it - which is what the gate's "the caller adds to its own list
afterwards" check is for.

`Tracks => _tracks;` works because `List<T>` implements `IReadOnlyList<T>`. Be
aware of what that does and does not promise: a caller who casts it back to
`List<string>` can still mutate it. `_tracks.AsReadOnly()` returns a genuine
wrapper that cannot, at the cost of an allocation - a real trade-off worth
being able to argue either side of.

`MoveUp` is `IndexOf` plus a swap:

```csharp
int index = _tracks.IndexOf(track);
if (index <= 0) return false;
(_tracks[index - 1], _tracks[index]) = (_tracks[index], _tracks[index - 1]);
```

`index <= 0` covers both the missing case (-1) and the already-first case (0)
in one test - which is neat, and worth a comment in real code so the next
reader does not think it is a bug.

## Hint 1

The field is `private readonly List<string>`; the property is
`IReadOnlyList<string>`. That pairing is the standard way to own a collection:
the class can add and remove, and callers can only look.

`List<T>` already has `Add`, `Remove` (which returns the bool you want) and
`IndexOf`. Most of this exercise is delegation.

## Hint 2

`_tracks.AddRange(tracks)` copies the incoming sequence rather than storing a
reference to it - which is what the gate's "the caller adds to its own list
afterwards" check is for.

`Tracks => _tracks;` works because `List<T>` implements `IReadOnlyList<T>`. Be
aware of what that does and does not promise: a caller who casts it back to
`List<string>` can still mutate it. `_tracks.AsReadOnly()` returns a genuine
wrapper that cannot, at the cost of an allocation - a real trade-off worth
being able to argue either side of.

`MoveUp` is `IndexOf` plus a swap:

```csharp
int index = _tracks.IndexOf(track);
if (index <= 0) return false;
(_tracks[index - 1], _tracks[index]) = (_tracks[index], _tracks[index - 1]);
```

`index <= 0` covers both the missing case (-1) and the already-first case (0)
in one test - which is neat, and worth a comment in real code so the next
reader does not think it is a bug.

-180..180. Two `Deconstruct` overloads: two components, and the same two plus

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Deconstruct` is a convention, not an interface: any method named `Deconstruct`
that returns `void` and takes only `out` parameters enables
`var (a, b) = thing;` on that type.

Overloads are chosen by *how many* variables the caller writes on the left, so
a two-part and a three-part version can happily coexist.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public void Deconstruct(out double latitude, out double longitude)
{
    latitude = Latitude;
    longitude = Longitude;
}
```

The three-part overload can call the two-part one and then fill in the extra:

```csharp
Deconstruct(out latitude, out longitude);
hemisphere = Latitude >= 0 ? "N" : "S";
```

Passing an `out` parameter straight through as another method's `out` argument
is legal and is the tidiest way to avoid repeating yourself.

The constructor validation is ordinary range checking - but note that the
bounds are *inclusive*, so `new Coordinate(90, 180)` must succeed. Off-by-one
at a boundary is the most common bug in validation code, and writing the test
case before the check is how you avoid it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Deconstruct` is a convention, not an interface: any method named `Deconstruct`
that returns `void` and takes only `out` parameters enables
`var (a, b) = thing;` on that type.

Overloads are chosen by *how many* variables the caller writes on the left, so
a two-part and a three-part version can happily coexist.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public void Deconstruct(out double latitude, out double longitude)
{
    latitude = Latitude;
    longitude = Longitude;
}
```

The three-part overload can call the two-part one and then fill in the extra:

```csharp
Deconstruct(out latitude, out longitude);
hemisphere = Latitude >= 0 ? "N" : "S";
```

Passing an `out` parameter straight through as another method's `out` argument
is legal and is the tidiest way to avoid repeating yourself.

The constructor validation is ordinary range checking - but note that the
bounds are *inclusive*, so `new Coordinate(90, 180)` must succeed. Off-by-one
at a boundary is the most common bug in validation code, and writing the test
case before the check is how you avoid it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the invariant down first: **`AvailableCount` always equals the number of
false entries in the array.** Every method then has one job - keep that true.

The consequence is that the counter may only move on the paths where the array
actually changed. A `Reserve` that decrements before checking whether the seat
was already taken breaks the invariant on the second call.

The other half is turning a (row, seat) pair into one index.

## Hint 2

A single `bool[]` of `rows * seatsPerRow` is enough; the mapping is

```csharp
(row - 1) * SeatsPerRow + (seat - 1)
```

for 1-based rows and seats. Multiply by the row LENGTH, not by the row count -
the gate's `Reserve(2, 3)` then `IsReserved(1, 3)` pair exists to catch that.

Put the bounds checks in one private helper that returns the index, and call it
from all three public methods. Validation written three times is validation
that will disagree with itself eventually.

Structure each mutator as: compute index (which validates), check the current
state, return false if nothing to do, otherwise change the array *and* the
counter together. Two lines that must always run together are a good candidate
for sitting next to each other with nothing in between.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A fluent builder is just methods that end with `return this;`. The state lives
in private fields - a nullable host, a list of segments, and something ordered
for the query parameters.

`Build` is where the string gets assembled, and where the "you never set a
host" error belongs.

## Hint 2

The query parameters need insertion order *and* replace-in-place, which a plain
`Dictionary<,>` does not promise. A `List<KeyValuePair<string, string>>` with a
linear scan is honest and fine at this size:

# d06 - Properties and initialisation drills

Eight problems on the members that look like fields and behave like methods:
private setters, computed properties, `init`, `required`, guarded setters,
caching, validation inside an init accessor, and an indexer. They drill lesson
03 - reread `03_classes_objects` if `{ get; private set; }` is not yet
automatic.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - a private setter

`Battery(capacityMah)` with `ChargeMah { get; private set; }`, computed
`Percent` (rounded to a whole number, halves away from zero) and `IsFull`, plus
`Charge` and `Drain` which clamp at capacity and at zero and reject negative
amounts.

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - init-only properties

`Invoice` has `Number`, `Subtotal` and `TaxRate` set through an object
initialiser, and three computed members: `Tax` (2 dp, halves away from zero),
`Total` (which must use the rounded tax) and `Label` (`"INV-1: 120.00"`).

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - required members

`MailMessage` has `required To` and `required Subject`, an optional `Body`
defaulting to `""`, and two computed members: `HasBody` and `Summary`
(`"To: ada@example.com | Hello (5 chars)"`).

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - a property with a body

`VolumeControl.Level` clamps to 0-100 rather than throwing, and setting it
unmutes. `Mute()` and `Unmute()` change `Muted` without forgetting the level,
and `Effective` is 0 while muted and `Level` otherwise.

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - computed every time, or computed once

`Basket.Total` adds the prices up on every read. `Basket.CachedTotal` does it
at most once between changes, and `TotalComputations` counts how often it
really added. `Add` must leave both answers correct.

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - a setter that refuses

`Password.Value` throws `ArgumentException` for null or anything under 8
characters, and a refused assignment leaves the previous value in place.
`Strength` scores one point each for length >= 12, a digit, an upper-case
letter, and a character that is neither letter nor digit; `IsStrong` is 3 or
more.

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - validation in an init accessor

`Reservation` has `required Name` and a `required Guests` whose **init
accessor** rejects anything below 1 with `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, an
optional `Note`, a `Describe` property, and `WithGuests(n)` returning a new
reservation that keeps the name and note and revalidates.

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - an indexer over defaults and overrides

`Settings(defaults)` copies the defaults. `settings[key]` reads the override,
then the default, then `""`. Assigning stores an override - unless the value
equals the default, in which case it clears the override instead. `IsModified`,
`ModifiedKeys` (sorted ordinally), `Reset(key)` and `ResetAll()` complete it.

Edit `src/Lessons/D06_PropertiesInit/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d06_properties_init ex8
```
