# Reading - csharp/d09_interfaces_contracts

## Notes

An interface is a promise with no implementation attached, and everything in
this set follows from one consequence of that: **the promise can be kept by
types that have nothing else in common, including types written later, in
another assembly, by somebody else.** A class hierarchy cannot do that; a
`struct` cannot join one at all.

The pattern that recurs is *narrowing*. `Document.Total` asks for
`IWordCount`, not for `Paragraph`. `Docs.LengthOf` asks for `IReadableDoc`, not
`MemoryDoc`. `Catalogue.Describe` asks for `IReadStore<T>`, not the store that
can also delete. Every one of those parameter types is a decision about how
little the method needs to know, and the payoff is that the method keeps
working when the world around it changes - and can be tested with a fake.

The second thread is that interfaces are where the framework meets your code.
`IComparer<T>` is how `List.Sort` learns your ordering; `IDisposable` is how
`using` knows what to unwind; `IEnumerable<T>` is how `foreach` works. Writing
those implementations correctly is not decoration - it is what makes your type
a first-class citizen of the BCL.

## ex1

Really testing: that an interface unifies unrelated types, including a struct.
The classic mistake is reaching for an abstract base class instead, which works
until you need a `struct` or a type you do not own to join in. `Largest`
starting at 0 handles the empty sequence without a branch, which is the same
"choose the identity value" trick from d01. The detail worth carrying away is
the cost: putting `ImageBlock` into an `IWordCount[]` **boxes** it, copying the
struct to the heap so a reference can point at it. That is why the guidance for
structs is to keep them small and to be wary of interface-typed collections of
them.

## ex2

Really testing: the difference between `IComparable<T>` - one natural order,
baked into the type - and `IComparer<T>`, an ordering that lives in its own
object so a type can be sorted several ways. The classic mistake is
`x.Seconds - y.Seconds`, which is right for small numbers and overflows for
large ones; `CompareTo` cannot. The second is omitting the tie-break:
`List<T>.Sort` is **unstable**, so equal elements can come back in any order
and that order can change between runs and framework versions. Any comparer
used for display needs a total order. And `Ordered` sorting a copy is not
politeness - a method that quietly reorders its argument is a bug generator.

## ex3

Really testing: that a class can implement many interfaces, and that the
interesting decision is in the *parameter* types. The classic mistake is
declaring `LengthOf(MemoryDoc doc)`, which compiles, works, and cannot be
called with a `FrozenDoc` or with a test fake. `CanWrite` shows the other half:
`is` asks about the object, so narrowing a variable to `IReadableDoc` loses
nothing. This is the interface-segregation principle in miniature - many small
contracts beat one big one, because a caller can then depend on exactly the
part it uses.

## ex4

Really testing: explicit interface implementation, which removes a member from
the class's own surface so it can only be reached through the interface. Three
legitimate reasons: keeping an infrastructure concern (`ToRow`) off a domain
type's API; disambiguating two interfaces that declare the same member; and
implementing an awkward legacy interface alongside its modern replacement. The
cost is real too - an explicit implementation on a struct is reachable only by
boxing, and a caller holding the concrete type has to know to cast. The gate
uses reflection because "does not appear on the class" is exactly the property
being bought.

## ex5

Really testing: default interface members, and the thing everyone gets wrong
about them. The body lives in the interface and is **not inherited into the
class**, so `new SalesReport(...).Summary()` does not compile - you must hold
the object as an `IReportable`. That is a feature, not an oversight: default
members exist so a library can add a member to a published interface without
breaking implementers, not as a way to share code (an abstract base class is
still the right tool for that). Note also that the default body calls the
interface's other members, which is what makes it useful at all.

## ex6

Really testing: the `IDisposable` contract, whose one hard rule is that
disposing twice must be harmless. A guard flag set *before* the work is the
whole implementation, and setting it first also protects against a child whose
`Dispose` re-enters the scope. The reverse order matters for the same reason
nested `using` blocks unwind backwards: a resource acquired later may depend on
one acquired earlier. The classic mistake is disposing in insertion order,
which usually works and fails exactly when a dependency exists. Worth having an
answer ready for "what if a child throws?" - you should still dispose the rest,
which is why real container code wraps the loop.

## ex7

Really testing: generic interfaces plus constraints, and splitting a contract
in two. `where T : class, IHasId` buys `Save` the right to read `item.Id` -
without it the compiler knows nothing about T. The split is the design point:
`Catalogue.Describe` takes `IReadStore<T>` so it *cannot* delete anything, and
a reader who sees the signature knows that without reading the body. The
classic mistake is one fat `IRepository<T>` with a dozen members, which forces
every consumer and every test double to care about operations it never uses.

## ex8

Really testing: the decorator pattern - a class that implements an interface
*and* wraps another implementation of it, so callers cannot tell the
difference. This is how caching, logging, retries, metrics and authorisation
get added in real systems without touching either the caller or the real
implementation. The subtle rule is in the ordering of the last three lines:
delegate, then store, then return - so an exception from the inner source
prevents the cache write, and the failure is not remembered. Caching a "not
found" would mean that adding the missing price later never takes effect, which
is the kind of bug that survives three deployments.

## Further reading

- [Interfaces](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/interfaces) - declaring, implementing, and what they may contain.
- [Explicit interface implementation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/interfaces/explicit-interface-implementation) - the syntax and the reasons.
- [Default interface methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/interface-implementation/default-interface-methods-versions) - the versioning problem they solve.
- [`IComparer<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.icomparer-1) and [`IComparable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.icomparable-1) - which to use when.
- [Implementing a Dispose method](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose) - the contract ex6 keeps.
- [Generic constraints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters) - what each constraint buys you.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - one contract, three implementers

`IWordCount` has a single `Words` property. `Paragraph` and `Heading` count
words separated by any run of whitespace; the `readonly struct ImageBlock`
answers 0. `Document.Total` and `Document.Largest` walk an
`IEnumerable<IWordCount>`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D09_InterfacesContracts/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d09_interfaces_contracts ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An interface is a list of members with no bodies. A type that says
`: IWordCount` promises to have them, and the compiler checks.

Note that one of the three implementers is a `struct`. Interfaces are not
limited to classes, and nothing about `Document.Total` needs to know which is
which.

`Text.Split((char[]?)null, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` splits on
any whitespace and drops the empties - the same call you used in d02 ex7.

## Hint 2

Each `Words` is one expression; `ImageBlock.Words` is the literal `0`.

`Total` and `Largest` are one `foreach` each over `IEnumerable<IWordCount>`,
reading `part.Words`. `Largest` starts at 0, which gives the right answer for
an empty sequence without a special case.

Worth knowing for the follow-up: putting an `ImageBlock` into an
`IWordCount[]` **boxes** it - the struct is copied onto the heap so the array
can hold a reference. That is the usual cost of a struct implementing an
interface, and it is why the guidance is to keep structs small and to be
careful about interface-typed collections of them.

## Exercise 2 - the ordering as a separate object

`ByLength` sorts shortest first with ties broken by title ordinally; `ByTitle`
sorts by title ignoring case. Both implement `IComparer<Track>`, and `Track`
itself has no ordering code. `Playlist.Ordered` sorts a **copy** and joins the
titles with `", "`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D09_InterfacesContracts/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d09_interfaces_contracts ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`IComparable<T>` puts the ordering *inside* the type - one natural order, and
only one. `IComparer<T>` puts it in a separate object, so a type can be sorted
several ways and `Track` needs no ordering code at all.

`Compare(x, y)` returns negative when x comes first, 0 when they tie, positive
when y comes first. The actual numbers do not matter.

## Hint 2

Delegate to comparisons that already exist rather than subtracting:

```csharp
int byLength = x.Seconds.CompareTo(y.Seconds);
return byLength != 0 ? byLength : string.CompareOrdinal(x.Title, y.Title);
```

`a.Seconds - b.Seconds` looks equivalent and overflows for large values -
`CompareTo` never does.

The tie-break is not decoration: without it, two tracks of the same length come
back in whatever order the sort happened to produce, and `List<T>.Sort` is
*unstable*, so that order can change between runs. Any comparer used for
display needs a total order.

`Ordered` must not sort the caller's list. `new List<Track>(tracks)` copies,
then `copy.Sort(comparer)`.

Left to you: how the comparers handle nulls. The framework may pass them; a
comparer that throws on null is a comparer that crashes on real data.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - two contracts, one class

`MemoryDoc` implements `IReadableDoc` and `IWritableDoc`; `FrozenDoc`
implements only the first. `Docs.LengthOf` takes the reading half,
`Docs.Exclaim` the writing half, and `Docs.CanWrite` answers about the object's
runtime type.

Edit `src/Lessons/D09_InterfacesContracts/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d09_interfaces_contracts ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A class may implement as many interfaces as it likes - `MemoryDoc` implements
both, so it can be passed to a method wanting either.

The design point is in the *parameters*: `LengthOf` takes `IReadableDoc`
because reading is all it does, and that is what lets a `FrozenDoc` be passed
to it.

## Hint 2

Each method is one expression. `MemoryDoc.Write` appends: `_text += text;`.

`CanWrite` is the interesting one:

```csharp
public static bool CanWrite(IReadableDoc doc) => doc is IWritableDoc;
```

`is` asks about the object's runtime type, so a `MemoryDoc` narrowed to
`IReadableDoc` still answers true. Testing the *variable's* type would be
meaningless - it is `IReadableDoc` by definition.

The general rule this is drilling: **ask for the narrowest interface that does
the job**. A method taking `IReadableDoc` can be called with anything readable,
including types written after it; a method taking `MemoryDoc` can only be
called with a `MemoryDoc`, and cannot be tested with a fake.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A class may implement as many interfaces as it likes - `MemoryDoc` implements
both, so it can be passed to a method wanting either.

The design point is in the *parameters*: `LengthOf` takes `IReadableDoc`
because reading is all it does, and that is what lets a `FrozenDoc` be passed
to it.

## Hint 2

Each method is one expression. `MemoryDoc.Write` appends: `_text += text;`.

`CanWrite` is the interesting one:

```csharp
public static bool CanWrite(IReadableDoc doc) => doc is IWritableDoc;
```

`is` asks about the object's runtime type, so a `MemoryDoc` narrowed to
`IReadableDoc` still answers true. Testing the *variable's* type would be
meaningless - it is `IReadableDoc` by definition.

The general rule this is drilling: **ask for the narrowest interface that does
the job**. A method taking `IReadableDoc` can be called with anything readable,
including types written after it; a method taking `MemoryDoc` can only be
called with a `MemoryDoc`, and cannot be tested with a fake.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An explicit implementation names the interface in the declaration and takes no
accessibility modifier:

```csharp
string IPersistable.ToRow() => ...;
int IPersistable.Version => 2;
```

The member then does **not** exist on `Customer`'s own surface. Only code
holding an `IPersistable` reference can call it.

## Hint 2

The three reasons to reach for this are worth knowing, because interviewers ask:

1. **Keeping an infrastructure concern off the domain type's API**, which is
   this exercise. `customer.ToRow()` would invite ordinary code to serialise
   things by hand.
2. **Two interfaces declaring the same member** with different meanings - each
   gets its own explicit implementation.
3. **Implementing an old, awkward interface** (the non-generic `IEnumerable`,
   say) alongside the modern one without cluttering the type.

`Persistence.Save` takes `IPersistable`, so passing a `Customer` converts
implicitly and the members become reachable - no cast is needed at the call
site.

Note the cost: an explicit implementation on a *struct* is reached only by
boxing, and a caller who has your concrete type has to know to cast. That is a
real trade-off, not a free tidy-up.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Since C# 8 an interface member may have a body. Implementers that say nothing
about it inherit that body; implementers that declare their own win.

The feature exists so a library can add a member to a published interface
without breaking every existing implementer - which used to be impossible.

## Exercise 6 - IDisposable and a scope

`Resource.Dispose` logs `"dispose NAME"` exactly once however often it is
called. `Scope` takes ownership of disposables, disposes them **last added
first** and only once, and throws `ObjectDisposedException` from `Add` after it
has unwound.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Dispose` has one hard rule: **calling it twice must be harmless.** A guard
flag checked at the top of the method is the whole implementation.

The scope owns its children, so disposing the scope disposes them - in reverse
order, because a resource created later may depend on one created earlier.
That is the same order nested `using` blocks unwind in.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (Disposed) return;
Disposed = true;
```

Set the flag *before* doing the work, not after: it makes the method safe
against a child whose `Dispose` somehow calls back into the scope.

Reverse iteration is the loop from d03 ex3:

```csharp
for (int i = _children.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--) _children[i].Dispose();
```

`ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(Disposed, this)` (since .NET 7) is the modern
one-liner for the `Add` guard.

Left to you: what should happen if one child's `Dispose` throws. This exercise
does not test it, and the production answer is that you should still dispose
the rest and then rethrow - which is why real container code wraps the loop in
a try/finally or collects the exceptions. Have an answer ready.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Dispose` has one hard rule: **calling it twice must be harmless.** A guard
flag checked at the top of the method is the whole implementation.

The scope owns its children, so disposing the scope disposes them - in reverse
order, because a resource created later may depend on one created earlier.
That is the same order nested `using` blocks unwind in.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (Disposed) return;
Disposed = true;
```

Set the flag *before* doing the work, not after: it makes the method safe
against a child whose `Dispose` somehow calls back into the scope.

Reverse iteration is the loop from d03 ex3:

```csharp
for (int i = _children.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--) _children[i].Dispose();
```

`ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(Disposed, this)` (since .NET 7) is the modern
one-liner for the `Add` guard.

Left to you: what should happen if one child's `Dispose` throws. This exercise
does not test it, and the production answer is that you should still dispose
the rest and then rethrow - which is why real container code wraps the loop in
a try/finally or collects the exceptions. Have an answer ready.

## Hint 1

`MemoryStore<T>` is a `Dictionary<string, T>` with five one-line members. The
interesting parts are the *signatures*: two interfaces rather than one, and a
constraint that lets the store index items by their own `Id`.

`where T : class, IHasId` says two things - T is a reference type (so `T?` and
`null` mean what you expect) and T has an `Id`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public T? Find(string id) => _items.TryGetValue(id, out T? item) ? item : null;
public void Save(T item) => _items[item.Id] = item;
public bool Delete(string id) => _items.Remove(id);
```

`Save` reading `item.Id` is only legal because of the constraint - without it
the compiler knows nothing about T and there is no `Id` to read. That is what
constraints are for: they buy you members.

## Exercise 8 - a decorator

`TablePriceSource` answers from a table, counting every lookup and throwing

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps and holds a
reference to it. Callers holding the interface cannot tell the difference,
which is what lets you add caching, logging, retries or metrics without
changing either the caller or the real implementation.

`CachingPriceSource.PriceOf` has exactly two paths: in the cache (a hit), or
not (a miss, delegate, remember).

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (_cache.TryGetValue(sku, out decimal cached)) { Hits++; return cached; }
Misses++;
decimal price = _inner.PriceOf(sku);
_cache[sku] = price;
return price;
```

The order of the last three lines is the exercise. `_inner.PriceOf` throws for
an unknown sku, so the assignment to `_cache` never runs and the failure is not
remembered - which is what the gate's repeated `"zz"` lookups check. Caching a
failure would mean that adding the missing price later never takes effect.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps and holds a
reference to it. Callers holding the interface cannot tell the difference,
which is what lets you add caching, logging, retries or metrics without
changing either the caller or the real implementation.

`CachingPriceSource.PriceOf` has exactly two paths: in the cache (a hit), or
not (a miss, delegate, remember).

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (_cache.TryGetValue(sku, out decimal cached)) { Hits++; return cached; }
Misses++;
decimal price = _inner.PriceOf(sku);
_cache[sku] = price;
return price;
```

The order of the last three lines is the exercise. `_inner.PriceOf` throws for
an unknown sku, so the assignment to `_cache` never runs and the failure is not
remembered - which is what the gate's repeated `"zz"` lookups check. Caching a
failure would mean that adding the missing price later never takes effect.

`TablePriceSource.Lookups` is incremented *before* the dictionary is consulted,
so failed asks are counted too - which is what makes the cache's behaviour
visible from outside.

Left to you: whether "not found" should really be an exception here.
`TryPriceOf(sku, out price)` would let the decorator cache the absence as well
- a better design for a real price service, and worth saying so.

# d10 - Records and structs drills

Eight problems on the two kinds of value-shaped type: positional records,
`with`, readonly structs, record inheritance, `record struct`, the `default`
hole, boxing a mutable struct, and nested records with positional patterns.
They drill lesson 06 - reread `06_structs_records` if `with` and `record`
are not yet automatic.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - what one line of `record` gives you

`Employee(Name, Department, Level)` is declared for you. `Staff.Describe`
deconstructs it into three variables; `Staff.Print` returns the generated
`ToString`; `Staff.SamePerson` uses the record's own `==`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - `with`, and what follows it

`Booking(Guest, Nights, NightlyRate)` needs a computed `Total` and `Label`.
`Bookings.Extend` and `Bookings.Reprice` return copies made with `with`,
leaving the original alone; `Extend` throws
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a negative number of extra nights.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a readonly struct

`Rgb(red, green, blue)` with `Hex` (`"#FF8000"`, upper case), a matching
`ToString`, and `Darken(amount)` that returns a **new** colour with every
channel reduced and clamped at 0.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - records inherit

`Truck : Vehicle` is declared for you. `Fleet.Replate` uses `with` on a
`Vehicle`-typed parameter - and gets a `Truck` back when that is what it was
given. `Fleet.PayloadOf` answers 0 for a plain vehicle. The gate also checks
that a `Vehicle` and a `Truck` with the same data are **not** equal.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - record struct, and the readonly one

`Tally(Wins, Losses)` is a mutable `record struct`; `Point(X, Y)` is a
`readonly record struct`. `Structs.BumpWins` modifies its parameter and returns
it - and the caller's tally must be unchanged. `Structs.Mirror` uses `with`;
`Structs.Score` deconstructs.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - the constructor you did not write

`Currency(code)` accepts exactly three letters and stores them upper-cased;
anything else is an `ArgumentException`. But `default(Currency)` bypasses it
entirely and leaves `Code` null - so `IsDefault` detects that and `Safe`
answers `"???"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - a mutable struct behind an interface

`MutableCounter` is a mutable struct implementing `ICounter`. Write the four
`Boxes` methods exactly as described, then predict each answer before running
the gate: `ViaLocal`, `ViaInterface`, `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal` and
`ViaArrayElement` do **not** all agree.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - nested records and positional patterns

`People.MoveCity` rebuilds the nested `Address` - `with` alone would share it.
`People.SameCountry` uses a positional pattern. `People.Classify` is one switch
expression with four arms, tried in order: country `"UK"`, then Paris/France,
then a name longer than 8, then everything else.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d10_records_structs

## Notes

Two ideas run through this set, and they are easy to confuse because they often
travel together. The first is **value semantics**: does copying this thing give
me an independent thing, and are two of them with the same contents "the same"?
The second is **immutability**: can it change after it is built? A `record` is a
class with value equality and a copy syntax; a `struct` is a value type that
copies on assignment; `readonly` is what actually stops mutation. You can have
any combination, and picking the wrong one produces a specific, recognisable
bug.

The drills split accordingly. ex1, ex2, ex4 and ex8 are about records - what
the compiler generates, what `with` copies, how inheritance behaves. ex3, ex5,
ex6 and ex7 are about structs - copying, the `default` hole, and what happens
when a mutable one meets an interface.

The rule of thumb worth carrying away is Microsoft's own: make a struct when
the thing is logically a single value, is small, is immutable, and will not be
boxed often. Every failure in ex6 and ex7 is one of those four conditions being
broken.

## ex1

Really testing: knowing what a single line of `record` actually produces - a
constructor, get-only properties, `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString`,
`Deconstruct`, `==`/`!=` and a copy constructor. The classic mistake is writing
`Print` by hand instead of calling the generated `ToString`, which misses the
point of the exercise; the second is comparing components one by one in
`SamePerson` when `==` already does it. Notice the gate checks `GetHashCode`
agrees for two equal records: that pairing is generated together, which is why
records are safe as dictionary keys and hand-written classes so often are not.

## ex2

Really testing: `with` as a copy-and-change expression, and the fact that
computed members follow the copy automatically. The classic mistake is thinking
`with` mutates - it does not, and the gate checks the original. The deeper
point is what `with` does *not* do: it calls the generated copy constructor,
not your primary constructor's body, so no validation runs. Any invariant has
to live in an `init` accessor or in the method doing the copying. That gap is
the one real weakness of records-as-immutable-data and a very common interview
question.

## ex3

Really testing: a `readonly struct` forcing you to return new instances rather
than mutate. The compiler enforces it, which is exactly why the modifier is
worth writing - it turns a convention into a rule. Two smaller traps live in
`Darken`: byte arithmetic promotes to `int`, so the result must be cast back;
and the clamp must happen *before* the cast, or a negative result wraps round
to a large byte. That is d01 ex8's lesson arriving in a different costume, and
it is the kind of bug that shows up as one weirdly bright pixel.

## ex4

Really testing: record inheritance, which is where records do something a
hand-written class rarely gets right. `with` on a base-typed variable produces
the *derived* type, because the copy constructor is protected and virtual - so
nothing is sliced off, and code that only knows about `Vehicle` cannot
accidentally discard a truck's payload. Equality is the other half: the
generated `Equals` compares a hidden `EqualityContract` (the runtime type)
before comparing components, so a `Vehicle` and a `Truck` holding the same data
are not equal. Getting both of those right by hand is genuinely hard, which is
the argument for the feature.

## ex5

Really testing: `record struct` versus `readonly record struct`, and struct copy
semantics. `BumpWins` mutates its parameter and the caller sees nothing -
write the same method for a class and both change. That difference is the whole
class-or-struct decision in three lines. The `default(Point)` check is a
deliberate set-up for ex6: for a point the zeroed value is meaningful, so
nothing is wrong; knowing which of your structs have a meaningful zero is the
difference between a safe value type and a trap.

## ex6

Really testing: that `default(T)` bypasses every constructor a struct has. A
`readonly struct Currency` looks watertight and still has a reachable state its
own constructor would reject - `default`, `new Currency[10]`, and an
uninitialised field all produce it, with `Code` null. The classic mistake is
assuming validation in a struct's constructor is a guarantee; it is only a
guarantee for instances that went through it. The three answers are to use a
class instead, to design the zero value to be meaningful, or to expose readers
that cope - which is what `IsDefault` and `Safe` do here. This is the standard
objection to "parse, don't validate" wrapper types being structs.

## ex7

Really testing: boxing, and why "make structs immutable" is advice rather than
pedantry. Assigning a struct to an interface-typed variable copies it into a
box on the heap; every subsequent call goes to that box, and the original is
untouched. `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal` returning 0 is the bug in its purest form,
and the line that caused it looks like an ordinary assignment. `ViaArrayElement`
is the counterpoint: an array element is a variable, so the mutation lands. Its
twin - `list[0].Increment()` on a `List<T>` - does not compile at all, because
the indexer returns a copy and C# refuses to let you mutate something about to
be discarded. Three different behaviours from three visually similar lines is
exactly why the guidance is to make the situation impossible.

## ex8

Really testing: that `with` is a **shallow** copy, and positional patterns.
Changing a nested value needs the nested record rebuilt - `person with { Home =
person.Home with { City = city } }` - and the gate checks that a plain
`with { Name = ... }` shares the very same `Address` object. That sharing is
safe here only because `Address` is immutable; with a mutable nested object it
is the classic aliasing bug. The pattern half shows what positional records buy
beyond deconstruction: `Person(_, Address(_, "UK"))` tests two levels without
naming a property, and arms are tried strictly in order - which is why a long
UK name still classifies as "UK".

## Further reading

- [Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record) - everything the compiler generates, including the copy constructor.
- [Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) - `readonly struct`, `record struct`, and the default constructor.
- [`with` expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/with-expression) - what is copied and what is not.
- [Choosing between class and struct](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/choosing-between-class-and-struct) - the four conditions.

# Reading - csharp/d10_records_structs

## Notes

Two ideas run through this set, and they are easy to confuse because they often
travel together. The first is **value semantics**: does copying this thing give
me an independent thing, and are two of them with the same contents "the same"?
The second is **immutability**: can it change after it is built? A `record` is a
class with value equality and a copy syntax; a `struct` is a value type that
copies on assignment; `readonly` is what actually stops mutation. You can have
any combination, and picking the wrong one produces a specific, recognisable
bug.

The drills split accordingly. ex1, ex2, ex4 and ex8 are about records - what
the compiler generates, what `with` copies, how inheritance behaves. ex3, ex5,
ex6 and ex7 are about structs - copying, the `default` hole, and what happens
when a mutable one meets an interface.

The rule of thumb worth carrying away is Microsoft's own: make a struct when
the thing is logically a single value, is small, is immutable, and will not be
boxed often. Every failure in ex6 and ex7 is one of those four conditions being
broken.

## ex1

Really testing: knowing what a single line of `record` actually produces - a
constructor, get-only properties, `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString`,
`Deconstruct`, `==`/`!=` and a copy constructor. The classic mistake is writing
`Print` by hand instead of calling the generated `ToString`, which misses the
point of the exercise; the second is comparing components one by one in
`SamePerson` when `==` already does it. Notice the gate checks `GetHashCode`
agrees for two equal records: that pairing is generated together, which is why
records are safe as dictionary keys and hand-written classes so often are not.

## ex2

Really testing: `with` as a copy-and-change expression, and the fact that
computed members follow the copy automatically. The classic mistake is thinking
`with` mutates - it does not, and the gate checks the original. The deeper
point is what `with` does *not* do: it calls the generated copy constructor,
not your primary constructor's body, so no validation runs. Any invariant has
to live in an `init` accessor or in the method doing the copying. That gap is
the one real weakness of records-as-immutable-data and a very common interview
question.

## ex3

Really testing: a `readonly struct` forcing you to return new instances rather
than mutate. The compiler enforces it, which is exactly why the modifier is
worth writing - it turns a convention into a rule. Two smaller traps live in
`Darken`: byte arithmetic promotes to `int`, so the result must be cast back;
and the clamp must happen *before* the cast, or a negative result wraps round
to a large byte. That is d01 ex8's lesson arriving in a different costume, and
it is the kind of bug that shows up as one weirdly bright pixel.

## ex4

Really testing: record inheritance, which is where records do something a
hand-written class rarely gets right. `with` on a base-typed variable produces
the *derived* type, because the copy constructor is protected and virtual - so
nothing is sliced off, and code that only knows about `Vehicle` cannot
accidentally discard a truck's payload. Equality is the other half: the
generated `Equals` compares a hidden `EqualityContract` (the runtime type)
before comparing components, so a `Vehicle` and a `Truck` holding the same data
are not equal. Getting both of those right by hand is genuinely hard, which is
the argument for the feature.

## ex5

Really testing: `record struct` versus `readonly record struct`, and struct copy
semantics. `BumpWins` mutates its parameter and the caller sees nothing -
write the same method for a class and both change. That difference is the whole
class-or-struct decision in three lines. The `default(Point)` check is a
deliberate set-up for ex6: for a point the zeroed value is meaningful, so
nothing is wrong; knowing which of your structs have a meaningful zero is the
difference between a safe value type and a trap.

## ex6

Really testing: that `default(T)` bypasses every constructor a struct has. A
`readonly struct Currency` looks watertight and still has a reachable state its
own constructor would reject - `default`, `new Currency[10]`, and an
uninitialised field all produce it, with `Code` null. The classic mistake is
assuming validation in a struct's constructor is a guarantee; it is only a
guarantee for instances that went through it. The three answers are to use a
class instead, to design the zero value to be meaningful, or to expose readers
that cope - which is what `IsDefault` and `Safe` do here. This is the standard
objection to "parse, don't validate" wrapper types being structs.

## ex7

Really testing: boxing, and why "make structs immutable" is advice rather than
pedantry. Assigning a struct to an interface-typed variable copies it into a
box on the heap; every subsequent call goes to that box, and the original is
untouched. `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal` returning 0 is the bug in its purest form,
and the line that caused it looks like an ordinary assignment. `ViaArrayElement`
is the counterpoint: an array element is a variable, so the mutation lands. Its
twin - `list[0].Increment()` on a `List<T>` - does not compile at all, because
the indexer returns a copy and C# refuses to let you mutate something about to
be discarded. Three different behaviours from three visually similar lines is
exactly why the guidance is to make the situation impossible.

## ex8

Really testing: that `with` is a **shallow** copy, and positional patterns.
Changing a nested value needs the nested record rebuilt - `person with { Home =
person.Home with { City = city } }` - and the gate checks that a plain
`with { Name = ... }` shares the very same `Address` object. That sharing is
safe here only because `Address` is immutable; with a mutable nested object it
is the classic aliasing bug. The pattern half shows what positional records buy
beyond deconstruction: `Person(_, Address(_, "UK"))` tests two levels without
naming a property, and arms are tried strictly in order - which is why a long
UK name still classifies as "UK".

- [Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record) - everything the compiler generates, including the copy constructor.
- [Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) - `readonly struct`, `record struct`, and the default constructor.
- [`with` expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/with-expression) - what is copied and what is not.
- [Choosing between class and struct](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/choosing-between-class-and-struct) - the four conditions.
- [Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) - what ex7 is really about.
- [Patterns](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/patterns#positional-pattern) - the positional pattern, in the specification.

## Exercise 1 - what one line of `record` gives you

`Employee(Name, Department, Level)` is declared for you. `Staff.Describe`
deconstructs it into three variables; `Staff.Print` returns the generated
`ToString`; `Staff.SamePerson` uses the record's own `==`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D10_RecordsStructs/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The record itself is already declared for you. What you write is the three
methods - and all three are one line.

`Describe` must *deconstruct*: a positional record generates a `Deconstruct`,
so `(string name, string department, int level) = employee;` works.

## Hint 2

```csharp
(string name, string department, int level) = employee;
return $"{name} works in {department} at level {level}";
```

`Print` is `employee.ToString()`. Do not build the string yourself - the point
is to see what the compiler generated: the type name, a brace, `Name = value`
for each component, a closing brace.

`SamePerson` is `a == b`. A record overloads `==` to compare by value, which is
the one thing a record does that a class does not do for free. Note the gate
also checks `GetHashCode` agrees - you get that automatically, and it is what
makes records safe as dictionary keys.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The record itself is already declared for you. What you write is the three
methods - and all three are one line.

`Describe` must *deconstruct*: a positional record generates a `Deconstruct`,
so `(string name, string department, int level) = employee;` works.

## Hint 2

```csharp
(string name, string department, int level) = employee;
return $"{name} works in {department} at level {level}";
```

`Print` is `employee.ToString()`. Do not build the string yourself - the point
is to see what the compiler generated: the type name, a brace, `Name = value`
for each component, a closing brace.

`SamePerson` is `a == b`. A record overloads `==` to compare by value, which is
the one thing a record does that a class does not do for free. Note the gate
also checks `GetHashCode` agrees - you get that automatically, and it is what
makes records safe as dictionary keys.

`Bookings.Extend` and `Bookings.Reprice` return copies made with `with`,

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`booking with { Nights = 5 }` makes a copy of the record with one component
replaced. It never modifies the original, and it is an expression - so it can
be returned directly.

The two computed properties go in the record's body, after the positional
parameter list, in braces.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public record Booking(string Guest, int Nights, int NightlyRate)
{
    public int Total => Nights * NightlyRate;
}
```

and

```csharp
return booking with { Nights = booking.Nights + extraNights };
```

`Total` is computed, so it follows the copy automatically - there is nothing to
keep in step.

The validation is worth noticing: `with` performs no checks at all. It calls
the copy constructor, not your primary constructor's body, so any invariant you
enforce has to live either in an `init` accessor (as in d06 ex7) or in the
method doing the copying. That is the one real gap in records-as-immutable-data,
and interviewers like asking about it.

## Hint 1

`booking with { Nights = 5 }` makes a copy of the record with one component
replaced. It never modifies the original, and it is an expression - so it can
be returned directly.

The two computed properties go in the record's body, after the positional
parameter list, in braces.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public record Booking(string Guest, int Nights, int NightlyRate)
{
    public int Total => Nights * NightlyRate;
}
```

and

```csharp
return booking with { Nights = booking.Nights + extraNights };
```

`Total` is computed, so it follows the copy automatically - there is nothing to
keep in step.

The validation is worth noticing: `with` performs no checks at all. It calls
the copy constructor, not your primary constructor's body, so any invariant you
enforce has to live either in an `init` accessor (as in d06 ex7) or in the
method doing the copying. That is the one real gap in records-as-immutable-data,
and interviewers like asking about it.

## Exercise 4 - records inherit

`Truck : Vehicle` is declared for you. `Fleet.Replate` uses `with` on a
`Vehicle`-typed parameter - and gets a `Truck` back when that is what it was
given. `Fleet.PayloadOf` answers 0 for a plain vehicle. The gate also checks

uv run dojo test csharp d10_records_structs ex4

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both records are declared for you. The two methods are one line each.

`Replate` is a `with` expression on a `Vehicle`-typed parameter. Before you
write it, predict what it returns when the argument is really a `Truck`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Vehicle Replate(Vehicle vehicle, string plate) => vehicle with { Plate = plate };
public static int PayloadOf(Vehicle vehicle) => vehicle is Truck truck ? truck.PayloadTonnes : 0;
```

The answer to the prediction: you get a `Truck`. A record generates a
**protected virtual copy constructor**, and `with` calls it through the object,
so the most derived copy constructor runs and nothing is sliced off. Writing
the same thing by hand with `new Vehicle(...)` would silently lose the payload -
which is the bug this arrangement prevents.

The equality assertion is the other half. Record equality compares an
`EqualityContract` - a hidden protected property returning the runtime type -
*before* it compares components, so a `Vehicle` and a `Truck` with the same
plate and wheels are not equal. That is usually what you want, and it is why
records handle inheritance better than a hand-written `Equals` normally does.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both records are declared for you. The two methods are one line each.

`Replate` is a `with` expression on a `Vehicle`-typed parameter. Before you
write it, predict what it returns when the argument is really a `Truck`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Vehicle Replate(Vehicle vehicle, string plate) => vehicle with { Plate = plate };
public static int PayloadOf(Vehicle vehicle) => vehicle is Truck truck ? truck.PayloadTonnes : 0;
```

The answer to the prediction: you get a `Truck`. A record generates a
**protected virtual copy constructor**, and `with` calls it through the object,
so the most derived copy constructor runs and nothing is sliced off. Writing
the same thing by hand with `new Vehicle(...)` would silently lose the payload -
which is the bug this arrangement prevents.

The equality assertion is the other half. Record equality compares an
`EqualityContract` - a hidden protected property returning the runtime type -
*before* it compares components, so a `Vehicle` and a `Truck` with the same
plate and wheels are not equal. That is usually what you want, and it is why
records handle inheritance better than a hand-written `Equals` normally does.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`record struct` is a value type with the record conveniences bolted on: value
equality, `ToString`, `Deconstruct`, `with`. Its components are **settable**,
so `tally.Wins++` compiles.

`readonly record struct` locks that down - nothing may be reassigned, and `with`
is the only way to get a changed copy.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Tally BumpWins(Tally tally)
{
    tally.Wins++;
    return tally;
}
```

That method modifies the parameter and the caller sees nothing, because a
struct parameter is a copy. Write the same method for a class and both change.
Which behaviour you want is exactly the class-or-struct decision.

`Mirror` is `point with { X = -point.X }`, and `Score` is a deconstruction:
`(int wins, int losses) = tally;`.

The `default(Point)` check is a hint about ex6: for a `Point` the zeroed
default is a perfectly good value, so nothing is wrong. That is not true of
every struct, and knowing which of your structs have a meaningful zero is the
difference between a safe value type and a trap.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the four methods exactly as their doc comments describe - do not try to
make them all agree. Two of them will disagree, and that is the exercise.

Before you run the gate, predict each answer, then check. The one worth
thinking hardest about is `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal`.

## Hint 2

The rule underneath all four: **assigning a struct anywhere makes a copy**, and
assigning one to an interface-typed variable copies it into a box on the heap.

- `ViaLocal` - one variable throughout: 2.
- `ViaInterface` - `new MutableCounter()` is boxed once, and every call goes to
  that single box: 2.
- `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal` - the local is copied into a box; both increments
  land on the box; the local is still 0.
- `ViaArrayElement` - an array element *is* a variable, so the call mutates it
  in place: 1.

The last one has a twin worth knowing: `list[0].Increment()` on a `List<T>` of
structs does not compile at all, because the indexer returns a copy and C#
refuses to let you mutate a value that is about to be thrown away. The array
version compiles because array indexing produces a variable reference.

This is why the guidance is "make structs immutable". Not because mutation is
slow, but because you cannot see, at the call site, which copy you are talking
to.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the four methods exactly as their doc comments describe - do not try to
make them all agree. Two of them will disagree, and that is the exercise.

Before you run the gate, predict each answer, then check. The one worth
thinking hardest about is `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal`.

## Hint 2

The rule underneath all four: **assigning a struct anywhere makes a copy**, and
assigning one to an interface-typed variable copies it into a box on the heap.

- `ViaLocal` - one variable throughout: 2.
- `ViaInterface` - `new MutableCounter()` is boxed once, and every call goes to
  that single box: 2.
- `ViaCopyThenReadOriginal` - the local is copied into a box; both increments
  land on the box; the local is still 0.
- `ViaArrayElement` - an array element *is* a variable, so the call mutates it
  in place: 1.

The last one has a twin worth knowing: `list[0].Increment()` on a `List<T>` of
structs does not compile at all, because the indexer returns a copy and C#
refuses to let you mutate a value that is about to be thrown away. The array
version compiles because array indexing produces a variable reference.

This is why the guidance is "make structs immutable". Not because mutation is
slow, but because you cannot see, at the call site, which copy you are talking
to.

## Exercise 8 - nested records and positional patterns

`People.MoveCity` rebuilds the nested `Address` - `with` alone would share it.
`People.SameCountry` uses a positional pattern. `People.Classify` is one switch
expression with four arms, tried in order: country `"UK"`, then Paris/France,
then a name longer than 8, then everything else.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`with` copies the record one level deep. `person with { Name = "X" }` gives a
new `Person` pointing at the *same* `Address` object - which is fine when the
address is immutable, and is the whole bug when it is not.

So changing a nested value means rebuilding the nested record too, and `with`
nests happily inside `with`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
person with { Home = person.Home with { City = city } }
```

For the patterns, a positional record can be matched by position:
`Person(_, Address(_, "UK"))` matches anyone whose home country is "UK",
without naming a single property. A pattern can also capture:
`Person(_, Address(_, string country))`.

`Classify` is one switch expression with the four arms in the order given.
Arms are tried top to bottom, which is why a long UK name still classifies as
"UK" - the gate checks exactly that.

Left to you: whether `SameCountry` reads better as a pattern or as
`a.Home.Country == b.Home.Country`. The property version is shorter and clearer
here; the pattern version generalises when you start needing several components
at once. Be able to argue for the one you chose.

lessons.briefing:
# d11 - Equality semantics drills

Eight problems on the question every type has to answer: when are two of these
the same? Reference versus value equality, `Equals`/`GetHashCode`,
`IEquatable<T>` on a struct, `==` disagreeing with `Equals`, a mutated
dictionary key, a custom comparer, the full operator contract, and the symmetry
break that inheritance causes. They drill lesson 06 - reread
`06_structs_records` if the `Equals`/`GetHashCode` pairing is still hazy.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D11_EqualitySemantics/`. Nothing here depends

# Reading - csharp/d11_equality_semantics

## Notes

"Equal" is not one question in .NET, it is five, and a type that answers them
inconsistently produces bugs that are extremely hard to see. The five are
`ReferenceEquals` (identity, never overridable), `Equals(object?)` (virtual,
the type decides), `Equals(T)` (from `IEquatable<T>`, typed and boxing-free),
`operator ==` (chosen at compile time from the static types), and
`GetHashCode` (which decides *where* the object is filed).

The rules that tie them together are short and non-negotiable. Equality must be
reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Equal objects must produce equal hash
codes. An object's hash code must not change while it is in a hash-based
collection. Every failure in this set is one of those four being broken.

The other theme is that the framework does not care which syntax you prefer.
`List<T>.Contains`, `Dictionary<K,V>`, `Distinct`, `GroupBy` and `Union` all go
through `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`, which uses `Equals` and `GetHashCode` -
never `==`. So a type whose `==` and `Equals` disagree behaves differently
depending on which collection method the caller happened to use, and nobody
will find that by reading the call site.

## ex1

Really testing: that the three questions are genuinely different.
`ReferenceEquals` is identity and cannot be overridden - which is exactly why it
exists, as the escape hatch when a type's own `Equals` is lying to you. A plain
class inherits identity for `Equals` too, and that is the *correct* default: a
type that has not said what equality means should not guess. `string` is the
counter-example everyone has internalised without noticing, because it
overloads `==` to compare characters. The classic confusion is assuming every
type does that. It is worth knowing that `"a" + "b"` is folded and interned at
compile time, so a demonstration of reference inequality needs a string built
at run time.

## ex2

Really testing: the `Equals`/`GetHashCode` pairing, and that the hash must be
derived from exactly the information the comparison uses. Compare
case-insensitively and hash case-sensitively and your `HashSet` will contain
two "equal" items, because they landed in different buckets and `Equals` was
never called. The classic mistake beyond that is
`Code.ToUpperInvariant().GetHashCode()`, which allocates a string on every hash -
`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Code)` does the same job without
the garbage. The `obj is Isbn other` pattern folds the null test and the type
test into one, which is why it has replaced the older two-line preamble.

## ex3

Really testing: why `IEquatable<T>` exists at all. A struct already gets
correct field-by-field equality from `ValueType.Equals` - but it is implemented
with reflection, and reaching it means boxing. Implementing `IEquatable<T>`
gives `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` a typed method to call, and the boxing and
the reflection both disappear. The classic mistake is implementing the typed
`Equals` and *not* overriding `Equals(object?)`, leaving a type whose answer
depends on how it was asked. Both must exist and both must agree; the object
version delegating to the typed one is how you guarantee that.

## ex4

Really testing: that `==` is not virtual. It is resolved at compile time from
the static types of its operands, so a class that overrides `Equals` without
overloading `==` has two different notions of equality living inside it. The
sting is `List<T>.Contains`, which uses `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` and
therefore `Equals` - so the collection says the tag is present while `==` says
the two tags are different objects. Both answers are correct and they
contradict each other. The guidance follows: if a type feels like a value,
overload `==` and `!=` alongside `Equals`, or make it a `record` and let the
compiler do all five.

## ex5

Really testing: the invariant that a hash-based collection depends on and
cannot enforce. `HashSet<T>` chooses a bucket from the hash *once*, when the
item is added. Change the item afterwards and every later lookup computes the
new hash, visits the wrong bucket and finds nothing. The entry is still there -
`Count` says so, enumeration finds it - but it is unreachable by any key at
all, including a fresh key with the original name, because the object living
in that bucket has since changed. The rule: anything used as a key must be
immutable in the parts that determine its hash. Records with `init` components,
strings and value tuples are safe; a class with public setters is not.

## ex6

Really testing: `IEqualityComparer<T>` as the way to define equality from
outside a type - because the type is not yours, or because it already has a
natural equality and you need a different one here. The two methods must agree
exactly as an overridden pair must, and the reliable way to guarantee that is a
single private helper producing the comparison value, used by both. The
domain-specific trap is `(int)` versus `Math.Floor`: a cast truncates toward
zero, so -1.2 and -0.4 land in the same cell, which is not what a map means by
a grid square. And the framework really does pass nulls while probing, so a
comparer that throws on null is a comparer that crashes on real data.

## ex7

Really testing: writing the whole contract once, deliberately. Five members,
and the one that bites is `operator ==`: writing `left == null` inside it calls
the operator again and stack-overflows, so the null test must be `left is
null`. The rest is discipline - `Equals(object?)` delegates to the typed
version, `GetHashCode` is built from the same fields with the same comparison
rules, and `!=` is `!(==)`. Note that the class is `sealed`, which is not
decoration: sealing removes the inheritance question ex8 is about and is what
lets a simple type test in `Equals` be correct. Most value-like classes should
be sealed for exactly this reason.

## ex8

Really testing: the symmetry break that `is`-based equality causes under
inheritance. Written with `obj is Point2`, a `Point2` at (1,2) considers a red
`ColouredPoint` at (1,2) equal while the coloured point disagrees - so
`a.Equals(b) != b.Equals(a)`, and any collection that happens to compare them
in the other order gets a different answer. `GetType() != obj.GetType()` fixes
it by making a base and a derived instance never equal, in either direction.
That has a real cost - a test proxy or a lazy-loading subclass is never equal
to the thing it stands for - which is why `record` picks the same rule via its
`EqualityContract`, and why value-like classes are usually sealed so the
question cannot arise.

## Further reading

- [Equality comparisons](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/statements-expressions-operators/equality-comparisons) - the whole map, reference versus value.
- [`Object.Equals`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.equals) - the reflexive/symmetric/transitive contract, spelled out.
- [`Object.GetHashCode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) - including "do not change while used as a key".
- [`IEquatable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.iequatable-1) - and why structs want it.
- [`IEqualityComparer<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.iequalitycomparer-1) - equality from outside the type.
- [`HashCode.Combine`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.hashcode.combine) - the modern way to build one.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - Equals and GetHashCode together

`Isbn` compares by code, ignoring case, ordinally - and hashes the same way, so
two equal ISBNs land in the same bucket. The gate puts them in a `HashSet`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D11_EqualitySemantics/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d11_equality_semantics ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Overriding `Equals(object?)` means you must override `GetHashCode` too, and the
rule joining them is one-directional: **equal objects must return the same hash
code**; unequal objects may share one.

So work out the comparison rule first, then build the hash from exactly the
same information. Here the rule is "same code, ignoring case".

## Hint 2

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj) =>
    obj is Isbn other && string.Equals(Code, other.Code, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

public override int GetHashCode() =>
    StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Code);
```

`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Code)` rather than
`Code.ToUpperInvariant().GetHashCode()`: the second allocates a string on every
hash, and a dictionary lookup in a loop turns that into real garbage.

The `is` pattern handles both the null case and the wrong-type case in one
test, which is why it has replaced the older `if (obj == null || GetType() !=
obj.GetType())` preamble for sealed-ish types.

Left to you: whether `Equals` should use `obj is Isbn` or
`GetType() == obj.GetType()`. They differ only when someone derives from
`Isbn` - which ex8 is entirely about.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Overriding `Equals(object?)` means you must override `GetHashCode` too, and the
rule joining them is one-directional: **equal objects must return the same hash
code**; unequal objects may share one.

So work out the comparison rule first, then build the hash from exactly the
same information. Here the rule is "same code, ignoring case".

## Hint 2

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj) =>
    obj is Isbn other && string.Equals(Code, other.Code, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

public override int GetHashCode() =>
    StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Code);
```

`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Code)` rather than
`Code.ToUpperInvariant().GetHashCode()`: the second allocates a string on every
hash, and a dictionary lookup in a loop turns that into real garbage.

The `is` pattern handles both the null case and the wrong-type case in one
test, which is why it has replaced the older `if (obj == null || GetType() !=
obj.GetType())` preamble for sealed-ish types.

Left to you: whether `Equals` should use `obj is Isbn` or
`GetType() == obj.GetType()`. They differ only when someone derives from
`Isbn` - which ex8 is entirely about.

## Exercise 3 - IEquatable on a struct

`Gram` implements `IEquatable<Gram>` with a typed `Equals(Gram)`, an
`Equals(object?)` override that delegates to it, and a matching `GetHashCode`.
The typed version is what stops `HashSet<Gram>` boxing on every comparison.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A struct inherits `ValueType.Equals`, which compares fields - correctly, but by
reflection, which is slow. `IEquatable<T>` gives the framework a strongly typed
`Equals(T)` to call instead, and generic collections look for it.

You need three members: `Equals(Gram)`, `Equals(object?)` and `GetHashCode()`.
The first is the real one; the second delegates to it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public bool Equals(Gram other) => Value == other.Value;
public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is Gram other && Equals(other);
public override int GetHashCode() => Value.GetHashCode();
```

The `Equals(object?)` override matters even though it looks redundant: code
that only knows `object` - the non-generic collections, `object.Equals(a, b)` -
will call it, and if it disagreed with the typed version you would have a type
whose answer depends on how it was asked.

The performance point is worth being able to state. Without `IEquatable<Gram>`,
`HashSet<Gram>.Contains` reaches `Equals(object?)`, which means **boxing** the
struct on every comparison. With it, `EqualityComparer<Gram>.Default` finds the
typed method and no boxing happens at all. That is the single best reason to
implement the interface on a struct.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A struct inherits `ValueType.Equals`, which compares fields - correctly, but by
reflection, which is slow. `IEquatable<T>` gives the framework a strongly typed
`Equals(T)` to call instead, and generic collections look for it.

You need three members: `Equals(Gram)`, `Equals(object?)` and `GetHashCode()`.
The first is the real one; the second delegates to it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public bool Equals(Gram other) => Value == other.Value;
public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is Gram other && Equals(other);
public override int GetHashCode() => Value.GetHashCode();
```

The `Equals(object?)` override matters even though it looks redundant: code
that only knows `object` - the non-generic collections, `object.Equals(a, b)` -
will call it, and if it disagreed with the typed version you would have a type
whose answer depends on how it was asked.

The performance point is worth being able to state. Without `IEquatable<Gram>`,
`HashSet<Gram>.Contains` reaches `Equals(object?)`, which means **boxing** the
struct on every comparison. With it, `EqualityComparer<Gram>.Default` finds the
typed method and no boxing happens at all. That is the single best reason to
implement the interface on a struct.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `HashSet<T>` puts each item in a bucket chosen by its hash code, once, when
the item goes in. It never looks again.

So if the item's hash changes afterwards, every later lookup computes the
*new* hash, goes to the *wrong* bucket, and finds nothing - while the item is
still sitting in the set, counted by `Count`, and reachable only by
enumerating.

## Hint 2

Write the four methods exactly as described - the point is to watch it happen,
not to prevent it:

```csharp
HashSet<MutableKey> set = new HashSet<MutableKey> { key };
key.Name = "changed";
return set.Contains(key);   // false
```

Predict all four answers before you run the gate. The surprising one is
`FoundByOldName`: constructing a *fresh* key with the original name hashes to
the right bucket, but the object living there now has the new name, so `Equals`
says no. The entry is unreachable by any key at all.

The rule this teaches: **anything used as a dictionary key or set member must
be immutable in the parts that decide its hash.** `record` types with `init`
components, `string`, and value tuples of those are safe. A class with public
setters is not, and no amount of care at the call site fixes it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `HashSet<T>` puts each item in a bucket chosen by its hash code, once, when
the item goes in. It never looks again.

So if the item's hash changes afterwards, every later lookup computes the
*new* hash, goes to the *wrong* bucket, and finds nothing - while the item is
still sitting in the set, counted by `Count`, and reachable only by
enumerating.

## Hint 2

Write the four methods exactly as described - the point is to watch it happen,
not to prevent it:

```csharp
HashSet<MutableKey> set = new HashSet<MutableKey> { key };
key.Name = "changed";
return set.Contains(key);   // false
```

Predict all four answers before you run the gate. The surprising one is
`FoundByOldName`: constructing a *fresh* key with the original name hashes to
the right bucket, but the object living there now has the new name, so `Equals`
says no. The entry is unreachable by any key at all.

The rule this teaches: **anything used as a dictionary key or set member must
be immutable in the parts that decide its hash.** `record` types with `init`
components, `string`, and value tuples of those are safe. A class with public
setters is not, and no amount of care at the call site fixes it.

## Exercise 6 - a comparer for someone else's type

`GridCellComparer` treats two `Reading`s as equal when both coordinates
**floor** to the same whole number, and hashes to match.
`Readings.DistinctCells` counts distinct cells with it. Nulls must be handled -
the framework passes them.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`IEqualityComparer<T>` is the answer to "I need a different definition of equal
here, and either the type is not mine to change or it already has a natural
one".

Two methods, one contract: `Equals(x, y)` and `GetHashCode(obj)` must agree,
exactly as an overridden pair must - so derive both from the same value.

## Hint 2

A private helper that produces the comparison value keeps them honest:

```csharp
private static (int, int) Cell(Reading reading) =>
    ((int)Math.Floor(reading.Latitude), (int)Math.Floor(reading.Longitude));
```

Then `Equals` compares two cells and `GetHashCode` hashes one -
`HashCode.Combine(cell.Item1, cell.Item2)` or the tuple's own `GetHashCode`.

`Math.Floor` rather than a cast: casting truncates toward zero, so -1.2 becomes
-1 and lands in the same cell as -1.8 *and* as -0.4. Flooring gives -2, which
is the cell a map would draw.

The framework passes nulls while probing, so handle them: two nulls are equal,
one null is not, and neither may reach `Cell`.

`Distinct(comparer)` is the LINQ overload that takes it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`IEqualityComparer<T>` is the answer to "I need a different definition of equal
here, and either the type is not mine to change or it already has a natural
one".

Two methods, one contract: `Equals(x, y)` and `GetHashCode(obj)` must agree,
exactly as an overridden pair must - so derive both from the same value.

## Hint 2

A private helper that produces the comparison value keeps them honest:

```csharp
private static (int, int) Cell(Reading reading) =>
    ((int)Math.Floor(reading.Latitude), (int)Math.Floor(reading.Longitude));
```

Then `Equals` compares two cells and `GetHashCode` hashes one -
`HashCode.Combine(cell.Item1, cell.Item2)` or the tuple's own `GetHashCode`.

`Math.Floor` rather than a cast: casting truncates toward zero, so -1.2 becomes
-1 and lands in the same cell as -1.8 *and* as -0.4. Flooring gives -2, which
is the cell a map would draw.

The framework passes nulls while probing, so handle them: two nulls are equal,
one null is not, and neither may reach `Cell`.

`Distinct(comparer)` is the LINQ overload that takes it.

## Hint 1

This is the full contract, written out once so you never have to guess again.
Five members, and each has a job:

- `Equals(Money?)` - the real comparison, from `IEquatable<T>`;
- `Equals(object?)` - delegates to it after a type test;
- `GetHashCode()` - built from the same fields;
- `operator ==` - handles nulls, then delegates;
- `operator !=` - `!(left == right)`.

## Hint 2

The operators are where the care goes, because they must not recurse:

```csharp
public static bool operator ==(Money? left, Money? right)
{
    if (left is null) return right is null;
    return left.Equals(right);
}
```

`left is null` rather than `left == null` - the second would call this operator
again and stack-overflow. The `is null` pattern is not sugar here; it is the
only safe test.

`Equals(Money? other)` needs `other is not null` and then the field comparison.
Compare `Currency` with `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` and hash it the
same way - `HashCode.Combine(Amount, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase.GetHashCode(Currency))`.

The class is `sealed`, which is deliberate: it removes the inheritance question
ex8 is about, and it is what lets `Equals` use a simple type test with a clear
conscience.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - equality and inheritance

`Point2.Equals` must use `GetType()` rather than `is`, so a `Point2` and a
`ColouredPoint` holding the same coordinates are never equal - **in either
direction**. `ColouredPoint.Equals` builds on `base.Equals` and adds the
colour. Both hash accordingly.

Edit `src/Lessons/D11_EqualitySemantics/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d11_equality_semantics ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Equality has to be **symmetric**: if `a.Equals(b)` is true then `b.Equals(a)`
must be too. Inheritance is where that breaks, and it breaks in a very specific
way.

Write `Point2.Equals` with `obj is Point2` and see what happens: a `Point2` at
(1,2) considers a red `ColouredPoint` at (1,2) equal, while the coloured point
does not agree. Then fix it.

## Hint 2

The fix is to compare the runtime types exactly:

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj)
{
    if (obj is null || GetType() != obj.GetType()) return false;
    Point2 other = (Point2)obj;
    return X == other.X && Y == other.Y;
}
```

`GetType() != obj.GetType()` is what makes a base instance and a derived one
never equal, in either direction - so symmetry holds however the comparison is
written.

`ColouredPoint.Equals` can then lean on it:

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj) =>
    base.Equals(obj) && Colour == ((ColouredPoint)obj!).Colour;
```

because `base.Equals` has already established that the runtime types match.

Hash codes must follow: `HashCode.Combine(base.GetHashCode(), Colour)`.

Left to you: `GetType()` equality also means a proxy or a subclass added for
testing is never equal to the thing it stands for. That is a real cost, and it
is a large part of why `record` picks the same rule and why value types are
usually `sealed`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Equality has to be **symmetric**: if `a.Equals(b)` is true then `b.Equals(a)`
must be too. Inheritance is where that breaks, and it breaks in a very specific
way.

Write `Point2.Equals` with `obj is Point2` and see what happens: a `Point2` at
(1,2) considers a red `ColouredPoint` at (1,2) equal, while the coloured point
does not agree. Then fix it.

## Hint 2

The fix is to compare the runtime types exactly:

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj)
{
    if (obj is null || GetType() != obj.GetType()) return false;
    Point2 other = (Point2)obj;
    return X == other.X && Y == other.Y;
}
```

`GetType() != obj.GetType()` is what makes a base instance and a derived one
never equal, in either direction - so symmetry holds however the comparison is
written.

`ColouredPoint.Equals` can then lean on it:

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj) =>
    base.Equals(obj) && Colour == ((ColouredPoint)obj!).Colour;
```

because `base.Equals` has already established that the runtime types match.

Hash codes must follow: `HashCode.Combine(base.GetHashCode(), Colour)`.

Left to you: `GetType()` equality also means a proxy or a subclass added for
testing is never equal to the thing it stands for. That is a real cost, and it
is a large part of why `record` picks the same rule and why value types are
usually `sealed`.

# d12 - Generics drills

Eight problems on writing code once for every type: generic methods, a generic
type with two parameters, the `class` / `struct` / `notnull` constraints,
`IComparable<T>` as a constraint, `new()` and a pool, several type parameters
with delegates, a memo, and a histogram with a tie-break. They drill lesson 07
- reread `07_generics` if constraints are still unfamiliar.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - generic methods

`Sequences.Repeat<T>(item, count)` returns a list of `count` copies, and an
empty list for a count of 0 or less. `Sequences.Interleave<T>(a, b)` takes from
each sequence in turn - `a1, b1, a2, b2, ...` - and then whatever is left of
the longer one.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - a generic type of your own

`Pair<TFirst, TSecond>` with `First`, `Second`, a `ToString` of
`"(a, b)"`, and `Swapped()` returning a `Pair<TSecond, TFirst>`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - three constraints

`Defaults.RefOrFallback<TRef>` (`where TRef : class`),
`Defaults.ValueOrFallback<TVal>` (`where TVal : struct`) and
`Defaults.CountBy<TKey>` (`where TKey : notnull`), which counts how many times
each key appears.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - constrained to be comparable

`Range<T> where T : IComparable<T>` with inclusive `Contains`, `Clamp` and
`Overlaps`. A low above the high is an `ArgumentException`. Everything is built
from `CompareTo` - `<` and `>` are not available on an unconstrained `T`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - the `new()` constraint

`Pool<T> where T : class, new()` with `Rent()`, `Return(item)`, `Created` and
`Available`. `Rent` reuses a returned instance before constructing a new one,
and throws `InvalidOperationException` when it would exceed its maximum.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - several type parameters

`Maps.Map<TSource, TResult>(items, selector)` projects a sequence.
`Maps.ToDictionary<TSource, TKey, TValue>(items, key, value)` builds a
dictionary in which a repeated key keeps the **later** value. Both infer every
type parameter from the arguments.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - a memo

`Memo<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull` with
`GetOrAdd(key, Func<TKey, TValue> factory)`, `Count` and `FactoryCalls`. The
factory runs once per key; a factory that throws must leave the memo unchanged
so the next call tries again.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a histogram with a tie-break

`Histogram<TKey> where TKey : notnull` with `Add(key)`, `CountOf(key)`,
`Distinct` and `TopKeys(n)`. Keys come back most frequent first, and keys with
the same count come back in the order they were **first seen**.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex8
```
