# Reading - csharp/d12_generics

## Notes

Generics let you write an algorithm once and have the compiler check it for
every type it will ever be used with. The mechanism is simple and the skill is
entirely in the **constraints**: a type parameter with no constraint is almost
useless (you may store it, pass it, and compare it with null), and every
constraint you add buys you exactly one more thing you may do.

That is the pattern running through all eight problems. `IComparable<T>` buys
`CompareTo`. `new()` buys `new T()`. `notnull` buys the right to be a
dictionary key. `class` and `struct` decide what `T?` even means. The design
question is always the same: what is the *smallest* promise this code needs?
Ask for more and you shut out callers; ask for less and you cannot write the
body.

The second thread is that .NET generics are real at run time, not erased.
`List<int>` is a distinct type with no boxing, `typeof(T)` works, and a
constraint is enforced by the runtime as well as the compiler. That is why
generic code in C# is fast rather than merely convenient - and why
`EqualityComparer<T>.Default` can find your `IEquatable<T>` implementation and
skip the boxing entirely.

## ex1

Really testing: that an unconstrained `T` is enough for anything that only
moves values around. Neither method inspects a `T` at all, so neither needs a
constraint - and adding one "just in case" would narrow the method for no
benefit. `Interleave` is the interesting half: it needs two enumerators
advanced independently, which `foreach` cannot express, so it drops to
`GetEnumerator` and `MoveNext`. The `using` on each enumerator is not optional
politeness - `IEnumerator<T>` is `IDisposable`, `foreach` disposes it for you,
and hand-written iteration has to do it itself.

## ex2

Really testing: a generic type with two parameters, and what happens when a
member reorders them. `Swapped()` returning `Pair<TSecond, TFirst>` looks
exotic and is ordinary substitution. The thing worth internalising is that
`Pair<int, string>` and `Pair<string, int>` are genuinely different types at run
time, with different static fields and no conversion between them - unlike
Java, where erasure makes them the same class. The naming convention (`TFirst`,
`TKey`, `TResult`) is a real readability tool once a signature has three of
them.

## ex3

Really testing: that `class`, `struct` and `notnull` are three different
promises. The one that catches people is that `T?` means different things under
each: an annotation on a reference type under `class`, `Nullable<T>` under
`struct`, and nothing at all without one. The other lesson is structural -
constraints do **not** participate in overload resolution, so two methods
differing only by constraint will not compile, which is why the two fallback
methods here have different names. `notnull` is worth knowing precisely: it is
a nullability constraint enforced by the compiler's flow analysis, not a
runtime check, and it exists because `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` demands it.

## ex4

Really testing: building an entire type out of one constrained member.
Everything in `Range<T>` is `CompareTo`, because `<` and `>` are not available
on a `T` the compiler knows nothing about. The classic mistake is getting a
comparison the wrong way round - it compiles perfectly and inverts the answer -
which is why reading each line out loud as a sentence is worth the ten seconds.
`Overlaps` rewards thinking about the negation: "they do not overlap when one
ends before the other begins", negated, is shorter and easier to check than
enumerating the overlapping cases.

## ex5

Really testing: the `new()` constraint, and one ordering decision. `new T()` is
only legal because of the constraint, and it compiles to an
`Activator.CreateInstance`-shaped call rather than a direct `newobj` - which is
why `new()` has a small but real cost and why a `Func<T>` factory parameter is
often the better design. The ordering matters: check the free list before the
limit, or a pool sitting at its maximum refuses to hand back an object it
already owns. `InvalidOperationException` is the right type for the same reason
as d05 ex8 - the arguments were fine, the object's state was not.

## ex6

Really testing: several type parameters at once, and delegates as parameters.
Every parameter here is inferred from the arguments, so callers never write
angle brackets - which is exactly how LINQ reads. The decision worth being
deliberate about is the duplicate key: this specification says the later value
wins (`dictionary[key] = value`), while LINQ's own `ToDictionary` throws. Both
are defensible and the surprise is expensive, so a method like this should say
which it does in its documentation - and this one does.

## ex7

Really testing: memoisation, which is d09 ex8's caching decorator generalised
to any key and value. The two details that separate a correct implementation
from a plausible one: the factory is called *outside* the dictionary write, so
a throwing factory leaves the memo unchanged and the next call retries; and
`FactoryCalls` counts real invocations, so the gate can prove the second lookup
did not recompute. The honest limitation is worth stating in an interview: a
memo with no eviction policy is a memory leak with a friendly name, and the
production versions add a size bound, an LRU policy or weak references.

## ex8

Really testing: counting, plus an ordering requirement a dictionary cannot
satisfy. `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` promises no enumeration order at all, so
"ties broken by first seen" needs the insertion order recorded separately. The
elegant part is that LINQ's `OrderByDescending` is a **stable** sort - equal
elements keep their input order - so ordering the first-seen list by count
gives the tie-break for free. That stability is a documented guarantee of the
LINQ `OrderBy` family and explicitly *not* of `List<T>.Sort` or `Array.Sort`,
and knowing which sorts are stable is the kind of detail that separates a
correct report from one that changes between runs.

## Further reading

- [Generics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) - the feature, from the top.
- [Constraints on type parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters) - every constraint and what it buys.
- [Generic methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/generic-methods) - declaration and type inference.
- [Differences between C++ templates and C# generics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/differences-between-cpp-templates-and-csharp-generics) - why .NET generics are real at run time.
- [`Func<T, TResult>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.func-2) - the delegate ex6 and ex7 take.
- [Sorting data with LINQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/sorting-data) - including the stability guarantee.

differing only by constraint will not compile, which is why the two fallback
methods here have different names. `notnull` is worth knowing precisely: it is
a nullability constraint enforced by the compiler's flow analysis, not a
runtime check, and it exists because `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` demands it.

## ex4

Really testing: building an entire type out of one constrained member.
Everything in `Range<T>` is `CompareTo`, because `<` and `>` are not available
on a `T` the compiler knows nothing about. The classic mistake is getting a
comparison the wrong way round - it compiles perfectly and inverts the answer -
which is why reading each line out loud as a sentence is worth the ten seconds.
`Overlaps` rewards thinking about the negation: "they do not overlap when one
ends before the other begins", negated, is shorter and easier to check than
enumerating the overlapping cases.

## ex5

Really testing: the `new()` constraint, and one ordering decision. `new T()` is
only legal because of the constraint, and it compiles to an
`Activator.CreateInstance`-shaped call rather than a direct `newobj` - which is
why `new()` has a small but real cost and why a `Func<T>` factory parameter is
often the better design. The ordering matters: check the free list before the
limit, or a pool sitting at its maximum refuses to hand back an object it
already owns. `InvalidOperationException` is the right type for the same reason
as d05 ex8 - the arguments were fine, the object's state was not.

## ex6

Really testing: several type parameters at once, and delegates as parameters.
Every parameter here is inferred from the arguments, so callers never write
angle brackets - which is exactly how LINQ reads. The decision worth being
deliberate about is the duplicate key: this specification says the later value
wins (`dictionary[key] = value`), while LINQ's own `ToDictionary` throws. Both
are defensible and the surprise is expensive, so a method like this should say
which it does in its documentation - and this one does.

## ex7

Really testing: memoisation, which is d09 ex8's caching decorator generalised
to any key and value. The two details that separate a correct implementation
from a plausible one: the factory is called *outside* the dictionary write, so
a throwing factory leaves the memo unchanged and the next call retries; and
`FactoryCalls` counts real invocations, so the gate can prove the second lookup
did not recompute. The honest limitation is worth stating in an interview: a
memo with no eviction policy is a memory leak with a friendly name, and the
production versions add a size bound, an LRU policy or weak references.

## ex8

Really testing: counting, plus an ordering requirement a dictionary cannot
satisfy. `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` promises no enumeration order at all, so
"ties broken by first seen" needs the insertion order recorded separately. The
elegant part is that LINQ's `OrderByDescending` is a **stable** sort - equal
elements keep their input order - so ordering the first-seen list by count
gives the tie-break for free. That stability is a documented guarantee of the
LINQ `OrderBy` family and explicitly *not* of `List<T>.Sort` or `Array.Sort`,
and knowing which sorts are stable is the kind of detail that separates a
correct report from one that changes between runs.

- [Constraints on type parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters) - every constraint and what it buys.
- [Generic methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/generic-methods) - declaration and type inference.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - generic methods

`Sequences.Repeat<T>(item, count)` returns a list of `count` copies, and an
empty list for a count of 0 or less. `Sequences.Interleave<T>(a, b)` takes from
each sequence in turn - `a1, b1, a2, b2, ...` - and then whatever is left of
the longer one.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A generic method declares its type parameter after the name -
`Repeat<T>(T item, int count)` - and then treats `T` as an ordinary type it
knows nothing about. That is the point: with no constraint you may store a `T`,
pass it around and compare it with `null`, and nothing else.

Neither method here needs to know anything about `T`.

## Hint 2

`Repeat` is a `for` loop adding `item` to a `List<T>`. A count of 0 or less
needs no guard - the loop condition is already false.

`Interleave` needs two enumerators advanced in step:

```csharp
using IEnumerator<T> left = a.GetEnumerator();
using IEnumerator<T> right = b.GetEnumerator();
bool hasLeft = left.MoveNext();
bool hasRight = right.MoveNext();
while (hasLeft || hasRight) { ... }
```

Take from each side when it still has something, then advance that side. The
`using` matters: `IEnumerator<T>` is `IDisposable`, and a `foreach` would
normally dispose it for you.

Left to you: two indexed loops over `ToList()` copies would also work and is
easier to read. It costs an allocation and it will not work on an infinite
sequence. Know which trade you made.

## Hint 1

A generic method declares its type parameter after the name -
`Repeat<T>(T item, int count)` - and then treats `T` as an ordinary type it
knows nothing about. That is the point: with no constraint you may store a `T`,
pass it around and compare it with `null`, and nothing else.

Neither method here needs to know anything about `T`.

## Hint 2

`Repeat` is a `for` loop adding `item` to a `List<T>`. A count of 0 or less
needs no guard - the loop condition is already false.

`Interleave` needs two enumerators advanced in step:

```csharp
using IEnumerator<T> left = a.GetEnumerator();
using IEnumerator<T> right = b.GetEnumerator();
bool hasLeft = left.MoveNext();
bool hasRight = right.MoveNext();
while (hasLeft || hasRight) { ... }
```

Take from each side when it still has something, then advance that side. The
`using` matters: `IEnumerator<T>` is `IDisposable`, and a `foreach` would
normally dispose it for you.

Left to you: two indexed loops over `ToList()` copies would also work and is
easier to read. It costs an allocation and it will not work on an infinite
sequence. Know which trade you made.

## Hint 1

A generic *type* puts the parameters on the class: `Pair<TFirst, TSecond>`.
Every member can then use them, and every distinct set of arguments -
`Pair<int, string>`, `Pair<string, int>` - is a genuinely different type at run
time.

`Swapped()` is the interesting member, because its return type is
`Pair<TSecond, TFirst>` - the same generic type with the arguments the other
way round.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public Pair<TSecond, TFirst> Swapped() => new Pair<TSecond, TFirst>(Second, First);
```

Nothing clever is needed; the compiler simply substitutes.

`ToString` is `$"({First}, {Second})"`. Interpolation calls `ToString` on each
component, and for a `T` that is null it produces the empty string rather than
throwing - which is worth knowing before you write a null check that never
fires.

Naming convention: type parameters start with `T`, and when there is more than
one they get descriptive names (`TFirst`, `TKey`, `TResult`). A bare `T` is
fine when there is only one and its role is obvious.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three constraints, three different promises:

- `where T : class` - T is a reference type, so `T?` means "may be null".
- `where T : struct` - T is a non-nullable value type, so `T?` means
  `Nullable<T>` and brings `HasValue` with it.
- `where T : notnull` - T may be either, but never a nullable one. This is what
  `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` requires of its key.

The two fallback methods have different names precisely because constraints do
**not** participate in overload resolution - two methods differing only by
constraint will not compile.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static TRef RefOrFallback<TRef>(TRef? value, TRef fallback) where TRef : class
    => value ?? fallback;

public static TVal ValueOrFallback<TVal>(TVal? value, TVal fallback) where TVal : struct
    => value ?? fallback;
```

They look identical and are not: in the first `TRef?` is an annotation on a
reference type, in the second `TVal?` is `Nullable<TVal>`, a different type
with a different `??`.

`CountBy` is a dictionary and a loop:

```csharp
counts[key] = counts.TryGetValue(key, out int existing) ? existing + 1 : 1;
```

The `notnull` constraint is what lets `TKey` be a dictionary key without a
warning. It is worth understanding that this is a *nullability* constraint, not

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three constraints, three different promises:

- `where T : class` - T is a reference type, so `T?` means "may be null".
- `where T : struct` - T is a non-nullable value type, so `T?` means
  `Nullable<T>` and brings `HasValue` with it.
- `where T : notnull` - T may be either, but never a nullable one. This is what
  `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` requires of its key.

The two fallback methods have different names precisely because constraints do
**not** participate in overload resolution - two methods differing only by
constraint will not compile.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static TRef RefOrFallback<TRef>(TRef? value, TRef fallback) where TRef : class
    => value ?? fallback;

public static TVal ValueOrFallback<TVal>(TVal? value, TVal fallback) where TVal : struct
    => value ?? fallback;
```

They look identical and are not: in the first `TRef?` is an annotation on a
reference type, in the second `TVal?` is `Nullable<TVal>`, a different type
with a different `??`.

`CountBy` is a dictionary and a loop:

```csharp
counts[key] = counts.TryGetValue(key, out int existing) ? existing + 1 : 1;
```

The `notnull` constraint is what lets `TKey` be a dictionary key without a
warning. It is worth understanding that this is a *nullability* constraint, not
a runtime one - it is enforced by the compiler's flow analysis, not by a check.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`where T : IComparable<T>` buys you exactly one member: `CompareTo`. Everything
in this class is built from it.

`a.CompareTo(b)` is negative when a comes first, 0 when they are equivalent,
positive when b comes first. Write the three methods in terms of that and do
not reach for `<` or `>`, which are not available on an unconstrained `T`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public bool Contains(T value) =>
    Low.CompareTo(value) <= 0 && High.CompareTo(value) >= 0;
```

Both bounds are inclusive, so both comparisons include the 0 case. Read that
line out loud - "Low is at or before value, and High is at or after it" - to
check the direction, because getting a `CompareTo` the wrong way round compiles
perfectly and inverts the answer.

`Clamp` returns `Low` when the value is below it, `High` when above, and the
value otherwise.

`Overlaps` is the one worth thinking about. The clean way is to ask when they
*do not* overlap - one ends entirely before the other begins - and negate:

```csharp
return Low.CompareTo(other.High) <= 0 && other.Low.CompareTo(High) <= 0;
```

Left to you: whether a range where `Low` equals `High` is legal. This one
allows it; a half-open range design usually would not, and the difference
matters as soon as you start joining ranges together.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`where T : IComparable<T>` buys you exactly one member: `CompareTo`. Everything
in this class is built from it.

`a.CompareTo(b)` is negative when a comes first, 0 when they are equivalent,
positive when b comes first. Write the three methods in terms of that and do
not reach for `<` or `>`, which are not available on an unconstrained `T`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public bool Contains(T value) =>
    Low.CompareTo(value) <= 0 && High.CompareTo(value) >= 0;
```

Both bounds are inclusive, so both comparisons include the 0 case. Read that
line out loud - "Low is at or before value, and High is at or after it" - to
check the direction, because getting a `CompareTo` the wrong way round compiles
perfectly and inverts the answer.

`Clamp` returns `Low` when the value is below it, `High` when above, and the
value otherwise.

`Overlaps` is the one worth thinking about. The clean way is to ask when they
*do not* overlap - one ends entirely before the other begins - and negate:

```csharp
return Low.CompareTo(other.High) <= 0 && other.Low.CompareTo(High) <= 0;
```

Left to you: whether a range where `Low` equals `High` is legal. This one
allows it; a half-open range design usually would not, and the difference
matters as soon as you start joining ranges together.

## Hint 1

`where T : class, new()` says T is a reference type with a public parameterless
constructor - which is what lets the pool write `new T()` without knowing
anything else about it.

The pool needs two counters and one stack of returned items. `Rent` either
reuses something returned earlier or makes a new one; `Return` puts it back.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (_available.Count > 0) return _available.Pop();
if (Created >= _max) throw new InvalidOperationException("The pool is exhausted.");
Created++;
return new T();
```

The order matters: check the free list *before* the limit, or a pool at its
maximum refuses to hand back something it already owns.

`Created` counts objects ever constructed, not objects currently out - which is
what makes the gate able to see that renting, returning and renting again
constructs only once.

`InvalidOperationException` rather than an argument exception, for the reason
from d05 ex8: every argument was fine, the *object's state* is the problem.

Left to you: what `Return` should do with an item the pool never created, or
with the same item twice. Real pools either track ownership or document that
double-returning is undefined; nothing here checks, and knowing that is part of
the answer.

## Exercise 6 - several type parameters

`Maps.Map<TSource, TResult>(items, selector)` projects a sequence.
`Maps.ToDictionary<TSource, TKey, TValue>(items, key, value)` builds a
dictionary in which a repeated key keeps the **later** value. Both infer every
type parameter from the arguments.

Edit `src/Lessons/D12_Generics/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d12_generics ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods have more than one type parameter, and the compiler infers all of
them from the arguments - so callers write `Maps.Map(items, x => x.Length)`
with no angle brackets at all.

`Func<TSource, TResult>` is a delegate: a method passed as a value. Calling it
is ordinary call syntax - `selector(item)`.

## Hint 2

`Map` is a loop:

```csharp
List<TResult> results = new List<TResult>();
foreach (TSource item in items) results.Add(selector(item));
return results;
```

`ToDictionary` is the same loop with two projections, and one decision to make:
what happens on a duplicate key. The specification here says the later entry
wins, which is `dictionary[key(item)] = value(item);` - the indexer replaces.
`Add` would throw instead, and LINQ's own `ToDictionary` does exactly that,
which is worth knowing before it surprises you in production.

The `where TKey : notnull` constraint is required because
`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` demands it. Constraints propagate: a generic method
that uses a constrained type must repeat the constraint.

Note how much the type parameters are doing for readability here. `TSource`,
`TKey`, `TValue` and `TResult` are the BCL's own names for these roles, and
following them makes a signature readable at a glance.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods have more than one type parameter, and the compiler infers all of
them from the arguments - so callers write `Maps.Map(items, x => x.Length)`
with no angle brackets at all.

`Func<TSource, TResult>` is a delegate: a method passed as a value. Calling it
is ordinary call syntax - `selector(item)`.

## Hint 2

`Map` is a loop:

```csharp
List<TResult> results = new List<TResult>();
foreach (TSource item in items) results.Add(selector(item));
return results;
```

`ToDictionary` is the same loop with two projections, and one decision to make:
what happens on a duplicate key. The specification here says the later entry
wins, which is `dictionary[key(item)] = value(item);` - the indexer replaces.
`Add` would throw instead, and LINQ's own `ToDictionary` does exactly that,
which is worth knowing before it surprises you in production.

The `where TKey : notnull` constraint is required because
`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` demands it. Constraints propagate: a generic method
that uses a constrained type must repeat the constraint.

Note how much the type parameters are doing for readability here. `TSource`,
`TKey`, `TValue` and `TResult` are the BCL's own names for these roles, and
following them makes a signature readable at a glance.

## Exercise 7 - a memo

`GetOrAdd(key, Func<TKey, TValue> factory)`, `Count` and `FactoryCalls`. The
factory runs once per key; a factory that throws must leave the memo unchanged

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`GetOrAdd(key, factory)` is the whole class: look the key up; if it is there,
return it; if not, call the factory, store the answer, return it.

The factory takes the key and returns a value - `Func<TKey, TValue>` - which is
what lets one memo serve many keys with a single function.

`FactoryCalls` must count only the times the factory really ran.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (_values.TryGetValue(key, out TValue? existing)) return existing;
FactoryCalls++;
TValue created = factory(key);
_values[key] = created;
return created;
```

Two details worth defending. First, the factory is called *outside* the
dictionary write, so a factory that throws leaves the memo unchanged and the
next call tries again - the same rule as d09 ex8's caching decorator. Second,
`FactoryCalls` is incremented before the call rather than after, so a throwing
factory still counts as an attempt; incrementing afterwards would be equally
defensible and you should know which you chose.

`where TKey : notnull` is required by `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`.

Left to you: this memo never forgets, which for an unbounded key space is a
memory leak with a friendly name. Say what you would add - a size limit, an
LRU policy, weak references - and why you did not add it here.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`GetOrAdd(key, factory)` is the whole class: look the key up; if it is there,
return it; if not, call the factory, store the answer, return it.

The factory takes the key and returns a value - `Func<TKey, TValue>` - which is
what lets one memo serve many keys with a single function.

`FactoryCalls` must count only the times the factory really ran.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (_values.TryGetValue(key, out TValue? existing)) return existing;
FactoryCalls++;
TValue created = factory(key);
_values[key] = created;
return created;
```

Two details worth defending. First, the factory is called *outside* the
dictionary write, so a factory that throws leaves the memo unchanged and the
next call tries again - the same rule as d09 ex8's caching decorator. Second,
`FactoryCalls` is incremented before the call rather than after, so a throwing
factory still counts as an attempt; incrementing afterwards would be equally
defensible and you should know which you chose.

`where TKey : notnull` is required by `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`.

Left to you: this memo never forgets, which for an unbounded key space is a
memory leak with a friendly name. Say what you would add - a size limit, an
LRU policy, weak references - and why you did not add it here.

# d13 - Lists and dictionaries drills

Eight problems on the two collections you will use every day: positional
surgery on a `List`, add-or-accumulate and add-or-overwrite on a `Dictionary`,
sorting in place versus sorting a copy, safe removal, tuple keys, nested
dictionaries, and the dictionary-powered two-sum. They drill lesson 08 - reread
`08_collections` if `TryGetValue` is not yet reflex.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/`. Nothing here depends
on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - insert, remove, and the indexes

`Agenda.MoveToTop` pulls an item to index 0 (false and no change when absent),
`AddAfter` inserts right after an anchor (or appends when the anchor is
missing), and `Swap` exchanges two positions. `IndexOf`, `Insert`, `RemoveAt`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - a counting dictionary with a remove rule

`Stockroom.Restock` accumulates delivered quantities per item (zero or
negative throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`). `Take` refuses (false, no
change) when there is not enough - and when a take empties a line exactly, the
key comes OUT of the dictionary.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - Add, overwrite, and TryAdd

`Roster.Assign` is add-or-move (the indexer). `AssignNew` is only-if-absent and
reports which happened (`TryAdd`, or `ContainsKey` then `Add`). `OccupantsOf`
answers "who is in this office?", which means scanning the values, A-Z.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - sorting in place and sorting a copy

Same ordering rule twice - score descending, player A-Z on ties - with
opposite contracts. `Leaderboard.SortInPlace` mutates via `List.Sort` and a
`Comparison<Entry>`; `Ranked` hands back a new list and leaves the caller's
alone.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - removing without tripping the enumerator

`Cleanup.DropBelow` removes every dictionary entry under a minimum - and
removing while foreach-ing the same dictionary throws, so collect the doomed
keys first. `DropWhere` is the `List` version, where `RemoveAll` does the whole
job and tells you how many went.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - a tuple is a perfectly good key

Route prices keyed by `(From, To)`. `Fares.Set` overwrites, `PriceOf` answers
null for a route not on file, and `CheapestFrom` scans one origin's routes for
the lowest price, destination A-Z on ties. `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` are different
keys - the gate checks you know that.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - a dictionary inside a dictionary

A gradebook: student -> subject -> score. `Gradebook.Record` creates the inner
dictionary on first sight and keeps the latest score. `ScoreOf` survives a miss
at either level. `SubjectAverage` averages over exactly the students who have
that subject, and throws `InvalidOperationException` when nobody does.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - two numbers that sum to a target

The interview classic. `PairFinder.FirstPairSummingTo` returns the positions of
the pair whose second position comes earliest (partnered with the earliest
earlier match), null when there is none - in ONE pass with a dictionary of
"value -> earliest position seen". `HasPairSummingTo` is the yes/no form.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex8
```

# Reading - csharp/d13_lists_dictionaries

## Notes

The skill this set drills is picking the operation that matches the question,
and knowing each operation's edge behaviour cold: what `IndexOf` says on a
miss, what the indexer does that `Add` does not, what happens when you remove
while enumerating. A `List` is about *positions* - insert here, remove there,
everything behind shifts. A `Dictionary` is about *keys* - and nearly every
dictionary bug in real code is one of three misses: indexing a key that is not
there, `Add`-ing a key that is, or mutating the collection mid-walk. The
pattern uniting the eight problems: decide what the missing case means
(`false`, `null`, zero, empty list, or an exception) before writing the happy
path, because the gate always probes the miss.

## ex1

Really testing: that `List` positions are live - `Insert` shifts everything
behind it, and an index from `IndexOf` is only valid until the next mutation.
The classic mistake is `AddAfter` on a missing anchor: `IndexOf` answers -1,
and blindly inserting at `-1 + 1` puts the item at the FRONT, which looks
almost right in a short test and is wrong. The model answer checks the -1
first, appends on a miss, and lets the list's own indexer guard `Swap` -
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` is already the correct exception, so adding your
own guard would only duplicate it.

## ex2

Really testing: the add-or-accumulate idiom and a deliberate remove rule.
`stock[item] = stock.GetValueOrDefault(item) + quantity` handles first-sight
and top-up in one line. The classic mistake is in `Take`: checking and
mutating in the wrong order, so a refused take still decrements, or leaving a
zero-quantity line in place. The model answer reads once with `TryGetValue`,
refuses early, and treats exact-empty as `Remove` - because "we stock zero
washers" and "we do not stock washers" must be indistinguishable to callers.

## ex3

Really testing: the three write operations and what each promises. The indexer
means "make it so" (add or overwrite), `Add` means "this must be new" (throws
otherwise), and `TryAdd` means "only if absent, and tell me". The classic
mistake is using `Add` for a re-assignment and meeting `ArgumentException` at
runtime. `OccupantsOf` makes the other point of the exercise: a dictionary
answers person -> office instantly, but office -> people means scanning every
pair - a dictionary is one-directional, and querying against the grain is a
linear walk (or a second dictionary, which is ex7's shape).

## ex4

Really testing: the mutate-versus-copy contract. `List.Sort` rearranges the
caller's list and returns nothing; `OrderBy...ToList()` builds a new one and
touches nothing. The classic mistake is sorting the caller's data when they
only wanted a ranked view - a bug callers find much later, far from the call.
The second skill is writing a `Comparison<Entry>`: negative, zero, positive.
Descending scores is `b.Score.CompareTo(a.Score)` - swap the operands, do not
negate the result (negating breaks on int.MinValue in the general case, and
reads worse). Ties fall through to an ordinal name comparison.

## ex5

Really testing: the remove-while-enumerating rule. `foreach` over a dictionary
while removing from it throws `InvalidOperationException`, so the model answer
materialises the doomed keys with `ToList()` - the snapshot ends the
enumeration before the mutation starts - then removes by key. For the `List`,
`RemoveAll` exists precisely so you do not write the backwards-index loop by
hand, and it returns the count the exercise asks for. The classic mistake is
`foreach (var pair in readings) readings.Remove(pair.Key)` which fails at
runtime, on the second iteration, only when something matched.

## ex6

Really testing: that value tuples make composite keys trivial. Tuples compare
by position with value equality and hash accordingly, so `(from, to)` just

# Reading - csharp/d13_lists_dictionaries

## Notes

The skill this set drills is picking the operation that matches the question,
and knowing each operation's edge behaviour cold: what `IndexOf` says on a
miss, what the indexer does that `Add` does not, what happens when you remove
while enumerating. A `List` is about *positions* - insert here, remove there,
everything behind shifts. A `Dictionary` is about *keys* - and nearly every
dictionary bug in real code is one of three misses: indexing a key that is not
there, `Add`-ing a key that is, or mutating the collection mid-walk. The
pattern uniting the eight problems: decide what the missing case means
(`false`, `null`, zero, empty list, or an exception) before writing the happy
path, because the gate always probes the miss.

## ex1

Really testing: that `List` positions are live - `Insert` shifts everything
behind it, and an index from `IndexOf` is only valid until the next mutation.
The classic mistake is `AddAfter` on a missing anchor: `IndexOf` answers -1,
and blindly inserting at `-1 + 1` puts the item at the FRONT, which looks
almost right in a short test and is wrong. The model answer checks the -1
first, appends on a miss, and lets the list's own indexer guard `Swap` -
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` is already the correct exception, so adding your
own guard would only duplicate it.

## ex2

Really testing: the add-or-accumulate idiom and a deliberate remove rule.
`stock[item] = stock.GetValueOrDefault(item) + quantity` handles first-sight
and top-up in one line. The classic mistake is in `Take`: checking and
mutating in the wrong order, so a refused take still decrements, or leaving a
zero-quantity line in place. The model answer reads once with `TryGetValue`,
refuses early, and treats exact-empty as `Remove` - because "we stock zero
washers" and "we do not stock washers" must be indistinguishable to callers.

## ex3

Really testing: the three write operations and what each promises. The indexer
means "make it so" (add or overwrite), `Add` means "this must be new" (throws
otherwise), and `TryAdd` means "only if absent, and tell me". The classic
mistake is using `Add` for a re-assignment and meeting `ArgumentException` at
runtime. `OccupantsOf` makes the other point of the exercise: a dictionary
answers person -> office instantly, but office -> people means scanning every
pair - a dictionary is one-directional, and querying against the grain is a
linear walk (or a second dictionary, which is ex7's shape).

caller's list and returns nothing; `OrderBy...ToList()` builds a new one and
touches nothing. The classic mistake is sorting the caller's data when they
only wanted a ranked view - a bug callers find much later, far from the call.

negate the result (negating breaks on int.MinValue in the general case, and
reads worse). Ties fall through to an ordinal name comparison.

while removing from it throws `InvalidOperationException`, so the model answer
materialises the doomed keys with `ToList()` - the snapshot ends the
enumeration before the mutation starts - then removes by key. For the `List`,

runtime, on the second iteration, only when something matched.

## Exercise 1 - insert, remove, and the indexes

`Agenda.MoveToTop` pulls an item to index 0 (false and no change when absent),
`AddAfter` inserts right after an anchor (or appends when the anchor is
missing), and `Swap` exchanges two positions. `IndexOf`, `Insert`, `RemoveAt`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three `List` members do all the work: `IndexOf` (answers -1 on a miss),
`RemoveAt`, and `Insert`. `MoveToTop` is remove-then-insert-at-0; `AddAfter`
is insert at anchor's index + 1 - but only when the anchor was actually found.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int index = items.IndexOf(anchor);
if (index < 0) { items.Add(item); } else { items.Insert(index + 1, item); }
```

For `Swap`, save one value in a local before overwriting (or use tuple
assignment: `(items[i], items[j]) = (items[j], items[i]);`). Do not guard the
indexes yourself - the indexer already throws the right exception.

## Hint 1

Three `List` members do all the work: `IndexOf` (answers -1 on a miss),
`RemoveAt`, and `Insert`. `MoveToTop` is remove-then-insert-at-0; `AddAfter`
is insert at anchor's index + 1 - but only when the anchor was actually found.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int index = items.IndexOf(anchor);
if (index < 0) { items.Add(item); } else { items.Insert(index + 1, item); }
```

For `Swap`, save one value in a local before overwriting (or use tuple
assignment: `(items[i], items[j]) = (items[j], items[i]);`). Do not guard the
indexes yourself - the indexer already throws the right exception.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - a counting dictionary with a remove rule

`Stockroom.Restock` accumulates delivered quantities per item (zero or
negative throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`). `Take` refuses (false, no
change) when there is not enough - and when a take empties a line exactly, the
key comes OUT of the dictionary.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Restock is the add-or-accumulate idiom: read the current count treating a
missing key as 0, add, write back through the indexer. `GetValueOrDefault`
gives you the 0 for free. Take must decide everything BEFORE mutating: read
once, refuse if missing or short, then either subtract or remove the key.

## Hint 2

```csharp
stock[item] = stock.GetValueOrDefault(item) + quantity;
```

In `Take`, `TryGetValue(item, out int available)` answers both "is it there?"
and "how many?". Refuse when it is absent or `available < quantity`. When
`available == quantity`, call `stock.Remove(item)` instead of writing a zero.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Restock is the add-or-accumulate idiom: read the current count treating a
missing key as 0, add, write back through the indexer. `GetValueOrDefault`
gives you the 0 for free. Take must decide everything BEFORE mutating: read
once, refuse if missing or short, then either subtract or remove the key.

## Hint 2

```csharp
stock[item] = stock.GetValueOrDefault(item) + quantity;
```

In `Take`, `TryGetValue(item, out int available)` answers both "is it there?"
and "how many?". Refuse when it is absent or `available < quantity`. When
`available == quantity`, call `stock.Remove(item)` instead of writing a zero.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two tools, two contracts. `List.Sort(Comparison<Entry>)` rearranges the
caller's list in place. `OrderByDescending(...).ThenBy(...).ToList()` builds a
NEW list and leaves the source alone. The gate checks both directions - if
`Ranked` uses `Sort` on the input, the "original untouched" assert catches it.

A `Comparison<Entry>` returns negative / zero / positive. Descending by score
means comparing the arguments in reverse order:

```csharp
entries.Sort((a, b) => a.Score != b.Score
    ? b.Score.CompareTo(a.Score)
    : string.CompareOrdinal(a.Player, b.Player));
```

Two tools, two contracts. `List.Sort(Comparison<Entry>)` rearranges the
caller's list in place. `OrderByDescending(...).ThenBy(...).ToList()` builds a
NEW list and leaves the source alone. The gate checks both directions - if
`Ranked` uses `Sort` on the input, the "original untouched" assert catches it.

## Hint 2

A `Comparison<Entry>` returns negative / zero / positive. Descending by score
means comparing the arguments in reverse order:

```csharp
entries.Sort((a, b) => a.Score != b.Score
    ? b.Score.CompareTo(a.Score)
    : string.CompareOrdinal(a.Player, b.Player));
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You cannot remove from a dictionary while foreach-ing that same dictionary -
the enumerator notices the mutation and throws InvalidOperationException. The
standard fix: build a LIST of the keys to remove first (the snapshot ends the
enumeration), then loop over that list removing by key. For the `List<int>`
half, one built-in method does removal, order preservation, and the count.

## Hint 2

```csharp
List<string> doomed = readings.Where(p => p.Value < minimum).Select(p => p.Key).ToList();
foreach (string key in doomed) { readings.Remove(key); }
return doomed.Count;
```

`DropWhere` is `values.RemoveAll(v => condemned(v))` - RemoveAll takes a
`Predicate<int>`, so wrap the `Func` in a lambda and return its answer.

## Exercise 6 - a tuple is a perfectly good key

Route prices keyed by `(From, To)`. `Fares.Set` overwrites, `PriceOf` answers
null for a route not on file, and `CheapestFrom` scans one origin's routes for
the lowest price, destination A-Z on ties. `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` are different
keys - the gate checks you know that.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A value tuple `(from, to)` is a complete dictionary key: it compares by
position with value equality and hashes to match, so no custom type is
needed. `Set` is the indexer; `PriceOf` is `TryGetValue` with the tuple key,
turning the miss into `null`.

## Hint 2

## Exercise 7 - a dictionary inside a dictionary

A gradebook: student -> subject -> score. `Gradebook.Record` creates the inner
dictionary on first sight and keeps the latest score. `ScoreOf` survives a miss
at either level. `SubjectAverage` averages over exactly the students who have
that subject, and throws `InvalidOperationException` when nobody does.

Edit `src/Lessons/D13_ListsDictionaries/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d13_lists_dictionaries ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The outer dictionary maps student -> inner dictionary; the inner maps
subject -> score. `Record` must get-or-create the inner one: try to fetch it,
and on a miss create it AND store it in the outer dictionary before writing
the score through it.

## Hint 2

`ScoreOf` chains two `TryGetValue` calls - the second only runs when the
first succeeded:

```csharp
return book.TryGetValue(student, out var subjects)
       && subjects.TryGetValue(subject, out int score)
    ? score : null;
```

## Hint 3

`SubjectAverage` never touches students who lack the subject: filter
`book.Values` with `ContainsKey(subject)`, project to the score as `double`,
and call `Average()`. Do not catch the empty case - `Average` throwing
InvalidOperationException is exactly the contract the gate asks for. The one
decision left: which level of the book you iterate to get there.

## Hint 1

The outer dictionary maps student -> inner dictionary; the inner maps
subject -> score. `Record` must get-or-create the inner one: try to fetch it,
and on a miss create it AND store it in the outer dictionary before writing
the score through it.

## Hint 2

`ScoreOf` chains two `TryGetValue` calls - the second only runs when the
first succeeded:

```csharp
return book.TryGetValue(student, out var subjects)
       && subjects.TryGetValue(subject, out int score)
    ? score : null;
```

## Hint 3

`SubjectAverage` never touches students who lack the subject: filter
`book.Values` with `ContainsKey(subject)`, project to the score as `double`,
and call `Average()`. Do not catch the empty case - `Average` throwing
InvalidOperationException is exactly the contract the gate asks for. The one
decision left: which level of the book you iterate to get there.

The interview classic. `PairFinder.FirstPairSummingTo` returns the positions of
the pair whose second position comes earliest (partnered with the earliest
earlier match), null when there is none - in ONE pass with a dictionary of
"value -> earliest position seen". `HasPairSummingTo` is the yes/no form.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One pass. For each position i, ask: "have I already seen the value
`target - numbers[i]`?" A dictionary from value -> the position it was FIRST
seen at answers that in constant time. If yes, you have your pair; if no,
record this value and move on.

## Hint 2

Order matters twice. Look up the complement BEFORE storing the current value
- that is what prevents position i from pairing with itself. And store only
the FIRST position of each value (guard with `ContainsKey`, or use `TryAdd`)
so `[1, 4, 1, 5]` pairs the 5 with the 1 at position 0.

## Hint 3

The skeleton, minus one line you decide:

```csharp
Dictionary<int, int> earliest = new Dictionary<int, int>();
for (int i = 0; i < numbers.Count; i++)
{
    if (earliest.TryGetValue(target - numbers[i], out int j)) { return (j, i); }
    // remember numbers[i] -> i, but only the first time
}
return null;
```

`HasPairSummingTo` should not repeat any of this - one call, one pattern test.

lessons.briefing:
# d14 - Sets, queues and stacks drills

Eight problems on the specialist collections: duplicate detection, set
algebra, subset and overlap questions, FIFO service with postponement, a
sliding-window rate limiter, an undo stack, browser back/forward, and a
postfix calculator. They drill lesson 08 - reread `08_collections` if
"which structure answers this question?" still takes thought.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/`. Nothing here depends
on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - a set spots the repeat

`Scanner.FirstDuplicate` returns the first id seen a second time (null when
all unique) in one pass - `HashSet<T>.Add` returns false for a repeat, which
is the entire algorithm. `CountUnique` counts distinct ids.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - intersect, except, and union

Two days of sign-ins. `Attendance.BothDays` (A-Z), `OnlyFirstDay` (A-Z), and
`TotalDistinct` are `IntersectWith`, `ExceptWith` and `UnionWith` wearing
domain names. Duplicate sign-ins count once.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - take, peek, and postpone

`Tickets.TakeNext` dequeues or answers null when empty. `Postpone` moves the
front ticket to the back and returns it. `UpNext` previews the next `count`
tickets without removing anything - a `Queue` enumerates front-first.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - an undo stack

`Draft.Type` appends to `Text`, first pushing the OLD text onto a history
stack; `Undo` pops it back (false when there is nothing to undo); `CanUndo`
reports whether there is. The order of push versus append is the exercise.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - a sliding window is a queue

`RateLimiter(limit, windowSeconds).Allow(second)`: first evict allowances
whose time is `<= second - windowSeconds` from the front, then grant only if
fewer than `limit` remain. Refused requests are not remembered. Times are
non-decreasing ints - no clocks, no timers.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - subset, overlap, and set equality

`Access.CanView` is "any shared role?" (`Overlaps`), `CanPublish` is "holds
them all?" (`IsSupersetOf`), `SameCrew` is "same set, ignoring order and
duplicates?" (`SetEquals`). Mind the empty cases: overlap with nothing is
false, superset of nothing is true.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - browser history: two stacks

`History` keeps `Current` plus a back stack and a forward stack. `Back` and
`Forward` shuttle pages between them; `Visit` pushes the old page onto back
and CLEARS forward - the classic interview design question, and the gate
checks exactly that clearing.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a postfix calculator

`Postfix.Evaluate("3 4 + 2 *")` is 14. Push numbers; each operator pops two
(first pop is the RIGHT operand), computes, pushes back. Unknown token:
`FormatException`. Too few operands or leftovers at the end:
`InvalidOperationException` - and `Pop` on an empty stack already throws the
right type for you.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d14_sets_queues_stacks

## Notes

Each of these structures answers exactly one question fast, and the drill is
matching structure to question without thinking. "Have I seen this?" is a
`HashSet`. "Who is next?" is a `Queue`. "What was most recent?" is a `Stack`.
The set problems (ex1, ex2, ex6) are about letting the built-in operations do
the work instead of hand-rolled loops; the queue problems (ex3, ex5) are about
front-first order and safe behaviour at empty; the stack problems (ex4, ex7,
ex8) all exploit the same property - a stack remembers not just how much
happened but the ORDER it happened in, so unwinding comes out backwards, which
is exactly what undo, back-buttons and nested arithmetic need.

## ex1

Really testing: that `HashSet<T>.Add` is a test and an insert in one call -
it returns false when the item was already present, so "first duplicate" needs
no `Contains` and no second pass. The classic mistake is `Contains`-then-`Add`,
which works but does two hashes per item, or collecting counts in a dictionary
when the question only needs membership. `CountUnique` is the constructor plus
`Count`: feeding a sequence into `new HashSet<string>(ids)` deduplicates as it
builds. One pass, one set, both answers.

## ex2

Really testing: the mutating set operations. `IntersectWith`, `ExceptWith` and
`UnionWith` all modify the set they are called on - so build a scratch set
from one argument, apply the operation with the other, and read the result.
The classic mistake is nested `Contains` loops that re-implement intersection
in O(n * m), or forgetting that day 1's duplicate sign-ins must count once
(the set eats them at construction). Ordering is not the set's job: sets have
no order, so the A-Z comes from `OrderBy` on the way out.

## ex3

Really testing: the difference between looking and taking. `UpNext` must not
mutate - enumerating a `Queue` (or `Take(count)` over it) walks front to back
without removing, while `Dequeue` removes. The classic mistake is implementing
the preview with `Dequeue` and re-`Enqueue`, which reorders nothing visibly in
a short test but wrecks the queue's state when it is short. `TryDequeue` gives
the null-on-empty contract in one call; `Postpone` is dequeue-then-enqueue and
is why round-robin schedulers are queues.

## ex4

Really testing: what to push and when. `Type` must push the text as it was
BEFORE the append - push-after gives an undo that restores the state you are
already in, an off-by-one that the gate's first `Undo` catches. The classic
mistake beyond that is undoing by string surgery (trimming the added suffix),
which breaks as soon as additions overlap; snapshots on a stack are dumb and
therefore correct. `Undo` checks `Count` before popping - an empty stack
throws on `Pop`, and "nothing to undo" is an answer, not an error.

## ex5

Really testing: the sliding-window idiom - a queue of timestamps where
arrivals join the back and expiries leave the front. Because request times
never decrease, the oldest allowance is always at the front, so eviction is a
`while` loop on `Peek`. Two classic mistakes: remembering REFUSED requests
(only grants occupy the window), and the boundary - an allowance at time t
dies at exactly t + window, so the eviction test is `<= second - window`. The
gate's second 10 request exists purely to catch a `<` where a `<=` belongs.

## ex6

Really testing: the query methods that do not mutate - `Overlaps`,
`IsSupersetOf`, `SetEquals` - and their empty-set edges. Overlap with an empty
requirement is FALSE (there is nothing to share), while superset-of-empty is
TRUE (nothing is missing); one is an existence claim, the other a universal
one, the same vacuous-truth logic as `All` over an empty sequence in LINQ.
The classic mistake is `SequenceEqual` for crew comparison, which is order-
and duplicate-sensitive - `SetEquals` accepts any `IEnumerable` and compares
membership only.

## ex7

Really testing: modelling a process with two stacks. Going back pushes the
current page onto forward; going forward pushes it onto back; each is the
other's inverse, which is why the same page shuttles between them. The design
decision the gate insists on: `Visit` clears the forward stack - after
branching to a new page, the old future is unreachable, exactly like a real
browser. The classic mistake is forgetting that clear, leaving a "forward"
that jumps to a page you never came from. Guard both moves with `Count`,
return false, and change nothing on the refusal.

## ex8

Really testing: why postfix notation and stacks are the same idea. Numbers
wait on the stack; an operator consumes the top two - and the FIRST pop is the
RIGHT operand, because it was pushed last, which is what makes "8 2 -" equal
6 and not -6. The classic mistake is popping into left-then-right order. Error
handling comes almost free: `Pop` on empty already throws
`InvalidOperationException` for the missing-operand case, so the only checks
you write are the unknown token (`FormatException`) and the end-state rule
that exactly one value remains. This is also how every expression compiler
evaluates its intermediate code, so the exercise is less artificial than it
looks.

## Hint 1

`IntersectWith`, `ExceptWith` and `UnionWith` each MUTATE the set you call
them on. So: build a fresh `HashSet<string>` from one day, apply the
operation with the other day, then read the result. Sets have no order -
the A-Z comes from you, on the way out.

```csharp
HashSet<string> result = new HashSet<string>(day1);
result.IntersectWith(day2);
return result.OrderBy(name => name).ToList();
```

`Tickets.TakeNext` dequeues or answers null when empty. `Postpone` moves the
front ticket to the back and returns it. `UpNext` previews the next `count`
tickets without removing anything - a `Queue` enumerates front-first.

## Hint 1

Three different intents, three different calls: `TryDequeue` removes (and
tells you whether it could), `Enqueue` re-adds at the back, and plain
enumeration - `queue.Take(count)` - looks without touching. `UpNext` must

`Postpone` is `TryDequeue` then `Enqueue`:


exercises.hints:
## Hint 1


letting `Pop` throw - and `CanUndo` is that same count as a bool.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - a sliding window is a queue

`RateLimiter(limit, windowSeconds).Allow(second)`: first evict allowances
whose time is `<= second - windowSeconds` from the front, then grant only if
fewer than `limit` remain. Refused requests are not remembered. Times are
non-decreasing ints - no clocks, no timers.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Keep a `Queue<int>` of the times at which requests were GRANTED. Because
times never decrease, the oldest allowance is always at the front - so
expiry is a `while` loop: peek, and dequeue while the front is old enough
to have aged out. Refusals are never enqueued.

## Hint 2

The boundary is `<=`: an allowance from time t is gone once
`t <= second - windowSeconds`.

```csharp
while (_granted.Count > 0 && _granted.Peek() <= second - _windowSeconds)
{
    _granted.Dequeue();
}
```

After evicting: refuse when `Count >= _limit`, otherwise enqueue `second`
and grant. `InWindow` is just the queue's `Count`.

## Hint 1

Keep a `Queue<int>` of the times at which requests were GRANTED. Because
times never decrease, the oldest allowance is always at the front - so
expiry is a `while` loop: peek, and dequeue while the front is old enough
to have aged out. Refusals are never enqueued.

## Hint 2

The boundary is `<=`: an allowance from time t is gone once
`t <= second - windowSeconds`.

```csharp
while (_granted.Count > 0 && _granted.Peek() <= second - _windowSeconds)
{
    _granted.Dequeue();
}
```

After evicting: refuse when `Count >= _limit`, otherwise enqueue `second`
and grant. `InWindow` is just the queue's `Count`.

## Exercise 7 - browser history: two stacks

`History` keeps `Current` plus a back stack and a forward stack. `Back` and
`Forward` shuttle pages between them; `Visit` pushes the old page onto back
and CLEARS forward - the classic interview design question, and the gate
checks exactly that clearing.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two stacks: `_back` and `_forward`. `Back` pushes `Current` onto `_forward`
and pops `_back` into `Current`; `Forward` is the mirror image. Each guard
is a `Count` check that returns false and touches nothing.

## Hint 2

`Visit` is three steps, and the third is the one people forget:

```csharp
_back.Push(Current);
Current = url;
_forward.Clear();
```

## Hint 3

Why the clear: after home -> a -> b, Back, Back, you are at home with
forward = [a, b]-ish state. Visiting c from home starts a NEW branch of
history; b and a are no longer "ahead" of anywhere you can reach. The gate
visits, goes back, visits somewhere new, and then insists `Forward()` is
false - if yours still moves, the old future leaked. Which stack the leaving
page goes onto in each method is the one decision left to you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two stacks: `_back` and `_forward`. `Back` pushes `Current` onto `_forward`
and pops `_back` into `Current`; `Forward` is the mirror image. Each guard
is a `Count` check that returns false and touches nothing.

## Hint 2

`Visit` is three steps, and the third is the one people forget:

```csharp
_back.Push(Current);
Current = url;
_forward.Clear();
```

## Hint 3

Why the clear: after home -> a -> b, Back, Back, you are at home with
forward = [a, b]-ish state. Visiting c from home starts a NEW branch of
history; b and a are no longer "ahead" of anywhere you can reach. The gate
visits, goes back, visits somewhere new, and then insists `Forward()` is
false - if yours still moves, the old future leaked. Which stack the leaving
page goes onto in each method is the one decision left to you.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - a postfix calculator

`Postfix.Evaluate("3 4 + 2 *")` is 14. Push numbers; each operator pops two
(first pop is the RIGHT operand), computes, pushes back. Unknown token:
`FormatException`. Too few operands or leftovers at the end:
`InvalidOperationException` - and `Pop` on an empty stack already throws the
right type for you.

Edit `src/Lessons/D14_SetsQueuesStacks/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d14_sets_queues_stacks ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split on spaces (`StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries`). For each token:
a number is pushed; an operator pops TWO values, computes, and pushes the
result. At the end, exactly one value may remain - that is the answer.

## Hint 2

Pop order is the classic trap: the first pop is the RIGHT operand (it was
pushed last), the second is the left.

```csharp
int right = stack.Pop();
int left = stack.Pop();
stack.Push(token switch { "+" => left + right, "-" => left - right, ... });
```

## Hint 3

You barely need to write error handling. `Pop` on an empty `Stack<int>`
already throws `InvalidOperationException`, which is the required behaviour
for "2 +" - so do NOT wrap it in try/catch. That leaves two checks of your
own: a token that is neither operator nor parseable int throws
`FormatException` (mention the token in the message), and after the loop a
stack whose `Count != 1` throws `InvalidOperationException`. Distinguishing
number from operator - `int.TryParse` versus matching the four operator
strings, and in which order - is the decision left to you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Split on spaces (`StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries`). For each token:
a number is pushed; an operator pops TWO values, computes, and pushes the
result. At the end, exactly one value may remain - that is the answer.

## Hint 2

Pop order is the classic trap: the first pop is the RIGHT operand (it was
pushed last), the second is the left.

```csharp
int right = stack.Pop();
int left = stack.Pop();
stack.Push(token switch { "+" => left + right, "-" => left - right, ... });
```

## Hint 3

You barely need to write error handling. `Pop` on an empty `Stack<int>`
already throws `InvalidOperationException`, which is the required behaviour
for "2 +" - so do NOT wrap it in try/catch. That leaves two checks of your
own: a token that is neither operator nor parseable int throws
`FormatException` (mention the token in the message), and after the loop a
stack whose `Count != 1` throws `InvalidOperationException`. Distinguishing
number from operator - `int.TryParse` versus matching the four operator
strings, and in which order - is the decision left to you.

# d15 - Iterators and yield drills

Eight problems on writing sequences with `yield`: simple generators, lazy
transforms, infinite sequences, single-pass pairing, the eager-validation
split, manual enumerators for weaving and merging, and a finale that maps out
exactly WHEN an iterator's body runs. They drill lesson 08's ex4 - reread
`08_collections` if "calling it runs nothing" still feels strange.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - two straightforward iterators

`Ranges.UpTo(first, last)` yields the inclusive range (empty when last is
below first); `Repeat(item, times)` yields one item over and over. Warm-up
mechanics: a loop around a `yield return`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - transforming lazily

`Transforms.Stutter` yields every item twice; `Numbered` yields `"1. ada"`
style lines with a 1-based counter. The gate's counting source proves you
built neither into a list: zero items read at call time, and taking 3
stuttered items reads only 2 source items.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - infinite sequences are fine

`Endless.Cycle(items)` repeats a list forever (an EMPTY list yields nothing
instead of spinning); `From(start)` counts upward without end. The gate takes
7 from a cycle and finds the first multiple of 7 in an infinite count -
laziness is what makes both safe.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - adjacent pairs from a single pass

`Pairs.Pairwise` yields each item with its successor; `Deltas` yields the
difference at each step. One walk of the source only - the gate counts walks,
so the Skip-and-Zip trick (two walks) fails. Remember the previous item in a
local.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - argument checks must not wait

`Sampling.EveryNth(items, n)` keeps positions 0, n, 2n... - and n below 1
throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` AT THE CALL. A body containing `yield`
postpones everything, guards included, so the method must be split: a plain
wrapper that validates, returning a private iterator that works.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - weaving two sequences

`Weaving.Weave` alternates items from two sequences and appends the leftovers
of whichever is longer. Two `foreach` loops cannot interleave - this is the
exercise where you call `GetEnumerator()` and `MoveNext()` yourself, inside
`using` declarations.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - merging two sorted sequences

`Merging.Merge` combines two ascending inputs into one ascending output,
keeping duplicates, lazily: always yield the smaller current item and advance
only that side. The gate meters both inputs - taking three merged items may
cost at most three pulls per side.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - when the body actually runs

`Tracing.Steps(log)` yields 1 and 2 around diary entries "start", "middle",
"end"; `Squares(log, count)` logs before each square it yields. The gate
drives `MoveNext()` by hand and checks the diary after every step, then
abandons a loop early and checks the rest of the body never ran. Write the
code in five minutes; spend the rest predicting the diary.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex8
```

# Reading - csharp/d15_iterators_yield

## Notes

An iterator method is a description of a sequence, compiled into a state
machine that runs one slice of the body per `MoveNext`. Everything in this set
follows from that single fact: calling the method runs nothing (ex2, ex8),
argument checks are postponed with the rest of the body (ex5), infinite loops
are harmless until someone demands everything (ex3), and abandoning a loop
midway simply never runs the remainder (ex8). The other skill drilled here is
the manual enumerator - `GetEnumerator`/`MoveNext`/`Current` inside a `using`
- which is what you need the moment two sequences must advance at different
rates (ex6, ex7). Write each iterator, then predict what the gate's counting
source will report before running it.

## ex1

Really testing: the basic shape - a loop around `yield return`, and the empty
case falling out naturally. `UpTo(7, 3)` is empty because the loop condition
is false immediately; no guard, no exception, no special case. The classic
mistake is building and returning a `List<int>`, which passes THIS gate but
is the habit the rest of the set will punish. Notice also that `Repeat` with
a negative count needs no check: a `for` loop that never starts is the check.

## ex2

Really testing: that transformation iterators do their work per-pull. Two
`yield return` statements inside one `foreach` is all `Stutter` is; the gate's
counting source proves nothing was read at call time and that `Take(3)` read
only two source items. The classic mistake is materialising (`Select` +
`ToList`, or filling a list) which produces identical output and fails the
pull-count asserts. `Numbered`'s counter is just a local - iterator locals
live in the state machine, so it survives between pulls.

## ex3

Really testing: that an infinite sequence is a legitimate value. `while
(true)` around a `foreach`, or a `for` with no condition, is safe because the
CALLER decides how much to consume - `Take(7)`, `First(...)`. Two classic
mistakes: trying to materialise (anything that walks to the end hangs), and
forgetting the empty-list guard in `Cycle` - cycling nothing must yield
nothing, not spin forever producing nothing, so check `Count == 0` and
`yield break` before entering the infinite loop.

## ex4

Really testing: single-pass thinking. The tempting implementation -
`values.Zip(values.Skip(1))` - enumerates the source TWICE, and the gate's
walk counter says so. The model answer keeps `previous` in a local, skipping
the yield on the first item: one `foreach`, one walk. This matters beyond
style: an `IEnumerable` might be a file, a network stream, or a query that
re-executes - walking twice is at best double cost and at worst different
data. `Deltas` is the same skeleton yielding `value - previous`.

## ex5

Really testing: the eager-validation split, one of the two famous iterator
traps. Because the whole body is postponed, a `throw` at the top of an
iterator does not fire at the call site - it fires later, wherever the
sequence is first enumerated, which may be another method entirely. The fix:
a public method with NO yield that validates and returns the result of a
private iterator method that does the work. The classic mistake is either
skipping the check or putting it inside the iterator and wondering why
`Teach.Throws` reports "no exception was thrown".

## ex6

Really testing: manual enumerators. Two `foreach` loops run one after the
other; interleaving needs both enumerators open at once, advanced
alternately. The shape to internalise: `using` on each enumerator (they may
hold resources), one `hasX = MoveNext()` before the loop, and after each
yield advance ONLY the side you consumed. The classic mistake is calling
`MoveNext` twice per turn - it advances, it does not peek - which silently
drops every other item.

## ex7

Really testing: the merge step of merge sort, written lazily. The invariant:
at every moment each side's `Current` is its smallest unconsumed value, so
yield the smaller and advance that side only. `<=` rather than `<` keeps the
merge stable and handles duplicates. The tail loops drain whichever side
remains. The classic mistake is buffering (`ToList` both, then sort or walk)
- correct output, but the gate's pull meters show everything was read to
produce three items. Real use: merging two sorted database cursors without
loading either.

## ex8

Really testing: the execution model, precisely. `MoveNext` runs from where
the body last paused to the NEXT `yield return`; the first call runs the code
before the first yield ("start"); the final call - the one that returns false
- runs the code after the last yield ("end"). Breaking out of a `foreach`
disposes the enumerator and the un-run remainder never happens, which is why
"middle" is missing in the abandoned run. The classic mistake is thinking of
an iterator as a method that ran and returned a collection; this exercise
exists to replace that model with slices-on-demand. Interviewers probe
exactly this with "what prints, and when?".

## Further reading

- [Iterators (C# guide)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/iterators) - yield, state machines, and the deferred body.
- [yield statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/yield) - the language reference, including the validation-split pattern.
- [IEnumerator<T>](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.ienumerator-1) - MoveNext/Current, what ex6 and ex7 drive by hand.
- [CA1851: possible multiple enumeration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca1851) - the analyser behind ex4's one-walk rule.

## Exercise 1 - two straightforward iterators

`Ranges.UpTo(first, last)` yields the inclusive range (empty when last is
below first); `Repeat(item, times)` yields one item over and over. Warm-up

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each method is a loop with a `yield return` inside. No lists, no early
returns - when the loop condition is false from the start, the sequence is
simply empty, which is exactly what the gate wants for `UpTo(7, 3)` and
`Repeat(_, 0)`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
for (int value = first; value <= last; value++)
{
    yield return value;
}
```

`Repeat` is the same shape counting `i` from 0 while `i < times` - a negative
`times` never enters the loop, so no guard is needed.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Stutter` is one `foreach` containing TWO `yield return item;` statements in
a row. Do not collect into a list - the gate counts how many items were read
from the source, and a list reads all of them immediately.

## Hint 2

`Numbered` keeps a counter local:

```csharp
int number = 1;
foreach (string item in items)
{
    yield return $"{number}. {item}";
    number++;
}
```

Iterator locals live inside the compiled state machine, so `number` keeps
its value between pulls - that is why this just works.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - infinite sequences are fine

`Endless.Cycle(items)` repeats a list forever (an EMPTY list yields nothing
instead of spinning); `From(start)` counts upward without end. The gate takes
7 from a cycle and finds the first multiple of 7 in an infinite count -
laziness is what makes both safe.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An infinite iterator is legal and safe: `while (true)` around a `foreach`
(for `Cycle`), or a `for` loop with no end condition (for `From`). The
caller's `Take`/`First` decides when to stop pulling - the body only runs
one slice per pull.

## Hint 2

The one guard that matters: `Cycle` of an EMPTY list must yield nothing, not
loop forever finding nothing to yield. Check `items.Count == 0` and
`yield break` BEFORE the `while (true)`. `From` is:

```csharp
for (int value = start; ; value++) { yield return value; }
```

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

An infinite iterator is legal and safe: `while (true)` around a `foreach`
(for `Cycle`), or a `for` loop with no end condition (for `From`). The
caller's `Take`/`First` decides when to stop pulling - the body only runs
one slice per pull.

## Hint 2

The one guard that matters: `Cycle` of an EMPTY list must yield nothing, not
loop forever finding nothing to yield. Check `items.Count == 0` and
`yield break` BEFORE the `while (true)`. `From` is:

```csharp
for (int value = start; ; value++) { yield return value; }
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `foreach`, and a local that remembers the PREVIOUS item. Skip the yield
on the very first item (nothing to pair with yet); from then on, yield the
pair and update the local. Anything built from `Skip(1)` or `Zip` enumerates
the source twice, and the gate counts walks.

## Hint 2

```csharp
bool first = true;
int previous = 0;
foreach (int value in values)
{
    if (!first) { yield return (previous, value); }
    previous = value;
    first = false;
}
```

`Deltas` is the identical skeleton yielding `value - previous`.

## Exercise 5 - argument checks must not wait

`Sampling.EveryNth(items, n)` keeps positions 0, n, 2n... - and n below 1
throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` AT THE CALL. A body containing `yield`
postpones everything, guards included, so the method must be split: a plain
wrapper that validates, returning a private iterator that works.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A method containing `yield` postpones its ENTIRE body - including your
`throw`. So the public method must contain NO yield: it validates n, then
returns the result of a second, private method that does contain the yield.
Calling the private iterator is instant; the check already ran.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static IEnumerable<T> EveryNth<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, int n)
{
    if (n < 1) { throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(n), n, "..."); }
    return Iterator(items, n);
}

private static IEnumerable<T> Iterator<T>(IEnumerable<T> items, int n) { ... }
```

Inside the iterator, count positions and yield when `position % n == 0`.

## Exercise 6 - weaving two sequences

`Weaving.Weave` alternates items from two sequences and appends the leftovers
of whichever is longer. Two `foreach` loops cannot interleave - this is the
exercise where you call `GetEnumerator()` and `MoveNext()` yourself, inside
`using` declarations.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You need both sequences open at once, each advanced at its own pace - that
means `first.GetEnumerator()` and `second.GetEnumerator()` held in locals
(wrap each in a `using` declaration), with `MoveNext()` telling you whether
a `Current` is available. Track each side's has-an-item flag in a bool.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using IEnumerator<string> a = first.GetEnumerator();
using IEnumerator<string> b = second.GetEnumerator();
bool hasA = a.MoveNext();
bool hasB = b.MoveNext();
while (hasA || hasB)
{
    if (hasA) { yield return a.Current; hasA = a.MoveNext(); }
    if (hasB) { yield return b.Current; hasB = b.MoveNext(); }
}
```

`MoveNext` advances - it never peeks - so call it exactly once per item you
consume.

## Exercise 7 - merging two sorted sequences

`Merging.Merge` combines two ascending inputs into one ascending output,
keeping duplicates, lazily: always yield the smaller current item and advance
only that side. The gate meters both inputs - taking three merged items may
cost at most three pulls per side.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Same manual-enumerator setup as ex6, different loop logic. Invariant: each
side's `Current` is its smallest unconsumed value (the inputs are sorted).
So while BOTH sides have items: yield the smaller `Current` and advance
ONLY that side. Afterwards, drain whichever side still has items.

## Hint 2

The comparison is `a.Current <= b.Current` - the `<=` keeps duplicates from
both sides and takes the left one first, which is what the gate's
"1, 2, 4, 4, 9, 30" expects.

The skeleton is: two `using` enumerators, two `hasX = MoveNext()` primers, a
`while (hasA && hasB)` doing the compare-yield-advance, then two drain loops
(`while (hasA) { yield...; hasA = a.MoveNext(); }` and the same for B). Do
not ToList anything - the gate meters the pulls. What remains yours: getting
the advance-only-the-consumed-side detail right inside the main loop.
