## Hint 1

Same manual-enumerator setup as ex6, different loop logic. Invariant: each
side's `Current` is its smallest unconsumed value (the inputs are sorted).
So while BOTH sides have items: yield the smaller `Current` and advance
ONLY that side. Afterwards, drain whichever side still has items.

## Hint 2

The comparison is `a.Current <= b.Current` - the `<=` keeps duplicates from
both sides and takes the left one first, which is what the gate's
"1, 2, 4, 4, 9, 30" expects.

## Hint 3

The skeleton is: two `using` enumerators, two `hasX = MoveNext()` primers, a
`while (hasA && hasB)` doing the compare-yield-advance, then two drain loops
(`while (hasA) { yield...; hasA = a.MoveNext(); }` and the same for B). Do
not ToList anything - the gate meters the pulls. What remains yours: getting
the advance-only-the-consumed-side detail right inside the main loop.

## Exercise 8 - when the body actually runs

`Tracing.Steps(log)` yields 1 and 2 around diary entries "start", "middle",
"end"; `Squares(log, count)` logs before each square it yields. The gate
drives `MoveNext()` by hand and checks the diary after every step, then
abandons a loop early and checks the rest of the body never ran. Write the
code in five minutes; spend the rest predicting the diary.

Edit `src/Lessons/D15_IteratorsYield/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d15_iterators_yield ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The code is genuinely five lines per method - log, yield, log, yield, log
for `Steps`; a loop that logs then yields for `Squares`. The exercise is the
TIMING: each `MoveNext` runs the body from where it paused to the next
`yield return`. Write the obvious code, then predict every gate assertion
before running.

## Hint 2

```csharp
log.Add("start");
yield return 1;
log.Add("middle");
yield return 2;
log.Add("end");
```

"start" appears on the FIRST MoveNext (not at the call); "end" appears on
the LAST MoveNext - the one that returns false.

## Hint 3

For the abandoned-loop check: `foreach ... break` after one item means the
state machine is disposed while paused at the first yield - the code after
that yield never executes, so the log holds only "start". In `Squares`, put
the `log.Add($"computing {n}")` immediately BEFORE its `yield return n * n`
- logging up front or after would shift the counts the gate expects. Which
loop form you use is up to you.

# d16 - Delegates and lambdas drills

Eight problems on treating behaviour as data: returning functions, combining
them, capturing variables in a closure, and building small engines out of
nothing but `Func` and `Action`. They drill lesson 09 - reread
`09_delegates_events_lambdas` if `Func<int, int>` still reads as noise rather
than as "int in, int out".

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/`. Nothing here depends
on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - a method handed back as a value

`Ops.ForName(name)` returns the arithmetic operation itself as a
`Func<int, int, int>` for `"add"`, `"sub"` and `"mul"`, and throws
`ArgumentException` for anything else. `Ops.Twice(transform, x)` applies the
transform to its own result: `Twice(x => x + 3, 10)` is `16`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - combining predicates, short-circuit included

`Predicates.Both(first, second)` and `Predicates.Either(first, second)` return
a new predicate. Both are generic in the item type, and both must short-circuit
exactly like `&&` and `||` do: `Both` never calls `second` once `first` has
said no, and `Either` never calls it once `first` has said yes. The gate counts
the calls.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a factory that closes over its parameter

`Factories.MakeDiscounter(0.25m)` returns a `Func<decimal, decimal>` that turns
`100` into `75` - the rate is captured by the returned lambda and stored
nowhere else. `Factories.MakeTagger("urgent")` returns a
`Func<string, string>` turning `"reboot"` into `"[urgent] reboot"`. Two calls
to the same factory must not interfere.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - wrappers that remember something

`Guards.Once(action)` returns an `Action` that runs the wrapped action on its
first call and does nothing afterwards. `Guards.After(times, action)` returns
an `Action` that does nothing until it has been called `times` times - it runs
on call number `times` and on every call after that. Two wrappers around the
same action must count independently.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - comparisons built out of comparisons

Three `Comparison<T>` combinators. `Comparers.ByKey(key)` orders ascending by
an `int` key. `Comparers.Reversed(inner)` turns any comparison upside down -
by swapping the operands, not by negating the answer. `Comparers.Then(first,
second)` uses `second` only when `first` returned `0`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - two lambdas over one variable

`Accounts.MakeAccount(opening)` returns a tuple of an `Action<int> Deposit` and
a `Func<int> Balance` that share one captured local - what the deposit writes,
the balance reads. Each call to `MakeAccount` makes a fresh, independent
balance. A negative deposit throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` and leaves the
balance alone.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - bind, flip and pipe

Three combinators, each fully generic. `Currying.Bind(f, first)` fixes the
first argument of a two-argument function. `Currying.Flip(f)` swaps its
parameters. `Currying.Pipe(f, g)` chains them so that `Pipe(f, g)(x)` is
`g(f(x))` - `f` runs first. Getting the type parameters lined up is most of the
work.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a rules engine made of predicates

`Validator<T>` holds a list of `(message, rule)` pairs. `Require` registers one
and returns the same validator so calls chain; `Check` returns every failing
rule's message in registration order (empty means fine); `IsValid` is true when
`Check` is empty. A rule answers `true` for GOOD data. The `Signup` record is
written for you.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d16_delegates_lambdas

## Notes

The skill being drilled is writing methods whose parameters and return values
are *other methods*. A `Func<A, R>` is not a special language feature you have
to think about; it is a value with a shape, and the only thing that makes it
feel strange at first is that the shape is "call me later with an A".

The pattern uniting all eight problems is the **returned closure**. In seven of
them a method builds a lambda, that lambda captures something from the
enclosing scope - a parameter, a local, a field - and the lambda outlives the
method that made it. The captured variable is hoisted onto a compiler-generated
object that lives as long as the delegate does, which is why `Once` can
remember whether it ran, why `MakeAccount` can hand out two lambdas that see
the same balance, and why two calls to `MakeDiscounter` do not interfere.

The second thread is **combinators**: functions that take functions and return
functions. `Both`, `Reversed`, `Then`, `Bind`, `Flip` and `Pipe` are all under
five lines each, and none of them does any work at the moment you call it -
they only build a new function whose body will do the work later. Once you can
write those six from memory, the entirety of LINQ stops being surprising.

## ex1

Really testing: that a `Func` is a value you can return, store and hand on. The
classic mistake is writing `ForName` so that it *does* the arithmetic - taking
the operands as parameters - because that is what a method usually does; the
signature is the whole point, and it says the operands are not available yet.
The second mistake is in `Twice`, where `transform(x) * 2` and
`transform(transform(x))` agree for doubling and disagree for everything else.
The model answer uses a `switch` expression whose arms are lambdas, so the
lambda is only created for the branch that is chosen.

## ex2

Really testing: that `&&` and `||` are short-circuiting, and that a combinator
built out of them inherits that. The classic mistake is
`item => first(item) & second(item)` - one character, and it turns two cheap
predicates into two expensive ones, or worse, calls a predicate that would
throw on the data the first one already rejected. That is not a hypothetical:
`Both(x => x != null, x => x.Length > 0)` is only safe because of the
short-circuit. The model answer is `item => first(item) && second(item)`, and
its correctness is entirely inherited from the operator.

## ex3

Really testing: capture of a *parameter*, which is the safe case. Each call to
`MakeDiscounter` gets its own `rate` variable, so each returned lambda closes
over a different one, which is why the two discounters are independent. The
classic mistake is thinking of the price rather than the rate as the fixed
thing and returning `rate * (1 - price)`; the second is returning the discount
amount rather than the discounted price. Contrast this with capturing a loop
variable, where every lambda closes over the *same* variable - that is the
famous trap, and the reason `foreach` was changed in C# 5 to give each
iteration a fresh one.

## ex4

Really testing: mutable state living in a closure. `bool ran` is a local, so it
would normally die when `Once` returns - but because a lambda uses it, the
compiler moves it onto a heap object that the delegate holds. The classic
mistake is a `static bool` field on `Guards`, which passes the first assertion
and then fails the moment a second wrapper is made, because all wrappers share
it. In `After`, the off-by-one is the other trap: `After(3, a)` fires on call
three, so the counter is incremented *before* the comparison and the test is
`>=`, not `==` - `==` would make it a one-shot.

## ex5

Really testing: that `Comparison<T>` is just a delegate, so ordering rules
compose like any other function. `Reversed` is written as
`(a, b) => inner(b, a)` rather than `-inner(a, b)` for a real reason: a
comparison is allowed to return any negative number, and `-int.MinValue`
overflows back to `int.MinValue`, so negation can report "less than" for a pair
that was greater. `Then` is the tie-breaker shape every multi-column sort uses,
and the classic mistake is adding or multiplying the two results instead of
consulting the second only when the first returned zero.

## ex6

Really testing: two delegates sharing one captured variable. This is where
closures stop looking like syntax and start looking like objects - the hidden
class the compiler generates has a field for `balance`, and both lambdas hold a
reference to the same instance of it. The classic mistake is capturing the
value instead of the variable, usually by copying `balance` into the lambda's
own local; then `Balance()` keeps reporting the opening figure forever. Note
also where the guard lives: inside the lambda, because the lambda is the only
door to the variable, and it throws before mutating so a refused deposit leaves
no trace.

## ex7

Really testing: reading and writing generic delegate signatures. The bodies are
one line each; the difficulty is entirely in the type parameters, and the way
to get them right is to write the desired call first and let it dictate the
signature. `Pipe<TIn, TMid, TOut>` is the instructive one - `TMid` appears as
`f`'s return type and `g`'s parameter type and nowhere in the result, which is
exactly what "f ends where g begins" means in types. The classic mistake is
composing in the other order and producing `f(g(x))`, which usually will not
even compile once the types differ, and that failure to compile is the type
system doing its job.

## ex8

Really testing: a whole feature built from stored predicates. The interesting
decision is the polarity - a rule answers `true` when the data is *good* and
its message is reported when it answers `false`. Getting that backwards is the
classic mistake and it reads fine until you see the output. The second is
returning a new `Validator<T>` from `Require`, which makes the fluent chain
silently drop every rule but the last. The model answer stores
`(string, Func<T, bool>)` pairs in a list and `Check` runs all of them - not
stopping at the first failure - because a form that complains once per submit
is worse than one that lists everything wrong at once.

## Further reading

- [Delegates](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/delegates/) - the language feature underneath `Func` and `Action`.
- [`Func<T, TResult>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.func-2) and [`Action<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.action-1) - the two built-in families.
- [Lambda expressions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions) - including the capture rules ex3, ex4 and ex6 depend on.
- [`Comparison<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.comparison-1) - the delegate ex5 builds, and what its return value means.
- [`List<T>.Sort`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1.sort) - note the explicit statement that the sort is unstable.
- [Boolean logical operators](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/boolean-logical-operators) - `&&` versus `&`, which is all ex2 is about.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - a method handed back as a value

`Ops.ForName(name)` returns the arithmetic operation itself as a
`Func<int, int, int>` for `"add"`, `"sub"` and `"mul"`, and throws
`ArgumentException` for anything else. `Ops.Twice(transform, x)` applies the
transform to its own result: `Twice(x => x + 3, 10)` is `16`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the return type first. `ForName` returns a `Func<int, int, int>`, not an
`int` - so its body never adds anything. It picks which operation to hand back
and hands it back; the caller supplies the operands later.

`Twice` is the mirror image: it receives behaviour and is the one that calls
it.

## Hint 2

A `switch` expression whose arms are lambdas is the tidiest shape:

```csharp
return name switch
{
    "add" => (a, b) => a + b,
    // ...
    _ => throw new ArgumentException($"unknown operation: {name}", nameof(name)),
};
```

For `Twice`, write down what `Twice(x => x + 3, 10)` should produce before you
code it: 10 goes in, the transform makes 13, and 13 goes back through the same
transform. So the result feeds the second call, and `transform(x) * 2` is a
different function that happens to agree when the transform is doubling.

`Factories.MakeDiscounter(0.25m)` returns a `Func<decimal, decimal>` that turns
`100` into `75` - the rate is captured by the returned lambda and stored

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The lambda you return uses `rate`, which is a parameter of `MakeDiscounter`.
That parameter would normally cease to exist when the method returns; because a
lambda uses it, the compiler keeps it alive for as long as the lambda lives.
That is a closure, and it is why nothing has to be stored in a field.

Work out the arithmetic on paper: a rate of `0.25m` applied to `100m` must give
`75m`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Func<decimal, decimal> MakeDiscounter(decimal rate)
{
    return price => price * (1m - rate);
}
```

Each *call* to `MakeDiscounter` gets its own `rate` variable, so each returned
lambda closes over a different one - which is why two discounters do not
interfere. Contrast that with capturing a loop variable, where every iteration
shares one variable unless the loop gives you a fresh one.

`MakeTagger` is the same shape with an interpolated string. Mind the single
space after the closing bracket.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The lambda you return uses `rate`, which is a parameter of `MakeDiscounter`.
That parameter would normally cease to exist when the method returns; because a
lambda uses it, the compiler keeps it alive for as long as the lambda lives.
That is a closure, and it is why nothing has to be stored in a field.

Work out the arithmetic on paper: a rate of `0.25m` applied to `100m` must give
`75m`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Func<decimal, decimal> MakeDiscounter(decimal rate)
{
    return price => price * (1m - rate);
}
```

Each *call* to `MakeDiscounter` gets its own `rate` variable, so each returned
lambda closes over a different one - which is why two discounters do not
interfere. Contrast that with capturing a loop variable, where every iteration
shares one variable unless the loop gives you a fresh one.

`MakeTagger` is the same shape with an interpolated string. Mind the single
space after the closing bracket.

## Exercise 4 - wrappers that remember something

`Guards.Once(action)` returns an `Action` that runs the wrapped action on its
first call and does nothing afterwards. `Guards.After(times, action)` returns
an `Action` that does nothing until it has been called `times` times - it runs
on call number `times` and on every call after that. Two wrappers around the
same action must count independently.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex4.cs`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Declare an ordinary local variable before the `return`, and mutate it from
inside the lambda. It looks like it cannot possibly survive the method
returning - it does, because the compiler moves it onto a hidden object that
the delegate holds a reference to.

A `static` field on `Guards` would look like it works, right up until the gate
makes a second wrapper.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Action Once(Action action)
{
    bool ran = false;
    return () =>
    {
        if (ran) { return; }
        ran = true;
        action();
    };
}
```

Set the flag *before* calling the action, not after, so an action that throws
still counts as having run.

For `After`, read the requirement carefully: `After(3, a)` does nothing on
calls one and two, runs on call three, and runs on every call after that. So
increment first and compare with `>=` - `==` would fire exactly once, which is
a different (and also useful) wrapper.

## Exercise 5 - comparisons built out of comparisons

Three `Comparison<T>` combinators. `Comparers.ByKey(key)` orders ascending by
an `int` key. `Comparers.Reversed(inner)` turns any comparison upside down -
by swapping the operands, not by negating the answer. `Comparers.Then(first,
second)` uses `second` only when `first` returned `0`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Comparison<T>` is a delegate: `(a, b) => int`, negative when `a` sorts first,
zero when they tie, positive when `b` sorts first. All three methods return one,
so all three bodies are `return (a, b) => ...;`.

`ByKey` should not compare the items at all - it compares what the key function
says about them.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Comparison<T> ByKey<T>(Func<T, int> key)
{
    return (a, b) => key(a).CompareTo(key(b));
}
```

For `Reversed`, resist `-inner(a, b)`. A comparison may legally return any
negative number, and `-int.MinValue` overflows straight back to `int.MinValue`,
so the negation reports "less than" for a pair that was greater. Swap the
operands instead.

`Then` needs to call `first` once, keep the answer in a local, and consult
`second` only when that answer was `0` - adding or multiplying the two results
gives orderings that are not even self-consistent.

## Exercise 6 - two lambdas over one variable

`Accounts.MakeAccount(opening)` returns a tuple of an `Action<int> Deposit` and
a `Func<int> Balance` that share one captured local - what the deposit writes,
the balance reads. Each call to `MakeAccount` makes a fresh, independent
balance. A negative deposit throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` and leaves the
balance alone.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One local variable, two lambdas, both mentioning it. That is the whole design.
The moment two lambdas use the same local, the compiler puts that local on a
single hidden object and gives both delegates a reference to it - so a write
through one is visible through the other.

Do not copy the balance into anything.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static (Action<int> Deposit, Func<int> Balance) MakeAccount(int opening)
{
    int balance = opening;

    Action<int> deposit = amount => { /* guard, then balance += amount; */ };
    Func<int> read = () => balance;

    return (deposit, read);
}
```

The guard belongs *inside* the deposit lambda, because the lambda is the only
way anyone can reach `balance` - and it has to throw before the `+=`, so a
refused deposit leaves no trace.

Each call to `MakeAccount` runs the `int balance = opening;` line again, which
is what makes two accounts independent. If you find yourself reaching for a
static field to hold the balance, you have written a class the hard way.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - bind, flip and pipe

Three combinators, each fully generic. `Currying.Bind(f, first)` fixes the
first argument of a two-argument function. `Currying.Flip(f)` swaps its
parameters. `Currying.Pipe(f, g)` chains them so that `Pipe(f, g)(x)` is
`g(f(x))` - `f` runs first. Getting the type parameters lined up is most of the
work.

Edit `src/Lessons/D16_DelegatesLambdas/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d16_delegates_lambdas ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every body here is one line. All the difficulty is in the signatures, so write
the call you want first and let it dictate the types:

```
Bind(divide, 100)      -> a function of ONE argument
Flip(divide)(4, 100)   -> divide(100, 4)
Pipe(f, g)(x)          -> g(f(x))
```

Note which argument `Bind` fixes: the first one.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Func<TSecond, TResult> Bind<TFirst, TSecond, TResult>(
    Func<TFirst, TSecond, TResult> f, TFirst first)
{
    return second => f(first, second);
}
```

`Flip` is the same trick with the parameters written in the other order: the
returned delegate is `Func<TSecond, TFirst, TResult>`, and inside it you call
`f(first, second)` with the names as they were.

## Hint 3

For `Pipe`, name the middle type. `f` is `Func<TIn, TMid>` and `g` is
`Func<TMid, TOut>`, so `TMid` appears twice in the parameters and never in the
result - that is what "f ends where g begins" means when written as types. The
body is `x => g(f(x))`.

If the compiler cannot infer the type arguments at a call site, that is not a
bug in your signature; sometimes there genuinely is nothing to infer from, and
the caller writes them out. Decide whether you want `Pipe`'s type parameters in
the order `TIn, TMid, TOut` - the gate calls it explicitly, so the order you
pick has to match the README.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Every body here is one line. All the difficulty is in the signatures, so write
the call you want first and let it dictate the types:

```
Bind(divide, 100)      -> a function of ONE argument
Flip(divide)(4, 100)   -> divide(100, 4)
Pipe(f, g)(x)          -> g(f(x))
```

Note which argument `Bind` fixes: the first one.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Func<TSecond, TResult> Bind<TFirst, TSecond, TResult>(
    Func<TFirst, TSecond, TResult> f, TFirst first)
{
    return second => f(first, second);
}
```

`Flip` is the same trick with the parameters written in the other order: the
returned delegate is `Func<TSecond, TFirst, TResult>`, and inside it you call
`f(first, second)` with the names as they were.

## Hint 3

For `Pipe`, name the middle type. `f` is `Func<TIn, TMid>` and `g` is
`Func<TMid, TOut>`, so `TMid` appears twice in the parameters and never in the
result - that is what "f ends where g begins" means when written as types. The
body is `x => g(f(x))`.

If the compiler cannot infer the type arguments at a call site, that is not a
bug in your signature; sometimes there genuinely is nothing to infer from, and
the caller writes them out. Decide whether you want `Pipe`'s type parameters in
the order `TIn, TMid, TOut` - the gate calls it explicitly, so the order you
pick has to match the README.

## Exercise 8 - a rules engine made of predicates

`Validator<T>` holds a list of `(message, rule)` pairs. `Require` registers one
and returns the same validator so calls chain; `Check` returns every failing
rule's message in registration order (empty means fine); `IsValid` is true when
`Check` is empty. A rule answers `true` for GOOD data. The `Signup` record is
written for you.

## Hint 1

A rule is a `Func<T, bool>` and a message is a string, and they belong
together - so store pairs, not two parallel lists. A `List<(string, Func<T,
bool>)>` is enough; the field initialiser runs per instance, which is what
keeps two validators apart.

Fix the polarity before you write anything: a rule answers `true` when the item
is *fine*, and its message is reported when it answers `false`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public Validator<T> Require(string message, Func<T, bool> rule)
{
    _rules.Add((message, rule));
    return this;   // `this`, not a new Validator<T>
}
```

them all.

loop; decide for yourself whether that is worth the extra list allocation on
the happy path, and what you would do instead if it were not.

lessons.briefing:
# d17 - Events drills

Eight problems on the publisher's side of an event: declaring one, raising it
without a `NullReferenceException`, carrying data in `EventArgs`, controlling
the subscriber list, and the two things a multicast delegate does badly - one
handler that throws, and handlers that return values. They drill lesson 09 -
reread `09_delegates_events_lambdas` if `+=` on an event is still mysterious.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D17_Events/`. Nothing here depends on anything
else here.

## Exercise 1 - raising an event nobody may be listening to

`Kettle.Heat(degrees)` adds to `Celsius` and raises the `Boiled` event on the
crossing from below 100 to 100 or above - once, not on every later call, and
not at all when nobody is subscribed. The sender is the kettle; the args are
`EventArgs.Empty`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - an event that carries data

`StockLowEventArgs` derives from `EventArgs` and carries `Sku` and
`Remaining`. `Warehouse` has `Receive`, `Remaining(sku)` (zero for an unknown
SKU) and `Ship`, which throws `InvalidOperationException` and changes nothing
when there is not enough stock, and otherwise raises `StockLow` whenever the
count left is strictly below `Threshold`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - many subscribers on one event

`Bell.Ring(note)` raises `Rung` for every subscriber, in subscription order and
without throwing when there are none. `Bell.Silence()` drops the whole
subscriber list at once - which is legal only inside the declaring class. The
gate also checks what `+=` and `-=` do with a duplicate handler.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - a subscription you can hand back

`Feed.Subscribe(handler)` registers the handler and returns an `Action` that
removes it again. Calling that action twice must not remove anybody else's
handler. `Feed.Publish(item)` calls every current handler in subscription
order.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - writing the add and remove accessors yourself

`Room.Entered` is declared with explicit `add` and `remove` accessors over the
private `_entered` field. `Subscribers` is the live count and
`PeakSubscribers` is the highest it has ever been. Removing a handler that was
never added must move neither number. `Enter()` raises the event with the room
as the sender.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - one bad handler must not silence the rest

`Broadcaster.BroadcastNaive` is written for you and shows the problem: the
first handler that throws ends the raise, so later handlers never run.
`Broadcaster.Broadcast(text)` must call every handler anyway and return the
exceptions it caught, in the order they happened - an empty list when all was
well.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - every handler's answer, not just the last one

`Poll.NaiveTotal` is written for you and shows the problem: invoking a
multicast `Func<int>` runs every handler and returns only the last one's
result. `Poll.AllVotes()` returns every handler's answer in subscription order,
and `Poll.Total()` sums them. No subscribers means an empty list and zero.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a typed event bus

`EventBus` keeps one handler list per message type in the supplied dictionary.
`Subscribe<T>`, `Unsubscribe<T>` (true when it removed one), `SubscriberCount<T>`
and `Publish<T>`, which delivers in registration order and returns how many
handlers ran. Publishing a type nobody subscribed to delivers to nobody. A
handler that subscribes during delivery must not receive the message being
delivered.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex8
```

## Notes

An event is a delegate field with two doors nailed shut. Outside the declaring
class you may only `+=` and `-=`; you cannot read it, assign it, or invoke it.
That single restriction is the whole feature, and it exists because a plain
public delegate field lets any caller overwrite every subscription or raise the
event on the publisher's behalf.

The pattern uniting these eight problems is that **the publisher owns the
list**. Every question worth asking about an event is a question about that
list: is it empty (ex1), what does it carry (ex2), what order does it run in
and what happens to duplicates (ex3), how does a subscriber get back off it
(ex4), who is counting it (ex5), and what happens when walking it goes wrong
(ex6 and ex7). Once you have written `GetInvocationList()` a few times, the
combined delegate stops being magic: it is an array of delegates and a loop.

Two of the problems exist because `Delegate.Invoke` on a multicast delegate is
a blunt instrument. It stops at the first exception and it throws away every
return value but the last. Neither is a bug - both are the documented
behaviour - but both are wrong often enough that real publishers loop by hand.

## ex1

Really testing: the two-line raise, and the crossing. The null-conditional
`Boiled?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty)` is the idiom, and the reason it matters
is that an event with no subscribers is `null`, not an empty list - so an
unguarded raise is a `NullReferenceException` on the very first call in
production and never in your tests. The classic mistake in the logic is testing
only the new temperature, which raises again on every subsequent heat; the
event is about the transition, so you have to remember what was true before.
(In multi-threaded code you would also copy the delegate to a local first, since
`?.` already does that for you.)

## ex2

Really testing: the `EventHandler<TEventArgs>` shape. A custom args class
derives from `EventArgs`, is immutable, and carries what the handler needs to
do its job without calling back into the publisher. The classic mistake is
putting the shipped quantity in `Remaining`; the second is raising the event
before the state has been updated, so a handler that reads `warehouse.Remaining`
sees the old number. Note also the order in `Ship`: validate, then mutate, then
raise - a refused shipment must leave no trace, which is why the check comes
before the subtraction rather than after.

## ex3

Really testing: that `+=` builds a list, not a set. Subscribing the same
handler twice really does register it twice and it really is called twice;
`-=` removes one copy, and specifically the last matching one. That surprises
people who use an event as a "register once" hook. `Silence` is the other half
of the lesson: `Rung = null` is a plain assignment that only compiles inside
`Bell`, because outside the class an event exposes nothing but its two
accessors. That is the difference between an event and a public delegate field,
and it is the reason to prefer the event.

## ex4

Really testing: the subscription token, and why it is needed. `-=` compares
delegates, and two separately written lambdas with identical bodies are
different objects - so `feed.Rung -= item => Log(item)` removes nothing at all
and the leak is silent. The fix is to keep the delegate instance, and the
tidiest way to hand it back is a closure that already holds it. The `removed`
flag is the extra care: without it a second call to the unsubscriber removes
one more copy of the same handler, which is somebody else's subscription when
the handler was registered twice. This is exactly the shape `IObservable<T>`
uses, with an `IDisposable` in place of the `Action`.

## ex5

Really testing: that the field-like event you normally write is shorthand. When
you write `public event EventHandler Entered;` the compiler generates a private
delegate field and a pair of accessors; spell them out and you can do anything
else you like in them. The instructive requirement is the stranger: `-=` for a
handler that was never added is a silent no-op on the delegate, so a naive
`Subscribers--` drifts below zero and the counter lies. Recomputing from
`GetInvocationList().Length` instead of tracking increments is the robust move,
and it is a good habit generally - derive state you can derive.

## ex6

Really testing: exception isolation across a multicast raise. `Message?.Invoke`
compiles into one call that walks the invocation list internally, so the first
handler to throw unwinds out of the publisher and the rest are simply skipped -
the publisher is now at the mercy of the worst subscriber it has. Looping over
`GetInvocationList()` with a `try` around each call is the standard fix, and
the important detail is that the caught exception object is stored as-is;
wrapping or rethrowing a new exception loses the original stack trace. Real
publishers usually finish by throwing an `AggregateException` when the list is
non-empty; here it is returned so the gate can inspect it.

## ex7

Really testing: what a multicast delegate does with return values. It calls
every handler and hands back only the last one's result - which is not a bug,
because there is nowhere else to put four answers, but it is almost never what
the author wanted. `GetInvocationList()` gives the array; casting each entry
back to `Func<int>` and calling it collects them all. The classic mistake is
assuming the earlier handlers did not run, and the classic *design* mistake is
using an event for something that needs answers at all - an
`IEnumerable<IVoter>` would say what is meant far more plainly.

## ex8

Really testing: everything above, generalised. The dictionary is keyed by
`typeof(T)`, which is what makes `Publish("hi")` reach the string handlers and
leave the int handlers alone; the values are `List<Delegate>` because a
dictionary cannot hold a differently-typed `Action<T>` in each slot, so the
cast back on the way out is unavoidable and is safe precisely because the key
guarantees it. The trap is re-entrancy: a handler that subscribes while the
message is being delivered mutates the list you are iterating, which throws
`InvalidOperationException`. Taking a snapshot with `ToArray()` first both
fixes that and gives the delivery a clear rule - this message goes to the
handlers that were registered when it was published.

## Further reading

- [Events](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/) - what the `event` keyword adds to a delegate field.
- [How to raise base class events](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/how-to-raise-base-class-events-in-derived-classes) - and the `OnXxx` protected-method convention.
- [`EventHandler<TEventArgs>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.eventhandler-1) - the standard shape ex1, ex2 and ex5 follow.
- [`Delegate.GetInvocationList`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.delegate.getinvocationlist) - the array behind every multicast delegate, and the key to ex6 and ex7.
- [How to implement custom event accessors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/how-to-implement-custom-event-accessors) - the `add`/`remove` form ex5 uses.
- [`AggregateException`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.aggregateexception) - what ex6's list of failures usually becomes.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - an event that carries data

`StockLowEventArgs` derives from `EventArgs` and carries `Sku` and
`Remaining`. `Warehouse` has `Receive`, `Remaining(sku)` (zero for an unknown
SKU) and `Ship`, which throws `InvalidOperationException` and changes nothing
when there is not enough stock, and otherwise raises `StockLow` whenever the
count left is strictly below `Threshold`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`StockLowEventArgs` is an ordinary class that derives from `EventArgs` and has
get-only properties set in the constructor. That is all `EventHandler<T>` asks
of it.

`Ship` does three things in a fixed order. Work out what they are before you
write the method - one of them being out of place is the mistake this exercise
is built around.

## Hint 2

The order is: validate, mutate, raise.

```csharp
int remaining = Remaining(sku);
if (quantity > remaining) { throw new InvalidOperationException(...); }
remaining -= quantity;
_stock[sku] = remaining;
if (remaining < Threshold) { /* raise with the count that is LEFT */ }
```

Validating first is what makes a refused shipment leave no trace. Raising last
is what lets a handler call back into `warehouse.Remaining(sku)` and see the
number the event just told it about.

`Remaining` should use `TryGetValue` so an unknown SKU reads as zero rather
than throwing - `_stock[sku]` on a missing key is a `KeyNotFoundException`.

## Hint 1

`StockLowEventArgs` is an ordinary class that derives from `EventArgs` and has
get-only properties set in the constructor. That is all `EventHandler<T>` asks
of it.

`Ship` does three things in a fixed order. Work out what they are before you
write the method - one of them being out of place is the mistake this exercise
is built around.

## Hint 2

The order is: validate, mutate, raise.

```csharp
int remaining = Remaining(sku);
if (quantity > remaining) { throw new InvalidOperationException(...); }
remaining -= quantity;
_stock[sku] = remaining;
if (remaining < Threshold) { /* raise with the count that is LEFT */ }
```

Validating first is what makes a refused shipment leave no trace. Raising last
is what lets a handler call back into `warehouse.Remaining(sku)` and see the
number the event just told it about.

`Remaining` should use `TryGetValue` so an unknown SKU reads as zero rather
than throwing - `_stock[sku]` on a missing key is a `KeyNotFoundException`.

## Exercise 4 - a subscription you can hand back

`Feed.Subscribe(handler)` registers the handler and returns an `Action` that
removes it again. Calling that action twice must not remove anybody else's
handler. `Feed.Publish(item)` calls every current handler in subscription
order.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`-=` compares delegates for equality, and two separately written lambdas with
identical bodies are two different objects. So a caller who wrote
`feed.Subscribe(item => Log(item))` has no way to remove that handler later
unless you give them one.

You have the handler right there in `Subscribe`. Return a lambda that closes
over it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public Action Subscribe(Action<string> handler)
{
    _handlers += handler;

    bool removed = false;
    return () => { /* guard on removed, then _handlers -= handler; */ };
}
```

The `removed` flag is not paranoia. Without it, a caller who invokes the
unsubscriber twice takes a second copy of the same handler off the list - and
if somebody else had subscribed that same handler, you have just cancelled
their subscription instead.

Note that `_handlers` here is a plain delegate field rather than an `event`,
because `Subscribe` needs to modify it and `Publish` needs to invoke it. Decide
for yourself whether you would expose it as an event as well.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`-=` compares delegates for equality, and two separately written lambdas with
identical bodies are two different objects. So a caller who wrote
`feed.Subscribe(item => Log(item))` has no way to remove that handler later
unless you give them one.

You have the handler right there in `Subscribe`. Return a lambda that closes
over it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public Action Subscribe(Action<string> handler)
{
    _handlers += handler;

    bool removed = false;
    return () => { /* guard on removed, then _handlers -= handler; */ };
}
```

The `removed` flag is not paranoia. Without it, a caller who invokes the
unsubscriber twice takes a second copy of the same handler off the list - and
if somebody else had subscribed that same handler, you have just cancelled
their subscription instead.

Note that `_handlers` here is a plain delegate field rather than an `event`,
because `Subscribe` needs to modify it and `Publish` needs to invoke it. Decide
for yourself whether you would expose it as an event as well.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`add` and `remove` are just method bodies. Inside them, `value` is the handler
being subscribed or unsubscribed, and `_entered` is the delegate field the
compiler would normally have generated for you.

So `add` starts with `_entered += value;` and `remove` with
`_entered -= value;`. The counting is the exercise.

## Hint 2

Do not write `Subscribers++` and `Subscribers--`. Derive the number instead:

```csharp
private int CurrentCount()
{
    return _entered?.GetInvocationList().Length ?? 0;
}
```

Call it at the end of both accessors. That handles the stranger case for free -
removing a handler that was never on the list leaves the delegate unchanged, so
the recomputed count is unchanged too, whereas a blind decrement would take it
to -1 and the counter would be lying from then on.

`PeakSubscribers` only ever moves up, so it is updated in `add` and never in
`remove`.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - every handler's answer, not just the last one

`Poll.NaiveTotal` is written for you and shows the problem: invoking a
multicast `Func<int>` runs every handler and returns only the last one's
result. `Poll.AllVotes()` returns every handler's answer in subscription order,
and `Poll.Total()` sums them. No subscribers means an empty list and zero.

Edit `src/Lessons/D17_Events/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d17_events ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Run the supplied `NaiveTotal` in your head first with three handlers returning
1, 2 and 3. All three run. The answer is 3. Nothing was skipped - the first two
results were simply discarded, because a single call can only hand back a
single value.

The fix is the same tool as ex6: walk the invocation list yourself.

## Hint 2

```csharp
foreach (Delegate entry in handlers.GetInvocationList())
{
    results.Add(((Func<int>)entry)());
}
```

The cast is safe because every entry in a `Func<int>`'s invocation list is a
`Func<int>` - the delegate type is what makes the list well-typed in the first
place.

Write `Total` in terms of `AllVotes` rather than duplicating the loop. And
notice what the gate checks with the same handler subscribed twice: the
invocation list is a list, so it votes twice. If that strikes you as wrong for
a poll, that is the real lesson here - an event is a poor way to ask a question
you need every answer to.

## Hint 1

Run the supplied `NaiveTotal` in your head first with three handlers returning
1, 2 and 3. All three run. The answer is 3. Nothing was skipped - the first two
results were simply discarded, because a single call can only hand back a
single value.

The fix is the same tool as ex6: walk the invocation list yourself.

## Hint 2

```csharp
foreach (Delegate entry in handlers.GetInvocationList())
{
    results.Add(((Func<int>)entry)());
}
```

The cast is safe because every entry in a `Func<int>`'s invocation list is a
`Func<int>` - the delegate type is what makes the list well-typed in the first
place.

Write `Total` in terms of `AllVotes` rather than duplicating the loop. And
notice what the gate checks with the same handler subscribed twice: the
invocation list is a list, so it votes twice. If that strikes you as wrong for
a poll, that is the real lesson here - an event is a poor way to ask a question
you need every answer to.

## Exercise 8 - a typed event bus

`EventBus` keeps one handler list per message type in the supplied dictionary.
`Subscribe<T>`, `Unsubscribe<T>` (true when it removed one), `SubscriberCount<T>`
and `Publish<T>`, which delivers in registration order and returns how many
handlers ran. Publishing a type nobody subscribed to delivers to nobody. A
handler that subscribes during delivery must not receive the message being
delivered.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The dictionary key is `typeof(T)` and the value is the list of handlers for
that type. `Subscribe<T>` finds or creates the list and adds the handler;
`SubscriberCount<T>` and `Unsubscribe<T>` look it up and do nothing when it is
missing.

`TryGetValue` is the tool for all three - a missing key is normal here, not an
error.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (!_handlers.TryGetValue(typeof(T), out List<Delegate>? forType))
{
    forType = new List<Delegate>();
    _handlers[typeof(T)] = forType;
}

forType.Add(handler);
```

The list has to be `List<Delegate>` because different slots hold different
`Action<T>` types, so `Publish<T>` casts each entry back with
`((Action<T>)entry)(message)`. That cast cannot fail: the key is what
guarantees the type.

## Hint 3

Re-entrancy is the last requirement, and it is the one the gate builds a
specific handler for. A handler that calls `Subscribe` while the message is
being delivered adds to the very list you are iterating, and `foreach` over a
`List<T>` that changed underneath it throws `InvalidOperationException`.

Take a copy before you start delivering - `ToArray()` is enough - and return
that copy's length. Beyond fixing the exception, it also settles a design
question you would otherwise have to answer case by case: this message goes to
the handlers registered when it was published, and nobody else.

lessons.briefing:
# d18 - LINQ filtering drills

Eight problems on the operators that make a sequence smaller or pick one thing
out of it: `Where`, `Any`/`All`/`Count`, the `First`/`Single` family, `Skip`,
`Take`, `TakeWhile`, `SkipWhile`, `Distinct`, `OfType` and the ordering that
goes with them. They drill lesson 10 - reread `10_linq_1` if the difference
between `First` and `Single` is still a shrug.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - restrict, then project

`Restrict.LongWordsUpper(words, minLength)` keeps the words at least
`minLength` characters long, upper-cases them with `ToUpperInvariant`, and
preserves the input order. `Restrict.Numbered(words)` turns each word into
`"1. ada"` with a 1-based position.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - questions with a yes-or-no answer

`Questions.AnyNegative`, `Questions.AllPositive`, `Questions.HasAny` and
`Questions.CountBetween(numbers, low, high)` - the last one counting the
numbers in an inclusive range. Work out what each of the first three should say
about an empty sequence before you write them; the gate checks all three.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - picking one element

Four ways to ask for the word starting with a given letter.
`Picks.FirstStartingWith` throws `InvalidOperationException` when there is
none; `Picks.FirstStartingWithOrNull` returns null instead;
`Picks.OnlyStartingWith` throws when there is none *and* when there is more
than one; `Picks.FirstStartingWithOr(words, letter, fallback)` returns the
fallback.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - slicing by position and by a running condition

`Slices.Page(source, pageNumber, pageSize)` returns one 1-based page; a page
past the end is empty. `Slices.WithinBudget(costs, budget)` returns the longest
run of costs from the front whose *running total* stays at or below the budget,
stopping at the first one that breaks it. `Slices.AfterFirstNegative(numbers)`
returns everything after the first negative number, dropping the negative
itself, and is empty when there is no negative.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - duplicates, and a stable order

`Dedupe.UniqueOwners(tickets)` gives each owner once in first-seen order.
`Dedupe.OnePerOwner(tickets)` keeps one whole ticket per owner - the first one.
`Dedupe.Ranked(tickets)` orders by `Priority` ascending with ties broken by
`Id` using `StringComparer.Ordinal`. None of them may modify the input.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - filtering by type, and filtering out nothing

`Narrow.IntsOnly(items)` keeps the items that really are `int`.
`Narrow.Meaningful(entries)` drops null, empty and whitespace-only entries and
trims what is left. `Narrow.Describe(items)` produces one description per item:
`"int:7"`, `"text:hi"`, `"null"`, or `"other:Double"` using the runtime type's
name.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - several filters, an ordering and a limit

`Reports.TopProducts(sales, allowedRegions, minRevenue, count)` keeps the sales
whose `Region` is in the allow-list and whose revenue (`Units * UnitPrice`) is
at least `minRevenue`, orders them by revenue descending with ties broken by
`Product` ordinal-ascending, cuts the result to at most `count` entries, and
returns the product names.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - optional filters, one page, and the total behind it

`Library.Search(books, author, fromYear, maxPrice, pageNumber, pageSize)`
applies only the criteria that were supplied - a null one means "do not filter
on that" - orders by `Year` ascending with ties broken by `Title` (ordinal),

# Reading - csharp/d18_linq_filtering

## Notes

The skill being drilled is choosing the right operator rather than writing a
loop that does the same thing more slowly. Every one of these eight problems
could be a `foreach` with an `if` in it; the reason to reach for LINQ is that
the operator names say what you meant, and a reader can check the intent
without simulating the code.

The pattern uniting them is the **pipeline**: restrict, then order, then cut,
then project - in that order. Almost every mistake in this set is an order
mistake. Taking before ordering gives an arbitrary top-N. Paging before
counting gives a total that is always the page size. Projecting before
filtering throws away the fields the filter needed. Once the shape is a habit,
the individual operators are trivia you can look up.

The other running theme is what each operator does with **nothing**: an empty
sequence, no match, a null element. `Any` says false and `All` says true;
`First` throws and `FirstOrDefault` does not; `Skip` past the end is empty
rather than an error. Those answers are not arbitrary, and knowing them is most
of what separates code that works on the happy path from code that works.

## ex1

Really testing: `Where` then `Select`, and the fact that neither one reorders
anything. The classic mistake is projecting first and filtering second - here
that still works because the length survives the upper-casing, but as soon as
the projection drops a field the filter needed, it does not. The second thing
being drilled is the `Select` overload whose lambda takes an index, which
removes the last honest reason to keep a manual counter beside a query. Note
that the index is the position in the sequence `Select` received, so putting a
`Where` in front of it renumbers everything.

## ex2

Really testing: the empty-sequence answers, which are the whole exercise.
`Any()` on an empty sequence is false and `All(...)` is true - vacuous truth,
the same rule that makes "every unicorn in this room is purple" true. It bites
in real code: a validation written as `orders.All(o => o.Total > 0)` passes
loudly for a customer with no orders. The other habit worth forming is `Any()`
over `Count() != 0`: `Any` stops at the first element, while `Count` walks the
entire sequence to answer a question the first element settled - and over a
lazy or remote source that difference is not a micro-optimisation.

## ex3

Really testing: four ways to fail, and picking the one that says what you mean.
`First` throws because for a sequence of ints there is no "no answer" value to
return; `FirstOrDefault` returns `default(T)`, which is null for a string and
*zero* for an int - a trap worth remembering, because zero is a perfectly
plausible value. `Single` is the interesting one: it is a claim that exactly
one thing matches, and it throws when two do. The classic mistake is using
`First` where `Single` was meant, which turns a broken assumption into a
silently arbitrary answer, and the second is using `Single` on a hot path,
since it must look at a second element to know it is alone.

## ex4

Really testing: the difference between filtering and slicing. `Where` looks at
every element; `TakeWhile` stops at the first failure and never looks again,
which is why `WithinBudget` refuses a cheap item that comes after an expensive
one. That is either exactly what you want or exactly what you did not,
and the operator name is the only thing that says which. `SkipWhile` is the
mirror: once it starts yielding it never tests again, so later negatives
survive. The paging arithmetic is the classic off-by-one - page 1 must skip
zero - and the pleasant surprise is that no bounds checking is needed anywhere,
because both `Skip` and `Take` are already total.

## ex5

Really testing: what "distinct" and "ordered" actually promise. `Distinct`
keeps the first occurrence and preserves order; it does not sort, and a result
that comes out sorted is a coincidence of the input. `DistinctBy` compares a
key and keeps the whole first item that had it, which is the operator people
hand-roll with a `HashSet` most often. The ordering half is about stability:
LINQ's `OrderBy` is a stable sort, so equal elements keep their relative input
order - but relying on that instead of writing the `ThenBy` means your tie-break
is an accident of the input rather than a decision, and `List.Sort` does not
make the same promise.

## ex6

Really testing: narrowing by type, and the difference between `OfType` and
`Cast`. `OfType<int>` filters - anything that is not an int is dropped, nulls
included. `Cast<int>` asserts - the first item that is not an int throws an
`InvalidCastException`. Using `Cast` where you meant `OfType` produces a crash
on data you thought you had excluded. In `Describe`, the ordering of the switch
arms is the lesson: `null` has to be handled first, because a type pattern
never matches null and the discard arm would then call `GetType()` on it. And
`Describe` projects rather than filters, so its output has exactly as many
entries as its input - a distinction the gate checks explicitly.

## ex7

Really testing: the pipeline order, under enough pressure that guessing does
not survive. Two independent filters, a two-level ordering, a limit, and a
projection - and the only arrangement that is correct puts `Take` after the
`OrderByDescending`/`ThenBy` pair and the `Select` last. Take first and you
get an arbitrary two rows sorted; project first and the revenue you need to
sort by is gone. The tie between two sales at 300 is deliberate: without the
`ThenBy` the result depends on input order, which is the kind of test that
passes today and fails when somebody adds a row. Note also that `HashSet`
membership is what keeps the region filter O(1) per row rather than a scan.

## ex8

Really testing: building a query conditionally, which is how every real search
endpoint works. Because the operators return a new `IEnumerable<T>` rather than
mutating, you can reassign a local inside an `if` and the query grows one clause
at a time - and nothing has run yet, so the cost of the branches is nothing. A
null criterion means *skip the filter*, not *match null*, and getting that
backwards makes an unfiltered search return zero rows. The second half is the
count: `TotalMatches` has to be taken after filtering and before paging, which
is exactly why the reference materialises the ordered sequence once and reads
both the page and the count off that list. Running two queries - one to count,
one to page - walks the source twice, which is wasteful over an array and
outright wrong over a sequence you can only read once.

## Further reading

- [LINQ overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/) - the standard query operators as a whole.
- [Filtering data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/filtering-data) - `Where` and `OfType`.
- [Quantifier operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/quantifier-operations) - `Any`, `All` and `Contains`, including the empty-sequence rules.
- [Partitioning data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/partitioning-data) - `Skip`, `Take`, `SkipWhile`, `TakeWhile`, `Chunk`.
- [`Enumerable.Single`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.single) - and exactly when it throws.
- [Sorting data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/sorting-data) - `OrderBy`, `ThenBy`, and the stability guarantee.

## Exercise 2 - questions with a yes-or-no answer

`Questions.AnyNegative`, `Questions.AllPositive`, `Questions.HasAny` and
`Questions.CountBetween(numbers, low, high)` - the last one counting the
numbers in an inclusive range. Work out what each of the first three should say
about an empty sequence before you write them; the gate checks all three.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

All four are one-liners built from `Any`, `All` and `Count`, each of which
takes an optional predicate. `Any` also has a parameterless form that just asks
"is there anything here".

Before you write them, answer this on paper: for an empty sequence, what does
`Any(...)` say, and what does `All(...)` say? They do not agree.

## Hint 2

`Any` on an empty sequence is **false** - it needs an element that satisfies
the predicate, and there is none. `All` on an empty sequence is **true** - it
needs no element that breaks the rule, and there is none of those either. That
is not a quirk; it is the same convention maths uses, and it is why
`orders.All(o => o.Total > 0)` passes cheerfully for a customer with no orders.

Prefer `Any()` to `Count() != 0`: `Any` stops at the first element while
`Count` walks the whole sequence to answer a question the first element already
settled.

`CountBetween` is inclusive at both ends, so both comparisons need the equals
sign.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

All four are one-liners built from `Any`, `All` and `Count`, each of which
takes an optional predicate. `Any` also has a parameterless form that just asks
"is there anything here".

Before you write them, answer this on paper: for an empty sequence, what does
`Any(...)` say, and what does `All(...)` say? They do not agree.

## Hint 2

`Any` on an empty sequence is **false** - it needs an element that satisfies
the predicate, and there is none. `All` on an empty sequence is **true** - it
needs no element that breaks the rule, and there is none of those either. That
is not a quirk; it is the same convention maths uses, and it is why
`orders.All(o => o.Total > 0)` passes cheerfully for a customer with no orders.

Prefer `Any()` to `Count() != 0`: `Any` stops at the first element while
`Count` walks the whole sequence to answer a question the first element already
settled.

`CountBetween` is inclusive at both ends, so both comparisons need the equals
sign.

## Exercise 3 - picking one element

Four ways to ask for the word starting with a given letter.
`Picks.FirstStartingWith` throws `InvalidOperationException` when there is
none; `Picks.FirstStartingWithOrNull` returns null instead;
`Picks.OnlyStartingWith` throws when there is none *and* when there is more
than one; `Picks.FirstStartingWithOr(words, letter, fallback)` returns the
fallback.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each of the four is exactly one LINQ call with a predicate. The whole exercise
is choosing which one, so read the summaries carefully - "throws when there is
more than one" names a specific operator.

The predicate itself needs care: `word[0]` on an empty string throws, so check
the length first.

## Hint 2

- `First(predicate)` - the first match, `InvalidOperationException` when none.
- `FirstOrDefault(predicate)` - the first match, `default(T)` when none.
- `FirstOrDefault(predicate, fallback)` - the two-argument overload, which
  saves you a null check at the call site.
- `Single(predicate)` - the one and only match; throws when there is none
  *and* when there are two.

`default(T)` is null for a string but **zero** for an int, which is why
`FirstOrDefault` over numbers cannot tell "no match" from "matched a zero" -
that is the case the fallback overload exists for.

Use `Single` when exactly one match is an assumption you want checked. It costs
an extra element read to prove the match was alone, and that cost is the point.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Each of the four is exactly one LINQ call with a predicate. The whole exercise
is choosing which one, so read the summaries carefully - "throws when there is
more than one" names a specific operator.

The predicate itself needs care: `word[0]` on an empty string throws, so check
the length first.

## Hint 2

- `First(predicate)` - the first match, `InvalidOperationException` when none.
- `FirstOrDefault(predicate)` - the first match, `default(T)` when none.
- `FirstOrDefault(predicate, fallback)` - the two-argument overload, which
  saves you a null check at the call site.
- `Single(predicate)` - the one and only match; throws when there is none
  *and* when there are two.

`default(T)` is null for a string but **zero** for an int, which is why
`FirstOrDefault` over numbers cannot tell "no match" from "matched a zero" -
that is the case the fallback overload exists for.

Use `Single` when exactly one match is an assumption you want checked. It costs
an extra element read to prove the match was alone, and that cost is the point.

`Slices.Page(source, pageNumber, pageSize)` returns one 1-based page; a page
past the end is empty. `Slices.WithinBudget(costs, budget)` returns the longest

itself, and is empty when there is no negative.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - duplicates, and a stable order

`Dedupe.UniqueOwners(tickets)` gives each owner once in first-seen order.
`Dedupe.OnePerOwner(tickets)` keeps one whole ticket per owner - the first one.
`Dedupe.Ranked(tickets)` orders by `Priority` ascending with ties broken by
`Id` using `StringComparer.Ordinal`. None of them may modify the input.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three one-liners. `Distinct` works on the values themselves, so `UniqueOwners`
has to project to the owner *before* de-duplicating.

For `OnePerOwner` you want the whole ticket, not the owner - which is a
different operator, added in .NET 6 precisely for this.

## Hint 2

```csharp
tickets.Select(t => t.Owner).Distinct()          // values
tickets.DistinctBy(t => t.Owner)                 // whole items, compared by key
tickets.OrderBy(t => t.Priority).ThenBy(t => t.Id, StringComparer.Ordinal)
```

Both `Distinct` and `DistinctBy` keep the **first** occurrence and preserve the
order the items arrived in. Neither one sorts, however sorted the result looks.

`ThenBy` takes an `IComparer<string>` as an optional second argument, and
`StringComparer.Ordinal` is the one that compares by code unit rather than by
culture - the only kind of string ordering that means the same thing on every
machine your code runs on.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three one-liners. `Distinct` works on the values themselves, so `UniqueOwners`
has to project to the owner *before* de-duplicating.

For `OnePerOwner` you want the whole ticket, not the owner - which is a
different operator, added in .NET 6 precisely for this.

## Hint 2

```csharp
tickets.Select(t => t.Owner).Distinct()          // values
tickets.DistinctBy(t => t.Owner)                 // whole items, compared by key
tickets.OrderBy(t => t.Priority).ThenBy(t => t.Id, StringComparer.Ordinal)
```

Both `Distinct` and `DistinctBy` keep the **first** occurrence and preserve the
order the items arrived in. Neither one sorts, however sorted the result looks.

`ThenBy` takes an `IComparer<string>` as an optional second argument, and
`StringComparer.Ordinal` is the one that compares by code unit rather than by
culture - the only kind of string ordering that means the same thing on every
machine your code runs on.

## Exercise 6 - filtering by type, and filtering out nothing

`Narrow.IntsOnly(items)` keeps the items that really are `int`.
`Narrow.Meaningful(entries)` drops null, empty and whitespace-only entries and
trims what is left. `Narrow.Describe(items)` produces one description per item:
`"int:7"`, `"text:hi"`, `"null"`, or `"other:Double"` using the runtime type's
name.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex6.cs`.


exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is an operator that filters a sequence down to the items of one type, and
a different one that insists every item already is that type. You want the
filtering one.

`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` handles all three of null, empty and spaces in a
single call.

## Hint 2

`OfType<int>()` keeps what matches and drops the rest, nulls included.
`Cast<int>()` would throw an `InvalidCastException` on the first string - that
is the whole difference, and picking the wrong one produces a crash on data you
believed you had excluded.

`Meaningful` filters and then projects, and the compiler needs help on the
projection: after the `Where` it still thinks the entry might be null, so
`entry!.Trim()` (or a pattern that reassures it) is what gets you past the
nullable warning.

For `Describe`, a `switch` expression inside `Select` reads best. Put the
`null` arm **first**: a type pattern like `int number` never matches null, so
without it the discard arm would call `GetType()` on a null reference.

is the whole difference, and picking the wrong one produces a crash on data you
believed you had excluded.

projection: after the `Where` it still thinks the entry might be null, so
`entry!.Trim()` (or a pattern that reassures it) is what gets you past the
nullable warning.

For `Describe`, a `switch` expression inside `Select` reads best. Put the
`null` arm **first**: a type pattern like `int number` never matches null, so
without it the discard arm would call `GetType()` on a null reference.

## Exercise 8 - optional filters, one page, and the total behind it

`Library.Search(books, author, fromYear, maxPrice, pageNumber, pageSize)`
applies only the criteria that were supplied - a null one means "do not filter
on that" - orders by `Year` ascending with ties broken by `Title` (ordinal),
and returns a `SearchResult` holding one 1-based page and the number of books
that matched *before* the paging. The gate also checks that the source sequence
is enumerated exactly once.

Edit `src/Lessons/D18_LinqFiltering/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d18_linq_filtering ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A LINQ operator returns a new sequence rather than changing the old one, which
means you can build the query up a clause at a time:

```csharp
IEnumerable<Book> matches = books;
if (author is not null) { matches = matches.Where(...); }
```

Nothing has run yet at that point, so the branches cost nothing. A null
criterion means *skip that filter entirely* - not *match books whose author is
null*.

## Hint 2

Order after all the filters, then materialise **once**:

```csharp
List<Book> ordered = matches
    .OrderBy(book => book.Year)
    .ThenBy(book => book.Title, StringComparer.Ordinal)
    .ToList();
```

Now the page is `ordered.Skip(...).Take(...)` and the total is `ordered.Count`.
Both come off the same list, which is what makes the gate's
enumerated-exactly-once assertion pass.

## Hint 3

The count is the part that is easy to get subtly wrong. `TotalMatches` is how
many books matched the criteria, **before** the paging - so it cannot be taken
after `Skip`/`Take`, where it would equal the page size on every full page and
the pager would have no idea how many pages exist.

The tempting alternative is `matches.Count()` and then a second query for the
page. It gives the right numbers for an array and it walks the source twice; if
the caller hands you a sequence that can only be read once - a file, a reader,
a generator - the second walk gets nothing. Deciding when that matters is worth
a minute of thought, and lesson d21 is entirely about it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A LINQ operator returns a new sequence rather than changing the old one, which
means you can build the query up a clause at a time:

```csharp
IEnumerable<Book> matches = books;
if (author is not null) { matches = matches.Where(...); }
```

Nothing has run yet at that point, so the branches cost nothing. A null
criterion means *skip that filter entirely* - not *match books whose author is
null*.

## Hint 2

Order after all the filters, then materialise **once**:

```csharp
List<Book> ordered = matches
    .OrderBy(book => book.Year)
    .ThenBy(book => book.Title, StringComparer.Ordinal)
    .ToList();
```

Now the page is `ordered.Skip(...).Take(...)` and the total is `ordered.Count`.
Both come off the same list, which is what makes the gate's
enumerated-exactly-once assertion pass.

## Hint 3

The count is the part that is easy to get subtly wrong. `TotalMatches` is how
many books matched the criteria, **before** the paging - so it cannot be taken
after `Skip`/`Take`, where it would equal the page size on every full page and
the pager would have no idea how many pages exist.

The tempting alternative is `matches.Count()` and then a second query for the
page. It gives the right numbers for an array and it walks the source twice; if
the caller hands you a sequence that can only be read once - a file, a reader,
a generator - the second walk gets nothing. Deciding when that matters is worth
a minute of thought, and lesson d21 is entirely about it.
