lessons.briefing:
# d19 - LINQ grouping drills

Eight problems on `GroupBy` and the things that live next to it: aggregating
inside a group, `ToLookup` versus `ToDictionary`, composite keys, `Aggregate`,
the `GroupBy` overloads nobody reads, top-N per group, and the buckets that
have to be reported even when nothing landed in them. They drill lesson 11 -
reread `11_linq_2` if `IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` is still an unfamiliar shape.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - the first grouping

`Tally.ByFirstLetter(words)` returns a `Dictionary<char, List<string>>` with
the words that share a first character, each group in input order.
`Tally.CountByLength(words)` returns `"3:2"` entries - length and count -
ordered by length ascending.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - aggregating inside each group

`Totals.UnitsByRegion(sales)` returns `"region=total"` ordered by total
descending, ties broken by region name (ordinal).
`Totals.BestSellerByRegion(sales)` maps each region to the product of its
largest single sale, ties broken by product name (ordinal).
`Totals.PeakSaleByRegion(sales)` maps each region to that largest number of
units.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - lookups and dictionaries are not the same thing

`Indexing.TitlesByAuthor(books)` returns an `ILookup<string, string>` - one
author, many titles - where an unknown key gives an empty sequence.
`Indexing.TitleById(books)` returns a `Dictionary<string, string>` and lets the
duplicate-key exception through. `Indexing.BookCountByAuthor(books)` counts
per author.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - a key made of two things

`Schedules.CountByDayAndRoom(visits)` returns `"Mon/A=2"` for every day-and-room
pair with any visits, ordered by day then room (both ordinal).
`Schedules.RoomHoppers(visits)` returns the people seen in more than one
*distinct* room, ordered by name.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - folding a sequence into one value

Three `Aggregate` overloads, one each. `Folds.TotalLength(parts)` uses the
seeded form and returns 0 for an empty sequence. `Folds.Deepest(paths)` uses
the seedless form - the path with the most `/`, first one winning a tie - and
throws `InvalidOperationException` when there is nothing. `Folds.Summarise`
uses the seed-and-result-selector form to gather count, min, max and sum in one
pass, throwing for an empty sequence.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - the GroupBy overloads that save you a step

`Shapes.NamesByDepartment(staff)` gives `"eng:ada,bob"` using the element-selector
overload, so each group holds names. `Shapes.HeadcountByDepartment(staff)` gives
`"eng=2"` using the result-selector overload, so no group object is created.
`Shapes.TopLevelByDepartment(staff)` gives `"eng=5"`. All three are ordered by
department (ordinal).

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - top N inside every group

`Leaderboards.TopTwoPerGame(scores)` gives `"chess:cleo,ada"` for each game,
games ordered ordinal, naming the two highest scorers with ties broken by
player name. A game with one player names one.
`Leaderboards.Consistent(scores)` returns the players who are in the top two of
more than one game, ordered by name.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a report, and the buckets that stay empty

`Analytics.ErrorReport(logs)` gives one line per service that logged at least
one `"error"`: `"api errors=2 slowest=1200"`, where slowest is the largest
`Millis` over *all* that service's entries. Ordered by error count descending,
ties broken by service name. `Analytics.LatencyHistogram(logs)` always returns
exactly `"fast=..."`, `"normal=..."`, `"slow=..."` in that order - fast is under
100ms, normal under 1000ms, slow is 1000ms or more - including buckets with a
count of zero.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d19_linq_grouping

## Notes

The skill being drilled is turning a flat sequence into a summary. `GroupBy`
does one thing: it walks the sequence, computes a key for each item, and hands
back one `IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` per distinct key - a key with the items
that had it hanging off it. Everything else in this set is what you do with
those groups.

The pattern uniting the eight problems is **group, aggregate, order,
project**, in that order. The grouping decides what a row is; the aggregate
decides what the row says; the ordering is over the *rows*, not the original
items, which is the step people most often put in the wrong place. Sorting the
input and then grouping usually gives the right answer by accident and the
wrong one as soon as the data changes.

The other thing worth internalising is what `GroupBy` will never do for you: it
never invents a group for a key nothing had. That is exactly right for
"customers by city" and exactly wrong for a histogram, where a bucket with zero
in it is the most interesting bucket on the chart. Ex8 makes that concrete.

## ex1

Really testing: the shape of what `GroupBy` returns. A group is not a list -
it is an object with a `Key` that also happens to be an `IEnumerable` of its
items, which is why `group.ToList()` and `group.Count()` both work on it
directly. The classic mistake is reaching for a `Dictionary<char,
List<string>>` and a `foreach` with a `ContainsKey` check, which is what
`GroupBy` plus `ToDictionary` does in one line. Note that both the groups and
the items inside them come out in first-seen order - documented behaviour of
the LINQ-to-Objects implementation, and worth relying on only there.

## ex2

Really testing: aggregating within a group and then ordering the results. Each
group gets `Sum`, `Max` or its own inner `OrderBy`, and the outer ordering
operates on the aggregated rows. The interesting one is `BestSellerByRegion`,
where the answer is "the item with the largest X" rather than the largest X
itself - `Max` gives you the number and throws away the row, so you either sort
the group and take the first, or use `MaxBy`. Both south sales are 40 units on
purpose: without the explicit tie-break the result depends on input order, and
a test that passes for that reason is not a test.

## ex3

Really testing: the difference between a one-to-many index and a one-to-one
one. `ToLookup` gives an `ILookup`, which is immutable, allows duplicate keys,
and returns an *empty sequence* for a key it does not have - so there is never
a null check and never a `ContainsKey`. `ToDictionary` insists each key appears
once and throws `ArgumentException` when it does not. That exception is a
feature: an id that repeats means the assumption behind the index is false, and
finding out here is much cheaper than finding out three screens later. The
third method shows the middle road - `GroupBy` then `ToDictionary` with
`Count()` - for when you want one value per key but the source has many.

## ex4

Really testing: composite keys. A value tuple `(visit.Day, visit.Room)` works
as a group key because tuples get structural equality and a matching hash code
for free, and the same is true of an anonymous type or a record. The classic
mistake is `visit.Day + visit.Room`, which quietly collides whenever the pieces
can run together ("Mo" + "nA" and "Mon" + "A" are the same string). The second
half is about `Distinct` inside a group: bob's two identical visits are one
room, so counting rows instead of distinct rooms would call him a room-hopper
on the strength of a duplicate.

## ex5

Really testing: the three `Aggregate` overloads and how they differ at the
edges. The seedless one starts with the first element and therefore throws on
an empty sequence - which is right for "the deepest path" and wrong for "the
total". The seeded one returns the seed for an empty sequence, and its seed can
be a different type from the elements, which is what lets a fold build
something. The third adds a result selector, which is how you carry a working
state - here a four-part tuple - and convert it to the answer at the end.
`Summarise` in one pass rather than four separate `Min`/`Max`/`Sum`/`Count`
calls is the point: four calls walk the sequence four times, which is invisible
over an array and impossible over a stream.

## ex6

Really testing: that `GroupBy` has four overloads and most people know one.
The element selector changes what the group *contains* - names rather than
employees - which is usually what you wanted and saves a `Select` inside the
`Select`. The result selector goes further and means no `IGrouping` object is
allocated at all: your lambda receives the key and the members and returns the
finished row. Neither is a performance argument at this scale; both are
readability arguments, and knowing they exist is what stops the deeply nested
`Select(g => new { g.Key, Names = g.Select(e => e.Name) })` that everybody
writes first.

## ex7

Really testing: top-N per group, which is the query people most often get
wrong. The ordering has to happen *inside* each group - `group.OrderByDescending
(...).Take(2)` - because a global sort followed by a group-wide `Take` takes
two rows from the whole sequence, not two from each. Pulling the per-group
ranking into a small helper is what makes the second half short, and the second
half is the other lesson: `SelectMany` flattens the per-game winners back into
one sequence of names, which can then be grouped *again* by name. Group,
flatten, group is a shape worth recognising; it is the same one SQL expresses
with a window function.

## ex8

Really testing: two aggregates over the same group with different filters, and
the limit of `GroupBy`. `Count(entry => entry.Level == "error")` and
`Max(entry => entry.Millis)` read the same group and answer different
questions, which is why the group has to be projected into a row before it is
filtered and ordered - filtering the *entries* to errors first would give the
wrong "slowest". The histogram is the more important half: `GroupBy` produces
a group only for a key that occurred, so an empty bucket simply is not there.
The fix is to state the buckets yourself and look each one up, which turns
"what did the data contain" into "what does the report always show" - a
distinction worth making explicitly every time you draw a chart.

## Further reading

- [Grouping data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/grouping-data) - every `GroupBy` overload, with examples.
- [`IGrouping<TKey, TElement>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.igrouping-2) - the key-plus-sequence type groups come back as.
- [`Enumerable.ToLookup`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.tolookup) - and the empty-sequence-for-a-missing-key rule.
- [`Enumerable.ToDictionary`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.todictionary) - including the duplicate-key exception.
- [Aggregation operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/aggregation-operations) - `Sum`, `Max`, `MaxBy`, `Average` and `Aggregate`.
- [`Enumerable.Aggregate`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.aggregate) - the three overloads ex5 is built from.

one sequence of names, which can then be grouped *again* by name. Group,
flatten, group is a shape worth recognising; it is the same one SQL expresses
with a window function.

## ex8

Really testing: two aggregates over the same group with different filters, and
the limit of `GroupBy`. `Count(entry => entry.Level == "error")` and
`Max(entry => entry.Millis)` read the same group and answer different
questions, which is why the group has to be projected into a row before it is
filtered and ordered - filtering the *entries* to errors first would give the
wrong "slowest". The histogram is the more important half: `GroupBy` produces
a group only for a key that occurred, so an empty bucket simply is not there.
The fix is to state the buckets yourself and look each one up, which turns
"what did the data contain" into "what does the report always show" - a
distinction worth making explicitly every time you draw a chart.

## Exercise 1 - the first grouping

`Tally.ByFirstLetter(words)` returns a `Dictionary<char, List<string>>` with
the words that share a first character, each group in input order.
`Tally.CountByLength(words)` returns `"3:2"` entries - length and count -
ordered by length ascending.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`GroupBy(word => word[0])` gives you one group per distinct first letter. A
group is an `IGrouping<char, string>`: it has a `Key`, and it *is* a sequence
of the words that had that key - so `group.ToList()` and `group.Count()` both
work on it without any unwrapping.

`ToDictionary` takes a key selector and a value selector, which is exactly the
pair you need for the first method.

## Hint 2

```csharp
words
    .GroupBy(word => word[0])
    .ToDictionary(group => group.Key, group => group.ToList());
```

For `CountByLength`, group by `word.Length` instead, order the *groups* by
`group.Key`, and project each one to `$"{group.Key}:{group.Count()}"`.

Note the thing the gate checks with the letter 'z': `GroupBy` never produces a
group for a key nothing had. That is right for most reports and wrong for a
histogram, which is what ex8 is about.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`GroupBy(word => word[0])` gives you one group per distinct first letter. A
group is an `IGrouping<char, string>`: it has a `Key`, and it *is* a sequence
of the words that had that key - so `group.ToList()` and `group.Count()` both
work on it without any unwrapping.

`ToDictionary` takes a key selector and a value selector, which is exactly the
pair you need for the first method.

## Hint 2

```csharp
words
    .GroupBy(word => word[0])
    .ToDictionary(group => group.Key, group => group.ToList());
```

For `CountByLength`, group by `word.Length` instead, order the *groups* by
`group.Key`, and project each one to `$"{group.Key}:{group.Count()}"`.

Note the thing the gate checks with the letter 'z': `GroupBy` never produces a
group for a key nothing had. That is right for most reports and wrong for a
histogram, which is what ex8 is about.

## Exercise 2 - aggregating inside each group

`Totals.UnitsByRegion(sales)` returns `"region=total"` ordered by total
descending, ties broken by region name (ordinal).
`Totals.BestSellerByRegion(sales)` maps each region to the product of its
largest single sale, ties broken by product name (ordinal).
`Totals.PeakSaleByRegion(sales)` maps each region to that largest number of
units.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each method groups by region and then asks the group a question: `Sum`, `Max`,
or "which item was biggest". The ordering in `UnitsByRegion` is over the
grouped rows, not over the sales - so the total has to exist before you can
sort by it.

Projecting the group into an anonymous type first makes that easy to say.

## Hint 2

```csharp
sales
    .GroupBy(sale => sale.Region)
    .Select(group => new { Region = group.Key, Total = group.Sum(s => s.Units) })
    .OrderByDescending(row => row.Total)
    .ThenBy(row => row.Region, StringComparer.Ordinal)
```

`BestSellerByRegion` is the interesting one: you want the *item* with the
largest units, not the largest units. `Max` gives the number and throws away
the row, so either sort the group and take the first, or use `MaxBy` - and if
you use `MaxBy`, decide what it does about the tie the gate builds into the
south region before you rely on it.

The tie is deliberate. Without the explicit tie-break, the answer would depend
on the order the sales happened to be in.

## Exercise 3 - lookups and dictionaries are not the same thing

`Indexing.TitlesByAuthor(books)` returns an `ILookup<string, string>` - one
author, many titles - where an unknown key gives an empty sequence.
`Indexing.TitleById(books)` returns a `Dictionary<string, string>` and lets the
duplicate-key exception through. `Indexing.BookCountByAuthor(books)` counts
per author.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is a one-call operator for each of the first two methods, and choosing
between them is the exercise. One of them allows a key to appear many times;
the other insists it appears once.

`ToLookup` takes a key selector and, optionally, an element selector - the same
pair `ToDictionary` takes.

## Hint 2

`Schedules.RoomHoppers(visits)` returns the people seen in more than one

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A group key can be anything with sensible equality, and a value tuple qualifies:

```csharp
visits.GroupBy(visit => (visit.Day, visit.Room))
```

The group's `Key` is then the tuple, and `group.Key.Day` and `group.Key.Room`
are both available for the ordering and the text.

Do not concatenate the two strings into one key.

## Hint 2

Tuples get structural equality and a matching hash code for free, which is
exactly what a key needs. `visit.Day + visit.Room` looks equivalent and is not:
`"Mo" + "nA"` and `"Mon" + "A"` are the same string, so two different pairs
would silently share a group. A record or an anonymous type works for the same
reason a tuple does.

For `RoomHoppers`, group by person and then ask each group how many **distinct**
rooms it saw:

```csharp
group.Select(visit => visit.Room).Distinct().Count() > 1
```

Counting the visits instead of the rooms would call anyone with two identical
visits a room-hopper - which is the case the gate builds for bob.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A group key can be anything with sensible equality, and a value tuple qualifies:

```csharp
visits.GroupBy(visit => (visit.Day, visit.Room))
```

The group's `Key` is then the tuple, and `group.Key.Day` and `group.Key.Room`
are both available for the ordering and the text.

Do not concatenate the two strings into one key.

## Hint 2

Tuples get structural equality and a matching hash code for free, which is
exactly what a key needs. `visit.Day + visit.Room` looks equivalent and is not:
`"Mo" + "nA"` and `"Mon" + "A"` are the same string, so two different pairs
would silently share a group. A record or an anonymous type works for the same
reason a tuple does.

For `RoomHoppers`, group by person and then ask each group how many **distinct**
rooms it saw:

```csharp
group.Select(visit => visit.Room).Distinct().Count() > 1
```

Counting the visits instead of the rooms would call anyone with two identical
visits a room-hopper - which is the case the gate builds for bob.

## Exercise 5 - folding a sequence into one value

Three `Aggregate` overloads, one each. `Folds.TotalLength(parts)` uses the
seeded form and returns 0 for an empty sequence. `Folds.Deepest(paths)` uses
the seedless form - the path with the most `/`, first one winning a tie - and
throws `InvalidOperationException` when there is nothing. `Folds.Summarise`
uses the seed-and-result-selector form to gather count, min, max and sum in one
pass, throwing for an empty sequence.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Aggregate` comes in three shapes:

```
Aggregate(func)                          // starts from the first element
Aggregate(seed, func)                    // starts from a seed you supply
Aggregate(seed, func, resultSelector)    // ...and converts the state at the end
```

The summaries say which one each method wants. Match them up before writing
anything - the difference between them is entirely about the empty sequence.

## Hint 2

`TotalLength` is the seeded form: `parts.Aggregate(0, (total, part) => total +
part.Length)`. The seed is what an empty sequence returns, which is why 0 is
the right one.

`Deepest` is the seedless form: `paths.Aggregate((best, path) => ...)`. With
nothing to start from, an empty sequence has no answer, and the operator throws
`InvalidOperationException` for you - no check needed. Use `>` rather than
`>=` in the comparison so the first of two equally deep paths wins.

## Hint 3

`Summarise` needs a state carrying four numbers, and a value tuple is the
cheapest way to hold one:

```csharp
numbers.Aggregate(
    (Count: 0, Min: int.MaxValue, Max: int.MinValue, Sum: 0),
    (state, number) => ( /* the four updated fields */ ),
    state => /* turn it into a Summary, or throw */);
```

The seed's `Min` starts at `int.MaxValue` so the first real number always beats
it, and `Max` starts at `int.MinValue` for the same reason - a trick worth
knowing, and also the reason the empty case has to be caught explicitly: the
seed alone would report a minimum of `int.MaxValue`, which is nonsense. The
result selector is where you notice `Count` is still zero.

## Exercise 7 - top N inside every group

`Leaderboards.TopTwoPerGame(scores)` gives `"chess:cleo,ada"` for each game,
games ordered ordinal, naming the two highest scorers with ties broken by
player name. A game with one player names one.
`Leaderboards.Consistent(scores)` returns the players who are in the top two of
more than one game, ordered by name.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The ordering has to happen **inside** each group. Sorting the whole sequence
and then taking two gives you two rows in total, not two per game.

Both methods need the same "top two players of this group" step, so write it
once as a private helper and call it from both.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private static IEnumerable<string> TopTwo(IEnumerable<Score> group)
{
    return group
        .OrderByDescending(score => score.Points)
        .ThenBy(score => score.Player, StringComparer.Ordinal)
        .Take(2)
        .Select(score => score.Player);
}
```

`Take(2)` over a group of one gives one - it never pads and never throws, so
the single-player game needs no special case.

## Hint 3

`Consistent` is group, flatten, group again. `SelectMany(group => TopTwo(group))`
turns the per-game winners into one flat sequence of player names, in which a
player who reached two podiums appears twice. Group *that* by the name itself
and keep the keys whose group has more than one member.

If you find yourself building a `Dictionary<string, int>` and incrementing, you
have written `GroupBy(x => x).Count()` the long way. Whether the long way is
clearer here is a fair question - but write the query version at least once,
because recognising this shape is what lets you read somebody else's.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The ordering has to happen **inside** each group. Sorting the whole sequence
and then taking two gives you two rows in total, not two per game.

Both methods need the same "top two players of this group" step, so write it
once as a private helper and call it from both.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private static IEnumerable<string> TopTwo(IEnumerable<Score> group)
{
    return group
        .OrderByDescending(score => score.Points)
        .ThenBy(score => score.Player, StringComparer.Ordinal)
        .Take(2)
        .Select(score => score.Player);
}
```

`Take(2)` over a group of one gives one - it never pads and never throws, so
the single-player game needs no special case.

## Hint 3

`Consistent` is group, flatten, group again. `SelectMany(group => TopTwo(group))`
turns the per-game winners into one flat sequence of player names, in which a
player who reached two podiums appears twice. Group *that* by the name itself
and keep the keys whose group has more than one member.

If you find yourself building a `Dictionary<string, int>` and incrementing, you
have written `GroupBy(x => x).Count()` the long way. Whether the long way is
clearer here is a fair question - but write the query version at least once,
because recognising this shape is what lets you read somebody else's.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - a report, and the buckets that stay empty

`Analytics.ErrorReport(logs)` gives one line per service that logged at least
one `"error"`: `"api errors=2 slowest=1200"`, where slowest is the largest
`Millis` over *all* that service's entries. Ordered by error count descending,
ties broken by service name. `Analytics.LatencyHistogram(logs)` always returns
exactly `"fast=..."`, `"normal=..."`, `"slow=..."` in that order - fast is under
100ms, normal under 1000ms, slow is 1000ms or more - including buckets with a
count of zero.

Edit `src/Lessons/D19_LinqGrouping/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d19_linq_grouping ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ErrorReport` needs two different aggregates from the same group: a `Count`
with a predicate for the errors, and a `Max` over *every* entry for the slowest.
So project the whole group into a row first, and only then filter and order.

Filtering the entries down to errors before you group would give you the
slowest error rather than the slowest request.

## Hint 2

```csharp
logs.GroupBy(entry => entry.Service)
    .Select(group => new
    {
        Service = group.Key,
        Errors = group.Count(entry => entry.Level == "error"),
        Slowest = group.Max(entry => entry.Millis),
    })
    .Where(row => row.Errors > 0)
```

`Where` after the projection is what removes the services that logged no
errors - and the gate deliberately gives one of those the slowest request of
the whole set, so a version that filters in the wrong place is easy to spot.

## Hint 3

The histogram is a different problem, and the trap is that `GroupBy` cannot
solve it. It produces a group for a key something landed in and no group at
all for a key nothing did - so a bucket with zero entries simply is not in the
result, and a report whose rows depend on the data is not a report.

State the three bucket names yourself and look each one up:

```csharp
string[] buckets = { "fast", "normal", "slow" };
```

Build a `Dictionary<string, int>` of the counts that do exist, then project the
`buckets` array through it with `TryGetValue` and a zero default. Decide for
yourself where the boundary function lives - the gate checks 99, 100, 999 and
1000, so being sure which side each one falls on is worth a moment.

# d20 - LINQ joins and flattening drills

Eight problems on putting sequences together: `Join`, `GroupJoin` and the left
join it builds, `SelectMany` in its two forms, `Zip`, the set operators,
composite join keys, a three-way report, and flattening a structure that nests
as deep as it likes. They drill lesson 11 - reread `11_linq_2` if `SelectMany`
is still the operator you look up every time.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/`. Nothing here depends
on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - the inner join

`Joins.CustomerAndProduct(customers, orders)` returns `"ada:book"` for every
order that has a matching customer, in the order the *orders* arrive.
`Joins.ProductsFor(customers, orders, name)` returns that customer's products
in order, and is empty for a name that does not exist.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - the left join, spelled out

`LeftJoins.CustomerBasket(customers, orders)` returns `"ada:book,lamp"` for
*every* customer, ordered by name, with `"(none)"` where the customer has no
orders. `LeftJoins.Idle` names the customers with no orders.
`LeftJoins.EveryRow` produces the flattened left join - one row per pair, plus
`"zoe/-"` for a customer with none - ordered by the whole string, ordinal.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - flattening

`Flatten.All(groups)` concatenates a sequence of sequences.
`Flatten.Letters(words)` gives every character of every word.
`Flatten.Pairs(lefts, rights)` gives the cross product as `"a-1"`, with the
left moving slowest.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - keeping the parent while you flatten

`Documents.AllLines(invoices)` gives `"INV1/paper"` for every line of every
invoice. `Documents.NumberedLines(invoices)` gives `"INV1#1: paper"` with the
numbering restarting at 1 *within* each invoice. `Documents.Blank(invoices)`
names the invoices with no lines - the ones flattening makes disappear.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - pairing up, and set arithmetic

`Combine.Labelled(names, scores)` zips them into `"ada=10"` and stops at the
shorter. `Combine.InBoth`, `Combine.OnlyInFirst` and `Combine.EitherOne` are
intersection, difference and union - each de-duplicating -
and `Combine.BothEndToEnd` is the one that keeps duplicates.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - joining on more than one column

`Rota.Covered(shifts, bookings)` returns `"Mon/A smith->ada"` for every booking
that has a shift on the same day *and* in the same room, ordered by day, room,
patient and nurse (all ordinal). Two shifts covering one booking produce two
rows. `Rota.Uncovered(shifts, bookings)` returns `"Tue/B/brown"` for the
bookings nothing covers, in the same ordering.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - a report across three sequences

`Registry.Transcript(students, courses, enrolments)` joins through both and
returns `"ada/Maths=90"`, ordered by grade descending, then student name, then
course title. `Registry.CourseAverages(courses, enrolments)` returns
`"Maths=77"` per course with at least one enrolment - the integer average,
rounded down - ordered by title. Read carefully which sequences each one
consults.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - flattening something that nests without limit

A `Category` holds child `Category` objects, to any depth. `Tree.Paths(root)`
returns the full path to every node - `"root/tools/hammer"` - depth first, each
parent immediately before its own subtree. `Tree.Leaves(root)` names the nodes
with no children in the same order. `Tree.Depth(root)` counts the levels; a
lone root is 1.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex8
```

# Reading - csharp/d20_linq_joins_flatten

## Notes

The skill being drilled is relating two sequences to each other, and the whole
subject is easier once you notice that LINQ has exactly two primitives for it.
`Join` matches items by key and produces one row per matching *pair*.
`SelectMany` takes each item, asks for a sequence, and concatenates the
results. Everything else here - the left join, the cross product, the recursive
walk - is one of those two wearing a hat.

The pattern uniting the eight problems is **what happens to the rows with no
partner**. An inner join drops them silently, which is right when a missing
partner is impossible and a disaster when it is merely rare. `GroupJoin` keeps
every outer item and hands you a possibly-empty group, which is the left join,
and `DefaultIfEmpty` is what turns that empty group into a visible row. The
invoice with no lines and the customer with no orders are the same problem in
two costumes, and both vanish from a naive flatten.

The third thread is order. `Join` yields the outer sequence's order; `Zip` runs
in lockstep and stops at the shorter side; `SelectMany` puts the outer item's
whole inner sequence out before moving on. None of these sorts anything, so
every ordering in this set is one you have to ask for - and every tie the gate
builds is there because a result that depends on input order is not a result.

## ex1

Really testing: reading `Join`'s four arguments. Outer sequence, outer key,
inner key, result selector - and the two key selectors have to return the same
type, which is the compiler's one contribution to getting this right. The
classic mistake is putting the sequences in the wrong order and then wondering
why the output is ordered strangely; the outer sequence is the one you call the
method on, and it drives both the order and the row count. The order for
customer 9 is the real lesson: it disappears with no exception, no warning and
no trace, and the only way to know is to have counted first.

## ex2

Really testing: that a left join in LINQ is two operators, not one. `GroupJoin`
is the left join in spirit - every outer item gets a row, with a group of
matches that may be empty. `SelectMany` with `DefaultIfEmpty` flattens it back
to one row per pair, using one null row where the group was empty, which is
exactly what SQL's `LEFT JOIN` produces. The classic mistake is forgetting the
`DefaultIfEmpty` and quietly getting an inner join back. Note also which side
is privileged: the orphaned order in this data is still not reported by any of
the three methods, because a left join is one-sided by definition - `Except`
in both directions is how you find the orphans on both sides.

## ex3

Really testing: `SelectMany` as concatenation. The one-argument form is the
whole operator - hand it a selector that returns a sequence and it strings the
results together - and `Flatten.All` shows it at its most naked, with the
selector being the identity. That a `string` is an `IEnumerable<char>` is worth
noticing on its own; it makes `words.SelectMany(word => word)` legal and is why
several string methods surprise people. The cross product is the same operator
with a selector that ignores its input, and the nesting order falls out of that:
the outer item's whole inner sequence is produced before the next outer item,
exactly like two nested `foreach` loops.

## ex4

Really testing: the two-lambda `SelectMany`, which exists precisely because the
one-lambda form loses the parent. Once you have flattened to lines, the invoice
number is gone; the result-selector overload hands you both, so `"INV1/paper"`
is one call rather than a projection to a tuple and a second `Select`. The
numbering is the sharper half: the index has to come from a `Select` on the
inner list, because an index over the flattened sequence would number `glue` as
3 rather than 1. And `Blank` is here to make the disappearing act explicit -
`INV2` contributes zero rows to the flatten, and reporting it needs a separate,
unflattened pass.

## ex5

Really testing: five operators that all combine two sequences and differ in
ways that are easy to get wrong under time pressure. `Zip` is positional, not
key-based, and it truncates rather than throwing - which makes it excellent for
paired data and dangerous for data you assumed was paired. `Intersect`,
`Except` and `Union` are set operations: they de-duplicate, they use the
default equality comparer, and `Except` is one-sided. `Concat` is the only one
that preserves duplicates, and reaching for `Union` when you meant `Concat` is
a bug that removes real rows and looks like nothing happened.

## ex6

Really testing: composite join keys. `(booking.Day, booking.Room)` works as a
key because value tuples have structural equality and a consistent hash code,
so the two key selectors just have to produce tuples of the same shape. The
alternative people reach for - concatenating the strings - collides whenever
the pieces can run together, and worse, it turns a type error into a silent
data error. The other lesson is the multiplication: two shifts cover Mon/A, so
each Mon/A booking produces two rows. A join is not a lookup, and if you wanted
one row per booking, that is a `GroupJoin` and a decision about which nurse.

## ex7

Really testing: chaining joins, and reading a specification carefully enough to
notice which sequences a query consults. `Transcript` joins through students
and courses, so an enrolment missing either partner vanishes. `CourseAverages`
joins only through courses - so the enrolment belonging to the non-existent
student 9 *is* counted, because nothing in that query ever looks at students.
That is not a trick; it is the most common real bug in report code, where two
numbers on the same page are computed over subtly different populations and
nobody notices until they are challenged to explain why they do not add up.
The integer division is a smaller version of the same care: `Sum / Count`
truncates, and that is a decision, not an accident.

## ex8

Really testing: recursion, expressed with `SelectMany`. A tree is the case
where you genuinely cannot write the query with a fixed number of joins,
because you do not know how deep it goes - so the flattening operator calls the
method that calls the flattening operator. `Paths` also demonstrates the
accumulator: the prefix is passed *down* the recursion, which is what lets each
node build its own path in constant work instead of walking back to the root.
The base cases are where the bugs are: a leaf is a node with no children, which
means a lone root is its own leaf and one level deep - and `Max` over an empty
child list would throw, which is why the leaf case is checked before the
recursion rather than inside it.

## Further reading

- [Join operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/join-operations) - `Join` and `GroupJoin`, with the left-join recipe.
- [`Enumerable.SelectMany`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.selectmany) - all four overloads, including the one that keeps the parent.
- [Projection operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/projection-operations) - `Select`, `SelectMany` and `Zip` side by side.
- [Set operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/set-operations) - `Distinct`, `Union`, `Intersect`, `Except` and the `...By` variants.
- [`Enumerable.DefaultIfEmpty`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.defaultifempty) - the one call that turns an empty group into a row.
- [Value tuples](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-tuples) - and why they work as dictionary and join keys.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - the inner join

`Joins.CustomerAndProduct(customers, orders)` returns `"ada:book"` for every
order that has a matching customer, in the order the *orders* arrive.
`Joins.ProductsFor(customers, orders, name)` returns that customer's products
in order, and is empty for a name that does not exist.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Join` takes four arguments in a fixed order: the inner sequence, the outer key
selector, the inner key selector, and a result selector that receives both
matched items.

Which sequence you call it *on* matters. The output keeps that sequence's order
and is driven by its rows - and the summary says the rows come out in order of
the orders.

## Hint 2

```csharp
orders.Join(
    customers,
    order => order.CustomerId,
    customer => customer.Id,
    (order, customer) => $"{customer.Name}:{order.Product}");
```

The two key selectors must return the same type; that is the only part of this
the compiler can check for you.

For `ProductsFor`, the tidiest route is to narrow the customers to the named
one before joining, so the join itself does the filtering. Note what the gate
checks at the end: an inner join gives the same empty answer for "this customer
ordered nothing" and "this customer does not exist", which is exactly the
ambiguity ex2 removes.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - flattening

`Flatten.All(groups)` concatenates a sequence of sequences.
`Flatten.Letters(words)` gives every character of every word.
`Flatten.Pairs(lefts, rights)` gives the cross product as `"a-1"`, with the
left moving slowest.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`SelectMany` takes a selector that returns a *sequence* for each item, and
concatenates the results. That is the entire operator, and `All` is the case
where the selector does nothing at all.

`Letters` works because a `string` already is an `IEnumerable<char>`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
groups.SelectMany(group => group)      // the selector is the identity
words.SelectMany(word => word)         // a string IS a sequence of chars
lefts.SelectMany(left => rights, (left, right) => $"{left}-{right}")
```

The cross product is the same operator with a selector that ignores its
argument and hands back the whole right-hand sequence every time. The nesting
order falls out of that: the first left is paired with every right before the
second left appears - identical to two nested `foreach` loops, which is worth
writing out once if the order surprises you.

An empty inner sequence contributes nothing rather than a gap, which is why the
empty group in the first test does not show up as a null.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`SelectMany` takes a selector that returns a *sequence* for each item, and
concatenates the results. That is the entire operator, and `All` is the case
where the selector does nothing at all.

`Letters` works because a `string` already is an `IEnumerable<char>`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
groups.SelectMany(group => group)      // the selector is the identity
words.SelectMany(word => word)         // a string IS a sequence of chars
lefts.SelectMany(left => rights, (left, right) => $"{left}-{right}")
```

The cross product is the same operator with a selector that ignores its
argument and hands back the whole right-hand sequence every time. The nesting
order falls out of that: the first left is paired with every right before the
second left appears - identical to two nested `foreach` loops, which is worth
writing out once if the order surprises you.

An empty inner sequence contributes nothing rather than a gap, which is why the
empty group in the first test does not show up as a null.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - keeping the parent while you flatten

`Documents.AllLines(invoices)` gives `"INV1/paper"` for every line of every
invoice. `Documents.NumberedLines(invoices)` gives `"INV1#1: paper"` with the
numbering restarting at 1 *within* each invoice. `Documents.Blank(invoices)`
names the invoices with no lines - the ones flattening makes disappear.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Flattening loses the parent - once you have a line, the invoice it came from is
gone. `SelectMany` has an overload for exactly that: a second lambda that
receives both the original item and the flattened one.

For the numbering, ask yourself which sequence the index has to be counted
over.

## Hint 2

```csharp
invoices.SelectMany(invoice => invoice.Lines, (invoice, line) => $"{invoice.Number}/{line}");
```

`NumberedLines` cannot use that overload, because the number restarts inside
each invoice. Do the numbering in the inner sequence instead:

```csharp
invoices.SelectMany(invoice => invoice.Lines
    .Select((line, index) => $"{invoice.Number}#{index + 1}: {line}"));
```

An index taken over the flattened result would number the third line 3 even
though it is the first line of its invoice - which is the bug this exercise is
built to catch.

`Blank` exists to make a point: an invoice with no lines contributes zero rows
to a flatten and therefore cannot be seen in one. Finding it needs a separate,
unflattened pass.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Flattening loses the parent - once you have a line, the invoice it came from is
gone. `SelectMany` has an overload for exactly that: a second lambda that
receives both the original item and the flattened one.

For the numbering, ask yourself which sequence the index has to be counted
over.

## Hint 2

```csharp
invoices.SelectMany(invoice => invoice.Lines, (invoice, line) => $"{invoice.Number}/{line}");
```

`NumberedLines` cannot use that overload, because the number restarts inside
each invoice. Do the numbering in the inner sequence instead:

```csharp
invoices.SelectMany(invoice => invoice.Lines
    .Select((line, index) => $"{invoice.Number}#{index + 1}: {line}"));
```

An index taken over the flattened result would number the third line 3 even
though it is the first line of its invoice - which is the bug this exercise is
built to catch.

`Blank` exists to make a point: an invoice with no lines contributes zero rows
to a flatten and therefore cannot be seen in one. Finding it needs a separate,
unflattened pass.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A join key does not have to be one field. Both key selectors just have to
return the same type, and a value tuple is the cheapest type that holds two
strings:

```csharp
booking => (booking.Day, booking.Room)
shift   => (shift.Day, shift.Room)
```

Do not build the key by concatenating the two strings.

## Hint 2

Tuples get structural equality and a matching hash code for free, which is
exactly what a key needs. `booking.Day + booking.Room` looks equivalent and is
not - `"Mo" + "nA"` and `"Mon" + "A"` are the same string, so two different
pairs would silently join. Records and anonymous types work for the same reason
tuples do.

Expect the multiplication: two shifts cover Mon/A, so each Mon/A booking
produces two rows. A join is not a lookup. If you want one row per booking,
that is a different query and a decision about which nurse to pick.

## Hint 3

`Uncovered` is the complement, and a join will not give it to you directly -
`Join` produces rows for matches, and you want the bookings with none.

Two routes. The tidy one is a `HashSet` of the shift keys and a `Where` that
asks whether it contains the booking's key; the other is a `GroupJoin` and a
`Where` on the empty groups. The set is O(1) per booking and reads as what it
means. Whichever you pick, note that a *shift* with no booking is not reported:
this report is about bookings, and the other direction needs the query run the
other way round.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A join key does not have to be one field. Both key selectors just have to
return the same type, and a value tuple is the cheapest type that holds two
strings:

```csharp
booking => (booking.Day, booking.Room)
shift   => (shift.Day, shift.Room)
```

Do not build the key by concatenating the two strings.

## Hint 2

Tuples get structural equality and a matching hash code for free, which is
exactly what a key needs. `booking.Day + booking.Room` looks equivalent and is
not - `"Mo" + "nA"` and `"Mon" + "A"` are the same string, so two different
pairs would silently join. Records and anonymous types work for the same reason
tuples do.

Expect the multiplication: two shifts cover Mon/A, so each Mon/A booking
produces two rows. A join is not a lookup. If you want one row per booking,
that is a different query and a decision about which nurse to pick.

## Hint 3

`Uncovered` is the complement, and a join will not give it to you directly -
`Join` produces rows for matches, and you want the bookings with none.

Two routes. The tidy one is a `HashSet` of the shift keys and a `Where` that
asks whether it contains the booking's key; the other is a `GroupJoin` and a
`Where` on the empty groups. The set is O(1) per booking and reads as what it
means. Whichever you pick, note that a *shift* with no booking is not reported:
this report is about bookings, and the other direction needs the query run the
other way round.

## Exercise 7 - a report across three sequences

`Registry.Transcript(students, courses, enrolments)` joins through both and
returns `"ada/Maths=90"`, ordered by grade descending, then student name, then
course title. `Registry.CourseAverages(courses, enrolments)` returns
`"Maths=77"` per course with at least one enrolment - the integer average,
rounded down - ordered by title. Read carefully which sequences each one
consults.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two joins chained: enrolments to students, then that result to courses. Each
join carries forward the fields the next stage needs, so an anonymous type in
between is the usual way to hold them.

Then read the two summaries again and notice which sequences each method is
given. They are not the same, and that is deliberate.

## Hint 2

```csharp
enrolments
    .Join(students, e => e.StudentId, s => s.Id, (e, s) => new { e.CourseId, e.Grade, s.Name })
    .Join(courses, r => r.CourseId, c => c.Id, (r, c) => new { r.Name, c.Title, r.Grade })
```

Order after both joins, over the finished rows.

## Hint 3

`CourseAverages` never receives the students, so it cannot filter on them - and
the gate builds one enrolment whose student does not exist but whose course
does. It counts. That is not a trap for its own sake: two figures on the same
report computed over subtly different populations is the most common real bug
in reporting code, and the only defence is to say out loud which rows each
number is over.

The average is integer division - `Sum / Count` truncates towards zero. Whether
that is the right rounding for a grade average is a decision somebody should
make on purpose; here the summary makes it for you.

## Hint 1

Two joins chained: enrolments to students, then that result to courses. Each
join carries forward the fields the next stage needs, so an anonymous type in
between is the usual way to hold them.

Then read the two summaries again and notice which sequences each method is
given. They are not the same, and that is deliberate.

## Hint 2

```csharp
enrolments
    .Join(students, e => e.StudentId, s => s.Id, (e, s) => new { e.CourseId, e.Grade, s.Name })
    .Join(courses, r => r.CourseId, c => c.Id, (r, c) => new { r.Name, c.Title, r.Grade })
```

Order after both joins, over the finished rows.

## Hint 3

`CourseAverages` never receives the students, so it cannot filter on them - and
the gate builds one enrolment whose student does not exist but whose course
does. It counts. That is not a trap for its own sake: two figures on the same
report computed over subtly different populations is the most common real bug
in reporting code, and the only defence is to say out loud which rows each
number is over.

The average is integer division - `Sum / Count` truncates towards zero. Whether
that is the right rounding for a grade average is a decision somebody should
make on purpose; here the summary makes it for you.

## Exercise 8 - flattening something that nests without limit

A `Category` holds child `Category` objects, to any depth. `Tree.Paths(root)`
returns the full path to every node - `"root/tools/hammer"` - depth first, each
parent immediately before its own subtree. `Tree.Leaves(root)` names the nodes
with no children in the same order. `Tree.Depth(root)` counts the levels; a
lone root is 1.

Edit `src/Lessons/D20_LinqJoinsFlatten/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d20_linq_joins_flatten ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You cannot write this with a fixed number of joins, because you do not know how
deep the tree goes. The flattening operator has to call the method that uses
the flattening operator:

```csharp
node.Children.SelectMany(child => Walk(child, ...))
```

Start each method by asking what it should answer for a node with no children.
That is the base case, and it is where the bugs live.

## Hint 2

`Leaves`: a node with no children is a leaf and contributes its own name; a
node with children contributes only what its children contribute, and nothing
of its own.

`Depth`: a leaf is 1; anything else is 1 plus the deepest child. Note that
`Max` over an empty sequence throws, so the leaf case has to be checked before
the recursion, not inside it.

## Hint 3

`Paths` needs an accumulator, so write a private helper that takes the node and
the prefix built so far:

```csharp
private static IEnumerable<string> Walk(Category node, string prefix)
{
    string path = prefix.Length == 0 ? node.Name : $"{prefix}/{node.Name}";
    return new[] { path }.Concat(node.Children.SelectMany(child => Walk(child, path)));
}
```

Passing the prefix *down* is what makes each node's work constant - the
alternative, walking back up to the root from each node, is the same answer
computed quadratically.

`Concat` of the one-element array with the flattened children is what puts each
parent immediately before its own subtree. Swap those two around and you have a
post-order walk instead, which is equally valid and not what the gate asks for.

lessons.briefing:
# d21 - Deferred execution drills

Eight problems on the fact that a LINQ query is a recipe, not an answer: when
it runs, how often it runs, what it captured, and what happens when the thing
it reads can only be read once. They drill lesson 10 - reread `10_linq_1`, and
its "the query is not the answer" exercise in particular, if `ToList` still
looks like noise.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D21_DeferredExecution/`. Nothing here depends
on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - a query is not an answer

`Deferred.BigOnes(numbers, min)` returns the query itself, so a later change to
the list is visible the next time it is enumerated.
`Deferred.BigOnesNow(numbers, min)` returns the answer, taken now. The gate
mutates the list between the two enumerations.

Edit `src/Lessons/D21_DeferredExecution/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d21_deferred_execution ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - two questions, one pass

`Passes.CountAndTotalTwice` is written for you and walks the sequence twice.
`Passes.CountAndTotal(numbers, predicate)` returns the same
`(Count, Total)` while enumerating the source exactly once and calling the
predicate exactly once per item. The gate counts both.

Edit `src/Lessons/D21_DeferredExecution/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d21_deferred_execution ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - what the lambda captured

`Captures.Above(numbers, threshold)` returns a query that reads

# Reading - csharp/d21_deferred_execution

## Notes

The skill being drilled is knowing *when* a query runs. `Where`, `Select`,
`Take`, `SelectMany` and their relatives do not compute anything when you call
them; they build an object that knows how to compute something later. The
computation happens when somebody enumerates that object - once per
enumeration, from the beginning, every time.

The pattern uniting these eight problems is that **the query holds references,
not values**. It holds a reference to the source sequence, so a change to the
source is visible next time. It holds the lambdas, so a variable one of them
captured is read again next time. Nothing was copied, so nothing is frozen -
and `ToList` is the one word that says "freeze this now", which is why it turns
up as the fix to about half the problems here.

Everything else follows from counting. How many times is the source
enumerated? How many times does each lambda run? Once you are in the habit of
asking, multiple enumeration stops being a mysterious performance note and
becomes something you can see in the code: two LINQ calls over the same
`IEnumerable` parameter is two passes, and over a network reader or a `yield`
method with a side effect, two passes is a bug rather than a slowdown.

## ex1

Really testing: the difference between an `IEnumerable<T>` returned from a
query and a `List<T>`. The query re-runs from scratch on each enumeration, so
it sees the `Add` that happened after it was written - which looks like magic
until you notice nothing had been computed yet. The classic mistake is
returning a deferred query from a method whose caller expects a value; the
caller then enumerates it three times and pays three times, or enumerates it
after the underlying data has changed and gets an answer nobody asked for. As a
rule of thumb: a method that returns a *result* should return a `List<T>` or an
array, and a method that returns a *query* should say so in its name.

## ex2

Really testing: multiple enumeration, counted. Two operators over the same
sequence are two passes, and each pass re-runs every lambda in the chain - so
the supplied version calls the predicate ten times for five items. Over an
array that is a rounding error; over a database query or a file it is two
round trips, and over a sequence with side effects it is wrong rather than
slow. The fix here is not a cleverer query - it is a `foreach` that accumulates
both answers at once, which is also the most readable thing on the page. LINQ
is not always the answer, and knowing when to leave it is part of knowing it.

## ex3

Really testing: what a lambda captures, combined with when it runs. The lambda
captured the `Threshold` *object*, and the query reads `Value` off it at
enumeration time - so mutating the object rewrites a query that was written
before the mutation. Copying the value into a local first is what freezes it,
because the lambda then captures a local nobody else has a reference to. This
is the same mechanism as the famous captured-loop-variable bug, seen from the
other side, and it is a genuinely useful technique when you *want* it: a query
whose parameters can be tuned between runs.

## ex4

Really testing: sources that can only be read once, which is what makes
multiple enumeration a correctness problem rather than a performance one. A
network stream, a `DataReader`, a `yield` method reading a file - all of them
behave like this, and none of them announce it in their type. `Count()`,
`First()` and `Last()` each start a fresh enumeration, so the tidy-looking
three-line version throws on the second call. Materialising once with `ToList`
is the whole fix, and the general rule follows: if you are handed an
`IEnumerable<T>` and need to look at it more than once, copy it first - or take
an `IReadOnlyList<T>` in the signature and make the caller do it.

## ex5

Really testing: which operators stream and which buffer. `Where`, `Select`,
`Take` and `TakeWhile` process one item at a time and can stop early, so a
pipeline made only of those reads exactly as far as it must - four items to
find two even numbers. `OrderBy`, `GroupBy`, `Reverse` and `ToList` are
buffering: they cannot yield their first item until they have seen the last
one. That is not an implementation detail to be optimised away; it is forced by
what they mean. The practical consequence is that a `Take(10)` after an
`OrderBy` still reads everything, and the surprise in the other direction is
`Take(0)`, which never asks the source for a first item at all.

## ex6

Really testing: counting how many times a selector runs. The two-pass version
looks perfectly idiomatic - `Min` then `First` - and calls the cost function
about twice per item, which is invisible until the cost is a database lookup or
a hash. Carrying the best item *and* its cost through a single loop is the fix,
and `MinBy` is the operator that does it for you (it evaluates the selector
once per element). The other detail is the tie: a strict `<` keeps the first of
two equal costs, `<=` keeps the last, and neither is wrong as long as it was a
decision.

## ex7

Really testing: everything above, turned into a reusable tool. `Memoized<T>`
has to be lazy - building it reads nothing - and it has to cache, so a second
enumeration replays from the list rather than the source. The interesting part
is that both enumerators share one cache and one source cursor, which is what
lets the interleaved case work: the second enumerator's first item is already
in the list. Real libraries ship this - `System.Interactive`'s `Memoize` is
the same idea - and the reason to write it once yourself is that it forces you
to say exactly what "enumerate at most once" means. Note that it deliberately
does not handle two threads; making it thread-safe is a different exercise and
a much longer one.

## ex8

Really testing: composing several answers out of one reading. Each of the three
figures is a one-liner in LINQ and all three together are three passes, which
the one-shot source turns from wasteful into impossible. Writing the loop by
hand is not a defeat: the loop states plainly that these three numbers are over
the same rows, which is exactly the property that gets lost when a report grows
by one query at a time. The distinct-words requirement is the small lesson
inside the big one - a `HashSet` answers "is this new" in constant time and a
`List` remembers the order, and using both together is what `Distinct` does
internally anyway.

## Further reading

- [Deferred execution and lazy evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/linq/deferred-execution-lazy-evaluation) - the concept, with the classic example.
- [Classification of standard query operators by manner of execution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/#classification-table) - which operators are deferred, streaming or buffering.
- [CA1851: possible multiple enumerations of an IEnumerable collection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca1851) - the analyser that catches ex2 and ex4 for you.
- [`Enumerable.MinBy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.linq.enumerable.minby) - the operator ex6 is asking you to hand-roll.
- [Lambda expressions and capture](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions) - what a closure actually holds.
- [`IEnumerable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.ienumerable-1) - and the fact that nothing in its contract promises a second enumeration will work.

`Passes.CountAndTotalTwice` is written for you and walks the sequence twice.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the supplied version and count. `numbers.Count(predicate)` walks the
sequence once; `numbers.Where(predicate).Sum()` walks it again. Two passes, and
the predicate runs on every item both times.

You cannot fix that by rearranging LINQ operators. Both answers have to come
out of the same walk.

## Hint 2

Write the loop:

```csharp
int count = 0;
int total = 0;
foreach (int number in numbers)
{
    if (predicate(number)) { count++; total += number; }
}
return (count, total);
```

That is not a step backwards. LINQ is excellent at expressing one question and
poor at expressing two questions that must share a pass - and a reader of this
loop can see immediately that both numbers are over the same items, which is
exactly the property that goes missing when a report grows one query at a time.

`Aggregate` with a tuple state would also work if you would rather keep it in
one expression. Decide which one you would want to meet in a code review.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the supplied version and count. `numbers.Count(predicate)` walks the
sequence once; `numbers.Where(predicate).Sum()` walks it again. Two passes, and
the predicate runs on every item both times.

You cannot fix that by rearranging LINQ operators. Both answers have to come
out of the same walk.

## Hint 2

Write the loop:

```csharp
int count = 0;
int total = 0;
foreach (int number in numbers)
{
    if (predicate(number)) { count++; total += number; }
}
return (count, total);
```

That is not a step backwards. LINQ is excellent at expressing one question and
poor at expressing two questions that must share a pass - and a reader of this
loop can see immediately that both numbers are over the same items, which is
exactly the property that goes missing when a report grows one query at a time.

`Aggregate` with a tuple state would also work if you would rather keep it in
one expression. Decide which one you would want to meet in a code review.

## Exercise 3 - what the lambda captured

`Captures.Above(numbers, threshold)` returns a query that reads
`threshold.Value` afresh every time it runs.
`Captures.AboveFixed(numbers, threshold)` returns a query whose threshold was
fixed at the moment the method was called. The gate changes the object in
between.

Edit `src/Lessons/D21_DeferredExecution/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d21_deferred_execution ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Above` is the naive version and it is already right: write the obvious
`Where` that reads `threshold.Value`, and it will follow the object because the
lambda captured the object and the query runs afresh each time.

`AboveFixed` needs one extra line *before* the query.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int fixedValue = threshold.Value;
return numbers.Where(number => number > fixedValue);
```

The lambda now captures a local that nobody outside this method can reach, so
nothing can change it afterwards. The read of `threshold.Value` happened when
the method was called, which is what "fixed" means.

This is the same mechanism as the famous captured-loop-variable surprise, seen
from the useful side: a query that follows a mutable object is a genuinely good
tool when it is what you meant, and a very confusing bug when it is not. The
only way to tell them apart is to have chosen.

## Exercise 5 - which operators can stop early

`Streaming.FirstMatching(numbers, predicate, count)` returns the first `count`
matches and must not read the source past the last item it needed.
`Streaming.LargestMatching(numbers, predicate, count)` returns the `count`
largest matches, descending - and cannot avoid reading everything. The gate
counts the reads for both.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are short LINQ chains. The exercise is not writing them - it is
knowing, before you run the test, how many items each one will read.

`Where` and `Take` process one item at a time. `OrderByDescending` cannot
produce its first item until it has seen the last one.

## Hint 2

```csharp
numbers.Where(predicate).Take(count).ToList();
numbers.Where(predicate).OrderByDescending(n => n).Take(count).ToList();
```

The first stops as soon as `Take` has what it wanted, so ten items in the
source does not mean ten items read. Put a `.ToList()` in the middle of that
chain and you have thrown the property away.

The second cannot stop early no matter how it is arranged, because "largest"
is a question about the whole sequence. That is not a flaw to optimise around;
it is what the operator means, and knowing which operators are like that is the
actual content of this exercise.

The `Take(0)` case in the gate is worth predicting before you run it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods are short LINQ chains. The exercise is not writing them - it is
knowing, before you run the test, how many items each one will read.

`Where` and `Take` process one item at a time. `OrderByDescending` cannot
produce its first item until it has seen the last one.

## Hint 2

```csharp
numbers.Where(predicate).Take(count).ToList();
numbers.Where(predicate).OrderByDescending(n => n).Take(count).ToList();
```

The first stops as soon as `Take` has what it wanted, so ten items in the
source does not mean ten items read. Put a `.ToList()` in the middle of that
chain and you have thrown the property away.

The second cannot stop early no matter how it is arranged, because "largest"
is a question about the whole sequence. That is not a flaw to optimise around;
it is what the operator means, and knowing which operators are like that is the
actual content of this exercise.

The `Take(0)` case in the gate is worth predicting before you run it.

`Costs.CheapestTwoPass` is written for you and calls the cost function more
than once per item. `Costs.Cheapest(items, cost)` returns the item with the
lowest cost - the first of any tie - calling `cost` exactly once per item and
enumerating the source once. It throws `InvalidOperationException` when there
are no items.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the supplied version and count the calls. `Min(cost)` runs the cost
function on every item, and then `First(item => cost(item) == lowest)` runs it
again on the items it looks at.

To call it once per item you have to remember two things as you go, not one.

## Hint 2

```csharp
string? best = null;
int bestCost = 0;

foreach (string item in items)
{
    int itemCost = cost(item);       // exactly once, and stored
    if (best is null || itemCost < bestCost) { best = item; bestCost = itemCost; }
}
```

Keeping `bestCost` alongside `best` is the whole trick: without it, comparing
the current item to the best one means asking the cost function about the best
one again.

`items.MinBy(cost)` does exactly this and evaluates the selector once per
element, so it is a perfectly good answer too - decide for yourself whether the
loop or the operator says it more clearly here, and note that they differ in
what they do when the sequence is empty.

The tie is a decision: `<` keeps the first of two equal costs and `<=` keeps
the last. The summary asks for the first.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two requirements pull in opposite directions. "Enumerate the source at most
once" says copy it; "read nothing until asked, and only what is asked" says do
not.

The resolution is to keep the source's *enumerator* and a cache list, and fill
the cache one item at a time as somebody asks for it.

## Hint 2

`OnePass.Analyse(lines)` reads the lines exactly once and returns a
`LineReport` holding how many there were, the longest line (the first of any

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three questions, one `foreach`. Each question needs one or two variables kept
outside the loop, and the loop updates all of them as each line goes past.

Do not reach for `lines.Count()`, `lines.OrderByDescending(...)` and
`lines.SelectMany(...)` - that is three enumerations, and the source the gate
hands you allows one.

## Hint 2

The three accumulators are a count, the longest line so far, and the words.
For the words you need two collaborating collections:

```csharp
List<string> words = new List<string>();
HashSet<string> seen = new HashSet<string>();
// ...
if (seen.Add(word)) { words.Add(word); }
```

`HashSet.Add` returns false when the item was already there, so one call both
tests and records. The list is what remembers first-seen order, which a set
alone cannot.

Split the line on whitespace with
`line.Split((char[]?)null, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` - passing a
null separator array means "any whitespace", and the option drops the empty
pieces that runs of spaces would otherwise produce.

The longest-line comparison needs a strict `>` so the first of a tie wins, and
the empty case is the one where you never assigned it at all.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three questions, one `foreach`. Each question needs one or two variables kept
outside the loop, and the loop updates all of them as each line goes past.

Do not reach for `lines.Count()`, `lines.OrderByDescending(...)` and
`lines.SelectMany(...)` - that is three enumerations, and the source the gate
hands you allows one.

## Hint 2

The three accumulators are a count, the longest line so far, and the words.
For the words you need two collaborating collections:

```csharp
List<string> words = new List<string>();
HashSet<string> seen = new HashSet<string>();
// ...
if (seen.Add(word)) { words.Add(word); }
```

`HashSet.Add` returns false when the item was already there, so one call both
tests and records. The list is what remembers first-seen order, which a set
alone cannot.

Split the line on whitespace with
`line.Split((char[]?)null, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` - passing a
null separator array means "any whitespace", and the option drops the empty
pieces that runs of spaces would otherwise produce.

The longest-line comparison needs a strict `>` so the first of a tie wins, and
the empty case is the one where you never assigned it at all.

lessons.briefing:
# d22 - Exceptions drills

Eight problems on failing well: what `finally` guarantees, an exception type of
your own with the cause attached, exception filters, the difference `throw ex;`
makes, disposal order, catch ordering and `AggregateException`, a retry policy
that retries only what is worth retrying, and turning an exception into a value.
They drill lesson 12 - reread `12_exceptions` if `when` on a `catch` is
unfamiliar.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - try, catch, finally, in that order

`Runner.Attempt(action, log)` returns `"ok"` when the action completes and
`"caught:<message>"` when it throws an `InvalidOperationException`. Any other
exception escapes. In all three cases `"cleanup"` is the last entry added to
the log, and the success path also logs `"done"` while the caught path logs
`"caught"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - an exception of your own, with the cause attached

`ImportException` carries a 1-based `Line` and an inner exception.
`Importer.SumLines(lines)` sums the lines as integers; the first line that is
not a number throws an `ImportException` with the message `"bad line 2"`, that
line number, and the `FormatException` as its `InnerException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a catch that can say no

`Filters.Classify(call, log)` returns what the call returned, or
`"handled:503"` when it threw a `HttpLikeException` with a status of 500 or
more. A lower status escapes unchanged, and so does any other exception type.
The decision must be made by an exception **filter**, and the filter adds
`"filter:<status>"` to the log as it decides - which is how the gate checks it
ran before the stack unwound.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - rethrowing without destroying the evidence

`Rethrow.Losing` is written for you and uses `throw ex;`.
`Rethrow.Keeping(action, log)` logs the same line and rethrows so the original
stack trace survives. `Rethrow.Wrapping(action)` replaces the exception with an
`InvalidOperationException` whose message is `"wrapped"` and whose
`InnerException` is the original.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - cleanup that happens anyway

`Resources.Use(name, log, body)` opens a `Probe`, runs the body, and disposes
the probe whatever happens, returning `"ok"` or `"failed:<message>"`.
`Resources.UseTwo(log, body)` opens `"outer"` then `"inner"`, runs the body,
disposes both - inner first - and lets any exception escape afterwards.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - catching the right thing, in the right order

`Sorting.Kind(action)` returns `"ok"`, `"null-arg"`, `"arg"`, `"format"` or
`"other"` depending on what the action threw. `Sorting.Leaves(exception)`
returns the messages of every leaf exception inside an `AggregateException`,
however deeply nested, comma-joined in order.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - retry the retryable, and only that

`Retry.Run(operation, attempts, log)` logs `"attempt:1"` before each try and
returns the first success. Only a `TransientException` is retried; anything
else escapes at once. When the last attempt also fails it throws an
`InvalidOperationException` with the message `"gave up after 3 attempts"` and
the last `TransientException` as its `InnerException`. An `attempts` below 1 is
an `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, thrown before anything is tried.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - an exception turned into a value, and back

`Safely.Capture(function)` returns a successful `Attempt<T>` or a failed one
carrying the exception's message - except `OperationCanceledException`, which
must escape. `Safely.Unwrap(attempt)` returns the value or throws an
`InvalidOperationException` whose message is the recorded error.
`Safely.Then(attempt, next)` runs `next` on the value only when the attempt
succeeded, capturing anything it throws, and otherwise passes the original
error through untouched.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex8
```
