# Reading - csharp/d22_exceptions

## Notes

The skill being drilled is deciding what a failure *means* before deciding what
to do about it. Almost every bad exception-handling decision comes from
skipping that step: a `catch (Exception)` that swallows a bug, a retry loop
that hammers a server over a malformed request, a wrapper that throws away the
stack trace that would have explained everything.

The pattern uniting these eight problems is **preserve the evidence and
classify honestly**. `throw;` rather than `throw ex;`; the inner exception
passed to every wrapper you construct; a filter that says no rather than a
catch that guesses; a retry that distinguishes "try again" from "this will
never work". None of that costs anything at runtime, and all of it is the
difference between a log entry that explains an outage and one that says
`InvalidOperationException` at a line inside your own error handling.

The third thread is `finally`, which is the only construct here that makes an
unconditional promise. It runs on success, on a handled failure and on an
exception heading for the caller - which is why `using` compiles into one, and
why cleanup should almost never live in a `catch`.

## ex1

Really testing: the order of the three blocks, including the case nobody tests
- an exception this method does not handle. `finally` runs on the way past, so
the cleanup happens even though the method is not returning normally and has
not caught anything. The classic mistake is putting cleanup at the end of the
`try`, where a throw skips it, or in the `catch`, where a success skips it.
The other thing worth noticing is that catching only `InvalidOperationException`
lets the `FormatException` through, which is the correct behaviour: a `catch
(Exception)` "to be safe" is how a bug gets logged as a warning and forgotten.

## ex2

Really testing: writing an exception type that is worth catching. Three
properties make it useful - a specific type, so a caller can catch exactly this
and nothing else; structured data (`Line`), so the caller does not have to
parse the message; and the `InnerException`, so the original cause survives.
The classic mistake is `catch (FormatException) { throw new
ImportException("bad line"); }` - the new exception looks tidier and has
destroyed the only record of what actually went wrong. Note also that the
constructor passes the inner exception to `base(message, inner)`; there is no
other way to set it.

## ex3

Really testing: exception filters, and the thing that makes them different
from a catch-and-rethrow. A filter is evaluated *before* the stack unwinds, so
at the moment it runs the original frames are still alive - which is why the
gate can see the filter's log entry appear before the callee's `finally`. That
matters for debugging: with a filter, a debugger breaking on an unhandled
exception still sees the real stack. The other lesson is that a filter
returning false leaves the exception completely untouched: same object, same
type, same trace, still in flight - which a `catch (X) { ... throw; }` cannot
claim.

## ex4

Really testing: the single most costly one-word difference in C#. `throw ex;`
rethrows the exception object but resets its stack trace to the current line,
so the frames between the original throw and here are gone for ever. `throw;`
rethrows the exception in flight and keeps them. The wrapping case is the third
option, and it is the right one whenever you are adding context: a new
exception type that means something to your caller, with the original hanging
off `InnerException`. (`ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex).Throw()` is the
fourth, for rethrowing outside the catch block, which is what `await` does with
a faulted task.)

## ex5

Really testing: `using` as a `try`/`finally` with better manners, and the order
two of them dispose in. Nested `using` blocks dispose in reverse - last opened,
first closed - which is not an arbitrary rule: the inner resource may well
depend on the outer one still being alive. The gate checks the disposal happens
even when the body throws and even when the exception is on its way to the
caller, which is the case people forget when they hand-roll the try/finally.
Note the `Disposed` guard in the supplied `Probe`: `Dispose` may legally be
called more than once, and it has to be harmless.

## ex6

Really testing: catch ordering, and `AggregateException`. Catch blocks are
tried in source order and the first *assignable* one wins, so a base type
before a derived one makes the derived one unreachable - the compiler catches
that for `Exception` first but not for `ArgumentException` before
`ArgumentNullException`, which is the trap. `AggregateException` is the other
half: it is a tree, because the tasks it collects may themselves have collected
tasks, and `Flatten()` turns that tree into one list. Reading
`InnerExceptions` without flattening finds the aggregates and misses the real
failures.

## ex7

Really testing: a retry policy that classifies. The distinction between
transient and permanent is the entire value of the exercise: retrying a
`FormatException` turns one bad request into three, and in a busy system that
is how a small outage becomes a large one. The other two details are the
budget - `attempts` counts total tries, not extra tries, and the loop stops at
the first success - and the give-up path, which must keep the last failure as
its `InnerException`. A retry loop that exhausts its budget and throws a bare
"gave up" tells the on-call engineer nothing at all. (A real policy adds
backoff and jitter; this one is deterministic so it can be tested.)

## ex8

Really testing: the exception-to-value conversion that turns up in every
codebase eventually. `Capture` has to catch broadly - the caller wants a value,
not a throw - which is exactly why the `OperationCanceledException` exclusion
matters: a cancellation means somebody asked to stop, and recording it as a
failure and carrying on is the wrong response. That exclusion is the one detail
people forget, and it is why `Task` treats cancellation as a separate state
rather than a fault. `Then` is the other half: it short-circuits on a failure,
so a chain of five steps runs no further than the first problem, and the error
that comes out is the first one rather than a cascade. Note also why `Ok` is a
separate field: `default(T)` is `0` for an int, so the value alone cannot tell
a failure from a real zero.

## Further reading

- [Exceptions and exception handling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/exceptions/) - the whole model, briefly.
- [`try`-`finally`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements#the-try-finally-statement) - what finally guarantees, and what it does not.
- [Exception filters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/exception-handling-statements#the-when-exception-filter) - and why they run before the unwind.
- [Creating and throwing exceptions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/exceptions/creating-and-throwing-exceptions) - including the inner-exception convention.
- [`AggregateException.Flatten`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.aggregateexception.flatten) - the tree, and how to level it.
- [`ExceptionDispatchInfo`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.exceptionservices.exceptiondispatchinfo) - rethrowing with the trace intact from outside a catch block.

## Exercise 1 - try, catch, finally, in that order

`Runner.Attempt(action, log)` returns `"ok"` when the action completes and
`"caught:<message>"` when it throws an `InvalidOperationException`. Any other
exception escapes. In all three cases `"cleanup"` is the last entry added to
the log, and the success path also logs `"done"` while the caught path logs
`"caught"`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `try`, one `catch (InvalidOperationException)`, one `finally`. Both the
try and the catch `return`, and the finally still runs after either of them -
that is what makes it the right place for the cleanup line.

Do not catch `Exception`. The gate throws a `FormatException` at you on
purpose.

## Hint 2

```csharp
try
{
    action();
    log.Add("done");
    return "ok";
}
catch (InvalidOperationException ex)
{
    log.Add("caught");
    return $"caught:{ex.Message}";
}
finally
{
    log.Add("cleanup");
}
```

The third case is the one worth pausing on: when the action throws something
this method does not catch, the exception carries on to the caller and the
`finally` still runs on the way past. Cleanup at the end of the `try` would be
skipped; cleanup in the `catch` would be skipped on success. Only `finally`
covers all three.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - a catch that can say no

`Filters.Classify(call, log)` returns what the call returned, or
`"handled:503"` when it threw a `HttpLikeException` with a status of 500 or
more. A lower status escapes unchanged, and so does any other exception type.
The decision must be made by an exception **filter**, and the filter adds
`"filter:<status>"` to the log as it decides - which is how the gate checks it
ran before the stack unwound.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `catch` can take a condition:

```csharp
catch (HttpLikeException ex) when (SomeTest(ex))
```

When the condition is false the catch does not run at all and the exception
carries on - which is not the same as catching it and rethrowing.

The logging has to happen inside the condition, so write the condition as a
method call.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private static bool Retryable(HttpLikeException exception, List<string> log)
{
    log.Add($"filter:{exception.Status}");
    return exception.Status >= 500;
}
```

The gate's last check is the reason filters exist. A filter is evaluated
*before* the stack unwinds, so its log line appears before the callee's
`finally` runs. A `catch` that inspects and rethrows would have unwound first,
and the order would be the other way round - and a debugger breaking on the
exception would have lost the original frames.

Note also what happens when the filter says no: same exception object, same
type, same stack trace, still in flight. Nothing you can write with catch and
`throw;` is quite that clean.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `catch` can take a condition:

```csharp
catch (HttpLikeException ex) when (SomeTest(ex))
```

When the condition is false the catch does not run at all and the exception
carries on - which is not the same as catching it and rethrowing.

The logging has to happen inside the condition, so write the condition as a
method call.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private static bool Retryable(HttpLikeException exception, List<string> log)
{
    log.Add($"filter:{exception.Status}");
    return exception.Status >= 500;
}
```

The gate's last check is the reason filters exist. A filter is evaluated
*before* the stack unwinds, so its log line appears before the callee's
`finally` runs. A `catch` that inspects and rethrows would have unwound first,
and the order would be the other way round - and a debugger breaking on the
exception would have lost the original frames.

Note also what happens when the filter says no: same exception object, same
type, same stack trace, still in flight. Nothing you can write with catch and
`throw;` is quite that clean.

## Exercise 4 - rethrowing without destroying the evidence

`Rethrow.Losing` is written for you and uses `throw ex;`.
`Rethrow.Keeping(action, log)` logs the same line and rethrows so the original
stack trace survives. `Rethrow.Wrapping(action)` replaces the exception with an
`InvalidOperationException` whose message is `"wrapped"` and whose
`InnerException` is the original.

## Hint 1

Compare the supplied `Losing` with what you need to write. The body is the same
except for one statement, and the difference is one word long.

`Wrapping` is a different decision: a new exception, with the old one attached.

## Hint 2

```csharp
throw ex;   // rethrows the object, and resets its stack trace to THIS line
throw;      // rethrows the exception in flight, trace intact
```

Inside a `catch` block a bare `throw;` is legal and means the second thing.
Outside one it is not.

For `Wrapping`, the constructor's second argument is what keeps the evidence:

```csharp
throw new InvalidOperationException("wrapped", ex);
```

Wrapping is the right move when you are adding context a caller needs - a type
that means something in your layer - and the wrong move when you are only
renaming the problem. Either way the original goes in `InnerException`, and a
wrapper that omits it is strictly worse than not wrapping at all.

## Exercise 5 - cleanup that happens anyway

`Resources.Use(name, log, body)` opens a `Probe`, runs the body, and disposes
the probe whatever happens, returning `"ok"` or `"failed:<message>"`.
`Resources.UseTwo(log, body)` opens `"outer"` then `"inner"`, runs the body,
disposes both - inner first - and lets any exception escape afterwards.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Probe` is written for you and already logs its own open and dispose. Your job
is to make sure the dispose happens - which is what `using` is for.

`Use` also has to catch, because it returns `"failed:..."` rather than
throwing. Think about where the `catch` goes relative to the `using`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using (Probe probe = new Probe(name, log))
{
    try { body(probe); return "ok"; }
    catch (Exception ex) { return $"failed:{ex.Message}"; }
}
```

The `using` compiles into a `try`/`finally`, so the dispose happens on the way
out of either `return`.

`UseTwo` stacks two of them and catches nothing:

```csharp
using (new Probe("outer", log))
using (new Probe("inner", log))
{
    body();
}
```

Predict the disposal order before you run the test. Nested usings unwind in
reverse - last opened, first closed - and that is not arbitrary: the inner
resource may need the outer one to still be alive while it shuts down.

## Exercise 6 - catching the right thing, in the right order

`Sorting.Kind(action)` returns `"ok"`, `"null-arg"`, `"arg"`, `"format"` or
`"other"` depending on what the action threw. `Sorting.Leaves(exception)`
returns the messages of every leaf exception inside an `AggregateException`,
however deeply nested, comma-joined in order.

Edit `src/Lessons/D22_Exceptions/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Catch blocks are tried in source order, and the first one whose type the
exception is assignable to wins. So the order of your four catches decides
which ones are reachable at all.

Check the inheritance: `ArgumentNullException` and
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` both derive from `ArgumentException`.

## Hint 2

Most specific first:

```
ArgumentNullException  ->  "null-arg"
ArgumentException      ->  "arg"
FormatException        ->  "format"
Exception              ->  "other"
```

Put `ArgumentException` first and the null case can never be reached - and
unlike a `catch (Exception)` in the wrong place, the compiler will not warn you
about that one.

For `Leaves`, an `AggregateException` is a tree: its `InnerExceptions` may
themselves be aggregates. `Flatten()` returns a new `AggregateException` whose
`InnerExceptions` are only the leaves, in order - so the whole method is one
`Flatten`, one `Select` for the messages and a `string.Join`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Catch blocks are tried in source order, and the first one whose type the
exception is assignable to wins. So the order of your four catches decides
which ones are reachable at all.

Check the inheritance: `ArgumentNullException` and
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException` both derive from `ArgumentException`.

## Hint 2

Most specific first:

```
ArgumentNullException  ->  "null-arg"
ArgumentException      ->  "arg"
FormatException        ->  "format"
Exception              ->  "other"
```

Put `ArgumentException` first and the null case can never be reached - and
unlike a `catch (Exception)` in the wrong place, the compiler will not warn you
about that one.

For `Leaves`, an `AggregateException` is a tree: its `InnerExceptions` may
themselves be aggregates. `Flatten()` returns a new `AggregateException` whose
`InnerExceptions` are only the leaves, in order - so the whole method is one
`Flatten`, one `Select` for the messages and a `string.Join`.

## Exercise 7 - retry the retryable, and only that

`Retry.Run(operation, attempts, log)` logs `"attempt:1"` before each try and
returns the first success. Only a `TransientException` is retried; anything
else escapes at once. When the last attempt also fails it throws an
`InvalidOperationException` with the message `"gave up after 3 attempts"` and
the last `TransientException` as its `InnerException`. An `attempts` below 1 is
an `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, thrown before anything is tried.


## Exercise 8 - an exception turned into a value, and back

`Safely.Capture(function)` returns a successful `Attempt<T>` or a failed one
carrying the exception's message - except `OperationCanceledException`, which
must escape. `Safely.Unwrap(attempt)` returns the value or throws an
`InvalidOperationException` whose message is the recorded error.
`Safely.Then(attempt, next)` runs `next` on the value only when the attempt
succeeded, capturing anything it throws, and otherwise passes the original
error through untouched.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d22_exceptions ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Capture` is a `try` that builds a successful `Attempt` and a `catch` that
builds a failed one. It has to catch broadly, because the caller asked for a
value rather than a throw - with exactly one exception, named in the summary.

`Unwrap` is the inverse, and `Then` is `Capture` with a guard in front.

## Hint 2

```csharp
try
{
    return new Attempt<T>(true, function(), null);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    throw;                       // a cancellation is not a failure to record
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    return new Attempt<T>(false, default, ex.Message);
}
```

The cancellation clause has to come first, because it is more specific. A
cancellation means somebody asked you to stop; recording it as a failure and
carrying on is the wrong response, and it is why `Task` treats cancelled as a
separate state from faulted rather than as an ordinary error.

## Hint 3

`Then` short-circuits:

```csharp
if (!attempt.Ok) { return new Attempt<TOut>(false, default, attempt.Error); }
return Capture(() => next(attempt.Value!));
```

Passing the *original* error through rather than inventing a new one is what
makes a chain of five steps report the first thing that went wrong instead of a
cascade of consequences.

Note why `Ok` is a separate field rather than "Error is null" or "Value is not
null": `default(T)` is `0` for an int, so the value alone cannot distinguish a
failure from a genuine zero. Decide for yourself whether you would rather model
this as a discriminated pair of types - C# is getting closer to making that
pleasant, and until then this shape is the usual compromise.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Capture` is a `try` that builds a successful `Attempt` and a `catch` that
builds a failed one. It has to catch broadly, because the caller asked for a
value rather than a throw - with exactly one exception, named in the summary.

`Unwrap` is the inverse, and `Then` is `Capture` with a guard in front.

## Hint 2

```csharp
try
{
    return new Attempt<T>(true, function(), null);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    throw;                       // a cancellation is not a failure to record
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    return new Attempt<T>(false, default, ex.Message);
}
```

The cancellation clause has to come first, because it is more specific. A
cancellation means somebody asked you to stop; recording it as a failure and
carrying on is the wrong response, and it is why `Task` treats cancelled as a
separate state from faulted rather than as an ordinary error.

## Hint 3

`Then` short-circuits:

```csharp
if (!attempt.Ok) { return new Attempt<TOut>(false, default, attempt.Error); }
return Capture(() => next(attempt.Value!));
```

Passing the *original* error through rather than inventing a new one is what
makes a chain of five steps report the first thing that went wrong instead of a
cascade of consequences.

Note why `Ok` is a separate field rather than "Error is null" or "Value is not
null": `default(T)` is `0` for an int, so the value alone cannot distinguish a
failure from a genuine zero. Decide for yourself whether you would rather model
this as a discriminated pair of types - C# is getting closer to making that
pleasant, and until then this shape is the usual compromise.

lessons.briefing:
# d23 - Async and tasks drills

Eight problems on `Task` as a value: starting work before waiting for it, what
runs at the call and what waits, `WhenAny` and the loser, the failures
`await` does not show you, chaining steps, reading a task's state without
touching it, preferring the first success, and coalescing many callers onto one
piece of work. They drill lesson 13 - reread `13_async_await` if `await`
still feels like "make this synchronous".

Every task in this set is driven by a `TaskCompletionSource` the gate controls,
so nothing here depends on timing. Every file lives in
`src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/`. Nothing here depends on anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - starting both before awaiting either

`Basics.BothAsync(first, second)` calls both factories *before* awaiting either
and returns `"<first>+<second>"` in parameter order.
`Basics.Immediate(value)` returns an already-completed task without being an
async method. `Basics.AlreadyFailed(message)` returns an already-faulted task
carrying an `InvalidOperationException` - returned, not thrown.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - what runs at the call, and what waits

`Timing.TraceAsync(gate, log)` adds `"before"`, awaits the gate, adds
`"after"`, and returns the log joined with `"|"`. The gate checks that
`"before"` is already there while the returned task is still pending.
`Timing.GreetAsync(name, ready)` returns `"hello ada"` once `ready` completes,
but throws `ArgumentException` **at the call** for an empty or null name.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - whoever gets there first

`Racing.FirstAsync(first, second)` returns the result of whichever finishes
first, leaving the other one untouched. `Racing.WinnerAsync(first, second)`
returns `"first"` or `"second"` naming which one it was.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - the failures await does not show you

`Failures.DescribeAsync(task)` returns `"ok:<result>"` or
`"failed:<message>"`, with the original exception's message.
`Failures.AllErrorsAsync(tasks)` waits for all of them and returns *every*
failure's message, in task order, comma-joined - an empty string when nothing
failed. Awaiting `Task.WhenAll` rethrows only the first.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - one step after another, without blocking

`Chaining.MapAsync(task, map)` applies a plain function to the task's result;
the function must not run before the task finishes.
`Chaining.ThenAsync(task, next)` runs a second asynchronous step on the first
one's result, starting it only when the first has finished - and not at all
when the first failed.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - asking a task how it is doing

`States.Describe(task)` returns `"pending"`, `"ok"`, `"cancelled"` or
`"faulted:<message>"` without awaiting or blocking.
`States.ResultOrFallback(task, fallback)` returns the result only when the task
has already succeeded, and the fallback in every other case - never awaiting,
never blocking, never throwing.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - the first one that actually works

`Preference.FirstSuccessfulAsync(tasks)` returns the result of the first task
to finish *successfully*, ignoring the ones that fail and carrying on waiting.
When every task has failed it throws an `AggregateException` holding all of
their exceptions in task order. An empty sequence is an `ArgumentException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - one piece of work, however many askers

`AsyncOnce<T>` calls its factory at most once and hands every caller the same
`Task` object, so callers arriving while the work is still running do not start
their own. `FactoryCalls` counts the calls. A factory whose task *fails* is not
cached: the next caller tries again.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex8
```

# Reading - csharp/d23_async_tasks

## Notes

The skill being drilled is treating a `Task` as an ordinary value. It is an
object you can hold, pass, store in a list, ask about, and wait on more than
once - and almost every async mistake comes from forgetting that and treating
`await` as a way of making code synchronous again.

The pattern uniting these eight problems is **start first, wait later**. A
method that returns a `Task` has already started the work by the time you have
the task in your hand; `await` only decides when you want the answer. So
`await A(); await B();` is two operations one after the other, while
`var a = A(); var b = B(); await a; await b;` is two at once, and the
difference is entirely in where the awaits go. Everything else here follows:
`WhenAny` gives you back a task rather than a result, `WhenAll` collects
failures onto the tasks rather than into what it throws, and a task you already
hold can be handed to a second caller instead of doing the work twice.

Every task in this set is a `TaskCompletionSource` the gate completes by hand.
That is not only for determinism in the test - it is the tool you reach for
whenever you need to turn something that is not task-shaped (a callback, an
event, a queue) into something that is.

## ex1

Really testing: where the awaits go. Calling the second factory before awaiting
the first is what makes the two operations concurrent, and the gate can see the
difference because it records the moment each factory is called. The other half
of the exercise is the pair of already-completed tasks. `Task.FromResult` and
`Task.FromException` build a finished task with no async machinery, no thread
and no allocation of a state machine - the right answers for a cache hit and a
validation failure respectively. Note what `AlreadyFailed` proves: a method can
*return* a failure rather than throwing it, which is what a caller holding a
`Task` expects.

## ex2

Really testing: that an async method runs synchronously until its first
`await`. The `"before"` line has already been written when the caller gets the
task back - the method did not go anywhere else to start. That is worth knowing
for two reasons: it means work before the first await happens on the caller's
thread, and it means an exception thrown before the first await *still* ends up
in the task rather than at the call. Which is exactly why `GreetAsync` cannot
be an `async` method: argument validation belongs at the call, so the pattern
is a plain method that validates and then returns an async local function's
task.

## ex3

Really testing: `Task.WhenAny`, and the thing it does not do. It hands back the
`Task` that finished - not its result - so getting the value needs a second
`await` and finding out *which* one won needs a reference comparison. The part
people miss is the loser: it is still pending, its work is still running, and
nothing about `WhenAny` cancels or tidies it. In a real timeout that matters -
you have stopped waiting, not stopped working, and if the loser eventually
fails with nobody observing it you have an unobserved task exception. A first
task that finished by *failing* still wins, which is the last assertion.

## ex4

Really testing: where `Task.WhenAll` puts the failures. The task it returns
faults with an `AggregateException` holding every failure, but `await`
deliberately rethrows only the first one, because rethrowing an aggregate would
make every `catch (SqlException)` in the world stop working. So a try/catch
around `await Task.WhenAll(...)` sees one failure and silently loses the rest.
The remaining failures are not gone - each one is on its own task - and reading
them off afterwards is the whole technique. (The other route is
`Task.WhenAll(...).Exception`, which gives the aggregate directly.)

## ex5

Really testing: composing asynchronous steps without ever blocking. Both
methods are two lines, and the point is what the gate measures: the mapping
function has not run while the task is still pending, and the second step has
not been *started*. `await` on the first line gives you both properties for
free, including the failure behaviour - an exception from the first step
propagates and the second step simply never happens, with no `if` anywhere.
This is `Task.ContinueWith` written the readable way, and the reason
`ContinueWith` has largely disappeared from modern code.

## ex6

Really testing: inspecting a task rather than waiting on it. The three terminal
states are distinct - `IsCompleted` is true for all of them, so the order of
the checks matters, and cancellation is not a kind of fault. `Exception` on a
faulted task is always an `AggregateException`, so the message worth logging is
one level in. The second method exists to make one point: `task.Result` on a
pending task *blocks the calling thread* until somebody else completes it,
which is the classic way to deadlock a UI or an ASP.NET request.
`IsCompletedSuccessfully` is the one test that excludes pending, faulted and
cancelled in a single call.

## ex7

Really testing: a `WhenAny` loop, which is the standard shape for "keep waiting
until something good happens". The list of pending tasks shrinks by one each
time round, and a task that finished by failing is dropped rather than
returned - which is exactly the behaviour plain `WhenAny` does not give you.
Two details are worth care. `finished.Status == TaskStatus.RanToCompletion` is
the success test, because `IsCompleted` is true for failures too. And the
give-up path reports the failures in *task* order rather than completion
order, because the caller is trying to understand a system, not a race.

## ex8

Really testing: everything above, in the shape real code needs. The key insight
is that the cached thing is the `Task`, not the value - which is what makes the
coalescing work, because a caller who arrives while the work is in flight can
be handed the same in-flight task. A cache that stores the *result* can only
help callers who arrive after it finishes, so the stampede it was built to
prevent goes straight through. The failure rule is the other half of the
design: caching a faulted task means one unlucky moment poisons the value for
the lifetime of the process, so a faulted task is dropped and the next caller
retries. (This version is deliberately not thread-safe; the real one wraps the
check in a lock or uses `Lazy<Task<T>>`, and knowing that you have not solved
that is better than assuming you have.)

## Further reading

- [Asynchronous programming with async and await](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/) - the model, and what await really does.
- [`Task.WhenAll`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenall) and [`Task.WhenAny`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenany) - including what each one does with failures.
- [`TaskCompletionSource<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.taskcompletionsource-1) - turning anything into a task, and the tool this whole lesson is tested with.
- [Task-based asynchronous pattern (TAP)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/task-based-asynchronous-pattern-tap) - the conventions, including where argument validation goes.
- [`Task.Status`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.status) - the full state machine behind ex6.
- [Async guidance: avoid blocking on async code](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/best-practices#avoid-blocking-calls) - why `.Result` on a pending task is a deadlock.

until something good happens". The list of pending tasks shrinks by one each
time round, and a task that finished by failing is dropped rather than
returned - which is exactly the behaviour plain `WhenAny` does not give you.
Two details are worth care. `finished.Status == TaskStatus.RanToCompletion` is
the success test, because `IsCompleted` is true for failures too. And the
give-up path reports the failures in *task* order rather than completion
order, because the caller is trying to understand a system, not a race.

## ex8

Really testing: everything above, in the shape real code needs. The key insight
is that the cached thing is the `Task`, not the value - which is what makes the
coalescing work, because a caller who arrives while the work is in flight can
be handed the same in-flight task. A cache that stores the *result* can only
help callers who arrive after it finishes, so the stampede it was built to
prevent goes straight through. The failure rule is the other half of the
design: caching a faulted task means one unlucky moment poisons the value for
the lifetime of the process, so a faulted task is dropped and the next caller
retries. (This version is deliberately not thread-safe; the real one wraps the
check in a lock or uses `Lazy<Task<T>>`, and knowing that you have not solved
that is better than assuming you have.)

## Exercise 1 - starting both before awaiting either

`Basics.BothAsync(first, second)` calls both factories *before* awaiting either
and returns `"<first>+<second>"` in parameter order.
`Basics.Immediate(value)` returns an already-completed task without being an
async method. `Basics.AlreadyFailed(message)` returns an already-faulted task
carrying an `InvalidOperationException` - returned, not thrown.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write out the two obvious versions of `BothAsync` and compare them:

```csharp
return $"{await first()}+{await second()}";      // one after the other
```

In that version, when is `second()` even called? Not until the first task has
finished. The gate records the moment each factory runs, so it can tell.

## Hint 2

Call both, then await both:

```csharp
Task<string> firstTask = first();
Task<string> secondTask = second();
return $"{await firstTask}+{await secondTask}";
```

A method that returns a `Task` has already started its work by the time you
hold the task, so both operations are in flight before either await. The order
you await them in does not change the answer - the output order comes from the
parameters.

For the other two, `Task.FromResult(value)` and
`Task.FromException<string>(new InvalidOperationException(message))` build
finished tasks with no async machinery at all. Note the second one *returns*
the failure rather than throwing it, which is what a caller holding a `Task`
expects.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write out the two obvious versions of `BothAsync` and compare them:

```csharp
return $"{await first()}+{await second()}";      // one after the other
```

In that version, when is `second()` even called? Not until the first task has
finished. The gate records the moment each factory runs, so it can tell.

## Hint 2

Call both, then await both:

```csharp
Task<string> firstTask = first();
Task<string> secondTask = second();
return $"{await firstTask}+{await secondTask}";
```

A method that returns a `Task` has already started its work by the time you
hold the task, so both operations are in flight before either await. The order
you await them in does not change the answer - the output order comes from the
parameters.

For the other two, `Task.FromResult(value)` and
`Task.FromException<string>(new InvalidOperationException(message))` build
finished tasks with no async machinery at all. Note the second one *returns*
the failure rather than throwing it, which is what a caller holding a `Task`
expects.

## Exercise 2 - what runs at the call, and what waits

`Timing.TraceAsync(gate, log)` adds `"before"`, awaits the gate, adds
`"after"`, and returns the log joined with `"|"`. The gate checks that
`"before"` is already there while the returned task is still pending.

but throws `ArgumentException` **at the call** for an empty or null name.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`TraceAsync` is the straightforward async method - log, await, log, return.
Predict what the gate will see before you write it: is `"before"` in the log
while the returned task is still pending?

`GreetAsync` is the one that needs a trick, and the summary says why: the
exception must arrive at the *call*, not in the returned task.

## Hint 2

An `async` method never throws at its caller. Everything, including an
exception before the first `await`, goes into the returned task. So the
validation has to live in a method that is not `async`:

```csharp
public static Task<string> GreetAsync(string name, Task ready)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(name)) { throw new ArgumentException(...); }

    return Greet();

    async Task<string> Greet()
    {
        await ready;
        return $"hello {name}";
    }
}
```

A local function keeps the two halves together. This is the standard shape for
argument validation in the task-based pattern, and it is the same problem
iterator methods have with `yield`.

## Exercise 3 - whoever gets there first

`Racing.FirstAsync(first, second)` returns the result of whichever finishes
first, leaving the other one untouched. `Racing.WinnerAsync(first, second)`
returns `"first"` or `"second"` naming which one it was.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Task.WhenAny(a, b)` returns a task whose result is **the task that finished**,
not that task's result. So there are two awaits: one for the race, and one for
the winner's value.

For `WinnerAsync` you do not need the value at all - only which task it was.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task<string> winner = await Task.WhenAny(first, second);
return await winner;                                  // FirstAsync
return ReferenceEquals(winner, first) ? "first" : "second";   // WinnerAsync
```

`ReferenceEquals` is the right comparison: `WhenAny` hands back one of the very
objects you passed in.

The assertion worth pausing on is the one about the loser. `WhenAny` does not
cancel it, does not dispose it and does not wait for it - it is still pending
and its work is still running. In a real timeout that is exactly the situation:
you have stopped waiting, not stopped working, and if the loser eventually
fails with nobody watching you have an unobserved exception.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Task.WhenAny(a, b)` returns a task whose result is **the task that finished**,
not that task's result. So there are two awaits: one for the race, and one for
the winner's value.

For `WinnerAsync` you do not need the value at all - only which task it was.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task<string> winner = await Task.WhenAny(first, second);
return await winner;                                  // FirstAsync
return ReferenceEquals(winner, first) ? "first" : "second";   // WinnerAsync
```

`ReferenceEquals` is the right comparison: `WhenAny` hands back one of the very
objects you passed in.

The assertion worth pausing on is the one about the loser. `WhenAny` does not
cancel it, does not dispose it and does not wait for it - it is still pending
and its work is still running. In a real timeout that is exactly the situation:
you have stopped waiting, not stopped working, and if the loser eventually
fails with nobody watching you have an unobserved exception.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - the failures await does not show you

`Failures.DescribeAsync(task)` returns `"ok:<result>"` or
`"failed:<message>"`, with the original exception's message.
`Failures.AllErrorsAsync(tasks)` waits for all of them and returns *every*
failure's message, in task order, comma-joined - an empty string when nothing
failed. Awaiting `Task.WhenAll` rethrows only the first.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`DescribeAsync` is a `try`/`catch` around an `await`. Note that `await`
unwraps: the exception you catch is the original one, not the
`AggregateException` that `.Result` would have handed you.

`AllErrorsAsync` is the interesting one. Await `Task.WhenAll`, catch, and then
look somewhere other than the exception you caught.

## Hint 2

`await Task.WhenAll(...)` rethrows only the FIRST failure, deliberately -
rethrowing an aggregate would break every `catch (SomeSpecificException)` in
the world. But the task WhenAll returns has all of them, and so does each
individual task:

```csharp
Task<string>[] all = tasks.ToArray();
try { await Task.WhenAll(all); } catch (Exception) { }

return string.Join(",", all
    .Where(task => task.IsFaulted)
    .Select(task => task.Exception!.InnerException!.Message));
```

Materialise the sequence first with `ToArray`, or you will enumerate it twice
and start each task's `WhenAll` registration on a different set of objects.

`task.Exception` is always an `AggregateException`, so the message you want is
one level in.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`DescribeAsync` is a `try`/`catch` around an `await`. Note that `await`
unwraps: the exception you catch is the original one, not the
`AggregateException` that `.Result` would have handed you.

`AllErrorsAsync` is the interesting one. Await `Task.WhenAll`, catch, and then
look somewhere other than the exception you caught.

## Hint 2

`await Task.WhenAll(...)` rethrows only the FIRST failure, deliberately -
rethrowing an aggregate would break every `catch (SomeSpecificException)` in
the world. But the task WhenAll returns has all of them, and so does each
individual task:

```csharp
Task<string>[] all = tasks.ToArray();
try { await Task.WhenAll(all); } catch (Exception) { }

return string.Join(",", all
    .Where(task => task.IsFaulted)
    .Select(task => task.Exception!.InnerException!.Message));
```

Materialise the sequence first with `ToArray`, or you will enumerate it twice
and start each task's `WhenAll` registration on a different set of objects.

`task.Exception` is always an `AggregateException`, so the message you want is
one level in.

## Exercise 5 - one step after another, without blocking

`Chaining.MapAsync(task, map)` applies a plain function to the task's result;
the function must not run before the task finishes.

one's result, starting it only when the first has finished - and not at all
when the first failed.

## Exercise 6 - asking a task how it is doing

`States.Describe(task)` returns `"pending"`, `"ok"`, `"cancelled"` or
`"faulted:<message>"` without awaiting or blocking.
`States.ResultOrFallback(task, fallback)` returns the result only when the task
has already succeeded, and the fallback in every other case - never awaiting,
never blocking, never throwing.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four states, and the properties that distinguish them are `IsCompleted`,
`IsCanceled` and `IsFaulted`. Watch the order: `IsCompleted` is true for a
failure and a cancellation as well as a success, so it cannot be the last test.

Nothing in this exercise awaits anything.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (!task.IsCompleted) { return "pending"; }
if (task.IsCanceled)   { return "cancelled"; }
if (task.IsFaulted)    { return $"faulted:{task.Exception!.InnerException!.Message}"; }
return "ok";
```

Cancellation is its own state rather than a kind of failure - `IsFaulted` is
false for a cancelled task - which is why it has to be checked separately.
`task.Exception` is always an `AggregateException`, so the readable message is
one level in.

For `ResultOrFallback`, `task.IsCompletedSuccessfully` is the single test that
excludes pending, faulted and cancelled at once - and it is what makes reading
`task.Result` safe on the next line. Reading `.Result` on a *pending* task
blocks the calling thread until somebody else finishes it, which is the classic
way to deadlock a UI or a request thread.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four states, and the properties that distinguish them are `IsCompleted`,
`IsCanceled` and `IsFaulted`. Watch the order: `IsCompleted` is true for a
failure and a cancellation as well as a success, so it cannot be the last test.

Nothing in this exercise awaits anything.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (!task.IsCompleted) { return "pending"; }
if (task.IsCanceled)   { return "cancelled"; }
if (task.IsFaulted)    { return $"faulted:{task.Exception!.InnerException!.Message}"; }
return "ok";
```

Cancellation is its own state rather than a kind of failure - `IsFaulted` is
false for a cancelled task - which is why it has to be checked separately.
`task.Exception` is always an `AggregateException`, so the readable message is
one level in.

For `ResultOrFallback`, `task.IsCompletedSuccessfully` is the single test that
excludes pending, faulted and cancelled at once - and it is what makes reading
`task.Result` safe on the next line. Reading `.Result` on a *pending* task
blocks the calling thread until somebody else finishes it, which is the classic
way to deadlock a UI or a request thread.

## Exercise 7 - the first one that actually works

`Preference.FirstSuccessfulAsync(tasks)` returns the result of the first task
to finish *successfully*, ignoring the ones that fail and carrying on waiting.
When every task has failed it throws an `AggregateException` holding all of
their exceptions in task order. An empty sequence is an `ArgumentException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A single `WhenAny` is not enough, because the first task to finish might have
finished by failing. You need to wait again, on what is left.

So: a list of pending tasks, and a loop that removes one each time round.

## Hint 2

```csharp
List<Task<T>> pending = new List<Task<T>>(all);

while (pending.Count > 0)
{
    Task<T> finished = await Task.WhenAny(pending);
    pending.Remove(finished);

    if (finished.Status == TaskStatus.RanToCompletion) { return await finished; }
}
```

`Status == TaskStatus.RanToCompletion` is the success test. `IsCompleted` would
be true for the failures too, and `!IsFaulted` would let a cancelled task
through and then throw when you awaited it.

## Hint 3

The give-up path needs every failure, and in **task** order rather than the
order they happened to finish - so keep the original list as well as the
shrinking one, and build the `AggregateException` from that:

```csharp
throw new AggregateException(all.Select(task => task.Exception!.InnerException!));
```

Reporting them in completion order would make the same set of failures produce
different-looking logs on different runs, which is exactly what you do not want
when you are trying to understand a system.

Decide for yourself what this should do about a task that was *cancelled* - the
gate does not test it, and the two defensible answers (treat it as a failure,
or let it out) say different things about what the method is for.

```csharp
    Task<T> finished = await Task.WhenAny(pending);
    pending.Remove(finished);

    if (finished.Status == TaskStatus.RanToCompletion) { return await finished; }
}
```

`Status == TaskStatus.RanToCompletion` is the success test. `IsCompleted` would
be true for the failures too, and `!IsFaulted` would let a cancelled task
through and then throw when you awaited it.

## Hint 3

The give-up path needs every failure, and in **task** order rather than the
order they happened to finish - so keep the original list as well as the
shrinking one, and build the `AggregateException` from that:

```csharp
throw new AggregateException(all.Select(task => task.Exception!.InnerException!));
```

Reporting them in completion order would make the same set of failures produce
different-looking logs on different runs, which is exactly what you do not want
when you are trying to understand a system.

Decide for yourself what this should do about a task that was *cancelled* - the
gate does not test it, and the two defensible answers (treat it as a failure,
or let it out) say different things about what the method is for.

## Exercise 8 - one piece of work, however many askers

`AsyncOnce<T>` calls its factory at most once and hands every caller the same
`Task` object, so callers arriving while the work is still running do not start
their own. `FactoryCalls` counts the calls. A factory whose task *fails* is not
cached: the next caller tries again.

Edit `src/Lessons/D23_AsyncTasks/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d23_async_tasks ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The thing you cache is the **`Task`**, not the value. That single decision is
what makes the coalescing work: a caller who arrives while the work is still
running can be handed the same in-flight task and will get the answer when it
arrives.

`GetAsync` is not `async` and does not await anything. It hands back a task.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (_task is null)
{
    FactoryCalls++;
    _task = _factory();
}

return _task;
```

That is the whole coalescing behaviour. Notice what a cache that stored the
*result* instead could not do: it would only be able to help callers who
arrive after the work finished, so the stampede it was built to prevent goes
straight through.

## Hint 3

The last requirement is the failure rule. A faulted task must not stay cached,
or one unlucky moment poisons the value for the lifetime of the process:

```csharp
if (_task is not null && _task.IsFaulted) { _task = null; }
```

at the top, before the null check.

the same moment could both see `null` and both call the factory. Making it safe
means a lock around the check, or `Lazy<Task<T>>` with
`LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication`. Decide which you would ship,
and note that knowing you have not solved it is worth more than assuming you
have.

# d24 - Mixed gauntlet

The last drill set, and the cumulative one: every exercise combines two or
three things from across the track rather than practising one. Records with
queries, an interface behind a generic constraint, a hierarchy read by a
pattern, delegates in a dictionary, your own comparer inside an iterator, an
event over a collection, tasks that partly fail, and a small repository that
uses most of the rest. If a problem here feels like guessing, the drill set it
came from is named in its section.

Every file lives in `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/`. Nothing here depends on
anything else here.

## Exercise 1 - records, a query and some formatting

*Draws on d10, d18 and d19.* `Roster.ByTeam(members)` returns
`"eng: ada(9), bob(4)"` for each team with at least one member scoring above
zero - teams ordered by name (ordinal), members by points descending with ties
broken by name. `Roster.Awarded(member, extra)` returns a copy with the extra
points added and leaves the original untouched.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - an interface, a constraint and a dictionary

*Draws on d09, d12 and d13.* `Catalogue.Cheapest<T>(items)` and
`Catalogue.Total<T>(items)` work for any `T : IPriced` - the cheapest being the
first of any tie, and empty being an `InvalidOperationException` for one and
zero for the other. `Catalogue.PriceList(widgets)` maps name to price with the
*last* widget of a repeated name winning.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a hierarchy, a pattern and a guard

*Draws on d07, d08 and d22.* `Rect` and `Circle` derive from `Shape`, override
`Area()`, and reject a non-positive dimension in the constructor with
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. `Shapes.Describe(shape)` returns `"rect 6"` or
`"circle 12.57"` - the kind from a type pattern, the area rounded to two places
and written with the invariant culture - and `"shape ..."` for anything else.
`Shapes.TotalArea(shapes)` sums the areas and rounds once at the end.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex3.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - delegates in a dictionary, with the errors named

*Draws on d16, d13 and d22.* `Commands.Register(name, handler)` stores a
handler and rejects a repeated name with `ArgumentException`, changing nothing.
`Commands.Names` lists them in registration order. `Commands.Run(name, arg)`
throws `KeyNotFoundException` for an unknown name, and wraps anything the
handler throws in an `InvalidOperationException` with the message
`"command failed: <name>"` and the original as its `InnerException`.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex4.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - your own comparer, streamed through an iterator

*Draws on d11, d15 and d21.* `CaseInsensitive` implements
`IEqualityComparer<string>` using an ordinal, case-insensitive comparison, with
a hash code that agrees with it. `Streams.FirstOfEach(source, comparer)` yields
the first occurrence of each distinct item lazily - nothing is read until the
result is enumerated, and only as far as the caller asks.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex5.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - an event, a collection and a query

*Draws on d17, d13 and d19.* `Basket.Add(item)` stores the item and then raises
`Added`; a null or empty item is an `ArgumentException` that neither stores nor
announces anything. `Basket.Duplicates()` names the items appearing more than
once, in first-seen order. `Basket.Tally()` returns `"apple=3"` per distinct
item, ordered by count descending with ties broken ordinally.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex6.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - many tasks, some of them broken

*Draws on d23, d18 and d22.* `Fetching.GatherAsync(tasks)` waits for all of
them and returns an `Outcome` holding the results that worked and the messages
of the ones that did not, both in task order.
`Fetching.LookupAsync(ids, fetch)` starts every fetch before waiting for any,
and returns `"id=result"` for the successful ones ordered by id (ordinal).

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex7.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a small repository that uses most of the track

*Draws on d13, d17, d19 and d22.* `Repository.Save(employee)` adds or replaces
by `Id` without changing the insertion position, then raises `Saved`.
`Get(id)` throws `KeyNotFoundException` when there is none. `Remove(id)`
reports whether there was one. `Query(predicate)` returns the matches in
insertion order, and `DeptTotals()` returns `"eng=170"` per department, ordered
by department (ordinal), formatted with the invariant culture.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/d24_mixed_gauntlet

## Notes

This set does not drill a feature. It drills the thing that actually makes
someone useful in C#: reaching for the right two or three tools at once and
getting the seams between them right. Every exercise here is small, and every
one of them fails for a reason that lives in the join rather than in any single
part.

The pattern uniting them is **decide, then compose**. What is a row? What order
is it in? What does "equal" mean here? What happens to the item that does not
fit? Each exercise makes you answer one of those questions explicitly, because
the parts on their own have no opinion: `GroupBy` will not tell you what to do
about the empty team, `Dictionary` will not tell you whether a repeat is a
mistake, `Task.WhenAll` will not tell you whether one failure should hide five
successes.

If a problem here feels like guessing, that is information rather than failure:
each section in the README names the drill sets it came from, and rereading one
of those is a better use of ten minutes than staring at this one.

## ex1

Really testing: records and a two-level query in the same breath. The query is
the familiar filter-group-order-project, and the trap is where the filter goes:
filtering before grouping is what makes the all-negative team disappear
completely, because `GroupBy` never invents a group for a key nothing reached.
The record half is `with`, and the assertions are chosen to show what it means
- the copy is a different object and an equal one, because records compare by
value. That combination is the whole reason to model a domain value as a
record.

## ex2

Really testing: an interface used as a generic constraint, which is the point
where "interfaces are for polymorphism" and "generics are for reuse" turn out
to be the same sentence. `where T : IPriced` gets you `.Price` inside the
method while the caller keeps their own type on the way out - no casting and no
`object`. The dictionary half is a deliberate contrast with d19: there a
duplicate key was a broken assumption worth throwing over, and here it is an
intended overwrite - so the indexer, not `Add` and not `ToDictionary`. Which
one is right depends entirely on what a repeat *means*, and that is a decision
the API cannot make for you.

## ex3

Really testing: a hierarchy, a switch over it, and validation in the
constructor. Putting the guard in the constructor is what makes every `Rect`
that exists a valid one, so no method downstream has to check - the shortest
route to code with no defensive noise in it. The `switch` is a type pattern
with a discard arm, and the arm matters: a pattern switch over a hierarchy
somebody else can extend needs an answer for the subclass you have not seen.
The formatting detail is small and real - `ToString()` on a double uses the
current culture, so on a machine with a comma decimal separator the same code
prints `12,57` and every string comparison in your test suite fails.

## ex4

Really testing: behaviour stored in a dictionary, and the two different
failures a dispatcher can have. "No such command" is the caller asking for
something that does not exist; "the handler threw" is the command failing at
its job. Reporting both as the same exception type makes them
indistinguishable, and wrapping the second one - with the original as its
`InnerException` - is what keeps the distinction while losing nothing. The
other detail is `Names`: a `Dictionary` makes no promise about enumeration
order, so a separate list is what remembers registration order. Relying on the
order a dictionary happens to give you is a bug that waits for a rehash.

## ex5

# Reading - csharp/d24_mixed_gauntlet

## Notes

This set does not drill a feature. It drills the thing that actually makes
someone useful in C#: reaching for the right two or three tools at once and
getting the seams between them right. Every exercise here is small, and every
one of them fails for a reason that lives in the join rather than in any single
part.

The pattern uniting them is **decide, then compose**. What is a row? What order
is it in? What does "equal" mean here? What happens to the item that does not
fit? Each exercise makes you answer one of those questions explicitly, because
the parts on their own have no opinion: `GroupBy` will not tell you what to do
about the empty team, `Dictionary` will not tell you whether a repeat is a
mistake, `Task.WhenAll` will not tell you whether one failure should hide five
successes.

If a problem here feels like guessing, that is information rather than failure:
each section in the README names the drill sets it came from, and rereading one
of those is a better use of ten minutes than staring at this one.

## ex1

completely, because `GroupBy` never invents a group for a key nothing reached.
The record half is `with`, and the assertions are chosen to show what it means

value. That combination is the whole reason to model a domain value as a
record.

## ex2

where "interfaces are for polymorphism" and "generics are for reuse" turn out
to be the same sentence. `where T : IPriced` gets you `.Price` inside the
method while the caller keeps their own type on the way out - no casting and no

duplicate key was a broken assumption worth throwing over, and here it is an
intended overwrite - so the indexer, not `Add` and not `ToDictionary`. Which
one is right depends entirely on what a repeat *means*, and that is a decision
the API cannot make for you.

## ex3

Really testing: a hierarchy, a switch over it, and validation in the
constructor. Putting the guard in the constructor is what makes every `Rect`
that exists a valid one, so no method downstream has to check - the shortest
route to code with no defensive noise in it. The `switch` is a type pattern
with a discard arm, and the arm matters: a pattern switch over a hierarchy
somebody else can extend needs an answer for the subclass you have not seen.

current culture, so on a machine with a comma decimal separator the same code
prints `12,57` and every string comparison in your test suite fails.

failures a dispatcher can have. "No such command" is the caller asking for

## Exercise 1 - records, a query and some formatting

*Draws on d10, d18 and d19.* `Roster.ByTeam(members)` returns
`"eng: ada(9), bob(4)"` for each team with at least one member scoring above
zero - teams ordered by name (ordinal), members by points descending with ties
broken by name. `Roster.Awarded(member, extra)` returns a copy with the extra
points added and leaves the original untouched.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex1.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The pipeline is filter, group, order the teams, order inside each team,
project. Getting the filter first is what makes the all-negative team vanish
rather than appearing empty.

`Awarded` is one line, and the keyword is `with`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
members
    .Where(member => member.Points > 0)
    .GroupBy(member => member.Team)
    .OrderBy(group => group.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal)
    .Select(group => $"{group.Key}: " + string.Join(", ", group
        .OrderByDescending(member => member.Points)
        .ThenBy(member => member.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal)
        .Select(member => $"{member.Name}({member.Points})")))
```

`member with { Points = member.Points + extra }` produces a copy. The original
is untouched, and the copy is *equal* to the original when nothing changed -

## Hint 1

The pipeline is filter, group, order the teams, order inside each team,
project. Getting the filter first is what makes the all-negative team vanish
rather than appearing empty.

`Awarded` is one line, and the keyword is `with`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
members
    .Where(member => member.Points > 0)
    .GroupBy(member => member.Team)
    .OrderBy(group => group.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal)
    .Select(group => $"{group.Key}: " + string.Join(", ", group
        .OrderByDescending(member => member.Points)
        .ThenBy(member => member.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal)
        .Select(member => $"{member.Name}({member.Points})")))
```

`member with { Points = member.Points + extra }` produces a copy. The original
is untouched, and the copy is *equal* to the original when nothing changed -
records compare by value, which is exactly why they suit a domain value like
this one.

Mind the separators: `": "` after the team and `", "` between members.

## Exercise 2 - an interface, a constraint and a dictionary

*Draws on d09, d12 and d13.* `Catalogue.Cheapest<T>(items)` and
`Catalogue.Total<T>(items)` work for any `T : IPriced` - the cheapest being the
first of any tie, and empty being an `InvalidOperationException` for one and
zero for the other. `Catalogue.PriceList(widgets)` maps name to price with the
*last* widget of a repeated name winning.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex2.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`where T : IPriced` is what lets the method say `item.Price` while the caller
keeps their own type on the way out. No casting, no `object`, and `Cheapest`
returns a `Widget` when you hand it widgets.

For `PriceList`, decide first what a repeated name *means* here. The summary
says.

## Hint 2

`Cheapest` is a loop that keeps the best item seen so far; use a strict `<` so
the first of a tie wins, and a `bool found` flag rather than comparing against
`default(T)` - `T` might be a value type with no meaningful default.
`items.MinBy(item => item.Price)` is also a fair answer; check what it does
about the empty case before you rely on it.

`Total` is `items.Sum(item => item.Price)`, and `Sum` already returns zero for
an empty sequence.

`PriceList` uses the indexer:

```csharp
prices[widget.Name] = widget.Price;
```

`Add` would throw on the repeat and `ToDictionary` would too - which was the
right answer in d19, where a duplicate meant a broken assumption. Here the
overwrite is intended, and the indexer is how you say so.

`where T : IPriced` is what lets the method say `item.Price` while the caller
keeps their own type on the way out. No casting, no `object`, and `Cheapest`

says.

## Hint 2

`Cheapest` is a loop that keeps the best item seen so far; use a strict `<` so
the first of a tie wins, and a `bool found` flag rather than comparing against
`default(T)` - `T` might be a value type with no meaningful default.
`items.MinBy(item => item.Price)` is also a fair answer; check what it does
about the empty case before you rely on it.

`Total` is `items.Sum(item => item.Price)`, and `Sum` already returns zero for
an empty sequence.

`PriceList` uses the indexer:

```csharp
prices[widget.Name] = widget.Price;
```

`Add` would throw on the repeat and `ToDictionary` would too - which was the
right answer in d19, where a duplicate meant a broken assumption. Here the
overwrite is intended, and the indexer is how you say so.

## Exercise 4 - delegates in a dictionary, with the errors named

*Draws on d16, d13 and d22.* `Commands.Register(name, handler)` stores a
handler and rejects a repeated name with `ArgumentException`, changing nothing.
`Commands.Names` lists them in registration order. `Commands.Run(name, arg)`
throws `KeyNotFoundException` for an unknown name, and wraps anything the
handler throws in an `InvalidOperationException` with the message
`"command failed: <name>"` and the original as its `InnerException`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Dictionary<string, Func<string, string>>` holds the handlers and a
`List<string>` remembers the registration order - a dictionary promises nothing
about the order it enumerates in, so you cannot get `Names` from it.

`Run` has two different failures to report, and they must not look the same.

## Hint 2

"No such command" is the caller asking for something that does not exist:
`KeyNotFoundException`, from a `TryGetValue` that came back false.

"The handler threw" is a different thing entirely - the command exists and
failed at its job - so it is caught and wrapped:

```csharp
catch (Exception ex)
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException($"command failed: {name}", ex);
}
```

Passing `ex` is what keeps the distinction useful: the caller can tell a
dispatch problem from a handler problem *and* still see what the handler
actually did.

In `Register`, check `ContainsKey` first and throw before touching either
collection, so a refused registration leaves the name list alone too.

## Hint 1

A `Dictionary<string, Func<string, string>>` holds the handlers and a
`List<string>` remembers the registration order - a dictionary promises nothing
about the order it enumerates in, so you cannot get `Names` from it.

`Run` has two different failures to report, and they must not look the same.

## Hint 2

"No such command" is the caller asking for something that does not exist:
`KeyNotFoundException`, from a `TryGetValue` that came back false.

"The handler threw" is a different thing entirely - the command exists and
failed at its job - so it is caught and wrapped:

```csharp
catch (Exception ex)
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException($"command failed: {name}", ex);
}
```

Passing `ex` is what keeps the distinction useful: the caller can tell a
dispatch problem from a handler problem *and* still see what the handler
actually did.

In `Register`, check `ContainsKey` first and throw before touching either
collection, so a refused registration leaves the name list alone too.

## Exercise 5 - your own comparer, streamed through an iterator

*Draws on d11, d15 and d21.* `CaseInsensitive` implements
`IEqualityComparer<string>` using an ordinal, case-insensitive comparison, with
a hash code that agrees with it. `Streams.FirstOfEach(source, comparer)` yields
the first occurrence of each distinct item lazily - nothing is read until the
result is enumerated, and only as far as the caller asks.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`IEqualityComparer<string>` has two members and they have to agree with each
other. Work out what `GetHashCode` must do given that `"Ada"` and `"ADA"` are
equal - two equal values that hash differently land in different buckets and a
`HashSet` never notices they match.

`FirstOfEach` is an iterator method. The word is `yield`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public bool Equals(string? x, string? y) => string.Equals(x, y, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
public int GetHashCode(string value) => value.ToUpperInvariant().GetHashCode();
```

Normalising before hashing is the usual trick: upper-case both and the hashes
agree because the strings do. (`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` would do the
whole job for you, and writing it out once is worth more here.)

```csharp
HashSet<string> seen = new HashSet<string>(comparer);
foreach (string item in source)
{
    if (seen.Add(item)) { yield return item; }
}
```

`HashSet` takes a comparer in its constructor, and `Add` returns false when the
item was already there - so one call both tests and records.

`yield return` is what makes it lazy: the body does not run until somebody
enumerates the result, and it stops as soon as they stop asking.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`IEqualityComparer<string>` has two members and they have to agree with each
other. Work out what `GetHashCode` must do given that `"Ada"` and `"ADA"` are
equal - two equal values that hash differently land in different buckets and a
`HashSet` never notices they match.

`FirstOfEach` is an iterator method. The word is `yield`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public bool Equals(string? x, string? y) => string.Equals(x, y, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
public int GetHashCode(string value) => value.ToUpperInvariant().GetHashCode();
```

Normalising before hashing is the usual trick: upper-case both and the hashes
agree because the strings do. (`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` would do the
whole job for you, and writing it out once is worth more here.)

```csharp
HashSet<string> seen = new HashSet<string>(comparer);
foreach (string item in source)
{
    if (seen.Add(item)) { yield return item; }
}
```

`HashSet` takes a comparer in its constructor, and `Add` returns false when the
item was already there - so one call both tests and records.

`yield return` is what makes it lazy: the body does not run until somebody
enumerates the result, and it stops as soon as they stop asking.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods have to start everything before waiting for anything, and both
have to treat a failure as something to record rather than something to
propagate.

`await Task.WhenAll(...)` rethrows only the FIRST failure - so catching it and
believing what you caught loses the rest.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task<string>[] all = tasks.ToArray();
try { await Task.WhenAll(all); } catch (Exception) { }

List<string> successes = all.Where(t => t.IsCompletedSuccessfully).Select(t => t.Result).ToList();
List<string> failures  = all.Where(t => t.IsFaulted).Select(t => t.Exception!.InnerException!.Message).ToList();
```

Materialise with `ToArray` first, or the two `Where` calls enumerate the source
twice and may not even see the same tasks.

## Hint 3

`LookupAsync` needs the id alongside its task, so project into a pair and
materialise immediately - the `ToList` is what starts every fetch before the
first await:

```csharp
var started = ids.Select(id => new { Id = id, Task = fetch(id) }).ToList();
```

Then wait for them (awaiting each in a `try`, or `Task.WhenAll` in one, it does
not matter as long as nothing escapes), and finally filter to
`IsCompletedSuccessfully`, order by `Id` with `StringComparer.Ordinal`, and
format.

Ordering by id rather than by who answered first is what makes the same data
produce the same output on every run - which is the difference between a report
and a race.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods have to start everything before waiting for anything, and both
have to treat a failure as something to record rather than something to
propagate.

`await Task.WhenAll(...)` rethrows only the FIRST failure - so catching it and
believing what you caught loses the rest.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task<string>[] all = tasks.ToArray();
try { await Task.WhenAll(all); } catch (Exception) { }

List<string> successes = all.Where(t => t.IsCompletedSuccessfully).Select(t => t.Result).ToList();
List<string> failures  = all.Where(t => t.IsFaulted).Select(t => t.Exception!.InnerException!.Message).ToList();
```

Materialise with `ToArray` first, or the two `Where` calls enumerate the source
twice and may not even see the same tasks.

## Hint 3

`LookupAsync` needs the id alongside its task, so project into a pair and
materialise immediately - the `ToList` is what starts every fetch before the
first await:

```csharp
var started = ids.Select(id => new { Id = id, Task = fetch(id) }).ToList();
```

Then wait for them (awaiting each in a `try`, or `Task.WhenAll` in one, it does
not matter as long as nothing escapes), and finally filter to
`IsCompletedSuccessfully`, order by `Id` with `StringComparer.Ordinal`, and
format.

Ordering by id rather than by who answered first is what makes the same data
produce the same output on every run - which is the difference between a report
and a race.

## Exercise 8 - a small repository that uses most of the track

*Draws on d13, d17, d19 and d22.* `Repository.Save(employee)` adds or replaces
by `Id` without changing the insertion position, then raises `Saved`.
`Get(id)` throws `KeyNotFoundException` when there is none. `Remove(id)`
reports whether there was one. `Query(predicate)` returns the matches in
insertion order, and `DeptTotals()` returns `"eng=170"` per department, ordered
by department (ordinal), formatted with the invariant culture.

Edit `src/Lessons/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex8.cs`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two fields, because neither structure gives you both things you need: a
`Dictionary<int, Employee>` for lookup by id, and a `List<int>` for insertion
order. Every method has to keep them agreeing.

Write down what each method does to *both* before you write any of them.

## Hint 2

`Save`: add the id to the order list only when it is new, then set the
dictionary entry either way, then raise. That is what makes a replace keep the
employee's original position.

`Get`: `TryGetValue`, and `KeyNotFoundException` when it says no - not null,
because a null forces every caller to check and most of them will not.

`Query` and `DeptTotals` both start from the order list and look each id up, so
they inherit insertion order:

```csharp
_order.Select(id => _byId[id])
```

## Hint 3

`Remove` is where this design goes wrong most easily. Removing the dictionary
entry and forgetting the order list leaves an id in `_order` that `_byId` no
longer has - and then `_byId[id]` throws inside `Query`, or worse, a version
that skips missing ids gives you totals that are right and queries that are
not. The gate checks the totals *after* a removal for exactly that reason.

`Dictionary.Remove` returns whether it removed anything, which is the value the
method wants anyway - so one call answers the question and does the work.

For the totals, format with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. Decide for yourself
whether `DeptTotals` should include a department whose only employee has just
been removed; the grouping answers that for you, and it is worth noticing which
way.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two fields, because neither structure gives you both things you need: a
`Dictionary<int, Employee>` for lookup by id, and a `List<int>` for insertion
order. Every method has to keep them agreeing.

Write down what each method does to *both* before you write any of them.

## Hint 2

`Save`: add the id to the order list only when it is new, then set the
dictionary entry either way, then raise. That is what makes a replace keep the
employee's original position.

`Get`: `TryGetValue`, and `KeyNotFoundException` when it says no - not null,
because a null forces every caller to check and most of them will not.

`Query` and `DeptTotals` both start from the order list and look each id up, so
they inherit insertion order:

```csharp
_order.Select(id => _byId[id])
```

## Hint 3

`Remove` is where this design goes wrong most easily. Removing the dictionary
entry and forgetting the order list leaves an id in `_order` that `_byId` no
longer has - and then `_byId[id]` throws inside `Query`, or worse, a version
that skips missing ids gives you totals that are right and queries that are
not. The gate checks the totals *after* a removal for exactly that reason.

`Dictionary.Remove` returns whether it removed anything, which is the value the
method wants anyway - so one call answers the question and does the work.

For the totals, format with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. Decide for yourself
whether `DeptTotals` should include a department whose only employee has just
been removed; the grouping answers that for you, and it is worth noticing which
way.
