## Challenge — the 45-minute task

> "Build me a small in-memory order service. I can place an order for a customer
> with some lines and get back an id. I can ask what an order cost. I can ask
> for the top N customers by spend. Validate the inputs properly, and make it
> `IDisposable` so we can shut it down cleanly."

Edit `src/Lessons/I2_InterviewDrills/Challenge.cs`. The full specification is in
the file's doc comments: id format, which exception for which bad input,
`KeyNotFoundException` for an unknown id, the top-customers report with its
tie-break, and `ObjectDisposedException` from every member after disposal.

Honest difficulty note: nothing here is hard on its own — it is lesson 03's
encapsulation, lesson 11's grouping and lesson 12's exceptions in one class.
The difficulty is *keeping all the rules in your head at once*, which is exactly
what the real version of this task tests. Read the whole specification and write
the rules down before you start typing.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i2_interview_drills challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Treat this like the real thing: read the whole specification first, write down
the rules, and only then start typing. There are four members and about eight
rules between them, and the ones people lose are the validation cases.

Order of attack that works: `Place` (storage plus validation), `TotalFor`,
`Dispose`, then `TopCustomers` last, because it is the only one that needs
thinking about.

## Hint 2

Storage: the dictionary field is already declared, keyed by id and holding the
customer and the lines. Ids are `$"ORD-{_nextId}"` with `_nextId` incremented
after use.

Validation order in `Place`: disposed first, then the customer, then the lines
being non-empty, then each line's quantity. Guard clauses, one per rule, in that
order — so the most fundamental problem is the one reported.

`TopCustomers` is lesson 11: group the stored orders by customer, sum
`Quantity * UnitPrice` across their lines, order by total descending with the
name as tie-break, take, and format `"name: total"`.

## Hint 3

Three details the gate checks and interviewers notice.

**`ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(_disposed, this)` at the top of every public
member.** Half-alive objects that quietly return empty results are worse than
ones that throw.

**The right exception per rule**: `ArgumentException` for a missing customer or
no lines, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a bad quantity, `KeyNotFoundException`

Treat this like the real thing: read the whole specification first, write down
the rules, and only then start typing. There are four members and about eight
rules between them, and the ones people lose are the validation cases.

`Dispose`, then `TopCustomers` last, because it is the only one that needs
thinking about.

## Hint 2

Storage: the dictionary field is already declared, keyed by id and holding the
customer and the lines. Ids are `$"ORD-{_nextId}"` with `_nextId` incremented
after use.

being non-empty, then each line's quantity. Guard clauses, one per rule, in that
order — so the most fundamental problem is the one reported.

`TopCustomers` is lesson 11: group the stored orders by customer, sum
`Quantity * UnitPrice` across their lines, order by total descending with the
name as tie-break, take, and format `"name: total"`.

## Hint 3

Three details the gate checks and interviewers notice.

**`ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(_disposed, this)` at the top of every public
member.** Half-alive objects that quietly return empty results are worse than
ones that throw.

no lines, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a bad quantity, `KeyNotFoundException`
for an unknown id. Using the precise type is free and tells the caller what to
fix.

collection the caller still owns; if they mutate it afterwards, your stored
order changes underneath you. That single `ToList()` is the kind of thing a
senior interviewer looks for specifically.

nothing unmanaged, so the argument for it is "make the failure obvious"; the
argument against is that `IDisposable` is for resources, not for lifecycle. Have
an opinion ready — that question is the interview.

## Exercise 1 — FizzBuzz, with a twist (10 minutes)

> "Everyone's done FizzBuzz. Do it again, but I want the rules to be data — I
> should be able to hand you `(3, "Fizz")` and `(5, "Buzz")`, or add a `(7,
> "Bang")` later without you touching the method. Return the sequence rather
> than printing it."

Edit `src/Lessons/I2_InterviewDrills/Ex1.cs`. For each number in the inclusive
range, join the words of every rule whose divisor divides it, in rule order; a
number matching nothing is its own text.

If your solution has `n % 15` in it, the twist has beaten you.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i2_interview_drills ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Say the rule out loud before you type: for each number, collect the words of
every rule that divides it, in rule order; if you collected nothing, use the
number itself.

That phrasing is already the algorithm, and it has no `if (n % 15 == 0)` in it
— which is the point of the twist. Hard-coding FizzBuzz stops working the
moment the interviewer adds a third rule.

## Hint 2

`Enumerable.Range(from, count)` generates the numbers; the count is
`to - from + 1`, and must not go negative.

For one number:

```csharp
string words = string.Concat(rules.Where(r => number % r.Divisor == 0).Select(r => r.Word));
return words.Length == 0 ? number.ToString() : words;
```

`string.Concat` over an empty sequence gives `""`, which is exactly the "no
rule matched" signal you need — no separate check for it.

## Hint 3

The classic interview follow-up is "now add a rule for 7" — and the answer
should be "pass another rule", with no code change at all. If your solution
cannot do that, it has the shape the question was testing for.

The second follow-up is usually "make it lazy" or "make it handle a billion
numbers". `Enumerable.Range` plus `Select` already is lazy; only the `ToList()`
at the end materialises. Returning `IEnumerable<string>` instead would let the
caller decide.

Left to you: whether to build the words with `string.Concat`, a
`StringBuilder`, or `string.Join("")`. All three are defensible; be ready to say
why you picked yours.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Say the rule out loud before you type: for each number, collect the words of
every rule that divides it, in rule order; if you collected nothing, use the
number itself.

That phrasing is already the algorithm, and it has no `if (n % 15 == 0)` in it
— which is the point of the twist. Hard-coding FizzBuzz stops working the
moment the interviewer adds a third rule.

## Hint 2

`Enumerable.Range(from, count)` generates the numbers; the count is
`to - from + 1`, and must not go negative.

For one number:

```csharp
string words = string.Concat(rules.Where(r => number % r.Divisor == 0).Select(r => r.Word));
return words.Length == 0 ? number.ToString() : words;
```

`string.Concat` over an empty sequence gives `""`, which is exactly the "no
rule matched" signal you need — no separate check for it.

## Hint 3

The classic interview follow-up is "now add a rule for 7" — and the answer
should be "pass another rule", with no code change at all. If your solution
cannot do that, it has the shape the question was testing for.

The second follow-up is usually "make it lazy" or "make it handle a billion
numbers". `Enumerable.Range` plus `Select` already is lazy; only the `ToList()`
at the end materialises. Returning `IEnumerable<string>` instead would let the
caller decide.

Left to you: whether to build the words with `string.Concat`, a
`StringBuilder`, or `string.Join("")`. All three are defensible; be ready to say
why you picked yours.

## Exercise 2 — an LRU cache (25 minutes)

> "Implement a cache with a fixed capacity. When it is full and something new
> arrives, throw out whatever was used least recently. Reads count as use. I
> want both operations O(1)."

`KeysNewestFirst` — the last one exists so the gate can check the ordering.

was used least recently; a list alone cannot find a key quickly. The two fields
declared in the file are the standard answer, and knowing *why* they are the

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The interviewer is looking for one thing above all: **O(1) for both operations**.
A `List` you scan to find the least-recently-used is O(n) and will be the first
thing they push back on.

Two structures working together give you O(1): a dictionary for "where is this
key?", and a linked list for "what order were they used in?". Both fields are
already declared for you.

## Hint 2

The invariant: `_order` holds the entries newest-first, and `_entries` maps each
key to *its node* in that list. Given a key, the dictionary hands you the node,
and `LinkedList<T>.Remove(node)` and `AddFirst(node)` are O(1) because the node
already knows its neighbours.

`TryGet`: find the node, move it to the front, hand back the value.

`Put`: if the key exists, update the node's value and move it to the front. If
it does not, evict `_order.Last` when the cache is full, then `AddFirst` the new
entry and record the node in the dictionary.

## Hint 3

Two details the gate checks that are easy to miss. **Reading counts as using**,
so `TryGet` must reorder — a cache where only writes refresh recency is not an
LRU. And evicting must remove the entry from **both** structures; forgetting the
dictionary leaves a key that reports present and has no node, which is the bug
that will bite in the interview's "what if I read that key now?" question.

The usual follow-ups, worth having answers for: *"is this thread-safe?"* (no —
wrap it in a lock, or use `ConcurrentDictionary` plus a lock for the order, and
note that the order list is the hard part). *"What if I want expiry as well?"*
(store a timestamp with the entry and evict lazily on read).

Left to you: whether `KeysNewestFirst` should be a snapshot or a live view. The
gate only reads it; a snapshot is safer for callers.

> "Given a chunk of text, give me the N most common words with their counts.

alphabetically, formatted `"word: n"`.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — a disposable resource wrapper (15 minutes)

> "We hand out database connections from a pool. Write me the wrapper the
> calling code puts in a `using`, so the connection goes back when the block
> ends. And make it obvious if somebody keeps using it afterwards."

Edit `src/Lessons/I2_InterviewDrills/Ex4.cs`. `Connection` hands back the
borrowed connection or throws `ObjectDisposedException`; `Dispose` returns it to
the pool exactly once however many times it is called.

The double-dispose rule is not pedantry here: returning the same connection to
the pool twice hands it to two callers at once.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i2_interview_drills ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two members, and the whole exercise is the two rules a wrapper must obey:
release exactly once, and refuse to be used afterwards.

The fields are already there. `_disposed` is your guard for both.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public void Dispose()
{
    if (_disposed) { return; }
    _disposed = true;
    _pool.Enqueue(_connection);
}
```

For the property, `ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(_disposed, this)` (since
.NET 7) is the one-liner; the older form is
`if (_disposed) throw new ObjectDisposedException(nameof(PooledConnection));`.

## Hint 3

Why "exactly once" matters here rather than being a formality: a double return
puts the same connection in the pool twice, and the pool then hands it to two
callers who both think they own it. That is a genuinely nasty production bug and
it is why the guard exists.

The interviewer's follow-ups: *"what if the caller forgets to dispose?"* (the
connection never comes back — a leak; a finaliser could return it, at the cost
of finalisation, and `SafeHandle` is the framework's answer for real handles).
*"What about async cleanup?"* (`IAsyncDisposable` and `await using`).

Left to you: whether `Dispose` should also close the connection rather than
pooling it. The class name is the specification — but noticing that the two
policies are different, and asking, is exactly what the interviewer wants to
see.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two members, and the whole exercise is the two rules a wrapper must obey:
release exactly once, and refuse to be used afterwards.

The fields are already there. `_disposed` is your guard for both.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public void Dispose()
{
    if (_disposed) { return; }
    _disposed = true;
    _pool.Enqueue(_connection);
}
```

For the property, `ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(_disposed, this)` (since
.NET 7) is the one-liner; the older form is
`if (_disposed) throw new ObjectDisposedException(nameof(PooledConnection));`.

## Hint 3

Why "exactly once" matters here rather than being a formality: a double return
puts the same connection in the pool twice, and the pool then hands it to two
callers who both think they own it. That is a genuinely nasty production bug and
it is why the guard exists.

The interviewer's follow-ups: *"what if the caller forgets to dispose?"* (the
connection never comes back — a leak; a finaliser could return it, at the cost
of finalisation, and `SafeHandle` is the framework's answer for real handles).
*"What about async cleanup?"* (`IAsyncDisposable` and `await using`).

Left to you: whether `Dispose` should also close the connection rather than
pooling it. The class name is the specification — but noticing that the two
policies are different, and asking, is exactly what the interviewer wants to
see.

## Exercise 5 — fix this async code (10 minutes)

> "A colleague wrote this and it's in production. It blocks a thread, it ignores
> the cancellation token it was given, and it swallows exceptions and returns
> zero. Fix all three."

Edit `src/Lessons/I2_InterviewDrills/Ex5.cs`. `TotalAsync(pages, token)` adds up
every page's count: awaiting rather than blocking, honouring the token both
before it starts and while it waits, and letting a failure travel to the caller.

Be ready to say what each of the three bugs actually does — the fix is three
lines and the explanation is the interview.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i2_interview_drills ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three bugs to avoid, and the fixed version is three lines. Name each bug before
you write anything:

1. blocking on `.Result` instead of awaiting;
2. accepting a `CancellationToken` and never looking at it;
3. `catch (Exception) { return 0; }` — a failure reported as a valid answer.

## Hint 2

```csharp
token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

int[] counts = await Task.WhenAll(pages).WaitAsync(token);
return counts.Sum();
```

The first line handles "already cancelled — do nothing". The `WaitAsync(token)`
handles "cancelled while we were waiting". And there is no `catch` at all, which
is what lets a failing page reach the caller.

## Hint 3

Bug 3 is the one candidates defend and should not. Returning 0 from a failed
total means the caller cannot tell "no pages" from "the database was down", and
the report goes out with a zero in it. If you cannot handle a failure, let it
travel to somebody who can.

Be ready for *"why not just `catch` and log?"* — because logging is not
handling: the caller still gets a wrong answer. Log **and rethrow**, or do not
catch.

Left to you: whether `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` at the top is redundant
given the `WaitAsync`. It is not quite — `WhenAll` over already-completed tasks
can finish before the token is ever consulted, and the gate checks that an
already-cancelled request does no work. Being able to explain that distinction
is worth more than the line itself.

## Hint 1

Three bugs to avoid, and the fixed version is three lines. Name each bug before
you write anything:

1. blocking on `.Result` instead of awaiting;
2. accepting a `CancellationToken` and never looking at it;
3. `catch (Exception) { return 0; }` — a failure reported as a valid answer.

## Hint 2

```csharp
token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

int[] counts = await Task.WhenAll(pages).WaitAsync(token);
return counts.Sum();
```

The first line handles "already cancelled — do nothing". The `WaitAsync(token)`
handles "cancelled while we were waiting". And there is no `catch` at all, which
is what lets a failing page reach the caller.

## Hint 3

Bug 3 is the one candidates defend and should not. Returning 0 from a failed
total means the caller cannot tell "no pages" from "the database was down", and
the report goes out with a zero in it. If you cannot handle a failure, let it
travel to somebody who can.

Be ready for *"why not just `catch` and log?"* — because logging is not
handling: the caller still gets a wrong answer. Log **and rethrow**, or do not
catch.

Left to you: whether `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` at the top is redundant
given the `WaitAsync`. It is not quite — `WhenAll` over already-completed tasks
can finish before the token is ever consulted, and the gate checks that an
already-cancelled request does no work. Being able to explain that distinction
is worth more than the line itself.

## Hint 1

This is ex2's idea with the difficulty removed: the same "most recently used
first, no duplicates, bounded length" behaviour, over a plain `List<string>`.

`Touch` is three steps in a fixed order. Say them out loud: remove it if it is
already there, put it at the front, drop the oldest if that took you over the
limit.

## Hint 2

```csharp
_items.Remove(item);      // no-op when it is not there
_items.Insert(0, item);
if (_items.Count > Capacity) { _items.RemoveAt(_items.Count - 1); }
```

`List<T>.Remove` returns a bool you can ignore, and does nothing if the item is
absent — which is why the dedupe needs no `if`.

`Items` should hand back something the caller cannot mutate: `_items.AsReadOnly()`.

## Hint 3

The performance answer, if asked: this is O(n) per touch because `Remove` and
`Insert(0, ...)` both shift the list. For a "recently opened files" menu of ten
entries that is completely fine, and reaching for a linked list plus a
dictionary here would be over-engineering. Knowing *when* the O(1) version
(ex2's) is worth the complexity is the actual skill.

Left to you: whether the eviction should happen before or after the insert. Both
orders can be made correct; only one of them is correct with the code above.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is ex2's idea with the difficulty removed: the same "most recently used
first, no duplicates, bounded length" behaviour, over a plain `List<string>`.

`Touch` is three steps in a fixed order. Say them out loud: remove it if it is
already there, put it at the front, drop the oldest if that took you over the
limit.

## Hint 2

```csharp
_items.Remove(item);      // no-op when it is not there
_items.Insert(0, item);
if (_items.Count > Capacity) { _items.RemoveAt(_items.Count - 1); }
```

`List<T>.Remove` returns a bool you can ignore, and does nothing if the item is
absent — which is why the dedupe needs no `if`.

`Items` should hand back something the caller cannot mutate: `_items.AsReadOnly()`.

## Hint 3

The performance answer, if asked: this is O(n) per touch because `Remove` and
`Insert(0, ...)` both shift the list. For a "recently opened files" menu of ten
entries that is completely fine, and reaching for a linked list plus a
dictionary here would be over-engineering. Knowing *when* the O(1) version
(ex2's) is worth the complexity is the actual skill.

Left to you: whether the eviction should happen before or after the insert. Both
orders can be made correct; only one of them is correct with the code above.
Work out which, and why.

# i3 — Interview rapid-fire

Four short problems and a review, all on the concepts `i1` marks [***] - the
ones to expect in any C# interview - and all of them you have already met,
all deliberately in a different shape from the lesson that taught them. Nothing
here takes more than five minutes; everything here is something an interviewer
can ask on a whiteboard while you are still taking your coat off.

This lesson exists for one reason: **spacing**. You met value semantics in
lesson 01, deferred execution in lesson 10, the hash contract in lesson 06 and
async in lesson 13 — and everything you learn decays unless it comes back. The
whole lesson is marked as review material, so `dojo review` will resurface it at
three days, a week, three weeks and two months. The ladder does the repetition;
you just have to keep answering.

Work these cold. No hints on the first pass, no scrolling back to the lesson,
no compiler until you have written the whole body. If it does not come out, that
is information — go back to the lesson named in the gate's failure message, and
let the ladder bring it round again.

## Exercise 1 — where does the copy happen? (3 minutes)

Edit `src/Lessons/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex1.cs`. The same struct in three
containers: an array (write straight through it), a `List<T>` (where the direct
write does not compile, so copy-modify-write-back), and a method parameter.

Three answers, one rule. Predict all three before you run the gate.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i3_interview_rapidfire ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the key contract (5 minutes)

Edit `src/Lessons/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex2.cs`. Override `Equals` and
`GetHashCode` on `Coordinate` so that two positions with the same X and Y are
one key, then count distinct positions with a `HashSet`.

Watch the hash: `X ^ Y` cannot tell `(5, 6)` from `(6, 5)`, which is legal and
turns your set into a linear scan.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i3_interview_rapidfire ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — lazy queries and captured variables (5 minutes)

Edit `src/Lessons/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex3.cs`. `Above` returns a query — not a
result — that compares against whatever the threshold function says **at the
moment it is enumerated**. `Indexes` builds three functions in a `for` loop that
return 0, 1 and 2, which the naive version does not.

The gate enumerates the same query twice with the threshold changed in between.
If your answer is the same both times, you materialised it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i3_interview_rapidfire ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — async outcomes (5 minutes)

Edit `src/Lessons/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex4.cs`. Both methods wait for **every**
task and then report on the outcomes without throwing: how many succeeded, and
the total of the successful ones.

Awaiting `Task.WhenAll` throws when any task failed, and rethrows only the
first exception — so the waiting and the answering are two separate steps.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i3_interview_rapidfire ex4
```

## Review

`review1` is three one-liners with no notes: what `Equals` says about two boxed
`7`s, whether `Trim` changed the caller's string, and what a box holds after the
variable moved. Two minutes, cold.

# Reading - csharp/i3_interview_rapidfire

## Notes

**Why this lesson is short and keeps coming back.** Everything here you have
already learned once. The problem is that "learned once" decays on a predictable
curve, and the fix — established by about a century of memory research — is
spaced retrieval: recall the thing at increasing intervals, from memory, with
effort. Not re-reading. Recalling. `dojo review` schedules these at 3, 7, 21 and
60 days precisely because that is roughly where the forgetting curve puts you.

**Retrieval has to be effortful to work.** If you glance at the hints first, you
have converted a retrieval exercise into a reading exercise, and reading
produces almost none of the strengthening. Attempt cold, get it wrong, *then*
look — that sequence is worth several times a comfortable re-read, and the
mild frustration is the feature.

**Say it, do not just write it.** Every gate here checks code, but the thing
you actually need on the day is a sentence. After each exercise goes green, say
the rule out loud in one sentence without looking. If you cannot, the code
passing did not mean what you hoped.

**What "[***]" means in practice.** These four concepts — value semantics,
the equality/hash contract, deferred execution and `Task.WhenAll` behaviour —
account for a startling share of C# interview questions, because each one is a
place where the language does something specific that you either know or do not.
There is no reasoning your way to "a `List<T>` indexer returns a copy" in the
room.

## ex1

Three containers, three behaviours, one rule underneath: a value type is copied
whenever it is assigned, passed or returned — and array indexing is the
exception, because it produces a *reference into the array's storage* rather
than a value.

That is why `array[0].Brightness = 9` compiles and works, `list[0].Brightness = 9`
does not compile at all (the compiler knows the write would be discarded, and
refuses rather than lying to you), and `Bump(pixel)` cannot touch the caller's
value.

The modern footnote worth knowing: `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list)` gives you a
`Span<T>` over a `List<T>`'s backing array, and indexing a span *is* a `ref`
return — so the direct write works there. You will not often need it; knowing
why it works is the same knowledge as knowing why the list version does not.

The sentence: **structs copy on assignment, argument passing and collection
reads; arrays hand out references into their storage.**

## ex2

The contract again, in a fresh shape: equal objects must return equal hash
codes, or the hashed collection never gets as far as comparing them. The
`HashSet` in `DistinctCount` is the demonstration — with no overrides at all it
returns 3, because a plain class inherits reference equality from `object`.

The hash-quality point is the one that separates a passing answer from a good
one. `X ^ Y` satisfies the contract (equal coordinates hash equally) and is a
bad hash, because `(5, 6)` and `(6, 5)` collide, as does every mirrored pair.
Collisions are legal and handled — by a linear scan within the bucket — so a bad
hash does not break correctness, it silently removes the performance you chose
the data structure for. `HashCode.Combine` mixes properly and is one call.

The type test in `Equals` handles both the wrong type and null in one
expression, which is why `obj is Coordinate other && ...` is the idiom rather
than a null check followed by a cast.

The sentence: **equal objects must hash the same, or the lookup looks in the
wrong bucket and never even calls your `Equals`.**

## ex3

Two mechanisms that are constantly confused with each other, deliberately put in
one exercise.

**Deferred execution** is about *when the query runs*: never at the point you
write it, always at the point something enumerates it, and again on every
subsequent enumeration. That is why moving the threshold between two
enumerations of the same query object changes the answer — and why a query is a
liability to hand to code that might enumerate it twice.

**Capture** is about *what the lambda remembers*: the variable, not the value.
One `for` loop variable shared by three lambdas gives three lambdas that all see
the loop's final value; a fresh local per iteration gives each its own. `foreach`
has declared a fresh variable per iteration since C# 5, which is why the same
mistake in a `foreach` no longer bites.

Put together, they explain a whole family of production bugs: a query built
inside a loop capturing the loop variable, evaluated after the loop finished.
Every element comes back matching the last iteration.

The sentences: **a query is a plan, re-run on every enumeration** and **a lambda
captures the variable, not the value.**

## ex4

`Task.WhenAll`'s three behaviours, all of which get asked:

1. It waits for **every** task, even after one has faulted. Usually right — no
   orphaned work continuing in the background — occasionally not, and `WhenAny`
   plus a cancellation token is the fail-fast alternative.
2. Awaiting it rethrows only the **first** exception. The rest are not lost:
   they are on the `WhenAll` task's `AggregateException` and on the individual
   tasks. When ten uploads fail, "one timed out" is a much worse log line than
   the full list, and getting the full list means looking at the tasks.
3. Each task knows its own outcome — `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`,
   `IsCanceled`, `Exception` — which is what makes "wait for everything, then
   report" a two-step operation rather than one.

The bare `catch` in the reference implementation is unusual and defensible
precisely because the next line inspects every outcome individually. The
question worth having an answer to: should a cancelled task count as a failure
here? For a "how many succeeded" report, probably yes; for anything that logs,
almost certainly not.

The sentence: **`WhenAll` waits for all of them and rethrows the first failure;
the outcomes live on the tasks.**

## review1

Three facts, three one-liners, no notes — and if any of them took more than
thirty seconds, the fix is not more code, it is `i1`'s question bank.

`Equals` on two boxed `7`s is true, while `==` on the same two variables typed
`object` is false: the operator is chosen at compile time from the static type,
the method is dispatched at run time on the actual object. `Trim` cannot change
the caller's string because no operation in .NET mutates an existing string.
And a box holds a copy taken at the moment of boxing, so moving the variable
afterwards leaves the box alone.

These are the three most commonly confused [***] facts in the language, and they
are all one sentence each. That is the standard to hold yourself to: not "I
could work it out", but "I can say it".

## Further reading

- [Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) — copy semantics, stated formally.
- [`CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.collectionsmarshal.asspan) — the `ref` view over a `List<T>`, and why it exists.
- [`Object.GetHashCode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) — the contract and the consequences of a poor hash.
- [Deferred execution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/linq/deferred-execution-lazy-evaluation) — which operators defer and which do not.
- [`Task.WhenAll`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.whenall) — the exception behaviour, spelled out in the remarks.
- [Lambda expressions and capture](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions#capture-of-outer-variables-and-variable-scope-in-lambda-expressions) — the official statement of what a closure captures.

            new Coordinate(1, 2),
            new Coordinate(3, 4),
        };

        Teach.Equal(2, Grid.DistinctCount(points),
            "Two of the three are the same position. Without an Equals override this returns "
                + "3, because a plain class compares by reference - reread README ex2.");

        Coordinate key = new Coordinate(5, 6);
        Coordinate twin = new Coordinate(5, 6);

        Teach.True(key.Equals(twin), "Same X and Y is the same coordinate.");
        Teach.True(!key.Equals(new Coordinate(6, 5)),
            "Order matters: (5, 6) is not (6, 5). If this failed you compared a sum or a "
                + "product instead of the two values.");
        Teach.True(!key.Equals("5,6"),
            "Equals takes an object and can be handed anything - a type test comes first.");

        Teach.Equal(key.GetHashCode(), twin.GetHashCode(),
            "Equal objects MUST hash the same, or the HashSet above never even calls your "
                + "Equals - reread README ex2.");

        Dictionary<Coordinate, string> cells = new Dictionary<Coordinate, string> { [key] = "here" };
        Teach.True(cells.ContainsKey(twin),
            "And this is what the contract buys: a lookup with a different but equal key.");
    }

    {

        IEnumerable<int> query = LazyAndClosures.Above(new[] { 1, 6, 10 }, () => limit);

        Teach.Equal("6, 10", string.Join(", ", query),
            "Above 5, at the moment of enumeration - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("10", string.Join(", ", query),
            "The SAME query object, enumerated again after the threshold moved, gives a "
                + "different answer - because a query is a plan, and the plan reads the "
                + "captured variable each time it runs. If you got \"6, 10\" again you "
                + "materialised it - reread README ex3.");

        Teach.Equal("0, 1, 2", string.Join(", ", indexes.Select(f => f())),
            "The naive for-loop version gives 3, 3, 3 - one variable, captured three times. "
                + "Copying it into a fresh local INSIDE the loop body gives each lambda its "
                + "own - reread README ex3.");

    public async Task Ex4_WaitForEverythingThenLookAtTheOutcomes()
    {
        Task<int>[] allGood =
        {
            Task.FromResult(1), Task.FromResult(2), Task.FromResult(3),
        };

        Teach.Equal(3, await AsyncRapid.CountSucceededAsync(allGood), "All three succeeded.");
        Teach.Equal(6, await AsyncRapid.TotalOfSucceededAsync(allGood), "1 + 2 + 3.");

        TaskCompletionSource<int> broken = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
        broken.SetException(new InvalidOperationException("nope"));
        Task<int>[] mixed = { Task.FromResult(4), broken.Task, Task.FromResult(6) };

        Teach.Equal(2, await AsyncRapid.CountSucceededAsync(mixed),
            "Two of three finished successfully. Awaiting WhenAll throws, so this needs a "
                + "try/catch and then a look at each task's own outcome - reread README ex4.");

        Teach.Equal(10, await AsyncRapid.TotalOfSucceededAsync(mixed),
            "4 + 6: the failed one contributes nothing, and reading .Result on it would "
                + "rethrow - filter on IsCompletedSuccessfully first - reread README ex4.");

        alsoBroken.SetException(new TimeoutException("slow"));
        Task<int>[] allBad = { broken.Task, alsoBroken.Task };

            "Everything failed, and the method still returned an answer rather than throwing. "
                + "Note WhenAll rethrows only the FIRST exception - the others are only "
                + "visible on the tasks themselves.");

parameter. `Ex2` counts distinct coordinates, checks `Equals` against a twin, a
mirror image, a string and a hash, then uses one as a dictionary key. `Ex3`
enumerates one query twice with the threshold moved in between, and calls the
three loop-built functions. `Ex4` counts and totals successful tasks across an
all-good list, a mixed one and an all-failed one. `Review1` is the
spaced-repetition variant.

## The teaching point

The concepts in this lesson are the ones that come back on the day, and they are
also the ones that decay fastest — because you use them constantly *without
thinking about them*, which is exactly the state in which you cannot explain
them.

So the value of a rapid-fire round is not the code. It is the sentence you say
afterwards: "a struct is copied on assignment, on argument passing and on a
`List<T>` read, but not on array indexing". "A query is a plan; enumerating it
runs it again." "Equal objects must hash the same or the lookup never even
compares them." "`WhenAll` waits for everything and rethrows the first failure."

Four sentences, each earned by writing the code that proves it. When those come
out in eleven seconds without a pause, you are ready — and `dojo review` is what
keeps them there.

That is the end of the C# track. `uv run dojo status csharp` shows the whole
tree; `uv run dojo review` will keep the important parts coming back.

# Reading - csharp/i3_interview_rapidfire

## Notes

**Why this lesson is short and keeps coming back.** Everything here you have
already learned once. The problem is that "learned once" decays on a predictable
curve, and the fix — established by about a century of memory research — is
spaced retrieval: recall the thing at increasing intervals, from memory, with
effort. Not re-reading. Recalling. `dojo review` schedules these at 3, 7, 21 and
60 days precisely because that is roughly where the forgetting curve puts you.

**Retrieval has to be effortful to work.** If you glance at the hints first, you
have converted a retrieval exercise into a reading exercise, and reading
produces almost none of the strengthening. Attempt cold, get it wrong, *then*
look — that sequence is worth several times a comfortable re-read, and the
mild frustration is the feature.

**Say it, do not just write it.** Every gate here checks code, but the thing
you actually need on the day is a sentence. After each exercise goes green, say
the rule out loud in one sentence without looking. If you cannot, the code
passing did not mean what you hoped.

**What "[***]" means in practice.** These four concepts — value semantics,
the equality/hash contract, deferred execution and `Task.WhenAll` behaviour —
account for a startling share of C# interview questions, because each one is a
place where the language does something specific that you either know or do not.
There is no reasoning your way to "a `List<T>` indexer returns a copy" in the
room.

## ex1

Three containers, three behaviours, one rule underneath: a value type is copied
whenever it is assigned, passed or returned — and array indexing is the
exception, because it produces a *reference into the array's storage* rather
than a value.

That is why `array[0].Brightness = 9` compiles and works, `list[0].Brightness = 9`
does not compile at all (the compiler knows the write would be discarded, and
refuses rather than lying to you), and `Bump(pixel)` cannot touch the caller's
value.

The modern footnote worth knowing: `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list)` gives you a
`Span<T>` over a `List<T>`'s backing array, and indexing a span *is* a `ref`
return — so the direct write works there. You will not often need it; knowing
why it works is the same knowledge as knowing why the list version does not.

The sentence: **structs copy on assignment, argument passing and collection
reads; arrays hand out references into their storage.**

## ex2

The contract again, in a fresh shape: equal objects must return equal hash
codes, or the hashed collection never gets as far as comparing them. The
`HashSet` in `DistinctCount` is the demonstration — with no overrides at all it
returns 3, because a plain class inherits reference equality from `object`.

The hash-quality point is the one that separates a passing answer from a good
one. `X ^ Y` satisfies the contract (equal coordinates hash equally) and is a
bad hash, because `(5, 6)` and `(6, 5)` collide, as does every mirrored pair.
Collisions are legal and handled — by a linear scan within the bucket — so a bad
hash does not break correctness, it silently removes the performance you chose
the data structure for. `HashCode.Combine` mixes properly and is one call.

The type test in `Equals` handles both the wrong type and null in one
expression, which is why `obj is Coordinate other && ...` is the idiom rather
than a null check followed by a cast.

The sentence: **equal objects must hash the same, or the lookup looks in the
wrong bucket and never even calls your `Equals`.**

## ex3

Two mechanisms that are constantly confused with each other, deliberately put in
one exercise.

**Deferred execution** is about *when the query runs*: never at the point you
write it, always at the point something enumerates it, and again on every
subsequent enumeration. That is why moving the threshold between two
enumerations of the same query object changes the answer — and why a query is a
liability to hand to code that might enumerate it twice.

**Capture** is about *what the lambda remembers*: the variable, not the value.
One `for` loop variable shared by three lambdas gives three lambdas that all see
the loop's final value; a fresh local per iteration gives each its own. `foreach`
has declared a fresh variable per iteration since C# 5, which is why the same
mistake in a `foreach` no longer bites.

Put together, they explain a whole family of production bugs: a query built
inside a loop capturing the loop variable, evaluated after the loop finished.
Every element comes back matching the last iteration.

The sentences: **a query is a plan, re-run on every enumeration** and **a lambda
captures the variable, not the value.**

## ex4

`Task.WhenAll`'s three behaviours, all of which get asked:

1. It waits for **every** task, even after one has faulted. Usually right — no
   orphaned work continuing in the background — occasionally not, and `WhenAny`
   plus a cancellation token is the fail-fast alternative.
2. Awaiting it rethrows only the **first** exception. The rest are not lost:
   they are on the `WhenAll` task's `AggregateException` and on the individual
   tasks. When ten uploads fail, "one timed out" is a much worse log line than
   the full list, and getting the full list means looking at the tasks.
3. Each task knows its own outcome — `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`,
   `IsCanceled`, `Exception` — which is what makes "wait for everything, then
   report" a two-step operation rather than one.

The bare `catch` in the reference implementation is unusual and defensible
precisely because the next line inspects every outcome individually. The
question worth having an answer to: should a cancelled task count as a failure
here? For a "how many succeeded" report, probably yes; for anything that logs,
almost certainly not.

The sentence: **`WhenAll` waits for all of them and rethrows the first failure;
the outcomes live on the tasks.**

## review1

Three facts, three one-liners, no notes — and if any of them took more than
thirty seconds, the fix is not more code, it is `i1`'s question bank.

`Equals` on two boxed `7`s is true, while `==` on the same two variables typed
`object` is false: the operator is chosen at compile time from the static type,
the method is dispatched at run time on the actual object. `Trim` cannot change
the caller's string because no operation in .NET mutates an existing string.
And a box holds a copy taken at the moment of boxing, so moving the variable
afterwards leaves the box alone.

These are the three most commonly confused [***] facts in the language, and they
are all one sentence each. That is the standard to hold yourself to: not "I
could work it out", but "I can say it".

## Further reading

- [Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) — copy semantics, stated formally.
- [`CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.collectionsmarshal.asspan) — the `ref` view over a `List<T>`, and why it exists.
- [`Object.GetHashCode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) — the contract and the consequences of a poor hash.

## Exercise 1 — where does the copy happen? (3 minutes)

Edit `src/Lessons/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex1.cs`. The same struct in three
containers: an array (write straight through it), a `List<T>` (where the direct
write does not compile, so copy-modify-write-back), and a method parameter.

Three answers, one rule. Predict all three before you run the gate.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i3_interview_rapidfire ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three tiny methods, each one three lines, each one a different container for the
same struct. Write them exactly as described — the differences between them are
the whole exercise.

If you find yourself wanting to change `Pixel` to a class, stop: that is the
comparison, not the fix.

## Hint 2

The array version is literally `pixels[0].Brightness = 9;` and it compiles.

The list version is not — `pixels[0].Brightness = 9;` is a compiler error — so
it is copy, modify, write back:

```csharp
Pixel copy = pixels[0];
copy.Brightness = 9;
pixels[0] = copy;
```

`Bump` sets `pixel.Brightness = 9` and returns it.

## Hint 3

The one-sentence answer, ready to say: **a struct is copied whenever it is
assigned, passed or read out of a `List<T>` — but array indexing gives a real
reference into the array's storage, so it is not copied there.**

That is why the array version works, the list version needs the write-back, and
the parameter version cannot touch the caller's value at all.

Left to you: work out what `List<T>`'s indexer would have to return for the
direct assignment to work. (A `ref` return — which `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`
can actually give you. Knowing that exists is a nice extra.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three tiny methods, each one three lines, each one a different container for the
same struct. Write them exactly as described — the differences between them are
the whole exercise.

If you find yourself wanting to change `Pixel` to a class, stop: that is the
comparison, not the fix.

## Hint 2

The array version is literally `pixels[0].Brightness = 9;` and it compiles.

The list version is not — `pixels[0].Brightness = 9;` is a compiler error — so
it is copy, modify, write back:

```csharp
Pixel copy = pixels[0];
copy.Brightness = 9;
pixels[0] = copy;
```

`Bump` sets `pixel.Brightness = 9` and returns it.

## Hint 3

The one-sentence answer, ready to say: **a struct is copied whenever it is
assigned, passed or read out of a `List<T>` — but array indexing gives a real
reference into the array's storage, so it is not copied there.**

That is why the array version works, the list version needs the write-back, and
the parameter version cannot touch the caller's value at all.

Left to you: work out what `List<T>`'s indexer would have to return for the
direct assignment to work. (A `ref` return — which `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan`
can actually give you. Knowing that exists is a nice extra.)

## Hint 2

```csharp
public override bool Equals(object? obj)
{
    return obj is Coordinate other && other.X == X && other.Y == Y;
}

public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(X, Y);
```

Two traps the gate checks. `Equals` is handed anything at all — a string, a null

predates records, or because you need equality on only *some* of the members.

Two one-liners-ish, both about *when* code runs rather than what it computes.

`Above` must stay a query, so no `ToList`. `Indexes` must keep its `for` loop
and still produce 0, 1, 2 — which means fixing the capture rather than the loop.

## Hint 2

```csharp
return numbers.Where(number => number > threshold());
```

`Where` is deferred, and the lambda calls `threshold()` afresh on every element
every time the query is enumerated — which is exactly what the doc comment asks
for.

For the loop, one extra line inside the body:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
{
    int captured = i;
    functions.Add(() => captured);
}
```

## Hint 3

Be able to say both mechanisms in one sentence each.

**Deferred execution**: a LINQ query holds the source and the lambdas and runs
nothing until enumerated — so it sees the world as it is at that moment, and
re-runs on every enumeration.

**Capture**: a lambda captures the *variable*, not its value. A `for` loop has
one variable for the whole loop, so three lambdas share it; declaring a fresh
local inside the body gives each iteration its own.

Left to you: the gate enumerates the same query twice with a changed threshold.
Work out what would have happened if `Above` had ended in `.ToList()` — and why
that is sometimes exactly what you want.

## Exercise 4 — async outcomes (5 minutes)

Edit `src/Lessons/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex4.cs`. Both methods wait for **every**
task and then report on the outcomes without throwing: how many succeeded, and
the total of the successful ones.

Awaiting `Task.WhenAll` throws when any task failed, and rethrows only the
first exception — so the waiting and the answering are two separate steps.

```
uv run dojo test csharp i3_interview_rapidfire ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both methods have the same two-part shape: wait for everything, then look at
what each task actually did.

The catch is that awaiting `Task.WhenAll` *throws* when any task failed — so the
waiting part needs a `try`, and the answering part comes after it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
try
{
    await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
}
catch
{
    // every task has finished either way
}

return tasks.Count(task => task.IsCompletedSuccessfully);
```

The empty catch is deliberate and deserves that comment: you are not ignoring
the failures, you are about to inspect them individually.

`TotalOfSucceededAsync` filters on `IsCompletedSuccessfully` before summing
`task.Result` — reading `.Result` on a faulted task would rethrow.

## Hint 3

Three facts this drill is checking, all of them [***] material:

- `Task.WhenAll` waits for **every** task even after one fails;
- awaiting it rethrows only the **first** exception — the others are reachable
  only from the tasks (or from `WhenAll`'s own `AggregateException`);
- a task knows its own outcome: `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`,
  `IsCanceled`, and `Exception`.

Left to you: a bare `catch` here is fine because the very next line examines
every outcome — but it would also swallow an `OperationCanceledException`. Decide
whether this method should treat cancellation as "just another failure", and be
ready to defend the answer.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both methods have the same two-part shape: wait for everything, then look at
what each task actually did.

The catch is that awaiting `Task.WhenAll` *throws* when any task failed — so the
waiting part needs a `try`, and the answering part comes after it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
try
{
    await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
}
catch
{
    // every task has finished either way
}

return tasks.Count(task => task.IsCompletedSuccessfully);
```

The empty catch is deliberate and deserves that comment: you are not ignoring
the failures, you are about to inspect them individually.

`TotalOfSucceededAsync` filters on `IsCompletedSuccessfully` before summing
`task.Result` — reading `.Result` on a faulted task would rethrow.

## Hint 3

Three facts this drill is checking, all of them [***] material:

- `Task.WhenAll` waits for **every** task even after one fails;
- awaiting it rethrows only the **first** exception — the others are reachable
  only from the tasks (or from `WhenAll`'s own `AggregateException`);
- a task knows its own outcome: `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`,
  `IsCanceled`, and `Exception`.

Left to you: a bare `catch` here is fine because the very next line examines
every outcome — but it would also swallow an `OperationCanceledException`. Decide
whether this method should treat cancellation as "just another failure", and be
ready to defend the answer.

  from `==`;

Left to you: whether `EqualsSays(null, x)` should be your problem. The gate never
passes null, and a production version would use `object.Equals(a, b)` — the
static one, which handles nulls on both sides. Worth knowing it exists.
